data:
The docs are in the order you’ll need them: getting devvm running, using it day to day, what changed in each release, staying safe, choosing a backend and comparing devvm with other tools, then every command, how devvm works and how to change it.
Getting started Installing devvm, making your first VM, and the commands you use most. Using devvm Images and toolchains, ports and size, coding agents, editors, settings, and what to do when something fails. Releases Each release’s changes in full: what was wrong, what changed and what to do. Staying safe The habits that keep you safe, network tiers, .git protection, and what devvm does about each attack. Backends What runs the VMs: Lima. Compared to other tools How devvm differs from Docker Sandboxes, other VM and OS sandboxes, and hosted ones. CLI reference Every command, with its arguments and flags. How it works How devvm builds images, forwards ports, confines VMs to their proxies and protects .git. Contributing Building, testing and writing docs, other hosts, and releases.

A backend is the program that runs devvm’s VMs and builds their images. devvm decides what goes into a VM, such as its image, its folders, its size and its network tier, and the backend runs it. Lima is devvm’s backend.
data.a-vms-backend#A VM’s backend:
Every new VM runs on Lima, and no flag or setting chooses another backend. A VM’s state records its backend, and the VM stays on that backend for as long as it exists. When a VM’s state names a backend this devvm doesn’t have, such as one a different build of devvm made, devvm stops and says so, and you use the devvm that made the VM.
The --json output of devvm ls, devvm images and devvm space names each VM’s, image’s and shared tool’s backend in a backend field, and devvm doctor --json names the backend it checks.
data.what-lima-gives-you#What Lima gives you:
Lima Each project gets a full VM with a kernel of its own Hosts macOS or Linux, on arm64 or x86_64 You need Lima, and on Linux QEMU and access to /dev/kvm (requirements, with the versions) Confined network tiers yes The docker layer yes The nix layer yes Limits paths with commas, and shrinking a disk (limits) On macOS, .git protection uses your machine’s file flags, so it doesn’t depend on the backend. On Linux it needs the backend to keep paths in the project folder read-only in the VM, which Lima does where the kernel lets devvm use a user namespace (.git protection on Linux hosts).
An image’s key includes its backend, so a backend never uses an image another backend built.
devvm doctor # Lima's features, and what devvm needs on this machine devvm doctor lists Lima’s features, which are what Lima does itself, what devvm builds from other parts of it, and what it can’t do. These are backend features, not the base image features you choose with devvm setup, even though devvm doctor calls both “features”. How it works › Backends explains them.
data.when-a-backend-lacks-something#When a ba:
When a VM needs something its backend can’t do, devvm stops and says so in one line, naming the VM and what to do. It never falls back to something weaker, so a VM on a confined tier never starts with an open network.
That holds for a new VM’s tier too, though allowlist is the default. When a backend can’t confine a new VM to its proxy, the VM can only be open, so devvm refuses to make it unless you give --network open, and it says so in one line (network tiers).

data: Lima is devvm’s backend, so every new VM runs on it (a VM’s backend). Each project gets a full VM with a kernel of its own, which runs on Apple’s Virtualization framework (vz) on macOS and on QEMU on Linux. How it works › Lima explains how devvm sets up, confines and clones Lima’s VMs.
data.cleaning-up#Cleaning up: devvm gc deletes devvm’s stale and unfinished Lima images and the shared tools that no VM has and that aren’t current, and it leaves your VMs as they are. devvm images rm deletes an image that’s current, except on Linux hosts one whose disk VMs use (cleaning up). Lima also keeps a download cache of its own, which holds Ubuntu’s cloud images that devvm’s builds downloaded, and which your own Lima VMs share. devvm gc --caches deletes the cloud images that devvm downloads and that no image of devvm’s names, after listing them and asking, and devvm never runs limactl prune, which empties the whole cache (what devvm keeps).
data.devvm-mount-cache-json#devvm mount-cache:
devvm mount-cache --json prints the VM’s mode, whether it was chosen, as the VM was made or with devvm mount-cache none, rather than kept from Lima, and the mode its next start gives it, when that differs:
{ "version": 1, "mode": "mmap", "chosen": true, "pending": "none" }
data.devvms-lima-home#devvm’s Lima home:
devvm keeps its VMs and images in a Lima home of its own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima (under $XDG_DATA_HOME when that’s set), whatever LIMA_HOME says. Your own Lima VMs stay where they are, and Lima settings you made for them don’t reach devvm’s VMs. Because of this, a plain limactl list doesn’t show devvm’s VMs, so run devvm limactl list instead (below). To keep devvm’s VMs somewhere else, such as a sandbox or a shorter path, set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to that folder.
Lima adds _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home to every VM it starts, so devvm refuses to start a VM while devvm’s Lima home holds either file, and you move them out of it to go on. devvm also refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it, because a second network would get around the VM’s proxy, so remove the networks: entries from the file that devvm names (why).
data.file-watchers#File watchers:
A dev server or a watcher that runs in the VM, such as Vite, webpack, tsc --watch or nodemon, learns about changed files from the VM’s kernel. The kernel sees every change made in the VM, so a file that a coding agent or a command in the VM’s shell writes reaches the watcher at once. Lima’s mounts don’t pass on the changes you make on this machine, though, so a watcher in the VM misses a file you save in your editor here, and the dev server doesn’t reload. On Linux the project folder is a 9p mount, and there a watcher also misses the VM’s own changes in the folder’s subfolders, and sees only those to files at the top of the folder.
To have a watcher see your edits, set it to poll the project folder, which costs some CPU in a large project:
Tool Setting chokidar, and tools built on it CHOKIDAR_USEPOLLING=1 Vite server.watch.usePolling: true in vite.config webpack watchOptions.poll in webpack.config.js, or WATCHPACK_POLLING=true nodemon nodemon --legacy-watch tsc --watch "watchOptions": { "watchFile": "fixedPollingInterval" } in tsconfig.json cargo watch cargo watch --poll Set the variables in the VM’s shell or in your project’s scripts, before the tool starts. Leave Lima’s own file event setting, mountInotify, off, because with it on, commands in the VM that write to the project folder, such as git init, fail at random (details).
data.limits#Limits: Folder names in VM names are cut short. Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket in the VM’s folder in its home, and a socket path has fewer than 104 characters. A long Lima home leaves less room for the name, so set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to a shorter folder if devvm says the home is too long, or that a VM’s name leaves no room for the folder’s name (VM names). Paths can’t contain commas. Lima and QEMU split mount options on commas, so devvm refuses to mount a project folder whose path has one, and it leaves out an agent’s folder whose path has one, with a warning. Disks can grow but not shrink. Mounts on Linux are 9p. A 9p share mounts once per guest, file watchers in the VM miss changes in its subfolders (file watchers), and SQLite’s WAL mode doesn’t work in the project folder, which a --clone VM avoids (SQLite and the cache). A VM that Lima reports as failed to start still starts, with a warning, when it’s running but degraded because one of Lima’s boot scripts failed. A VM that doesn’t answer over ssh within a minute is stopped instead, and its console log is in its Lima folder (serial*.log).
data.programs-that-map-files-for-writing#Prog:
With none, a program in the VM can’t map a file in the project folder for shared writing, or map one it opened for writing at all, and it fails at once with Invalid argument, so nothing is lost. LMDB, numpy’s memmap in r+ or w+ mode, Java’s read-write MappedByteBuffer and the mold linker do this, while git, npm, Vite, webpack, esbuild, jest, Go, cargo with Rust’s own linker, GNU ld, lld, Gradle, DuckDB, ccache and Terraform work as they do on any disk. LMDB is what Parcel’s .parcel-cache and Gatsby’s cache use.
For a program that maps its files, keep them on the VM’s own disk, such as in its home folder: for mold, a CARGO_TARGET_DIR there, or lld instead. Or use a --clone VM, whose repo is on the VM’s own disk. The VM’s own disk is also far faster than the shared folder, so a --clone VM suits large repos and heavy builds: on a Fedora 43 host, npm ci of 369 packages took 4.8 s in the shared folder and 2.8 s on the VM’s disk, a debug cargo build of ripgrep 8.5 s and 4.8 s, and a cold git status of an 18,000-file tree 23 s and 1 s.
data.requirements#Requirements: macOSLinux macOS 13 or newer, on arm64 or x86_64. Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide. Linux on arm64 or x86_64. Lima 2.2 or newer, with limactl on your PATH. Install it with Homebrew, brew install lima, or see Lima’s install guide. QEMU from your package manager: qemu-system-aarch64 (or qemu-system-x86_64) and qemu-img. Read and write access to /dev/kvm. That means virtualization is turned on in the firmware (or nested virtualization, in a VM), and your user is in the kvm group. Every command that needs Lima checks these first and stops at the first one that’s missing. devvm doctor lists them all, each with the command that installs it where there’s one to run. That’s Homebrew’s command for Lima when you have Homebrew, your package manager’s for QEMU (apt, dnf, pacman or zypper), and sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER for /dev/kvm, after which you log in again. devvm never runs them itself (details).
data.running-limactl#Running limactl:
devvm limactl ARGS... runs limactl with ARGS on devvm’s Lima home, in devvm’s place. Its input, output, terminal and exit code are limactl’s, and devvm passes every option on to it, --help included. devvm help limactl shows devvm’s own help for the command.
devvm limactl list devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img- It runs from devvm’s data folder, as devvm’s own limactl commands do, so give files by their absolute path. It runs without your SSH agent, so a VM never gets your agent through it, whatever its SSH agent choice says (why). A VM you start this way, with devvm limactl start or shell --start, runs unconfined, whatever its tier, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced (confinement). Start project VMs with devvm.
data.sqlite-and-the-cache#SQLite and the cach: SQLite’s default journal works in the project folder. WAL mode doesn’t, because SQLite maps its shared index and fails with disk I/O error, unless the connection sets PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE before PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL. That keeps the index in memory, and lets only that connection use the database. A project whose database is in WAL mode works in a --clone VM, or with the database outside the project folder, such as in the VM’s home folder or /tmp.
data.the-project-folders-cache#The project fo:
On Linux, QEMU shares the project folder with the VM over 9p, and the VM’s kernel can cache the folder’s files as it reads and writes them. devvm gives every new VM the cache mode none, so the VM reads and writes straight through to the folder on this machine, and what you edit on either side is what the other side sees.
Lima’s own default for a writable folder is mmap, which caches the files’ contents in the VM, and Linux’s 9p client loses data with it in two ways. When a program reads a file’s size while another write is making the file longer, the VM can take the older size from this machine and drop the new data, even after fsync succeeded, so the file ends up empty or cut to 4096 bytes, and Claude Code’s edits are one way to set it off. And when a program locks a file it has written, its next read of that file returns zeros. That stops SQLite at its second write with file is not a database, whatever its journal mode, and Gradle’s second build with Unexpected lock protocol found in lock file.
A VM made before devvm chose none keeps mmap, and devvm doesn’t change its mount on its own, so each launch of such a VM warns until you switch it:
devvm mount-cache # how this folder's VM caches its project folder devvm mount-cache none # switch it to none from the VM's next start devvm mount-cache none switches the mode from the VM’s next start, so in a terminal devvm offers to restart a running VM now. none is the only mode devvm sets, so any other value is refused.
A --clone VM mounts no project folder, so it has no cache mode until devvm clone off mounts the folder, which then gets none. On macOS, VMs share the project folder with virtiofs, which has no cache mode to choose, so there devvm mount-cache refuses. On Linux it refuses the same for a VM whose project folder isn’t a 9p mount, such as one whose Lima config you gave another mount type.
data.when-the-cache-mode-changes#When the cac:
The VM gets none at its next start, and that start mounts the project folder again once the VM runs, before devvm sets the VM up or opens its shell. The VM’s first mount of the folder at boot still has the old mode, because the guest reads its new mount options only after it has mounted the folder. devvm then checks the folder:
When the folder is mounted with none, the VM goes on as usual. When the folder is still mounted with the old mode, isn’t mounted at all, or the VM doesn’t answer the check, devvm restarts the VM once, before it sets it up or opens its shell. The folder can be left with the old mode when the VM couldn’t unmount it, because something it started at boot, such as a container, was using it, or when the VM’s start was degraded. It can be left unmounted when the VM unmounted it but couldn’t mount it again, as happens on an Alpine VM. The restart’s boot mounts the folder with none, and devvm checks it again. After the restart, devvm checks the folder once more and doesn’t restart the VM again:
When the folder is mounted with none, the VM goes on as usual. When the folder is still mounted with the old mode, devvm warns and goes on, though the folder can lose writes under that mode. When the folder isn’t mounted at all, or the VM doesn’t answer the check, devvm stops the VM before it sets it up or opens its shell, because files written there would go to the VM’s own disk and vanish once the folder is mounted over them. In both cases a restart of your own repeats what failed, so look first at why the VM’s boot didn’t mount the folder with none. Its console log, which A VM won’t boot shows where to find, has what the boot said, and the run log has what the VM’s umount and mount said and why devvm restarted the VM (logs).
When devvm can’t stop the VM for the restart, a folder still mounted with the old mode is warned of and the VM goes on as it runs. Otherwise the launch fails, saying the VM didn’t stop, because it may still be running. Pressing Ctrl+C while devvm mounts or checks the folder, or stops the VM for the restart, stops the VM, without a restart. A launch into a running VM checks too that its project folder is mounted, and refuses to open a shell in one whose folder isn’t, naming devvm restart.

data.examples#Examples: devvm # open this folder's VM, choosing what a new one gets devvm --agents claude # create the VM with Claude Code and the toolchains the folder needs devvm --tools node --agents none --layers docker # create the VM with node and the docker layer alone devvm --clone # create the VM with its own clone of this repo devvm ls # list every VM
data.options#Options: --agents LIST the LIST of coding agents a new VM gets, such as claude,codex, or none (default: devvm setup's) --clone create the VM with its own clone of this repo, or of each repo in this folder, instead of mounting the folder --cpus N the N CPUs the VM gets (default: devvm size -g, else the image's) --disk GiB the VM's disk in GiB, at least the image's (default: devvm size -g, else the image's) --from IMAGE the container IMAGE base starts from, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu's cloud image (default: $DEVVM_FROM) -h, --help help for devvm --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside --layers LIST the LIST of layers a new VM's image gets, bottom first, such as docker,mine, or none (default: devvm setup's) --memory GiB the VM's memory in GiB, such as 16 or 16G (default: devvm size -g, else the image's) --network TIER the network TIER a new VM gets: open, internet, allowlist or none, or learn for internet while it learns the hosts it needs (default: devvm network -g's, else allowlist) --no-devcontainer create the VM without reading the folder's devcontainer.json --no-git-protect create the VM without .git protection --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own --ports PORTS the PORTS the VM forwards: all, none or a list like 5173,8000-8010 (default: devvm ports -g, else all) --repos LIST the repos a --clone VM of a folder of repos gets: all, none or a LIST of their paths, such as frontend,backend (default: a picker in a terminal) --ssh-agent create the VM with your SSH agent forwarded, so anything in it can use your keys while you're connected --ssh-config add devvm's Include line to ~/.ssh/config without asking --tools LIST the LIST of toolchains a new VM gets, such as node,python, or none (default: those the folder's files call for) --unsafe-folder mount a folder devvm refuses, such as your home folder -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line --version print devvm's version

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
Open a shell in this folder’s VM, at the same path, and create the VM first when the folder has none. devvm shows what a new VM gets, and in a terminal you can customize its toolchains, coding agents, layers, tier, ports and size, which –tools, –agents, –layers, –network, –ports, –cpus, –memory and –disk choose without asking. The VM mounts only this folder read-write, and with –clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead.

Check for newer versions of the shared tools, build them, and move this folder’s VM to them, then open a shell in it. Nothing in the VM’s disk changes, because its tools are mounted.
devvm tools update [flags]

data: Bring this folder’s VM up to date, then open a shell in it
data.docs#Docs: The docs page for devvm update explains it in full.
data.examples#Examples: devvm update # move the VM to the newest tools, and to its image's new build after asking devvm update --force # the same without asking, as a script must devvm update --clean-home # start from the image's home folder too
data.options#Options: --clean-home give the VM the image's home folder instead of keeping its own -f, --force don't ask to confirm, which devvm needs without a terminal or with --no-input -h, --help help for update --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside --no-export don't export the agents' history first --no-worktree-check with --clean-home, don't check the agents' worktrees in the VM for uncommitted changes first, which are lost --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
Move this folder’s VM to the newest shared tools, as devvm tools update does, then open a shell in it. When its image changed since devvm made the VM, or the folder’s devcontainer.json did, devvm then asks to make the VM again from the image’s new build and the file as it is now, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, and everything else on its disk is lost. When its image has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, unless you give –no-export.
devvm update [flags]

data.docs#Docs: The docs page for devvm upgrade explains it in full.
data.examples#Examples: devvm upgrade # install the newest release, asking first devvm upgrade --check # say whether a newer release is out devvm upgrade --force # install it without asking, as a script must devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0 # install that release, even an older one devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 # install a prerelease, which only --to installs

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
Install devvm’s newest release the way this devvm was installed, after asking. The install script’s devvm gets the release once its signature and checksum check out, and Homebrew’s runs brew upgrade devvm, or brew upgrade devvm-rc for the formula that follows prereleases. –check only says whether a newer release is out.
devvm upgrade [flags]

data:
devvm gives each project folder a VM of its own on your machine, with the project’s toolchains shared read-only between VMs, a proxy on this machine that confines the VM’s network, and your secrets kept outside the VM. Other tools sandbox coding agents in other ways: in a microVM, in an OS sandbox around the agent’s process, or on a vendor’s servers. This page sets devvm beside the ones you’re most likely to weigh it against.
Note
Last checked on 2026-11-08, against each tool’s own docs, which the sources list. These tools change every week, so check a tool’s own docs before you rely on a row here, and open an issue when a row is out of date.

data.how-devvm-differs#How devvm differs:
Beyond the tables, these are the differences you’re most likely to weigh:
Shared toolchains. Of the tools on this page, only devvm shares toolchains read-only between VMs, so a second project that needs node uses the same copy as the first, and nothing in a VM can change it. devvm detects the toolchains from the project’s files and reads a project’s devcontainer.json. .git protection. devvm locks the hooks and config of a folder’s .git against the VM, and those of each repo nested up to four folders below it, so the VM can’t add a hook that runs on this machine, which Docker Sandboxes’ docs say its direct mode doesn’t prevent. On Linux the locks need no root, and where the kernel doesn’t allow them, such as on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, devvm watches .git instead and names what changed (.git protection). A clone of your repo as it is. With --clone, the VM works on a clone of its own instead of your folder, and the clone gets your local branches, tags, uncommitted changes, stash, the repo’s settings and hooks, its submodules and its Git LFS files. devvm clone fetch brings the VM’s work back as branches, and devvm rm checks for work you haven’t fetched before it deletes the VM (working on a clone). Confinement from outside the VM. devvm enforces the network policy from outside the VM, so it holds even against root in the VM. Transparent mode also sends tools that ignore the proxy settings, such as static Go binaries and containers, to the VM’s proxy, on every tier but open. Learning a VM’s hosts. A VM can learn the hosts it needs on the internet tier, and devvm network lock then keeps the ones you choose, much as OpenShell shows you the hosts it blocked so that you can approve them. Your own secrets. Any API key that a tool sends in a header can be a secret of your own, so the VM gets a placeholder, and its proxy puts the real value only into requests to the hosts, methods and paths you give it (your own secrets). Agents’ logins on this machine. devvm keeps each agent’s login on this machine, so a confined VM never holds it, and Docker Sandboxes does the same for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Droid. In both, one login for each agent serves every VM. On devvm’s open tier, a program in the VM can go around the proxy and keep a login that it makes there. Images from the clipboard. devvm paste sends an image, a PDF or a file you copied on this machine into the VM, and puts its path in the VM on your clipboard for the agent’s prompt. It never reads text from the clipboard (pasting images).

data.other-tools#Other tools: Clawk is closer to devvm in shape, with a VM for each folder on your machine. It denies outbound traffic by default, but it forwards your SSH agent, and its tip for Claude Code signs every sandbox in with your Claude Code token. agent-vm also gives each folder a VM on your machine, and it runs Lima as devvm does. It makes every .git read-only for the VM from your machine and asks you before the VM writes files such as .envrc and .vscode/tasks.json, but the VM reaches the whole internet unless you add domain rules. Lima’s own recipe for coding agents mounts only the project folder, or syncs it and asks before the VM’s changes reach your machine, and it leaves the network and API keys to you. Dev Containers run in a container, which shares this machine’s kernel or Docker’s VM, and set no network policy. Claude Code’s reference container adds a firewall allowlist, and its docs warn that it doesn’t stop a malicious project from sending out what’s in the container, Claude Code’s login included. Hosted sandboxes, such as E2B, Vercel Sandbox, Fly.io Sprites and exe.dev, run on the vendor’s servers, so your code and keys go there, and each needs an account.

data.what-devvm-doesnt-do#What devvm doesn’t: devvm runs on macOS and Linux, on Lima, and Windows support is coming soon. Docker Sandboxes, microsandbox, smolvm and Codex CLI run on macOS, Linux and Windows. Its rules apply to the whole VM, while OpenShell’s rules can also name the program that may reach each host. It has no snapshots of a VM, which smolvm’s checkpoints and Docker Sandboxes’ templates give. It has no SDK or API for driving VMs from a program, though most commands have --json output. It checks at most once a day whether a newer release is out, which release-check = false turns off, and it sends nothing else. Known limits and Attack vectors list the rest.

data: Docker Sandboxes, the sbx command, is the tool closest to devvm: each sandbox is a VM with its own kernel on your machine, the project folder is mounted read-write, outbound traffic goes through a proxy on your machine, and API keys and agents’ logins stay outside the VM. This page sets the two side by side. Last checked on 2026-11-08 against Docker’s docs, which each row links to, and against Docker’s isolation and network rules pages again on 2026-11-12.
data.choosing-between-them#Choosing between t: Choose Docker Sandboxes if you need Windows, rules by URL query, one of the agents devvm doesn’t support, a sandbox saved as a template, or a sandbox you can move to Docker’s cloud. Choose devvm if you want open source without an account, toolchains shared between projects, .git protected from the VM in the folder you work in and in the repos nested in it, or a VM that learns the hosts it needs before you lock its allowlist.

data.whats-the-same#What’s the same: A VM with its own kernel. Docker’s sandboxes are microVMs with their own Linux kernel and Docker Engine, and the agent runs as a user with sudo (isolation). devvm’s VMs are full Lima VMs, whose user also has sudo. The folder mounted, or a clone. Both mount the project folder read-write by default, and both have a mode in which the VM works on a clone of its own instead (isolation, working on a clone). Placeholders for API keys. In both, the VM holds a placeholder, and a proxy on your machine puts the real value into requests (credentials, secrets). Agents’ logins on your machine. Both keep the logins of the agents they support outside the VM and give the VM placeholders, and in both, one login for each agent serves every VM. Docker Sandboxes does this for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Droid (credentials), and devvm for Claude Code, Codex, opencode and Cursor’s CLI, and for pi’s API keys (coding agents). Rules by method and path. Both let a rule for a host name its HTTP methods and its path, so a VM can read from an API without changing anything there (network rules, rules by method and path).

data: The rules for working in the repo, for people and coding agents alike, are in AGENTS.md. The codebase-standards skill turns what reviews of devvm’s code kept finding into a short checklist for a commit and a review, says how new code matches the code already there, and lists what guards each rule. Why devvm is built the way it is, what was tried and dropped, and what’s still open are in the design notes, with each emulation’s threat check and the tests that prove it.
data.building-from-source#Building from sourc:
devvm is built with Go, pinned in mise.toml. With mise installed:
mise install mise exec -- go build -o devvm ./cmd/devvm ./devvm --help The binary has devvm’s own files (assets/) built in, so it runs from anywhere: link to it from your PATH, or copy it there.
ln -s "$PWD/devvm" ~/.local/bin/devvm After editing anything in assets/, build again before a manual run: a binary keeps the files it was built with.
data.go-conventions#Go conventions:
The linters above check most of these, and the structure test checks others (the structure test). How a command fails, prints and cleans up is in CLI conventions.
One binary, no C. devvm builds with CGO_ENABLED=0, which mise.toml and .goreleaser.yaml set, and only the test tasks turn cgo on, for the race detector. internal/proxy and internal/daemon build only on unix systems for now, because they use syscall.Kill, Setsid and Flock. External tools are commands, never linked. devvm runs limactl, docker, security, git, chflags and the other tools it needs as commands, and it uses the standard library where that does the job rather than shelling out. A string that goes into a shell is quoted with shell.Quote. Code for one system goes behind build tags in internal/platform, in files named *_darwin.go, *_linux.go and *_other.go. The exceptions are the packages that the proxy imports, which can’t import internal/platform, so each one keeps its own few such files: internal/safefile’s flags, internal/daemon’s spawn_*.go, internal/proxy’s socketpair, touch_*.go and confineself_*.go, and internal/landlock, the proxy’s child’s confinement on Linux. Test seams are fields that a test sets, such as Host, Exec, Runner, OS and Reporter, and never package variables, which reassign keeps any package from setting in another. internal/proxy’s seams are fields of its server, which each test makes. A new dependency needs the maintainers’ yes before it goes on depguard’s list.
data.go-lint-rules#Go lint rules:
golangci-lint enforces most of the Go conventions in .golangci.yml:
Rule Enforces forbidigo only internal/ui prints (fmt.Print*, os.Stdout, os.Stderr); only cmd/devvm calls os.Exit; only internal/ui and cmd/devvm make a context (context.Background, context.TODO), every other function takes its caller’s; only internal/platform reads the host’s CPUs, memory and free space, which the rest reads through platform.Host; only internal/cli calls testbuild.On; only internal/daemon and internal/platform signal a process by its pid (os.FindProcess, syscall.Kill, unix.Kill, os.Process’s Kill and Signal); only internal/fetch makes an HTTP client or a transport (http.Client, http.DefaultClient, http.Transport, http.DefaultTransport, http.Get and the like), which the rest names as fetch.Client; nothing calls os.UserHomeDir, because the home folder is paths.Dirs.Home; only internal/state calls os.WriteFile or os.Create or opens a file with os.O_TRUNC, and the rest writes a file whole through state.WriteFile, or state.WriteFileMode for a mode other than 600; nothing but daemon.Ready changes devvm’s own environment (os.Setenv, os.Unsetenv, os.Clearenv and syscall’s), and a command gets its own through its Env; only the code that must use a secret’s value calls redact.Secret’s Reveal, each call with a nolint saying why (Secrets in the code) depguard the allowed modules, which are cobra, pflag, cobra’s doc package for the CLI reference, go-i18n, BurntSushi’s toml, golang.org/x/text, x/term and x/sys, and only the blake2b package of x/crypto, for minisign’s prehashed signatures; the tests may also use go-internal. Nothing imports a module that cobra’s doc package uses but isn’t on the list. internal/proxy, internal/daemon, internal/safefile, internal/vmname and internal/redact use only the standard library and each other, and their tests may use internal/leaktest and internal/memnet, which use only the standard library too nolintlint every //nolint names its linters and says why, and is still needed reassign no package reassigns another package’s variables, tests included revive at most 100 statements or 160 lines a function (function-length), and a cognitive complexity of 75 (cognitive-complexity) govet besides its defaults, nilness (a nil pointer dereferenced, or a nil check that is always true or always false), unusedwrite (a field written to a copy of a struct that nothing reads again), hostport (an address built as host + ":" + port, which breaks on IPv6, where net.JoinHostPort belongs) and waitgroup (WaitGroup.Add called inside the goroutine it counts) nilnesserr a function that checks an error and then returns a different error that is always nil, which reports success for a failure durationcheck two time.Duration values multiplied together, which gives nanoseconds squared instead of a duration canonicalheader an HTTP header named other than its canonical form, such as WWW-Authenticate or X-Request-ID errchkjson a JSON encoding’s error is checked when the value could fail to encode (it holds an any, a float, a channel or a custom marshaler), and dropped as _ when errchkjson proves it can’t fail, so a value that changes type gets its check back. It also reports a struct with no exported fields, which encodes as {}. The tests may drop the error of a value they built or decoded themselves forcetypeassert a type assertion without its ok, which panics on any other type. The tests are exempt, because a panic there fails the run and names the line contextcheck a function given a context that calls one making a context of its own, instead of passing its caller’s along gochecksumtype a type switch on a sum type names every type in it, even when the switch has a default A function passes its caller’s context along, even to work that must outlive it. Work that many requests share, such as a lookup whose value is cached for all of them, uses context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), …), which keeps the caller’s values and drops its cancel, so no one request’s end stops it. A fresh context is the exception, for code with no caller’s context to take, such as a cleanup that outlives a canceled run or the proxy’s own start, and it takes //nolint:forbidigo // . contextcheck can’t follow a request’s own context through httputil.ReverseProxy’s Rewrite, and it doesn’t count context.WithoutCancel alone as deriving one, so those few places take //nolint:contextcheck // .
A sum type is an interface whose implementations are a closed set. It has an unexported method, so only its own package can add one, and its doc comment ends with a //sumtype:decl line. gochecksumtype then fails any type switch on it that leaves out one of its types, as exhaustive does for a switch on an enum’s constants. The login file formats (format in internal/agentlogin) are one. A new interface with a fixed list of implementations, which code switches on by type, is declared the same way.
testdata/lint/forbidigo.go breaks each forbidigo rule once, on a line that ends in // want forbidigo. mise run lint:code lints it with forbidigo alone and fails unless forbidigo reports exactly those lines, so a rule whose pattern stops matching fails there. A new rule gets its line in the file. ./... leaves testdata out, so the file never fails the lint run of the code itself.
data.nil-checks#Nil checks:
mise run nilaway # where a nil value may reach a dereference in devvm's code, and which findings are new nilaway follows nil values across functions and packages and reports each place one may be dereferenced: a field read, a method call, an index or a slice. It reads only the packages under github.com/devvmhq/devvm, and it leaves out the tests and their helpers, internal/stubtest and internal/backend/backendtest, because a nil panic there fails a test. It checks the code as built for the system it runs on, so the files that build only for macOS or only for Linux need a run on each.
Its findings include false positives, so the ones already triaged as false positives are in testdata/nilaway-baseline.txt. scripts/nilaway.sh, which the task runs, prints every finding and then the ones the baseline doesn’t have. A finding’s key in the baseline is its file and its trace without line or column numbers, so moving code doesn’t make a triaged finding new. The baseline has a line for each finding, so when two findings share a key, such as two unchecked os.Stat results in one file, the key is there twice, and a third finding with that key is new.
The script exits with status 3 when there’s a new finding. It exits with status 1 when nilaway can’t run, when nilaway’s output has a finding the script can’t read, and when a baseline line is stale or isn’t a group and a key, so a change in nilaway’s output can’t leave the check comparing nothing. TestNilawayBaseline in internal/structure checks each of these with a stand-in nilaway.
The task isn’t part of lint, and it never fails CI. When there’s a new finding, CI’s nilaway job warns on the run and lists the new and stale findings, then every finding, in the run’s summary. The job fails when the script exits with status 1, and even then it blocks nothing.
A warning in a green run is easy to miss, and a finding’s key is its code path, so code that only moved can read as new. So before a push to main, mise run nilaway:linux must pass. It runs the same script with GOOS=linux, so nilaway checks the code as built for Linux, as CI’s job does, even on a Mac, and it also checks the files that build only for Linux. A new finding or a stale baseline line fails it, and gets a fix or a baseline change before the push.
Each finding starts with the place a nil value is dereferenced and then traces where it came from, one line for each step. A new finding that is a real bug gets a fix and a test that would have panicked without it. A false positive goes into the baseline as the key the script prints after new:, one line for each time it’s printed, with one of the baseline’s groups in front:
checked: a value used only once its error was checked, in a way nilaway doesn’t follow, such as err == nil && fi.Mode(). bounds: a slice indexed only within its length or sliced where nil is safe, or a variadic parameter that every caller passes. mapkey: a map read with a key taken from the same map, or after its ok. nilsafe: a method that checks for a nil receiver itself, or values that are always set together. The script lists the baseline’s lines that match no finding any more after stale:, and you remove one line for each.

mise installs every tool at the version pinned in mise.toml, checked against mise.lock:
Tool Used for go building and testing golangci-lint Go linters and formatters (.golangci.yml) gotestsum running the tests govulncheck checking dependencies for known vulnerabilities nilaway finding where a nil value may be dereferenced goreleaser release builds (Maintaining) hugo the docs site vale, markdownlint-cli2, lychee linting the docs node running markdownlint-cli2, and drawing the docs site’s diagrams with pele, which docs/package.json pins (diagrams) shellcheck linting shell scripts actionlint, zizmor linting the GitHub workflows, and checking them for security problems minisign signing releases Run the tasks with mise run :
Task Does fmt formats Go code lint runs lint:code and lint:docs lint:code runs golangci-lint, shellcheck, actionlint and zizmor lint:docs draws the diagrams (docs:diagrams), runs the docs linters, the message link check, the command line check and the user pages’ prose check, and builds the site, which fails on any warning test runs the tests with the race detector, then checks each package’s coverage against its baseline coverage runs the tests, then raises each package’s coverage baseline to what they reach (scripts/test.sh --raise) vuln runs govulncheck on the code as built for Linux and as built for macOS nilaway reports where a nil value may be dereferenced in devvm’s own code, not the tests’, and the findings that testdata/nilaway-baseline.txt hasn’t triaged (Nil checks) nilaway:linux runs nilaway on the code as built for Linux, as CI’s job does, from any system, and must pass before a push to main deadcode lists functions nothing calls outside the tests: only backendtest’s, stubtest’s, upgradetest’s, msg.IDOf, msg.NamesOf, msg.Recorder and msg.Fake, which the tests use, and anything else it lists gets a caller or goes cli-docs generates the CLI reference docs:diagrams installs pele with npm ci and draws the docs site’s diagrams, which every build of the site needs first. mise skips it when no page, the script or pele’s pins changed, and it reinstalls pele only when the lock changed and draws only the diagrams that changed (diagrams) docs generates the CLI reference and draws the diagrams, then serves the docs site e2e runs the end-to-end tests against real VMs mise run test needs a C compiler for the race detector: Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, gcc on Linux. It gives each package 30 minutes rather than go test’s 10, because the CLI tests run the built binary against many stubs and take far longer on a busy machine. Both test tasks run scripts/test.sh, which gives the tests a throwaway HOME.
Before and after every change, mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test must pass. Before a push to main, mise run nilaway:linux must pass as well, because CI’s nilaway job only warns, so a new finding hides in a green run (Nil checks).
CI runs lint and test on macOS and Linux, and vuln and nilaway in jobs of their own. Its nocgo job runs internal/landlock’s and internal/proxy’s tests on Linux with CGO_ENABLED=0, as devvm ships. The test tasks turn cgo on for the race detector, and with cgo the proxy’s child can’t confine every thread of itself (syscall.AllThreadsSyscall), so only that job runs a child under Landlock and the seccomp filter. A weekly workflow also scans main and the binaries of the latest releases (Known vulnerabilities). A change that touches only the docs and Markdown files skips them: the Docs workflow runs lint:docs and builds the site instead, and on every push to main it deploys next.devvm.dev (the docs sites).

data.cli-conventions#CLI conventions:
devvm’s commands follow one set of rules, so that a user who knows a few of them can guess the rest. A bare verb acts on this folder’s VM, anything else goes under its noun, and a bare noun shows or lists. A setting shows bare, changes with a value and takes -g for what new VMs get. The cli skill holds every rule, with a checklist for adding a command and a review for changing one, and its judgment.md explains, with examples, the rules that only a reviewer can check. The reasoning behind most of them is in the Command Line Interface Guidelines, and Cobra’s own mechanics are in Cobra’s docs.
The tests check every rule that a machine can, and mise run test runs them. The cli skill says which test checks each rule and which rules a reviewer checks by hand, and The CLI rule tests says what each test checks. After changing a command’s Use, Short, Long, Example or flags, run mise run cli-docs and commit the CLI reference it writes.
Each command gets the run’s services from one app, in internal/cli/app.go, which NewRoot makes for the run’s UI and hands to every command’s constructor. The app holds devvm’s folders (dirs), a test build’s overrides, the secrets store, the backends’ registry, the shared tools, the environment of the commands on this folder’s VM (vmEnv) and the image builder of the backend new VMs get (builder, the VM environment’s Builder). It makes each one the first time a command asks for it and keeps that one, or its error, for the rest of the run, so the retention that runs before a command and the command itself share them. A command on this folder’s VM runs in a.env, which returns the command’s failure with its message for an error that isn’t one. A new command takes its services from the app rather than making its own.
A command fails by returning its error from RunE, as failed(err, what) when the error may not be a message: what makes the message from the error’s text, such as msg.LsFailed. execute shows what the command returned in showFailure, and it’s the one place a failure is printed. A backend.LoggedError shows the end of the run log, then its message (ErrorLogged). A message, or an error that carries one, shows as it is, and any other error shows in what’s message, or in output_failed when the command didn’t say what failed. The run then exits with 1, and ui.Main runs the cleanups. Once the run is interrupted, a failure prints nothing, because the interrupt is the reason. The root’s layout check (checkLayout) returns its failure the same way, from PersistentPreRunE. Only the UI ends a run itself, in die, where no command can return: a question that gets no answer, and a run log that can’t be opened.
INT, TERM and HUP cancel the run’s context in ui.Main, which then waits for the logged command that’s running to end. When there are cleanups to run, it also waits for the command’s own code to return, for up to 2 seconds (returnGrace), before it runs them and exits with 130. So a cleanup never undoes a command’s work while that command still runs, and a command that can’t stop delays the exit by no more than those 2 seconds. A question waiting for its answer isn’t waited for at all, because reading its answer doesn’t end at Ctrl+C, and an answer read once the run is interrupted is refused, so nothing goes ahead after it. A run with no cleanups exits at once, because nothing could undo its work, so the proxy and devvm’s other background processes stop as soon as they’re told to. A second signal during the cleanups is ignored, so they aren’t stopped halfway.
Ctrl+C reaches every process in the terminal’s group, so it can end a command that devvm runs before devvm itself sees the interrupt. When a command ends by a signal, or exits with a code of 128 or more, devvm waits up to 1 second for its own interrupt (interruptGrace), so that the run ends as interrupted, printing nothing, instead of showing the command’s failure.
Whatever a failure would leave behind, such as a build VM or a temporary file, registers a cleanup with the UI’s AddCleanup and removes it, with the function AddCleanup returns, once there’s nothing left to clean up. The cleanups run when the run ends, last added first, whether it ended normally, failed or was interrupted. They run after the command returned and the run’s context is canceled, so each one gets a fresh context of its own. A cleanup that only undoes unfinished work after an interrupt checks Interrupted(), and the command leaves it registered once the run is interrupted, because the cleanups run only after the command returns.
devvm runs every external command through the UI’s LoggedCmd(ctx, step, cmd), which a backend gets as its Runner. The command’s output goes to the run log, a terminal’s status line shows step, and a failure after it is returned as backend.Logged(m), which shows the end of the log with the message. WithSteps(ctx, n) starts a phase of n steps, and each LoggedCmd with the context it returns is numbered, as [2/5] running base.sh, on its status line and in the log.
data.colors#Colors:
Only internal/ui adds color, through a style for each stream that onTerminal makes, and colorOn decides each one: NO_COLOR or DEVVM_MESSAGES=names turns it off, then FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE (but 0) turns it on, then TERM=dumb turns it off, and otherwise the stream gets color only when it’s a terminal. Names mode stays plain in a terminal too, so end-to-end checks that run devvm under script read the names as they are. A UI from New, as tests make, has no terminal, so it’s plain unless the environment it reads sets FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, which is how cli’s tests get a colored one.
The colors are SGR codes from the 16 base colors only, which the theme maps to its own shades. devvm uses no bright colors (90–97), because Solarized maps them to greys and bright black is Solarized Dark’s background, and it uses no backgrounds, 256 colors or truecolor. The codes go on labels, links, log text and a message’s values, never on the template’s own words:
A message’s values are bold (1), on the status line and in prompts too. msg.M.Segments renders the template with each value between two private-use runes, U+E000 and U+E001, after dropping those runes from the values, so a value can’t start or end a marking of its own. It returns the text cut into segments, each one the template’s words or a value, beside the doc link. Joined, the segments are Text, and String and names mode don’t change. Every value goes through msg.OneLine as the message renders, in Text, Segments and Names alike, so a value has no newline or other control character, whoever made it, bold or not. The log end that ErrorLogged prints is the message on one line without bold, because bold inside dim would cancel it. Error’s devvm: label is bold red (1;31), and Warn’s is bold yellow (1;33). A doc link is underlined blue (4;34). msg.M.Segments gives the doc link apart from the text, so ui colors the link alone. Info’s ==> is bold (1). The run log’s end that ErrorLogged prints, with its --- lines, the log text on the status line, and the log’s lines that -v streams (SetVerbose: LoggedCmd and LogWriter copy the log to stderr through msg.Printable, with no status line) are dim (2). The done mark that a slow step leaves is green (32). The codes are added after msg.Printable and msg.OneLine, so they’re the only ones devvm prints. Those two are devvm’s one cleaner, and msg.Safe is its one rule for which characters reach the terminal. They drop every character that msg.Safe refuses but newline and tab (which OneLine drops too), and a lone C1 byte. msg.Safe takes a graphic character in any script, such as an accented letter, a CJK character or an emoji, so a VM’s file names still read as they are. It refuses the control characters (C0, DEL and C1), the bidi controls such as U+202E, which reorder the text after them so a name could read as another, the format characters, such as the zero-width space and joiners, the word joiner, the soft hyphen and the tag characters, the variation selectors, and the fillers that show as nothing, such as U+3164 and the braille blank U+2800, which could hide or fake text in a prompt. The diff of devvm agent save writes each character that msg.Safe refuses as its code instead, and the names of the files it saves must hold none. The status line, the run log’s end, Pick, devvm network log and the port forwarder’s log use them as well. The status line cuts and counts its plain text with style.fit before painting it, so it still fits the terminal’s width and clears the right number of rows. The run log is never colored.
Tables on Stdout() are colored as stdout is. A command gets a ui.Table from u.Table() and adds a header, rows of ui.Cells and a totals row, and cli never reads the environment itself. Each cell has a ui.Role: Good is green (32), Attention yellow (33), Bad red (31), Secondary dim (2), and Plain stays in the default color, while the header and totals rows are bold. Table pads each cell on its plain text before painting it, because text/tabwriter counts the codes’ bytes as width, and a plain table is byte for byte what text/tabwriter writes with a padding of 2 (TestTableLikeTabwriter). The roles for each table’s values are next to the code that writes it:
devvm images: current is good, stale, unfinished, unused and not built need attention, and digests and keys are secondary. devvm ls: Running and the .git protections on and clone are good, Stopped needs attention, and any other status, such as Broken, is bad, as is the tier unenforced, while a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, is good and open stays plain. devvm space: only copy and leftover in KEPT need attention. devvm doctor: native is good, emulated needs attention, and unreviewed and none are bad. Every command’s --json output is for scripts and stays plain.
mise run test unsets NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and CLICOLOR_FORCE, and the end-to-end tests unset the last two, so your own settings never change what they check.
data.command-arguments#Command arguments:
Each command checks its arguments and flags before it does anything else, so a usage error never looks for a VM, applies the retention settings or changes a file. internal/cli/args.go holds the checks:
A command’s Args is one of noArgs, exactArgs(n), maxArgs(n) and minArgs(n), never Cobra’s own validators, whose errors are in English. Each one names the arguments the command’s Use shows (KEY_FILE, [all|none|LIST]), and with ValidArgs set, it refuses any other value. noArgs on a command with commands of its own says the word isn’t one of them and lists them. Values are checked in Args too. A command adds its own check with cobra.MatchAll, such as settings.ParsePorts for devvm ports or netpolicy.Rule for devvm network allow, returning the same message the command would fail with later. Flag values are checked by name in checkFlagValue, because one flag name has one meaning: --cpus, --memory, --disk, --ports, --lifetime, --older-than, --tools, --agents and --layers. Flags that can’t be given together are marked with exclusive(cmd, a, b), which checkFlags checks first, in place of Cobra’s MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive alone. The parser’s own flag errors (an unknown flag, one without its value, a value its type refuses) become messages in flagError, set as the root’s SetFlagErrorFunc. checkCommands wraps every command’s Args in these checks when NewRoot builds the tree. A message one of them returns is a usage error: Execute prints it, then usage_help naming the command’s own --help, and exits with 2. usage_error is only the fallback for a parser error devvm doesn’t know. What a command’s RunE returns once it ran is a failure, which execute shows and exits with 1. TestUsageErrorsEveryCommand runs every command with an unknown flag, without the argument it needs, with too many and with each flag’s value blank, and checks that each is a usage error and nothing runs.
devvm itself takes no arguments, so a layer may have a command’s name. The root’s Args is noArgs, which for the root runs checkWord (internal/cli/word.go): a word that isn’t a command is a usage error. When the word, or each name in it joined with + or a comma, is a part’s name, from the same partNames that checkPartFlag reads (image.Toolchains, image.Agents and the build env’s layers), the error is no_command_part, with the flags that choose them. Any other word gets the closest command, from Cobra’s SuggestionsFor with SuggestionsMinimumDistance 2 (msg.SuggestDistance, which msg.Closest also uses). devvm’s own help command and the root’s help func run the same check, so devvm help WORD and devvm WORD --help fail as devvm WORD does. The help func can’t return an error, so it panics with a wordPanic that execute recovers. --tools, --agents and --layers are checked in checkFlagValue through checkPartFlag: none alone, or a list of the part’s names. A name of another part’s is refused with that part’s flag (part_other_flag), and any other name it doesn’t know with the closest name (vm.CheckPart).
data.doc-links#Doc links:
A message links a docs page through the docs map in internal/msg/docs.go, from message ID to a page in docs/content/docs and a heading on it. The page is its path without .md, and a section’s own page, its _index.md, is the section’s folder:
var docs = map[string]string{ "vm_outdated": "using/images#outdated-vms", "backend_lacks": "backends#when-a-backend-lacks-something", } devvm prints the page’s address on the docs site on the line after the text.
After editing en.toml, run:
mise exec -- go generate ./internal/msg It writes internal/msg/messages_gen.go, with one function per message. The parameters are the template’s fields in sorted order, in camelCase, and count int for plural messages: [no_vm] becomes msg.NoVM(dir string) msg.M, and a value that’s missing or extra is a compile error. msg.M is also an error: one made from another error carries it with .Because(err), so errors.Is and errors.As see through it, while the text stays the message’s own.
The tests fail when:
messages_gen.go is stale; a message doesn’t render with sample values, or shows ; a generated function is never called outside the generated file and the tests; a doc link names a message that isn’t in en.toml, or a page or heading that doesn’t exist. mise run lint runs this check too.
data.json-output#JSON output:
Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which jsonFlag in internal/cli/json.go adds. The command builds a struct of its own with snake_case json tags, next to the code that writes its table, and writes it with printJSON, which puts "version": 1 (jsonVersion) first, writes HTML characters as they are and refuses anything but an object. A list it prints is never nil, so it’s [] rather than null, and a field that doesn’t apply is omitempty. Sizes are bytes unless the field’s name gives the unit, as in memory_gib.
The root command’s PersistentPreRun calls u.DataOnly() for any command given --json, so Say, Info and LogNote print to stderr from then on, and stdout gets only the JSON. A settings command that also changes its setting with a value wraps its Args in showsOnly, which refuses the value with --json (json_shows_only) before anything else runs.
TestJSONShapes in internal/cli/json_test.go holds each command’s shape, a path: type line for each field of a sample with every field set. A field renamed, removed or given another type fails it. Shapes only gain fields, so a new field goes into the sample and the test, and any other change raises jsonVersion. A new command that shows or lists something gets --json, a row in that test, a CLI test and a section on its page with an example, which output for scripts links to.
data.messages#Messages:
Every message devvm prints is a table in locales/en.toml, and Go code calls it through a function generated from it. internal/msg renders messages but never prints them; the run’s ui.UI does. Only cmd/devvm and internal/cli hold it. Every other package prints and asks through the one msg.Reporter interface, which ui.UI implements: a package’s type embeds it, its constructor takes it, and cli gives it the run’s UI. A package that takes no Reporter gets the answer instead, because cli asks the question first and passes the answer in. Where a package’s warnings also say where the run log is, as Lima’s and the shared tools’ do, its type has its own Warn method over the Reporter’s. A Go test gives a package a msg.Fake instead, a Reporter that prints nothing and refuses every question unless the test sets its fields, and records what it says with a msg.Recorder.
Prose is never built with fmt: every sentence devvm shows the user is a message. A message made from an error carries that error with .Because(err), rather than only its text from err.Error(). Data output, such as a table or --json, isn’t a message, and neither is text in a script that runs somewhere else. Data goes to the UI’s Stdout(), and a log line that isn’t a message goes to its Stderr().
The locale files are in go-i18n’s TOML format, with only go-i18n’s own message fields, so go-i18n’s loader reads them as they are and its goi18n tools work on them:
[no_vm] other = "There's no VM for {{.dir}}. Run devvm to make one." [gc_tools] one = "{{.count}} shared tool image is unused ({{.size}})." other = "{{.count}} shared tool images are unused ({{.size}})." [gc_tools_no_vm] description = "tools lists the tool images, as \"node 24.21.0, claude 2.1.295\"" one = "{{.count}} current shared tool image no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}." other = "{{.count}} current shared tool images no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}." The ID is the table’s name, in snake_case. other is the text: a Go template whose fields are snake_case ({{.vm_name}}). Only plain fields are allowed, no logic. Fields’ types: the generator makes each field a string parameter of the message’s function, except count, which is an int, and vm and vm_name, which are vmname.VM. A field that may hold something other than a VM’s name, such as an image’s name or a VM’s name as the user typed it, is named what or name instead. one is the text for a count of 1, when the wording changes with the count. Both texts then take {{.count}}. description is an optional note for translators. Nothing else: the generator refuses keys go-i18n doesn’t know, nested tables, plural forms English doesn’t use (zero, two, few, many) and leftDelim/rightDelim. Voice: a message’s text follows the docs-voice skill’s Messages rules, which set its length (an error or a warning has at most two sentences, and a prompt at most two lines of context), and the mechanism goes in its doc link rather than its text. One line: a value renders on one line without control, bidi or invisible characters, because msg.OneLine cleans every value as the message renders. Text from a VM that devvm shows as data goes through msg.Printable instead, which keeps its newlines and tabs. Colors says what the two drop.
data.names-mode#Names mode:
With DEVVM_MESSAGES=names, a message prints as its ID and its values in sorted key order, so tests check which message devvm printed and with what, never its wording or language:
! exec devvm _msg nope stderr 'msg_unknown name=nope$' Every CLI test runs in names mode unless it sets env DEVVM_MESSAGES=.
Names mode belongs to internal/ui, which reads it once, with the rest of a stream’s style, in New: a msg.M itself always renders as its text, so its String and Error are the same whatever the environment says. Whatever shows a message as data, a table’s cell or a --json field, goes through the UI’s Text, or a Table’s, to get the names in names mode. New takes the function it reads the environment with, os.Getenv for devvm’s own UI, so a Go test makes a UI in names mode without setting the environment and can run in parallel; cli’s testUI does. A Go test that checks a message without a UI compares Names, msg.IDOf or msg.NamesOf.
devvm _msg NAME key=value… prints a message’s text (never its names), for end-to-end tests that look for it in a VM’s output. It’s hidden from the help.
data.questions#Questions:
A prompt asks a msg.Question, never a bare message, so every question declares what answers it where devvm can’t ask: without a terminal, with --no-input, or once the input ends. A message becomes a question in one of two ways. msg.X(...).AnsweredBy("--force") names the flag or command that answers it, and its refusal is no_input, which names that answer and shows the question first when the prompt wasn’t printed. RefusedWith(msg.Y(...)) makes a question that no flag answers, and its refusal is the message given, which says what to do instead. About(...) adds the messages said before the question, which devvm shows only when it asks.
The Reporter’s Ask, Confirm, Answer and Secret take the question and, where devvm can’t ask it, return its *msg.Refusal, an error whose Msg is the refusal’s message. A command returns it as it would any failure, and a caller with something to fall back on does that instead, so no caller checks for a terminal itself. TestQuestionsDeclareAnswers checks every question in the code, as The CLI rule tests says, and a CLI test answers one with ttyin or DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS=1, as CLI tests says.
data.status-lines#Status lines:
Any work that can take noticeable time runs under a status line, so that the user sees what devvm is waiting for. Such work is a host command, host git, a command in a VM, a backend’s own commands, such as limactl list, a request over the network, a walk of a folder the user owns, a lookup of a folder’s disk with macOS’s diskutil, and a wait for a lock, a timeout or another process. A logged command shows its step on its own. Other slow work shows one with the Reporter’s Status, whose label is a message in locales/en.toml: a lowercase phrase in -ing, such as reading_vms, with a description that says what runs under it. For example:
func ListAll(ctx context.Context, e *Env) ([]Listed, []Known, error) { defer e.Status(msg.ReadingVMs())() inv, err := ReadInventory(ctx, e.Dirs, e.Registry, AllBackends) The status line shows only in a terminal, without -v and until the run is interrupted, because nothing would clear one started after that. The UI keeps status lines as a stack. A logged command or a Status inside another shows its own line until it ends, and then the UI draws the outer one again, so a phase can show one line around steps that show their own. A message said under a status line, whether Info, Warn, Note or data on Stdout(), clears the line, prints, and draws the line again below it, so a warning never lands on the status line. A question, the picker and ui.Terminal, which a command in the VM that draws on the terminal gets, hold the status line until they’re done, so its redraw never goes over a prompt or what the user types.
A wait for a lock that another devvm holds shows a status line only while it waits, never when the lock is free. platform.LockFile, platform.LockFileShared and platform.LockDir take a platform.Waiting, which they call once they find the lock held, and they call its end once the wait ends. msg.Waiting(status, label) makes one from a Reporter’s Status and a label, such as vm_state_waiting. internal/state, for a VM’s lock or the layout’s, and internal/trust take no Reporter, so they alone take the run’s Status from the context (msg.StatusOf), which the run’s root sets (msg.WithStatus), and forbidigo keeps it to them. The layout’s migration shows layout_migrating while it runs. An agent’s login file is locked by its folder’s lock (platform.LockDir), which the proxy holds while it refreshes the login, so it takes its wait as agentlogin.File’s Waiting (agent_login_waiting), and its wait ends with the caller’s context, as every lock’s does. Only a lock that never waits, such as one on a file just made, passes platform.NoWait, which shows nothing, and the structure test’s status-lines rule holds it to statusSites, as it does a nil. msg.Waiting with no status, as in a process with no UI, gives a wait that shows nothing, never nil. A test build’s locks panic on a nil one (platform.CheckWaiting, which the root’s run calls in every test build), so the CLI tests and the end-to-end tests catch one that the rule can’t see, such as a zero agentlogin.File’s. They don’t catch a msg.Waiting given a nil status, which only a review finds. A forbidigo rule refuses syscall.Flock and unix.Flock outside internal/platform, the proxy’s log rotation, the stubs and tests, so every lock goes through internal/platform’s.
Work that takes the terminal never runs under a status line, because its redraw would go over what the work shows. That work is a VM’s shell, ssh-add asking for a key’s passphrase (checkAgent, Agent.Ensure) and an agent’s login in the VM. A launch shows its status lines around those steps rather than across them. A background process, such as the proxy, a forwarder or a link session, has no terminal and shows none.
Tests check the label rather than a terminal. A msg.Fake gives each status line’s label, and each logged command’s step, to its OnStatus, and Showing returns the one showing. So a seam that the slow work goes through records what showed meanwhile, as TestAgentImportStatus does with the Opencode and ExcludeFromBackup seams, and a backendtest.Fake gives each call to its OnCall. TestLaunchStatusLines runs a new, a running and a stopped VM’s launch and fails on any backend call made with no status line showing, except the shell’s, which takes the terminal, and Running’s, which reads the VM’s pid files. TestCommandStatusLines does the same for the commands that show, list, change, export, stop and delete a running or a stopped VM, including devvm network lock’s picker, devvm restart, the restart that devvm mount-cache asks for, links, and a group with a second VM that runs, stops and goes. It answers their questions in a terminal through the msg.Fake, checks that the picker and the restart are asked, and fails on a question asked under a status line, or a proxy or link session started with none. testProxy runs each link session as a sleep that says each of its links is carried, as its links change. TestVMLockWaits, TestCheckLayoutWaits and each lock’s own test check a wait’s status line. TestSSHAddOffStatusLine fails on an ssh-add that runs under one, on the user’s agent or devvm’s own, and chflagsCalls fails a clone test on a lock or unlock of .git with none. The structure test’s status-lines rule fails on a function that does slow work it knows by name and shows no status line of its own. That slow work is a host command, host git, a walk of a folder, a volume’s lookup, a request through internal/fetch, a wait for a lock that shows nothing, or a backend’s command outside a step. The rule passes a function when statusSites lists it with why, such as the status line of the caller it runs under (The structure test).
data.the-cli-rule-tests#The CLI rule tests:
The Go tests in internal/cli walk the command tree, so a command that breaks one of the command line’s rules fails mise run test, whether it’s new or changed. Each exception says why, in its test’s list or in the command’s own about:
TestEveryCommandsHelp checks that every command users see has a Short in sentence case without a full stop, a Long of one to three sentences, an Example and a docs page in its about, and that each of the root’s commands is in a group. devvm help is the exception, as Cobra lists it apart and the CLI reference leaves it out. TestAboutGroupsAreHelpGroups checks that each group a command names is one of helpGroups. TestPersistentFlags checks that every command takes -h/--help, --no-input and -v/--verbose and has no other persistent flag. TestFlagNames checks that each shorthand is in its list, -h, -v, -f, -g and -n, for one flag only, that no command takes --yes, and that a flag has one help text wherever it appears, except the names in manyUses. TestFlagNamesHaveOneMeaning checks that a flag name has the same shorthand, type and value everywhere. TestDurationFlags checks that a flag whose value is a DURATION is read with state.ParseDuration in checkFlagValue, and that no flag is a Go time.Duration. TestShowCommandsTakeJSON checks that every command users see takes --json or says why not in its about’s noJSON, and TestJSONShapes checks that every command with --json has a shape. TestCommandNames checks that command names are lower case without aliases, that no command is named list, show, get, delete, remove or ls but devvm ls, that a command named unX has a sibling X, and that each argument in a Use is a PLACEHOLDER or a word, with |, [] and ... only. TestUseMatchesArgs runs every command with the arguments its Use shows, from argSamples, and with none when they’re optional, and checks that it runs, so its Args takes what its help shows. TestUnknownWord checks that devvm WORD, devvm WORD --help and devvm help WORD fail alike for a word that isn’t a command, and that a toolchain’s, an agent’s or a layer’s name, alone or joined with others, points to its flag while any other word gets the closest command. TestCommandLines reads every devvm command line in the repo: the docs, the generated CLI reference among them, the README, AGENTS.md, locales/en.toml, Go’s comments and strings, assets/, install.sh, the CLI tests and their stubs, the scripts, the workflows and the skills. It checks that each one’s command exists, that each flag is one that command takes, that a placeholder is one its Use shows and a flag’s value the one its help shows, such as DURATION, and that a word after a command with commands of its own isn’t a command from elsewhere in the tree. A command line written to be typed, in a code block, a code span or a CLI test’s exec, also has its values checked with checkFlagValue, and when it has nothing to fill in, it runs in a tree whose commands do nothing, where it mustn’t be a usage error. Prose has only its command and its flags checked, because its words after the command are English. The lines written to show a refusal are in refused, each with why, and a CLI test’s ! exec lines are left out, as they’re meant to fail. mise run lint:docs runs it too, so a docs change that names a command that doesn’t exist fails there. TestCheckCommandLine checks that it finds each kind of stale line. TestQuestionsDeclareAnswers in internal/cli finds every question the code makes, outside tests. A question is a msg.Question, which Ask, Confirm, Answer and Secret take, and only two methods of a message make one: AnsweredBy("--force") names the flag or command that answers it, and RefusedWith(msg.X(...)) gives a question that no flag answers the refusal that says what to do instead. The test checks that each AnsweredBy names a string, that each flag in it is one its command takes and each command one devvm has, and that each RefusedWith gives a message, so no question is asked without its answer declared. TestCheckAnswer checks that it finds each kind of wrong answer.
data.translations#Translations: A translation is locales/.toml (de.toml) with the same tables, one and other translated (and the language’s other plural forms, such as few), loaded by go-i18n the same way. Doc links are the same in every language: the docs site is English. devvm picks the language from the first of LC_ALL, LC_MESSAGES and LANG that is set (de_DE.UTF-8 is German); C and POSIX are English. A message missing from a translation is shown in English.

data: For contributors: why devvm is built the way it is, what was tried and dropped, and what’s still open. How each part works is on its own page in How it works, and the rest of Contributing has the repo’s layout and rules. Why devvm is written in Go is under Why Go, with the processes it runs.
data.a-ca-per-vm#A CA per VM:
To put a secret in, a VM’s proxy shows the VM certificates from a CA that the VM trusts, and inside the VM that CA vouches for any site. So each VM has CAs of its own, and the design keeps two things: a CA’s key never leaves this machine, and no VM’s proxy can make a certificate that another VM accepts (how).
What it’s built from: trust.InitCA, at each launch, whatever the VM’s tier, readies the VM’s current CA and its next one in vms//run/ca/ (paths.VM.CA): ECDSA P-256, 30 days and an hour each, the next one starting a week and an hour before the current one ends. The proxy’s config names the four files (ca, ca_key, ca_next, ca_next_key) and their certificates’ SHA-256 (ca_sha256, ca_next_sha256), so a replaced CA starts the proxy again. The proxy signs with the next CA from an hour after its start (ca.signer), and the VM’s setup installs both certificates, devvm-proxy.crt and devvm-proxy-next.crt, so the switch needs neither a launch nor a new proxy. The guest never fetches a CA: its trust comes only from the setup that devvm sends over ssh at each launch.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its data isolation and lifecycle companion). Leads, each ruled out, fixed or listed:
One VM’s CA signing for another: ruled out. Each proxy’s config is devvm’s, mode 600 in the VM’s own run folder, and names only that VM’s files, and a VM reaches no other VM’s proxy without that VM’s password. A VM trusts only the certificates its own setup sends, and the setup removes any other devvm-*.crt. The keys reaching a VM: ruled out. The setup sends the two certificates and nothing else from the folder, /ca.pem serves certificates only, and no VM mounts devvm’s data folder. The CLI tests check the setup’s files for a private key, and e2e searches the VM’s /etc, /home, /root and /usr/local for each key. Key files: the folder is mode 700 and each key mode 600, written whole through a temporary file. Fixed: the proxy read the CA’s files through tls.LoadX509KeyPair, which follows links and takes any mode, and it now reads them as the user’s own regular files, not links, with a key no one else may read or write, of at most 64 KiB (loadCA, readPrivate). On macOS each VM’s CA folder is kept out of Time Machine at each launch. Expiry and rotation: a CA lasts 30 days and an hour, and each certificate it makes a day, never past the CA’s end. Listed: the next CA’s key is on disk for up to 23 days before that CA starts, so a copy of it taken then works until that CA ends, up to 53 days after the copy. A VM that isn’t opened again stays verifiable for at least 30 days less an hour after its last launch, which is the trade the successor buys. Two launches of one VM at once: fixed. InitCA holds the CA folder’s lock, run/ca/lock, while it reads and writes the CAs, so two launches at once take turns and never leave a key and a certificate from different runs (TestInitCATogether). Lifecycle: a remake keeps the VM’s folder and its CAs. devvm rm, devvm gc --orphans and the deletion of a VM whose creation was interrupted delete the folder with the keys. A change of tier keeps the CAs, because every tier’s proxy signs with them. Issuer confusion: fixed before it could arise: each CA’s name holds its serial, so a VM’s two CAs never share a subject, which some verifiers look issuers up by. Clock skew: the switch waits an hour past the next CA’s start, so a VM whose clock is up to an hour behind still accepts the certificates. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, network): two confined VMs have different CAs; each VM trusts its own two and none of the other’s, and its /etc/ssl/devvm.pem holds the next one; no key is anywhere in the VM, and the keys are mode 600; each proxy serves its own CAs at /ca.pem, and a certificate it presents for a bound host verifies with its own VM’s CAs and not with the other’s; devvm rm deletes one VM’s CAs and leaves the other’s. The switch itself is checked by unit tests (TestNextCASigns, TestInitCASwitch), because it happens weeks after a launch.
data.a-company-proxy#A company proxy:
Behind a company proxy, nothing reaches the internet without going through it, so each VM’s proxy goes through it too (how), and each build goes through a proxy of devvm’s for the build alone, which goes through it. The design keeps two things: the proxy still decides every request by the name the VM asked for, and the company proxy’s password reaches nothing of a VM’s or a build’s.
