What it’s built from: the host’s HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, read from devvm’s environment (backend.ReadHostProxy) when a VM’s proxy starts, or config.toml’s [proxy] when the environment sets neither proxy (settings.HostProxy), checked (HostProxy.Upstream: only http:// proxies), and written into the proxy’s config, proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, vms//run/ (mode 600), as upstream (internal/proxy/upstream.go). config.toml is a file people copy and keep with their dotfiles, so it never holds the password: its URL names the user, and the password is the proxy secret (proxy.UpstreamSecret), in the Keychain or devvm’s secrets folder, which the proxy looks up through IO.Secret as it starts (upstreamPassword), so no file of devvm’s holds it either. It’s a host-only secret (secrets.Secret.HostOnly): no VM is ever bound to it. The proxy opens its own CONNECT through the company proxy, by name, with Proxy-Authorization: Basic from the URL, for tunnels and for the TLS connections it makes to put secrets in, which check the server against the system’s roots and the user’s CAs. Plain HTTP goes to the company proxy in absolute form. A change to the settings starts the VM’s proxy again at devvm’s next run, and an old proxy that won’t stop fails the start (proxy_stop_failed) rather than run on with its old settings.
What an upstream changes: the proxy resolves a name and dials the addresses it checked only when it connects directly. Through a company proxy, the company proxy resolves the name, so the floor can’t hold it to checked addresses:
An address the VM asks for is judged as before, and localhost, *.localhost and loopback and unspecified addresses never go upstream, so the floor refuses them as before unless a rule names them. A host whose last label is all digits or starts with 0x (127.1, 2130706433, 0x7f000001) is refused as no host name (hostOK), because a company proxy that reads it as inet_aton does would reach an address the floor never judged. A name is refused when this machine’s resolver answers with any internal or denied address (floorUpstream). The proxy looks it up absolute, as it does for a direct connection (egress.lookupName), so this machine’s DNS search domain never turns api into api.corp.example.com, a name that no rule judged. A name this machine can’t resolve within three seconds goes upstream unjudged only when the policy names it, as itself or under *.domain (policy.byName). When only ** allows it, the proxy refuses it (errUnresolved), because ** would otherwise send the company proxy any name the VM makes up, and the company proxy may resolve such a name to its own network’s hosts. The company proxy may still resolve a name differently, or later, than this machine did (DNS rebinding between the two lookups). It may also add its own search domain to any name it’s sent, before or after it tries the name as written, depending on its resolver. A Kubernetes pod’s resolver, for example, uses ndots:5, so it tries the search domain first for any name with fewer than five dots. So a name that a rule names, such as jenkins, may reach jenkins.corp.example.com through it, and a name that resolves here may reach another under the company’s search domain there. A VM that controls a name under an allowed domain can choose the unjudged path: its name server can fail, or answer after the proxy’s three seconds, and then answer the company proxy with an internal address. So under a name the policy lists, a VM reaches whatever the company proxy reaches: its company’s internal hosts, and the company proxy’s own host, including this machine’s loopback when the company proxy runs on this machine (a local proxy that a VPN client runs, for example). Address denies apply only to the addresses this machine resolves. The allowlist stays the limit: a name the VM’s policy doesn’t allow never reaches the company proxy. The proxy reads at most 64 KiB of the company proxy’s answer to CONNECT (maxConnectReply), so an answer whose headers never end fails the request instead of filling memory. The company proxy sees every allowed host name and port, and with a CA in the user’s CA folder, it reads TLS too, as it does for this machine. Credentials: the company proxy’s user and password are in no process’s arguments (only the file’s path is), in no log (the event log’s upstream field and the proxy’s own log name the company proxy as host:port, and the URL the proxy’s HTTP transport uses has no user), and in no request but the company proxy’s own: the proxy drops the VM’s Proxy-Authorization and sets the company proxy’s only for a request it sends there. The VM never sees them, not even in a refusal, which names the company proxy by host:port and its status code.
Builds: a build runs code that isn’t devvm’s: layer scripts run third-party installers, and with --from, the container image’s own shell and package manager run as root in the build VM. So a build never gets the company proxy’s settings. Behind a company proxy, each build goes through a proxy of devvm’s on the host for that build alone (backend.ProxyStarter). It’s devvm _proxy -config with the same config as a VM’s proxy (proxy.Config): a policy file of **, which allows any host on ports 80 and 443 but the host’s own and internal addresses, a new random password, the company proxy’s settings as its upstream, and its lifeline on the build VM’s hostagent, all in one file of mode 600. The build gets only http://devvm:@:, in each proxy variable the host sets, and the host’s NO_PROXY. When the build ends, devvm stops that proxy and deletes its config, which holds the password and the company proxy’s, and a successful build’s folder goes too. The password is worthless once the proxy has stopped, and the build never sees the company proxy’s address, user or password. Without a company proxy, builds start no proxy and get no proxy settings.
Lima: the build VM (an image’s, the tools build’s or --from’s conversion VM) reaches the proxy at 192.168.5.2, the host’s address on Lima’s user-mode network, with vz and with QEMU, and on macOS its Seatbelt profile allows that one port of the host’s loopback alongside its ssh port. The proxy runs on the host, so a company proxy on this machine’s loopback, such as one a VPN client runs, works for builds on macOS too. Lima’s propagateProxyEnv would write the host’s proxy settings into the guest’s /etc/environment between #LIMA-START and #LIMA-END at each boot (Lima’s 07-etc-environment.sh), and a stopped build VM’s disk would keep that block, so build VMs start with propagateProxyEnv: false, and only a VM on Lima’s own network whose guest doesn’t name devvm’s proxy (NetDirect without Confinement.GuestProxy) starts with it on. Every project VM names its proxy, an open one’s included, so every project VM starts with it off, and its first start makes that change in the edit that adds its proxy to its environment. Lima also logs the proxy settings it reads, password and all, into devvm’s run log, so devvm runs limactl without them, and only a start with propagateProxyEnv on gets them back. Each build script gets the build proxy’s variables exported at its start, on its input with the script (internal/backend/lima/buildproxy.go), and /etc/sudoers.d/devvm-build-proxy keeps them for sudo until the scripts end. The build proxy’s files and logs are in the build VM’s folder, in run/builds//run/build-proxy/ in devvm’s data folder. --from’s conversion: oci/build.sh runs as root with the build proxy’s variables for crane. The container image’s own code runs only in a chroot under env -i: the /etc/os-release check gets PATH alone, and chroot_run (bootify.sh, the CAs’ ca.sh) gets PATH, HOME, LC_ALL and the build proxy’s variables, for bootify.sh’s package downloads. The build’s policy is ** alone, so on its own the build’s proxy would refuse every name this machine can’t resolve, and where only the company proxy resolves outside names, a build would reach nothing by name. Lima’s build proxies start with upstream_unresolved in their config, which sends such names on to the company proxy unjudged. The refusal would protect little there, because without a company proxy those builds are on Lima’s user-mode network and reach internal addresses directly.
End-to-end checks (Lima):
images: a layer built with a fake company proxy’s password in HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY (a closed port, NO_PROXY=*): its script and sudo see the build’s proxy at 192.168.5.2 with user devvm, never the password, the build’s proxy is gone afterwards, and neither the image’s whole disk, nor Lima’s files for it, nor devvm’s logs hold the password; from: a company proxy of the run’s own with a password, and a --from alpine:3.21 base, with every feature, and a layer on it: the registry, Alpine’s mirror and the layer’s own download reach the company proxy through the builds’ proxies; what the layer’s commands and sudo have is the build’s proxy with a password of its own; and the password is in no converted disk, image, log, build file or process’s arguments; network: a company proxy of the run’s own (a devvm _proxy with a password, allowing any host): the VM’s next launch with it in devvm’s environment starts the VM’s proxy again with -upstream; an allowed host goes through it by name (its event log) and the VM’s event log names it; a host the VM’s policy doesn’t allow gets 403 and never reaches it; its password is in no process’s arguments, no log and nothing of the VM’s; the launch after, without it, starts the VM’s proxy again going directly. Not covered: https:// and socks5:// company proxies, which devvm refuses (upstream_proxy_scheme); proxy auto-configuration (PAC) files and the macOS system proxy, which devvm doesn’t read; Kerberos or NTLM authentication. An open VM goes through its proxy as every VM does, so no project VM gets the host’s settings in its /etc/environment. What devvm’s redaction of Lima’s logs leaves open is under your company proxy’s password.
data.a-folders-volume#A folder’s volume:
A VM’s state records its folder’s volume beside the folder’s device, inode and birth time, so a folder that moved while a restart gave its disk another device number keeps its VM (one VM per folder). The volume is macOS’s volume UUID, from diskutil info -plist for the mount point and device read from the folder opened with no link on its path, or Linux’s f_fsid on ext4, Btrfs and ZFS, read from that open folder. It’s bound to the folder’s inode and birth time, so a record that an older devvm left beside another folder names no volume.
The volume tells two disks apart that each have a folder with the same inode and birth time, which happens by chance or when a copy of a disk gets a volume ID of its own. It doesn’t tell a disk from a copy that keeps the volume ID, and it isn’t a secret or a signature:
Who can forge one: whoever can write a volume’s metadata. On macOS that’s root, any program running as you, which can attach a disk image it made with hdiutil without root and without asking, or anyone who makes a disk image, sets the UUID in its bytes and gets you to attach it. On Linux, tune2fs -U and btrfstune need write access to the block device, which is root’s, and a crafted image needs a loop mount, which is root’s unless your desktop lets you mount images. A crafted disk or image can set the inode and birth time too. What it gets them: what a copy of the disk that keeps all three already gets. At another path, devvm offers the VM to the folder only when nothing is left at the old path and the folder is yours, and moves it only after you confirm. On a disk image or an external disk mounted with its owners ignored, as macOS mounts them by default, a folder can read as yours whoever made it, so that check holds little there. At the folder’s own path, the forged disk has to be mounted over the folder’s path, and then it gets the VM as the folder’s disk would. What a VM can do: nothing here. A VM can’t attach a disk or write a volume’s metadata on the host, and devvm reads the folder’s identity, its owner, its mount point and its device from the folder opened with no link on its path, so a link a VM puts in a folder’s place can’t pass another folder off as it. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, with its data isolation companion):
Lead What holds it Check A folder on another volume with the same inode and birth time, at the folder’s own path after a restart A renumbered folder at its own path must be on the recorded volume when both are known (platform.KeepsVolume), checked when devvm finds the VM and again when the start records the new device Unit tests (TestKeepsVolume, TestRenumberedOnAnotherVolume) A link swapped in while devvm reads the folder The identity, owner, mount point, device and f_fsid come from one folder opened with no link on its path (platform.StatFolder), and diskutil’s answer must name that mount point and device Unit tests (TestStatFolderAndVolumeUUID, TestStatFolder, TestMovedFrom) A diskutil that hangs or fails A lookup within 1 or 5 seconds, none after one fails in a run, and a volume that can’t be told records no volume and matches no moved folder, while a renumbered folder at its own path is then judged by its device, inode and birth time alone, as for a state that records no volume Unit tests (TestVolumeOfCache, TestRecordFolder) A disk the user mounts in its place Not held, because a disk mounted at the folder’s path with the folder’s volume ID, inode and birth time is the folder to devvm, as it is to any program Documented here and in one VM per folder
data.a-vm-made-again#A VM made again:
devvm layer add and devvm layer rm make a VM again from a new image, and devvm update from its own image’s new build, while keeping devvm’s state for it and its home folder (making a VM again). All three use the one remake, and three choices shape it.
Option B, a new disk. The layer’s script never runs in the existing VM. Running it there would run a third-party installer next to the project’s files, as root, on a disk the VM’s own code has changed, and the image’s key would then describe a disk that no longer matches it. A new disk from the image keeps every VM a copy of an image whose key hashes everything in it. Taking a layer out works the same way, because a layer has no script that undoes it, and only a new disk from an image without the layer leaves nothing of it behind.
The old disk is kept until the new VM has started. devvm stops the VM and renames its machine to devvm--old (backend.Backend’s Rename, limactl rename on Lima, which keeps the disk whole) before it makes the new one by the VM’s name, rather than deleting it first. So a failed create, start or home copy puts the old VM back as it was, and only a remake that got its new VM started with its home folder deletes the old disk. Every backend renames a stopped VM, so none deletes the old disk early. The aside name is no project VM’s name (vmname.IsVM), which keeps it out of devvm ls, the ssh config, the mounts devvm’s SSH agent checks and devvm space’s strays. It’s 24 characters for every VM, two more than the shortest name a project VM can have, so in a Lima home whose path leaves room for fewer, the rename is refused (lima_home_too_long) before anything else changes, and the VM stays as it was, stopped.
The VM keeps its ID. A link records its target’s id so that a different VM in the target’s folder, made after devvm rm, never inherits the link (links between VMs). A remake isn’t that case. The user runs it in the folder, on the host, and it keeps the VM’s name, its state, its folder and its project, so its links, its group and its published ports are the user’s choices for this project, and none of them is worth losing to a layer. A new ID would make every client’s link to the VM replaced, and the user would have to add each again in every client’s folder, which gives nothing a check needs: the clients reach the same project’s published ports, on a VM the same person made again from an image devvm built. What changes is the VM’s disk and its host keys. devvm reads the new host keys from the new disk’s system files, which the home folder’s copy never reaches, as for any VM that starts, and a link session’s master to the target ends when the target stops, so the next one reads the new keys. A remake of a confined VM keeps it, with the same proxy password and salt, so the links’ policy rule holds throughout.
data.bases-image-and-packages#Base’s image an:
base starts from the newest Ubuntu cloud image on each machine, and its packages are the newest when each key of base first builds, so devvm’s own files pin neither and need no bumps (how, packages). What it trusts, and where:
The image: Ubuntu’s cloud image key alone, pinned in devvm’s files. devvm checks the release’s SHA256SUMS signature itself, in Go, so a host without gpgv checks it too, and a bad signature is refused, never passed over for an older release. The listing that names the newest release is unsigned, so a server or network that can change it can only hold devvm back to an older signed release, over HTTPS. The signed SHA256SUMS names files, not its release, so such a server could also serve an older release’s files under a newer release’s name, which devvm then records as the pin; that holds base back the same way, and it makes the package check’s date stricter, not looser. The pinned SHA-256 then decides every later download. The packages: Ubuntu’s archive key, through apt in the build VM, which holds nothing but Ubuntu’s image and devvm’s own scripts while it records. A mirror only serves files, and apt checks each against the archive key, so ubuntu-mirror can’t install a package Ubuntu didn’t publish. Ubuntu’s InRelease files carry no Valid-Until, and the build VM has no lists before, so a stale or hostile mirror, or anyone on an http:// path to one, can serve an older signed state of the archive. devvm refuses one older than the archive state the pinned cloud image was built from, naming the mirror (packages_stale_mirror, packages_stale without one): every pocket but the release’s must be dated no more than a day before the image’s release, and the release pocket no earlier than Ubuntu’s release day (Release.Stale). So a recorded state is never older than the pinned image. A mirror that fell behind after the pinned release still gets recorded, so freshness past the pin’s date rests on the mirror, and on HTTPS for Ubuntu’s own. The cache: a first build records what its own apt checked, and devvm checks it again on this machine before it keeps anything. The build hands back the InRelease files and package lists apt used, and devvm verifies each InRelease with Ubuntu’s archive key, pinned in its files, in Go (pgp.go’s clearsigned messages). Each list must be one a verified InRelease gives the SHA-256 and size of, and each package one a list gives the SHA-256 of, so the recording VM can’t add a package Ubuntu didn’t publish, even with root, and the set keeps the archive’s own entry for each package. devvm keeps each file under its own SHA-256 and each key’s set once. What comes back from the VM is checked for shape, hashes and size (at most 20,000 entries and 16 GiB of packages, 2 GiB of lists) before anything is kept, so a build VM can’t put a file under another file’s name, change another key’s set, or write outside the cache. A key’s set is never written again, so a later build can’t change it either. The recording VM can’t record an older version than apt would install either: the build must hand back resolute-updates’ and resolute-security’s InRelease files with lists for the recorded packages’ architectures, and every non-empty list that each InRelease it hands back gives for the recorded packages’ architectures, and devvm refuses a package that the release pocket, -updates or -security lists a newer version of, ordered as dpkg --compare-versions orders them (packages_lists_missing, packages_not_newest). apt in the build takes phased updates too, so the newest version is what it installs. A replay checks each file’s SHA-256 on this machine before it sends it, and apt in the VM checks it again against the set’s entry. Replays trust apt’s entries as recorded (trusted=yes on a local repository of files devvm checked), because the archive’s signature covers the archive’s lists, not a set of packages taken from them. What it doesn’t stop: anything with root in the recording VM before apt.sh end (a feature’s script, a compromised pinned download) chooses which of Ubuntu’s signed packages get recorded, because the host checks that each package is the archive’s and the newest that the lists handed back have, not that apt chose it. It can record a package base doesn’t ask for, or one from -backports, but never one from -proposed. It can also hand back an older signed state of -updates and -security than the archive’s newest, dated as early as a day before the pinned image’s release, which the stale check allows, and record the newest versions of that state. Every later build of that key replays what it recorded, as the same image would. It can also change the image itself, which the image’s key doesn’t cover. devvm rebuild base records anew. Packages for --from bases and for layers come from their sources as they are, unpinned. Breakage from upstream: users now build from images and packages that e2e hasn’t run. If the newest image doesn’t boot, a first build tries the release before it (how), which covers a release whose kernel Lima can’t start, but not packages that break base.sh or a VM later. A scheduled build of base from the newest image and packages, on CI or the test machines, should catch a break before users do; it isn’t built yet.
data.claude-codes-plugins-a-seed-and-a-folder:
Claude Code writes into its plugins folder whenever it runs: each plugin’s data, which a plugin reaches as ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, the plugins it installs, its marketplaces’ copies and their updates, its MCP bundles and its records. devvm’s agent store holds one plugins folder for every VM with Claude Code, mounted read-only, so if that folder were each VM’s ~/.claude/plugins, every one of those writes would fail. A plugin that keeps data would break, and no plugin could be installed in a VM. Making the store’s folder writable would fix the writes, but every VM shares it, so a VM could then change the plugins, hooks and MCP servers’ commands that Claude Code runs in every other VM, and keep a foothold in each of them after you delete it. That isn’t an escape to this machine, but it breaks the line between VMs that the store’s read-only mounts hold for every other agent folder.
So each VM’s plugins folder is its own, on its own disk, and the store’s folder is Claude Code’s seed, a plugins folder that Claude Code reads but never writes, which it supports for container images and CI (how). Its two variables, CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR, are Claude Code’s own, so devvm patches nothing in Claude Code and copies nothing into the VM at a launch, and the seed stays one mount that every VM reads. What a VM writes stays in that VM, and what it installed reaches the store, and every VM, only through devvm agent save, whose diff you read before you answer yes. The import and the save copy only the entries a seed has, the marketplaces’ records, their copies and the plugins’ cache, because the rest of the folder is each machine’s own. Each plugin’s data can hold its own logins, and this machine’s plugins’ data in the store would reach every VM.
The save never takes a plugin out of the store, because a VM’s folder holds only what that VM installed, not the store’s plugins, which it reads from the seed, so a plugin missing from it isn’t one the VM removed. Taking out what the VM’s folder lacks would empty the store of every plugin the VM didn’t install itself. The VM’s marketplaces’ records join the store’s for the same reason, and only a record whose copy is in the store’s marketplaces folder joins, so the records that Claude Code made of the seed’s own marketplaces stay as the store has them, and a record can’t point other VMs elsewhere.
Not covered:
A marketplace in a folder on this machine reaches a VM only when that folder is in the VM too, because Claude Code reads such a marketplace where it is, and a seed holds no copy of it. A plugin’s data stays in its VM. A new VM, or one made from an export of another’s history, starts each plugin’s data afresh, and so does every VM after you install a plugin there, as the export leaves the VM’s plugins folder out. A plugin installed in a VM runs in that VM with whatever it does, as a plugin does on this machine. devvm keeps it from the other VMs until you save it, and the save’s diff shows what it adds. Threat check (the security-audit skill, a hostile VM writing what other VMs or this machine run):
Lead What holds it Check A VM writing the store’s plugins, which every VM runs The store’s folder stays mounted read-only, and the VM’s writes go to its own folder TestClaudePluginsSeed, sync’s links and own-dirs, e2e’s project section A save that sends more than the seed’s entries, such as a plugin’s data The VM’s script sends only the seed’s entries, and devvm saves nothing when the stream has any other entry of the folder TestReadSentClaudePlugins, TestAgentSaveScriptClaudePlugins, agent_save This machine’s plugins’ data reaching every VM The import copies only the seed’s entries, through links too TestAgentImportClaudePlugins, agent This machine’s plugins’ data that devvm 0.1.0’s import left in the store Every start takes the store’s entries that a seed lacks out before the VM runs, from devvm’s config folder as a root, refusing a link anywhere on the path and following none among the entries, and a VM with Claude Code doesn’t start while they can’t go TestCleanSeeds, TestCleanSeedsFails, fixture_v010_plugins A VM’s paths in the records it saves The records’ paths to the VM’s plugins folder are renamed to the store’s, only a record whose copy is in the store’s marketplaces by a clean path joins the store’s, and a records file that isn’t a JSON object is left out TestAgentSaveClaudePlugins A name in the VM’s plugins folder that the save’s script would read as a pattern It’s sent rather than excluded, and devvm refuses the save TestAgentSaveScriptClaudePlugins A plugin’s data, or what a VM installed, reaching another VM through an export The export and the import leave out the VM’s plugins folder, and the import leaves out the seed’s link TestClaudePluginsHistory An export that names the VM’s plugins folder another way, such as .claude/./plugins, past the import’s excludes, as the folder is writable The import refuses a name with a ., .. or empty part, and deletes what it leaves out by its path once unpacked. The review found it first, and it’s fixed TestHistoryImportRuns
data.devcontainerjson#devcontainer.json:
A new VM gets what the project’s devcontainer.json says, as far as devvm does it (its page).
The guarantee: nothing from the file runs on or reaches this machine: it reads none of its environment, files, credentials, Docker images or registry logins, adds no mount, writes nothing to the project folder, and weakens no confinement (the network tier, .git protection). It shapes only what’s in a new VM and what runs in it, as the VM’s user. devvm’s own handling of it (reading, parsing, state, the environment file, commands, ports, the image lookup) can’t be turned against this machine or devvm. Reviewed: the threat check’s leads are fixed, ruled out or listed below.
The problem: the file is the project’s, so the VM’s: the VM writes the folder, and a cloned repo’s file is whoever wrote it. Dev Containers runs much of it on the host (initializeCommand, ${localEnv:…}, builds, mounts, runArgs, docker-outside-of-docker’s socket), pulls images with the user’s logins, and forwards ports at will.
How it’s kept:
Reading: only in the folder, through os.Root (a link out of it isn’t followed, .. included), opened without blocking (a FIFO the VM made in its place opens at once and is refused) and checked as a regular file on the open descriptor, at most 1 MiB. It’s read once, at plan; what the VM is made from is the parsed plan, recorded in its state, never the file read again. Later launches only hash it and warn. Parsing: comments and trailing commas are blanked at the same offsets, strings untouched, then encoding/json; values of the wrong kind, a NUL, an environment variable’s name that isn’t one, and every variable devvm doesn’t fill in are refused before anything’s made, ${localEnv:…}/${env:…} above all. Nothing is filled in from this machine: ${containerWorkspaceFolder} is the folder’s path (the same in the VM), ${containerEnv:X} the VM’s own X, left to its shell. Mapped, or refused, or ignored: build/Dockerfiles/Compose are refused; initializeCommand never runs; mounts, runArgs, privileged, capAdd, securityOpt, workspaceMount and the rest are ignored, named. Features map only to devvm’s own layers (docker-in-docker to the docker layer, a toolchain’s name to that toolchain); no feature’s script is fetched, docker-outside-of-docker is refused, everything else too. The image: --from’s path, but only an image its registry gives anyone: asked anonymously (from.Lookup.Public, never Docker’s store), pinned to that digest, which the build pulls by. A registry named localhost or by an address that isn’t the internet’s is refused by name, and the lookup’s client (from.NewPublicRegistry) connects only to the internet’s addresses, whatever a name resolves to, its token service’s included; offline, only a registry digest recorded for that reference stands in. The docker layer: the backend’s own rules for it, as when it’s named; the file never changes the VM’s tier. The environment: each variable’s value is built as a shell word (single-quoted text, "${X}" for the VM’s own), stored as JSON in the VM’s state, and written as export NAME=word into the VM’s environment file before devvm’s own (which win); a name is checked again when it’s written. Commands: stored as argv in the VM’s state; run by the backend’s Exec (on Lima, one sh -c string, each word in single quotes), as the VM’s user, in the folder, after the self-check, .git’s locks and a --clone VM’s clone: confined like anything in the VM. Their output goes to the run log, shown only through printable. Ports: only numbers and localhost:N/127.0.0.1:N, added to the user’s ports as devvm ports add adds them (filePorts, through AddPorts and RemovePorts; --ports wins when the VM is made): with every port forwarded, the default, they’re among them already. The ones the file added are recorded (devcontainer.ports_gave), so devvm update takes out only those the file no longer lists and never brings back one devvm ports rm took out. Forwarded on this machine’s loopback alone, as any listed port, by the one forwarder, never a host port of another program’s (ports_taken). A repo’s file can so widen a list the user narrowed, to more of this machine’s loopback, which is the user’s decision to accept by opening the folder; --no-devcontainer skips it. What it relies on: os.Root and O_NONBLOCK; encoding/json; Lima’s Exec passing arguments unchanged; the registry’s digest naming what’s pulled (a pull checks it); the backend’s own confinement of the VM and its builds.
What could break it: a backend whose Exec runs its arguments through a host shell; a new property mapped without the same review; a host proxy that reaches this machine or its network for a public-looking name (Not covered).
Not covered:
The project’s own VM and the lookup through a host proxy (HTTPS_PROXY), where only names are checked, not what the proxy resolves them to: Attack vectors lists both, under its devcontainer.json entries. Its image is any public image, whose code runs as root in the build VM, as with --from. A name that resolves to the internet for devvm and to this machine’s network for the backend’s pull (DNS rebinding) gets only content with the digest the public registry gave, which only someone who has that content can give. Threat check (the security-audit skill; its local IPC, data isolation and supply chain companions). Leads, each confirmed and fixed, or ruled out:
An image only this machine or its network has (localhost:5000/…, a private address, a name that resolves to one, its token service on one): confirmed: a backend that pulls it from this machine reaches this machine’s loopback, and the lookup was made on this machine; fixed: refused by name and by address (publicHost, NewPublicRegistry), a recorded digest included; unit-, CLI- and end-to-end-tested. forwardPorts over a user’s port list (added to devvm ports -g’s list, or to none, a limit the user set): accepted: the file’s ports are added to the user’s list, on this machine’s loopback alone, as the Ports entry above says, so opening the folder accepts them, and --no-devcontainer skips them; CLI- and end-to-end-tested. The JSONC stripper and parser (comments in strings, an unterminated comment or string, a BOM, trailing commas): ruled out: blanking keeps offsets and leaves strings alone; anything else is invalid JSON; fuzzed (FuzzParse): no panic, every variable a shell word, nothing of this machine’s environment kept. Reading (a link out, .., a FIFO, a device, a huge file, a swap between the check and the read): ruled out: os.Root, a non-blocking open, the descriptor’s own Stat, 1 MiB; one read per new VM; unit-tested (links, a FIFO). Variables (${localEnv:…}, ${env:…}, nested or unterminated): ruled out: refused, or left as text for the VM’s shell; nothing is read from this machine. The environment file and state (newlines, quotes, $(), a name like A;rm): ruled out: values are shell words, JSON-escaped in state (one line), names checked twice; the file is the VM’s own. Command quoting (', newlines, an argument starting with -): ruled out: devvm runs bash -lc 'exec "$@"' with the argv after it, and Lima quotes each word. Messages (the file’s values in this machine’s terminal): ruled out: every message value goes through msg.OneLine as it renders, the image through from.Valid, errors’ causes aren’t printed, the log tail goes through msg.Printable. Commands before confinement: ruled out: they run after the self-check (which stops a VM whose policy fails), .git’s locks, and a clone’s seeding. A digest the registry made up (Docker-Content-Digest): ruled out: sha256: and 64 hex digits, and every pull checks content against it. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, project): a VM made from a file: its variables in the shell, postCreateCommand once and postStartCommand at each start, in the VM and folder, its port forwarded and no other, nothing written to the folder, a changed file only warned about; a file whose image is on this machine’s registry refused, nothing made.
data.devvms-own-lima-home#devvm’s own Lima ho: Lima merges _config/default.yaml and override.yaml of its home into every VM. In ~/.lima, a networks: [{vzNAT: true}] there gave a confined VM a second network card with a default route around its proxy (the self-check caught it), and an extra mount went unnoticed. Hence a Lima home of devvm’s own, which refuses those files and any network devvm didn’t give a VM (details). The costs: plain limactl list doesn’t show devvm’s VMs, and VM names are shorter, as the path of Lima’s ssh socket has fewer than 104 characters.
data.emulated-features#Emulated features: When devvm builds a backend feature from other parts of the backend, the feature is emulated, and it gets a note here before its review. The note says what the feature is built from, the guarantee it keeps, what could break it, and which end-to-end checks prove it. The threat check comes next, and only then is the feature marked reviewed. Every feature Lima has is native except its ports, which devvm’s forwarder emulates (below).
data.failed-attempts#Failed attempts: Claude’s host login in VMs: on macOS it’s in the Keychain, which can’t be shared. VMs get a login made in a VM instead, which the VM’s proxy captures. The first token saved by hand was the code the browser shows, so devvm secret set claude refuses one without the sk-ant-oat01- prefix. krunkit (Lima on libkrun) to return freed memory: it didn’t visibly return any. Debian’s cloud kernel for --from: on arm64 it has no gpio_keys, so it ignored Lima’s stop request; Lima hard-killed the VM after 30 s, and node, bun and dockerd in the image came out corrupted. On x86_64 it has no 9p, so on a Linux host every mount of the VM’s was an empty folder: Lima mounts them with nofail, and the shared tools’ build failed at its first cd. --from uses the generic kernel on both. With it, a Debian VM on QEMU first booted with its network card named enp0s4, which cloud-init couldn’t rename to Lima’s eth0 once the card was up, so the VM got no ssh host keys. Debian’s kernel command line has net.ifnames=0, which keeps the name eth0 from the start. Every layer as a Docker build stage, flattened: it worked, but each image became its own full disk (3.7 GB for node). Shared read-only layers: each Docker layer as an EROFS file, stacked as / with overlayfs over each VM’s own disk by an initramfs of devvm’s own. It worked (node took 1.0 GB of layers instead of a 1.8 GB disk), but devvm owned the boot path (the initramfs, an exit initramfs for clean shutdowns, kernel extraction), and cold program starts were 10–50 ms slower. Shared tools, and overlays on Linux, give the same savings without it. A read-only mount for .git/hooks in the VM: root in the VM can unmount it and write hooks through the project mount underneath. Locking .git itself (uappnd) breaks git, and a locked placeholder .git/commondir makes git fail. Hence chflags uchg on hooks and config on macOS, plus detection, and on Linux read-only binds in QEMU’s own namespace, which the VM can’t reach (details, read-only paths on Linux). Keeping git on this machine out of submodules the VM adds (strict): diff.ignoreSubmodules = all in the locked .git/config, which devvm git-protect strict sets in devvm 0.1.0 and 0.1.1-rc.1, can’t hold. The VM writes .gitmodules, whose ignore line beats it, and git reads the index’s or HEAD’s copy when the working tree has none. git add -A, -u and . enter a submodule whatever the settings say, git diff-index, git diff-files and git describe --dirty enter one that .gitmodules doesn’t name, git fetch and git pull recurse into one that fetched commits move, and --ignore-submodules on the command line beats config. A per-name submodule..ignore holds only for the name the VM picks, and locking .gitmodules would put a file in the working tree and leave checkouts across it stale on macOS. The submodule’s own config runs either way, because the git that the host’s git starts in it reads that config, and no setting refuses it. Only --clone keeps the VM’s code away from git on this machine, so devvm git-protect strict is a usage error that names devvm clone on, and a VM left strict is on from its next check that finds it stopped (VMs that were strict). A root helper for Linux’s immutable attribute: a helper with CAP_LINUX_IMMUTABLE, installed with sudo, could lock .git as macOS’s flag does, but it would put a privileged program on every host that the VM’s repo could aim at. QEMU’s own namespace needs no privilege. Kernel extraction trying gzip first: Ubuntu’s arm64 kernel is an EFI executable with a zstd payload. mke2fs -d from a tarball: it needed libarchive and a UTF-8 locale. A directory works.
data.groups#Groups:
A group is a named set of VMs that reach each other’s published ports by name: you run devvm group join web in each VM’s folder, and every member gets a link to each port that every other member publishes. Groups are built on links alone. A group adds nothing below the link session, so every connection of a group’s link goes through the same session, sockets, proxy entrance and checks as a link made with devvm link add, and everything above holds for it.
The rules:
A VM is in one group at a time. devvm group join refuses a VM that’s in another group (group_other), naming devvm group leave, and devvm group leave takes no name. One tier. Every member of a group is on the same tier. devvm group join refuses a VM whose tier differs from the members’ (group_tier_mismatch), and a group with a member whose network section can’t be read, and devvm network is refused for a member (group_tier_fixed), naming the group and devvm group leave. So every link a group makes keeps the links’ tier rule, and each of its connections is still checked against the states, with the target’s tier enforced as it runs, and warned of with link_target_unenforced when the group makes the link. Membership is recorded on the host, in each member’s own state under ~/.local/share/devvm, as group and group_as in its links section, never in a project folder or a VM. A VM made again after devvm rm gets new state with a new ID, so it’s in no group, and the links to the old VM, which record its ID, don’t apply to it. devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update keep the VM’s state, so the VM stays in its group (a VM made again). A group’s links are links, recorded in each member’s links state with a mark of their own, so devvm group leave removes only those, and devvm link rm refuses them (link_from_group) while they still apply. Every connection of one is also checked against membership: a group’s link applies only while its client and its target are in the same group (ungrouped otherwise), so a link that a leave cut short, or a race between two devvm commands, left behind carries nothing, and devvm link rm removes it. devvm group leave removes the leaver’s own group links before it takes it out of the group, and running devvm group join again works out every member’s links again. Each takes the client’s address for that member and the member’s name in the group: its folder part, or the name it joined with (--as NAME). devvm works out a member’s group links again whenever a member joins or leaves, publishes or unpublishes a port, or adds or removes a link of its own, and it records and applies only the members whose links changed, naming the links each gains or loses (group_links_added, group_links_removed). A running member gets them at once, as devvm link add gives them, and a stopped one at its next start. The user’s links take precedence. A link made with devvm link add stays as it is: a port it links gets no group link, its name names that member’s group links too, and when its name is another member’s name in the group, that member’s group links aren’t made in that client, which is warned of (group_link_name_clash). Names are unique in a group. devvm group join refuses a name another member has, as its name or its folder part (group_name_taken), and localhost (group_name_host). It also refuses a VM whose own hostname, its folder part, is another member’s name, whether that’s the member’s folder part or the name it joined with (group_name_hostname), because the name would resolve to the joining VM itself, whatever name it joins as. The refusal names the fix: the other member leaves and joins again with another name, or the project goes in a folder with another name. So no member’s name is another member’s hostname, and groupLinks makes no link by such a name, or by localhost, all the same. Joins take turns. Each devvm group join and devvm group leave, each publish and unpublish that works the members’ links out again, and devvm rm of a VM hold a lock on the host, ~/.local/share/devvm/groups.lock (lockGroups), from reading the members’ states to writing them. A join checks the group once before it asks to widen a parent folder’s VM, and again once it holds the lock, with the VM’s state read again, so two VMs joining at once are checked one after the other, and the second sees the first as a member. So the one tier and the names hold however the joins overlap. A devvm that waits for the lock does so under a status line (group_waiting). The lock is an OS lock (flock) on an open file, which the system lets go of when the process holding it ends, however it ends. devvm rm of a member takes it out of its group, after devvm rm’s removal of every link to it, and the group goes with its last member. What a group adds to the link threat check. A group joins the trust of every member: code in any member can often run code in the others through the ports they publish, and then has their network, secrets and project folder. A member joining later gets that reach into every member, and they into it, without a command in their folders, so devvm group join says so on every join (group_trust). Nothing reaches more than the published ports on each member’s own loopback, and the one tier keeps every member’s tier whole.
Not covered:
Every member trusts every other, which what a VM does through a link lists. A published range gives a link for each port in it, in every other member. A wide range means as many forwards in each member and as many sockets on the host, so publish only the ports you mean the group to reach. devvm link add or devvm link rm at the same moment as a group’s change can each write the same member’s links whole, because those two don’t take the groups lock, so the later write wins. A group link left that way is refused as ungrouped, and the next change works the links out again from the states. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC, data isolation and resource exhaustion companions), what a group adds to the links’ rows above:
Lead What holds it End-to-end check A member reaching every other member’s published ports Accepted, bounded by the links’ rules: only published ports, only on each member’s loopback, and said on every join (group_trust) Three members reach each other’s published ports by name within seconds of the last join, and a port published by a member reaches the others at once A member joining later It needs devvm group join in its own folder, on the host; membership is in each member’s state on the host, which no VM writes. Every join says the group joins every member’s trust The third VM’s join gives the other two links to its published port and it links to theirs, and group_trust is said A member reaching one on a lower tier One tier at devvm group join, checked again under the groups lock, devvm network refused for a member, and every connection checked as for any link An allowlist VM is refused by an open group, and an open one by an allowlist group; devvm network allowlist for a member is refused. Unit tests (TestGroupJoinsAtOnce) and the CLI tests join an allowlist VM and an open one at once, and only one gets in, every time A member’s name taking over a name the user chose The user’s links take precedence, a name is unique in the group, localhost is refused, and so is a VM whose own hostname is a member’s name The CLI tests refuse a taken name, another member’s folder part, localhost, and a VM whose folder part is a member’s folder part or the name it joined with, and drop a member’s group links whose name one of the user’s links has Leaving or removing a member leaving links behind devvm group leave and devvm rm remove the group’s links in every member, and the user’s stay After devvm group leave, the leaver’s and the others’ group links are gone and their names don’t resolve, while a link made with devvm link add still answers A group’s link outliving its group, from a leave cut short or a race Each connection checks that the client and the target are in the same group (ungrouped), and a leave removes the leaver’s group links first Unit tests (TestCheckGroupLink) refuse a group’s link once either VM is in another group or none, and keep the user’s own A VM made again inheriting membership Membership is in the VM’s own state, which devvm rm deletes, so a VM made after it starts in no group. devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update keep the state, because they make the same VM again (below) The CLI tests: devvm rm of a member takes it out, and the last one’s leaving removes the group
data.links-between-vms#Links between VMs:
A link lets a program in one VM, the client, reach a TCP service in another VM, the target, by name, as in postgres://db:5432/app. Links work on every tier, within the tier rule below. You run devvm link publish 5432 in the target’s folder to offer the port to any of your VMs, and devvm link add db 5432 in the client’s folder to reach it as db:5432 and db.devvm.internal:5432. A link carries its connections over ssh through the host, so it uses neither VM’s network, and the design keeps every guarantee that the tiers’ confinement and port forwarding give. The review of the code checks it against the threat check below.
The rules:
A link is reached only by its name. The client reaches the target’s port at the link’s short name and at NAME.devvm.internal, and never at its own 127.0.0.1 or ::1, so localhost:PORT in the client stays the client’s own. The short name is the target’s folder part, or the name given with --as NAME, and the target’s full VM name is never a hostname. .internal is reserved for private use, so NAME.devvm.internal names no host on the internet. The target publishes. A port is reached only once the target’s folder has published it with devvm link publish, which offers it to any of your VMs. Each link is still made from the client’s folder, with devvm link add. A client links only to a target on its own tier or a stricter one. A link joins the two VMs’ trust (below), so a client linked to a target on a lower tier would reach more through the target than its own tier allows: an allowlist client linked to an internet or open target would reach the internet through it. devvm checks the rule when the link is made, at each launch of the client, on every connection, and when devvm network gives the target a tier lower than the client’s or the client one higher than a target’s, both of which it refuses while such a link exists (link_tier_mismatch). For a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must also be enforced as the target runs (netpolicy.Listed), not only recorded in its state: devvm network allowlist on a running open target takes effect at its next start, and a target whose self-check failed may reach the internet directly, so until then the connection is refused as unenforced. devvm link add, devvm link publish of a port such a client links to, and the client’s launch warn of a running target in this state with the same check (link_target_unenforced), refusing nothing, and a stopped target isn’t warned of, because its tier applies when it next starts. An open client may link to a target on any tier. A connection never starts a VM. A connection to a stopped target fails, and devvm logs why in the client’s event log, but the target stays stopped. devvm records links on the host, in each VM’s state under ~/.local/share/devvm, never in a project folder or a VM. The client’s VM gets only the names and addresses it needs, which devvm checks before it sends them. A link joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s own service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets its proxy puts into requests, and its project folder. devvm doesn’t try to stop that, because it’s the service’s own behavior. So a link is safe only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach, and devvm link add says so when it makes one. The tier rule above keeps a link from widening the client’s tier.
What it’s built from:
A VM’s identity. Every VM gets a random ID when devvm makes it, recorded in its state. A link records the target’s VM name and its ID when it’s made, so a VM made again in the target’s folder, which has the same name and a new ID, isn’t the linked target, and a second VM with the same folder name that appears later changes nothing. Which VM a link names. devvm link add TARGET PORT takes a VM’s full name, its ssh alias (devvm-, as its state records it), a folder’s path, or a folder’s name, which is matched against the folder that each VM’s state records, so a VM whose backend cut its name still matches its whole folder name. A folder name that matches several VMs is refused, with each VM and its folder listed. The published ports are in the target’s state, a list of ports and ranges as devvm ports takes them, without all. devvm link unpublish takes ports out of the list, and a link to a port that isn’t published is refused on its next connection. An address per target. Each target a client links to gets an address of its own in 127.77.0.0/16, chosen when the first link to it is made and kept for every port of that target in that client, so two targets can share a port. The client listens on the target’s own port, so devvm link add db 80 listens on port 80. The addresses are internal and appear only on these pages. Names in the client. The setup that devvm sends at each launch writes a block marked # devvm links begin and # devvm links end into the client’s /etc/hosts, with a line 127.77.x.y NAME NAME.devvm.internal for each target, and replaces the block whole, writing the file in place rather than renaming over it. devvm sends the same block over ssh as root when links change on a running client, and it applies at once. No link name goes into NO_PROXY or no_proxy, which name the VM alone, because a running VM can’t take a new environment: HTTP clients with the VM’s proxy settings reach a link through the proxy (below). So a change of links changes no VM’s environment, restarts no daemon, and on Lima runs no limactl edit, which would give the VM new ssh host keys. The client’s sshd. Every VM’s sshd allows remote forwards to 127.77.0.0/16 alone, with one rule written when the image is built, so no link rewrites or reloads it. That’s 00-devvm.conf from assets/layers/base.sh, which sets AllowTcpForwarding all, GatewayPorts clientspecified and PermitListen 127.77.*:*, and keep AllowStreamLocalForwarding local, PermitTunnel no and X11Forwarding no. Without clientspecified, sshd would bind every remote forward on the VM’s loopback, 127.0.0.1. sshd matches the address a request names against the rule as text, so 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost and * are refused, and only devvm on the host asks for these forwards, always with a numeric address. The rule is a safeguard for an honest VM, because root in the VM can change sshd, and the boundary is the host’s ssh client (below). Low ports. At each start, the setup sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start to 0 where it’s 1024, which is on Lima’s Alpine VMs, so sshd can listen on a link’s port below 1024 for the VM’s user. Lima’s Ubuntu and Debian VMs already have 0, so devvm leaves it there. The link session. For each running client with links, a hidden command, devvm _links, runs on the host as one detached process. It keeps an ssh connection of its own to the client, never the forwarder’s master, with the options of internal/vmssh: -F none, BatchMode, the VM’s key alone (IdentitiesOnly, IdentityAgent=none), its pinned host key, ForwardAgent=no, ForwardX11=no, Tunnel=no, PermitRemoteOpen=none, PermitLocalCommand=no and ProxyJump=none. It starts that connection as a master with ClearAllForwardings=yes, so the master asks for nothing at first, and adds each link with ssh -O forward -R 127.77.x.y:PORT: and removes it with ssh -O cancel, at its start and while the client runs. A cancel keeps the connections that are open, and the master ending drops them. Each link is its own -O forward, never ExitOnForwardFailure for all of them, so a link whose address a program in the client already holds fails alone, with an error naming the link (link_port_taken). The sockets. Each link’s forward ends at a unix socket on the host, mode 600 in devvm’s run folder ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700), named by a hash of the client, the address and the port, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. The masters’ control sockets are in the same folder, named by a hash of the client, and for a master to a target, of the target and its start too. A stale socket at the path is replaced, anything else there is refused, and the socket goes when its link or the process ends. Each connection. When a program in the client connects to a link’s address, the client’s sshd opens a channel to the host for the forward, and the host’s ssh connects it to that link’s socket. devvm _links then reads the links state again and checks that the link still exists, that the target’s ID matches, that the port is published, that the tier rule holds, that the target runs as its backend says, and, for a client on a confined tier, that the target’s tier is enforced as it runs. The connections to one target share what its backend says of its run, which is whether it runs, its start and its ssh. One lookup is in flight for each target, and its answer is reused for one second (linkRunFor), so a burst of 256 connections asks the backend once rather than once for each. A connection that closes while its lookup runs finds the target stopped, but that lookup isn’t kept, and the connections waiting on it look again, so they get the target’s real answer. A target that stops is noticed within that second, and the connection’s other checks, the tier’s as the target runs included, are made for each connection. That tier check asks the backend again, and a stopped VM never runs confined, so for a client on a confined tier it notices at once that the target stopped. When the backend then says the target no longer runs on the start that was looked up, the connection is refused as link_target_stopped, not as unenforced. It then carries the connection with ssh -S -o ProxyCommand=/usr/bin/false -W 127.0.0.1:PORT through a master to the target that it keeps, one per target, with the target’s key and pinned host key. The target’s sshd connects to the target’s own loopback. When the master is gone, -S alone would make a connection of its own, and ProxyCommand=/usr/bin/false makes that connection fail, so a channel goes through the master or nowhere. A target’s master ends when the target stops, and the next one reads the target’s known hosts again, because a VM whose Lima config changed gets new host keys when it boots. Each relay’s ssh (-W) waits for the target’s sshd to end its channel, so each runs with a context of its own (vmssh.relayConns, which the port forwarder’s forwards also use). The link’s removal and its master’s replacement close its connection and cancel that context under the session’s lock, which kills the ssh (exec.CommandContext), and a relay that ends by itself releases its context. So a removed link’s open connections end with it, and a target that never ends a channel can’t keep the relay’s ssh process, or one of the 256, past either. A link whose address and port lead to another target at the next sync, as a link removed and another added within one second would, cuts the old target’s connections and starts a new set for the new one, and a connection accepted before that change is cut with the old set. While a link lasts, the relay’s grace (pipeSSH, as for the forwarder) kills an ssh whose client in the client VM has closed and whose target has sent nothing for 30 seconds. devvm never starts the target. At most 256 connections are carried at once, and the next one is refused and logged. A link’s socket holds 128 connections waiting to be accepted on macOS, and the process accepts nothing while it starts an ssh, so its accept loop only accepts, and hands a burst on whole once 5 ms pass with nothing more waiting, the first has waited 50 ms, or 257 wait. Another goroutine then carries or refuses each connection in it, logging each refusal before it closes the connection, while the loop goes on accepting the next burst, and the loop waits for that goroutine only once 257 of the next burst wait. So every connection in a burst is carried or refused with link_limit, and none is refused by the socket unlogged. The proxy’s entrance. In a client on any tier, an HTTP client that honors HTTP_PROXY sends db:5432 to the VM’s proxy, and the proxy is a second entrance to the same socket, so a link added while the client runs works at once without a restart. devvm _links writes every link the client has, carried or not, to links.json in the client’s run folder, vms//run/ (mode 600, written whole) whenever they change or the file is gone, with each link’s names, address, port, target and socket. A link it doesn’t carry has no socket, and a session that ended leaves its list, so the proxy refuses those links (502, link_refused) instead of asking its rules, which could send db to a host the host’s resolver or a company proxy finds by that name. devvm removes the list with the VM. devvm puts the path in the proxy’s config as links, and its run folder, where the sockets are, as link_sockets, so internal/proxy stays standard library only, and the proxy reads the list for every request, after the VM’s password and before any rule, as it does for devvm.proxy. It matches CONNECT NAME:PORT and absolute-form GET http://NAME:PORT/ exactly, after one normalization: lower case, one trailing dot dropped, and NAME.devvm.internal as the list names it. It takes an entry only when the entry’s socket is the one that proxy.LinkSocket names from devvm’s run folder, this VM, the entry’s address and its port, which is also the name vmssh.Links.Socket gives the socket. It then connects to the socket and passes the bytes as they are: no SNI check, no interception, no secret put in, even when a secret’s hosts would match, and no rule asked. An absolute-form request goes over a new connection to the socket for each request, without the proxy’s headers, and HTTPS in absolute form gets 400. devvm _links’s checks of each connection apply to both entrances unchanged, and it logs the connection once, as link. A stale entry fails there, or finds no socket, which the proxy answers with 502 and logs as link_refused (not carried). The proxy also refuses any other name under devvm.internal, logged as a refused block, so a long name never reaches the rules. An absolute-form request to a link ends when the client gives it up, so a target that never answers can’t hold the client’s 256 connections. Anything else not on the list meets the floor and the rules as before, so a short name the client has no link for, before its first session lists it, is the rules’ to decide. Events. devvm _links writes link, link_refused (with why), link_target_stopped and link_limit events to the client’s event log, in the proxy’s JSON-lines format, with the link’s name as the host and the target VM as target, so devvm network log shows them. Every client gets an event log for them, whatever its tier. devvm _links writes it with the proxy’s own writer, which rotates it past 10 MiB by the proxy’s rule and follows the file to its new name when the other writer rotated it, so the two writers never lose each other’s lines. The forwarder skips links. The port forwarder (vmssh.Forwarder) forwards a server on any loopback address of the VM’s, so it would put a link’s listener on the host’s 127.0.0.1 and ::1. It never forwards a listener whose address is in 127.77.0.0/16, on any VM, so a server of the client’s own on 127.0.0.1 with the same port is forwarded as usual. Lima’s own forwards don’t take it either, because devvm’s rules ignore every port first, and Lima’s fallback rule matches 127.0.0.1 and the bind addresses 0.0.0.0, :: and ::1 alone. In VMs’ lives. A launch starts devvm _links once the client runs and its setup is done, warns once for each stopped target (link_target_stopped) without starting it, and skips a link whose tier rule no longer holds, with link_tier_mismatch. For a client on a confined tier, it also warns once for each running target whose tier isn’t enforced (link_target_unenforced). devvm link add and devvm link rm on a running client change its setup and its running devvm _links at once, and on a stopped client they apply at its next start. devvm stop stops devvm _links with the client, which ends its connections and removes its sockets, and the process also ends once the client no longer runs the start it was made for, as the forwarder does, or has no links left. devvm rm of a client removes its links with its state, and devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from every client’s state and names the clients that lost one, deleting nothing else of theirs. devvm link unpublish of a port with links names the clients that link to it. Both backends must have the link feature, which needs ssh on both VMs, and devvm checks it with Review.Require when a link is made and at each launch. What keeps a link from carrying a VM out. Every connection starts on the host, and neither VM’s network carries it:
A confined VM reaches only its proxy and the links you made. The link’s bytes travel inside ssh connections that the host opens, so no backend’s confinement changes, and the client’s own connections, including sshd’s, stay confined as before. Through its proxy, a VM reaches only the sockets of its own links: a request names a host and a port, never a socket, the proxy’s list is in the VM’s run folder, which no VM can write, and the proxy takes an entry only when its socket is the one devvm names for that VM’s link at that address and port. The VM can’t choose where its connections go on the host. OpenSSH’s client accepts a forwarded channel only for a listener it asked for, and connects it only where it chose, which is the link’s socket. A channel the client’s sshd opens for any other address or port, or of any other kind, is refused, whatever sshd root in the client runs. The forwarder’s master asks for no remote forward, and the link session is a connection of its own, so links don’t change what the ports note says. Other users and VMs can’t use a link. Its end on the host is a unix socket of yours, mode 600 in a folder of mode 700, so no other user on the host reaches it, and neither does a VM that reaches the host’s loopback. Programs of yours on the host can connect to it, as they can already ssh into the target by the name devvm host shows. A target’s service isn’t put on the host’s localhost. -W reaches the target’s loopback through its sshd, and the forwarder never forwards 127.77.0.0/16, so a link listens nowhere on the host. Each VM’s own ssh rules hold. Host keys are pinned, each VM has its own key, and no agent is forwarded (ForwardAgent=no, IdentityAgent=none), as for the forwarder. devvm takes a client’s or a target’s ssh only as its backend gives it on the host’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with a user and a key, and it refuses any other address, as the ssh config’s entries do. Why not a shared network, the proxy, or a host port:
A network shared between VMs would bypass the proxy and the VMs’ confinement. On Lima it needs a root helper, and QEMU can’t make one. CONNECT through the proxy as the only way in would work only for programs that use the VM’s proxy settings, and a raw TCP client in every VM would need a tool of devvm’s to make the connection. The proxy is a second entrance instead, for HTTP clients, beside the ssh forward that carries every link on every VM. The target’s port forwarded to the host’s localhost is refused by the proxy’s floor, is reached by any open VM and any program on the host, and is a port that a host program can take first. What the prototype showed. devvm’s prototype ran in the e2e sandbox, and nothing needed the link feature off:
macOS’s ssh 10.3p1 and Linux hosts’ ssh 9.6p1 and 10.2p1 accept -R 127.77.x.y:PORT:, and -O forward and -O cancel work on a master started with ClearAllForwardings=yes. A cancel keeps open connections, ending the master drops them, and a session keeps the PermitListen it connected with. sshd 9.2p1 (Debian 12, --from), 10.2p1 (Ubuntu 26.04) and 10.3p1 (Alpine), with GatewayPorts clientspecified and PermitListen naming one address, bind that address alone and refuse 0.0.0.0, 127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost, *, other ports and port 0. The glob 127.77.*:* works the same way and matches the requested address as text. All of them honor ip_unprivileged_port_start, which is 0 by default on Lima’s Ubuntu and Debian VMs, and 1024 on Lima’s Alpine VMs. SIGHUP keeps sessions and open connections under systemd and OpenRC. Lima’s Ubuntu VMs (an sshd per connection over vsock) read the config at every connection. sshd’s rule is written once, so links don’t depend on either. ssh -W through a kept master works over Lima’s ssh, and a new master after the target restarts reads its rewritten known hosts, while Lima keeps its key. Without a master, -S connects on its own unless ProxyCommand=/usr/bin/false. glibc 2.36 and 2.43 and musl 1.2.6 resolve /etc/hosts names in 127.77.0.0/16, and Go, Node 18, 22 and 24, curl, Python and libpq 15 and 18 reach db and db.devvm.internal. HTTP clients honor NO_PROXY with db,.devvm.internal, Node 22 needs the leading dot, and Node 18’s fetch ignores proxies. devvm’s port forwarder put a link’s listener on the host’s 127.0.0.1 and ::1, which is why it skips 127.77.0.0/16. The prototype didn’t run confined VMs, so the end-to-end checks do. What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client accepting forwarded channels only for listeners it asked for, and connecting each one only where it chose. It also relies on -O forward and -O cancel changing one master’s forwards, on ProxyCommand=/usr/bin/false keeping -S from connecting without its master, and on the host’s unix socket permissions. The pinned host keys are the ones the forwarder and ssh rely on. Lima’s rules must ignore every port ahead of its fallback rule, and devvm’s state on the host must hold each link’s target, ID and port. The proxy’s entrance relies on devvm’s run folder and the VM’s being yours alone, and on the proxy checking each entry’s socket against the one it names itself from the VM, the address and the port.
What could break it: an OpenSSH release whose client accepts a channel for a listener it didn’t ask for, which the end-to-end checks would see as a host connection devvm didn’t make. A Lima release that forwards a listener on a 127.77 address despite the rules would put a link on the host’s loopback, which the forwarder’s own skip doesn’t cover, and the end-to-end checks look for it on the host. A backend that started a target for a connection would break the rule that a connection never starts a VM, but devvm never asks a backend to start one then.

A link that goes, by devvm link rm, devvm rm of its target or a group’s change, ends its open connections (above). A target can’t get a tier lower than a client’s that links to it, because devvm network refuses it then, so no open connection breaks the tier rule. A program in the client can take a link’s address and port first, and that link then fails with link_port_taken until the program lets it go. Root in the client can also edit its own /etc/hosts, which changes only what the client reaches. A link name hides a name the client would otherwise resolve, such as db under its search domain. devvm refuses localhost, the client’s own hostname, another link’s name and anything that isn’t one DNS label. A remote forward you ask for into a VM, with ssh -R through devvm’s ssh config, may bind an address in 127.77.0.0/16 in that VM, as remote forwards you add says. sshd matches the rule as text and then resolves what it matched, which is why a host name that begins with 127.77. binds whatever address it resolves to in the VM. devvm’s own forwards name addresses only. data.links-out-of-an-agents-folder#Links out:
devvm’s agent store reaches every VM with the agent: its folders are mounted read-only, its files are copied in at every launch, and the hooks, MCP servers’ commands and plugins in it run in each of those VMs. So whatever devvm agent import copies is something every such VM reads and runs. A link in an agent’s folder that leads out of it can lead anywhere on this machine, such as to ~/.ssh, to another agent’s login, or into a folder that a VM can write, such as a dotfiles repo that is also a devvm project. Following such links unasked would let a mistaken link put a secret into every VM, and let a VM that writes the folder a link leads into change what every other VM’s agent runs. That’s why the import follows no link out of an agent’s folder by default, and reads each folder through itself as an os.Root (how).
Dotfiles repos keep settings as links all the same, and copying them into the store by hand is lost at the next import, so devvm follows them when you allow it, in two ways:
config.toml’s follow-links names folders, such as ~/dotfiles, whose links devvm follows without asking. You choose a folder once, for every import, so devvm checks the folder as a whole: one that is, holds or is inside a refused place fails the import, because a link inside it can lead anywhere in it. --follow-links, or a yes to the question, follows one run’s links after naming each and where it leads, so you see every target before anything is copied. Without a terminal, no link out is followed unless the flag is given, and each is named in a warning, so a script never follows a link it didn’t ask for. The folder each is read through is the link’s own target, or a linked file’s own folder. Whichever allows it, the same rules hold:
Resolved first, read inside. devvm resolves every link on the way to the target, checks that target, then reads it through the allowed folder as a root, which it opens one folder at a time from /, never through a link. A link inside what it copies is read only when it leads to a file inside the same root. Always refused. devvm never follows a link to the home folder or a folder holding it, to devvm’s config, data or Lima folders, to ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/Library/Keychains, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.netrc, ~/.config/gh, ~/.docker or ~/.kube, or to any agent’s logins or history, nor into one of them or to a folder holding one. The home folder holds all of them, devvm’s folders hold its CA keys, binaries and every VM’s disk, and the agents’ logins and history are what the store exists to keep apart from VMs. The named folders are the places that commonly hold credentials, and the list can’t name every one, which is why the question names each target and the setting takes folders you choose. A VM’s folder warns. A target in a VM’s project folder, or a --clone VM’s source folder, is followed with a warning naming the VM, because that VM can change what every VM’s agent reads from the next import on. Refusing it would refuse the common case of a dotfiles repo that you also work on in a VM, and the warning leaves the choice with you. A chain that passes through a link in a VM’s folder to a place outside it is refused, though, because the VM chose that place, and it could name any file the refused list doesn’t. Compared by identity. devvm compares a target with the refused places and the VMs’ folders by name and by file identity, because a Mac’s file system ignores case, so ~/.SSH names ~/.ssh. Copies only. The store gets a copy of each file and folder, never a link, and the next import replaces or takes out each copy as it does the agent’s own files. devvm agent save still refuses a link the VM sends. Bounded. One import copies at most 20,000 files and folders, 128 MiB and a file of 16 MiB through links, the bounds of devvm agent save, so a link to a large tree can’t fill the store. Not covered:
The copy is as the target was at the import. A VM that writes a followed folder later changes nothing in the store until the next import, which then copies what it wrote. The warning names that VM. A refused place under another name, such as a credential folder that the list doesn’t name, is copied when a link you allowed leads to it. A huge folder is read before the bounds stop it. devvm lists each folder whole before it counts its entries, so a folder of millions of entries costs memory on this machine before the import leaves it out. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, an independent review of the code):
Lead What holds it Check A VM swapping a link into the path of an allowed folder, or into what’s being read The root is opened one folder at a time from /, never through a link, and everything below it is read through it as a root, without blocking and without following a swapped-in link TestOpenPhysical, TestAgentImportNestedLinks A VM choosing the target through a link in its project folder Every link on the way is kept, and a chain through a VM’s folder to a place outside it is refused, whatever allows it TestAgentImportLinkThroughProject; the review found it first, and it’s fixed A refused place spelled another way, such as ~/.SSH on a Mac Targets are compared with the places by identity as well as by name TestAgentImportRefusedOtherCase; the review found it first, and it’s fixed A link to a secret, a login or devvm’s own files The refused places, checked on every target and every follow-links folder TestAgentImportRefusedPlaces, TestAgentImportRefusedRoots A write outside the store Names come from real folder entries under the link’s own path, and the store’s clean-up goes through the store as a root Reviewed A FIFO, a device, a huge or growing file, a loop Reads refuse anything but a regular file, the bounds are checked when listing and again when reading, and loops end at the bounds or the system’s TestAgentImportLinkBounds, TestLinkSourceGrown, TestLinkHops A link followed without the user seeing it Without a terminal nothing is followed unless the flag is given, and each link followed is named TestAgentImportFollowsLinks, agent_import_links What VMs get Copies only, mounted read-only like the rest of the store e2e’s project section reads the linked skill’s copy in a VM and finds root can’t write it
data.linux-hosts-overlays-instead-of-copies#L: Lima on QEMU keeps one qcow2 disk per VM, and a clone copies it (2.0 GB for base). A project VM’s disk is a qcow2 overlay of its image’s instead (details): 196 KB new, 12 MB after booting, the same speed except fsync writes (1.8–2.5 s vs 1.2–2.1 s per GiB). Flattening one (qemu-img rebase -b "") took 8 s, if it’s ever needed.
data.nested-repos#Nested repos:
A folder often holds git repos of its own besides its submodules, such as a workspace of several repos with no repo at its top. Every one of them is in the VM’s mount, so .git protection covers each as it covers the folder’s own repo (nested repos). Two other designs were weighed. Refusing such folders, or warning only, leaves the most common multi-repo layout without protection. A --clone of every repo keeps the VM out of the working trees altogether, which is what a workspace clone does for a user who doesn’t need the VM to write them, so both are built.
The guarantee: in a VM made by this devvm, or one devvm git-protect on set, nothing in the VM can change the hooks and config of a nested repo that a walk of the stopped VM’s folder found, with the same locks, pins and watch as the folder’s own repo, and with the same reports at each check. It holds from the check that found the repo: a repo the VM makes while it runs, or a folder of its own the VM puts in a protected repo’s place on Linux, is git’s to use on this machine until the next stopped check names it, and what the walk can’t find or the bound leaves out is named, or counted, not protected. A VM an earlier devvm made keeps protecting only its own repo until devvm git-protect on, because locking a repo’s config breaks git config there, which the user didn’t ask for. It’s told once.
