What could break it: the walk finding the wrong folders or too many; a lock or a read outside the mount through a nested repo’s paths, which now have two bounds, the repo’s top folder and the mount; the VM hiding a nested repo behind another one’s protection; two VMs protecting one repo, where one’s unlock would take the other’s locks off; taking a strict VM’s diff.ignoreSubmodules out, which unlocks a config to write it; and the cost of a check, which the VM can raise by making repos.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion’s local-file and race classes, with two independent reviews of the change, the second adversarial, which proved its two highs with real host git running a VM-planted core.fsmonitor). Leads, each fixed, ruled out or listed:
A nested repo hidden behind another’s protection: fixed. The first version left a nested repo to any repo whose scan locked its git folder as a submodule’s, and the VM writes the index that names submodules, so a gitlink with a .git file naming b/.git hid b’s own submodules and worktrees from every scan (TestNestedGitlinkCantHide). The second left one to any repo whose .git its git folder was below, so a src/.git file naming a .git/evil the VM made, or a .git/modules/x whose commondir leads to one, was neither locked nor named. A repo is now left to another only when its git folder is one that repo’s scan locks whole: its .git, a git folder under .git/modules that reads its own config, or a linked worktree whose commondir leads back. Anything else is scanned on its own and named (TestNestedIntoTopGit). A protected nested repo made to look gone: fixed. devvm took a folder for a repo by a narrower test than git’s, which also takes a HEAD with a commondir, and objects and refs that are files, so the VM could rename a protected repo’s objects and refs, add a commondir to a git folder of its own, or rename .git to .GIT on macOS, or make it unreadable, and devvm dropped the repo as gone while git still used it, its pins and watch with it. The walk now takes anything named .git, any case on macOS, hostsafety.IsGitDir follows git’s test, and a recorded repo stays while anything is at its .git (TestNestedNotGone, TestIsGitDir). git_nested_gone is a warning. A bare repo the VM makes: listed, named. git takes a folder shaped like a git folder for a bare repo, and its config can name a work tree, so git run below one runs its core.fsmonitor. devvm names the ones it finds, and devvm doctor gives a tip until git’s safe.bareRepository is explicit (git 2.38 and newer), which refuses them; devvm never changes your git config. A path outside the mount: ruled out. Every lock, unlock and pin goes through realInDir, which takes the mount as its bound and refuses a path with a symlink in it below the mount, so a nested repo whose folder became a symlink is reported, not locked (TestLockNeverThroughSymlinks, TestRealInDirPins). The walk follows no symlink and stays on the mount’s file system. The state records nested repos by local relative paths only. Two VMs, one repo: fixed. On macOS both VMs set the same flag, so an unlock leaves what another VM’s protection still covers, and names that VM (TestNestedUnlockKept, the git_nested script’s nested VM). Unlocking a kept config for a moment, to take a strict VM’s diff.ignoreSubmodules out, would let a running VM race it, so devvm skips a kept config there, and locks a config again when git can’t change it (TestUnstrictKept, TestUnstrictFails). The ownership check fails closed: a state that can’t be read keeps every path in the folder its state’s folder is named after, and a VMs’ folder that can’t be read keeps everything (TestGitKeeper). Locking and recording, and unlocking, take one host lock (paths.Dirs.GitLock), so two commands at once can’t unlock what the other just locked. A repo devvm stops protecting keeps its record in made.left, so its locks come off with the rest, and one that left the folder is named, as only chflags reaches it then (TestNestedLeftUnlocked). A repo whose git folder is outside the folder: named. Its .git file is locked, and the VM can’t reach where it leads, but another project’s VM may write it, as for a submodule’s (git_nested_gitdir_outside). The watch hiding a change: fixed. The watch records a new or gone nested repo’s sums without naming them, and it first skipped every path under such a repo’s folder, so a repo nested in it went unwatched for a check. It now skips only the paths whose deepest repo is that one (TestRepoOf). The bound used to hide a repo: fixed. The VM can make up to 100 repos cheaply, and the walk keeps the first 100, so the count past the bound is now named at every check, with the first ten of them, not only when it grows, as the VM could keep the count and change which repos are past it. The .git the walk sees where it doesn’t look for repos, which a set-id walk on Linux sees, and the folders on other disks it doesn’t enter, are counted and named. Cost: fixed, and listed. A scan followed gitlinks that led back to a git folder it had followed, through a symlinked folder, up to eight deep, so the VM could make it run git without end; it now follows each git folder once, and one check’s scans follow 1,000 in all, across every repo, and name a repo past that (TestEmbeddedOnce, TestScanBudget). A launch into a running VM scans no nested repo, so it costs what it did before them. A check scans eight repos at once, so 50 nested repos take under a second on an M3 Max, walk and locks included (BenchmarkNestedCheck). Listed: the watch’s bounds grow with the repos, at most 2,000 sums for the folder’s own repo and 200 for each nested one, each file read up to 16 MiB, so a VM that fills them makes a stopped check slow; a hooks folder filled to blind the watch is named at every check (git_watch_blind). A nested repo’s folder renamed on Linux: listed, reported. A pin makes .git a mount point, which the guest can’t rename, but a nested repo’s own folder isn’t one, so the guest can rename ws/a, .git and all, and put another repo in its place, which git on this machine then reads until the next check names it (git_replaced). Pinning every folder down to each nested repo would refuse the VM’s own moves of those folders. macOS has the same gap for every repo, the folder’s own included. A repo the VM makes while it runs: listed, reported. devvm can’t lock what it hasn’t found, so a repo the VM clones while it runs is git’s repo for its folder from then on, shell prompts and editors included, and the VM’s until the next stopped check names it, with the config keys and hooks in it that run programs (git_nested_appeared_runs), and locks it as it is. One deeper than four folders or under a skipped name is never named, only counted where a set-id walk sees it. The pins’ file: ruled out. A VM with many nested repos has more pins than one environment variable holds (MAX_ARG_STRLEN is 128 KiB), so the start writes them to run/git-pins.json in the VM’s folder, private and whole, which the VM can’t reach, and devvm _qemu reads it through no symlink, capped, and checks it again (TestPinsOrder, TestPinsRefused). The keeper’s inotify watches are a few folders for each repo, far below the kernel’s limit for 100 repos. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, the project section): a folder of two repos without one of its own gets a VM whose root can’t add a hook or change the config of either repo, on macOS and on a Linux host that pins; on a Linux host that can’t pin, devvm stop names the config the VM changed; devvm rm takes the locks off both; a repo whose .git file names a git folder the VM made under the folder’s own .git is named at devvm stop; and a protected repo whose objects and refs the VM renamed, with a commondir to a git folder of its own, or whose .git it renamed to .GIT on macOS, stays protected. Unit tests: TestWalkRepos, TestIsGitDir, TestNestedIntoTopGit, TestNestedNotGone, TestScanBudget, TestRunsProgram, TestNestedLeftUnlocked, TestGitKeeper, TestBareExplicit, TestNestedProtected, TestNestedNoTopRepo, TestNestedExistingVM, TestNestedWatch, TestNestedPins, TestNestedGitdirInside, TestKeeps, TestMadeJSON and the 0.1.0 fixture’s tests, whose state reads as a VM whose protection covers its own repo alone.
data.network-tiers#Network tiers:
A VM’s network is one of four tiers, open, internet, allowlist and none, from the lowest to the highest (what each reaches). The design keeps two things: every VM’s requests go through its own proxy, whatever its tier, and only the open tier ever runs a VM unconfined.
What it’s built from: netpolicy.Tier, in the VM’s net section as tier. An unknown tier fails to read (Tier.UnmarshalJSON), and TierOf reads a section it can’t read as none, never as open; a section without a tier reads as allowlist. Tier.Net maps the tier to the backend’s confinement: NetProxy for every tier but open, and NetDirect with the proxy’s port and password for open (Confinement.GuestProxy). netpolicy.Policies gives each tier its policies (PolicySet), and Prepare writes them into the proxy’s config: builtin_policies for the built-in policies and policies for your files on the allowlist tier, deny_policies for the user’s files on internet and none, whose allows the proxy drops as it reads them, and open for the open tier, which allows every host and address with no floor and takes no policy at all (Config.check). Every tier’s proxy has the VM’s CAs and its bindings file, an open VM’s included, and every VM’s setup sends the same placeholders and redacted copies (stageSecrets), so no VM holds a real secret and the tier decides only the confinement and the rules. A running VM keeps the confinement it started with: one made open while it runs confined stays on NetProxy until its next start, with an open proxy. Every Prepare reads the tier from the VM’s state as it is then, so a command that read the state before a tier change never starts the proxy with the tier before.
Rules: ** covers addresses as well as names, and :* any port 1 to 65535. Neither lifts the floor, because only an address rule can (policy.addrAllowed), so the internet tier’s **:* reaches every public host and address and no internal one.
Lima: an open VM runs as a VM without a proxy would, with no Seatbelt profile and no restrict=on from the QEMU wrapper, and its guest reaches its proxy at 192.168.5.2, the host’s loopback on Lima’s user-mode network, on macOS and on Linux. propagateProxyEnv is off for it, so the host’s proxy settings never reach the guest, and its NO_PROXY adds Lima’s names for the host.
Links: a client links only to a target on its tier or a stricter one (policyRule), and a group’s VMs are all on one tier. A tier change that would break either is refused (tierLinked, group_tier_fixed).
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode). Leads, each ruled out, fixed or listed:
The open flag reaching a confined VM’s proxy: ruled out. Open is set only for the open tier, a config with open and any policy is refused, and an unknown or unreadable tier reads as none. A confined VM reaching the host or the LAN: ruled out. The confinement is the tier’s (Tier.Net), the floor still judges every address the proxy dials on a confined tier, and ** and :* lift no floor (TestAnyPort, TestFloor). A tier change racing the proxy’s config: fixed. Prepare read the tier from the state its caller had read, so a command started before devvm network changed the tier could start the proxy again with the looser one; it now reads the tier from the VM’s state as it is then. Listed: two devvm commands at once can still interleave between that read and the proxy’s start, and the next launch puts the right config back. A running confined VM made open: listed, by design. Until its next start it stays confined, but its proxy is open’s, so through the proxy it reaches this machine’s loopback and the LAN, as the open tier you asked for does. devvm network open asks first in a parent folder (widen), and the VM keeps its CAs, which its open proxy goes on signing with. Other programs or VMs using an open VM’s proxy: ruled out. Every request needs the VM’s own random password, which is in no process’s arguments: the proxy’s config is mode 600, and the open self-check names $HTTPS_PROXY, not its value (TestSelfCheckOpen). The company proxy’s password: improved. An open VM no longer gets the host’s proxy settings, so neither the shell’s password nor config.toml’s reaches its guest. An open VM spending a secret past its proxy: ruled out. Its environment, its git credential helper and its agents’ copies hold only its placeholders, which end in its own salt, so a request it sends directly carries a placeholder that the secret’s host refuses, and only a request through its proxy, with its password, gets the real value. An open VM’s proxy putting secrets into another host’s requests: ruled out. The open flag lifts the rules and the floor, not the bindings: the proxy intercepts and puts a secret in only for the binding’s own hosts on :443, and a request inside the tunnel that names another host gets 421, as on every tier (TestInterceptOpen; TestPrepareOpen and sync.txtar for the VM’s CAs, salt, bindings and placeholders). An open VM’s CA: listed, as on every tier. The VM trusts its own CA, whose key stays on this machine, so its proxy can impersonate the secrets’ hosts to that VM alone. ** matching addresses on the allowlist tier: listed. A policy with ** now allows public address literals too, which it refused before. Old VMs: listed. A VM made before tiers reads as allowlist, so one that was open starts confined, and a running one shows as unenforced until devvm restarts it. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e): network: open from its next start, a direct connection works, its proxy is set, answers the self-check and carries the VM to this machine’s loopback and its LAN address, while the allowlist tier refuses this machine’s loopback; the open VM holds no real secret, its proxy puts the token in over TLS the VM verifies with its own CA, and a request around the proxy carries only the placeholder and gets a 401; open behind a company proxy, the guest gets its own proxy and never the shell’s settings, which go through the VM’s proxy alone; internet reaches a host off the allowlist and another port but not this machine’s LAN address, and a direct connection still fails; none refuses github.com, lets Claude Code’s API through, and keeps a deny. link: an allowlist client’s link to a none target goes on, and to an internet one is refused and warned of.
data.one-binary#One binary: devvm’s own files (assets/ in the repo: base.yaml, prelude.sh, layers/, features/, shared-tools/, network/, guest/, oci/) are embedded in the binary (assets.FS), so devvm installs, moves and upgrades as one file and can’t find a mismatched copy beside it. Code reads them from that file system; scripts reach VMs on their standard input, never by path or file mode. The binary is the only copy: no shared folder on disk holds devvm’s files, because a copy there could be edited and still be used. A VM’s proxy is devvm itself, so it reads its built-in policies from the binary (its config’s builtin_policies, by name), once, and its policies carry only your files. limactl create reads base.yaml on its standard input (-). Only --from’s build on Lima needs a path, because its build VM mounts the conversion’s scripts from oci/ read-only (root there reads them), and none of the folder’s other files, with guest/ca.sh beside it when you have company CAs. It writes them into its own temporary folder, devvm-oci., beside vm/ and never inside it, files 600 and folders 700, and the build’s cleanup deletes the folder however the build ends. Image keys hash the embedded files, so what goes into an image is always what its key describes.
data.one-form-of-a-host#One form of a host:
Every check that judges or compares a host reads it in one form, proxy.NormHost’s, so a deny, a binding, a risk or a warning can never hold for one spelling of a host and miss another. NormHost lowercases a host of printable ASCII, in ASCII alone, and drops its one trailing dot, unless the host is an address, whose dot can only be its IPv6 zone’s. Any other host keeps its case and its dots, and HostOK refuses it, because Unicode’s case folding turns some letters into ASCII ones, such as the Kelvin sign into k. A host with two trailing dots or more keeps them all, which HostOK refuses, so NormHost gives the same host however many times it runs, and a caller that reads a host again can’t turn evil.test.. into evil.test. A matcher takes a proxy.Host, which only NormHost makes, and the structure test refuses another copy (the checks on owners).
The shapes each reader meets. Each reader has a differential fuzz target (FuzzHostSites in internal/proxy, and one beside each reader elsewhere), which checks it against a frozen copy of the readers that each folded and trimmed a host its own way, and allows only these differences:
A rule’s host and its ! read exactly as the frozen copy reads them, so a line is the same rule or no rule, and a line that starts with ! but isn’t a rule is a broken deny, which makes the policy deny everything, never a valid deny. The frozen state’s policy files, bindings and links read the same too (TestFixtureHosts). Two trailing dots in a request’s host, an SNI or a host Allows or Denies judges stay, where the copy drops one. The proxy answers 400 to both, and no rule but ** matches either spelling, while ** matches both. The policy’s own matching (rulesFor, quiet, byName) and devvm network lock’s risks and ticks don’t fold a host that isn’t ASCII, where the copy folds it in Unicode. Neither meets such a host, because the proxy refuses it before the policy sees it, and the lock judges only hosts the proxy took. Brackets hold only an IPv6 address, one pair of them, as in a rule, so HostOK and Host.Addr take an address bare or as [::1], never with a stray bracket, and NormHost keeps a dot after a bracket ([::1].), so that’s no address either. A request for [evil.com]:443, [1.2.3.4]:443, 1.2.3.4] or [[::1]] gets 400, where net.SplitHostPort or a trim took the brackets off and the name or address in them was judged. An SNI in brackets is refused as no host name rather than as an address. An IPv6 address whose zone ends in a dot keeps it, so ::1%. is the zoned address it is, where the copy dropped the dot and left ::1%, an empty zone, which is no address. The proxy answers 400 to both, and an address with a zone is never the internet’s (proxy.Public), so a promisor remote at one counts as private and --from’s registry at one isn’t public. A host with a stray bracket around an address is an address, so an MCP server there (https://1.2.3.4]/, whose hostname Go’s URL parser gives as 1.2.3.4]) gets no binding. A line that isn’t a rule, which devvm network rm and its duplicate check compare as text, matches another line only when the two differ in nothing but the case of ASCII letters and one trailing dot, so a Kelvin sign typed for a k never names the rule with the k, such as the deny !kubernetes.io. An SNI’s trailing dot on the transparent path is dropped, as a request’s is. crypto/tls refuses such a ClientHello, so none reaches it. A NO_PROXY name that isn’t ASCII matches no host, so the Kelvin sign’s kubernetes.io doesn’t send kubernetes.io directly, and the request goes through the company proxy. A NO_PROXY entry with port 0, which no request has, sends nothing directly, as one with a port past 65535 doesn’t, where the copy read git.test:0 as git.test on every port (found by FuzzNoProxy). Neither does an entry whose port isn’t in plain decimal, such as git.test:080 or git.test:+80, which Go’s clients match against no request, where the copy read it as port 80. A secret’s --host or an MCP server’s host that isn’t ASCII is refused, as the proxy refuses it, rather than taken as the ASCII host its letters fold into. --from’s registry isn’t on the internet when its name is one the proxy doesn’t take (HostOK), such as one with anything but printable ASCII, a bracket that a trailing dot hid ([::1].) or a shorthand address (10.1), none of which a registry’s name is, so a registry is never more public than the copy finds it. A partial clone’s promisor remote loses its trailing dot, so a warning names example.com rather than example.com., and localhost. or 127.0.0.1. counts as private, as the proxy refuses it. The Kelvin sign isn’t folded. A remote’s ssh host, which finds a VM’s alias in the ssh config, keeps its own reading, lowercased with its trailing dot kept, as ssh reads it, because it’s no host a policy judges.
data.open-work-and-risks#Open work and risks:
User-facing limits are in Known limits, and what devvm leaves open is in Attack vectors.
--from: a moved tag is noticed only at the next build, not when listing images; devvm doesn’t log in to registries, so private images work only through Docker; registries over plain HTTP (localhost:5000) aren’t supported. Alpine: rc-status as a normal user shows acpid and syslog as crashed, as their pid files are root’s (sudo rc-status is clean). Free-space floors: the free space devvm wants before each build and new VM (free space) is set by Lima’s own package, and for shared tool images in internal/backend/disk.go, where the comments give what each number was measured from. The measurements are free space, read with statfs before, during and after each step, in e2e runs on macOS with Lima vz, and for shared tool images also with devvm’s data folder on a tmpfs of its own on Linux. On Linux hosts, Lima’s numbers add a copy of base’s disk to an image’s and a tools build’s, but they haven’t been measured there yet. A --from base converts its image in the host’s temporary folder, which devvm doesn’t check, because on Linux that’s often a small tmpfs. Workspace clones: each repo’s seed is copied one after another, so a folder of many big repos takes a copy per repo; copies in parallel, bounded, aren’t built. A repo made in the VM stays there until the user clones it out by hand, and nothing of the folder’s own files comes back (workspace clones). x86_64 hosts are untested on real hardware; on Intel Macs, --from’s kernel is untested with vz. Linux hosts: the QEMU wrapper depends on the shape of Lima’s -netdev user,id=net0,… argument. If Lima changes it, the wrapper refuses to start QEMU rather than run it unrestricted. Network tiers, not built: approving blocked hosts as they’re hit. Claude Code’s login is captured on a path Anthropic doesn’t document. devvm reads Claude Code’s token endpoint, its client ID, its requests and replies and the .credentials.json format from Claude Code 2.1’s bundle, and refreshes the login on the host as Claude Code would (logins made in a VM). A release that changes any of them can break the login in VMs, or the host’s refresh, without warning. The network end-to-end section drives the real Claude Code’s claude auth login against a fake endpoint, so a change to its requests fails that section, and a Claude Code token from claude setup-token, which Anthropic documents, stays the fallback. Network tiers, risks of the mechanism: sandbox-exec is deprecated. If Apple removes it, macOS needs another way to confine the hostagent: an egress filter upstream (gvisor-tap-vsock#609 and #631; Lima’s hostLoopback: false, lima#5581), a user-v2 daemon of devvm’s own (lima#5464), or QEMU with the Linux mechanism on macOS too (it works there, slower than vz). The self-check catches it breaking silently. VMs started outside devvm (limactl start, limactl shell starting a stopped VM, Lima’s start at login) aren’t confined: devvm reports them unenforced. An override.yaml setting a dead HTTPS_PROXY might harden this (untested). A Lima upgrade that adds a hostagent connection fails closed: the start hangs until Lima gives up (10 minutes in the experiment). devvm should time-box the start and say it’s the sandbox. That includes unix sockets: the profile allows only those in the VM’s Lima folder and the forwarded agent’s. Allowing every unix socket would let a compromised hostagent reach docker.sock or another ssh agent. Tunnels the proxy doesn’t read are decided by the CONNECT host and checked against the TLS server name, so domain fronting through a shared CDN may still reach other hosts (attack vectors).
data.opencodes-database-in-history-exports#op:
opencode 2 keeps its sessions and its logins in one SQLite database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db (opencode-.db for another channel’s build), in WAL mode. An export of agents’ history goes to this machine and can go into another VM of the folder, so it must carry the sessions without the logins. Leaving the database out would lose opencode’s history, and opencode’s own opencode session export runs opencode and its server once per session, which an export before devvm rm can’t count on. devvm copies the database in the VM with the sqlite3 that base installs (sqlite3 on Debian and Ubuntu, sqlite on Alpine), as the VM’s user, in a temporary folder in ~/.cache (opencodeClean):
VACUUM INTO copies the database as one snapshot, with what its -wal file holds, so a login that opencode saved last, which is still only in the WAL, is in the copy and taken out with the rest. In the copy, devvm drops every trigger, so none can put a row back, and empties the tables that hold logins: opencode 2.2’s credential (its logins and API keys), account and control_account (its console’s access and refresh tokens) and account_state, the session_share table of an earlier opencode (each share’s secret), and any other table whose name has credential, account, auth, secret, token or share in it, or that has a column such as secret, api_key, access_token or password, so a table that a later opencode adds for its logins is emptied too. It also deletes the rows of the kv table whose key starts with wellknown:config:, because each holds an organization’s remote config, which opencode fetched with that organization’s well-known login and which can hold the organization’s keys. opencode fetches the config again once it has the login. It also empties what would run without asking in the VM that imports the copy (opencodeUnattended): opencode 2.4’s automation table, each automation’s trigger and the shell command it runs, which opencode approved once, as the automation was made, and never asks about again, its permission table, the requests you said always to allow in a project, its job table, the subagents’ jobs, and its session_inbox table, a session’s queued messages, which its service starts again when it starts (restart.ts), and any table whose name starts with one of those names. It sets to NULL, in every table, a column named time_suspended, which marks a session whose turn the service resumes on its own, and one named commands, a project’s commands, whose start command opencode runs with bash -lc for each worktree it makes (opencodeNulled). It drops every view, as a view in an emptied table’s name could show a renamed table’s rows, and its check fails on any table with a generated column, which pragma_table_info doesn’t list. Each session’s own rules are the permission column of session_v2, a JSON array of rules, each with an effect of allow, deny or ask, so in every table with a permission column, its name in any case, devvm keeps only the deny and ask rules with a text action, and a value that isn’t such an array becomes no rules (opencodeAllowRules). It writes each kept rule again from the values that sqlite3 read, because sqlite3 reads a key written twice by its first value and opencode’s JSON.parse by its last, so "effect":"deny","effect":"allow" would otherwise stay as an allow rule for opencode. A kept rule whose resource is missing or isn’t text gets *, which matches every resource, because opencode’s rules need one. It reads that JSON only where a CASE has found it valid, because sqlite3 may read both sides of an AND and fail on text that isn’t JSON. It takes out the record of opencode’s migration that imports auth.json (20260805200742_import_legacy_credentials), so the opencode that next opens the copy imports the logins that devvm’s setup wrote in its own VM’s auth.json, as it does when it first makes its database. It turns WAL off, with secure_delete on, and runs VACUUM, which writes the file again, so no free page keeps a deleted row and no -wal or -journal file is left. It checks what sqlite3 printed, not only that it succeeded. Right after VACUUM INTO, the copy must have as many tables as the database, and at least one. At the end, devvm counts the triggers and views, the generated columns, the rows of each table it emptied, the values left in each column it set to NULL, the rows whose permission still holds anything but deny and ask rules, and the kv rows it deleted, and each count must be 0, so a sqlite3 that runs nothing and prints nothing fails the check too. When a check or any step fails, the database is left out of the export and the run log says why. The export’s tar leaves out the database and its -wal, -shm and -journal files as they are, matched within opencode’s folder, and adds the copy at the database’s path (--transform, which leaves symlinks’ targets alone). The import does the same to an export it unpacks, in the VM, before anything reaches the home folder: it deletes the -wal, -shm and -journal files and any database that isn’t a regular file, and puts in each database’s copy, or deletes the database when the VM has no sqlite3 or the copy fails. Each sqlite3 runs with trusted_schema off, so an imported database’s schema can’t call the CLI’s functions that write files.
Not covered:
A secret that’s in a session itself, such as a key you pasted into a prompt, stays in the session, as it does in Claude Code’s and Codex’s transcripts. A plugin’s own storage and a remote workspace’s binding stay. opencode keeps each plugin’s storage in its kv table, under the plugin’s own prefix, and each remote workspace’s binding, the record its provider needs to reconnect, in its workspace table. opencode’s built-in plugins keep model catalogs and session records there, but a plugin you install, or a workspace provider, that keeps a token there takes it into the export. A VM without sqlite3, made from an image built without it, exports and imports no opencode database, and opencode’s sessions are lost from that export. opencode’s own agents keep their rules. A session keeps its agent, and a turn is checked against that agent’s built-in rules too, such as explore’s, which allow its shell commands. With no suspended session, job or queued message, no turn starts until you send one. A host password that looks like a variable’s name or a number. Settings’ copies keep a value that looks like an environment variable’s name or a switch (envName, plainValue), so a service password set by hand in that form reached VMs as it was, with no devvm-redacted for the setup’s clean-up to find; the release page says what to do. The event table stays as it is. It holds the events that opencode’s sessions were made from, a session.permissions event’s rules among them, and opencode 2.4.1 writes an event into session_v2 as it publishes it (its session projector), not when it opens a database, so the copy’s rules are the ones opencode reads. A later opencode that rebuilt its sessions from that table would read the allow rules again. A remake’s home folder copy keeps opencode’s database with its logins, and its home key, because it’s the same VM’s data going into the same folder’s new VM (the home folder’s copy). opencode 2.4 keeps the private Ed25519 key of its home, which every machine it pairs with opencode machine add trusts and which it never replaces, in a file of its own, ~/.local/state/opencode/machine/home-key, not in the database. The database’s machine table holds each paired machine’s name and the public key it logs in to the home with, so it’s the VM’s own pairings, and the copy empties it with the login tables (opencodeLogins). The key’s folder, the background service’s registration (service.json, or service-.json on a channel other than latest, dev, beta or next, with the service’s password, written through ..tmp, and .pty-handoff, a terminal’s handoff ticket, written through .pty-handoff..tmp) and the terminals’ daemons (pty, their sockets and access tokens) are opencode’s HistoryOwn in the agents’ registry: the export leaves them out and the import never writes them, while a remake keeps them. The registrations are patterns, service-*.json, service.json.* and service-*.json.*, which the export’s GNU tar --exclude and the import’s tar --exclude and its clean-up loop, a shell glob, all expand.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, with its data isolation companion):
Lead What holds it Check A key typed into opencode in the VM reaching this machine’s export The export holds only the copy, whose login tables are empty and whose file is written again by VACUUM Unit tests (TestOpencodeClean, TestHistoryExportRuns) plant a credential, an account’s tokens, a share’s secret and a later table’s key, the credential only in the WAL of an open connection, and find none of them in any byte of the copy or the export; e2e’s network section plants a key with the VM’s sqlite3 and finds neither it nor the login’s placeholders in the export The WAL or journal file carrying the rows They never go into an export, and an import deletes them TestHistoryExportRuns and TestHistoryImportCleansOpencode An export with the logins in it reaching another VM The import makes the same copy in the VM before anything reaches its home folder, or leaves the database out TestHistoryImportCleansOpencode, with and without sqlite3 A trigger putting a row back as it’s deleted Every trigger is dropped first, and the rows are counted after TestOpencodeClean plants one A hostile VM’s export running a command, or allowing one, without asking in the VM that imports it The copy empties automation, permission, job and session_inbox, and every table whose name starts with one of those names, sets time_suspended and commands to NULL, keeps only the deny and ask rules of each permission column, written again, drops views and refuses generated columns; the counts after must be 0. The export leaves out opencode’s git repositories (snapshot, repos, worktree), and the import never writes them TestOpencodeCleanSchema plants a row in each from opencode 2.4.1’s schema, an allow rule, a suspended session and a project’s commands; TestOpencodeCleanSessionRules plants rules that aren’t deny or ask, a key written twice, values that aren’t rules and a column in upper case; TestOpencodeCleanHidden a view and a generated column; TestHistoryExportRuns and TestHistoryImportRuns the git folders opencode’s home key reaching this machine’s export or another VM The export leaves out its machine folder, service.json, service-.json, their handoff and temporary files, and pty, and the import never writes them, by their paths after it unpacks too; the copy of the database empties its machine table, the paired machines’ public keys TestHistoryExportRuns, TestHistoryImportRuns and TestHistoryImportV010 plant them; TestOpencodeCleanSchema empties machine from opencode 2.4.1’s schema; TestHomeSkipsEveryLogin keeps them in a remake A hostile database’s schema running code in the VM trusted_schema is off, and it runs as the VM’s user on the VM’s own files, which the export’s code could reach anyway Reviewed
data.pasting-images#Pasting images:
devvm paste gets an image, a PDF, or one copied file, from this machine’s clipboard to an agent in the VM (how). It keeps four things. The VM gets the clipboard only when you run the command, and only an image, a PDF or a copied file. A copied file goes only after you say yes to its path on this machine (paste_file_ask), because the clipboard can name any file of yours, such as one a web page or another program put there. Nothing the VM says reaches your clipboard. And devvm leaves no process of its own running for it.
--send-file answers the question only for a file below the folder the VM mounts, which the VM can read already. confirmFile decides with sendFileAnswers: inFolder compares the cleaned path that OpenNoLinks opened with the folder’s physical path, and OpenNoLinks must have followed no link at all, because a root-owned link below the folder, such as one a root container made on a Linux host, can lead anywhere. It never answers for a --clone VM. A file anywhere else is refused where devvm can’t ask (paste_file_outside), and so is one reached through a link (paste_file_through_link), so a hotkey or a script can’t send a file it never showed. There’s no list of credential folders that devvm refuses outright, because it could never name every place a key is kept, and the question shows every path.
What it’s built from: internal/platform’s clipboard readers, vm.Paste, and config.toml’s paste-dir.
On macOS, clipboard_darwin.go runs osascript with a JavaScript for Automation script through NSPasteboard. The script takes a PDF (com.adobe.pdf) first, as it is, before the picture of it and the temporary file of its own that Preview puts beside it. Then it asks for file URLs alone (readObjectsForClasses with NSPasteboardURLReadingFileURLsOnlyKey), counts several and reports one’s path. Otherwise it writes a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP as it is, or a TIFF made a PNG, to a file in a private folder devvm makes and deletes, only when it’s within the cap. The copy back is pbcopy. Both tools run by their paths in /usr/bin, never found on PATH.
On Linux, clipboard_linux.go runs wl-paste --list-types and --type on Wayland, and xclip’s TARGETS and -t on X11, taking application/pdf before a file reference and the image types. The copy back is wl-copy or xclip -i. Each comes from the first of /usr/bin, /bin, /usr/local/bin and NixOS’s /run/current-system/sw/bin that has it, never from PATH, because PATH can hold a project’s folder, such as direnv’s PATH_add or node_modules/.bin, and the VM writes those.
Every clipboard tool runs with exec.CommandContext (clipboard_tool.go), and devvm reads its output, never through the run log, so the image stays out of it. Each tool is stopped after 30 seconds, as a tool waits on a program that holds the clipboard and doesn’t answer: a read gives paste_tool_slow, and a copy back gives a warning. Its pipes are closed a second after it ends, as a child of its may keep them.
vm.Paste (internal/vm/paste.go) finds the VM as every command does, refuses a stopped one, and reads the clipboard before touching the VM. It names the file on this machine: paste-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS-8hex, then the image’s or the PDF’s extension, or the copied file’s when it’s letters and digits alone and at most 16 of them, and nothing else of the file’s name. It runs assets/guest/paste.sh in the VM as sh -c’s script, so nothing of it is left on disk. config.toml’s paste-dir (settings.PasteDir) is the folder in every VM, which each launch makes through sync.sh (DEVVM_PASTE_DIR), mode 700 and the user’s own.
Why push, not pull. A VM that pulls the clipboard on Ctrl+V, through a stand-in xclip and a channel to this machine, would need three things. It would need a server of devvm’s on this machine for as long as a session lasts, and devvm runs limactl shell in its own place, so no devvm process exists during a session. It would need a remote forward into the VM’s sshd, which allows them on 127.77.0.0/16 alone, for links. And anything in the VM could read your clipboard at any moment while a session is open, a screenshot of your password manager included. With push, only the host starts the transfer, and only an image, a PDF or a file crosses. Stand-ins for xclip and wl-paste in the VM would reach only Claude Code and pi, because Codex and opencode read X11 or Wayland in their own process, and both already handle a pasted path.
What the VM can’t do. It can’t ask for the clipboard, because devvm reads it once, when you run the command. devvm asks only for a file’s reference, a PDF and image types, never text, then checks an image’s or a PDF’s bytes against the type (http.DetectContentType, for which a PDF starts with %PDF-). Text is never taken for a file. AppleScript’s the clipboard as «class furl» makes any text a path, /Users/you/.ssh/id_ed25519 as it is and hello as /hello, so the macOS reader asks NSPasteboard for file URLs alone, which text never gives. A copied file whose path can’t be found is refused (paste_file_gone) rather than Finder’s icon beside it sent.
It can’t write to your clipboard. The path is built on this machine from paste-dir and a name devvm picks, both from a fixed set of characters, before the VM runs anything. Of a copied file’s own name only its extension is kept, letters and digits alone, because a file in the project folder is named by the VM. So what reaches your clipboard is devvm’s own path, with no space, quote or newline in it, which can’t run anything when you paste it into a terminal.
It can’t keep devvm reading or waiting. The one thing devvm reads back from the VM is a count, parsed as a whole number from bounded output. Each of paste.sh’s commands is stopped once it prints past 32 bytes on stdout or 4 MiB on stderr, so a VM that prints without end can’t keep devvm reading. It’s also stopped past its time, 10 minutes for put, which carries up to 64 MiB, and 2 for count and rm, so a VM that never answers can’t keep devvm waiting. The command then fails as it does for any other failure of the script (paste_not_sent, paste_count_failed, paste_rm_not_done). It gets no SSH agent, because the writes and counts go through the backend’s Exec as it is, never target.exec, as the clone checks do.
It can’t send a file of yours through a link. A copied file may be in the project folder, which the VM writes, so its path is cleaned, never resolved first, and opened as named following no link but the system’s. platform.OpenNoLinks opens each component from its parent with O_NOFOLLOW, through golang.org/x/sys/unix’s Openat, because the standard library exports no Openat on macOS and internal/safefile is standard library only. It reads a link on the way with Readlinkat and follows it only when Fstatat says root owns it, and the folder’s Fstat says root owns that too and neither its group nor others can write it, as for macOS’s /tmp, /var and /etc in /, for at most 40 hops. Root owning the link isn’t enough on its own, because a link of root’s can be hard-linked into a folder of yours, and in a folder only root can change, no one else can swap the link between its Fstatat and its Readlinkat. It never follows the file itself, and it opens it with O_NONBLOCK and O_NOCTTY, so a FIFO never makes devvm wait and a terminal never becomes devvm’s.
A link the VM makes in a mount is the user’s on this machine, never root’s. So a link in the file’s place, a folder’s link planted before the copy or swapped in after it, and a copied folder’s reference whose trailing slash hid a link all fail (paste_file_link) rather than send what they point to, and your own links do too. Every step goes through a file descriptor, so there’s no moment for a swap between a check and the open. The file opened is then checked and read as every file a VM can write is, by internal/safefile (Checked, then ReadAll): a regular file within the cap of 64 MiB, the cap an image is held to as well.
In the VM, paste.sh writes with umask 077 to a .part name and renames it, and it refuses a paste-dir that’s a link, not a folder or not the user’s. Its count and rm see only regular files at the folder’s top level with devvm’s names, never anything else in a folder that may be yours. Root in the VM can get around any check the VM runs, which gives it nothing it couldn’t do to a file in the project folder.
What’s left on this machine: on Linux, wl-copy or xclip serves the path until you copy something else, because a Linux clipboard’s contents live in the program that copied them. It isn’t devvm’s process, and devvm runs it with no pipes on its output, because Go’s Wait waits for a child that inherited them. On macOS, nothing.
End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, the project section): with stand-in clipboard tools in a test build’s DEVVM_CLIP_TOOLS, devvm paste --json puts the copied image into the running VM, where its SHA-256 matches, mode 600 in the folder of mode 700, and the stand-in copier got the path. devvm paste rm --force deletes it and leaves a file of the user’s in the folder, and a stopped VM is refused before the clipboard is read.
The CLI tests (testdata/script/paste.txtar, paste_rm.txtar) drive the rest against the stubs: the types read, the bytes sent, each refusal, the launch’s offer and config.toml’s paste-dir. On macOS, TestReadClipPasteboard runs the real script against a pasteboard of the test’s own, never the clipboard. Text that’s a path or a file:// URL is no file, nor is a file:// URL as public.url. A file URL with Finder’s .icns icon beside it is the file, a file reference URL is resolved, two files are counted, and a file that’s gone is refused. A PNG and a TIFF are read as PNGs, beside text too. A PDF is read as it is, beside its picture and beside the temporary file a thumbnail copied in Preview names, while a file URL beside a JPEG, as Photos copies, is the file. One past the cap is refused before it’s written.
Not covered: the real clipboard, which no automated check reads. The copies of Finder (one file URL per file, with an .icns icon), Photos (a JPEG and a file URL), Preview (a PDF with a TIFF, and a thumbnail’s temporary file beside them), and Safari, Chrome and Firefox (a TIFF or a PNG) were checked by hand on macOS, and TestReadClipPasteboard writes the same types to its own pasteboard, so a change in what an app copies would need checking by hand again. Also not covered: image types other than PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and TIFF, which devvm doesn’t read on macOS; whether macOS asks before osascript reads the clipboard, which depends on the release and its privacy settings; Linux’s clipboard tools, which only the stubs stand in for; and the agents’ own reading of a pasted path, which their releases change.
data.ports-on-lima#Ports on Lima:
The guarantee: when a VM forwards every port, each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in it listens on, on its loopback or on all its addresses, is forwarded to the same port on the host’s loopback, and only to its loopback. When a VM lists its ports, only those are forwarded, however many it lists, by the same rules. The forwarder never takes a port that a program on the host has on any address when the forward is made, or a port devvm records for another VM. Forwarding gives the VM no way out that it doesn’t already have, because every connection starts on the host. Lima’s own forwards listen with SO_REUSEADDR, so on macOS, whenever a server in the VM starts, Lima takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. That’s why Lima forwards nothing and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t depend on Lima for that, because its hostagent’s sandbox refuses it every port but its ssh port, so Lima can’t forward a port of the VM’s even if it ignored its rules. The emulation is reviewed, with the threat check’s findings fixed or listed below, which is why the host key read is capped, reports are paced and the log is limited, and the end-to-end checks prove the rest.
What it’s built from:
Lima’s forwards off. Each VM’s portForwards holds three ignore rules, each for every guest port and protocol (any, which is TCP and UDP). They’re on 127.0.0.1, which Lima also matches for ::1, on 0.0.0.0 and on ::, which together match servers on all addresses. They come ahead of Lima’s own last rule, which forwards everything. CreateVM sets them with limactl clone --set. Start sets them only where limactl list shows other rules, because an edit gives the VM new host keys at its next boot. Lima’s ssh is its VM driver’s forward (ssh.localPort), not a rule, so the ignore rules leave it alone, and they cover the guest’s own ssh port like any other. The sandbox’s binds (macOS, confined tiers). The hostagent of a confined VM runs under a Seatbelt profile (confinement) that denies every network bind but two kinds. It may bind the VM’s ssh port over TCP, which devvm chooses and records in the VM’s state (the ports section’s host.ssh), and unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, which hold the hostagent’s own socket (ha.sock), the VM’s network (default_ep.sock, default_fd.sock) and ssh’s control socket. Seatbelt matches a bind by its port alone, on any address, even when the rule names localhost, and it can’t allow an ephemeral bind (port 0) without allowing every port. It matches a unix socket by its path with links resolved, so a link in the Lima folder doesn’t let the hostagent bind a socket elsewhere. Lima’s host resolver binds two ephemeral ports for its DNS server, so a confined VM starts with the resolver off and 127.0.0.1 as its DNS server, as on Linux, where nothing listens and lookups fail at once. The hostagent reaches the guest agent over vsock, which needs no bind. This list comes from starting a VM under a profile that reported every bind, then under one that denied the rest: Lima logs a forward it’s refused (failed to listen) and carries on, while a refused resolver ends the start. Which ports. Which ports each VM forwards, all, none or a list, is in its state (ports.forward), and the backend never hears of them: neither Start’s Want nor any other call of the backend’s has them. vmssh.Forwards.Start, the one owner of the forwarder, reads them from the VM’s state each time it starts one, after a start of the VM and when devvm ports changes a running VM’s ports, without editing Lima’s config. A stopped VM’s change is its state’s alone, because its next start reads it. When the VM lists ports, the forwarder forwards those less the ports a program on the host has, which the owner leaves out with a ports_taken warning. When none is left, no forwarder runs. A forwarder per VM, on the host. The forwarder is vmssh.Forwarder, which isn’t a backend’s. Its owner, vmssh.Forwards, runs it detached as devvm _ports, one per VM, for project VMs alone, because only a project VM’s start goes through it, and builds’ starts don’t. The owner starts it once the backend’s Start returns, and again on a running VM when its ports change, each after stopping any forwarder the VM had, which ends the connections open through it. devvm finds that one by its pid file, which it checks against the process’s arguments, as it does for the proxy. It sends that forwarder SIGTERM and kills it if it hasn’t ended within 2 s, so its ports are free before devvm asks which listed ports a host program has. devvm holds a lock of the VM’s own (ports.lock, beside its pid file ports.pid in the VM’s run folder) from stopping the old forwarder until the new one has started, so two devvm runs at once, such as a start and devvm ports, leave one forwarder, the one its pid file names. The owner waits up to 10 s for the forwarder to say it forwards while it runs. The forwarder says so in a status file of its own beside its pid file (ports.status), which holds its pid and which devvm removes before each start. If it doesn’t, devvm warns with ports_forward_failed, naming its log, and leaves it to keep trying while the VM runs on. Reaching the VM. The forwarder makes one ssh connection, a master (ssh -F none -M -S ), to the VM’s sshd on Lima’s ssh port on the host’s loopback. Lima’s SSH gives the port with the user and the key, the first IdentityFile of Lima’s ssh config, and devvm refuses that target unless the config names 127.0.0.1 (vmssh.FromTarget, the check links and the ssh config use too). It logs in as Lima’s user with Lima’s key alone (IdentitiesOnly, IdentityAgent=none), _config/user in devvm’s Lima home, which every VM there authorizes, and never with the user’s agent. The master reads none of the user’s configuration and forwards nothing either way, with ClearAllForwardings, PermitRemoteOpen none, ProxyCommand none, and no agent, X11 or tunnel. The VM’s sshd allows local forwarding, and remote forwards only to 127.77.0.0/16 for links (base.sh), and -W is local forwarding. Its control socket is in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700) and is named by a hash of the VM’s name, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. When the connection is lost, the forwarder closes its forwards and makes the connection again every 2 s while the lifeline holds. What listens. The master’s session runs ports.sh (assets/guest/ports.sh) as the VM’s user (sh -s). It prints the local addresses of the VM’s listening TCP sockets, which are the state 0A lines of /proc/net/tcp and tcp6, whenever they change and every 10 s regardless, so it ends soon after the connection does. The forwarder treats the report as untrusted. A line over 128 bytes or a report over 4096 lines ends the connection, and anything that isn’t a hex address and port is skipped. Reports are applied at least 500 ms apart, and one that comes sooner waits, holding up the VM’s ssh channel with it, so the VM can’t make the forwarder bind, dial and read devvm’s state at its own pace. The VM can make the forwarder write to its log, with ports coming and going and with the session’s stderr, so the log takes 200 writes at once and then one every 10 s. Each write is at most 512 bytes, without control characters other than newlines and tabs, C1 included, and the log is rotated before it passes 1 MiB, its end kept in ports.log.1. A forwarded port’s connections go to 127.0.0.1 for a server on all IPv4 addresses or on that address, and to ::1 for a server on all IPv6 addresses or on that address. A server on another 127.x address alone gets its connections there. Servers on other addresses alone aren’t forwarded. How many. With every port, the forwarder takes ports from 1024 up, because the ports below are the host’s system services. With listed ports, it takes those alone (-only), a listed port below 1024 included, because the user asked for it, and a bind the host refuses is logged. Either way the forwarder takes at most 256 ports at once (vmssh.MaxForwards). It records why it couldn’t take each port in ports.forwarded, by the bind’s error: in use (EADDRINUSE), past its limit, or refused (EACCES or EPERM, such as below 1024 on Linux), and devvm ports warns each with its own message (ports_taken, ports_limit, ports_refused). Any other error, such as EMFILE, ENOBUFS or EADDRNOTAVAIL, says nothing about the port, so it’s logged, not recorded, and the port is tried again at the next report, the log’s limit capping the repeats. A port past the limit is tried again at the next report once the forwarder forwards fewer. A record from before the reasons, whose third line holds every port it couldn’t take, is read as giving no reason, so it warns of none rather than call a refused port in use. It reads the reserved ports (below) again with each report, and while it can’t read them, it takes no new port and keeps those it has. A port it has that has since become reserved, such as one another VM’s start has chosen, is given up at that report, though the VM still listens on it, and also within 10 s on the host’s own clock (Forwarder.Recheck), whether or not the VM reports, so a VM that holds its session open and stays silent can’t keep it. A reserved port the VM listens on waits and is tried again at each report until it’s no longer reserved. A port that a host program has, or that the host refused, is tried again only once the VM’s server on it goes and comes back. Listening. The forwarder listens on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, or on IPv4 alone on a host without IPv6, which a bind on ::1 reports as EADDRNOTAVAIL, EAFNOSUPPORT or EPROTONOSUPPORT. EACCES or EPERM on ::1 alone, with 127.0.0.1 bound, also gives IPv4 alone, with a line in the log, because that’s a host denying IPv6 rather than a port it refuses. Any other error on ::1 closes the port’s 127.0.0.1 listener and counts as that bind’s error would on 127.0.0.1, recorded or tried again at the next report as the bullet above says, so a passing error such as EMFILE never leaves a forward on IPv4 alone until its port is opened again. It binds without SO_REUSEADDR (platform.ListenExclusive). With that option, which Go and Lima set, macOS lets a socket take 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. Without the option, the bind is refused when another program has the port on any address. This was checked on macOS for a program on 0.0.0.0, on :: (IPv4 and IPv6 at once, as Node’s and Go’s servers listen), on IPv6 alone and on 127.0.0.1, each with and without SO_REUSEADDR of its own. A port held only by ended connections (TIME_WAIT, with nothing answering on it) is taken as usual, so a server that restarts gets its forward back. When a bind is refused, the forwarder dials the port and takes it only if the dial is refused. A full backlog times out, which counts as taken. A port the forwarder took on 127.0.0.1 but finds in use on ::1 is given up, so localhost never reaches two programs. On Linux, SO_REUSEADDR stays on. Linux refuses that bind with the option too while another socket listens on the port, and without it, the forwarder’s own ended connections (TIME_WAIT) would keep anyone from listening on the port for a minute, its next forwarder included. Each connection. Each forwarded connection is a channel of the master’s (ssh -S -W HOST:PORT), with one process per connection and at most 256 at once. The VM’s sshd opens it to the VM’s own loopback from inside the VM. The channel’s ssh has the master’s options. If the master is gone, ssh connects on its own, and it then reaches the VM’s sshd the same way, never the host’s. Each relay’s ssh runs with a context of its own, which closing its forward cancels, so the ssh is killed with the forward even when the VM never ends its channel. pipeSSH, which carries every relay of the forwarder’s, the link sessions’ and a login’s callback, also cancels that context once the client on the host has closed its side and the VM has sent nothing for 30 seconds (relayGrace), and once the client can take nothing more and the ssh hasn’t exited within 30 seconds. Each write of the VM’s bytes to the client starts the grace again once it’s done, and the grace doesn’t run while that write waits for the client, so a client that closes for writing alone and waits still gets an answer the VM keeps sending, however slowly it reads. The VM must send something at least every 30 seconds, its first byte included, so a client that half-closes and waits longer than that for a first byte, such as nc -N in front of a slow query, is cut. The timer (graceTimer) runs only once the client’s side has closed, or once the copy to the client has ended, with a write that failed or the VM’s EOF, and a relay that ends stops it for good, so the client’s goroutine, which can outlive the relay, never starts it again. The relay’s own context, its owner’s, also closes the client’s connection when it ends, so a write that waits on a client that stopped reading ends with its forward, its link or LoopbackForward.Close. Reserved ports. The forwarder never takes the VM’s own Lima ssh port, which Lima’s SSH names, or its proxy port, which its state records, and the owner passes both as -reserve. It also never takes the ssh, proxy and desktop ports devvm chooses and records in any VM’s state, the ports another VM’s running forwarder forwards now, as its ports.forwarded record says, or the ports another VM lists while it has a claim on them, which is while its forwarder runs or while devvm holds its ports.lock to start one again, unless this VM lists them too (ports.Reserved). A stopped VM’s listed ports aren’t reserved from other VMs’ forwarders, but the ports devvm chooses still avoid them (ports.Used). Every Lima VM’s ssh port is one of those, whatever its tier: devvm chooses it when it makes the VM, sets it with limactl clone --set .ssh.localPort, and records it in the VM’s ports section before the clone (ports.Allocator.SSH). One allocator, ports.Allocator, chooses every host port devvm chooses, the ssh, proxy and desktop ports, and records it while it holds the VM’s lock and then the claims lock (run/claims.lock, state.VM.Claim) until the VM’s state is written, so two devvm commands making or starting VMs at once never choose the same one. A build VM has no state, so devvm chooses its ssh port too, on every host, through the same allocator (ports.Allocator.Build), under the claims lock alone (state.Claims), and on macOS the build’s Seatbelt profile names that port. It records the port by the build VM’s name (run/build-ports/), where ports.Used reads it, until limactl start returns, and by then Lima has bound the port or the start has failed. The devvm that starts the build holds a file lock on that record until then, and the kernel lets go of the lock when that devvm ends, even when it’s killed. Each time devvm chooses a port, under the claims lock, it first deletes the records whose lock no process holds and that are over 15 minutes old. The age matters because a killed devvm leaves its limactl start running, which may still bind the port for up to Lima’s 10 minutes of waiting for the VM’s ssh. So a devvm killed while its build VM starts reserves that port for 15 minutes, and then only until the next port is chosen. A stopped VM gets a new one only when a program on the host has its port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, or when the VM lists it to forward, and its start then sets it with an edit. Lima binds the port only once the VM boots, a few seconds after its start, so a port Lima picked itself would be free for another VM’s forwarder in that window, and Lima’s own ssh, which checks no host key, would then reach the other VM (the threat check below). The host key. devvm keeps one record of a VM’s host keys for each of its starts, vms//run/known_hosts (vmssh.PinHostKeys). It removes the record before each start and reads the keys once the VM runs, whatever ports the VM forwards, and a command that finds the VM running without a record of its current start reads them too (starter.pinHostKeys). It reads them through limactl shell, at most 64 KiB for at most 30 s, keeping only lines whose key decodes and names its own type (vmssh.ParseHostKeys). The record’s first line names the start it was read for (backend.Run.ID), so a record of another start, such as one before a limactl start outside devvm, is read again, and keys read while the VM started again aren’t recorded. The forwarder checks the VM against that record, with HostKeyAlias and StrictHostKeyChecking yes, as the ssh config, links’ sessions and a --clone VM’s git do. All of them reach the VM through one function, vmssh.Checked, which checks the backend’s ssh and adds the record: the forwarder and the ssh config pin the keys when the record is another start’s, and links’ sessions and git take only a record of the current start. The pin keeps the forwarder from talking to a program on the host that takes the ssh port. It doesn’t guard against the VM itself, which is already the other end of the connection. Its lifeline. The forwarder follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid, the lifeline Lima’s Running gives), as the proxy does, and exits once the file is gone, holds anything else, or its process is gone. devvm stop stops it with the VM, and devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it before they delete its files with the VM’s folder. A VM that stops some other way, such as when its self-check fails or a restart stops it, ends its forwarder through the lifeline, and the next start stops any forwarder that’s left before it starts its own. What keeps a forward from carrying the VM out: every connection starts on the host. A program connects to the forwarder’s port, and the forwarder asks the VM’s sshd to connect to the VM’s loopback. The VM opens nothing to the host through the forwarder, because the master asks for no remote forward, agent, X11 or tunnel, and OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel that the server opens unasked, whatever sshd root in the VM runs. The only remote forwards devvm asks a VM for are a client’s links, on a link session that is a connection of its own, never the forwarder’s master (links). What the VM sends back goes to the program that connected, as with any forward. On a confined tier, the VM’s own connections stay confined by Seatbelt or QEMU’s restrict=on, while the forwarder runs on the host as devvm, outside the hostagent’s sandbox.
What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels and honoring -F none, the kernel refusing a bind without SO_REUSEADDR where another socket has the port (checked on macOS), devvm’s state listing every VM’s ports, each running forwarder’s record of the ports it forwards, and the forwarders’ pid files and locks saying which VMs have a claim on their listed ports. It also relies on Lima binding its ssh forward on the host’s loopback alone, on the host key that devvm pins at the start, and on Lima honoring the ignore rules ahead of its own rule. On macOS, a confined VM relies on Seatbelt refusing the hostagent’s binds instead of on the rules, and on the Virtualization framework’s own process, which runs outside the profile, binding nothing: the VM’s network goes through the hostagent’s unix sockets.
What could break it: a Lima release that forwards despite the ignore rules, or that forwards from somewhere other than portForwards. On macOS, a confined VM keeps the guarantee even then, because its sandbox refuses the binds. An open VM, and every VM on Linux, where QEMU’s restrict=on doesn’t cover the hostagent’s own binds, still relies on Lima honoring the rules. A Lima release that needs a new bind for a confined VM, such as a resolver that can’t be turned off, fails its start closed, and Lima’s log names the refused bind. The end-to-end checks look at the rules, and use lsof or ss to check that the hostagent has no TCP or UDP port of the VM’s and that a host program keeps its port. A program on the host could take Lima’s ssh port while the VM is stopped, and the pinned host key refuses it. Lima’s key logs in to every VM in devvm’s Lima home, as it does for Lima’s own ssh, but public key authentication never sends the key to the VM.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion; the sandbox’s binds and the ssh port). Leads, each confirmed and fixed, ruled out, or listed:
Another VM answering for this one’s ssh: confirmed, fixed. An ssh port that Lima picks at a VM’s start, and binds once the VM boots, is one devvm doesn’t record, so no forwarder reserves it. Another VM forwarding every port, with a server on that port in the window, has its forward take it. Lima then carries on with its other ssh forward and waits on the port (seen with a host program holding it), and Lima’s own ssh checks no host key (StrictHostKeyChecking no), so limactl shell, the host keys devvm reads and pins after the start, and devvm’s setup and shell would reach the other VM. The fix: each VM’s ssh port is devvm’s, whatever its tier, recorded before the clone and reserved by every forwarder. It’s unit-tested and checked by the CLI tests, and end to end, the port a VM’s state records is the one Lima listens on. A guest port bound around the rules: ruled out on macOS on a confined tier. Lima forwards a port only by binding it on the host, and the sandbox refuses every port but the ssh port. End to end, with Lima’s own rule put back for one start inside the sandbox, Lima tries the guest’s TCP and UDP ports, is refused (operation not permitted), and has no port but its ssh port, while devvm’s forwarder forwards the TCP port. The ssh port on every address: listed. Seatbelt allows the ssh port on any address, so a Lima that bound it on 0.0.0.0 would put the VM’s sshd on the network, where it still takes only keys. Lima binds it on 127.0.0.1, and the end-to-end checks look at the hostagent’s listeners. The rule allows the port over TCP alone, so the guest’s UDP server on that port number can’t get a forward from it; checked end to end. A program holding a stopped VM’s ssh port: ruled out, but for a race. A start looks for the recorded port with a bind on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 as well as a connection, so a program that has the port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, gives the VM a new port. Only a program that takes the port between that check and Lima’s bind, a few seconds later, gets Lima’s ssh, which is listed under not covered below. End to end, a VM whose port a host program holds starts on a new one, recorded, and the program keeps its own. Two VMs choosing the same ssh port: confirmed, fixed. Without a lock, two devvm commands making VMs at once could each choose the same port from the ports other VMs record, and the second VM’s Lima would wait on a port that the first one’s has. devvm chooses and records a port while it holds the claims lock, run/claims.lock in its data folder, after the VM’s own lock (locks). A build VM’s ssh port: confirmed, fixed. A port that Lima picked at a build’s start would be one that no VM’s state records, so another VM forwarding every port could take it in the window before Lima binds it, and Lima’s ssh would then run the build’s scripts in that VM. The fix: devvm chooses every build VM’s ssh port, on macOS and Linux, under the claims lock, and records it in run/build-ports/, which every forwarder reserves, until the build VM’s start returns. A record that a killed devvm leaves is deleted the first time devvm chooses a port once the record is 15 minutes old, because no process holds its lock, and until then it keeps the port from any VM while the start that the killed devvm left may still bind it. Builds carry no credentials, an image is the build VM’s own disk, and a tool build writes its images through a folder that only its own VM mounts, so even a VM that reached a build’s ssh another way could break that build but couldn’t learn a secret from it or choose what an image or a tool image holds. It’s unit-tested on both systems, and the CLI tests check that a build’s start sets the port. A browser reaching a VM’s ssh port: confirmed, fixed. Lima listens on the ssh port on this machine’s loopback, and root in the VM can make what answers on port 22 speak HTTP, so a page opened as http://localhost:PORT, by a link or by a VM that opens URLs, would reach a server the VM controls with the cookies of the apps you use on localhost, even in a VM that forwards no ports. The fix is that every VM’s ssh port, and every build VM’s, is one of the Fetch standard’s bad ports from 1024 up that Chromium’s kRestrictedPorts also blocks (ports.SSHPorts, 17 of them, because Chromium lacks 4190 and 6679, which headless Chrome 157 loads). Every browser engine refuses every request to these ports, navigations and WebSockets included. The one allocator chooses them (ports.Allocator.SSH and Build, through freeSSH), its other ports never take one, and a proxy or desktop port that an older devvm chose there moves at the VM’s next start. No forwarder takes one unless its VM lists it (ports.Reserved), so a guest forwarding every port can’t fill them, and a stopped VM’s listed ports don’t keep them from a start. That allows at most 17 running VMs, and a start past that fails with ports_ssh_limit or ports_ssh_limit_all, naming the VMs whose ports are in use, or ports_ssh_limit_others. An older devvm’s VM moves onto the list at its next start, in the start’s one limactl edit, and each launch warns of a running VM still on an old port (ports_ssh_old). A start holds its port, kept or new, for a minute (run/ports.ssh-hold in the VM’s folder), because a stopped VM’s port that it keeps would otherwise look free to another start in the window before Lima binds it. The hold is time-limited, so a backend that takes over a minute to bind can lose the port to another start and fail, and its next start gets another. It’s unit-tested (TestSSHPorts, TestSSH, TestSSHHolds, TestSSHListed, TestOffList, TestBuild, TestReserved, TestStartBuildSSHPort, TestPrepareRestartsTheProxy, TestDesktopListener), checked by the CLI tests (ssh_ports, the frozen 0.1.0 fixture’s launches), and end to end each VM’s ssh port is on the list. What a failed start or create leaves: ruled out. A VM whose create fails, other than by an interrupt, keeps its state, and with it its recorded port, until devvm rm deletes it, so the port stays reserved and nothing else takes it. devvm rm deletes the state, which frees the port. Unix sockets: ruled out as a way out. The hostagent binds them only in the VM’s Lima folder, which only Lima’s own commands and devvm use. DNS around the proxy: ruled out. With Lima’s resolver off, the guest’s DNS server is 127.0.0.1, which transparent mode’s dnsmasq answers inside the VM with one stand-in address and no upstream, or nothing answers when it’s off, and Lima’s network’s DNS address and the host’s address on it answer nothing even when root asks them directly with transparent mode stopped, because the sandbox denies the hostagent the host’s DNS service and every connection but the proxy’s; checked end to end, with transparent mode stopped and running. A compromised hostagent: listed. The bind rules stop a Lima that misbehaves, not code an attacker runs in it, which the profile still lets read and write your files. Starts without the sandbox: listed. Only confined starts on macOS run under it. A build keeps Lima’s host resolver, so its binds aren’t denied, and an open VM starts unconfined. Such a VM could run under a profile that denies binds alone, as its ssh port is fixed, but it would need Lima’s resolver off too, which changes how it resolves names (the user-mode network’s own DNS instead of the host’s resolver), so that’s proposed rather than done. Threat check for listed ports (the security-audit skill, its local IPC companion). Listed ports use the same forwarder with -only, so these leads are what listed ports add, each confirmed or ruled out:
A port the VM chooses: ruled out. -only comes from the VM’s state, less the ports a host program has, both read on the host by the forwarder’s owner, and the VM’s reports can’t add to it. A listed port is forwarded only while a server in the VM listens on it, as with every port. Port 22 listed: ruled out as a collision. Port 22 in the VM is its sshd, and Lima’s ssh forward comes from another host port, so a listed 22 forwards the VM’s sshd to the host’s port 22 as it would forward any server. The VM’s sshd still takes only keys. A host whose own sshd has port 22 keeps it, with a ports_taken warning. A listed proxy port: ruled out. The forwarder reserves the VM’s own proxy port whether or not it’s listed, and every other VM’s as well. A listed port below 1024: taken because the user asked for it. A host service that has the port keeps it, and a bind the host refuses is logged and recorded as refused, never as in use, so devvm ports warns ports_refused rather than ports_taken. One that isn’t running yet is under Not covered. A forwarder left behind: ruled out. devvm stop stops it, devvm rm stops it and removes its files, any other stop ends it through its lifeline, and a start or change whose listed ports are all taken runs none. Two devvm runs that start a VM’s forwarder at once take turns on the VM’s lock, so the second stops the first one’s forwarder, and neither leaves one that its pid file doesn’t name, which nothing would stop. A tier’s confinement: ruled out. Listed ports take fewer ports than every port, never more, and every connection still starts on the host. Another VM takes a stopped or restarting VM’s listed port: mitigated. Only a running VM holds a port, so while VM V is stopped, another VM E may forward V’s listed port, and a hostile E could then try to keep it, such as by forwarding every port and holding its ssh session open without reporting again. Three things stop that. First, the host decides when a port is given up: every forwarder closes each forward whose port is now reserved within 10 s on its own clock, whatever its VM reports, so E gives V’s port up once V runs and lists it. Closing a forward also closes every connection it accepted that’s still open, so a browser’s keep-alive connection to localhost:5173, opened while E had the port, ends then too, and the browser’s later requests, with V’s cookies, never reach E over it. Second, V’s start, a change of its ports and devvm ports warn with ports_held and name E in held_by, whether E lists the port or forwards every port, so V never waits silently. Third, V’s listed ports stay reserved while devvm holds V’s ports.lock, from stopping V’s old forwarder until its new one runs, so no other VM takes them in that window. A stale ports.forwarded can’t hold a port either: devvm removes it under that lock before each start, each forwarder writes an empty one when it starts, and a record counts only while its pid is the VM’s running forwarder. A relay the VM holds open: confirmed, fixed. Closing a forward closed the connections it had accepted, but each connection’s ssh (-W) waits for the VM’s sshd to end its channel, so a hostile VM that ignored the EOF kept that ssh process, and one of the forwarder’s 256 relays, until the forwarder ended. Up to 256 such ssh processes could pile up on the host for each VM, and the VM’s forwards would then refuse every new connection. Each relay now runs with a context of its own, which closing its forward cancels, under the forwarder’s lock as the close already runs, so the ssh is killed (exec.CommandContext), and a relay that ends by itself releases its context. Unit-tested with an ssh stand-in that never exits on its own: the relay ends, its process is gone and its slot is free once the forward closes (TestForwarderEndsStuckRelay), with no goroutine or file descriptor left under -race. A relay the VM holds open after its client has gone: mitigated. While a forward lasts, a VM that ignores EOF would keep each relay whose client on the host had closed, its ssh process and one of the 256, so a hostile VM could fill the forwarder’s relays with connections a browser had already closed. Each relay’s ssh is killed once its client has closed and the VM has sent nothing for 30 seconds, or 30 seconds after the client can take nothing more, so a VM keeps such a relay only by sending to it, and only for as long as the client keeps its side open for reading. The grace doesn’t run while a write waits for a slow client, so a client that stops reading holds the relay and its ssh itself, as it could by staying open, until it reads again, closes, or the relay’s forward or link goes. Unit-tested with an ssh stand-in that never exits: a closed client’s relay and a half-closed one’s both end after the grace when the stand-in is silent, and one the stand-in keeps talking to goes on past it, while a fully closed client’s relay, and one whose writes to its client fail, end within the grace however much the stand-in sends. A half-closed client that doesn’t read for many graces still gets all of the stand-in’s answer afterwards, and a relay whose write waits on a client that stopped reading ends when its context does (TestPipeSSHGrace, TestPipeSSHGraceWriteError, TestPipeSSHGraceSlowClient, TestRelayGrace, TestRelayGraceWriteError, TestRelayGraceSlowClient, TestRelayCancelEndsBlockedWrite, TestGraceTimer).
