The price is a client that half-closes and waits more than 30 seconds for an answer’s first byte, which is cut. A forward on IPv4 alone: ruled out except on a host without IPv6 or one that denies it. A bind on ::1 that fails with an error that says nothing of the port, such as EMFILE or ENOBUFS, closes the port’s 127.0.0.1 listener, is logged, and has the port tried again at the next report, so localhost never reaches the VM on one address and another program, or nothing, on the other. Only EADDRNOTAVAIL, EAFNOSUPPORT and EPROTONOSUPPORT, a host without IPv6, give IPv4 alone, and so do EACCES and EPERM on ::1 alone, logged, as a security module that denies IPv6 sockets would otherwise stop every forward. On such a host, a program that the module lets use IPv6 could still take ::1 on a forwarded port, and localhost would then reach it there, which is listed rather than refused because the alternative is no forwarding at all. Unit-tested with each error on ::1 (TestForwarderIPv6Failures). A forward’s listener out of files: confirmed, fixed. The loop that accepts a forward’s connections ended at any error, EMFILE included, while its listener stayed open, so a burst that ran the forwarder out of open files left that port taking connections that nothing answered until the forward went. The fix is that it tries again after a wait that starts at 5 ms and doubles with each failure in a row, up to a second, and logs only the first failure of a run (daemon.AcceptRetry), as the link session, a login’s forward and the proxy’s SSH agent relay do. A login’s forward also carries at most 16 connections at once, an ssh process each (TestAcceptRetry, TestForwarderAcceptRetries, TestLinksAcceptRetries, TestForwardLoopbackLimit). Channels the VM never closes in the master: listed. A hostile VM that never sends CLOSE for a killed relay’s channel can leave small channel entries, with no file descriptor, in the forwarder’s ssh master. At most 256 relays run at once, which bounds them, and no code change is needed. Not covered:
While a VM is stopped, another VM that serves on its listed port, such as localhost:5173, gets that port’s browser origin, with the site data, storage and service workers your browser keeps for it, as two projects on one port would on any host. A service worker that the other VM’s page registers there can still answer for that origin after the first VM takes the port back.
A VM can take a free port from 1024 up, or a listed one, on the host’s loopback that a program there expects to be its own, such as one that isn’t running yet or is restarting. What the VM serves there reaches whatever connects, so a page it serves to the user’s browser can reach the internet from the host, past the VM’s tier.
A host program that starts on a port while the VM has it forwarded still binds it when it listens on all addresses with SO_REUSEADDR, as most servers do (checked on macOS). Its loopback connections then reach the VM, because the forward’s address is the narrower one. A program that binds without SO_REUSEADDR is refused.
The VM can make the forwarder dial a host loopback port that’s in use and then close the connection at once without sending anything, because that’s how the forwarder checks for a port held only by ended connections. This happens at most once per port every second, as the VM’s listener on the port goes and comes back.
Servers only on the VM’s other addresses, such as its network address or a container’s, aren’t forwarded.
Other users on the host reach the forwards, because they’re on the host’s loopback.
UDP isn’t forwarded. Ports shows how to tunnel it over TCP.
A server that keeps a port while its forward couldn’t be made, because the host had the port, isn’t forwarded until it stops and starts again.
Another user on the host can take a VM’s ssh port while the VM is stopped or booting. Lima’s own ssh would then reach that user’s program, as it checks no host key, while devvm’s forwarder and ssh config pin the VM’s.
A VM started outside devvm, such as with devvm limactl start, or one whose forwarder ended, runs without forwarded ports until its next start through devvm, or until devvm ports changes its ports, which starts a forwarder with the host key devvm pinned at its last start.
End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, project, and network for the sandbox’s binds):
Lima’s rules ignore everything, the forwarder runs with the host key devvm pinned for the VM, and Lima’s ssh listens on the port the VM’s state records. A stopped VM whose ssh port a host program holds, on 127.0.0.1 alone and accepting no connections, starts on a new port that its state records, and the program keeps its own. A VM server on a port answers at the host’s 127.0.0.1 through the forwarder, while Lima’s hostagent has neither that port nor a UDP server’s port. The forward listens on the host’s loopback alone. A port that a host program has on every address keeps that program’s localhost connections while a server in the VM listens on it, and the forwarder logs that port as not forwarded. With listed ports, only those reach the host, whatever address the VM’s server is on. A listed port that a host program has is left out with a warning, and forwarded again once it’s free. On a running VM, devvm ports changes the forwarder’s ports at once. A port that devvm ports add lists has its server reach the host at once, and once devvm ports rm takes it out, it doesn’t. The VM’s boot ID is the same throughout, so it never restarted. devvm stop stops the forwarder, limactl stop outside devvm ends it (on macOS), and rm stops it and deletes its files. On macOS, a confined VM has a profile that denies every bind but its ssh port’s over TCP and unix sockets in its Lima folder, and the same binds that work outside the profile, a TCP port and a UDP socket on the ssh port, fail under it. Its hostagent listens on its ssh port alone, with Lima’s resolver off. Started again with Lima’s own forwarding rule put back inside the sandbox, the hostagent tries a VM server’s TCP and UDP ports and is refused, and has neither. The VM still works: ssh by name, devvm’s forwarder (on the host’s loopback alone), the proxy and the self-check. Its next start puts the ignore rules back. On a confined tier, with transparent mode stopped, DNS fails at once, because the guest’s programs ask 127.0.0.1 alone, and Lima’s network’s DNS address and the host’s address on it give no answer for a name, with transparent mode running too.
data.read-only-paths-on-linux#Read-only paths:
macOS locks .git’s hooks and config with the user-immutable flag, which Linux has only for root, so on Linux devvm makes them read-only where the VM sees them instead (.git protection on Linux hosts). Lima’s read-only-paths feature is native: QEMU serves the project folder over 9p from its own mount namespace, and devvm binds each path over itself there. Landlock, a FUSE layer and a 9p server of devvm’s own were ruled out: Landlock can’t make paths read-only below a folder it allows writes in, and the other two would put devvm’s code between the VM and every file of the project.
The guarantee: while a VM whose protection is on runs, nothing in it, root included, can write, replace, remove or rename .git’s hooks, config and the rest of what’s locked, of .git and of the submodules the check before its start found, or rename .git and those git folders. git in the VM commits as before. Nothing changes for this machine’s own git, and nothing persists once QEMU ends. Where the host can’t do it, the start is refused, or, for a VM made there, protection is off and devvm says so at each launch. devvm reports a VM that’s on and runs without its pins, at each launch of it and at devvm stop. One gap is listed, not closed: a file that a git command on this machine renames over a pinned one while the VM runs is the guest’s until it’s pinned again, and devvm names it afterwards.
What could break it: a path that’s a symlink, or under one, which mount(2) would follow out of the project folder; a file with another name; a host whose kernel refuses the namespace’s capabilities; a pinned file that a git command on this machine replaces while the VM runs; QEMU, or a process it starts, undoing a pin; what keeps the pins ending while QEMU runs; a pin reaching this machine’s own mounts; a VM started without devvm’s wrapper.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion’s privileged-helper and local-file classes). Leads, each ruled out, fixed or listed:
A symlink at a pinned path, or above one: ruled out. The check that lists the paths skips any that isn’t real (realInDir), and devvm _qemu pinned opens each path with openat2 beneath the project folder with RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS, refuses anything but a file or a folder, and binds the descriptor it opened, never the path. A refused path stops the start (TestRunPinned’s symlinked hooks folder). The VM isn’t running while QEMU’s namespace pins, so only this machine’s own programs could race the check. The guest undoing a pin: ruled out. The guest has no way into QEMU’s mount namespace, and 9p carries file operations, not mounts. A rename or removal of a mount point gets EBUSY, and a write EROFS (TestRunPinned; e2e). QEMU undoing a pin: ruled out for QEMU as it runs. It runs as you, with no capability in any namespace (CapInh, CapPrm, CapEff and CapAmb 0; its bounding set stays whole, which gives nothing with no new privileges) and no-new-privileges, and the pins belong to the namespace devvm made, where only CAP_SYS_ADMIN could unmount them. Listed: a guest that breaks out of QEMU runs as you, and can reach .git through a process outside the namespace (/proc//root), as it can every file of yours. devvm _qemu pinned, which keeps CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the namespace: ruled out as a way in. It reads only DEVVM_QEMU_PINS, which devvm gives it, binds only those paths with the same checks, and ends with QEMU. The guest can make it work by filling .git with files, but each burst of changes makes one look at the pins. What keeps the pins ending while QEMU runs: fixed. A separate keeper could end (an inotify limit, a misread parent) with QEMU running on, so devvm _qemu pinned runs QEMU as its child, killed when it ends, and a watch it can’t set up on any of the folders refuses the start. A change to a pin that goes unrecorded: fixed. devvm _qemu pinned refuses the start when it can’t write the events file’s first line. An event it can’t add later goes to Lima’s log with a warning, and to the file as a mark when it can, and the check names a record that’s unreadable, holds a mark or a line that isn’t an event, or lost its first line (git_pins_unrecorded). A file it can’t write at all after the start stays listed, with Lima’s log as its record. A git command on this machine replacing .git/config: listed, and reported. The new file isn’t pinned until devvm _qemu pinned pins it again, within milliseconds of the change, and in that window the guest can write it, put a file of its own in its place, which then gets the pin, open it for writing, a handle the pin doesn’t take back, or give it another name. A guest that loops can win that window. Each pin made again, or that can’t be, is recorded and named once the VM stops, and the watch’s sums, which run on Linux with the pins too, name a file whose contents changed. macOS’s flag has no such window. A file with another name (a hard link): fixed. A bind covers one name, and the guest could write the file through another, so a regular file to pin, or one in a folder to pin, with more than one name is refused at the start (git_pin_linked), and one that gets another name while the VM runs isn’t pinned again and is named. A VM that’s on running without its pins: fixed, reported. Each launch of a running VM and devvm stop read QEMU’s mounts and name each pin it lacks, .git and the git folders as mount points and the rest read-only (git_pins_missing). A pin reaching this machine’s mounts: ruled out. The namespace’s mounts are private, and a mount namespace owned by a user namespace gets none of its pins back to its parent’s (checked on Fedora: this machine’s mountinfo has none of them while the VM runs). What’s pinned, from the guest’s index: ruled out. The VM writes the index, so it can add submodules, but devvm pins only real git folders inside the project folder (hostsafety.IsGitDir), so the worst it can do is make a folder of its own project read-only to itself. DEVVM_QEMU_PINS: ruled out. devvm sets it for the start alone, _qemu checks that the folder is absolute and clean and that every path is relative and below it, and devvm takes it out of QEMU’s environment. An AppArmor profile for Ubuntu: ruled out for now. A profile with the userns rule for devvm’s binary, in a folder you can write, would let any program running as you put itself there and get what Ubuntu’s restriction holds back, so devvm offers none, and Ubuntu with the restriction on only watches .git. .git/commondir: listed. A file has to be there to be pinned, and devvm puts nothing in .git that git doesn’t, so the VM can still make one, which devvm reports at each check, as on macOS. A VM started without devvm: reported. limactl start runs QEMU without devvm’s wrapper, so without pins, as it runs without the network confinement (unenforced in devvm ls), and the next launch or devvm stop names its missing pins. Start VMs with devvm. Files owned by another user: listed. QEMU’s namespace maps only you, so a file in the project folder that another user owns shows as nobody’s in the VM. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, the project section on a Linux host, run on Fedora 43 and Debian 13): QEMU runs in a namespace with .git/config and .git/hooks mounted read-only, with no capability and no-new-privileges; root in the VM can’t add a hook, change, replace or remove the config, rename .git or move the hooks folder; git in the VM commits; git config on this machine reaches the VM, and the new config is read-only in the VM again; a submodule the VM adds is named by devvm stop, nothing of the namespace outlives the stop, and the next start pins the submodule’s config but not a folder that isn’t a git folder; devvm git-protect off on a running VM applies at its next start, which pins nothing; a VM left strict is on at its next launch, its diff.ignoreSubmodules = all taken out, and pinned again, and its next stop names nothing. Unit tests: TestRunPinned (a file renamed over a pinned one is pinned again and recorded; a hard link refuses the start), TestPinsInNamespace, TestKeep and TestProbePin on a Linux host, TestPinsOrder, TestPinsRefused, TestStartPins, TestPins, TestBindsWatch, TestReportPinEvents (a path’s repeats in one line, each record it can’t trust named), TestRecordPinEvent, TestPinWaits (a folder it can’t watch fails the watch) and TestPinsMissing (.git not a mount point, a config not read-only).
data.rules-by-method-and-path#Rules by method:
A rule can narrow a host name to some of its requests, by method, by path or both (how to use them, how the proxy judges them), and a secret of yours can go in for some methods alone. The design keeps two things: a request that a deny names doesn’t reach its host by any spelling of its method or its path that the threat check below covers, and an allow lets through only what it names, as every server would read it. What it leaves open, such as a form’s _method field and methods outside the list, is listed there.
What it’s built from: the policy files’ one line per rule, with the methods and then the path after the host (proxy.parseRule), --method and --path on devvm network allow, deny and rm (netpolicy.Rule), the proxy’s interception with the VM’s CA, which the secrets already use, and one matcher, proxy.match in internal/proxy/request.go, for rules and for secrets’ bindings, whose path check (plainPath) is the one that custom secrets’ --path had.
Decisions:
One line per rule, in the files there are. A rule stays a line of a policy file, api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/, which the one parser reads for the proxy, devvm network and devvm doctor (ParsePolicy), so layers’ and your own policies, -g’s and each VM’s take it as they are. A TOML or table form would be a second grammar beside the line one, for the same files. Every line that was a rule before means what it did, any method and any path. A line with spaces in it wasn’t a rule, so a hand-written one that has the new form gains a meaning: example.com GET, which the proxy skipped, now allows GET, and !example.com GET, a broken deny that denied everything, now denies GET alone. Both are what the line says, and devvm writes such lines only from --method and --path. Flags, not a quoted rule. RULE stays one word, as the cli skill has an argument, and --method and --path say how the rule narrows, so devvm network allow takes api.github.com --method GET,HEAD. The same flags on devvm secret set narrow a secret of yours, with none for every method, as --path and --scheme have it, so a saved secret’s methods can go without deleting it. A path is one value, as --path has one wherever it appears, so two paths are two rules. Allows add up, and a deny beats any allow, as before. An allow that narrows allows its host for the connection and only its requests one by one, and a deny that narrows refuses only its requests. So narrowing a host that a rule allows whole, devvm’s built-in GitHub among them, takes a deny, and devvm network allow warns when an allow by method and path would narrow nothing because the VM’s allowlist, or every VM’s with -g, allows its host whole (proxy.Allowlist.CoversWhole, rule_narrows_nothing). An allow that replaced the whole allows of earlier policies was ruled out: adding an allow would then take access away, and a user’s file would silently override devvm’s. Methods from a closed list. proxy.Methods are RFC 9110’s, PATCH and QUERY, without CONNECT. A method outside them isn’t a rule, so a typo in a deny, such as PSOT, is a broken deny, which denies everything until it’s fixed, rather than a deny of nothing. Paths as patterns, judged only in a plain form. * within a segment, ** for one segment or more, and a last / for everything below, which is what a binding’s path below which its value goes in already meant. Rather than decode and clean a path, which servers do differently, the matcher takes only a path that every server reads alike (plainPath), as custom secrets’ --path did. An allow, and a binding, match exactly, in case too, and never a path in another form, while a deny matches broadly, so each fails closed in its own direction. A deny matches in any case, every path that isn’t plain, the path above one that ends with /, as /gists is to /gists/ for most servers, and a last segment cut at its first ., as Rails and Spring route /admin.json to /admin and some servers drop a trailing dot. Cutting at the first dot rather than the last covers /admin.tar.gz too, and it refuses a few more requests than a deny names, which is the side a deny errs on. The cost is that a request to a host with path rules whose path has an encoded character, such as a file name with a space, is refused unless a rule without a path allows it. Rules that need requests force interception, or a refusal. A host whose requests the rules judge (hostRules.byRequest) is decrypted on :443 with the VM’s CA, and refused on any other port and without a CA, never tunneled unjudged. A host that a whole allow covers, with no deny that narrows, stays a tunnel, so the cost falls only where the rules need it. No host is spliced by name: devvm already decrypts GitHub, Anthropic’s API and the agents’ token endpoints for secrets, and git, the GitHub CLI and Claude Code work through it. A client that pins its certificates or ignores the VM’s CA fails its handshake, which devvm network log shows as TLS with the VM failed, so devvm notes that a host is now decrypted when a rule narrows it (rule_narrows) rather than refusing the rule. Addresses, CIDRs and ** can’t narrow, because an address has no name to make a certificate for and ** would decrypt every host. Methods a request names besides its own. Some frameworks take the method from a header, X-HTTP-Method-Override and its kin, which Rack and CGI read with _ for -, or from a _method parameter. The proxy reads every override-like header (overrideLike) and the query’s _method, and while a rule narrows a host by method, it refuses a request whose value isn’t exactly one method, such as a list, which servers read apart, rather than guess. Judging a _method in the query, rather than refusing every request with one, keeps a GET that names GET working, and an allow still needs every method named to be its own. A form’s _method in a POST’s body isn’t read: the proxy forwards bodies unread, so it’s judged as the POST it is. Every request is judged. The intercepted tunnel’s own HTTP server calls the handler for each request, HTTP/1.1 kept alive or HTTP/2, and so does each absolute-form request, so the rules and the bindings are asked for each one, with the files as they are then. A connection’s verdict and whether its requests are judged come from one read of the files (hostRules). A WebSocket is judged by its upgrade request, and an upgrade to anything else, such as h2c, and a CONNECT inside the tunnel are refused, as the bytes after them would pass unread. A tunnel opened before a rule narrowed its host stays a tunnel until it closes, as tunnels do for every new deny, and rule_narrows says so. The shared Nix cache’s own fetch from cache.nixos.org is judged as a GET of the path the VM asked for, so its rules apply there too. A proxy from another binary. A running proxy is the devvm binary that started it, and one from before this change reads a rule by method and path as a line that isn’t a rule: an allow it skips and a deny that denies everything. So devvm network allow, deny and rm warn, naming the VM, when they change such a rule while the VM’s proxy runs from another binary than their own (proxy_other_binary, by the devvm_sha256 of the config it started with, and when that config or this binary can’t be read, as devvm can’t tell), and the VM’s next launch starts the proxy again. A change to a host’s rule doesn’t warn, as every binary reads it alike. The bindings file stays version 1 while every binding has no methods and no path but a prefix longer than / that ends with / and has no *, so devvm secret set and rm, which write every VM’s file, don’t take an older proxy’s bindings away, logins included. Such a file reads alike to a proxy from after bindings gained paths; a 0.1.0 proxy ignores the path, which for the built-in bindings only widens OpenRouter’s key to all of openrouter.ai, as 0.1.0 bound it, until the VM starts again. Writing version 2 instead would cut those proxies’ logins. It’s version 2 only for a binding with methods or a pattern, which such a proxy refuses, so it puts no value in rather than put one in for every method, and devvm warns about each such VM whenever it writes one, from devvm secret set, rm and use or devvm agent login –api-key (Proxy.SecretsWritten, secrets_other_binary). A path of /, which that proxy’s prefix check refused with the whole file, is no path, as it’s every path. A custom secret’s path that devvm writes is marked a pattern (path_pattern), so a path saved as a prefix whose * was itself is refused rather than read as a wildcard. A blocked request gets 403 and a blocked event with its method and path, which devvm network log, /blocked and devvm-why show. A deny’s refusal is marked refused, so no allow is suggested, and a request that no allow covers suggests the allow of the whole host, never a path, which the VM chose. Learning stays by host: devvm network lock adds whole hosts, which you then narrow, because a log of methods and paths would turn every request a VM made while it learned into a rule to review. The floor and secrets. A rule that narrows names a host, so it lifts no floor: an internal address still needs an address rule. A secret of yours narrowed by --method goes in by the same matcher as an allow. A built-in secret’s or an agent’s login’s binding isn’t narrowed per VM: a deny by method and path in the VM’s own file already keeps the token from those requests, and refuses them outright rather than sending them with a placeholder, which is stricter, while narrowing the binding would need a per-VM record of known secrets and logins and a second way to the same end. What could break it: a spelling of a method or a path that a server reads as one a deny names and the matcher doesn’t; an allow letting through a request it doesn’t name; a host whose requests the rules judge reaching the far end without being judged; a request after the first on a connection going unjudged; the matcher being made slow by a VM’s path; and the bindings’ methods widening a secret.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode). Leads, each ruled out, fixed or listed:
A path’s spelling past a deny (case, a trailing slash, the prefix itself, a format’s suffix or a trailing dot, percent-encoding, .., //, \, ;): fixed. A deny of /gists/ let /gists through, and a deny of /admin let /admin.json and /admin. through, which it now refuses (TestDenyBypasses, TestMatchPath; FuzzDenyBypass checks, with a deny of /gists/ alone, that no path that a server could read as /gists or below, decoded once or twice, with \ as /, without ;’s parameters, cleaned and with its last segment’s suffix dropped, gets through). A deny of /config.json let /config.json. through, and every segment now matches with its trailing dots dropped too. Listed: a server that routes /admin-x or /admin~ to /admin isn’t covered. A method’s spelling past a deny: fixed. The deny compared each of three override headers’ whole value, so X-HTTP-Method-Override: DELETE, GET, X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE: DELETE and ?_method=DELETE got past a deny of DELETE. Now every override-like header in any spelling and the query’s _method are read, each word of a list is judged, and a value that isn’t exactly one method is refused while a rule narrows the host by method. Go’s url.ParseQuery skips a pair with a ; in it, so ?a=1;_method=DELETE hid its _method; a query with a ;, or one ParseQuery can’t read whole, is refused there too (TestDenyBypasses, TestAllowNarrowed, TestForRequestMethods, and FuzzDenyBypass, with a header of its choosing and an oracle that splits the raw query at & and ; itself). Listed: a method outside proxy.Methods, such as WebDAV’s, can’t be named, so a deny of writes doesn’t refuse PROPFIND, which a server that doesn’t speak WebDAV refuses itself; a _method field in a POST’s body, which the proxy doesn’t read, is judged as the POST it is; a header of another name that a framework is set to read the method from isn’t. An allow letting through more than it names: ruled out. It matches the method as written, every method the request names besides, and only a plain path in its own case (TestAllowNarrowed, TestPathWithin, which the bindings share). An allow that narrows nothing: fixed. An allow by method and path for a host that a whole allow covers, such as api.github.com, changed nothing, while devvm said the host was now decrypted; devvm network allow now warns that it narrows nothing, naming the VMs, with -g by each VM’s own allowlist, its file, layers and shared tools included, and names the deny instead. Where the whole allow names port 443 alone, the warning says the rule narrows only port 80’s plain HTTP (TestCoversWhole, network_narrow.txtar). Two reads of the rules for one connection: fixed. The CONNECT’s verdict and whether its requests are judged each read the files, so a change between them could tunnel a host whose new rules needed its requests; both now come from one read (hostRules). The shared Nix cache past the rules: fixed. Its fetch from cache.nixos.org asked only whether the host was allowed, and now meets rules by method and path as a GET of its path (TestNixCacheRulesByPath). A proxy or a saved secret from before this change: fixed. A proxy from another binary, or one devvm can’t tell, gets a warning when a rule by method and path changes (TestOtherBinaries). devvm wrote every bindings file as version 2, so a devvm secret set or rm after an upgrade took every running older proxy’s bindings away, its agents’ logins included, without a word; the file is version 1 now unless a binding needs 2, which an older proxy refuses rather than put a value in for every method, and writing one for such a proxy warns, devvm agent login –api-key’s write included (TestReadBindings, TestRefreshSecretsOtherBinary, TestDefine’s path of /). Checking whether an allow narrows anything after it’s written warns about a VM whose rules can’t be read rather than fail the change (TestNarrowNotesUnreadable). devvm 0.1.0’s own state, frozen in the repo, is the check that none of this moves what 0.1.0 wrote: its bindings files read as version 1 and are written again byte for byte, its proxies’ configs read and name the binary that started them, its grammar’s lines and verdicts are a table of their own (TestFixtureBindings, TestFixtureProxyConfig, TestV010Rules), and its app VM takes an allow that narrows nothing, a deny by method, a launch that leaves its bindings file as 0.1.0 wrote it, and a secret by method that makes it version 2 (fixture_v010_network.txtar). A custom secret’s path with a * saved as a prefix is refused (TestCustomsUnreadable). A host whose requests the rules judge, tunneled unjudged: ruled out. Its CONNECT is intercepted on :443 and refused anywhere else and without a CA, logged as a refused block (TestNarrowedNotDecrypted). Requests after the first, or smuggled in one: ruled out. Go’s HTTP server parses every request on the decrypted connection and calls the handler for each, HTTP/1.1 kept alive and HTTP/2 alike, and the proxy sends each to the host as a request of its own through its reverse proxy, so no bytes of the VM’s pass unparsed (TestInterceptRules over both). An upgrade other than WebSocket and a CONNECT inside the tunnel are refused. Listed: what a WebSocket carries after its upgrade request passes unread. Another host’s requests in the tunnel: ruled out, as before: a request that names another host gets 421. A VM’s path making matching slow: ruled out. Matching is a table over the pattern’s segments, at most 32, and the path’s, so a path of 20,000 segments against several ** takes well under a second (TestMatchPath). A rule a typo turned into nothing: ruled out for methods and paths, which a line that isn’t a rule can’t hold, so a deny with one is a broken deny that denies everything (network_narrow.txtar). A binding’s methods widening a secret: ruled out. A binding goes in only where its match allows, and the lookup checks a binding’s methods against the secret’s as it’s saved (fits), so a bindings file edited to drop them gets nothing (TestForRequestMethods, TestInterceptSecretMethods). Interception breaking a client: listed. A tool that doesn’t trust the VM’s CA fails at a host once a rule narrows it, which devvm says when the rule is added and devvm network log shows. What an allowed request carries: listed. A rule judges a request’s method, the methods it names and its path, not its body or its other headers, so a POST that an allow lets through, such as GitHub’s GraphQL, carries whatever the VM sends there, and a deny of POST refuses GraphQL’s reads too. A deny of git-receive-pack blocks pushes over HTTPS alone, not over ssh on github.com:22 or through GitHub’s Git Data API. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, network): a host that only devvm network allow --method GET --path allows, faked by the run’s company proxy, is decrypted with no secret bound to it. Two GETs below the path reach it, while a POST to the same path, a GET elsewhere, and a GET that names POST in X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE or in ?_method= get the proxy’s 403, never reach it, and are logged as blocked with their method and path, which devvm network log shows. A secret of yours with --method GET,HEAD goes into a GET and leaves the placeholder in a POST to the same host and path.
data.shared-tools#Shared tools:
Each tool version is one compressed EROFS image, loop-mounted read-only in each VM from a read-only share (details).
Measured (macOS): ten tools take 0.85 GB as images (1.5 GB installed), once for every VM and mix. Start times from an image match a local disk warm (node -e 0 13 ms vs 14 ms, claude --version 3 ms), and are 10–30 ms slower cold. Mounting five images takes 0.15 s; VM start is unchanged. Why images, not a shared folder: tools run from a virtiofs folder were about 3× slower warm (node -e 0 38 ms, claude --version 30 ms), the Mac’s case-insensitive disk collided 33 file names in Python’s terminfo, and mise’s version links failed in a read-only folder. Why not per-tool layers: an image chain for every mix of languages and agents repeats each agent’s files in every mix. Where they build: a tool image is shared by every VM whose tools need its key, and its build runs whatever runs as root in its build VM, so the key alone can’t keep one VM’s base out of another VM’s tools. A glibc tool image therefore always builds in a clone of devvm’s own Ubuntu base, on every backend, even for a VM on a --from Debian or Ubuntu image, whose code would otherwise run as root in the build of images that Ubuntu VMs then mount. --from VMs mount those images, because the tools are their projects’ own prebuilt releases, which run on any glibc new enough, and devvm still refuses a tool that needs a newer glibc than the image has (shared tools and glibc). A musl tool image can only build on Alpine, so it builds in the VM’s own --from base, and its key hashes that base’s digest, so it’s only ever another VM’s on the same container image. Before it builds, devvm checks the base’s record against what the images are for, and refuses any other base (tools_wrong_base, building tools). The cost is a build of devvm’s own base for a --from VM’s first glibc tools when it isn’t built yet. A VM for each tool: a tool’s installer runs as root in its build VM, and a tool image’s key hashes only its own tool’s inputs, so tools built together in one VM could write into each other’s images: through a shared work folder, a process left running until the next tool’s mkfs.erofs, or root replacing mise or mkfs.erofs itself. A fresh folder for each tool and killing its processes wouldn’t stop root, so each tool builds in a VM of its own, with an output folder of its own, and only that tool’s image leaves it (building tools). Measured on Fedora 43 (bare-metal x86_64, Lima with QEMU and KVM), building node, pnpm and bun took about 16 s in one VM and about 34 s in three, the same in two runs each, so each extra tool costs about 9 s, once for each tool version. Why a tool that doesn’t mount fails the launch: mise would otherwise download the same version into the VM on first use, which gives that VM a private copy, a download nobody asked for, and one that the VM’s tier may block, all without a word (how). Instead of Nix: Nix and NixOS were weighed as the way to deliver the shared tools and rejected, because NixOS breaks prebuilt binaries, and a Nix hidden under the tools shows through in read-only-store errors. The nix layer is separate, and you choose it. It gives a project that uses Nix a Nix of its own in its VM, with its own store and daemon, and the shared tools stay as they are beside it.
data.ssh-into-vms#ssh into VMs:
ssh for editors is native on Lima, so it isn’t an emulation, but its sessions keep a guarantee of devvm’s own: ssh and editors reach a VM by name through the entries devvm writes (security model), and a session gives the VM no way out it doesn’t already have, on a confined tier nothing past its proxy, whatever the VM runs as sshd.
What keeps a session from carrying the VM out. An ssh session can carry the VM’s traffic only through channels the host’s ssh asks for: remote forwards (-R, RemoteForward, a remote SOCKS forward), X11, a tunnel and the agent; OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel the server opens unasked. Root in the VM runs whatever sshd it likes, so the guarantee is the host’s ssh’s: devvm’s entry (first in ~/.ssh/config, so its options win over a Host *) sets ForwardX11 no, ForwardX11Trusted no, Tunnel no, PermitRemoteOpen none (so devvm needs OpenSSH 8.7 or newer; no IgnoreUnknown for older ones, as its first value wins and would replace a user’s Host * one, such as macOS’s for UseKeychain), ForwardAgent as the agent choice the VM’s current start was made with says, AddKeysToAgent no (no key of the host’s lands in an agent the session forwards), ProxyJump none and ProxyCommand none (no hop through something else), UpdateHostKeys no (the VM can’t add host keys; devvm reads them itself) and HashKnownHosts no. A RemoteForward can’t be turned off without refusing ssh -R on the command line too, so it isn’t (Not covered). VS Code’s Remote-SSH uses local and dynamic forwards (-L, -D) and is unaffected. Then sshd’s own settings, a defence for an honest VM (assets/layers/base.sh, /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-devvm.conf, first so it wins; Lima’s own forwards are local; it applies only where the image’s sshd_config includes sshd_config.d, as Ubuntu’s and Debian’s do, so for some --from images not at all, which only an honest VM’s defence loses):
Local forwarding (-L, -D, -W) is allowed: the VM itself connects, from its own network, which its tier confines like any other connection of the VM’s (checked). VS Code’s Remote-SSH reaches its server this way. Remote forwards bind only 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, and remote socket forwards are refused. A remote forward makes the host connect on the VM’s behalf, so one the host’s ssh asked for by mistake could reach anything the host reaches, its loopback services and sockets (docker.sock, agents) included, around the VM’s confinement. GatewayPorts clientspecified binds the address a request names, and PermitListen 127.77.*:* matches that address as text, so a request for localhost (ssh’s default), 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Only devvm on the host asks for a forward in that range, always by number. X11 and tunnels are refused too. Agent forwarding is allowed: the entry decides it from the SSH agent choice the VM’s current start was made with (ForwardAgent and IdentityAgent naming the VM’s proxy’s relay of that agent, yours or devvm’s own, which passes on only listing keys, signing and session-bind@openssh.com, so the VM can’t remove, lock or add the agent’s keys, as the SSH agents says). Refusing it would break devvm ssh-agent on in editors. These settings guard against the host’s ssh asking for a forward that devvm’s entry doesn’t pin (a RemoteForward under Host *, ssh -R), and only while root in the VM leaves sshd as it is. They’re a safeguard for an honest VM, and the boundary is the host’s ssh, which accepts a channel only for a forward it asked for.
What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels, and devvm’s Include line first in ~/.ssh/config, so its entries’ options win.
What could break it: host ssh settings that come before devvm’s entries.
Not covered:
A remote forward you ask for (ssh -R, a RemoteForward of yours): remote forwards you add lists what it leaves open. Sessions see the proxy’s password, as devvm’s own shells do, and VS Code and Cursor relay what VS Code and Cursor describes.
data.the-9p-cache-on-linux#The 9p cache on Li:
On a Linux host, Lima’s QEMU shares the project folder over 9p, and Lima mounts a writable 9p share with cache=mmap unless the VM’s config says otherwise (read-only ones with fscache). The guest kernel’s 9p client has a race in that mode, which Pierre Barre’s patch describes and which isn’t merged. A stat() that runs while a write() makes a file longer refreshes the inode from the server, which still has the old size, so the client takes that size over its own, and writeback then drops the pages past it. fsync succeeds, yet the file reaches the host empty or cut to 4096 bytes. Claude Code’s Edit tool sets it off, and so can any editor or build that stats files as they’re written. macOS isn’t affected, because Lima’s vz VMs mount the folder with virtiofs.
mmap has a second bug on the guest kernel devvm’s base boots (Ubuntu 26.04’s 7.0), which doesn’t depend on timing. After a process writes a file and takes a POSIX lock or an flock on it, its next read of that data returns zeros, though the host has the data and another process reads it. On such a lock, the 9p client writes the file’s pages back and drops them, and the next buffered read through netfs returns zeros. SQLite takes a shared lock at the start of each transaction, so its second transaction reads page 1 as zeros and stops with SQLITE_NOTADB (“file is not a database”), in its default journal mode as in WAL mode, and Gradle’s daemon, which keeps its lock files in .gradle/ open across builds, fails from its second build with “Unexpected lock protocol found in lock file”.
none, the one mode devvm sets. With cache=none, the client caches neither pages nor sizes, so every write goes to the host as it’s made, no stat can roll a size back and no lock drops data. It takes away shared writable mmap, which 9p allows only with writeback caching: a shared mapping of a file opened for writing fails with EINVAL, even one that’s only read. That fails at once, so nothing is lost, and only programs that keep a database or an index in the folder do it: SQLite’s WAL mode, whose -shm index is such a mapping, unless the connection sets locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE first, which keeps the index on the heap; LMDB, which Parcel’s .parcel-cache and Gatsby’s cache use; numpy’s memmap in r+ or w+ mode; Java’s read-write MappedByteBuffer; and the mold linker, which maps its output. Each of them works on the VM’s own disk, in its home folder or in a --clone VM, faster than under any 9p mode. mmap is faster than none only for large sequential files, about 7 to 12 times for 1 GiB, 1.3 to 1.5 times for cargo, and within 10 to 20% for git, npm, Vite, Go and rg, while the VM’s own disk is faster still by far, from about 2 times for npm ci to over 20 for a cold git status (measured on a Fedora 43 host). So devvm doesn’t offer mmap, which would trade two ways of losing data for what the VM’s own disk does better. It doesn’t offer loose or fscache either: they allow the same mappings, share mmap’s SQLite failure in a worse form, as the database can’t be opened again at all, and cache files’ contents and metadata in the guest without asking the host, so the guest misses edits you make on this machine, which devvm’s mounted folder exists for.
Existing VMs opt in. A VM made before devvm chose none has no mode in its state, and its starts leave its mount’s cache as it is, so an upgrade changes nothing in how such a VM uses its folder. Each launch of such a VM warns of the risk and names devvm mount-cache none, which ends the warning. none is the only value the command takes, so there’s no default to choose and no -g or config.toml key: every new VM gets none, and so does the folder devvm clone off mounts.
Build VMs’ output folders get none too. The shared tools’ build writes its EROFS images into a writable mount with mkfs.erofs, and --from’s conversion writes its disk into one with mke2fs, and neither maps its output for shared writing, so none takes nothing from them. The read-only mounts, agents’ folders and the shared tools, keep Lima’s fscache: the guest can’t write them, so the race has no write to drop.
One edit. The mode is a mount’s 9p: cache: option, which devvm compares with what limactl list shows and sets only where it differs, in the start’s one limactl edit, as any edit gives the VM new ssh host keys. limactl list fills each mount’s other 9p and sshfs settings in, at Lima’s defaults where lima.yaml sets none. A rewrite of the mounts keeps only the settings devvm knows (9p’s security model, protocol version and message size, sshfs’s cache, symlinks and SFTP driver) where they differ from Lima’s defaults, as the VM’s own, and drops the rest, so no default gets written into lima.yaml, where a later Lima’s would never reach it. A setting devvm doesn’t know, such as one a later Lima adds, is dropped too, for Lima to fill in, as devvm can’t tell its default from a value someone gave: it has no YAML parser to read lima.yaml itself. Editing only devvm’s own fields with --set instead (.mounts[0]["9p"].cache = "none", which Lima takes) would keep everything else as it is, but a moved folder or other agents’ folders would then need edits by index and by selector, which the CLI tests’ limactl stub doesn’t model, so devvm rewrites the mounts whole. The defaults are the ones in the golden fixture of real Lima’s limactl list (Lima 2.2), which TestMountRoundTrip checks, so a later fixture that changes them fails that test; until then, a known setting whose default a later Lima changes keeps the old default through a rewrite.
The remount. Lima’s cloud-init writes the new options into the guest’s /etc/fstab at the boot after the edit, but systemd has mounted the folder by the old line by then, and a 9p share keeps its tag. So that start unmounts the folder and mounts it again from /etc/fstab once the VM runs, with a minute’s limit and its output in the run log, then checks it with mountpoint and the folder’s line of /proc/self/mountinfo, which a POSIX awk picks by its mount point, as mountinfo escapes it (a space as \040). The check is portable: it runs with any guest’s awk, busybox’s too, and depends on no util-linux tool, such as findmnt, but mountpoint, which busybox has as well. devvm reads at most 4 KiB of the answer and only its last line, the mount visible at the folder where mounts are stacked, takes the mount’s options and its file system’s from it, refuses an answer that isn’t a mountinfo line, and names any mode but none and mmap as unknown. The remount’s and the check’s output pipes close a second after the commands end or time out, as limactl shell’s ssh can leave a child that holds them open.
The restart. A folder that isn’t mounted, one still mounted with the old mode, or a check that gets no answer gets one restart. The remount fails when something the VM started at boot holds the share, when a degraded start mounted it again by the old line, or on an Alpine guest with OpenRC, whose mount after a successful umount finds the share already mounted or busy. The Lima backend writes why in the run log, stops the VM under one status step, and fails the start with a RemountError, and the start’s caller (starter.start) starts the VM again once, all of it: a new proxy that follows the new hostagent, the .git pins applied in QEMU’s new namespace, the host keys read again for the new start, and the start recorded. The caller restarts the VM, not the backend, because the proxy follows one start’s hostagent and exits when the VM stops. The guest’s /etc/fstab has the new mode by then, so the restart’s boot mounts the folder with it, and that start’s Want.CheckCache asks the backend for the same check without the remount. That check is the last, and nothing it finds restarts the VM again. A folder that isn’t mounted stops the VM and fails the start before its setup or shell, as an agent’s writes there would land on the VM’s disk and vanish under the share at its next mount (mount_cache_unmounted, which names devvm restart), and so does a check that gets no answer (mount_cache_unchecked). A folder still mounted with the old mode is warned of (mount_cache_remount_failed). When the restart’s stop fails, a folder still mounted with the old mode is warned of the same way and the VM goes on with its proxy, and any other failure fails the start as a stop that failed (stop_failed, with the run log’s end), as the VM may still be running. The retry runs the whole start again, so the UI says each warning once a run, and the first start’s warnings aren’t repeated. An interrupt during the remount, a check or the restart’s stop, on any tier, leaves a cleanup that stops the VM, which stays until that stop returns, and an interrupt gets no restart. A known race, older than the restart, fails closed: another devvm command can start the VM between the restart’s stop and its start again, and the two starts then contend as any two starts of one VM do.
A running VM’s folder. A launch into a running VM whose folder has a cache mode checks it’s a mount point, one mountpoint -q over the VM’s ssh, and refuses one that isn’t (project_unmounted), or whose check fails to run or gives no answer (project_unchecked). The guest answers in words, as mountpoint’s exit codes differ between util-linux (32) and busybox (1).
Tool images built before. A shared tool’s build wrote its EROFS image into a writable 9p mount with Lima’s mmap before devvm chose none, so an image built then could reach the share empty or cut to 4096 bytes. devvm reads each EROFS image’s superblock when it asks whether the image is built: one that ends before its superblock does (1,064 bytes), empty included, or is shorter than the block count its superblock gives, counts as not built, and the next build makes it again. A build whose output is cut short is refused (tool_bad_output). It costs a 40-byte read per image, and a file that isn’t EROFS’s at all is left to the guest’s mount to refuse.
End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, the project section on a Linux host): a new VM’s folder mounts with none, as its state says, which /proc/self/mountinfo shows as no cache option at all, as the kernel leaves it out for none, where it shows cache=0x5 for mmap; 40 files written in 4 KiB extending writes with fsync, while a loop stats each, all reach the host whole under none; SQLite’s WAL mode fails in the folder under none and its default journal works; a shared writable mmap of a file there is refused with EINVAL, and SQLite’s WAL with locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE works and opens again; a VM whose state loses its mode, and whose lima.yaml gets Lima’s mmap by hand, keeps mmap with its lima.yaml unedited by devvm, and warns at each launch; and devvm mount-cache none gives it none at its next start, devvm restart, which mounts the folder again, and the warning stops. The tools and from sections build the shared tools and --from bases with their output folders under none, and the from section’s Alpine VM, given Lima’s mmap with no mode chosen, gets none from devvm mount-cache none at its next start, through the restart its failed remount gets, its folder checked by the portable check. On macOS, the project section checks that the folder is virtiofs and that devvm mount-cache refuses the VM’s. Two things under mmap are run and reported, not checked: the same loop, as the race is timing’s, which left 1 file of the 40 short in one run on Fedora 43 and none in others, and five new SQLite databases in the default journal mode, for the lock bug. The research behind dropping mmap (every tool above under each mode, on a Fedora 43 host with devvm’s Ubuntu 26.04 guest) was run by hand, outside the end-to-end tests. Unit tests: TestProjectCache, TestMountRoundTrip, TestStartSetsProjectCacheOnce (the remount’s outcomes, each failure a restart), TestStartRechecksProjectCache (the restart’s check, with no second restart), TestRemountInterrupted, TestRemountRestartStop (the cleanup kept through the restart’s stop, and a stop that fails), TestOptionsOfMountinfo, TestMountinfoPath and TestLastMount (real mountinfo lines: 9p with and without cache=0x5, stacked mounts, a path with a space) in the Lima backend, TestCutShort and TestBuiltCutShort in the shared tools, TestGuestMountOptions in the stubs, TestUpCacheMode, TestWarnMountCache, TestCacheAtNextStart, TestSwitchCache, TestSetMountCache and TestRemountRestart (one start again, with a proxy of its own), TestRemountRestartConfined (each start’s interrupt undo, an interrupt between the starts, a start again whose proxy fails), TestWarnOnce in the UI, and the CLI tests mount_cache (with the stubs’ remount-fails, and a policy line warned of once), clone_switch and the 0.1.0 fixture, whose VMs keep mmap and warn.
data.the-desktop#The desktop:
devvm desktop shows a VM’s desktop on this machine with VNC, and keeps two things: no one on this machine or the network reaches the desktop without the VM’s password, and the desktop gives the VM no new way out. Both hold whatever the VM’s own server does, because root in the VM can replace it (how).
What it’s built from: the built-in desktop layer (assets/layers/desktop.sh): Xfce and TigerVNC’s Xvnc from the distribution’s archive, and /usr/local/bin/devvm-desktop, which starts Xvnc on a socket of the VM’s user’s own (/run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock, mode 600 in a 700 folder), with no TCP port and no password, then an Xfce session. On this machine, internal/desktop’s Relay, which devvm desktop runs (internal/vm/desktop.go): a listener on 127.0.0.1 alone (platform.ListenLoopback, without address reuse), on the port the VM’s state records (the ports section’s host.desktop, chosen by ports.Allocator and among ports.Used), and for each viewer that passes its check, an ssh -W channel to the socket through devvm’s ssh config’s entry for the VM. Only a VM made with the layer has the desktop (image.DesktopLayer), because it adds about 370 MB to an image, so base and the VMs without it stay that much smaller.
Why devvm’s own relay, not the port forwarder: the forwarder forwards every port a VM listens on from its start, on the same port number. A VNC server on a port would have been on this machine’s loopback at every start, without anyone running devvm desktop, on a port another VM’s desktop or macOS’s own Screen Sharing server (5900) can have. The relay is open only while devvm desktop runs, on a port of the VM’s own, and checks the password itself, which the forwarder, a byte copier, can’t.
The password: VNC’s own authentication (RFB security type 2: DES of a 16-byte challenge, desktop.Response) is what macOS’s Screen Sharing speaks to a server that isn’t a Mac, and it takes 8 characters. devvm’s are random, from 31 characters (about 40 bits), checked one at a time with a second’s wait after a wrong one, so an online guess takes thousands of years. The relay checks it before it starts any ssh, so a wrong viewer costs the VM nothing. It’s kept in the VM’s state (the desktop section’s made.password, mode 600), shown only with the address (desktop_ready, a message, not the run log), and never sent to the VM, so a VM can’t use it to reach its own desktop’s port. Screen Sharing gets the address alone (open vnc://127.0.0.1:PORT), not the password, which would be in open’s arguments where any process on this machine reads them.
What keeps the VNC connection from carrying the VM out. Every connection starts on this machine: a viewer connects to the relay, and the relay asks devvm’s ssh for a local channel (-W) that the VM’s sshd connects to the VM’s own socket. The ssh asks for no session, agent, X11, tunnel or remote forward, and OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel the server opens unasked, as for the forwarder. What the VM sends back goes only to the viewer that connected. The VM’s server reaches nothing on this machine, so the VM’s tier holds as it is: the VM’s own connections still reach only its proxy, and devvm allows no new host for the desktop.
The clipboard: off unless --clipboard. Without it, Xvnc starts with AcceptCutText, SendCutText, SetPrimary and SendPrimary off, and the relay drops every ClientCutText from the viewer, extended clipboard ones too (internal/desktop/filter.go). It reads the viewer’s messages by their lengths (RFC 6143’s and the extensions TigerVNC offers: fences, continuous updates, desktop size, xvp, GII, QEMU’s key and audio events) and ends the connection on a type it doesn’t know, so nothing it can’t read reaches the VM. The other way, from the VM to the viewer, isn’t read: following the server’s ServerCutText would mean decoding every screen update’s encoding. A VM whose server was changed can send its clipboard to the viewer, so Screen Sharing’s Use Shared Clipboard setting is what keeps it off this machine then.
The local proxy, for browsers: Chrome, Chromium and Firefox ignore the password in the VM’s HTTP_PROXY and ask for it on every site, so the desktop’s session uses devvm-local-proxy instead (how), which the guest setup writes (assets/guest/sync.sh) and socat serves. It gives no program a power it lacked, because the password it adds is the one the VM’s environment already holds, and every program in the VM can read it there. What it must not do is hand the password to anything outside the VM, or send it anywhere but the VM’s proxy:
Where it listens: 127.0.77.1:3128 (proxy.LocalProxyAddr, proxy.LocalProxyPort), on the VM’s loopback alone (bind=), taking connections from 127.0.0.0/8 alone (range=). The port forwarder never forwards a server on that address (vmssh’s dialAddr, proxy.IsLocalProxyAddr), so a VM that forwards every port doesn’t put a proxy that needs no password on this machine’s localhost, where other users and programs would reach the VM’s proxy, and its secrets, without the password. Where the password goes: only to the VM’s proxy, whose address is written into the script with the password, never to an address a request names. It’s in the one Proxy-Authorization header the local proxy adds, after it drops the client’s, and devvm’s proxy removes that header before it forwards a request. A CONNECT’s tunnel carries nothing of the local proxy’s after its head. Web pages: a page can reach the loopback as a server, but its requests are in origin form (GET /), which the local proxy refuses with 400 before it connects anywhere. A page can’t send a CONNECT or an absolute-form request line, and DNS rebinding changes only the Host header, so a page can’t use the local proxy to reach the VM’s proxy. One request per connection: a request that isn’t a CONNECT goes with Connection: close, because the local proxy reads only a connection’s first head, so no later request on the connection reaches the VM’s proxy without the password, as it would otherwise get 407 and the browser’s prompt. The file: /usr/local/bin/devvm-local-proxy holds the password, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s, which is stricter than the VM’s /etc/environment, where the same password already is. The tier holds as it is: the VM’s proxy decides each request the local proxy sends, and a host the tier doesn’t allow gets its 403.
End-to-end checks (tests/e2e):
desktop (Lima): a VM of base without the desktop’s programs, which devvm desktop refuses (desktop_no_layer); then a VM with the desktop layer on the allowlist tier: the relay on 127.0.0.1 alone, its port and password in the VM’s state; a wrong password refused, the password let in, with the VM’s ServerInit and a screen update (TestE2EDesktop); Xvnc on its user’s socket (700, 600) and no TCP port, the clipboard off; the password in no file of the VM’s, no run log and no host process’s arguments while devvm desktop started; the self-check passed and no direct connection out, nor to the desktop’s port on this machine; the Xfce session’s proxy variables set to the local proxy, which listens on 127.0.77.1:3128 alone, takes curl without a password to an allowed host, gives a blocked one the proxy’s 403 (CONNECT and plain HTTP), refuses an origin-form request with 400, and isn’t forwarded to this machine; root’s own server in place of Xvnc (no password, its socket anyone’s, recording what reaches it): a wrong viewer never reaches it, and the viewer’s clipboard never does while its key event does; Ctrl+C closing the port; --clipboard on the same port, the clipboard on. Not covered: the VM’s clipboard sent to a viewer that takes it, by a server root changed; Screen Sharing itself, which no check drives, so its messages are the relay’s reading of the protocol; a program on this machine with the password, which reaches the desktop as you do; a program on this machine, or a VM that reaches this machine’s loopback, that keeps the relay’s 8 connections busy or keeps failing its check, which keeps viewers out for as long as it does, and gets no further; the browsers themselves, which no check drives, so that they read the session’s proxy variables rests on Chrome’s and Firefox’s documented behavior on Xfce, and the local proxy’s handling of requests on its unit test (netpolicy’s TestLocalProxy) and curl.
data.the-home-folders-copy#The home folder’s:
The old VM’s home folder is the VM’s own data, which nothing on the host trusts. devvm runs tar --one-file-system --ignore-failed-read in the old VM as its user, so the stream holds nothing from a mount, such as the project folder or an agent’s folder, and devvm reads it on the host with Go’s archive/tar and compress/gzip (copyHome). Nothing unpacks it on the host. Each entry is kept or dropped there, and only what’s kept is written, gzipped again, to home.tar.gz in the VM’s folder, 600 in folders that are 700:
Types: regular files, folders and symlinks, and a hard link only to a regular file kept before it. Devices, FIFOs and anything else are dropped, so the new VM’s tar creates none. Paths: each is cleaned, and one that’s absolute, has .. above the home folder or holds a control character is dropped, and so is the home folder’s own entry, so its mode stays the new image’s. So is any entry below a symlink kept before it, which tar would follow out of the home folder. Modes and owners: the setuid, setgid and sticky bits are dropped, and so are the entry’s owner and group, so the new VM’s tar makes everything its user’s. What devvm writes itself: ~/.config/devvm (its environment, which holds the placeholders of the VM’s secrets), ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, every agent’s login files, whichever agents the VM has, but Claude Code’s ~/.claude.json, whose per-folder state is history, the agents’ folders that devvm links to their mounts and the files it copies from the host, all of which the new VM’s setup writes again, and ~/.cache. devvm puts the file into the new VM once it has started confined, as the VM’s user, with tar --skip-old-files, so a file or folder the new image put in the home folder, ~/.bashrc among them, stays the image’s, its metadata included, and the shell that runs tar there reads only the image’s files. devvm’s setup runs after it and writes its own files again. The file is deleted once the new disk has it, when the remake is undone, and with the VM’s folder.
Not covered:
The home folder is as trusted as the old VM was. What its code wrote there, such as a shell snippet in ~/.bashrc.d, a ~/.ssh/config entry or an agent’s settings, runs in the new VM as it would have in the old one. The new VM is the same project’s VM, with the same reach, so this is no new access, and --clean-home starts from the image’s home folder instead. Its size isn’t bounded. A VM can make its home folder as large as its disk, and the copy then takes as much room on the host, besides the old disk and the new one. A VM can already fill the host’s disk through the project folder, which it writes, so this adds no new way to do it, and devvm checks for a VM’s free space before the remake. It’s on the host’s disk for the remake’s minutes, with whatever the VM keeps in its home, such as keys or logins it made itself. The VM’s disk holds the same data in devvm’s Lima home, with the same permissions, so a backup of the data folder sees it either way. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, with its data isolation and lifecycle and resource exhaustion companions):
Lead What holds it Check A hostile home folder writing outside the new VM’s home through .., an absolute path or a symlink it planted copyHome drops each, on the host, before the new VM’s tar sees the stream, and that tar runs as the VM’s user Unit tests (TestCopyHome) keep files, folders, symlinks and hard links to kept files, and drop .., absolute paths, control characters, devices, FIFOs, setuid bits, owners, hard links out of the home folder and entries below a symlink A hostile stream attacking the host It’s parsed by memory-safe stdlib readers and never unpacked on the host, and it’s written only into the VM’s own folder, which only devvm writes TestCopyHome refuses a stream that isn’t gzip devvm’s own files or the user’s secrets carried across ~/.config/devvm, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the agents’ logins and the files and folders devvm copies or links from the host are left out, and the new VM’s setup writes them again TestCopyHome leaves them out, and the CLI tests check that a saved home holds .bash_history without ~/.config/devvm The old VM’s code influencing the new VM’s setup or the restore itself The restore keeps what the image put in the home folder, its folders’ metadata included (--skip-old-files), so the shell that runs it reads the image’s ~/.bashrc, and devvm’s setup runs after it The CLI tests check the restore’s command and order; e2e checks that a file in ~ survives a remake and that the VM opens a shell afterwards A remake halfway losing the VM The old machine is kept aside until the new one has started with its home folder, the cleanup puts it back on any failure or interrupt before then and never deletes the new one after, and a killed devvm leaves the remake section, which the next devvm finishes, while devvm gc --orphans skips the VM and devvm rm deletes both machines. data.the-proxys-broker#The proxy’s broker:
A VM’s proxy reads every byte the VM sends out, and it runs as you, with your Keychain, your files and every socket of yours. A bug in it that a VM could drive, such as a parser that a crafted request takes over or a path that leads out of its folder, would reach all of that. So devvm _proxy is split in two: a broker, which keeps what only the host should do and stays unconfined, and a child, which reads the VM’s network and can be confined. The design keeps four things. A child that a VM takes over holds nothing of this machine’s beyond what it held for that VM. It can’t make the broker act for another VM, another secret or another file. It connects to no address that the VM’s rules and the floor refuse, such as this machine’s loopback, except for what a company proxy reaches for it. And the VM’s connections stay the child’s. Of each request, only the host name it looks up and the address it connects to cross to the broker, which opens the connection and hands it to the child, so no byte that the connection carries passes through the broker. Of a request’s own bytes, only a login’s token exchange reaches the broker, as captures in the broker below describe. Processes describes the two processes as they run, and this note is their design, with its threat check. On macOS the child runs under Seatbelt, and on Linux it confines itself with Landlock and a seccomp filter (the child’s sandbox), and on both its sandbox refuses it every connection of its own, so the broker looks up each name and opens each connection that the child asks for, once its own policy and floor allow the address.
Why a broker, and not values handed over at the start: the proxy looks each bound value up when a request needs it, in the Keychain, devvm’s secrets folder or an agent’s login file, which it refreshes on the host when it’s due (how the proxy puts them in). A login’s value changes with each refresh, and the proxy keeps it for 30 seconds, and any other value for 5 minutes. The proxy also saves the logins that a VM makes, and writes the VM’s bindings again. Values handed over once would be stale within the minute, and the child would need to write the store of logins. So the broker runs beside the child for as long as it does, and answers its questions.
What runs where:
Part Side Why The VM’s proxy port, every request and tunnel, the rules and the floor, the SNI check, interception, putting values into headers, transparent mode, devvm.proxy’s endpoints, and the bounds on what a VM makes the proxy hold (maxConns and admit, maxConnects, maxRequests) child they read the VM’s bytes, which is what the child is for The event log, network.jsonl, and the child’s own lines in proxy.log child each request logs an event, so a hop to the broker would sit on every request’s path The shared Nix cache, its fetches and its files child its fetches go through the floor and the company proxy as the VM’s requests do, and each VM’s Nix checks what it gets The company proxy as the requests’ upstream, with its credentials child, with the proxy secret’s value from the broker the company proxy takes its password with each plain HTTP request, so whatever sends those requests holds it Looking up a name, and opening a TCP connection to an address or to the company proxy broker, which hands the connection to the child, and judges each address again with its own policy and floor a sandbox can’t tell this machine’s loopback, its own addresses and the LAN apart from the internet as a rule changes (below), so the child’s sandbox refuses it every connection of its own Each value’s lookup: the Keychain through security, devvm’s secrets folder, an agent’s login file and its OAuth refresh (IO.Secret) broker they need the Keychain and your files Capturing logins: the token request to the endpoint, its reply, saving the login and writing the bindings again (IO.Capture) broker the endpoint’s reply holds the login’s real tokens, its refresh token among them, which never enter the child The SSH agent’s relay, its socket and its connections to the agent broker its filter is the guarantee, and a child with the agent’s socket could send the agent anything Holding the backend’s logs to their cap (IO.KeepLogs, Config.VMLogs) broker they’re in Lima’s folder for the VM, beside its disk and its lima.yaml, which a child must never write Connecting to a link’s socket broker, which hands the connection to the child devvm’s run folder holds every VM’s link sockets and agents’ relays, and the ssh masters’ control sockets, each a way into a VM Finding a request’s host in the links’ list child, checked again by the broker the child decides for each request whether it’s for a link, before any rule proxy.json, the CAs’ files, the lifeline, the status file and the pid file broker the child gets what it needs of them over the socket, so it needs no read of the VM’s run folder The files that change while the proxy runs: the policy files, the bindings file and the links’ list the child looks at them, the broker reads them below The files that change. The proxy reads each of these files again when its modification time, size or inode changes, which it checks with a stat on every request. The child keeps that check, because Landlock leaves stat unrestricted and Seatbelt can allow it alone (file-read-metadata), and asks the broker for the file only when it has changed. The broker reads the file with the proxy’s usual checks, its owner, its mode, at most 1 MiB, and a symbolic link followed or refused as each file allows, and returns its bytes with the stamp of the file it read. The child parses them and keeps that stamp, so a change still applies to the next request, and an unchanged file costs no hop. Both write proxy.log, each line saying which side wrote it. A rotation takes the file’s lock and checks its size again, as the event log’s does, so the two writers rotate it once, and the broker reads, copies and empties the file through the descriptor it was given, never by its path.
The folders the child writes are the VM’s. A child that a VM takes over can put anything in the folders it writes, so the unconfined code that later opens them reads them as it reads a file a VM can write. The child may create only regular files there. On Linux it never gets Landlock’s rights to make a link, a FIFO, a socket, a device or a folder, and the Nix cache’s nar/ folder is made before it confines itself. On macOS its profile refuses creating anything but a regular file, and hard links, which the follow-up checks there. devvm, devvm _links, devvm network log, devvm network lock, the port forwarder, the link session, devvm gc’s trim of the Nix cache and the cache’s lock open, rename, empty, change and delete files in those folders through internal/safefile, never following a link and taking only a regular file with one link that’s yours, or through an os.Root of the folder. The broker makes the cache’s nar/ folder and sets both folders’ modes the same way (makeNixFolders), deleting anything at nar/ that isn’t a folder, a link as itself, and making a folder in its place, which its log warns of, so its chmod never reaches a folder of yours. A confined child can’t leave a link there, so this is for one that runs without Landlock or Seatbelt. So a link that a child leaves where proxy.log, network.jsonl, links.log, ports.log or nar/ was never leads devvm to your files, and a FIFO there never hangs a command. A build’s child writes events.jsonl and proxy.log in a logs/ folder of its own inside the build proxy’s folder, apart from its config, its policy and its status file.
What the child needs, which what confines it holds it to:
Its descriptors: standard input from the null device, proxy.log as its output and its error output, the socket to the broker as descriptor 3, and the VM’s proxy port’s listener, which the broker opened, as descriptor 4. Its environment: TZ, SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR when devvm has them, so the roots it trusts on Linux are the proxy’s usual ones, and GODEBUG, to which it adds updatemaxprocs=0, so Go’s runtime doesn’t read its cgroup’s CPU limit again as it runs. It gets nothing else, so it never sees a token in the environment of the shell that started devvm, or the status file’s name. Files to read and write: the VM’s logs folder, vms//logs/, where it creates, appends to, reads, empties and renames its two logs and takes the event log’s lock, which devvm _links takes too, and for a VM with the nix layer, the shared Nix cache, cache/nix-cache/ and its nar/ folder, where it creates, writes, reads, lists, deletes and renames regular files, from the top folder into nar/ among them, and takes .lock. A build’s child writes its own logs/ folder instead. Files to look at only: the policy files, the bindings file and the links’ list, with stat. What the system gives it: what a Go program reads to start, the system’s roots, its time zone, and the host’s own addresses. On Linux, it loads the roots and its time zone before it confines itself. On macOS, crypto/x509 asks trustd through com.apple.trustd.agent, after CoreFoundation looks at the metadata of the program’s folder for its bundle. The floor reads the host’s addresses every 30 seconds (hostAddrs), through a netlink route socket on Linux and the route sysctl on macOS. It needs no resolver, because the broker looks up its names. The network: no connection of its own. It accepts on its listener, reads and writes the connections it accepted and those that the broker hands it, and on Linux binds its netlink route socket, which reaches the kernel alone. It sends no UDP, and it listens on nothing. Nothing else: no read of your home folder or of devvm’s data, config or run folders, no Keychain, no unix socket but its own two descriptors, no Lima folder, no signal to another process, no tracing, and no fork or exec. The floor fails open if it reads no addresses for the host, because hostAddrs then refuses none of them, so the child’s check after it confines itself needs a read of the host’s addresses that isn’t empty, and a later read that fails keeps the last good one.
The protocol. The broker makes one unix stream socketpair, close-on-exec from the start (SOCK_CLOEXEC on Linux, and syscall.ForkLock held with CloseOnExec on macOS), so no program the broker runs, such as security, holds an end, and the child’s end is its descriptor 3. Each message is a frame: a 4-byte big-endian length, then a JSON object of at most 2 MiB with its type, its id and its fields, which the reader decodes refusing unknown fields. Bytes, such as a file, a body or a header’s value, cross as []byte, which JSON holds in base64, so encoding/json never changes bytes that aren’t UTF-8 and a 1 MiB file takes about 1.4 MiB of a frame. Every read is a recvmsg with room for one descriptor, and a read whose control data was cut short (MSG_CTRUNC) breaks the rules. Each read asks for no more than the bytes left in its frame, and the writer sends each frame whole under one lock, with its descriptor on the frame’s first bytes, so a descriptor always arrives with the frame it belongs to. The broker’s first frame is start, with the protocol’s version, 1, the SHA-256 of the broker’s own executable, which the broker reads first thing as it starts, and everything the child runs with, as the start below says. The child answers ready, with the same version, the SHA-256 of its own executable, which it reads before it confines itself on Linux and through its profile on macOS, the address it serves and how it’s confined, or failed, with why. After that only the child asks, and the broker answers each request with a frame of the same id, in any order:
Request What the child sends What the broker answers value a binding’s kind, agent and name (valueKey) the value and when the broker looked it up, or an error file a watched file’s number in the start’s list the file’s bytes and the stamp it read, or that it’s missing or refused, and why link a request’s host and port a connection to the link’s socket, as the frame’s one descriptor (SCM_RIGHTS), or an error token a captured request’s host, its clean path, method and query, its headers, at most 64 KiB, and its body, at most 64 KiB (captureRequestMax) the reply the VM gets, its status and its few headers, and the agent whose login it was, or an error lookup a host name, absolute, with its one trailing dot its addresses, or an error dial an address and a port, or which company proxy, https or http a TCP connection to it, as the frame’s one descriptor, or an error cancel the ID of a lookup or a dial it gave up on, as the frame’s own nothing of its own: that request ends with an error Only a lookup and a dial can be cancelled, with a cancel frame of the request’s ID, below. A value’s lookup and a token exchange run to their 20 seconds whatever happens to the VM’s request, so the broker keeps a value it looked up for the next request. The child stops waiting for a reply once its request has ended, drops the reply when it comes, and holds the request’s place under its type’s cap until then, so it never has more under way than the broker allows, and it closes a link’s or a dial’s connection that it no longer wants. A reply that wouldn’t fit in a frame is sent as an error instead, so no request waits for one that never comes, and the few headers a token’s reply keeps are 1 KiB each at most. An error reaches the child as one of a few codes, not_found, refused, busy, too_long or failed, or for a lookup, no_such_host, timeout or temporary, which the child turns back into the resolver’s error that its block’s reason and its second try need, and the broker’s own log keeps its text, which can name a lookup’s or an endpoint’s details. The broker’s start frame has the start’s deadline to be written, so a child that never reads can’t hold the broker either.
Bounds, and failing closed. The broker serves one value at a time, as the proxy’s lookups go one at a time, at most 8 tokens at once, as captureReads allows, 4 files, 256 links, which is the link session’s own cap on a client’s connections, 256 lookups and 1024 dials, as many as the child’s tunnels at once (maxConnects).
