It answers a request past its cap with an error, which a child that keeps the same caps never gets, because the broker gives a request’s place back as its reply starts to go, before the child can send the next. A reply that waits for the socket keeps its place, so a child that stops reading holds no more of the broker’s answers than the caps. It keeps each value it looked up for as long as the proxy keeps it, so a child that asks again and again makes the broker look a binding up at most once in 30 seconds or 5 minutes, and on macOS run security that often. It keeps a failed lookup for 5 seconds, so a child can’t make it run security or try a refresh back to back. The child keeps a value only until the broker’s lookup is that old, so no value is kept longer than the broker keeps it. The broker keeps its own watch on the bindings file, the links’ list and the policy files, as the proxy does (watched), looking at the first two on every value, link and token request, and at the policy files on every dial, whatever the child asks, so a binding or a link that devvm takes away is gone for the next request, and a change to the bindings file drops the broker’s values and its failed lookups, as it drops the proxy’s values, so a secret set right after a failure goes in at the next request. Some frames end the pair: one over 2 MiB, one that isn’t JSON or has a type or a field that the version doesn’t know, a second start, a reply to no request, a frame that carries a descriptor from the child, and a ready whose version or executable’s SHA-256 differs. The child takes a descriptor only with a link or dial reply that says it carries one, and closes any other. For each, the broker stops the child, logs the rule the frame broke but never its bytes, and exits, and the VM has no network until devvm starts its proxy again. A request that the broker refuses, such as one for a binding that isn’t in the file, gets an error instead, which the child handles as it handles a failed lookup. No value goes in, a capture gets 502, a link gets link_refused, a name that the broker can’t look up gets the block of any name that doesn’t resolve, and a connection that the broker refuses or can’t open gets connect failed.
Naming nothing but its own VM’s. Every request names something in the broker’s own config, which is one VM’s, so the child can’t reach another VM’s binding, any other secret or any file:
value: the broker finds the key in its own read of the bindings file that its config names, and looks the value up with its own copy of that binding, never the child’s, so the binding’s id and its methods are checked as for any binding (fits). A key that the file doesn’t hold now gets an error, the company proxy’s secret’s included, which no binding names. file: a number in the broker’s list, which is the bindings file, the links’ list and the policy files in the config’s order, so no path crosses the socket. link: the broker finds the host and port in its own read of the links’ list (links.find), and connects to LinkSocket of its run folder, its VM, the entry’s address and its port, only for an address in 127.77.0.0/16, trying a few times for a full backlog as the proxy does. token: the broker finds the endpoints in its own captures that the host, the path and the method match, which gives the agents, refuses a request that matches none, and puts in the VM’s name itself (Exchange.VM). lookup: the broker takes only a host name in the proxy’s own form (NormHost, HostOK), with its trailing dot, and no address, and looks it up as the proxy does, so a child learns no more than it could ask this machine’s resolver. dial: the broker connects to an address only once its own read of the VM’s policy files and its own read of the host’s addresses allow it, as the floor does, and to a company proxy only at the address of its own config. Captures in the broker. For a captured request, the child does what the proxy does for any request up to the request’s body. It judges the host and the request by the VM’s rules, intercepts it and reads the body. Then it sends the request in token. The broker runs IO.Capture’s Request, and sends the request to the endpoint’s host from its own config, on port 443, through the company proxy when there is one, and trusting the system’s roots and upstream_cas, as an OAuth refresh does. It reads the reply, runs Response and returns what the VM gets. The broker does what the proxy does with a captured request. It drops a 1xx, refuses an upgrade, leaves gzip to Go’s transport, sends the VM’s headers on without the hop-by-hop ones and Proxy-Authorization, takes a successful reply of at most 1 MiB and returns only keepHeaders’ headers with it. It returns an error reply as it is, up to the same 1 MiB, rather than streaming it through, and gives one that’s longer a 502. An error reply to a request whose body Request changed comes back as its OAuth error code alone (errorReply). The child logs the login event, naming the agent that the broker returned, and guard stays in the child, for the host’s other replies. So the real tokens in an endpoint’s reply, a new login’s refresh token among them, and the id_token that Request puts into Codex’s API-key exchange, never enter the child, and a child can’t save tokens that the endpoint didn’t issue.
Connections through the broker. The child judges each request as the proxy does, by the VM’s rules, then the floor, which looks the name up and keeps the addresses that aren’t internal or that a rule names. It asks the broker for each lookup, and then for a connection to each address it kept, one at a time, as the proxy dials them, or for a connection to the company proxy when one applies. The broker answers a dial for an address only when that address passes its own copy of the floor’s check: no deny names it, and it’s neither internal nor this machine’s own, or a rule names it, by the broker’s own read of the VM’s built-in policies, its policy files, which it looks at on every dial, and the host’s addresses, which it reads every 30 seconds, or the config says the VM is open. Then it connects over TCP, with the proxy’s 15-second timeout, and hands the connection to the child as it hands a link’s. So a child that a VM takes over connects to this machine’s loopback, its own addresses and the private and link-local ranges only where a rule names the address, as the VM does, and it reaches the internet as the VM does. Two ways stay open, as they do for the VM: a company proxy, which the child speaks to with its password and which reaches whatever it reaches, this machine’s loopback included when it runs on this machine, and a host on this machine’s network whose address is public, such as a neighbour’s global IPv6 address, which the floor counts as the internet.
A rule applies from the next connection. devvm network allow 127.0.0.1:5432 changes the policy file, the child sees its new stamp at the next request and asks for it, and the broker’s own look at the file at the dial that follows sees it too. A rule taken away is gone for the broker’s next dial as well, so a connection opened as a rule goes may fail, but never one that no rule allowed. The broker also looks at its own copy of the policy files at each file request for one of them, so its copy is never older than what it gave the child, but in the moment between the two looks. A rule for a name, such as localhost:5432, judges the name, and the floor needs a rule for the address too, such as 127.0.0.1:5432. Which addresses: the broker judges each address as the floor does, unmapped, so an IPv4-mapped ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is 127.0.0.1, a NAT64 or 6to4 address is judged by the IPv4 address in it, ::1 and every address in 127.0.0.0/8 are loopback, and 0.0.0.0 and ::, which reach this machine’s own services, are internal. It refuses an address with a zone, such as fe80::1%en0, which no rule can name, and a port outside 1 to 65535. The company proxy: the child asks for https’s or http’s, and the broker connects to the address in its own config, by name, through the system’s resolver, so a company proxy on this machine’s loopback, such as a VPN client’s, works, and the child can name no other address that way. The child still speaks CONNECT and plain HTTP to it, with its password, so the company proxy, not the broker, decides where those go. The host’s addresses: the broker reads them before it starts the child, and a read that fails or finds none fails the start, as the child’s own check does, and a later read that fails keeps the last good one. A request given up on: the child sends cancel with a lookup’s or a dial’s ID once the VM’s request has ended, or a lookup’s own deadline has passed, and the broker ends that lookup or connection, answers it with an error and frees its place, so slots that a VM’s abandoned requests held don’t fill the caps. A cancel gets no answer of its own, and one for an ID that isn’t under way is dropped. Lookups: the broker looks each name up through this machine’s resolver, as the proxy does, so the child sends no DNS, and a resolver on this machine’s loopback, such as systemd-resolved’s 127.0.0.53 or a dnsmasq on 127.0.0.1, answers the broker. The child sends no UDP at all. What doesn’t change: the open tier’s broker allows every address, as the floor does there. Transparent mode’s connections, the Nix cache’s fetches and the connections that put a value in go through the same dial. A link’s connection is the broker’s already, through its link request, and a capture’s token request is the broker’s own. The sandboxes: on macOS the child’s profile allows no network out at all, neither TCP nor UDP to any address, nor any unix socket, and Seatbelt checks every connect and every send with an address, while writes on a connection it accepted or was handed need no rule. On Linux, Landlock from ABI 4 refuses every TCP connect, and from ABI 10 every UDP bind and send, as the child’s ruleset handles those rights and allows no port, and the seccomp filter refuses the child every socket but a netlink route socket, connect and socketpair outright, and MSG_FASTOPEN on sendto, sendmsg and sendmmsg, because TCP Fast Open connects a socket as it sends, and the listener, once a shutdown has closed it, is a TCP socket that could connect again. A filter reads only a call’s arguments, never what they point to, and these checks need nothing else, so no other thread of the child can change what the filter checked. Without the sandbox: a child that runs unconfined, or on a Linux kernel without seccomp filters, still asks the broker for every connection, but nothing stops a child that a VM took over from connecting itself, so its confinement says so (partial with no-seccomp, or none), and devvm doctor warns of it. The Secret type on the socket. The frames are the third kind of file that holds values, after proxy.json and vm.json, so they get wire types of their own, as those files have (where secret values live). The start’s password, the company proxy’s password, the CAs’ keys, and a value or token reply’s value each cross as a string in a wire struct. Only the protocol’s encoder fills that string, with Reveal and its //nolint:forbidigo on the line, and the decoder makes it a redact.Secret at once. Nothing logs a frame, and an error names only its type and the rule it broke. The company proxy’s URLs from the environment cross as strings, as they are in proxy.json.
The start:
devvm starts the broker as it starts the proxy, devvm _proxy -config FILE, detached, with its output in proxy.log, and waits up to 5 seconds for its status file. The broker reads the config, looks up the company proxy’s password when the config names the proxy secret, reads the CAs’ files, listens on the VM’s proxy port, starts the agent’s relay and the keeping of the backend’s logs, and makes the socketpair. It starts the child, devvm’s own binary with the arguments _proxy-child -for FILE, through daemon.Spawn, which gains the descriptors to pass (ExtraFiles) and an environment that its caller chooses. On Linux it runs /proc/self/exe, which is its own file even once an upgrade has replaced the file at its path. -for names the config only so the child can be told apart, and the child never opens it. Once the child runs, the broker closes its own copies of the listener and of the child’s end of the socketpair. It sends start, which also says how the broker started the child, under Seatbelt or unconfined and why. The child checks the executable’s SHA-256 against its own, makes its server from the start, opens its logs and the Nix cache, loads the system’s roots and its time zone, checks that it can read the host’s addresses, confines itself where its platform does that in the process, checks that the confinement holds by opening its broker’s config, which it must be refused, and answers ready with how it’s confined. Within 4 seconds of its own start, the broker writes the child’s pid file, run/proxy-child.pid, and how it’s confined, run/proxy.confined, which devvm doctor reads only while the broker runs, and which Proxy.Stop removes with the pid file, and then the status file with its own pid and the address (daemon.Ready), which is what devvm waits for. The status keeps the address alone, which devvm compares with the config’s. When the child answers failed, or doesn’t answer in time, the broker stops it and exits with the reason in proxy.log, so devvm reports proxy_start_failed. The end. The two end together, and neither starts the other again:
The lifeline is the broker’s. When the VM’s hostagent ends, the broker closes the socket, and the child closes its listener first, then closes its connections, waits up to 5 seconds for its handlers as the proxy does, and exits. The broker waits for it, and kills it a second past that, then removes the agent’s socket and exits. devvm stop’s SIGTERM reaches the broker through its pid file. The broker sends the child SIGTERM through its daemon.Handle, which ends it at once, as SIGTERM ends the proxy, and kills it if it hasn’t ended within a second, inside the 2 seconds that devvm waits before its own SIGKILL. So a stop ends both, and the next start finds the port free. A broker that ends any other way, SIGKILL included, leaves the socket closed, because nothing else holds its end, and the child reads its end, closes its listener and exits. The child reads the socket for as long as it runs, so this needs no signal. A child that a VM has taken over can ignore the socket’s end, so on Linux the broker also starts the child with PR_SET_PDEATHSIG set to SIGKILL, from a goroutine that holds its thread (runtime.LockOSThread) until the child is reaped, because Linux ties that signal to the thread that started the child rather than its process. A child that ends, crashed or killed, ends the broker, which logs how it ended and removes the agent’s socket. Neither starts the other again, so a child that fails at once can’t loop, and the VM has no network until devvm’s next command starts its proxy again, as after a proxy’s crash. Finding them. To devvm, the broker is the proxy. Its pid file, its status file and its arguments, _proxy -config FILE, which daemon.Proc matches, stay as they are. The broker signals the child through the daemon.Handle that Spawn returned, which reaps it. devvm also finds the child as a daemon.Proc, by run/proxy-child.pid and its arguments, _proxy-child -for and the VM’s config, so Proxy.Stop and devvm gc --orphans stop a child that outlived its broker, checking its arguments before each signal as they do for every background process. The broker writes that pid file only once the child said it’s ready, after sandbox-exec has run it, so the arguments are already the child’s own. Its arguments don’t contain _proxy -config, so every pattern that finds a VM’s proxy finds only the broker. The testscript runner’s pkill -f of _proxy -config in the sandbox ends the brokers and so their children, and the runner also ends _proxy-child -for in the sandbox, in case a test killed a broker in a way that kept its child. The end-to-end checks find the child by [_]proxy-child -for and the config, and a check that a proxy is gone checks both.
The build proxy is the same broker and child, which backend.ProxyStarter starts and stops through its daemon.Handle, and which ends the child as devvm stop does. Its broker has no secrets, captures, links, agent or backend logs to keep, so it only looks up the proxy secret when config.toml’s company proxy names one, and follows the build VM’s lifeline. Its child writes events.jsonl and proxy.log in the build proxy’s logs/ folder and reads nothing else, so the end-to-end checks that look for a build’s logs look there. One way for both keeps one code path, and a build runs code that devvm trusts no more than a VM’s.
Upgrades. The config doesn’t change. proxy.json keeps its fields and ConfigVersion stays 1, so every release’s frozen configs still read and write back byte for byte (TestV010ProxyConfigs), and the implementation starts a broker and its child on each of them. A proxy that a devvm before the split started runs as one process until the VM’s next launch, which starts it again because its config’s devvm_sha256 differs, as every upgrade does, so a running VM keeps its network through the upgrade. An older devvm that stops a VM’s proxy after a downgrade finds the broker by the same pid file and arguments, and the child ends with it.
Confining the child. Two follow-ups hold the child to what it needs, as listed above, and where a platform can’t, the child runs unconfined, says so in ready, the broker logs a warning and writes it to run/proxy.confined, and devvm doctor warns of it for each running VM. The child says how it’s confined in one line of words from a fixed set, its level, full, partial or none, then what confines it, and for a child that isn’t fully confined, why (proxy.Confinement, in internal/proxy/confine.go), which the broker refuses unless it parses, so devvm never prints what a child wrote (the child’s sandbox has the table). Both follow-ups share it, the check that the confinement holds (checkConfined, which opens the broker’s config) and the hook where the child confines itself in the process (confineSelf, by platform), which on Linux calls internal/landlock and turns what it got into the line (landlockConfinement), and which confineChild bounds to 2 seconds (confineWait). The child gets the hook through IO’s confine, which ChildMain sets, so a test’s child in the test’s own process confines nothing, and a confinement that fails, rather than one the kernel can’t give, fails the start. Each follow-up’s start fits in the broker’s 4 seconds, so a sandbox that refuses what the child needs fails the start rather than hang it, and on macOS a broker and its child under Seatbelt are ready in about 40 ms, or 350 ms for the first start of a binary that macOS hasn’t run before.
macOS, with Seatbelt: the broker starts the child through /usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p PROFILE, with a profile that denies everything by default, so the child is confined from its first instruction, and the profile is an argument, never a file on disk. internal/seatbelt owns it (ChildProfile), with the quoting and the real paths that Lima’s hostagent’s profile uses too, and the broker gets it through proxy.IO.Seatbelt, which only devvm _proxy on macOS sets, because internal/proxy imports the standard library alone. The profile imports the system’s dyld-support.sb, the rules that Apple keeps for starting a program, so dyld and the system’s libraries in their cryptexes load as Apple changes them. It allows exec and reading of devvm’s binary by its real path alone, which sandbox-exec needs to run it and the child needs for its SHA-256, and the metadata of its folder, which CoreFoundation looks at for the program’s bundle before Security checks a certificate. It allows reading /usr/lib and /System/Library and the time zone, and the metadata of the links on the way, /etc, /var and /tmp, because a sandboxed lookup through a link needs it. It allows reading and writing in its folders, making only regular files there (vnode-type REGULAR-FILE), no hard link anywhere (file-link), no folder removed, and no change to a file’s flags, ACL, owner, set-id bits or extended attributes, so the broker makes the Nix cache’s folders before the child starts. It allows file-read-metadata alone on the watched files, on their targets when they’re links, and on every link on the way to any of its files and folders (seatbelt.Links), the mach services com.apple.trustd and com.apple.trustd.agent, reading sysctl but its kern.proc names, and signals to itself. It allows no network out at all, to any address or unix socket, and accepting on its listener, and reading and writing the connections it accepted and those that the broker handed it, need no rule. It allows no bind, no fork, no look at another process (process-info, the process list), and none of the Keychain’s services. The list of what the child needs came from the sandbox’s own log of what it refused (log show --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "devvm("'), and the profile leaves refused what the child does without: com.apple.logd, com.apple.system.notification_center, com.apple.system.opendirectoryd.libinfo, /Library/Preferences/com.apple.networkd.plist, /etc/passwd, /dev/fd, the interfaces’ link addresses (net.link.addr), AF_SYSTEM sockets and the binds that the system’s network code tries. crypto/x509’s checks don’t need com.apple.SecurityServer, which the profile never allows. A watched file whose link points elsewhere after the start gets its stat refused, which the child takes as a file to ask the broker for at every request (watched.get), so a change still applies to the next request. The broker starts the child again unconfined, within the same 4 seconds, only when sandbox-exec failed before devvm’s code ran, which the child’s end shows: it ended before it answered, with sandbox-exec’s own exit status, 65 for a profile it refused or 71 for a program it couldn’t run, or killed by SIGABRT or SIGKILL, as dyld aborts a program that the profile refuses what it needs to load, which the broker decides before its own stop of the child. A ready that names a sandbox the broker didn’t start the child under breaks the protocol’s rules (Confinement.fits). ChildProfile refuses a path that isn’t absolute or that is the root, as resolved. A missing sandbox-exec starts it unconfined too. Anything else fails the start, so nothing a VM left in the child’s folders can turn a confined start into an unconfined one. Linux, with Landlock: the child sets no_new_privs on every thread and restricts itself (landlock_restrict_self, through syscall.AllThreadsSyscall, or with ABI 8’s TSYNC where the kernel has it) before it reads a byte of the VM’s, and the files it opened before then are its logs and the Nix cache. It keeps the rights above on its folders, to make regular files alone, binds and connects no TCP port (ABI 4), binds and sends no UDP (ABI 10), scopes abstract unix sockets and signals to itself (ABI 6), and connects to no named unix socket (ABI 9). Landlock’s network rules match only ports, so they can refuse the child an address only by refusing it every connection, which is what the child needs, and the seccomp filter refuses the same on every kernel, TCP Fast Open included, which Landlock’s check of connect doesn’t see. It reads no file outside its folders, because it needs no resolver. The Nix cache renames a NAR’s temporary file from its top folder into nar/, which Landlock allows only from ABI 2 (REFER), so the floor is ABI 2, unless the cache makes each temporary file in the folder that its file goes to. A child on a kernel below ABI 4 or 6 is partly confined, which it says in ready and devvm doctor reports. A kernel at ABI 6 or 7 without Landlock’s erratum 2, which lets a process’s threads signal each other across the domains each made in turn, would refuse the signals that syscall.AllThreadsSyscall sends each thread and hang the start, so there the child leaves signals unscoped and says so (landlock-signals). A kernel without Landlock, or at ABI 1, confines no files, and the child runs with the seccomp filter alone and says so (partial seccomp no-landlock), which devvm doctor warns of: the VM keeps its network rather than lose it on such a kernel. internal/landlock (Self) does all of it, with the standard library alone, behind its own build tags, as the proxy can’t import internal/platform, and checks after confining that the child lists its folders and fails to list / and to read /etc/hosts. Linux, with seccomp: no Landlock ABI can refuse the child an address, a kernel before ABI 9 can’t refuse it a named unix socket, and one before ABI 4 can’t refuse it a port, so the child also installs a seccomp filter on every thread (SECCOMP_FILTER_FLAG_TSYNC) that refuses socket for every family but a netlink route socket (AF_NETLINK with NETLINK_ROUTE), socketpair, connect, listen, MSG_FASTOPEN on sendto, sendmsg and sendmmsg, socketcall, and io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter and io_uring_register, whose operations would pass a filter of system calls. It kills the child for a system call of any architecture but its own, and on amd64 for the x32 numbers, so the 32-bit calls can’t get around it. socketcall is a 32-bit call alone, so the check of the architecture is what refuses it. The filter also refuses ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev and pidfd_getfd, which Landlock restricts to the child’s own domain but nothing does on a kernel without it, and which would let the child read the memory, or take the descriptors, of another process of yours, such as an ssh master. Changed in review, it refuses what Landlock doesn’t restrict at any ABI: a file’s mode, owner, extended attributes and times changed by its path (chmod, fchmodat, fchmodat2, chown, lchown, fchownat, the six xattr calls, utime, utimes, futimesat, and utimensat with a path), truncate, which Landlock restricts only from ABI 3, the kernel’s keyrings (add_key, request_key, keyctl), another process’s limits and scheduling (prlimit64 on another pid, setpriority, ioprio_set and the four sched_set calls), watches that would tell it of files outside its folders (inotify_init, inotify_init1, inotify_add_watch, fanotify_init, fanotify_mark), and what the child never does: execve and execveat, fork, vfork and a clone that isn’t a thread, a namespace (unshare, setns, a clone with a namespace’s flag), bpf, userfaultfd and perf_event_open, with clone3 refused as ENOSYS, as its flags are behind a pointer. The calls on a descriptor the child opened stay (fchmod, fchown, ftruncate, utimensat without a path), and the Nix cache marks a file used through its descriptor. The review’s own check: the filter’s interpreter, and TestSelf on Fedora 43 (ABI 11), Ubuntu 26.04 (ABI 8) and Debian 13 (ABI 6), where Go’s runtime still starts new threads under it. The child needs none of these, as the broker looks up its names and opens its connections. Once confined, the child checks that it can’t make a unix or an IPv4 socket, nor connect or send with MSG_FASTOPEN on any socket, which the filter refuses before the kernel looks at the descriptor. The filter is classic BPF written out by hand (internal/landlock’s filter), a unit test runs its bytes in an interpreter of its own for amd64 and arm64, and a test’s child confines itself under it on the Linux test hosts and in CI’s nocgo job (TestSelf). A kernel without seccomp leaves the filter out, and the child says so (no-seccomp). Performance. The path of the VM’s requests is the child’s alone: no request, tunnel or byte in them crosses the socket. The child asks the broker only for a value that its cache doesn’t hold, at most once for each binding in 30 seconds or 5 minutes, for a watched file after it changed, for each connection to a link, which is a new connection for each plain HTTP request to a link, for each token request, and for each lookup and each connection that a request opens upstream. Those last two add a round trip on the socketpair to each lookup and each connection, a JSON frame each way and a descriptor, which is small beside a lookup’s or a TCP handshake’s own time, and a kept-alive connection or a tunnel costs it once. A start costs one more process and its exec, and each VM’s proxy takes a second Go process’s memory: on an Apple silicon Mac, an idle broker and its child each take about 19 MB resident.
Options weighed:
Values handed to the child at the start: ruled out, above. The child reading the changing files itself: it would need to read the VM’s run folder and devvm’s config folder. Landlock keeps a rule for a file on that file itself, so a file that devvm replaces whole would lose it, and only a rule on the folder would hold. Asking the broker after a change keeps the check on each request without a hop. The broker sending changes to the child as they happen: the broker would have to watch each file, and the standard library can only poll, so a change would wait for the next poll, while with the stamp’s check it applies to the next request. The broker speaking to the company proxy and handing over the tunnel: that would keep the company proxy’s password out of the child for tunnels, but the company proxy takes it with each plain HTTP request, which would put the broker on that path, parsing what the child sends. So the broker opens the TCP connection to the company proxy alone, and the child speaks to it. Seatbelt refusing localhost:* alone, with the broker connecting to loopback only: Seatbelt’s network filter names a host only as * or localhost, so the child would still reach this machine’s own LAN addresses, where a server that listens on every address answers, such as Docker’s published ports, and the LAN, and whether localhost covers all of 127.0.0.0/8, 0.0.0.0 and the mapped forms is Apple’s to say. A profile that allows nothing out, with the broker judging every address, holds for all of them, and keeps one way for both systems. seccomp’s user notification on Linux, with the broker as the supervisor of connect, sendto and sendmsg: the broker would read the address from the child’s memory, which another thread of the child can change after the read, so it could never let the call go on, and would make every connection itself and put it in the child (SECCOMP_IOCTL_NOTIF_ADDFD), which costs what the dial request does. Reading the child’s memory needs ptrace’s access, which Yama’s ptrace_scope 2 or 3 refuses, the broker couldn’t tell a TCP socket from a UDP one without taking it (pidfd_getfd, the same access), the listener’s descriptor would have to come from the child, which the protocol refuses, and ADDFD needs Linux 5.9. The filter on arguments works on every kernel with seccomp filters, with no access to the child’s memory. A network namespace for the child with nothing but its own loopback, with the broker dialing every connection: it costs what the dial request does, it needs an unprivileged user namespace, which Ubuntu’s AppArmor restricts from 24.04 and other systems turn off, and which the child’s filter refuses (unshare), so the broker would have to make it. The filter refuses the same connections without a namespace. The broker signing the interception’s certificates: the child already sees every byte of its VM’s traffic, so the VM’s CA key gives it nothing more, and no other VM trusts that CA. The agent’s relay in the child, through a connection from the broker: that connection would carry whatever the child sends, so the broker would have to filter it, which is the relay’s whole job. A process each for the relay, the logs and the lookups: each would be unconfined, as the broker is, so more processes would add lifecycles but no boundary. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, with its local IPC, protocols, data isolation and resource exhaustion companions, on this design, and an independent review of it against today’s code, whose findings are folded in). Leads, each ruled out by the design, changed in review, or listed:
The child naming another VM’s binding, another secret or a file: ruled out. Each request is a key, a number, a host and port, or an endpoint that the broker resolves in its own config and its own reads of its VM’s files, and no path, VM name or binding crosses the socket. The values bound to its VM: listed. A child that a VM takes over can ask for every value that its VM’s bindings file names, such as a secret of yours, a GitHub token or an agent’s access token, and use it anywhere the child reaches, while the VM itself holds only placeholders. It gets no other VM’s value, no value that isn’t bound to its VM, and no login’s refresh token. The company proxy’s password: listed. The child holds it, as the proxy does, because the company proxy takes it with each plain HTTP request, so a child that a VM takes over can send it anywhere it reaches. Its VM’s password and CAs: listed. The child holds its VM’s password and both CAs’ keys, which only that VM trusts, and it already sees all of that VM’s traffic. A forged token reply: ruled out. The broker gets the endpoint’s reply itself, over TLS that it checks, from the host in its own config, so a child can’t save tokens that the endpoint didn’t issue. Listed: a real exchange of a code that the VM got for an account of its own saves that account’s login for every VM with the agent, as a VM can do without the proxy taken over (logins made in a VM). A binding or link that devvm took away: changed in review. The broker read the bindings file and the links’ list only when the child asked for them, which a child that a VM takes over never does, so a secret unbound or deleted, or a link removed, stayed within its reach. The broker now looks at both on every request that uses them, and drops its values when the bindings file changes. Flooding the broker: listed. Frames have a cap, each request type has a cap on how many run at once, the broker’s cache holds a lookup to once a binding in 30 seconds or 5 minutes, a failed lookup is kept for 5 seconds (changed in review, as a failure wasn’t kept, so a child could make the broker run security or try a refresh back to back), and a frame that breaks a rule ends the pair. A child can still run up to 8 token exchanges at once with your login, one after another, as a VM can, and make the broker write a line in proxy.log for each connection it refuses or can’t open, which pushes older lines out of the log’s rotation, as the child’s own lines can. The broker’s own parsing: listed. The broker still reads bytes that a VM chooses, in four bounded places: the child’s frames, at most 2 MiB each, which encoding/json decodes, the agent’s relay’s messages, at most 256 KiB each, read by their length and type alone, the backend’s logs, which it scans for passwords, and a token request and its reply, at most 64 KiB and 1 MiB, which internal/agentlogin parses as the proxy’s process does. The network: changed, and listed. The rules and the floor were the child’s own code, and the sandboxes allowed it TCP and UDP to any address, so a child that a VM took over reached this machine’s loopback, its own LAN addresses and the LAN, such as your dev servers, Docker’s published ports and other VMs’ proxies, whatever the rules said. A profile can’t follow a rule that applies from the next connection, and Landlock and a seccomp filter can’t refuse an address, so the sandboxes now refuse the child every connection of its own, and the broker, which judges each address with its own read of the policy files and the host’s addresses, opens each one for it. Listed: the child still reaches any public address on the internet, as an open VM’s proxy does, over TCP alone, and an address that a rule names. Changed in review, the note no longer says the LAN is out of reach: the floor counts a host on this machine’s network whose address is public as the internet, such as a printer’s or a NAS’s global IPv6 address on most networks with IPv6, or any host on a network of public IPv4 addresses, so the child, as the VM, reaches those, and the floor counting this machine’s own networks as internal is a change of its own, for the VM as much as the child. The child reaches no unix socket, so neither the ssh masters’ control sockets, nor docker.sock, nor an SSH agent. The dial and lookup requests: ruled out, and listed. A dial names an address and a port, which the broker judges as the floor does before it connects, or a company proxy of its own config, and nothing else, so a child can’t make the broker connect where the floor refuses, nor reach a unix socket, nor send UDP through it. A lookup takes a host name alone, and the broker returns its addresses, which the child could ask this machine’s resolver for, split DNS, /etc/hosts and .local names included. Listed: a child can make the broker look up any name, which carries data out in the name as a VM’s own lookups through the proxy can, and hold 256 lookups and 1024 connections under way at once, each for at most its timeout, as it could hold them itself before. Changed in review: a lookup or a connection that the child gave up on held its place until its timeout, so a VM whose requests went away while DNS or IPv6 hung could fill the caps, and now the child cancels it. The broker logged a line for each failed lookup and connection, which a VM that asks for one refused address after another drives, and now it logs at most 20 a minute, then one that says it stops, as the child does for the lookups it gives up on. The connections the child holds: changed in review, and listed. The caps count a connection only while it opens, and Go raises a process’s limit on open files to its hard limit, so a child could keep every connection the broker handed it and use up this machine’s ports for outgoing connections. The child now lowers its own limit, soft and hard, to 8448 files before it confines itself, four times maxConns and room for its logs and the Nix cache, so it holds at most that many, which a process can’t raise again. Listed: that lowers the risk but doesn’t remove it, as macOS gives out its outgoing ports from one range of 16,384 for every process, so a few children that VMs took over, or one on a busy machine, could still use them up. A connection connected again: ruled out. A child holds connected TCP sockets, those it accepted and those the broker handed it, and its listener. On Linux, the filter refuses connect, which could otherwise disconnect a TCP socket (AF_UNSPEC) and connect it elsewhere, and MSG_FASTOPEN, which would connect the listener once a shutdown has closed it. On macOS, Seatbelt checks every connect and every sendto with an address against the profile, which allows none. A rule as it changes: ruled out, and listed. The child and the broker each read the policy files when their stamp changes, and the broker looks at them at each dial, after the child’s own look, so a rule that the child saw is one the broker sees. A rule taken away as a connection opens makes that connection fail, which fails closed. Changed in review: the broker’s copy and what it gave the child were two reads, and a file that keeps its last rules when it can’t be read, as a policy file does, could leave the broker’s copy older than the child’s, with a rule the child no longer had, so the broker now looks at its copy at each file request for a policy file too. Listed: a file that changes and can’t be read between those two looks, which only you can make happen, still leaves the broker’s copy a version behind until the file reads again. The company proxy: listed. A child that a VM takes over can connect to the company proxy of its config, wherever it is, loopback included, and send it what it likes with the password it holds, as the proxy does: CONNECT and plain HTTP to any host and port, which the company proxy, not the floor, decides on, so it reaches whatever the company proxy reaches, this machine’s loopback included when the company proxy runs here. The broker speaking CONNECT itself would keep tunnels to the floor, but plain HTTP takes the password with each request, so the child would still hold it and reach the same through http’s company proxy. Other processes’ details: changed in review. The first profile allowed every sysctl and process-info, so a child could list your processes and read their paths and arguments, a token on a command line among them. The profile now denies process-info for any process but the child, the process list, and sysctl’s kern.proc names. macOS answers kern.procargs2, a process’s arguments, to a sandboxed process only for the processes of its own process group, and the child is alone in a session of its own (daemon.Spawn’s Setsid), so it’s refused every other process’s, its broker’s included, which TestChildProfileConfines checks. Changing the shared folders’ files: changed in review. The first profile allowed every write in the child’s folders, so a child could set a flag such as uchg on a file in the shared Nix cache, or remove its nar/ folder, and stop every VM’s cache and devvm gc’s trim from changing it. The profile now refuses changing a file’s flags, ACL, owner, set-id bits and extended attributes, and removing a folder, and leaves the mode and times, which the child changes. A child can still delete or rewrite the cache’s files, as the disk’s row says. The seccomp filter’s way around: changed in review. A filter of socket alone lets a child reach a unix socket through the 32-bit system calls (socketcall, or the x32 numbers) or through io_uring, which doesn’t pass the filter, and before ABI 9 that filter is all that keeps the ssh masters’ control sockets from it. The filter now kills any other architecture’s calls and refuses socketcall and io_uring, on every thread. The folders the child writes: changed in review. A child that a VM takes over could leave a link or a FIFO in its logs folder or the Nix cache, and devvm opened proxy.log again by its path at the next start, copied and emptied it by its path at each rotation, opened links.log and ports.log, read the event log, and trimmed the cache through nar/, each following the link. That would have written the VM’s bytes into a file of yours, copied one into the log the child reads, emptied or deleted yours, or hung a command on a FIFO. The child now makes regular files alone, and devvm opens everything in those folders through internal/safefile or an os.Root, never following a link, and rotates proxy.log through its descriptor. The disk: listed. Only the child’s own code bounds its logs and the shared Nix cache, so a child that a VM takes over can fill the disk, write what it likes into its VM’s logs, which devvm network log and devvm network lock read, replace links.log and ports.log with files of its own, so the link session’s report after a start can show warnings it forged or miss real ones, and write what it likes into the cache. Each VM’s Nix checks a cached NAR against cache.nixos.org’s signature and its NarHash, so the other VMs fetch such a NAR again rather than trust it. The Nix cache’s lock and its names: changed in review, and listed. A child that held .lock forever would have hung every other VM’s /nix/ requests and devvm gc’s trim, so each takes the lock with a deadline of a few seconds, trying it without blocking, and past it answers 404 or skips the trim and says so. A child can still slow the cache down by holding the lock, and list the store paths that other VMs fetched. The logs’ locks: changed in review, and listed. The broker and its child share proxy.log’s lock, and the child and devvm _links the event log’s, so a child that held one for ever would have stopped the broker at its next line, and the broker logged before it closed the socket when the hostagent ended, so the pair would have outlived the VM. Now the broker closes the socket and starts its kill’s timer before it logs anything, and every writer tries each log’s lock without blocking for at most 200 ms, then writes its line without the lock or skips the rotation. A child can still make each of the broker’s lines wait that long, and make a rotation lose the lines written as it copies. A log made huge: changed in review, and listed. A rotation of proxy.log read the whole file into memory, so a child that made it huge, or sparse at a terabyte, could have made the broker run out of memory and write as much. Now a rotation copies at most the last twice its limit, 20 MiB, from a line’s start, streamed into its copy. A child can still fill the disk, as the disk’s row says. What stat shows: listed. Landlock doesn’t restrict stat, so a child that a VM takes over on Linux learns whether any file of yours exists, its size and when it changed, though not what it holds. Changed: it read every file below /etc that you can, which its resolver needed, and now that the broker looks up its names, it reads none. On macOS the profile refuses stat outside the child’s files, but a refused path answers EPERM and a missing one ENOENT, so a child there learns whether a path exists, though nothing else of it. The services the profile allows on macOS: listed, and changed. A child that a VM takes over can ask trustd to check certificates, which reads your trust settings, and that holds no secret of yours and isn’t the Keychain. trustd can fetch a missing issuer’s certificate or an OCSP answer from the URL in a certificate, from its own unconfined process, which a review raised as a way to send a request to loopback or the LAN. Checked: a leaf whose issuer was missing and whose issuer, OCSP and CRL URLs named a server on this machine’s loopback or its LAN address made trustd fetch nothing, through Go’s verifier under the profile and without it, and through security verify-cert, which allows network fetches, with revocation required or not, on macOS 27. Listed: when it fetches is Apple’s to change, and the worst it could do is a request, whose answer the child never sees, to loopback or the LAN. The profile allowed mDNSResponder’s socket for the resolver, so a child could browse the local network’s Bonjour services, announce services of its own there, and register any .local record it liked (DNSServiceRegisterRecord), and now that the broker looks up its names, the profile allows no unix socket. com.apple.trustd.agent also takes changes to your trust settings, which macOS asks your password for through its authorization services (com.apple.authd), and the profile allows neither those nor com.apple.SecurityServer, so a child can’t trust a CA of its own. devvm’s tests didn’t try such a change. A confined start made unconfined: ruled out, and changed in review. The broker starts the child again unconfined only for a failure of sandbox-exec itself, an exit status of its own or SIGABRT or SIGKILL before the child answered, which comes before devvm’s code runs and reads nothing of a VM’s, so a child that a VM took over, or what it left in its folders, can’t make the next start unconfined. The broker counted any signal, after its own stop of a child that hadn’t answered in time, so a child that hung, which its stop then ended with SIGTERM, counted as the sandbox’s failure. It now decides before its stop, only for a child that had already ended, and only for those two signals. Listed: a program of yours that kills the child in that moment makes the start unconfined, which the proxy’s log and devvm doctor say. A child that fails after that, such as on a planted file, or that hangs, fails the start, which leaves the VM without a network until its next start, as before. A child that claims more: changed in review. The broker took any confinement the child’s ready named, so a child could say full seatbelt when the broker had started it unconfined. The broker now refuses a ready that names a sandbox it didn’t start the child under, or another than the one it did (Confinement.fits), which ends the pair. Other processes: ruled out where the child is confined. Landlock scopes signals to the child (ABI 6) and lets it trace only processes in its own domain, and the profile allows signals only to itself. Listed: on a Linux kernel before ABI 6, or at ABI 6 or 7 without erratum 2, a child that a VM takes over can signal any process of yours, which devvm doctor warns of. Changed in review: Landlock’s scope of signals doesn’t cover a process’s limits or scheduling, and a review killed another process from a fully confined child on ABI 8 by setting its RLIMIT_CPU to 1 with prlimit64, so the seccomp filter refuses prlimit64 on any pid but the child’s own (0), and setpriority, ioprio_set, sched_setaffinity, sched_setscheduler, sched_setparam and sched_setattr outright. The seccomp filter refuses ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev and pidfd_getfd on every kernel, but on a kernel without Landlock the child can still open /proc//mem and /proc//fd/ of another process of yours, unless the kernel’s Yama restricts tracing (ptrace_scope 1 or more, Ubuntu’s default), and so read its memory and its files. Changed in review: the broker sets itself undumpable (PR_SET_DUMPABLE 0), so its own memory and descriptors, which hold the VM’s secrets, are root’s alone there. A port of another VM’s: changed in review, and ruled out where the seccomp filter or Seatbelt holds. Before ABI 4, Landlock can’t refuse the child a port, so a child could bind another VM’s proxy port while that proxy starts again, and take that VM’s password from its requests. The seccomp filter refuses listen, and now every new socket but a netlink route socket, so the child has no socket to bind, as the ones it holds are bound already, and the profile refuses a bind on macOS. Listed: without either, the child can still bind such a port, so that VM’s proxy fails to start until it’s free again. No confinement, or part of it: listed. Where Landlock or Seatbelt isn’t there, the child runs with the broker’s access, and the split then only keeps the lookups, the captures, the relay and the logs’ keeping out of the code that reads the VM’s network. Without the seccomp filter, or on macOS without Seatbelt, a child that a VM took over can also connect anywhere itself, loopback included. A kernel below ABI 4 or 6 confines the child in part, which ready, run/proxy.confined and devvm doctor say. Changed in review: ABI 6, 7 and 8 with the seccomp filter and scoped signals count as full, as the filter refuses every unix socket that ABI 9 would refuse by path, and every connection and datagram of the child’s own, which ABI 10 would refuse only for UDP, so doctor warns of nothing that a user could close. On macOS, sandbox-exec is deprecated, and if macOS drops it, or it fails to start the child, the child runs unconfined, and the proxy’s log and devvm doctor say so, so the VM keeps its network. The floor without the host’s addresses: changed in review. A confinement that refused the read of the host’s addresses would have left the floor with none, and so let the VM reach this machine’s own public addresses. The child’s check after it confines itself needs a read that isn’t empty, and a later read that fails keeps the last good one. Descriptors and the environment: ruled out. The child inherits only its four descriptors, the socketpair is close-on-exec so no other program holds an end, the child closes any descriptor that a frame brings that it didn’t ask for, and it gets only TZ, SSL_CERT_FILE, SSL_CERT_DIR and GODEBUG from the environment. The pid and status files: ruled out. The child can’t write the run folder, the status file’s name isn’t in its environment, and the status names the broker’s pid, which daemon.Proc checks, so a child that a VM takes over can’t make devvm signal another process. The broker writes the child’s pid file, and devvm checks the child’s arguments before it signals it. A child that outlives its broker, or starts again: ruled out, changed in review. The child ends when it reads the socket’s end, which a killed broker leaves because no other process holds it, and the broker ends with its child, and neither starts the other. A stop gave the broker 2 seconds and the child’s close took up to 6, so a child could have kept the port and its old config as the next start began. Now SIGTERM ends the child within a second, and devvm finds a child that outlived its broker by its pid file and stops it. Listed: a child that a VM has taken over can ignore the socket’s end and change its own arguments, which daemon.Proc then doesn’t match, so devvm leaves it alone. On Linux PR_SET_PDEATHSIG kills it with its broker, but on macOS such a child outlives a broker that was killed, confined, with its VM’s values and port, and the VM’s next start reports its proxy’s port as taken. A binary that changed under the broker: changed in review. The protocol’s version alone can’t tell two builds apart, so the start and the answer carry each side’s executable’s SHA-256, and a child from another build fails the start, and the VM’s next launch starts the pair again. On Linux the child is the broker’s own file anyway. A file that changes between its stamp and its read: ruled out. The child keeps the stamp of the file that the broker read, so a write after that read changes the stamp, and the child asks again. Memory and CPU: listed. A child that a VM takes over can use memory and CPU without a bound, as the proxy can. End-to-end checks that the implementation adds, in network, link, nix, images, tools and from: a VM’s proxy runs as a broker and a child, with the child’s arguments and descriptors above and no environment but the four variables. A bound secret goes in, a login is captured from the fake token endpoint, a link connects and the Nix cache fills, each through the child. devvm stop leaves neither process, and the next launch starts on the same port at once. A symbolic link, a FIFO and a hard link planted in the VM’s logs folder and the Nix cache lead no command of devvm’s, the next start or a rotation to their targets, and hang none. A broker killed with SIGKILL takes its child with it within a second, a child killed takes its broker and the agent’s socket with it, and nothing starts again until the next launch. A build behind a company proxy goes through a broker and a child, and both are gone after the build. The two follow-ups add the checks that the confined child can’t read a file in the home folder, reach the Keychain or connect to a unix socket, on each platform. On Linux, network checks that the VM’s proxy says Landlock in run/proxy.confined, and that the child’s /proc entry shows no_new_privs and a seccomp filter, and TestSelf, in internal/landlock, runs its test binary again as a child that confines itself, which writes, renames and lists in its folder, reads the host’s addresses and writes to a TCP connection it held before, and is refused a file outside its folder, /etc/hosts, listing /, its own executable, a folder, a link and a FIFO in its folder, a unix socket that stands in for an ssh master’s, a socketpair, a listen, an IPv4 and an IPv6 socket, a netlink socket of another family than routes, connecting a TCP socket it held before to a loopback server, MSG_FASTOPEN from its listener once a shutdown has closed it, from ABI 4 a bind and from ABI 6 a signal to its parent. By hand, devvm’s release build ran a broker whose child was confined on Ubuntu 26.04 (AppArmor, ABI 8), Fedora 43 (SELinux, ABI 11), Debian 13 (ABI 6) and Ubuntu 26.04 on arm64, served a request, refused a blocked host and reached the Nix cache’s endpoint. On macOS, network checks that the VM’s proxy says full seatbelt in run/proxy.confined, which means the child started under sandbox-exec and its own check held, and TestChildProfileConfines, in internal/seatbelt, runs its test binary again under the child’s profile, which writes a regular file in its folder, renames it, changes its mode, removes it, looks at its policy file, and writes to a TCP connection it was handed and to one it accepted on a listener it was handed, and is refused a link, a folder, a FIFO and a hard link there, changing a file’s flags, removing a folder, reading its policy file, reading or looking at a file outside, opening the broker’s config, connecting to a unix socket, connecting over TCP to a loopback server on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 or to any other address, sending UDP, running a program, listening on a port, signalling its parent and listing the processes. The broker’s judgment is unit tests: a dial to a loopback port that no rule names is refused, 127.0.0.1 and ::1 alike, and so is one to this machine’s own address, while one that a rule names connects, from the dial after the rule is written, and not after it’s gone, and the open tier’s broker connects to any. FuzzBrokerFrames sends the broker any lookup and dial, and checks that it looks up only a host name and connects only where its own floor allows, and the in-process tests run the whole proxy with every lookup and connection through the broker. By hand, devvm’s release build ran a broker whose child was confined, and a helper under the child’s profile was refused ~/.zshrc, ~/.ssh, ~/Library/Keychains and the login keychain’s file, ~/.local/share/devvm and ~/.config/devvm, running security, and an ssh master’s control socket, and reached example.com. The fallback and its limits are unit tests (TestStartChildSandbox), as a broken sandbox-exec can’t be made on a real Mac.
data.the-shared-nix-cache#The shared Nix cach:
VMs with the nix layer share their downloads from cache.nixos.org through a cache that only the host fills (how). It’s the first thing that VMs share, so the design keeps two things: each VM’s Nix store stays its own, and no VM can change what another VM gets.
Why a cache the host fills, not a shared store: one store, or one daemon, shared between VMs is what Nix’s own store vulnerabilities break. CVE-2026-110450 (the daemon’s store corrupted through repair), CVE-2026-39860 and the CVE-2024-27297 family (a fixed-output derivation that changes its output after Nix registered it) each let a client of the daemon change paths in its store, and in a shared store, every other VM would then trust those paths. A VM’s own builds are worse: a path a VM built has no signature that another VM could check, short of a key that trusts that VM, and then every VM trusts every other. A binary cache keeps the trust where Nix already has it. Each VM’s Nix fetches from the cache as from cache.nixos.org, checks cache.nixos.org’s signature and the NarHash itself, and adds the path to its own store, so the cache only saves downloads.
What the host checks, and what each VM checks:
The proxy (internal/proxy/nixcache.go) takes only GET and HEAD of nix-cache-info, <32 nix32>.narinfo and nar/<52 nix32>.nar with no suffix or .xz, .zst or .bz2, with no query and nothing escaped (nixPath, fuzzed by FuzzNixPath), and 400 for anything else. It makes up nix-cache-info itself. It fetches from https://cache.nixos.org alone, only when the VM’s policy allows cache.nixos.org:443 and, by method and path, a GET of the path the VM asked for (policy.judge), through the floor or the company proxy (dialOut), with the system’s roots and the user’s CAs, following no redirect, and sending only its own GET and User-Agent. A narinfo is kept when its StorePath is the path asked for, its URL is a NAR path of the pattern above, its hashes are SHA-256 in Nix’s base 32, each reference is a store path’s base name, and a Sig by cache.nixos.org-1 (the Ed25519 key pinned in nixKey) verifies over 1;StorePath;NarHash;NarSize;References, the references as full store paths, sorted and joined by commas (parseNarinfo, against a narinfo of cache.nixos.org’s own in internal/proxy/testdata/nix/). The bytes kept are cache.nixos.org’s, as they came. A narinfo’s URL must be named by its own NarHash or FileHash, since the URL isn’t signed. A NAR is fetched only after a narinfo this proxy checked names its URL (nixKnown, at most 65536 entries), and kept only when its SHA-256 and size are that narinfo’s FileHash and FileSize, read through a limit of FileSize plus one byte. A HEAD never fetches one. Each VM’s Nix checks the signature again and the NarHash, which the host can’t: the compression is xz or zstd, which aren’t in Go’s standard library, and internal/proxy takes nothing else. The spike showed a VM’s Nix refuses both a narinfo with an added reference and a corrupted NAR. Files go into a temporary file in the folder (.tmp-*, 600) and are renamed into place, in folders of 700. Not-found answers and errors are never kept, and the VM gets 404, so its Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself. The cap: nix-cache.size, 10 GiB when it’s off, passed in the proxy’s config as nix_cache_max. Before a proxy writes a file, it takes the file’s room under an exclusive flock on .lock (reserve), in whole 4 KiB blocks. When .size, the running total, is missing or the new file would pass the cap, it counts the folder again, each file by the larger of its size and its blocks, and deletes the least recently used files, by modification time, which a hit sets, down to nine tenths of the cap. A NAR being fetched is made its full size at once and counts, but is never deleted, so a fetch that would pass the cap with them is refused. A fetch that fails gives its room back. One proxy fetches each NAR once however many requests ask for it, and at most four at once. A NAR whose FileSize is over the cap isn’t fetched. devvm gc, its --nix-cache and the daily retention run trim under the same lock (TrimNixCache). A temporary file over an hour old is a dead proxy’s, and the next count deletes it.
What stays open:
Timing and filling the cache: Attack vectors lists what one VM learns of another by how fast the cache answers, and how a VM that fills the cache to its cap pushes other VMs’ paths out. Hiding the timing would mean waiting as long as a fetch on every hit, which is the saving. Private caches (Cachix, a netrc) are never shared: only root in the VM can add a substituter, and Nix reaches it through the allowlist directly. Options weighed:
Nix’s local overlay store, the VM’s store over a read-only lower store shared from the host. It works on Lima, but it’s still experimental in Nix 2.35, the lower store can’t change while it’s mounted, so sharing new paths means remounting, and a garbage collection by a daemon not set up for it writes whiteouts that hide lower paths from that VM for good. Packages fetched into an image, by a custom layer that runs nix build while the image builds (the recipe). Clones share them on disk at no cost, but only what’s in the image, and a changed flake.lock needs a rebuild. Open VMs: every VM has its own proxy, an open one’s included, so open VMs share the cache through it, with the VM’s password, as confined ones do. Ruled out: a shared loopback listener without a password, because anything on the host or any VM that reaches the host’s loopback could use it; and the cache folder mounted read-only into VMs, which leaves the VM’s Nix to read the files and the host with nothing to fill it. Review (the security-audit skill, on nixcache.go, its callers and the VM’s setup):
What a VM sends (headers, a body, a query, an escaped path, another method): ruled out: nixGet makes a request of its own from the checked path, the VM’s User-Agent and path go only to its own event log, and what’s kept is cache.nixos.org’s body under a name of the pattern. A path out of the folder (.., %2e, a symlink): ruled out: the names hold only Nix’s base 32, which has no /, . or %, and can’t be .lock, .size or .tmp-*; the folder is in devvm’s data folder, which no backend mounts, so nothing in a VM can put a file or link there. Upstream elsewhere (a redirect, DNS rebinding, a company proxy): ruled out: every dial is dialOut(cache.nixos.org, 443), through the floor or the company proxy as any request, ServerName is fixed and no redirect is followed; the client is made after the user’s CAs are read. A NAR kept under another NAR’s name: confirmed, fixed. A narinfo’s URL, FileHash and FileSize aren’t signed, so a bad upstream (or a CA in the user’s CA folder) could pair a real narinfo with another NAR’s URL and a file of its own, and every VM would then get that file for the other NAR, which its Nix refuses, until a trim. parseNarinfo takes a URL only when it’s named by the narinfo’s own NarHash or FileHash, and a hit whose size isn’t that of the narinfo this proxy checked is dropped and fetched again; unit-tested. The cap under many proxies: confirmed, fixed. Files being fetched didn’t count and were written before any room was taken, so one VM’s parallel requests could put many NARs’ worth on the host’s disk past the cap, and a small narinfo takes a whole block. Now a fetch takes its room under the lock first, makes its file its full size at once, and is refused when the files being fetched leave no room (reserve); sizes count whole blocks; one proxy fetches each NAR once, however many ask, and at most four at once (fetchOnce); a narinfo is written under the lock; unit-tested (40 writers at once, a full cache, eight requests for one NAR). A HEAD that downloads: confirmed, fixed: a HEAD for a NAR the cache doesn’t have answers 404 without fetching it. Parser differences (spaces, \r, a key twice, references twice): ruled out: they only refuse, and each VM’s Nix parses and checks the bytes again, so no narinfo the host keeps means something else to Nix. One VM learning of another: timing only: hits and fetches answer with the same bytes and headers (no Last-Modified or ETag), events go to the VM’s own log, /blocked holds none of them, and errors in the body say nothing of the host. The VM’s own settings: ruled out: devvm-cache.conf and the !include line are root’s, in that VM; only root is a trusted user, and root in a VM changes only its own Nix, while the cache takes nothing from any VM. Memory: ruled out: a narinfo is read up to 1 MiB, and nixKnown holds at most 65536 entries per proxy. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, nix): the VM’s Nix has the cache first and cache.nixos.org’s key alone; nix run nixpkgs#hello comes through the cache, fetched by the host into the folder (files 600, folders 700); a VM’s PUT and POST, a URL in the path, a query and .. get 400, a NAR no checked narinfo names and a path cache.nixos.org doesn’t have get 404, and the host keeps none of them; a second VM gets the first’s paths as hits and fetches none; after devvm network open, the open VM’s nix-daemon still goes through its proxy and keeps the cache first.
data.the-state-layout#The state layout:
devvm keeps its state in plain files in two folders, which State files describes. The layout follows a few rules:
One folder per VM, keyed by identity. A VM’s folder, vms//, is named by the hash that ends the VM’s name, the hash of its project folder’s physical path when devvm made it. The VM’s name, its backend and its ssh alias are chosen once, when devvm makes the VM, and recorded in its state, so devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder, first by the path’s hash, then reads the name and the backend from the state. A folder that moves keeps its VM, whose state records the new path while its name and folder stay (a moved folder). A backend’s limit on names, or another VM taking the same folder name, never changes which VM a folder finds. Every file devvm keeps for a VM is in its folder, so deleting a VM stops what runs for it, removes what it has outside the folder, and then deletes the folder whole, and devvm space and devvm gc count folders. A list of a VM’s files, kept in each place that deletes or counts them, would drift, and one of those places would miss a file. Only sockets stay outside, in run/ and named by hashes, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. The folder says who writes a file. ~/.config/devvm holds what you write, and devvm never rewrites a file of yours there: it changes single lines of policy and keeps the rest, comments included, and it writes the folder’s version. Everything devvm writes is in ~/.local/share/devvm. A default comes from a flag, then config.toml, then settings.json, then devvm’s own, and a command that would save a default that config.toml sets refuses, naming the file and the key, because the saved value would never apply. Two formats. What you edit is TOML, read strictly, so a typo stops the command and devvm names the file and the line, rather than the key being ignored. What only devvm writes is JSON, through encoding/json, and devvm ignores fields it doesn’t know, so a newer devvm’s additions don’t stop an older one. A change that an older devvm would read wrongly goes through the layout version instead. One section per package. vm.json has the core fields every VM has, and each package that keeps something of a VM’s owns one section of it, with its own type, so internal/state imports none of them. Each section keeps what you asked for apart from what devvm made, which sits under made, so a value is never stored twice under two names. The lock rule. Each change to a VM’s state holds that VM’s lock, reads the file again, and writes it once, so a command’s changes land together, and reads take no lock, because each write renames a whole file over the old one. A command holds at most one VM’s lock at a time. A change across VMs, such as removing every link to a VM being deleted, lets go of the first VM’s lock, then takes each other VM’s lock in turn and reads its state again before writing it. The claims lock is taken only after a VM’s own lock, never before, so no two devvms can each wait for the lock the other holds. Test builds and the tests check this order as each lock is taken (internal/state’s held): a second VM’s lock, a VM’s lock under the claims lock, or a lock the same goroutine holds already panics, naming both locks, before it waits. The check is per goroutine. It follows the locks each goroutine holds, by the goroutine’s number, which it reads from the goroutine’s stack, so two goroutines that each hold one VM’s lock pass, and a goroutine that a change starts while it holds a lock isn’t checked against that lock. A release build checks nothing. A layout version. Each folder records its layout version in version. A newer devvm that changes the layout raises it and adds a migration from the version before, an older layout is migrated before a command runs, and a newer one is refused, because this devvm would read it wrongly. testdata/script/layout.txtar lists every file and folder a confined VM, a port, a link and a secret leaves, so a change to the layout changes a listing and fails the test until someone decides whether it needs a new version (changing the state layout). devvm’s own files stay in the binary, as one binary describes, so neither folder holds a copy of assets/. Why not a database. SQLite or bbolt would give transactions, but either one is a new dependency, and devvm builds without cgo, so SQLite would mean a large pure-Go port. State would also stop being files that you can read with cat or jq, back up, and check by hand. Files written whole and renamed into place, with an OS file lock for each VM, give what devvm needs: one writer to a VM at a time, and readers that never see half a file.
data.things-learned#Things learned: Lima vz never returns freed guest memory to the Mac. sbx returns it with a VM monitor of its own; libkrun has MADV_FREE, with a stronger fix still an open PR. APFS clones cost nothing until written, and du overcounts them: real use was 5.5 GB where du said 12.7 GB. Lima locks each additional disk to one running VM, so images shared across VMs go through a shared folder (virtiofs on macOS, 9p on Linux) and are loop-mounted from it. Read-only mounts are enforced by the host: even root in the VM can’t write to them, but root can unmount a nested one and reach what’s underneath. Codex and opencode refreshing their OAuth logins in a VM can rotate the token and sign the host out. On every tier the VM holds only placeholders, and devvm refreshes the logins on the host when the proxy asks it for their values (internal/agentlogin). Codex decodes id_token’s claims and the access token’s exp without checking signatures, so placeholders are unsigned JWTs with the real account claims and a far-off exp. On macOS, a socket in transit over SCM_RIGHTS can lose the data it held and read as ended when the same process closes, at that moment, a unix socket that still holds descriptors no one received. It fails closed, as an ended connection. The broker and its child close such a socket only as the pair ends, and the test that reads a handed-over link’s data asks for the link once more when it reads empty. A process passes the files it was given on to the processes it starts, unless they’re marked close-on-exec. Go marks only the files it opens itself, so a terminal, an editor or a test harness that gives devvm another one (a pty on descriptor 3, the end of a pipe) would have it held by devvm’s proxy, its port forwarder and Lima’s processes, which keep that terminal or pipe open for as long as they run. So devvm marks every file it was given past standard input, output and error close-on-exec as it starts, and keeps them open itself. No existing tool gives Lima Dockerfile-style layers with sharing at run time; nerdbox and Kata do it on VM runtimes of their own. Where devvm fits, next to sbx and Colima: sbx puts agents first; devvm gives a full Linux VM per project, with agents optional.
data.transparent-mode#Transparent mode:
A confined VM’s tools that ignore the proxy settings, such as workerd under wrangler dev, a static Go binary or a container made through Docker’s API, reach the VM’s proxy by the names they look up (how). The design keeps three things: no DNS query and no connection leaves the VM but through its proxy, the host the proxy judges is the host it dials, and nothing new listens on the host or takes part in the backends.
What it’s built from: internal/proxy/transparent.go: the reserved target TransparentHost (transparent.devvm.proxy), the stand-in address SentinelAddr (198.18.0.1, in benchmarking’s 198.18.0.0/15, which clients such as workerd’s kj count as public and the floor counts as internal), transparent’s serve, tls, handler and refusePage, sniHost, and policy.transparentPorts behind /transparent/ports. routeFor is the order every connection is judged in, CONNECT’s and the transparent path’s alike, and carry is the one tunnel, its SNI check included. Event.Via is dns for the path’s events (withVia for its requests). In the guest, assets/guest/transparent.sh is devvm-transparent, its ruleset (render), its slots and its service, set up by sync.sh when netpolicy.TransparentAddr gives the setup the stand-in address: the VM runs confined (backend.NetProxy) and its mode is on (netpolicy.TransparentOf: the VM’s net.transparent, else config.toml’s transparent-proxy, else on). layers/base.sh installs dnsmasq, socat and nftables, which changes base’s key.
Choices against the first design:
Listeners on the stand-in address, not on 127.0.77.1: Docker’s containers reach a local address on the VM over its bridges, but a loopback one only with route_localnet=1, the hole of CVE-2020-8558, which would open every loopback service of the VM to them. The port forwarder forwards only loopback and wildcard listeners, and vmssh.dialAddr refuses the stand-in address by name too. dnsmasq on the stand-in address alone: a listener on 127.0.0.1:53 could be forwarded to this machine’s loopback when you list port 53, giving the host’s programs the stand-in address for every name and putting their names in the VM’s log. A rule sends the VM’s own 127.0.0.1:53 to dnsmasq instead, so nothing of transparent mode listens on loopback, and the forwarder never sees it. DNS to public servers, not daemon.json: Docker gives containers 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4 when the host’s only name servers are on loopback, and an edit of daemon.json would restart Docker and need undoing on the open tier. A rule sends DNS to any public address to dnsmasq, from the VM and the bridges, which also catches resolvers that tools hard-code, and so does DNS to the VM’s own name servers but loopback’s: Lima’s DHCP adds one beside 127.0.0.1, which systemd-resolved falls back on and Docker gives containers once it drops the loopback one, and the e2e run showed both failing without it. Other private, link-local, CGNAT and loopback addresses are left alone, so a DNS server on a container’s or the LAN’s address still answers. Every other port refused, Docker’s published ports included: the NAT chains run at -110, before Docker’s at -100, and give every TCP and UDP port of the stand-in address a mapping, to its listener, to dnsmasq, or to a port where nothing listens. Without that, Docker’s DOCKER chain, which takes every local address but loopback, would send db.example.com:5432 to a container that publishes 5432, and a test suite would write into a local database. The ports from the proxy: the proxy owns the policy and reads its files again when they change, so devvm-transparent fetches /transparent/ports every 10 seconds rather than devvm finding every command and hand edit that changes a rule. The first bytes decide on every port: HTTP and TLS each work on every redirected port, so a rule such as api.internal.example:8080 works for plain HTTP too. devvm.proxy reserved whole: a name under it never reaches a link, a rule, a resolver or a company proxy, and neither does CONNECT devvm.proxy:P, which has no endpoint; only absolute-form requests for http://devvm.proxy/ reach the endpoints. Never 22 or 53: SSH names no host in its first bytes, and the VM’s ssh goes through ProxyCommand already. 53 is the VM’s own names'. A link’s name refused on both ways: dnsmasq gives a link’s name its /etc/hosts address, never the stand-in address, so only a crafted client reaches a link through the reserved target, and both the TLS and the HTTP way refuse it, so the two agree. Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, on the reserved target, the guest’s rules and the setup). Leads, each ruled out, fixed or listed:
Naming one host and reaching another: ruled out. The host is the SNI’s, or each request’s Host, and the proxy dials that host by name after routeFor judged it, then checks the replayed ClientHello’s SNI again (carry). An interception’s leaf names the SNI host alone, and every request whose Host or :authority differs gets 421 (TestTransparentIntercept). Domain fronting and ECH’s outer name are what CONNECT with the password reaches already. Secrets on the wrong host, or in plain HTTP: ruled out. Interception is chosen from the SNI host alone, on 443, and a plain request is always forwarded as http://, which never gets a secret (TestTransparentHTTP). SNI and Host shapes: ruled out. No SNI, an address, a trailing dot, two names, a ClientHello split across records or cut short, a name HostOK refuses and a name under devvm.proxy are refused before the policy (TestTransparentSNI, FuzzTransparent). A name with anything but printable ASCII is refused before its case is folded, so the Kelvin sign never becomes k, and the same holds for CONNECT’s target and its SNI check (TestHostsNotASCII). Holding the proxy’s memory or slots: fixed. A transparent connection counts toward the 1024 tunnels and gets 10 seconds for its first bytes. A ClientHello record longer than 16 KiB and 256 bytes is never read, and on every tunnel a ClientHello that has started must arrive whole within 10 seconds (TestTunnelHelloDeadline, TestPeekClientHelloCap). The 403 page’s TLS connection and an intercepted tunnel took 1 MiB of a request’s headers, where the proxy’s own listener takes 64 KiB.
