With the fix, every connection that the proxy serves HTTP on takes 64 KiB, and HTTP/2 inside one asks for at most 100 requests at once, where Go’s default is 250, each a request upstream (serveOne, TestServeOneHeaderLimit, TestServeOneStreamsLimit). Requests left running, and idle connections: fixed. A plain HTTP request, the transparent path’s included, went on after its client had gone, because the proxy can’t tell that from a half-close, so a VM could leave requests waiting on a host that never answers, past the connections it holds. Once its client stops sending, a request ends after a minute with nothing to pass on, while an answer that keeps coming still reaches a client that half-closed. A connection to the proxy waits at most 10 minutes between requests, and one without the password is closed after its 407. Only tunnels counted toward a limit, so the fix holds the proxy to at most 2048 connections of every kind at once, a request that outlives its client included, as net/http closes its connection only once the handler returns (maxConns). A connection counts from its first request with the password, and the ones that haven’t sent it wait in a pool of 128 where a new one closes the oldest (maxWaiting), so an open VM that reaches another VM’s proxy port can’t take that VM’s room by holding connections through their 30 seconds for headers. Tunnels’ HTTP/2 streams were bounded only for each tunnel, and every request upstream is a connection of its own, so 1024 tunnels could open about 100,000 connections to hosts. The proxy has at most 2048 requests upstream at once (maxRequests). Each limit’s line in proxy.log comes once a minute at most (everyMinute). A plain ws:// upgrade got 502, because the request’s writer hid the hijack it needs, and with the fix it gets its 101 (TestPlainHTTPEndsWithClient, TestProxyConnectionBounds, TestProxyConnectionLimit, TestProxyWaitingConnections, TestUpstreamRequestLimit, TestPlainWebSocket). A flood of connections to another VM’s proxy: listed. Connections without the password wait in their own pool, so holding them can’t take a VM’s room, but an open VM or a program on this machine that opens connections as fast as the host accepts them fills the kernel’s accept queue, and the VM’s own connections wait in it with them, or are evicted from the pool before their first request arrives. That slows the VM’s proxy for as long as the flood lasts, and ends with it. A ClientHello sent a byte, then late: fixed, found in review. The deadline first made a record header that didn’t come whole read as “not TLS”, so a tunnel that sent 0x16, waited past it, then sent a ClientHello naming another host was carried unchecked, which the SNI check had refused before. A stream whose first byte is 0x16 is TLS from then on: a header that doesn’t come whole, or whose version byte isn’t 3, is refused, and the far end gets nothing (TestTunnelHelloStall, FuzzClientHello). A split ClientHello on an address’s tunnel: fixed, found in review, older than transparent mode. A tunnel to an address may carry no server name, and a ClientHello that didn’t parse read as one without a name, so one split across two records, naming another host in the second, went on unchecked. Only a ClientHello that parsed whole counts now: one that doesn’t is refused, on every tunnel (TestTunnelAddressSplitHello). Other bridges and protocols reaching Docker’s DNAT through the stand-in address: fixed, found in review. The NAT chains map TCP and UDP alone, and only for lo, docker0 and br-*, so a published SCTP port, or a connection from Podman’s or LXD’s bridges, could reach a container through the stand-in address. Two filter chains at -150 drop both before any NAT chain (TestTransparentRuleset). The proxy’s endpoints without the password: fixed, found in review. socat adds the VM’s password for any client, so a container without the proxy settings reached devvm.proxy’s CA, ports and Nix cache through Host: devvm.proxy. On the transparent path that host reaches /blocked alone (TestTransparentHTTP). Names under the search domain: listed. dnsmasq can’t tell a single-label name the resolver extended from a name a tool names whole, so every name under this machine’s network’s search domain gets no answer through transparent mode, git.corp.example.com under corp.example.com included. Such a host needs the tool’s proxy settings, as its address on the LAN or a company network would anyway. A DNS server on the VM’s 127.0.0.1:53: listed. The rule that sends the VM’s resolver to dnsmasq takes every connection to that address and port, a forward of port 53 that the user listed included. The via label: listed. Whether a connection came through transparent mode is the VM’s own doing, as its User-Agent is, so devvm network lock’s heading for such hosts is a hint, not proof. DNS out of the VM: ruled out. dnsmasq has no upstream, the proxy asks the policy before it resolves a name, and the 403 page resolves nothing, so a blocked name never reaches the host’s resolver. Root that gives dnsmasq an upstream, or stops the service, meets the host’s confinement, which the e2e checks prove with the service stopped. New exposure on the host: ruled out. No listener, socket or sandbox rule is added on the host. socat’s connections are the VM’s own, to its own proxy, with its own password, which /etc/environment gives every VM process already. The listeners reached from the host or another network: ruled out. Nothing listens on loopback, the forwarder refuses the stand-in address, and an input rule keeps every interface but lo and Docker’s bridges off it. The VM’s password in arguments: ruled out. The setup reads the proxy’s URL on stdin, and socat and curl read the password from root’s files, so ps and the journal never show it. Containers without the proxy settings: listed, within the threat model. A container made through Docker’s API, or with its proxy variables emptied, had no way out before, and now reaches what the VM’s policy allows, as every program in the VM does. --network none gives a container no network, and an --internal network’s containers reach nothing. What /transparent/ports tells the VM: listed. It’s the ports the VM’s rules name, the shared ~/.config/devvm/policy’s included, never their hosts. The VM can’t read its policy otherwise, and it can’t learn a rule’s port by trying without a host that matches it, so the list is a small disclosure that reaches nothing. Learning: listed. Tools that failed silently before, such as telemetry, now succeed on the learn tier and would be learned, so devvm network lock lists the hosts that only they reached apart, under a heading of their own. A tunnel event needs a dial that succeeded, so a VM can’t make learn list a host it never reached. An open start after a confined one: listed. The service is enabled at boot until that launch’s setup takes it out, a few seconds later. In that window its connections reach the VM’s proxy, which is open by then, so they reach what the open tier allows anyway, and its answers have a time to live of 0, so nothing keeps them after. A running VM’s tier changed: listed, by design. The setup decides by the confinement the VM runs with, so a confined VM made open keeps transparent mode on an open proxy until its next start, which reaches what the open tier allows. Unprivileged in the VM: listed. dnsmasq and each socat connection’s process run as devvm-transparent, while socat’s listeners stay root’s, because socat drops its user only in each connection’s process. That’s hardening inside the VM, which the threat model doesn’t rely on. End-to-end checks (tests/e2e): network, on macOS and on a Linux host: the service runs, the stand-in address is on lo, and dnsmasq and socat listen on that address alone; every name with a dot resolves to it, IPv6 has none at once, /etc/hosts’ names keep theirs, and a name without a dot that isn’t there resolves to nothing, though the VM’s resolver appends this machine’s network’s search domain to it; curl without proxy settings and a static Go client with its own resolver reach github.com with its own certificate, logged without proxy settings; a blocked host gets the 403 over the VM’s CA; port 5432 of a name is refused at once and devvm-why names it; a port a rule names is redirected while the rule is there and refused at once after; your own servers bind 0.0.0.0:443 and :80; the service comes back when it’s killed or its table flushed; devvm network transparent off takes it out at the next launch and on puts it back; open, there’s none and names resolve with Lima’s DNS; with the service stopped, direct connections, DNS to Lima’s addresses and TCP to a public server’s port 53 still fail, and with it running a public DNS server and Lima’s DNS addresses answer only with the stand-in address, TTL 0, or nothing. In a VM of the docker layer, containers without proxy settings reach github.com on the default bridge and on a network of their own, a blocked host is logged, a container reaches no other port of the stand-in address and none of its listeners directly, a container’s published 5432 isn’t reached through the stand-in address from the VM or from another container, its published 443 doesn’t take the VM’s connections, and an --internal network reaches nothing. from: a Debian 12 VM and an Alpine one each pass the same checks on the allowlist tier, and with the service stopped, Lima’s DNS and a public server answer nothing.
data.where-secret-values-live#Where secret va:
devvm handles values that let whoever holds them act as you or as a VM: a VM’s proxy password, a build proxy’s, the company proxy’s password, the secrets you save and the keys and tokens in agents’ login files. Each one lives in a few places, and only there: the Keychain or the secret’s file in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/, the proxy’s proxy.json, the VM’s vm.json for its proxy password, the agent store’s login files, the proxy’s memory for the values it caches, and the VM’s own proxy settings for its password, which the VM must send. In devvm’s code, each such value is a redact.Secret from the moment it’s read until the place it’s used, except for the two that Not covered names (secrets in the code).
Printing never shows the value. String, GoString and Format write for every verb, so a %v of a struct in an error, a log line in the proxy’s own log or a line of devvm’s run log can’t hold it. fmt can’t call Format on a value in an unexported field, and prints such a field as it is, so the value is behind a pointer, and the field shows only its address. The run log’s own redaction, redact.String, still takes proxy keys and URL passwords out of the output of the commands devvm runs, which no type can reach. Encoding fails rather than writing a stand-in. MarshalJSON and MarshalText return redact.ErrEncode. A MarshalJSON that wrote would look safe, but a struct written to the file that should hold the value, such as proxy.json or vm.json, would then lose it, and a VM would lose its proxy or you your login, with no error. A file that holds a value has a wire type of its own instead, which writes the value as a string, so the two kinds of file can’t be confused. There’s no LogValue. devvm has no log/slog logging, so a slog.LogValuer would have no caller, and Format already covers the proxy’s log.Logger. Reveal is the one way to the value, and forbidigo refuses every call to it outside tests, so each place that uses a value carries a //nolint:forbidigo with its reason: the proxy’s password check, the headers it puts values in, the company proxy’s credentials, the VM’s CA key as it signs, its config file and the broker’s frames to its child; the secrets’ store, which writes the Keychain and the file; the VM’s proxy URL and vm.json; and internal/agentlogin’s login files, refreshes and claims. A new use is a choice someone made, with its reason on the line, which the review sees. The structure test refuses a struct that embeds a Secret, which would take on its Reveal, and an interface that declares Reveal() string, through which a value could pass without a call forbidigo sees. The wire types keep each file’s bytes as they were, so a frozen release’s proxy.json writes back byte for byte (TestV010ProxyConfigs), its Sum doesn’t change and no running VM’s proxy starts again for an upgrade. An agent’s login file stays the agent’s own format, read and written as a map so that fields devvm doesn’t know are kept, and a key or token is a redact.Secret once it leaves the map, through a lookup, a refresh or a capture.
Not covered. The company proxy’s URLs as your environment gives them, HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY, can hold a password, and they stay strings, because devvm passes them on as they are, to proxy.json and to the programs it runs on the host. So do the URLs proxy.Upstream.WithPassword returns, which hold the saved password for devvm’s own clients and the programs it runs. The VM’s proxy URL, which holds its password, is a string too, because it goes into the VM’s Lima config and environment, where the VM needs it. redact.String and redact.In take the passwords in such URLs out of devvm’s run log and Lima’s logs (your company proxy’s password). Two values are strings by design:
The Keychain’s value, which platform.KeychainGet returns and KeychainSet takes as a string, because internal/platform imports no devvm package. secrets.Store makes it a Secret at once in saved, and reveals it only for KeychainSet in save. devvm desktop’s VNC password, 8 characters that you must see to type into a VNC viewer. devvm keeps it in the desktop section of vm.json and shows it in desktop_ready.
data.workspace-clones#Workspace clones:
devvm --clone in a folder of repos gives one VM a clone of each repo the user picks, each at its own path, so the paths between them work as on the host (folders of repos). It extends the one-repo clone rather than adding a mode beside it: the clone section’s repos lists the repos by their paths relative to the folder, and a clone of the folder’s own repo, the only kind devvm 0.1.0 made, reads as one repo at . with its remote and seed in made, so its state needs no migration. Every step that a one-repo clone takes for its repo, a workspace clone takes for each: the checks of --clone (checkRepoTop, cloneSource, gitprotect.OwnRepo), a remote of its own (freeRemote), a copy of its branches through the VM’s own command channel to that repo’s path (the copy into a clone VM), and at devvm rm or devvm clone off, the check of its work and the removal of its remote. The repos are found by the walk that .git protection makes (starter.walk), so the same depth, skipped folders and bound apply, and they’re recorded once, when the VM is made or at devvm clone add, never at a launch.
Four choices keep it small. The seed copies each repo’s refs as a one-repo clone’s seed does, every branch, tag and remote-tracking branch, so a workspace repo behaves in the VM as a repo of its own does; the seed sends one pack for each repo, so this costs about what a clone of the repo does. A repo --clone can’t copy is listed and left out, never fatal, so one odd repo doesn’t stop the rest; the same holds for a repo whose three remote names are taken. The folder’s own files outside every repo are copied once and never back, as a tar the host makes from what it reads beneath the folder, so a Makefile or a compose file works in the VM without becoming a sync. And devvm in one of the repos opens the folder’s VM at that repo’s path, because the VM has the repo there and mounts nothing of the host, so the finder’s reason to pass over a parent’s VM below a repo of its own, that the parent’s VM can write that repo, doesn’t hold; --here still makes the repo’s own VM.
rm’s check reads every repo at once: one script sent with the command (cloneState, never a copy on disk) prints each repo’s branches, its status and its linked worktrees below the folder with their statuses, as length-prefixed records, so ten repos cost one ssh session, not thirty. devvm reads it as it reads anything from a VM, capped, by a parser that takes only what it asked for.
The guarantee: a workspace clone’s VM gets nothing of the host but the branches the user’s repos already have, the files outside them that devvm copied once, and the shared tools and agent folders every VM gets. Nothing from the VM runs on the host, changes a ref outside a repo’s remote-tracking branches for the VM, or writes outside those repos’ .git. Everything the VM says, its branch names, paths and statuses, is untrusted, checked before it’s used and made printable before it’s shown.
What could break it: a host file outside the folder reaching the VM through the copy, by a link, a hard link, a swap during the read or a special file; host git run in a folder the state names, or by what the VM serves; refs written outside refs/remotes//; the clone check’s answer read without a bound, or a path in it that leads out of the folder; the finder taking a VM that mounts the folder for one that doesn’t.
Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion’s local-file class, and two independent adversarial reviews of the change, “the review” and “the second review” below). Leads, each fixed, ruled out or listed:
A host file through the copy: fixed. devvm first walked the folder by paths beneath an os.Root, which follows a link in the middle of a path while it stays in the root, so another VM that mounts a subfolder could swap a folder there for a link to an unchosen repo, or its .git, as the walk reached it, and the copy took that repo’s files and config (the adversarial review). The walk now opens each folder from its parent’s handle and checks it’s the folder it listed (safefile.Root.OpenDir, TestOpenDir), and opens each file by its own name in its folder, without following a link at its end, checked to be a regular file once open, and refused when it has another hard link, which could be any file on its disk (OneLink). A folder shaped like a git dir, such as a bare mirror, was copied as plain files, which the review found too; it’s now left out and counted. A link is copied as a link only when its target is relative and stays in the folder, never read through. Other disks, sockets, FIFOs and devices stay on the host, and files keep their permissions without set-id bits (TestWorkspaceFiles). A workspace clone copies the folder’s files, so devvm refuses the folders it refuses to mount, such as the home folder (checkUnsafe). Listed: a secret the user keeps at the folder’s top, such as an .env, is copied as any file is, which the docs say. Host git in a folder the VM chose: fixed. Host git runs only in the repos devvm’s state records, which only devvm writes, each at a clean path below the folder, and repos passes over any other. The review found that only the seed checked a recorded repo again, so once another VM, or the user, removed a repo’s .git or put another folder in its place, devvm clone fetch and rm’s fetch wrote the VM’s objects and refs into whichever repo git found there, the folder’s own above it included. Every fetch into a repo, and devvm clone off’s undo adding its remote again, now checks first that the folder is still the top of a repo of its own (checkRepoTop): devvm clone fetch leaves it alone and names it, and rm and devvm clone off refuse and keep the VM (the clone_workspace script). Every host git command goes through hostgit, so no hook, fsmonitor, filter or GIT_* of the environment runs, and the push and fetch connect to the VM alone, whatever the repo’s config says (gitSSHCommand). Refs from the VM: ruled out. devvm clone fetch fetches with --refmap= and one refspec, +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes//*, so the VM’s branches land only under that repo’s remote for the VM, whose name devvm chose, and host git refuses a ref name it can’t take. rm’s fetch writes new saved/ branches only, never over one (savedPrefix). The names devvm lists are host git’s, read back, and shown through msg.Printable. The clone check’s answer: ruled out. devvm reads at most 8 MiB, and fails the check past that or after 2 minutes; each record must be whole, of a repo asked for, and each worktree’s path clean, relative and below the folder, once, followed by its status (TestParseCloneState, TestWorktreePathPins). A VM that hides its work only loses its own work, which the docs say: devvm checks what the VM answers, not that it answers everything. A repo whose clone isn’t at its path in the VM first read as having nothing to check, so a clone moved in the VM went with its work without a question (the review); it’s now asked about, as uncommitted changes are (TestCloneChangesAcrossRepos). The finder’s carve-out: ruled out. It applies only to a state whose clone section is on and a workspace, which never mounts the folder; a VM made again with the folder mounted clears that section first (TestCoversRepo, the clone_workspace script). A repo another VM can swap: fixed. A VM that mounts a subfolder holding a workspace repo, or the repo itself, can swap it for a link to another repo between devvm’s check and its push or fetch, which would send another repo’s history into the clone VM, or write the clone’s refs into another repo (the second review). devvm now refuses such a repo when it finds the repos, at devvm clone add and before each push and fetch, and rm’s check runs no host git in it, naming the VM (finder.mountsRepo, stillRepo, the clone_workspace_repo script); the check and git still race for a VM that mounts it only later, which the next command names. A repo with worktrees or repos of its own: fixed. The second review found that a repo holding a linked worktree, as the docs’ .worktrees/NAME layout makes, or a repo below it, became a workspace: --no-input scripts that 0.1.0 ran now refused, the worktree was copied as a repo of its own, recording a remote in the config it shares with its repo, and the folder’s own clone showed the other clones as untracked, so rm always asked. A folder that’s a repo gets its own clone unless --repos is given, a linked worktree of a repo in the folder is never a repo of its own (worktreeIn), each repo’s remote is chosen once the one before is added, and the folder’s own clone excludes the other clones and what the host’s info/exclude names (repoExcludes, TestFindRepos, TestRepoExcludes, the clone_workspace_repo script). A folder of repos inside another repo’s working tree is refused, as its copy would take that repo’s files. Work lost to a copy that didn’t finish: fixed. devvm clone add records a repo before its copy, and a failed copy left it recorded and unseeded, which the command then called added, and rm passed over, so a push that reached the VM without its record went unchecked. A recorded, unseeded repo is now copied again by devvm clone add, fetched when its remote is recorded, and checked by rm when its clone is in the VM (the clone_workspace script’s failed add, then its retry). The verification pass: fixed. devvm clone add . gave the folder’s own clone no excludes, so it showed the other clones as changes and rm always asked; it now gets every other repo’s and the host’s. A linked worktree whose repo another VM mounts wasn’t refused; devvm now checks the repo its common dir is in too (mountingVM). Exclude lines took a repo’s folder name as a pattern, so lib[2] wasn’t left out, and a name with a line break could write a line that left out every new folder, hiding work from rm; git’s pattern characters are now escaped, each line is anchored at both ends, and a repo whose name has a character msg.Safe refuses, a line break among them, is refused (TestRepoExcludes runs real git on them). A repo another VM mounts failed rm for the whole workspace; rm now reads its clone in the VM, checks every other repo, and asks before its work goes, never running host git in it. The VM’s folder never made failed the check; it now reads as every repo gone. Each repo is checked again after rm’s question, before its fetch. A retry whose push had landed sent it again, which the VM refused once its branch moved on; a repo the VM has with a commit is now left as it is, and only its remote added. The branches’ bound of 10,000 is for all the repos of a check together. A worktree hidden by the bound: fixed. The clone check’s script counted the worktrees outside the folder towards its 101 before leaving them out, so 101 outside ones hid a changed one inside, and rm deleted without asking, for a one-repo clone too; it counts only those inside now (TestCloneStateScript). The repos’ branches are capped at 10,000 in all per check, as each costs host git a lookup. Cost: listed. The walk is .git protection’s, bounded at 100 repos; the copy at 5,000 entries and 64 MiB, each file at 10 MiB. A VM can serve a pack without end, or many branches, which devvm clone fetch writes into the repo until the disk is full or the user presses Ctrl+C, as git fetch devvm would; a cap on what host git reads from the VM’s ssh isn’t built. The read of the clone, by rm and devvm clone off, shares the bounds of the read of the agents’ worktrees (answer). devvm stops the VM’s command past 8 MiB and gives up past 2 minutes, so when a VM writes without end, slowly or not, or never answers, the check fails and devvm keeps the VM, and --no-clone-check is the way out (TestWorkCheckBounded). End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, the clone section): a folder of two repos and a file of its own gets one VM that mounts only the shared tools, with each repo’s clone at its path holding every branch and the folder’s file; an agent-like commit in each repo comes back with devvm clone fetch, listed as one branch with both repos; devvm clone add copies a third; rm without a terminal refuses with unfetched work in one repo, naming it, and keeps the VM; --no-clone-check deletes it and removes every repo’s remote. Unit tests: TestDefaultBranch, TestSeedTips, TestIsWorkspace, TestChooseRepos, TestPickRepos, TestFindRepos, TestWorkspaceFiles, TestCloneChangesAcrossRepos, TestFetchedByBranch, TestCloneRepos, TestFixtureClonesReadAsOneRepo, TestCoversRepo, TestParseCloneState, TestCloneStateScript, TestOpenDir and TestRepoExcludes.

data.a-commands-help#A command’s help:
Every command’s help, which its reference page also shows, has the same shape. Short is an action in sentence case without a full stop, such as List the project VMs. Long is one to three short sentences on what the command does, and the rules and edge cases go on its docs page. Example comes from examples in internal/cli/help.go, which takes each command line with a short comment and lines the comments up, the most common invocation first. A flag’s description is short, and its long explanation goes on the page.
Each command describes itself where it’s made, so its docs page and group are in its own file, not in tables elsewhere. Its Annotations come from an about in internal/cli/help.go: docs, the user page that covers it as page#anchor; group, its section of the root’s help; and noJSON, why a command without --json has none. addDocs gives the root Cobra’s usage template with a Docs section at the end, which shows the address of the command’s page, and the root’s help also ends with the issue tracker, msg.IssuesURL. The CLI reference links each command’s page too, and TestDocLinks in internal/msg reads those links from the reference and checks that each page and heading exists and is a user page. helpGroups in the same file lists the root’s sections, in order, and addGroups adds each group that has a command and sets its commands’ GroupID, so a group whose commands don’t exist yet stays out of the help. A subcommand can name a group too, such as layer add in Change your VM, when it belongs in another group than its parent. addGroups then adds that group to the parent, so the parent’s own help groups its subcommands the same way, and the usage template lists the subcommand by both names in the root’s group, after the group’s own commands. Cobra lists a group’s commands in alphabetical order, and help goes in Cobra’s own Additional Commands.
The tests fail when the checked-in pages are stale: TestReferenceIsCurrent in internal/cli/docgen generates the reference into a temporary folder and compares it with docs/content/docs/cli/, and it checks each generated block against its page too, which TestStaleBlockIsCaught proves it catches. mise run docs regenerates it before serving the site.
data.building-the-site#Building the site: mise run docs draws the diagrams, then serves the site at http://localhost:1313/ and reloads on every change except a diagram’s, which needs mise run docs:diagrams again. After you run mise run docs:diagrams, mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify builds the site into docs/public/, as the Docs workflow does for devvm.dev, and mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml builds the site as next.devvm.dev has it, with its banner and its noindex (the docs sites).
data.the-cli-reference#The CLI reference:
The CLI reference in docs/content/docs/cli/ is generated from devvm’s commands with Cobra’s docs generator, and checked in. Don’t edit it: change the command’s Use, Short, Long, Example or flags, or its docs page in internal/msg/docs.go, then run:
mise run cli-docs It runs internal/cli/docgen, which replaces every page in that folder: _index.md, listing the commands, and a page per command named after its path (devvm_build.md), with title and explainer front matter, the explainer being the command’s Short, and links to the other pages as files. Each page has the command’s examples, and a Docs section before See also that links to the command’s docs page on the site. Hidden commands (_msg, _qemu) and Cobra’s help command are left out. The pages carry no dates, so the same commands give the same files. They carry no weight either, so Hugo sorts the section by title, and a new command adds its own page and changes only _index.md and the root’s devvm.md; TestPagesHaveNoWeight checks this. The .gitattributes file marks the pages as generated, so GitHub collapses them in a diff.
mise run cli-docs also writes the generated blocks of hand-written pages, which cli.DocBlocks in internal/cli/docblocks.go lists: the Supported agents table in using/coding-agents.md, and the README’s list of the agents. Each block sits between two HTML comments that name it, and docgen replaces only the text between them, from the registry of agents, agents.Defs, and each agent’s policy in assets/shared-tools/. So don’t edit a block by hand: change the agent’s Def, its Docs included, or its policy, then run mise run cli-docs.
data.writing-docs#Writing docs:
The site is Hugo with the Hextra theme, built from docs/. Hextra is a Hugo module pinned in docs/go.mod; update it with hugo mod get github.com/imfing/hextra@ in docs/.
Pages are Markdown files in docs/content/docs/, one per topic, in a folder per section of the sidebar. The sections run in the order a new user needs them: getting-started/, using/, releases/, safety/, backends/, compared/, cli/, internals/, then contributing/. Each folder’s _index.md is the section’s own page, which lists its pages. Update the page for any behavior you change, in the same change. The README stays high level: it says what devvm is and links to the pages for the rest. What goes where: the user pages, in getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/ and compared/, say what devvm does, what you type and what you see, and they name no repo paths, Go identifiers or message names. How it works, in internals/, explains how devvm does it, for readers who want to check a claim, and it holds the mechanisms and the message names that come from them. Contributing, in contributing/, covers changing devvm, so repo paths, Go identifiers, version bumps, releases and tests go there, and so do the design notes, which say why devvm is built as it is and hold each emulation’s design note and threat check. A user page links once to its How it works page where there is one. Current behavior, but for releases: every page describes how devvm works now, and none mentions older behavior, what changed or what moved, because that goes in the changelog and on the release pages. Releases, in releases/, is the one place the docs describe history. It has a page for each minor release, such as releases/0.2.0.md, which covers the release and its release candidates and is written as the release is made. Each change there has a section of its own, under Breaking changes, Changes, Fixes or Hardening, that tells its full story: what was wrong or missing, how it showed, how devvm works now, at the level of the user pages, and what you do, with links to the user or How it works pages for anything deeper. The changelog’s entry links each section, as Releasing says. These pages follow the docs voice, but they aren’t user pages, so the rules for leading with a command don’t apply. User pages lead with doing: a task on a user page, in getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/ or compared/, shows its command, in a copyable block or numbered steps, and a short explanation follows. One paragraph of why next to its command is fine, but two or more paragraphs back to back mean the mechanism belongs on the How it works page, under a heading that the user page links to, with every fact moved rather than dropped. The docs-voice skill’s SKILL.md has the rule, under Commands first on user pages, with an example, and its scan.sh -p paras and scan.sh -p long list the runs and the long paragraphs. Front matter sets title, shown as the page’s heading, weight, the page’s place in its section, or a section’s place in the sidebar for an _index.md, and explainer, the line under the title on the page’s social card, which Social cards below describes. Start the body at ##. Links to other pages point at their files ([Contributing](_index.md)), so the linters can check them. Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks, fenced with mermaid, which a script draws as SVGs before Hugo builds the site, so no page loads Mermaid or any other diagram JavaScript. A diagram goes where it helps the reader follow the text, with at most one sentence to introduce it, and the text keeps every fact the diagram shows. Drawing them: mise run docs:diagrams installs pele with npm ci --ignore-scripts, at the version and integrity that docs/package.json and docs/package-lock.json pin, and then runs docs/render-diagrams.mjs. The script draws each block in docs/content as an SVG in docs/.build/diagrams/, which git ignores, with a JSON file of the diagram’s size beside it. It names both files for the block’s key, which is a hash of the salt and the block’s text. The salt is a hash of pele’s version and the script itself, and the script writes it to that folder too. mise run docs and mise run lint:docs run it first, and so do the Docs workflow’s builds. Caching: a run with nothing changed takes a few hundredths of a second. mise skips the task when the drawings’ folder is newer than every page in docs/content, the script, docs/package.json and the lock, so the script updates the folder’s time on every run. The task runs npm ci only when the lock’s SHA-256 differs from the one it wrote to docs/node_modules/.devvm-lock-sha256 after its last install. The script keeps every drawing that’s already there, draws only the blocks it has no drawing of, and deletes the files no block’s key names, so a changed diagram is drawn again on its own, and a new pele or a change to the script draws them all again. The CI workflow’s check job caches npm’s downloads, keyed on the lock, and the Docs workflow, which publishes, keeps no cache and draws every diagram. Putting them in pages: hugo.yaml mounts that folder at assets/diagrams, and the render hook, docs/layouts/_markup/render-codeblock-mermaid.html, which takes the place of Hextra’s, reads the salt, computes each block’s key from it and the block’s text, and puts the SVG in the page. A block without its SVG fails the build, so run mise run docs:diagrams again after you change a diagram, even while mise run docs serves the site, because the server doesn’t redraw them. The theme is in custom.css, which sets pele’s --pele-* variables from the site’s palette, so a diagram never sets its own colors or font. Panels are on the surface color with blue borders, lines and arrows are lime, subgraphs, lifelines and notes use the border color, and text is in Departure Mono at 14px, larger than the home page’s art so labels read easily. The layout is pele’s own, with the Mermaid settings that render-diagrams.mjs passes, such as right-angled edges. A diagram can set its own layout in front matter, as Staying safe’s three columns set minNodeWidth, but never its own colors or font. pele lays subgraphs out from left to right in the order they’re written. Measuring labels: the script measures each label by Departure Mono’s metrics, where every character is 350/550 of the font size wide, so labels fit their boxes. pele draws edge labels, messages and notes at seven-eighths of the size, 12px, and has no option to change it, so the measurer gives that text its width at 14px and the script then writes it at 14px. A self-check, before anything is drawn, fails the run when pele no longer measures and writes that text as the script expects, and every group of small text that pele draws must carry the 12px size the script replaces. The script also puts a newline after each label, where the SVG draws nothing, so the site’s search sees one label’s last word apart from the next label’s first. Size: each diagram is drawn at its own size and never scaled to fit. The hook sets each diagram’s width on it, and a diagram wider than the text reaches into the page’s right margin, the article’s padding, as far as it needs, and into the padding on the left for whatever the right margin can’t hold, so it never covers the table of contents. A diagram wider than the text and both paddings scrolls sideways, as the widest ones do on a narrow screen. custom.css gives each one content-visibility: auto, so the browser draws it only when it nears the screen, and the hook sets the diagram’s height as its contain-intrinsic-block-size, so the page doesn’t jump while you scroll. Accessibility: every diagram has an accTitle and a one-line accDescr, which become the SVG’s title and description that screen readers read, and the script fails on a diagram without them. The description says in full sentences what the diagram shows. Labels: keep labels short, and break a long one with . In a label, write < as #lt; and > as #gt;. pele’s version is pinned exactly, and scripts/bump.sh pele moves it (updating pinned versions). Style: succinct and direct. Commands are written as devvm x or in backticks, never in quotes. No please, simply or note that. The home page is docs/content/_index.md, on Hextra’s hextra-home layout: its hero shortcodes, then plain Markdown. custom.css styles it through the one div that the layout wraps its content in. After the hero, the page has a quick start, what’s supported, why to use devvm with its feature cards, a short FAQ, and a closing call to action with the hero’s buttons. It keeps a marketing tone, but each of its claims matches the docs page it links to, it uses the same terms, and it says each thing once. The quick start shows the three commands to run first, each after a comment short enough to fit a phone’s width, because a comment after its command would scroll out of view there. Feature cards on the home page come from two shortcodes in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, which make a {{< features >}} grid of {{< feature title="Ready in seconds" icon="high-voltage" art="copies" >}} cards, each closed with {{< /feature >}}. A card shows its title as a heading, after the pixel icon its icon names, drawn in the title’s own color at 24px, then the Markdown inside it, then its illustration, which is optional. The cards are in one centered column on smaller screens. From 1024px wide, they go into two columns, the first, third and so on on the left and the rest on the right, and each card is as tall as its content, so no card leaves a gap under it. features places them: feature renders its card through docs/layouts/_partials/feature-card.html and hands it over, and each card’s order style keeps the page’s order when the columns stack. What’s supported uses the same cards with smaller illustrations, and Quick start uses them with a terminal in each card. {{< features columns="3" >}} puts three in a row from 1024px wide, and level="3" on a card makes its title an h3, under the section’s own heading. Art beside a section’s text comes from {{< beside art="blast-radius" >}}, closed with {{< /beside >}}, in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/beside.html. It renders the Markdown inside it, then the illustration it names. From 1024px wide, the text and the drawing each take half the column, with the drawing on the right, centered on the text. On narrower screens, the drawing goes below the text. Why use devvm? uses it. Install commands come from {{< install >}} in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/install.html, which the home page and Installing use. The commands are written in one place, docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, which the tabs and the pages’ Markdown copies both read. It renders Hextra’s tabs with a macOS tab, which has the Homebrew command, and a Linux tab, which has the install script. The macOS tab is selected in the HTML, so it shows when JavaScript is off. A small script in docs/layouts/_partials/install-os.html selects the Linux tab as the page loads when the browser’s platform or user agent string says Linux, apart from Android. To check the Linux tab in headless Chrome, pass --user-agent= with a Linux user agent string. custom.css styles the tabs on a blue line, with the selected tab in lime. Other content per operating system goes in {{< os-tabs >}}, with a {{< os-tab name="macOS" >}} and then a {{< os-tab name="Linux" >}} inside it, each holding Markdown, as Installing’s requirements tables do. It uses the same tabs, styles and script as the install commands, so the visitor’s system is selected, and the build fails unless the tabs are macOS’s, then Linux’s. Colors: the site is dark only (hugo.yaml’s params.theme). Its palette is in docs/assets/css/custom.css: a black background and one lime accent, #7fff00, which sets Hextra’s primary color. The home page’s illustrations also use #0086b3, the blue that Hextra’s syntax highlighting gives commands like cd, and #ff5370 (--devvm-red), the JustBlack theme’s red, which marks only what an attack has compromised. The red’s contrast is 6.7:1 on the black and 6.0:1 on the surface color, and it’s much darker than the lime, so the two stay apart for readers who can’t tell red from green. Fonts: the site uses Instrument Sans for text, Martian Mono for code, and Departure Mono, a pixel font, for the logo and the home page’s headings, badge and buttons. All three are in docs/static/fonts/, each in its own folder with its license, and docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html declares them. Instrument Sans and Martian Mono are upstream’s variable WOFF2 files, so one file holds every weight, and the partial’s comment records where each font came from, at which commit or release, and its SHA-256. To update a font, download the new version from the same place, check its SHA-256, and update the comment. Departure Mono is sharp at multiples of 11px and has one weight. No third-party requests: devvm.dev and next.devvm.dev load every script, stylesheet, font and image from the site itself, so a visitor’s browser asks no other host for anything. mise run lint:docs checks this after it builds the site: TestNoThirdPartyLoads in internal/cli/docgen/site_test.go reads every page and stylesheet and fails on a link, script, image, frame or CSS url() that points at a host other than the ones in hugo.yaml’s and next.yaml’s baseURL. Hugo fetches FlexSearch, which Hextra’s search uses, when it builds the site, and the site serves it itself, so it passes. Diagrams are SVGs inside the pages, so they load nothing. Links that a visitor clicks, such as GitHub’s, aren’t loads, and the check ignores them. The social cards draw it from docs/assets/fonts/departure-mono/, which has the same release’s OTF and license, because Hugo can’t draw text from a WOFF2. The logo in the navbar is the branding page’s devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at its own size, which hugo.yaml’s params.navbar.logo names, with the site’s title as its alt text. Right-clicking it opens the branding page instead of the browser’s menu, through a script in docs/layouts/_partials/custom/footer.html. A left click, or Enter on the focused logo, still goes to the home page. The branding page is docs/content/branding.md, at /branding/, on its own layout, docs/layouts/branding.html, which is Hextra’s home layout with the home page’s look and the script that copies a swatch’s hex. Its front matter keeps it out of the sidebar. It has the logo as box-drawing text in a code block, the logo’s SVGs and PNGs, the icons, the social card, the palette, the fonts, how to use the logo and the credits. Its downloads are in docs/static/branding/, and {{< brand-asset >}} tiles inside {{< brand-assets >}} show each one on its background, with a link to each file. The build fails when a file doesn’t exist, and it reads each PNG’s size for its link. devvm-logo-on-dark.svg and devvm-logo-on-light.svg are the logo, drawn on a pixel grid as the favicon is, made from Departure Mono’s 11px glyphs. The prompt and devvm are at twice the glyphs’ size, the box is in 1-pixel lines, and the lock, a block with a keyhole under a 2-pixel arch, sits on the box’s bottom-right corner, with the box’s lines stopping short of it so that the arch stands clear. The version for light backgrounds is black, with its prompt in the dark lime, #408000 (--devvm-accent-dark), which is the lime’s hue at half its lightness, with a contrast of 4.9:1 on white, where the lime has 1.2:1. Each logo’s PNG is its SVG at four times its size on a transparent background, and devvm-icon-64.png to devvm-icon-1024.png are docs/static/favicon.svg at 4 to 64 times its size. After changing an SVG, render its PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the exact size, passing --default-background-color=00000000 for the logos’ transparency, and look at each one. The palette comes from {{< palette >}}, which reads the colors that docs/data/palette.yaml lists, with each one’s name and use, and takes each hex from its variable in custom.css, so the page always shows the site’s colors. The build fails when a variable isn’t there. A new color goes in both files. The fonts each come from {{< font-sample >}}, which shows a line of text in the font, with a link to the license the site serves for it. The favicon is the same mark drawn on a 16-pixel grid in docs/static/favicon.svg: the box, a lime prompt in its middle and a small lock centered on its bottom-right corner, overhanging it by 2 pixels each way, its shackle a closed arch, with the box’s lines stopping a pixel short of the lock, on black, with a pixel of black around the whole mark. Hextra links its icons by name, and the ones in docs/static/ take the place of its own: favicon-16x16.png and favicon-32x32.png, favicon.ico, which holds those two PNGs, apple-touch-icon.png, which is the grid at 160px with 10px of black around it, and the two android-chrome-*.png icons that site.webmanifest lists. Each PNG is the SVG at a whole multiple of its size, so its pixels stay sharp. The social card in docs/static/images/social-card.png is the 1200x630 card that the branding page offers for links to devvm. It has devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at twice its size, the home page’s headline and tagline in Departure Mono, and the site’s colors. After changing the SVG or the card’s text, render the PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the image’s exact size, and look at each one. Social cards: every page gets a 1200x630 card of its own, which Hugo draws when it builds the site, and which sites and chat apps show when someone shares the page’s link. The card is docs/assets/images/og-template.png, which is social-card.png with the headline and tagline painted out in the background’s black, so it has the logo, devvm.dev and the lime bar, in the same four colors and nothing else. docs/layouts/_partials/og-image.html draws three things on it with Hugo’s images.Text, in Departure Mono: the page’s section in lime capitals at 22px, its title in white at 66px, or at 55px or 44px when a smaller size fits it in two lines, and its explainer in gray at 33px. A docs page’s section is its section’s title, such as Using devvm, a section’s own page has Docs, and the home page and the branding page have none. The text is centered between the logo and devvm.dev. Each size is a multiple of 11px and each line starts at a whole pixel, so the text is as sharp as the logo, and the card keeps only the template’s four colors. docs/layouts/_partials/og-wrap.html wraps the lines at spaces, and because the font is monospaced, a line’s width is its length. The explainer is the explainer in each page’s front matter: a few plain words on what the reader gets from the page, such as Install devvm and check what it needs, without a full stop. It isn’t the page’s description, which search engines and llms.txt show, because that’s a sentence or two, and most pages have none. The home page’s card shows its cardTitle, the hero’s headline, in place of its title, because the logo already says devvm. The CLI reference’s pages get their command’s Short as their explainer when mise run cli-docs writes them. TestExplainers in internal/cli/docgen fails when a page has no explainer, or when its explainer takes more than two lines of 48 characters or its title more than two lines of 36, which are the card’s lines at 33px and 44px. The tags: docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes og:image with its type, width, height and og:image:alt, and twitter:image:alt, whose text is devvm docs, the title and the explainer. docs/layouts/_partials/_funcs/get-page-images.html takes the place of Hugo’s own, which its Twitter card and schema templates call for a page’s images, so twitter:image and the schema’s image are the same card. hugo.yaml names no params.images, so Hextra’s Open Graph template writes no second og:image. A card’s address is the site’s, so next.devvm.dev’s pages show next.devvm.dev’s cards. The illustrations on the home page are SVGs in docs/assets/home/, and {{< art "name" >}} inlines one into the page, so that it gets the page’s fonts and colors. A feature card’s art parameter inlines one the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/art.html. Each one is drawn on Departure Mono’s 11px cell, 7 pixels wide and 14 tall, so its text and shapes are sharpest at its own size or at twice its size. The art shortcode shows it at twice its size, 728px wide. A card shows it as wide as the card, at whatever scale that takes. Each card’s drawing shows what its text says, and nothing more. The big cards’ drawings are 364 by 140 pixels, or 168 for isolated.svg: zero-config.svg shows a dev server’s forwarded port, devvm code and a commit authored by you, copies.svg the base image and its copies, isolated.svg the mount and the proxy, agents.svg the agents’ mounts, the history that stays and the token, and make-it-yours.svg the stack of base, your layer and the VM, with --from. The What’s supported cards’ drawings are 224 by 70 pixels: toolchains.svg, coding-agents.svg and layers.svg, which shows the image docker+nix as a stack and the built-in layers beside it. The Quick start cards’ drawings are terminals of 254 by 181 pixels, which a card shows at most twice their size: step-cd.svg types cd ~/some-project on your machine, step-pick.svg types devvm, shows a short version of the new VM’s summary and presses enter at Customize it? [y/N], and step-agent.svg types claude in the VM’s shell. Why use devvm?’s drawing, blast-radius.svg, is 364 by 210 pixels and shows the same four attacks as its text on two machines. Without devvm, they light up on your machine, and the project, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh and another project turn red one after another. With devvm, they light up in the VM, each one’s path toward your machine ends at the VM’s border with a cross, and your machine’s folders stay as they are. Every text element holds one run of characters at its own x, because Hugo’s --minify removes the spaces between tspan elements. A gap of a cell is 7 pixels added to x. Animations are CSS keyframes in custom.css, which classes in the SVGs turn on. pulse dims and brightens a lime arrow every 3 seconds, and pulse-2 and pulse-3 start a part of the arrow 0.3 and 0.6 seconds later, so the pulse runs along it. pulse-slow does the same every 4 seconds. lit lights a text’s fill and lit-chip a chip’s opacity for most of a 4-second loop, and lit-2, lit-3 and lit-4 start them 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds later, so they light one after another. blink turns a cursor on and off every 2 seconds. mover marks a block that travels a path, mover-token along the token’s line, under the proxy and down to the API in 3 seconds, and mover-egress under the proxy, down to the allowlist and back, then out to the internet in 4 seconds. A block is drawn before the shapes it passes under. attack-1 to attack-4, path-1 to path-4 and reach-1 to reach-4 tell blast-radius.svg’s story in an 8-second loop, and every part of the drawing stays in place all along, so the story only changes colours and draws lines. Each attack’s chip turns from gray to lime at 0.4, 1.6, 2.8 and 4 seconds. In the VM, its path then draws itself down to the VM’s border, and when it gets there, the cross at the border turns lime and, on the machine without devvm, the folder it reaches turns red. Everything holds from 5.2 seconds, and from 6.6 seconds the colours go back and the paths draw back up, so the drawing rests from 7.2 seconds until the story starts again. Each step has its own keyframes, so that all of them end together. The SVG draws each part in its end colour, and --rest in custom.css gives the colour it has before its step, so a drawing without animation shows the end of the story. The Quick start terminals each loop on their own. type marks a cover over a command, which shrinks from the right one cell at a time while caret moves the cursor along, both in --chars steps across --width, and caret-blink keeps the cursor solid while it types and makes it blink after. In step-pick.svg, pick-summary shows the summary once devvm is typed, pick-ask shows the question after it, and key lights enter as it’s pressed. Their styles in custom.css are each part’s end state too, and their keyframes start from the beginning. When the visitor’s system asks for reduced motion, prefers-reduced-motion turns every animation off and hides the blocks. To see an animation’s state in a screenshot, pause the animations with a stylesheet of your own and set each class’s animation-delay to minus the time you want, because headless Chrome’s --virtual-time-budget barely moves CSS animations. Icons are pixel icons in docs/assets/icons/, one SVG per icon. Most come from Dinkie Icons, which is MIT licensed, and the folder keeps its license and a README that names the version they were copied from. The penguin, prompt, warning and light bulb icons are drawn for devvm in the same style. {{< icon "rocket" >}} inlines one through docs/layouts/_partials/icon.html, so it takes the text’s color, and the build fails when no icon has that name. An icon is 0.75em square, which makes each of its pixels one screen pixel in 16px text, and it sits on the text’s baseline. Screen readers skip it, unless a second argument gives it a label, as in {{< icon "warning" "Warning" >}}, for an icon that says something the text doesn’t. To add a Dinkie icon, copy its path data from the same version of the @dinkie-icons/react npm package into a new file named after the icon in kebab case, with the same svg attributes as the others. A new icon of your own uses the same 12-pixel grid and 1-pixel lines, and the README lists it. Each section’s icon is chosen once, in docs/data/sections.yaml, which maps a section’s folder under docs/ to an icon’s name, as in getting-started: rocket. A new section gets a line there. The section cards and the sidebar both read it, so they always show the same icon, and the build fails when the list names a section or an icon that doesn’t exist. Section cards on the docs’ first page are Hextra’s {{< cards >}} holding a {{< section-card path="getting-started" >}} for each section, with its one-line description inside, closed with {{< /section-card >}}. The shortcode takes the section’s title and link from its page under docs/, and its icon from sections.yaml, and the build fails when there’s no such page. Hextra’s card takes an icon only from Hextra’s own set, so the shortcode puts ours in the card’s title, at 24px. It’s dimmed as Hextra dims its own cards’ icons, and it turns lime on hover. The sidebar’s top-level items show their section’s icon at 12px, in the link’s color, so it’s gray, and lime for the section you’re in. Hextra’s sidebar has no icons, so docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes a CSS rule for each section when the site builds, keyed to the section page’s address, with the icon from docs/assets/icons/ as a mask. Nothing is generated into the repo, so there’s no step to rerun. The OS tabs of install and os-tabs show the Apple icon before macOS and the penguin before Linux, which docs/layouts/_partials/os-tab-name.html adds to each tab’s name. ✓ and ✗ go before a table cell’s word: {{< yes >}} yes puts a lime check before it, and {{< no >}} doesn't a gray cross. They go only in cells that are a plain yes or no, or what stands for one, such as the install script’s offers it, never in cells that are sentences, and the word stays, because screen readers skip the icon. Icons in tables are 12px, because a table’s text is smaller than 16px. Buttons take an icon before their text: docs/layouts/_shortcodes/hextra/hero-button.html is Hextra’s hero-button with an icon parameter, as in {{< hextra/hero-button text="Install" link="docs/getting-started/install/" icon="download" >}}, drawn at 24px like the headings’ icons. The 404 page’s two buttons have their icons in its layout, a rocket for Getting started and the open book for the docs, as the home page’s Read the docs has it. The navbar’s GitHub link uses Dinkie’s GitHub icon, which docs/data/icons.yaml adds to Hextra’s own icons as dinkie-github, and hugo.yaml’s menu names. Hextra’s icon partial reads only that data, so an icon for the navbar goes there as its SVG, not in docs/assets/icons/. Heading icons: a heading gets an icon before its text with an icon attribute, as in ## Quick start {icon="rocket"}, which the home page’s section headings use. docs/layouts/_markup/render-heading.html takes the place of Hextra’s heading render hook and adds the icon after Hugo makes the heading’s anchor, so the anchor comes from the text alone, such as quick-start. On the home page, custom.css draws these icons in lime at 24px, so each icon pixel is two screen pixels, as each of Departure Mono’s pixels is at 22px. Callouts are GitHub’s alerts: a blockquote whose first line is [!NOTE], [!TIP] or [!WARNING], which GitHub shows the same way. docs/layouts/_markup/render-blockquote-alert.html takes the place of Hextra’s alerts and draws each one on the surface color with a line down its left side, and a title with its icon: information-circled in blue for a note, the light bulb in the soft lime for a tip, and warning in lime for a warning. Any other type fails the build. Hextra’s own callout shortcode isn’t used. Use a callout only for a real warning, such as what the VM’s boundary rests on, or a tip that saves the reader trouble, such as keeping a VM on a strict tier, and move the sentence into it instead of repeating it. For agents and other tools that read the site, hugo.yaml turns on three things that Hextra has. The site’s root has llms.txt, which lists every section and its pages. Each page has a Markdown copy beside its HTML, such as /docs/using/clone.md beside /docs/using/clone/, and a section’s copy is index.md in its folder, such as /docs/using/index.md. Each docs page has a Copy page menu beside its title, which copies the page’s Markdown or opens it. hugo.yaml lists every output for the home page, the sections and the pages, so the home page and the sections keep their RSS feeds, and the search index is built apart from these outputs. llms.txt comes from docs/layouts/llms.txt, which takes the place of Hextra’s. It has the site’s title and description, then each section under its title, with the section’s own page first and its pages after it. Each one is a link to its Markdown copy, as the llms.txt convention prefers, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-link.txt writes, and a line of plain text, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-summary.txt writes. A page without a copy gets a link to its HTML page instead. The line is the page’s description from its front matter when it has one, and otherwise its first paragraph, cut at 200 characters. A description is also the page’s description for search engines and link previews, so give a page one when its first paragraph doesn’t say what the page covers, as Coding agents has. llms.txt also lists the CLI reference, with each command’s one-line summary. The Markdown copies come from docs/layouts/page.markdown.md and section.markdown.md, which take the place of Hextra’s and both use docs/layouts/_partials/markdown-copy.md. A copy is the page’s title as a heading, then its Markdown with its shortcodes rendered. In a copy, a link to a section’s _index.md points at index.md, the section copy’s name, so the links work between the copies, and a link written in code stays as it is. Each shortcode that docs pages use has a Markdown version beside its HTML one in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, named after it with .markdown.md, which renders it in the copies. install writes each system’s name in bold, then its commands, which come from docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, the same partial its tabs use. os-tabs writes its tabs the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/os-sections.md. section-card makes a list item that links the section’s copy, and Hextra’s cards keeps only what’s inside it. yes and no become ✓ and ✗. A shortcode without a Markdown version puts its HTML into the copy. The home page and the branding page are mostly shortcodes, and neither layout shows the menu. hugo.yaml gives the home page no Markdown copy, and its front matter sets contextMenu: false. The branding page’s front matter sets outputs: [html], contextMenu: false and llms: false, so it has no copy, no menu and no line in llms.txt. Any other page can set llms: false to stay out of llms.txt, or contextMenu: false to have no menu. After you add a page or a shortcode, build the site and read the page’s line in llms.txt and its Markdown copy. The line should say what the page covers, and the copy should have no shortcode left in it, such as {{< os-tabs >}}, and no HTML from one. A shortcode that docs pages use gets its Markdown version. To try the menu, serve the site with mise run docs and open a docs page. custom.css gives the menu the site’s border and secondary text, lime on hover, and its list the surface color. The 404 page is docs/layouts/404.html, which takes the place of Hextra’s and uses the site’s navbar and footer. It shows a VM’s terminal answering cd ./this-page with “no such page”, drawn like the home page’s art in docs/assets/home/not-found.svg with the blink cursor, then Hextra’s search box and links to Getting started and the docs. Build the site and open /404.html to see it. mise run lint:docs, which mise run lint includes, checks docs/ with:
Linter Checks Config markdownlint-cli2 Markdown .markdownlint-cli2.yaml Vale the style rules .vale.ini, .vale/styles/devvm/ lychee (--offline) links to pages and files It also builds the site with Hugo’s --panicOnWarning, into a temporary folder it removes, so any warning fails it. That includes a deprecation, such as a template that reads site.Data where Hugo wants hugo.Data, so a Hugo upgrade that deprecates something the templates use fails here before the feature is removed. It runs TestExplainers too, so a page without an explainer fails it, and TestUserPageProse (internal/cli/docgen/prose_test.go), which holds the user pages to lead with doing: it fails a run of three or more paragraphs back to back where two are over 80 words, and any paragraph or list item over 150 words. It counts words as scan.sh does, a code span as one word and a link by its text, and a paragraph of 40 words or fewer that ends with a colon introduces what follows, so it isn’t in a run. proseExempt names the pages that another branch is rewriting, each with why, until that branch lands. TestChangelogShape (internal/cli/docgen/changelog_test.go) holds CHANGELOG.md to the shape that Releasing gives an entry, and TestChangelogProblems checks that each of its rules fails an entry that breaks it.

data.adding-a-coding-agent#Adding a coding ag:
Each coding agent is one agents.Def in internal/agents/agents.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the agents and every fact of one from there: its shared tool (image.SharedTools makes its entry, glibc-only or not), its settings folders and files with each file’s format, its Seeds, its Names and NamedValues, the folder that devvm agent import copies from, which of that folder’s entries are each machine’s own (its FolderOwn), which neither the import nor the save copies and no VM gets, its login files and their kinds, its history and what an export leaves out of it (its logins, and what’s the VM’s own as a machine, its HistoryOwn, which a VM made again keeps), where in that history it makes git worktrees, which devvm rm and a remake with --clean-home check for uncommitted changes first (its Worktrees), the environment that every VM’s shells get, which turns off its self-update and telemetry, the secret every VM with it uses, how devvm agent login logs it in (its Login: the command lines of its own login, with a code and for a setup token, and whether the login comes back to a forwarded port or you paste a code back; or API keys alone), whether config.toml’s [pass-keys] takes it, and its row in the docs’ Supported agents table (its Docs). Its Seeds are the folders it reads in a VM as a seed of a folder of the VM’s own, such as Claude Code’s plugins. Each one has the link that the VM’s home puts the store’s folder at and the entries that devvm agent import and devvm agent save copy, which agents.MachineOwn judges. Its Names and NamedValues are the tables in its settings files whose keys are names you choose, such as its MCP servers’, which agentlogin.Redact doesn’t judge as keys, read from the agent’s own docs. The commands’ help, --agents, the picker, shell completion, the messages and the CLI tests’ lists of the agents all come from the registry too. A new agent that works like one devvm has needs these files and nothing else:
internal/agents/agents.go: its Def and its name’s constant. assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: its line in [tool_alias], the backend it comes from, and in [tools], its version. assets/shared-tools/.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows. testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: its lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second. docs/content/docs/using/coding-agents.md: a section on its login when it has one. CHANGELOG.md: its entry. tests/e2e/network_test.go: its name in the network section’s --agents list, which launches one VM with every agent, and the checks of its allowlist, its login and its copies there. assets/guest/sync.sh, only when it needs setup in the VM beyond its settings and logins, as Claude Code’s link in ~/.local/bin and Codex’s lines in its config.toml do. When it keeps a login file: a format for each of its kinds in a file of its own in internal/agentlogin, named for the agent, with the format interface’s methods, kind naming its kind (and keyFormat or chatGPTFormat when its Def says it saves API keys or holds a ChatGPT login, and captureFormat when the VM’s proxy captures its logins: its token endpoints, the start of its User-Agent when another agent shares an endpoint, its capture and its reply to the VM’s own refresh), added to the list in formats in format.go, with its fixture in goldenLogins (internal/agentlogin/golden_test.go) and its golden file, and its format’s section in internals/network.md. Then mise run cli-docs writes the agent’s row in the Supported agents table, its name in the README’s list and the CLI pages whose help lists the agents, and the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its paths with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden. TestDefsComplete, TestFormatsCoverLogins, TestSharedToolsPolicies, TestConfigTools and TestReferenceIsCurrent fail until those files match the registry. Code of the agent’s own, such as a settings filter or a login of its own, goes in a file named for the agent, such as claude.go or agentlogin_claude.go, and names the agent by its constant in internal/agents, so the code for every agent calls a hook there rather than asking which agent it has. The structure test fails on a string literal elsewhere that is the agent’s name or holds its folder, on code outside the agent’s own files that compares with its constant, has a case for it, looks for it or keys a map on it, on a list in Go that names every agent, tests included, and on a CLI test script’s line that lists agents as a message does, which $AGENT_CHOICES, $LOGIN_AGENTS and $KEY_AGENTS stand in for. The network section of the e2e tests drives every agent, so the new one gets its checks there.
data.adding-a-provider#Adding a provider: The model providers whose API keys the VM’s proxy puts in for the agents with a key for each provider, opencode and pi, are one table, agents.Providers in internal/agents/agents.go. Each agents.Provider holds the provider’s ID, which is its entry’s name in both agents’ auth.json, its name as people know it, the hosts the agents send its key to, its Path when the agents send the key below one path of those hosts alone, such as OpenRouter’s /api/, the Headers they send it in, most often one but two for OpenRouter, whose Anthropic models take the key in x-api-key, and its Prefix, which starts the key’s placeholder when an agent checks how the provider’s keys start: pi takes an OpenAI key that doesn’t start with sk- for a Sign in with ChatGPT login, so OpenAI’s is sk-. The opencode and pi formats’ bindings, agentlogin.KeyProviders, which devvm agent login --provider takes and its help lists, and the allowlist lines of each binding’s hosts all come from it. A new provider is its entry there, in the order of its ID, and its row in the table in using/coding-agents.md’s API keys the proxy puts in, which TestProvidersComplete checks against the registry. Read the hosts, the paths, the headers and any check of how a key starts in both agents’ own source first, and in the SDK that each one sends its requests with, because a header that differs from the agents’, or one that an agent uses for some models alone, leaves the key’s placeholder in the request, and a host that the agents never send the key to would get the key anyway. The proxy puts a provider’s key in only when the header’s value is the placeholder alone, or Bearer and the placeholder in Authorization, so check that both agents send the key that way too. A Path starts and ends with /, is clean, and goes into each binding as its Path, below which pathWithin takes a request’s path, so set one only when every request of both agents with the key goes below it. Then mise run cli-docs writes the CLI page whose help lists the providers, and UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/agentlogin -run Golden writes the golden files that list them.
data.adding-a-toolchain#Adding a toolchain:
Each toolchain is one image.ToolDef entry in image.SharedTools, in internal/image/tool.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the toolchains and every fact of one from there: its members in the lock, the files in a project folder that call for it, its installer, the environment that every VM’s shells get, the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, and the members whose version files mise reads. --tools, devvm tools, the picker, shell completion, the new VM’s summary and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps list the toolchains from the table too, and every launch writes the environment, the PATH folders and the version files into the VM, so a new toolchain changes no image. A new toolchain that mise installs from the lock’s checked downloads, as it installs node, python and go, needs these files and nothing else:
internal/image/tool.go: its entry, with its Env, PathDirs and VersionFiles when it has them. assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: a line in [tools] for each member, with its hold, and a line in [tool_alias] for each member that isn’t one of mise’s own (core:), naming the backend it comes from. assets/shared-tools/.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows, such as its package registry and the downloads of the versions a project asks for. testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: each member’s lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second. docs/content/docs/using/toolchains.md: its row in the table, in the registry’s order, its section, with what it brings, the files that call for it, its version files, its global installs and its allowlist, and its row in the glibc table of Which bases they run on. tests/e2e/tools_test.go: its checks, such as a project’s VM that its files call for, a global install and a version file’s own version. Then the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its environment, its PATH folders and its version files with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden, and a reviewer reads their diff. TestToolchainsComplete, TestToolchainGuest, TestSharedToolsPolicies and TestConfigTools fail until those files match the table, and the structure test fails on a string literal elsewhere that is its name or a member’s.
A toolchain that needs more than mise’s install gets code of its own, which the table can’t hold. A step in each VM, such as rust’s rustup in ~/.cargo, go’s telemetry switch or dotnet’s /etc/dotnet/install_location, is a block of assets/guest/sync.sh that reads the toolchain’s version from the VM’s tool list. An install that mise can’t check, such as rust’s, which rustup checks against its own signed manifest, or dotnet’s, whose SDK archive devvm adds to the lock with its SHA-512, is an Installer of its own, with its branch in assets/shared-tools/build.sh and its handling of the lock in internal/tools.
data.how-a-backend-plugs-in#How a backend plu:
devvm runs every VM on Lima, but the rest of devvm reaches Lima only through the backend.Backend interface in internal/backend, so another backend is an addition rather than a change to the callers. A backend lives in a package of its own under internal/backend, and it does four things:
It implements backend.Backend and returns its errors instead of ending the run: a msg.M, or backend.Logged(m) once a logged command failed, so the command shows the run log’s end before the message. Backend is the backend’s Name and Caps and four roles, each an interface of its own that every backend implements in full:
backend.Host is what the backend needs of this machine and where it keeps its VMs there. Problems lists what the host lacks for it, and backend.Check(ctx, b) returns the first of them, so a backend doesn’t write a check of its own. NameMax is the longest VM name it takes, Location is where its VMs live when that can change between runs (backend.LocationOf), and DiskDirs and Floors are the folders its disks are in and the free space it wants there (backend.Space). A backend whose VMs can’t move returns "" from Location, and one whose disks aren’t on this machine returns no DiskDirs. backend.Images builds images and the shared tools’ images and keeps the images. BuildImage runs the spec’s Recipe (image.Recipe, which internal/build puts together and image.Input hashes) as it is, each image.Step with its arguments and as root when it says so. Origin is the backend’s own steps that base starts with, such as the Ubuntu image Lima pinned on this machine, a --from image’s conversion, base’s disk size (backend.BaseDiskGiB) and base.yaml. Base’s size is backend.BaseCPUs, backend.BaseMemoryGiB and backend.BaseDiskGiB, never read from a backend’s files. internal/build puts them first in base’s recipe, as its Origin, so base’s key hashes them, and BuildImage is given them back and runs those rather than reading its own files again. PinOrigin pins what base starts from on this machine, which internal/build asks for before it keys a build (backend.PinFirst): on Lima, that’s the newest Ubuntu cloud image (state.UbuntuPin, found by ubuntu.Finder). A base build’s ImageSpec.Packages, a backend.Packages, sends its packages into the VM’s backend.PackagesDir before the steps and takes them out after, which internal/build/packages.go records or replays and checks, and a step that exits backend.ExitUnreachable fails as build_sources_unreachable. backend.Machines makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, lists them, and runs commands and shells in them. A stopped VM changes only at Start, which first checks with backend.Validate that it can apply the VM’s backend.Want, such as a disk no smaller than the VM’s own, and then applies what the Want asks where it differs from the VM. Start leaves a running VM as it is, and the callers, not the backend, warn that a change waits for the VM’s next start. On Lima, Start owns the config’s env:, propagateProxyEnv, dns and hostResolver, and a project VM’s size, agent mounts and forwardAgent, which it compares with the VM’s before its one edit (what devvm sets on a VM). Ports are never the backend’s: vmssh.Forwards forwards them over the backend’s SSH. Running says how a VM runs now, in one backend.Run: the ID of its current start, whether it’s confined to its proxy, and its lifeline, the file that the VM’s proxy and port forwarder follow. The backend runs no port forwarder of its own, and SSH says how ssh, links and devvm’s forwarder (vmssh.Forwards) reach a running VM’s sshd, a target that vmssh.FromTarget checks. Every ssh of devvm’s to a VM, its port forwarder’s included, refuses a target that isn’t on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with vmssh.FromTarget (what each backend emulates). All three get it through vmssh.Checked, which checks the review lets the backend’s ssh through, checks the target, and adds the VM’s host keys for its current start, reading the record (vmssh.ReadKeys) or pinning the keys first (vmssh.PinKeys). A VM whose ssh isn’t usable fails with a *vmssh.UnusableError and one without host keys with vmssh.ErrNoHostKeys, which the ssh config skips on. Exec passes its backend.ExecOpts streams on as they are. When they’re a terminal’s files, the command must get a terminal in the VM, as a shell does, because an agent’s login that draws full-screen needs one, and any other streams are pipes (TestExecStreamsAsGiven on Lima). backend.Housekeeping is what devvm space and devvm gc ask: Usage, Strays, and DevvmCache and DeleteCache for its own caches. A backend that can’t tell returns none. backend.Forgetter is the one role a backend may leave out, for the files it keeps for a VM besides the VM. Lima keeps none.
