Lima’s type, lima.Lima, holds the backend’s fields, Name, Caps and the helpers its roles share, and it embeds one type for each role, host, images, machines and housekeeping, each over the Lima it’s part of. backendtest.Fake is split the same way. So no type has more methods than the structure test allows, and a new method goes on the type of its role.
It declares Caps, saying for each of backend.Features whether it has the feature natively, emulates it, or lacks it (features). It lists every feature by hand, None included, and Registry.Register refuses Caps that leave one out or rate a feature better than the one Feature.BuiltOn says it’s built on (Caps.Check). The callers, not the backend, decide what a VM needs, and they check it with the registry’s Review.Require(b, vm, spec.Features()...) before they act. A feature the backend lacks fails in one line that names the VM and what to do, and devvm never falls back to something weaker. An emulation stays refused until its review passes: a design note in the design notes, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove its guarantee.
It’s registered in registry.New (internal/backend/registry), the only place besides internal/cli that imports a backend. The registry hands the backend out behind its guard, which checks every CreateVM, Start, BuildImage and BuildTools call before the backend sees it. The guard refuses a spec that needs a feature Review.Require would refuse, using the specs’ own Features, and a build spec whose ImageSpec.Validate or ToolsSpec.Validate fails, such as one with a network that isn’t a build’s or a key that isn’t one. So a caller that forgets Require still can’t reach a backend with a feature it lacks, and the backend doesn’t check those specs itself. The guard has every role’s methods, its own in place of the backend’s for those calls, so a guarded backend handed on as a backend.Images or a backend.Machines is still guarded. The guard’s type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so code that looks for an optional role, such as backend.Forgetter, uses backend.As instead of a type assertion, and the structure test fails on a type assertion to a backend package’s type anywhere but the guard.
It names its images by key, and an image’s key hashes the backend’s name, so two backends never share an image.
It passes the conformance suite, backendtest.Conformance(t, factory), which checks the contract that backend.Backend’s documentation gives. The backend’s tests call it with a factory that returns a new backendtest.Subject for each check, and each check runs as a subtest. The subject is the backend, holding one image, whose key is Image, and no VMs. Dir is a folder of the check’s own for the folders its VMs mount, Boots says whether its VMs start, and Restart starts a running VM again outside Start, as a command of the user’s own would. The suite checks every role’s answers and the empty answers each role allows, that a VM is made, renamed and deleted as its spec says, and that a missing VM is backend.ErrNotFound. It also checks that Running gives a stopped VM its lifeline with an empty ID, that every start gets another ID, that a VM is Confined only while it runs on a start Start made with NetProxy, and that the registry’s guard still refuses what the backend lacks when the backend is used as backend.Images or backend.Machines alone. checkProxyURL checks what the open tier needs of every backend, which has no feature of its own (features): a VM on the backend’s own network (NetDirect) reaches a port on the host’s loopback, and the guest’s proxy settings come from the confinement (Confinement.GuestProxy, ProxyURL). When Boots is false, the checks that need a running VM are skipped with the reason, and when Restart is nil, so is the one that needs it. backendtest.Fake runs the suite in internal/backend/backendtest, and TestConformance in internal/backend/lima runs it on Lima twice: on the limactl stub, whose VMs start, and on real Lima’s dummy instances, which can’t boot, so the checks that need a running VM are left to the end-to-end tests. The real Lima run skips when limactl isn’t on PATH. TestConformanceFinds checks the suite itself: each of a set of fakes that breaks the contract in one method fails the check meant to catch it.
The registry’s For chooses a VM’s backend: a VM that exists gets the one its state records in backend=, and a new VM gets backend.Default, which is lima. Tests set the registry’s NewVMs to give new VMs a fake backend (backendtest.Fake). The command line has no way to choose a backend, so a second backend would also add one, following the cli skill, together with its column in the tables that list VMs, images and caches. --json output already names each VM’s, image’s and shared tool’s backend.
A new backend gets a design note and a threat check with the security-audit skill before any of its emulations is marked reviewed, and that check covers what Lima gets from its VMs’ design. A VM started outside devvm must not forward an agent devvm didn’t choose, a VM whose root can change its own network must not count as confined, a secret the proxy needs goes in a private file and never in a command’s arguments, and a socket on this machine goes in a private folder.

data: For maintainers: version bumps and releases. Run the scripts with mise, which puts the pinned GoReleaser and minisign on PATH: mise exec -- scripts/release.sh.
data.checking-base-against-ubuntus-newest#Che:
The end-to-end tests pin base to e2eUbuntuRelease, so they never build base the way a user’s first build does, from Ubuntu’s newest cloud image and the mirrors’ newest packages. An upstream change can break those builds before any test sees it. For example, vz’s direct kernel boot needs an uncompressed arm64 kernel, and a VM shuts down only when its kernel has gpio_keys. mise run e2e -- --newest-base builds base as a user’s first build does and runs the checks that prove it works: images, then project (a VM that boots, stops, starts again and shuts down) and tools. --only chooses other sections in their place.
The run gives devvm no release to pin. It reads the newest release from Ubuntu’s listing, as scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu does, and prints it at its start next to e2eUbuntuRelease. It runs in a sandbox of its own, which is slot 0’s with -newest added to its Lima home, state folder, Keychain service and lock (~/.lt-e2e-go-newest, /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-newest, devvm-go-e2e-newest and /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-newest.lock), with each fixed port slot 0’s plus 1000. So the cached pinned images in the other sandboxes stay as they are. Each run first deletes its sandbox’s images, tool images and package cache, so base is built from nothing, with its packages from the mirrors. The images section checks that devvm pinned the release Ubuntu listed as its newest and that base booted from it. When the newest doesn’t boot, a user’s devvm falls back to the release before it (origin_no_boot), so that check fails on the fallback. Its times go in timings/plain-newest/ in slot 0’s state folder, apart from the cached runs’. --newest-base can’t be combined with --slots or --slot.
Run it before each release and every week or two between them, on an arm64 Mac (vz) and on a Linux host (QEMU) when you can, because the two boot base differently. At its end, it prints the release Ubuntu listed and the release devvm pinned. When a check fails, it says UPSTREAM DRIFT and names the release, because a user’s first build of base gets the same failure now. Then:
Read the failed check’s output and the run log of base’s build, which the build’s output names (log_details), in the sandbox’s state folder under data/devvm/logs/runs/. Run mise run e2e -- --only images on the pinned release. If it passes, the failure is upstream’s, from the newer image or its packages. If it fails too, the fault is devvm’s own, so fix that first. Fix devvm for the new release, such as a change to assets/layers/base.sh or to the Lima template. Then run --newest-base again until it passes. Bump e2e-ubuntu to that release once it passes, so the other end-to-end runs test it too. Until a fix ships, users can still build base, because devvm’s fallback to the release before covers a newest release that doesn’t boot. A package that breaks base has no fallback, so a fix for one goes in the next release.
data.fuzzing-failures#Fuzzing failures:
The Fuzz workflow (.github/workflows/fuzz.yml) fuzzes every target each night and keeps its failures in one issue, “Fuzzing found failing inputs”, which names each failing target and links the night’s run. For each target there, download its crash- artifact from that run, and fix it as Fuzzing says:
cp ~/Downloads/crash-FuzzNoProxy/* internal/proxy/testdata/fuzz/FuzzNoProxy/ # the input, in its target's seeds go test -run '^FuzzNoProxy$' ./internal/proxy # fails until the code is fixed Commit the input with the fix and its test. The input stays in the target’s corpus, so the target fails on it each night until the fix is on main, and the issue closes on the first night every target passes (the nightly run).
data.known-vulnerabilities#Known vulnerabilit:
govulncheck checks devvm against the Go vulnerability database. mise run vuln scans the code twice, once as built for Linux and once as built for macOS, because some files build for only one of them, and it reports a vulnerability only when devvm’s code calls the vulnerable function. Two workflows run it:
CI’s vuln job runs mise run vuln on every push and pull request that CI runs on, as a job of its own, so a vulnerability published since the last change fails that check alone, and lint and test still report. The Vulnerabilities workflow (.github/workflows/vuln.yml) runs every Monday, and you can start it by hand from the Actions tab. It scans main’s code for both systems, then downloads the archives of the latest release and of the newest release, prerelease or not, and checks that SHA256SUMS lists each archive and matches it. Then it scans each platform’s binary with govulncheck -mode=binary, because a release’s binaries keep the Go and modules they were built with. A binary’s scan works differently from the code’s. It reports the vulnerable code that the binary holds rather than the calls into it, and it can name a package that isn’t linked into the binary at all. Before you release for a vulnerability that only a binary’s scan found, check that the binary has it, with go version -m BINARY for its Go and modules and govulncheck -mode=binary -show traces BINARY for the code it holds.
The workflow keeps its findings in one issue, “Known vulnerabilities in devvm”, which lists each scan’s vulnerabilities with the version found and the version that fixes it, and links each one’s entry in the database. It comments on the issue whenever the findings change, so a new vulnerability notifies you, and closes the issue once every scan finds nothing. When govulncheck itself fails, the job fails and leaves the issue as it is. Only a scan job with read access runs govulncheck. A second job, the only one that can write issues, reads the scan’s findings and updates the issue, and it does so only in a run on main, so a run started on another branch never closes it. The scans cover devvm’s Go code alone, not the packages in the VM images, the pinned tools, Lima, or releases older than the two they scan.
To fix a vulnerability, move what it’s in to the version that fixes it:
mise run vuln # what govulncheck finds in your checkout, and the calls that reach it scripts/bump.sh go # Go's newest patch release, for one in the standard library scripts/bump.sh go-minor # Go's newest minor release, when only a newer minor has the fix scripts/bump.sh go-mods # the direct modules' newest patches and minors, for one in a module A module that only go.mod’s indirect requirements hold moves with go get @ and go mod tidy. Once main is fixed, its scan passes, but the issue stays open while the latest release or the newest release still has the vulnerability, and it closes only when a release with the fix is the latest. A vulnerability that affects devvm’s users calls for a release (Releasing), and one that devvm’s code reaches only in a way that doesn’t matter can wait for the next one.
data.releasing#Releasing:
Once, the keys: a minisign key for releases, minisign -G -p packaging/minisign.pub -s ~/.minisign/devvm.key (commit packaging/minisign.pub; the secret key and its password never go in the repo), and a key git signs tags with (git config user.signingkey, GPG, or SSH with gpg.format ssh) that git tag -v verifies on this machine. Commit its fingerprint in packaging/release-signer, one per line (# comments): the GPG fingerprint (gpg --fingerprint, no spaces), or the SSH key’s SHA256:… (ssh-keygen -lf KEY.pub). release.sh refuses a tag signed by any other key, even one git trusts. To rotate, add the new key’s line, tag with it, then remove the old one.
Between releases, each change on main that someone could notice adds its line to the ## Unreleased section at the bottom of CHANGELOG.md, in the group of the people who notice it, and its full story as a section of the next release’s page in releases/, in the same commit. A line under the page’s title links Unreleased, so the top of the page shows the latest release. Unreleased has no Highlights, because they’re written at the release, and a change that affects nobody, such as a refactor, adds no line.
Before the release commit, sort the lines by audience. List every Unreleased line in a table for the maintainer, with the group it goes in, who notices it and the line itself, and name the close calls, the lines that could go in either of two groups, with the case for each. Once the maintainer approves the table, write the Highlights and the lines as it says. Then someone who didn’t write the lines, such as a fresh agent, reviews them with the docs-voice skill, reading the visible part as a user would on GitHub and then each collapsed group, and flags what’s vague, padded, repeated across groups or about the notes themselves. Fold in the fixes until the review finds nothing to change.
Each release: bump VERSION, move the Unreleased lines to the top as the release’s ## entry, leaving the empty ## Unreleased section at the bottom, and commit it on main. Then tag main’s HEAD with git tag -s v and run mise exec -- scripts/publish.sh, which asks for the minisign password once and asks once more before it publishes anything. The secret key never leaves this machine, and only minisign reads it, so no CI job and no GitHub secret ever has it.
If a final release changed the state format, freeze testdata/v/ once the tag exists: run its generate.sh against the tag on a Mac and on Linux, and add its tests, as Freezing a release’s state says. A release that changes nothing on disk adds no fixture, and a release candidate adds none either, because its final release’s fixture holds the state it changed.
A prerelease, such as a release candidate or a beta, goes out the same way, with a version of the form x.y.z-.N: VERSION holds 0.2.0-rc.1, CHANGELOG.md gets an entry ## 0.2.0-rc.1, and the tag is v0.2.0-rc.1. The word is lowercase letters, such as rc, beta or alpha, and release.sh refuses any other form of VERSION. scripts/publish.sh marks a prerelease’s GitHub release as a prerelease, passing --prerelease to gh release create and gh release edit, so GitHub’s latest release skips it, and so do the install script’s default, devvm upgrade and the daily release check. In the tap it changes only Formula/devvm-rc.rb, the formula that follows prereleases, in a commit titled devvm-rc , so the formula devvm stays on the last release. At the end, it prints how to check the prerelease with brew upgrade devvm-rc or brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc, and the prerelease’s install script line.
The tap’s two formulas are devvm, the newest release’s, and devvm-rc, the newest prerelease’s or release’s, whichever is newer. devvm-rc only moves forward: each publish, a release’s or a prerelease’s, points Formula/devvm-rc.rb at the version it publishes, unless the tap’s devvm-rc already names a newer one. So a release moves devvm-rc users onto it once it’s newer than their prerelease, and a patch release of an older line, or a prerelease older than the tap’s, leaves devvm-rc where it is. The printout says which way it goes, and when nothing in the tap changes, as for such a prerelease, it has no tap step and prints the install script line and devvm upgrade --to for checking it.
The changelog’s entry is sorted by who notices each change. Each line goes where a reader asking “does this affect me?” looks for it, so the question for a line is who notices it: everyone upgrading, the users of one feature, only a hostile VM, or nobody in practice. The entry starts with a paragraph that says which release it is and how to install it, then a line that links the release page, then its groups in this order, each one only when it has something:
Highlights: three to five concrete lines on what the release means for you, such as what now works or which reported bugs are fixed. A highlight never refers to the notes themselves, such as by pointing at What to do. What to do: numbered steps, each an action that someone upgrading takes, such as running devvm update or restarting each running VM, with why when it isn’t plain. A breaking change goes here when it asks something of you. Fixed: the bugs that users reported, with their issues, and the ones a typical user plausibly hit. If you use…: a collapsed block for each feature, such as If you use a Linux host , holding the changes that only that feature’s users notice. Security hardening: a collapsed block whose summary starts Security hardening: and says what the hardening means for you, such as Security hardening: a VM that tries to attack your machine can now do much less , with one line for each change that matters only when a VM is hostile. Internal changes: a collapsed block, Internal changes , for rare conditions, limits nobody meets, pins, logs, status lines and the rest. A collapsed block renders its list on GitHub only with a blank line after its … line and another before its . markdownlint allows details and summary and no other inline HTML. Each line is one outcome sentence, then its links. The sentence says what changes for you and what to do, if anything, in at most 35 words, not counting its links or a credit, and how devvm does it goes on the release page. A step in What to do may run longer, but it says only what to do and why. A line that covers several changes keeps every link of each. The links come in this form and order: the user page to act on, for a step in What to do or a breaking change, then the change’s section on the release page, then its issue, then its commit, as in ([details](https://next.devvm.dev/docs/releases/0.2.0/#claude-codes-setup-token-login), [#57](https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/issues/57), [6965efc](https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/commit/6965efcc0a97f7f6334f00d0530007ecf459972c)). The issue is a full link, such as [#57](https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/issues/57), or /pull/N in place of /issues/N for a pull request, because a bare #57 links only in GitHub’s view of the release’s notes, and not in CHANGELOG.md or anywhere else the entry is read. gh api repos/devvmhq/devvm/issues/N --jq .pull_request tells them apart: it prints nothing for an issue. Every reference to an issue or a pull request in the changelog is written this way, a credit’s included, and the release page writes them the same way. The commit is the one that made the change, or the main one of several, linked by its full SHA and shown by its first seven characters. Find each one with git log v..main and its messages, and git log -G on CHANGELOG.md names the commit that added a line. Credits, such as thanks for a report, stay in the line’s text, after its sentence and before its links. The links point at next.devvm.dev in a release candidate’s entry, because devvm.dev shows the latest release’s docs, which don’t have its release page yet, and at devvm.dev in a release’s entry. Each anchor is the heading’s ID as Hugo makes it, such as #a-no_proxy-entrys-port for A NO_PROXY entry’s port, so check a new one against the built page. lychee checks the docs’ links offline, so it doesn’t check these. TestChangelogShape keeps the shape, in internal/cli/docgen/changelog_test.go, which mise run lint:docs and mise run test run. For each entry from 0.2.0-rc.1 on, and for Unreleased once it has a line, it checks the groups and their order, three to five Highlights in a release’s entry, each collapsed group’s , and blank lines, each line’s 35 words outside What to do, its details link to a releases/ page, and a full link for every issue and pull request. The entries before 0.2.0-rc.1 are history, and the test leaves them as they are. The release page holds each change’s full story, and it is docs/content/docs/releases/..0.md, such as releases/0.2.0.md, which covers the release and its release candidates. Each release candidate adds its changes there, in the same commit as its changelog entry, so the page is written as the release is made. Each change gets a section of its own with its full story, under Breaking changes, Changes, Fixes and Hardening, as Writing docs describes, and the Releases section’s own page lists the page. Every fact a changelog line leaves out is in its section, so a line can stay one sentence. A change that two lines describe, such as a step in What to do and a line in Fixed, can share one section, which both link, and a line that covers several changes links each one’s section.
A prerelease’s changelog entry lists what changed since the version before it, whether that’s a release or another prerelease, and it becomes that prerelease’s notes on GitHub. When the release itself goes out, its entry, such as ## 0.2.0, replaces its prereleases’ entries and lists everything since the last release, so someone who upgrades from that release reads one entry. Each prerelease’s notes stay on its GitHub release.
Before it builds, scripts/publish.sh checks what it needs and stops with nothing done when a check fails. The tag v has to pass release.sh’s own checks, so it exists, is signed, and is signed by a key in packaging/release-signer. The tag’s commit has to be main’s HEAD, and origin’s main has to be an ancestor of it, so that the push is a fast-forward. If origin already has the tag, it has to be the same tag. The working tree has to be clean, gh has to be installed and logged in (gh auth status), and minisign has to be installed. A published GitHub release for the tag is refused unless it already has every file, which is the case when an earlier run stopped after it, and unless GitHub marks it as a prerelease exactly when the version is one. The refusal names the gh release edit command that fixes the mark. The tap’s checkout, a clone of devvmhq/homebrew-tap, has to exist, be clean and be on main, for a prerelease too, and its origin has to have no commits that its main lacks. The checkout is DEVVM_TAP_DIR, or ../homebrew-tap next to this repo by default.
Then it builds and shows the release. It runs scripts/release.sh, which builds dist/ and signs SHA256SUMS, and where minisign asks for the password. It prints the version, the tag’s commit, each file with its size and SHA-256, the release notes, which are the CHANGELOG.md entry for the version, and the tap’s changes as a git diff of each formula it writes: Formula/devvm.rb for a release, and Formula/devvm-rc.rb, with a line saying when a release moves it too, or when it stays on a newer version. It lists the four steps, each marked done or to do, and when nothing in the tap changes, the fourth says so. Then it asks Publish devvm ? [y/N] on the terminal, and any answer but y stops it with nothing published. --dry-run stops before the question, so it pushes and publishes nothing and makes no commit in the tap, and --help describes the script.
Then it publishes, in this order. It pushes main and then the tag to origin. It makes the GitHub release devvmhq/devvm v with gh release create --verify-tag, titled devvm , with the release notes and the archives, the source tarball, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig and install.sh. The release starts as a draft and is published only once every file is uploaded, so nobody sees a release that is missing files. Last, it copies dist/devvm.rb to the tap’s Formula/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb to its Formula/devvm-rc.rb, each only when it’s one the tap gets and it differs, commits them in one commit, devvm for a release or devvm-rc for a prerelease, with the tap’s own commit signing, and pushes the tap. It uses gh for GitHub and never puts a GitHub token on a command line. At the end it prints how to check the release: brew update && brew upgrade devvm, or brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm and then brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm, with devvm-rc in place of devvm for a prerelease, and the install script’s curl line.
When a step fails, it says which steps it published and which it didn’t. Fix what failed and run it again, because every step skips what’s already done: a pushed main or tag, a published release whose SHA256SUMS matches the new build’s, and a tap whose formulas are already this build’s. A draft release that an earlier run left gets this build’s files again before it’s published. A release published from another build, whose SHA256SUMS doesn’t match, is refused. To finish by hand instead, run the steps it didn’t do in order: git push origin main, git push origin v, the gh release create above (or gh release upload --clobber to a draft, then gh release edit v --draft=false), each with --prerelease for a prerelease, and then copy the formulas the printout listed, dist/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb, to the tap’s Formula/, commit them and push it.
scripts/release.sh checks the tag with git tag -v and its signer against this checkout’s packaging/release-signer, then builds dist/ from the tagged commit with GoReleaser (.goreleaser.yaml), in a clone of its own, so only what’s committed goes in, with one goreleaser release --skip=publish. It checks that the binary built for this host prints the version, writes install.sh and adds its checksum to SHA256SUMS, then signs SHA256SUMS with ~/.minisign/devvm.key (or DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY) and verifies it with packaging/minisign.pub. Nothing is published, because publishing is scripts/publish.sh’s. scripts/release.sh --check runs only the tag’s checks and the build’s preconditions, prints the tag’s commit and builds nothing, and scripts/publish.sh runs it first.
dist/ then holds:
File What devvm---.tar.gz the binary, its files (assets/) embedded, with README.md, CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE, for darwin and linux, arm64 and amd64 devvm-.tar.gz the source, attached to the release for whoever wants to build devvm themselves SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig their checksums and install.sh’s, and the signature install.sh the install script, set to this release and to packaging/minisign.pub’s key devvm-rc.rb the Homebrew formula devvm-rc, which follows prereleases, set to each platform’s archive, its URL and its checksum from SHA256SUMS devvm.rb for a release, not a prerelease, the Homebrew formula devvm, set the same way scripts/release.sh --head builds from HEAD’s commit instead, for testing, with VERSION’s version, a release’s or a prerelease’s. It’s unsigned unless DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY names a test key; DEVVM_MINISIGN_PUB names its public key in place of packaging/minisign.pub. DEVVM_RELEASE_URL points the formula at a test location. A commit without install.sh is refused.
scripts/release.sh --formula-from DIR writes only the formulas, for VERSION’s release once it’s published, and builds nothing: dist/devvm-rc.rb, and dist/devvm.rb too when VERSION isn’t a prerelease. Download the release’s SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.minisig into DIR first. The script checks the signature against packaging/minisign.pub, and that its trusted comment is devvm for VERSION’s version, so it refuses another release’s files. Then it fills in the formulas the same way a build does, from that SHA256SUMS.
To try dist/install.sh on such a build, copy dist/ to DIR/releases/download/v/, then in a throwaway HOME with DEVVM_PREFIX under it: DEVVM_INSTALL_TEST=1 source dist/install.sh, set repo_url=file://DIR and protos='=https,file' (it downloads over HTTPS only), and run main --no-deps. Without --no-deps it offers to install what the host lacks: answer no, or run it with no terminal.
Every build sets the version with -X github.com/devvmhq/devvm/internal/cli.version=: devvm doesn’t read VERSION. The formula template (packaging/homebrew/devvm.rb) is both formulas’ one source, and it builds nothing. It has an archive for each of macOS and Linux on arm64 and Intel, the same archives the install script installs, and it installs the binary alone from the one for this machine. release.sh fills in each formula’s class, Devvm or DevvmRc, and the other formula, which it conflicts with by its full name, devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc or devvmhq/tap/devvm, because both install the devvm command. It also fills in each archive’s URL and its checksum, which it reads from the SHA256SUMS it just wrote, on every line that isn’t a comment. Both generated formulas pass brew audit --strict --online and brew style.
Publishing is the maintainer’s call, so an agent asks first and never runs scripts/publish.sh without --dry-run on its own. The script’s tests (testdata/script/publish.txtar) run it against a local bare repo as origin, a local bare tap and a fake gh.
data.the-docs-sites#The docs sites:
The docs have two sites, and the Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) deploys both. devvm.dev shows the docs of the latest release, so what users read matches the devvm they install. next.devvm.dev shows the docs on main, for the next release, which is what someone trying a prerelease reads. A pull request that touches the docs gets their lints and a build, and it deploys nothing, so a pull request from a fork never reaches either site or its keys.
devvm.dev is GitHub Pages, in the repo’s github-pages environment, which accepts deployments from main and from v* tags, and only admins can create a v* tag. When a release is published, and it isn’t a prerelease, the workflow builds the docs in that release’s tag and deploys them. A release event runs the workflow file that the tag has, so a release whose tag predates this workflow doesn’t deploy on its own. Pushes to main never change devvm.dev. To deploy a release’s docs by hand, for a release that didn’t deploy on its own or to put devvm.dev back on a release, run the Docs workflow from main in the repo’s Actions tab, or with gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=devvm.dev -f ref=v0.1.0. The site is devvm.dev unless you choose another one, and the ref is the release’s tag, which has to look like v0.1.0, so a prerelease’s tag is refused. Without a ref, the workflow deploys the latest release, as gh release view names it. next.devvm.dev is Cloudflare Pages, serving the files on the main branch of the repo devvmhq/docs-next, and Cloudflare builds nothing. On each push to main that touches the docs, the workflow lints and builds main’s docs for next.devvm.dev, then replaces everything in devvmhq/docs-next but its README.md with the build, and commits it as Build from devvm . When the build is the same as the last one, it commits nothing. gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=next.devvm.dev runs it by hand. Nobody edits devvmhq/docs-next by hand, because the next build replaces it. Every build draws the diagrams first, with mise run docs:diagrams, so each of the workflow’s jobs installs Node through mise. A release whose tag predates the drawing script, docs/render-diagrams.mjs, loads Mermaid in its pages instead, so the release job draws them only when the tag has that script. The deploy key that pushes to devvmhq/docs-next is the secret DOCS_NEXT_DEPLOY_KEY in the docs-next environment, which only main can deploy from. It’s an ed25519 key with write access to devvmhq/docs-next and to nothing else. The workflow checks that repo out with it only after the site is built, so the build never sees the key. To rotate it, make a new key, add its public half to devvmhq/docs-next as a deploy key with write access, put its private half in the secret, then delete the old deploy key. The next build is hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml, which reads docs/next.yaml over docs/hugo.yaml. It sets the site’s address to https://next.devvm.dev/ and puts a banner on every page that says these docs are for the next devvm and links to devvm.dev. It also sets noindex, so Hextra gives every page a noindex, nofollow robots meta tag, and docs/layouts/robots.txt disallows everything, so search engines don’t index the site. devvm.dev’s build, hugo -s docs --minify, never reads docs/next.yaml, so it has no banner, its pages say index, follow, and its robots.txt allows everything.
data.updating-pinned-versions#Updating pinned:
scripts/bump.sh moves every version pinned in the repo, so preparing a release’s pins is one command:
scripts/bump.sh --check # every pin, by group, against upstream; changes nothing scripts/bump.sh # every patch and minor bump, then a summary for the commit message scripts/bump.sh docker pele # only these tools, with a named images or e2e tool's major --check prints each group’s pins under its name in brackets, such as [go], with each pin’s current version and upstream’s newest, and whether a bump would be a patch, a minor or a major, or a new digest, commit, checksum or release for a pin that isn’t a version. A held pin says which version holds it, and a line that the run wouldn’t apply says how to apply it. When upstream’s latest is older than a pin, as when a release marker hasn’t moved yet, --check says the pin is newer and bump.sh leaves it as it is. With no tools named, bump.sh applies every patch and minor bump. It never applies a major, a held pin or a tool that it applies only when named. Naming an images or e2e tool also applies its major. e2e-tools always applies one, because users get the shared tools’ new majors as well, and assets/shared-tools/mise.toml holds what stays. It writes a value only if it has the shape of a pin (a version, a 64-hex checksum, a dated release, a commit, an image digest), since some of the edited files run on the host, and it edits nothing unless every value is good. Then it runs the commands that finish a bump: mise lock for Go and the dev tools, go get and go mod tidy for the modules, go get and hugo mod tidy in docs/ for Hextra, npm install --ignore-scripts in docs/ and then mise run docs:diagrams for pele, and actionlint and zizmor for the workflows. If one of those fails, the pins are already edited, and bump.sh says so. It needs curl and jq, mise for Go, the dev tools, the end-to-end lock and pele, go to apply the modules and Hextra, and gh for the actions. Every Monday the Pins workflow (.github/workflows/pins.yml) runs scripts/bump.sh --check and opens or updates one issue, “Pinned versions to bump”, which lists the outdated pins under their groups, and closes it once none is left. It never bumps anything, so you run scripts/bump.sh, then the --from tier of the end-to-end tests when an images or e2e pin moved, because those bumps change images. The tools, by group, as --check prints them:
Group Tools What they move images docker, nix, direnv, nix-direnv, mise, git-lfs, rustup, crane, omb, eza, tealdeer the downloads pinned in assets/, and devvm’s host mise, so scripts/bump.sh nix direnv nix-direnv moves the nix layer’s three pins shared-tools cursor, only when named Cursor’s CLI in assets/shared-tools/mise.toml, the one shared tool pinned for users e2e e2e-tools, e2e-from, e2e-curl, e2e-ubuntu, e2e-lima the end-to-end tests’ own pins go go, go-minor only when named, go-mods, deadcode Go, its modules and the deadcode task dev-tools dev-tools mise.toml’s tools except Go, with their mise.lock entries ci ci-mise, actions the mise the workflows install, and their actions docs hextra, pele only when named the docs site’s theme, and pele, which draws its diagrams go moves Go to its newest patch release of the minor that go.mod names, from go.dev/dl. It edits the go lines of go.mod and docs/go.mod, mise.toml’s go, and its mise.lock entries. --check reports a newer minor on the go-minor line, and scripts/bump.sh go-minor moves the same files to it. go-mods moves go.mod’s direct modules, the ones the depguard allowlist allows and the tests’ own, to their newest patch or minor release from the Go module proxy, with go get and go mod tidy. The indirect ones move as go mod tidy needs them. A module’s next major has a new path, so --check reports it and you move it by hand. deadcode moves the deadcode task’s version in mise.toml to golang.org/x/tools’ newest release. dev-tools moves each of mise.toml’s tools except Go to mise’s newest version of it, edits its line and runs mise lock, so mise.lock keeps every platform’s checksum, and markdownlint-cli2’s lock folder in .mise/locks/ moves with it. nilaway has no releases, so its pin is a pseudo-version, which mise latest prints nothing for. dev-tools moves a Go tool pinned to a pseudo-version to its newest commit’s, from the Go module proxy’s @latest for the module that holds the tool, the longest prefix of its path that the proxy has. A tool with no newest version stops the run with an error, never a change, and so does any failed request to the proxy, except its answer that a prefix isn’t a module. ci-mise moves the version that the workflows give jdx/mise-action to base’s mise, as the run leaves it, so scripts/bump.sh mise ci-mise moves both. actions moves each workflow’s uses: to its newest release’s tag, as the tag’s commit from gh api, with the tag in the comment after it, and reports a newer major without applying it. An action in a folder of its repo, such as actions/cache/restore, moves with its repo’s releases. hextra moves the docs site’s theme in docs/go.mod, and it reminds you to compare the copies of Hextra’s files in docs/layouts/ with the new release’s. pele moves pele only when named, because the diagrams need a look on the built site. It runs npm install in docs/ with the exact version and no install scripts, which writes docs/package.json and docs/package-lock.json, and then draws the diagrams again with mise run docs:diagrams. The drawing script’s self-check fails that step when the new pele no longer measures and writes its small text, such as edge labels, as the script expects (diagrams). cursor moves Cursor’s CLI only when named, to the release that Cursor’s install script fetches, with each platform’s SHA-256 computed from its download, because Cursor publishes no checksums. devvm’s login and proxy code was read against the pinned release, so read the new one where that code names it, then run e2e-tools. A hold keeps a pin below a version, and --check shows the newest version beside it. Go modules and actions take Dependabot’s ignore list in .github/dependabot.yml, which keeps pflag below 1.1.0, because pflag 1.1 prints every boolean flag with [=true|false] in the help. The other holds are in bump.sh’s holds, which keeps Node, the one in mise.toml, on its major. bump.sh’s header lists every pin with the tool that moves it, or with - and the reason it’s left, as # pin lines. TestBumpCoversPins in internal/structure finds the pins in assets/, mise.toml, both go.mod files, the workflows, tests/e2e-mise.lock, tests/e2e’s consts, docs/hugo.yaml and docs/package.json’s dependencies, without the network, and fails on a pin that no line covers or on a line that covers nothing, so a new pin gets a tool or a reason. The header also says why the pins outside those files are left as they are, such as the Lima that install.sh installs, which is the newest release checked against its SHA256SUMS, and the Homebrew formula, whose URLs and checksums release.sh fills in. base’s Ubuntu cloud image and its apt packages have nothing to bump: devvm pins the newest image on each machine at its first build of base, and records the newest packages for each key of base at its first build (Ubuntu’s cloud image, base’s packages). docker moves Docker’s packages (assets/layers/docker.sh), read from its repository for base’s Ubuntu release, and its signing key. Packages added to assets/layers/base.sh or assets/features/ need no pin of their own: they change base’s key, whose first build records them. mise moves base’s mise (assets/layers/base.sh) and devvm’s host mise (internal/tools/mise.go) together: the host one writes the lock base’s installs from. TestMisePins fails when their versions or Linux checksums differ, and base’s mise version is in the key of each tool image mise installs, so a bump builds them again. The shared tools aren’t pinned for users, except Cursor’s CLI. Holds go in assets/shared-tools/mise.toml (node = "24" stays on that major). testdata/mise.lock is a fixed lock for the tests. Their backends are named in mise.toml’s [tool_alias] table, for every tool that isn’t one of mise’s own core: tools, because mise’s registry can move a tool to another backend in any release (versions). A new shared tool gets its alias there, and TestToolBackendsNamed fails when a tool that isn’t a core: tool has none, or when its alias isn’t the backend that tests/e2e-mise.lock resolved. When opencode’s major version changes, or a bump of e2e-tools moves opencode to a version that adds migrations, refresh internal/vm/testdata/opencode-.sql, the schema of opencode’s database that TestOpencodeCleanSchema cleans. Print it with sqlite3 ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db .schema in a VM with that opencode, after opencode auth list has made the database, and copy only the schema, never rows. You can also make the file from the release’s packages/core/src/database/schema.gen.ts in opencode’s repo: unwrap its SQL and add the migration table’s line at the end, and it matches .schema line for line. Name the file for the version, and in the test put each new table in its list of tables that devvm empties or keeps, which the test asks for. A table or a column that holds a login also goes into opencodeLogins (internal/vm/agents.go) and the design note’s opencode’s database in history exports. e2e-tools, e2e-from, e2e-curl and e2e-ubuntu move the end-to-end tests’ own pins, which keep their cached images valid between runs. e2e-tools resolves tests/e2e-mise.lock again, with devvm’s pinned host mise, for both architectures’ glibc and musl VMs, and refuses a tool whose download has no checksum on every platform yet. e2e-from moves the digests of node:24, alpine:3 and ubuntu:26.04 in tests/e2e/from_test.go to Docker Hub’s. e2e-curl moves curlImage in tests/e2e/transparent_test.go, the curl image that the network checks run in containers, to curlimages/curl’s newest release, by its digest. e2e-ubuntu moves e2eUbuntuRelease in tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go, the dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image that e2e pins base to in place of the newest, to the newest Ubuntu lists. Ubuntu removes dated releases after a few months, and e2e’s going stops its first builds of base: bump e2e-ubuntu before that. Run e2e-tools after any change to assets/shared-tools/mise.toml, because the end-to-end tests refuse a lock resolved from another one (end-to-end tests). mise run test catches it first: TestE2ELockPins checks the lock’s first line against mise.toml and that it locks each of its tools, and TestE2EUbuntuPins checks that e2eUbuntuRelease is a dated release of base’s Ubuntu release, which e2e-ubuntu lists, and that scripts/bump.sh and tests/e2e name only that release. e2e-lima moves the Lima release that CI’s end-to-end workflow installs, LIMA_VERSION in .github/workflows/e2e.yml, to Lima’s newest release, and LIMA_SHA256 to its Linux-x86_64 tarball’s line in that release’s SHA256SUMS. Lima’s release notes print the SHA-256 of SHA256SUMS itself, so e2e-lima checks the downloaded file against that value first and edits nothing when they differ. assets/layers/ubuntu-cloud.gpg is Ubuntu’s cloud image signing key (fingerprint D2EB44626FDDC30B513D5BB71A5D6C4C7DB87C81), from keyserver.ubuntu.com. If Ubuntu changes it, pinning a new image (a first build of base, or devvm rebuild base) stops with ubuntu_bad_signature: fetch the new key, check its fingerprint against Ubuntu’s announcement, and replace the file (gpg --export FPR). assets/layers/ubuntu-archive.gpg is Ubuntu’s archive signing key, “Ubuntu Archive Automatic Signing Key (2018)” (fingerprint F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C), fetched from keyserver.ubuntu.com by that fingerprint, checked against the fingerprint that Ubuntu’s security team lists, and exported with gpg --export-options export-minimal --export FPR. devvm checks the InRelease files of a first build of base against it (ubuntu.ArchiveKeyring). If Ubuntu signs the archive with a new key, that build stops with packages_refused: fetch the new key, check its fingerprint the same way, and replace the file. The key must be RSA, because internal/ubuntu/pgp.go checks only RSA signatures. Moving base to a new Ubuntu release (ubuntu.Series, ubuntu.Version) also moves ubuntu.Released, the day Ubuntu released it, which is the date of that release’s own InRelease (dists//InRelease), because devvm refuses a release pocket dated before it. Edited scripts change image keys, so the affected images rebuild on next use. An edit to assets/prelude.sh changes the key of every image and every shared tool image. Build them in a sandbox of their own (LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME) before committing (devvm build docker, or a VM made with the tools whose build script changed), then devvm gc, and run the end-to-end tests.

data.agreement-tests#Agreement tests: When two places must agree but can’t be one, a test checks that they agree. TestEveryPartHasAPolicy checks that every image part has its policy, TestSharedToolsPolicies that the policies in assets/shared-tools/ are one for each shared tool in image.SharedTools, TestConfigTools that assets/shared-tools/mise.toml lists each shared tool’s members and nothing else, TestBuiltinPolicies that every policy devvm ships parses, TestEveryMessageIsUsed that every message has a caller, TestDocLinks that every doc link is a message and a heading, TestPreludeUsers that only the scripts that get the prelude use it, TestDefsComplete that every coding agent has its [tool_alias] line and its row in the docs’ Supported agents table, TestProvidersComplete that every provider in agents.Providers has its row in the docs’ table of the API keys the proxy puts in, TestToolchainsComplete that every toolchain has files that call for it and its row and section on the toolchains page, which names those files and its PATH folders, TestFormatsCoverLogins that every agent’s login file has its format in internal/agentlogin, TestBumpCoversPins that scripts/bump.sh moves every pin it finds, or says why it’s left (updating pinned versions), and TestReferenceIsCurrent that the CLI reference matches the commands. A new pair of places that must agree gets such a test.
data.changing-the-state-layout#Changing the s:
State files describes the layout, and the design note says why it’s built that way. Every path in it comes from internal/paths. paths.Dirs names the shared folders and files, and Dirs.VM(name) gives a VM’s paths.VM, whose methods name each file in the VM’s folder: Dirs.VMDir(hash), vms//, for a project VM, and run/builds// for a build VM. A new file of a VM’s gets a method on paths.VM, so it lands in the VM’s folder, and vmFolders.teardown in internal/vm/teardown.go deletes it with the folder, with no list of files to update. A new socket goes in Dirs.Run(), named by a hash, and TestSocketsFit checks the longest path against paths.SocketMax. A new record that only devvm writes is JSON, read with encoding/json, which ignores fields it doesn’t know, and written whole with state.WriteFile. A new default goes in internal/settings, which reads config.toml strictly and saves settings.json, and a new lock is an OS file lock (platform.LockFile and its kin) on a file that paths names.
The data folder and the config folder each hold a version file with their layout version, state.Layout in internal/state/layout.go. Before each command that reads them, state.CheckLayout takes version.lock in the data folder and compares both files with state.Layout. A folder without the file gets this devvm’s version, the same version goes on, and a newer one stops the command with layout_newer, because a newer devvm changed the folders. An older one runs the migrations from that version to this one, in order, and then writes state.Layout into both files. skipsLayout in internal/cli/root.go lists the commands that skip the check: help, completion, the version and devvm’s own hidden commands.
testdata/script/layout.txtar makes two VMs on the allowlist tier, a forwarded port, a link and a secret, lists every file and folder under the data and config folders, and compares the lists with the ones at the end of the script, one for macOS and one for Linux. A change to the layout, such as a new file, a renamed folder or a file that moves, changes a listing, so the test fails until you update it. When it does, decide whether the change needs a new layout version:
A change that an older devvm would read wrongly, or a file that moves, raises state.Layout by one. It adds a state.Migration at the end of migrations(), which changes the folders from the version before to the new one. A migration takes paths.Dirs, and a run that it fails stops before the versions change, so the next run tries it again. TestMigrations checks that there’s one migration for each version before this one, and TestCheckLayout runs fake ones. It updates the listings in layout.txtar. A new file that an older devvm doesn’t need to know about, or a field added to a JSON file, which an older devvm ignores, keeps the version and changes only the listings.
data.changing-what-devvm-does-with-state#Chan:
A change that reads or writes state, such as a new command, a new section in vm.json or a new field in a record, runs its new commands on every fixture in the same commit, and reading the files isn’t enough. Add the steps to each release’s scripts, as fixture_v010_network.txtar runs rules by method and path on 0.1.0’s app VM and fixture_v010_clone.txtar runs devvm clone add on its web VM. When a fixture’s test fails, today’s devvm breaks the state that the release’s users have. Fix devvm, or add a migration, but never change the fixture.
A change in what devvm does with existing state gets a line in CHANGELOG.md, in the Unreleased section at the bottom until its release moves it to the top: a step in What to do when the user has to act on it, and otherwise a line in the group of the people who notice it, as Releasing says. When the user has to do something about it, such as run a command, devvm also tells them once, at the first launch after the upgrade.
data.freezing-a-releases-state#Freezing a rel:
At release time, after the tag exists, a final release that changed the state format gets its fixture. A release candidate gets none, even when it changed the state, and its final release’s fixture holds that state:
Copy the newest fixture’s generate.sh, generate.txtar and README.md into testdata/v/. Set the tag, the version and the script’s name in generate.sh, and add the VMs and commands to generate.txtar that make the state the release added. Run generate.sh on a Mac and on Linux, which writes darwin/ and linux/. 0.1.0’s were made on an arm64 Mac and on x86_64 Fedora. Add the release’s entries in stateFixtures, fixtureBinaries and storeFixtures, and its scripts, made from the newest release’s scripts with checks of its own VMs. Commit the folder as the run left it. The older fixtures stay as they are.
data.one-owner-for-each-concern#One owner for: Each concern in devvm has one owner, the package or function that does it, such as internal/hostgit for every git command devvm runs on the host, internal/paths for every folder and file devvm uses, internal/settings for every default (settings.Read and settings.Save, over config.toml and settings.json, with each value’s parser), and locales/en.toml for every message. Before you add a helper, a parser, a path, a file reader, a message or a table, find its owner and extend it. A second copy drifts from the first, and then one of them is wrong. Code with no owner yet can have a second copy, because a copy can be cheaper than the wrong shared helper, so extract an owner at the third copy. A judge, such as proxy.Public or NormHost, gets its owner at once, because its two copies would disagree on what’s allowed. The packages says what each package owns, and the failures of the checks below name the owners too.
data.released-state#Released state: Someone who upgrades devvm keeps their VMs, defaults, agent store and secrets as the release they came from left them. Until 1.0, an upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 has to work. Each final release that changed what devvm writes on disk has a frozen copy of the state it left, called its fixture, and the tests run today’s devvm on every fixture, so a change that breaks an older release’s state fails the gate.
data.secrets-in-the-code#Secrets in the code:
A value that lets whoever holds it act as you or as a VM is a redact.Secret, from the moment devvm reads it until the place it’s used. That covers a VM’s proxy password (netpolicy.Key, proxy.Config.Password, backend.Confinement.ProxyPassword) and a build proxy’s, a secret’s value (secrets.Store.Value, Get and Save, and what ui.UI.Secret reads), the company proxy’s password and the Proxy-Authorization the proxy sends it, the values the proxy caches for a VM’s bindings (proxy.Lookup), and an agent’s API keys and tokens once they leave its login file (agentlogin.File.Get and SetKey, and the tokens a capture or a refresh brings). Two such values stay strings, as where secret values live explains: the value on its way through platform.KeychainGet and KeychainSet, which secrets.Store makes a Secret at once, and devvm desktop’s VNC password, which you must see. A Secret prints as with %v, %s, %q, %x, %#v and every other verb, so a log line, an error or a struct printed with %+v never shows it. Its value is behind a pointer, because fmt prints a value in an unexported field without calling its Format, and such a field then shows only an address. Two Secrets are equal with == only when they’re the same one, so compare their values with Reveal, or the structs that hold them with reflect.DeepEqual.
Reveal is the only way to the value, and forbidigo refuses every call to it except in tests. So each place that must use a value says why in a //nolint:forbidigo // on that line. Those places are the proxy’s password check and the headers it puts values in, the store’s file and the Keychain, the VM’s proxy URL and a login’s file, its refresh and its claims. Anywhere else, pass the Secret on. testdata/lint/forbidigo.go keeps a call to Reveal that the rule must report. The structure test refuses a struct that embeds redact.Secret outside internal/redact, which would take on its methods, and an interface that declares Reveal() string, whose calls forbidigo wouldn’t see. It reads the source alone, so it doesn’t see a Secret embedded through another type or reached through reflection.
Encoding a Secret as JSON or as text is an error (redact.ErrEncode), never , so a value written somewhere by accident fails at once rather than losing your login. A file that must hold the real value therefore writes it through its own wire type, a struct with the value as a string that only that file’s reader and writer use:
The proxy’s config, proxy.json, is configFile, with Config’s fields in Config’s order, so its bytes, and the Sum that decides whether a running VM’s proxy starts again, match what earlier releases wrote. TestConfigFile holds the two types together. A VM’s key in vm.json is netpolicy.NetMade’s own MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON, through netMade. A secret’s file without a Keychain is the value and a line’s end, which secrets.Store.save writes and saved reads. A login’s file is the agent’s own format, read and written whole as a map so that fields devvm doesn’t know stay, and a key or token leaves the map through agentlogin’s token and goes into it through setToken. To add a field that holds a secret, give it the type redact.Secret. If a struct with it is written to a file, add the field to that file’s wire type, and check that a frozen release’s files still read and write the same bytes: TestV010ProxyConfigs does it for proxy.json, TestFixtureVMStates for vm.json’s sections, TestFixtureStoreGet for a secret’s file on Linux, and TestFixtureAgentStore for the agents’ login files, which every read leaves as they were.
data.the-checks-on-owners#The checks on owner:
An owner gets a check only when a second copy would be a bug or a security hole, and only when the check is exact, so that it never fails on code that’s right. Each check’s failure names the owner. The table is written from ownerDocs in internal/structure/owners_doc_test.go, which TestOwnersDoc checks it against and TestOwnersAgree checks against the structure test’s own tables, so a change to a check changes its row there, and go test ./internal/structure -run TestOwnersDoc -update writes the table again:
Check Owner Allowed elsewhere forbidigo, testbuild.On internal/cli, whose readOverrides is the only code that asks whether this is a test build nowhere: other packages take the overrides as fields forbidigo, os.FindProcess, syscall.Kill, unix.Kill and os.Process’s Kill and Signal internal/daemon, which signals a background process only while its pid file and its arguments say it’s still that process (Proc), or through the process it started (Handle) internal/platform; tests, which signal the children they started; and a child that hasn’t been waited for yet, whose pid is still its own, with a nolint saying so forbidigo, unicode.IsGraphic, IsPrint, IsControl and Bidi_Control msg.Safe in internal/msg/safe.go, the one rule for which characters reach the terminal, which msg.Printable, msg.OneLine, the UI’s renderers and devvm agent save’s diff follow, so a second rule can’t let through what this one refuses (Colors says what it refuses) a check that isn’t about the terminal, such as a path one line long, with a //nolint:forbidigo saying so forbidigo, HTTP clients internal/fetch, whose NewClient sets each client’s timeout and redirect policy (HTTPSOnly or SameScheme), and whose Retry, Transient, ReadCapped, Get, Resolve and Download try again after the failures that may pass, cap what a body or a download may hold, follow a HEAD’s redirects to where they end and check a download’s SHA-256 before anything uses it. fetch.Client is its own type, so a client that NewClient didn’t make, such as &fetch.Client{}, fails every request, and a caller changes a client’s transport through its Transport method internal/proxy, which is the standard library only, and tests, which make their own servers’ clients forbidigo, netip.Addr’s IsPrivate proxy.Public in internal/proxy/proxy.go, the one judge of whether an address is on the internet: netip’s classes, the table of the other ranges that aren’t (notPublic), and the IPv4 address in a NAT64 or 6to4 address. The proxy’s floor, devvm network lock, a --clone VM’s partial-clone remotes and --from’s registries all ask it, so a range added to it holds for each internal/proxy forbidigo, redact.Secret’s Reveal; the structure test, a struct that embeds redact.Secret and an interface that declares Reveal() string redact.Secret in internal/redact/secret.go, the type of the values that let whoever holds them act as the user or a VM, but for those Secrets in the code names: a VM’s proxy password, a secret’s value, a login’s keys and tokens once they leave its file, and the company proxy’s password and its Proxy-Authorization. Every way of printing one shows or, in an unexported field, an address, and encoding one as JSON or text is an error, never a stand-in, so a file that holds the real value writes it through its own wire type, and a value can’t be lost by going somewhere it isn’t meant to where the value is used, each call to Reveal with a //nolint:forbidigo that says why: the proxy’s password check, its config file, the headers it puts values in, the company proxy’s credentials, the VM’s CA key as it signs and the broker’s frames to its child; the store’s file and Keychain; the VM’s proxy URL and its key in vm.json; a login’s file, its refresh and its claims; and tests. No struct embeds redact.Secret and no interface declares Reveal() string outside internal/redact forbidigo, os.WriteFile, os.Create and os.O_TRUNC internal/state, whose WriteFile and WriteFileMode write a file whole through a temporary file in its folder, renamed over it, so a reader never sees half of it internal/proxy, which imports only the standard library and has its own writer, writeAtomic; internal/msg/gen, which imports no devvm package; internal/stubtest; tests; and, with a nolint saying why, a file written another way: a log that a process writes as it runs, a download that streams into its file, and internal/daemon’s pid and status files, each written in one write that a reader takes as missing until its line ends forbidigo, os.Open, os.OpenFile, os.ReadFile, os.OpenRoot, os.OpenInRoot, os.DirFS and os.Root’s Open, OpenFile, ReadFile and FS, in the code that reads files a VM can write or swap: internal/gitprotect, internal/agentlogin, internal/vm’s devcontainer.go, detect.go, paste.go and agentsave*.go, internal/netpolicy/rules.go, internal/vmlog, and internal/proxy’s config.go, policy.go, rotate.go and nixcache.go internal/safefile, which imports only the standard library, so the proxy reads with it too. Its Read and Open open a file without blocking and, unless the caller passes Follow, without following a symbolic link at the path’s end. They then check the file they opened, not its name, so a FIFO, a device or a folder is refused with ErrNotRegular, a file past its cap with ErrTooLong, and, with OneLink, a file with another hard link with ErrLinked. A FIFO that the VM swaps in after a check can’t hold devvm, and a link to /dev/zero can’t flood it. Checked checks a file its caller opened another way in the same way, such as devvm paste’s copied file, which platform.OpenNoLinks opens following no link but the system’s, through openat, which the standard library doesn’t have on macOS. OpenRoot opens beneath a folder through os.Root, never through a link out of it, and its FS lists and stats what’s there but opens only regular files and, never through a link at the name’s end, folders to list. Walk walks a folder that a VM can fill, reading each folder in batches and stopping at its bound on the entries it reads, as devvm agent import walks an agent’s folder every other file, which is devvm’s own or the user’s; tests, which make their own fixtures; and, with a nolint saying why, what opens a file to write it or a folder to lock it, such as the proxy’s logs and the Nix cache’s lock, each opened never through a link or waiting on a FIFO and checked once open forbidigo, os.Chmod, os.Chtimes, os.Chown, os.Lchown and os.Truncate, in the code that changes files a VM can write or swap: internal/proxy, internal/vmlog and internal/vmssh the file’s own descriptor, from internal/safefile, an os.Root or the proxy’s OpenLog: os.File’s Chmod, Chown and Truncate, an os.Root’s methods, and the proxy’s touchFile (futimes, or utimensat with no path), because a VM can swap a name for a link between the open and the change, which would then reach a file of yours every other package, whose files are devvm’s own or the user’s; tests, which make their own fixtures; and, with a nolint saying why, a unix socket devvm has just made in its own folder (the proxy’s SSH agent relay and the link session’s sockets), whose mode only its path can set forbidigo, os.Setenv, os.Unsetenv, os.Clearenv and syscall’s each command’s own environment, its exec.Cmd’s Env, because every command and background process devvm starts inherits devvm’s. A VM’s SSH agent is one: the finder’s target carries its socket, its proxy’s relay (netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare), which goes to the backend in backend.ExecOpts.Agent, backend.ShellOpts.Agent and Confinement.AgentSocket, and Lima sets SSH_AUTH_SOCK on that VM’s limactl commands alone, so a run that reaches several VMs never gives one another’s daemon.Ready in internal/daemon/status.go, which takes the status file’s name out of a background process’s own environment; stubtest.NoGitRepo, which takes git’s variables that pick a repo out of a test’s environment until the test ends; and tests, which use t.Setenv the structure test’s owners, host commands the runners: the UI’s LoggedCmd, which a package takes as a field and which runs a command into the run log, a backend’s Runner, and internal/hostgit. A host command that one of them doesn’t run is made only in the files execSites lists: those that make the command a runner then runs, such as Lima’s limactl and mise’s, and those whose command can’t go into the run log, because it streams for as long as a link, the port forwarder or the desktop’s relay lasts, asks on the terminal, outlives the run, or carries a secret tests the structure test’s owners, a backend’s other interfaces backend.As in internal/backend/guard.go, because the registry’s backends are behind its guard, whose type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so a type assertion to backend.Forgetter or *lima.Lima on one is always false tests the structure test’s owners, git internal/hostgit, which runs git without the repo’s fsmonitor, hooks, filters or signing programs, over ssh only, without the environment’s GIT_* variables, prompts, replace refs or grafts. It’s also the only package whose string literals may be "push", whole (names), and none is: a --clone VM’s copy goes through the backend’s Exec (internal/vm/cloneseed.go), never git’s transport, whose receive-pack refuses shallow and SHA-256 repos. Nor may any other package’s be "diff-files", which enters each submodule, where that repo’s own config can name a filter: hostgit.DiffFiles doesn’t. In tests, which run plain git to make their repos, it’s internal/stubtest’s Git, which leaves out git’s variables that pick a repo, its files or its config (GitEnv), so a git that runs the tests, such as a hook’s or git rebase --exec’s, never sends a test’s git to the checkout itself nothing else forbidigo, os.UserHomeDir, and the structure test’s owners, HOME paths.FromEnv in internal/paths/dirs.go, which reads HOME once into paths.Dirs.Home, so a test or an e2e run that sets its own HOME moves every path devvm takes from it tests the structure test’s owners, DEVVM_ variables readOverrides in internal/cli/overrides.go, which reads a test build’s stand-ins, while a release reads none the settings in envSettings, and tests the structure test’s owners, shell quoting internal/shell, whose Quote and QuoteJoin quote words for a POSIX shell, so a value never runs as a command, and QuoteLine a word on one line for bash tests the structure test’s owners, the VM-name grammar internal/vmname, whose IsVM tells a project VM’s name from an image’s, so gc never takes a project VM for an image tests the structure test’s owners, VM names internal/vmname, whose VM is the name of every machine devvm runs on a backend: a project VM, an image’s machine, a build VM, or a VM’s old machine while a remake makes the new one. A name is made a VM only where it’s read: Parse takes a project VM’s name from an argument or a file name, and also reads vm.json’s name and runs in project.Nth, ParseListed one a backend lists, VM.UnmarshalText one in a JSON file (one path element that doesn’t start with -, or none, and any machine’s, so a field that must hold a project VM’s is still checked with IsProject), Image names an image’s machine and VM.Aside a remake’s old one, and a backend’s build VMs are typed constants. A struct field, a parameter or a result named for a VM (vm, vms, otherVM, vmName) whose type is a string, a pointer to one, a list of them or a map keyed on them fails, and so do a conversion of anything but a literal to vmname.VM and a type alias of it, so a path, an alias or a folder’s name is never passed for a VM’s name. The check goes by names, so it doesn’t see a VM’s name in a string named otherwise (target, client, parent, to, name), vmname imported with a dot or reached through a type parameter, or a VM joined to a string constant, whose type is still vmname.VM (l.VM+lineNoLinks in internal/vmssh/links.go) msg.M.VM in internal/msg/msg.go, which reads back the VM a message’s function took; internal/stubtest, whose stubs stand in for limactl and ssh, whose arguments are strings; the names notNames lists that aren’t a VM’s, such as backend.Registry.NewVMs, a backend’s name; and tests the structure test’s owners, hosts internal/proxy/host.go, whose NormHost reads a host as the proxy judges it, the one form every judge of a host compares: a host of printable ASCII lowercased, in ASCII alone, and its one trailing dot dropped unless it’s an address, whose dot can only be its IPv6 zone’s, and any other host left as it is, which HostOK refuses, so no Unicode fold makes another name match. An address is bare, or an IPv6 address in one pair of brackets, never one with a stray bracket. Its Host is what a matcher takes, such as a rule’s matchHost and NO_PROXY’s. A call to package strings that drops a dot (Trim, TrimLeft or TrimRight with a cutset that holds ., TrimSuffix or CutSuffix with "."), or that folds or trims an argument named for a host (ToLower, ToUpper, EqualFold, TrimFunc, TrimLeftFunc or TrimRightFunc of host, sni or u.Hostname()), fails, and so does a conversion to proxy.Host of anything but a literal. The check goes by names and calls, so it doesn’t see a host’s case folded in a variable named otherwise, a dot dropped by slicing, or a host mapped rune by rune (strings.Map) the functions free lists by file and name, each with why: trimDots in internal/proxy/request.go, which drops a path’s segments’ trailing dots; urlHost in internal/vm/cloneseed.go, which reads a remote’s ssh host as ssh does, to find a VM’s alias, its case folded and its trailing dot kept; safeIndexPath in internal/vm/cloneworktree.go, which drops a path segment’s trailing dots and spaces as Windows does; and machines.fillPassword in internal/backend/lima/start.go and transportHelper in internal/vm/cloneconfig.go, which check that a string has only the characters of a set that holds .; and tests the structure test’s owners, the coding agents internal/agents, whose Defs hold every fact devvm keeps of each agent, so no copy of an agent’s list or paths goes stale when one is added. A string literal that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, or that holds an agent’s folder below the home folder, fails, and code of one agent’s own names the agent by its constant there. Comparing with that constant, or with one named after it such as secrets.ClaudeToken, a case for it, looking for it with slices.Contains or slices.Index, looking it up in a map, a map literal keyed on it and strings.HasPrefix, HasSuffix, EqualFold or Contains with it fail too, outside the files named for the agent, such as claude.go, so the rest of devvm asks the agent’s Def and a new agent changes none of it. A list that holds every agent’s name, tests included, fails as a copy of agents.Names(), and so does a CLI test script’s line that lists agents as a message does, for which the runner gives $AGENT_CHOICES, $LOGIN_AGENTS and $KEY_AGENTS (adding a coding agent) internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for, and tests; for a name, the value of a constant that devvmNameFree lists with its reason and the only files that may use it: vm.CursorCommand, the Cursor editor’s cursor command, which devvm cursor runs and isn’t the agent’s, used in internal/vm/ssh.go and internal/cli/cursor.go alone and compared with as an agent’s constant is; for the comparisons, the files whose names hold the agent’s name as a word, and the constants devvmSwitchFree lists in one file each with its reason: the claude secret’s own checks, which are a secret’s, and Codex’s binding name in logins.go the structure test’s owners, the toolchains internal/image, whose SharedTools holds every fact devvm keeps of each toolchain: its members, the files that call for it, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files. A string literal that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, fails, so code elsewhere asks the table, and a new toolchain is an entry there (adding a toolchain) internal/stubtest, and tests the structure test’s owners, image names internal/image, whose Name is an image’s name and splits it into its layers (Layers, Parent, Has), whose NameOf joins layers into one, and whose ParseName reads the name the user gives, which build.Names’ Parse checks against the layers there are. devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm read their names there once, and the rest of devvm passes the image.Name on tests the structure test’s owners, state.ReadHash and project.Parents the finder in internal/vm/finder.go, whose target finds the VM every command acts on: the folder’s own, the nearest parent folder’s under --here and --parent (resolveFolder), or one named (devvm rm VM). It finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder (finder.state, by the path’s hash first, then recorded), offers to move a VM whose folder moved there (moveHere in internal/vm/move.go, the match here.movedFrom), and names a new VM by the first of the folder’s names whose VM folder is free (newName, project.Nth). Its need says what the command needs of the VM, and need.check is the one place that refuses one that isn’t there, one made for an earlier folder at its path, one whose remake didn’t finish and one whose creation didn’t, the last with refuseUnfinished, which every start (starter.bringUp in internal/vm/start.go) makes too. It reads the folder devvm runs in only then, so the commands that act on no folder’s VM run in a folder that’s gone. The VM it finds is a target (internal/vm/target.go). It holds what the VM’s backend told the finder, which each start and stop of the VM then updates, and it runs what a command does with that VM: exec, shell, stop, running, ownSSH and the name of its ssh config entry internal/state, and tests the structure test’s owners, hostsafety.Walk the start in internal/vm/start.go, whose starter.walk walks a VM’s project folder once for each check of the folder on the host, for the git repos nested in it, which .git protection goes by (gitprotect.Protector.Nested), and on Linux hosts its set-id files, so a check never walks the folder twice. It walks when a VM is made and when a check finds it stopped, at a launch or at devvm stop (starter.hostChecks), and at devvm git-protect on a stopped VM, never at a launch into a running VM internal/hostsafety, and tests the structure test’s owners, state.ReadAll the inventory in internal/vm/inventory.go, which reads every VM’s state (ReadStates), and with ReadInventory the backends’ lists too, each within its wait, for every listing of VMs: devvm ls, devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc, the ssh config, devvm gc --orphans, the links, devvm secret’s list, finding a VM by its name and the mounts that devvm’s SSH agent checks a key against. Its one failure policy is that a backend that can’t list fails a listing (Inventory.Err) only when some VM’s state names it, and that a state that can’t be read is a row of its own, which the readers leave out and ToolsInUse and Mounts fail on. state.VMNames, which fails on such a state, stays for the readers below internal/vm that must count every VM: netpolicy’s secrets, ports and sshconfig.ChooseAlias; state.ReadableVMs, which leaves such a state out, is for those that only warn: netpolicy’s warnings of every VM and doctor’s policy warnings internal/state, and tests the structure test’s owners, paths.Dirs.AgentSettings and paths.Dirs.AgentLogins devvm’s agent store: agentStore in internal/vm/agents.go for the agents’ settings, which the mounts, the setup’s copies, a remake’s home and devvm agent import take, and secrets.LoginFile in internal/secrets/secrets.go for their logins, which the setup’s copies and the proxy read, so nothing reads an agent’s files from the home folder but vm.AgentImport internal/paths, and tests the structure test’s owners, paths in devvm’s folders internal/paths, whose Dirs and VM name every file and folder devvm keeps, so the layout, its golden listing in testdata/script/layout.txtar and a VM’s teardown miss none. A filepath.Join onto a Data or Config field fails, and so does an os.MkdirTemp or os.CreateTemp there whose name is a literal; a name from paths, such as paths.ToolsBuildPrefix, passes tests forbidigo matches only the function a call names, so the checks that look at a call’s arguments are in the structure test. It finds a host command in an exec.Command or exec.CommandContext call that names it, as a literal or as a constant, whatever name the file imports os/exec under. It finds a DEVVM_ variable in a call to any function or field named Getenv or LookupEnv, in any case, so t.Getenv and a getenv parameter count as well as os.Getenv, and it finds HOME the same way. The settings envSettings lists are the ones users set, DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_FROM; names mode, DEVVM_MESSAGES, which any build has; and the variables devvm sets for its own processes, DEVVM_GUESTFWD for devvm _qemu and DEVVM_DAEMON_STATUS for each background process internal/daemon starts.
The structure test also finds a copy of an owner’s code by its text, in literals. A string literal outside tests that holds '\'', the escaped quote a shell quoter writes, belongs in internal/shell, and one that holds [0-9a-f]{14}, the hash at the end of a project VM’s name, belongs in internal/vmname. A quote written as a rune, such as '\'' in Go, isn’t a string literal, so it doesn’t count. One that holds a coding agent’s folder below the home folder, such as .codex/ or .pi/agent, belongs in internal/agents, and so does one that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, such as "opencode" (names), so code of one agent’s own names it by its constant there, such as agents.Opencode, and a longer text that mentions an agent, such as a command’s example, doesn’t count. A literal that is a toolchain’s name or one of its members’, whole, such as "dotnet" or "pnpm", belongs in internal/image in the same way, so code elsewhere finds a toolchain’s facts in its image.SharedTools entry. A literal that is "push", whole, belongs only in internal/hostgit, which holds none, so no package passes push to git: a --clone VM’s copy goes through the backend’s Exec instead (internal/vm/cloneseed.go, the copy into a clone VM), because git’s receive-pack refuses shallow and SHA-256 repos, and a second transport would drift. A literal that is "diff-files", whole, belongs only in internal/hostgit too, whose DiffFiles adds --ignore-submodules=all, because git diff-files otherwise runs git status in each submodule or embedded repo, where that repo’s own config can name a filter that devvm’s git doesn’t turn off.
