In the same way, separators finds a copy of a parser by what it splits on: a call to any function of package strings with + as an argument, as a literal or as a constant, splits or joins an image’s layers, so it belongs in internal/image. A call with another argument that holds a +, such as strings.ContainsAny(arg, "+,"), doesn’t count.
The shared tools have one owner too, the table image.SharedTools in internal/image/tool.go, whose agents’ entries it makes from the coding agents’ registry, agents.Defs (adding a coding agent). Each entry, an image.ToolDef, holds a tool’s name, its kind (a toolchain or an agent), its members (the tools in the lock that its name stands for, such as pnpm and bun for node), the files in a project folder that call for it, and its installer, which is mise for every tool but rust, which rustup installs, and dotnet, which assets/shared-tools/build.sh unpacks from Microsoft’s SDK archive. A toolchain’s entry also holds the environment that every VM’s shells get for it, such as NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX and .NET’s telemetry switch (Env), the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, where its global installs go (PathDirs), and the members whose version files mise reads in a project (VersionFiles). mise locks dotnet’s version without a download, because its own installer runs Microsoft’s install script, which checks nothing, so devvm adds each platform’s archive and its SHA-512 from Microsoft’s release metadata to the lock (withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go), and Share.Build passes them to build.sh (image.OwnDownload), which checks the archive with devvm-fetch. image.Toolchains, image.Agents, image.GroupTools, the files that make devvm choose a toolchain for a new VM, the lock’s check for downloads (image.NoDownload) and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps to a toolchain all come from it. So do the files that every launch’s setup writes for the toolchains: /etc/devvm/toolchains.sh, with every toolchain’s environment and PATH folders (image.GuestEnv and image.GuestPath), which base’s /etc/profile.d/devvm-tools.sh reads in every shell, as it reads the agents’ /etc/devvm/agents.sh, and the VM’s mise setting that names the tools whose version files it reads (image.VersionFileTools). The image builds read none of them, so a toolchain’s environment changes no image. The structure test fails on a string literal outside internal/image that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, so code elsewhere asks the table, through image.Def, an entry’s Installer or its other fields, rather than naming a toolchain. Adding a toolchain and adding a coding agent list the files a new shared tool needs, and the agreement tests fail until the table and those files match.
The scripts that devvm’s builds run with bash have one owner for the machine they run on, assets/prelude.sh, whose $devvm_arch, $devvm_libc and devvm_sha give each script its architecture, its C library and its pinned checksum for each download (the scripts’ prelude). A script reads them rather than run uname -m or look for apk itself, and checks that the prelude came first with : "${devvm_arch:?}" for each variable it reads, which also tells shellcheck that the variable is set. Go reads each of those scripts through image.OwnScript, which puts the prelude before it, so a recipe, a tool image’s key and the conversion’s copy of oci/build.sh all hold the two together. TestPreludeUsers in internal/image fails when a script that doesn’t get the prelude, such as assets/oci/bootify.sh or assets/guest/’s, uses it, or when a script reads a variable without that check. testdata/script/prelude.txtar checks which pin devvm_sha picks from each script’s pins on arm64 and amd64, with glibc and with musl. A CLI test or a Go test that sources one of these scripts sources assets/prelude.sh first.
internal/paths also owns how a path on the host is resolved and compared with a folder, in resolve.go, whose comment says which resolver each question takes. paths.Physical resolves every symlink as far as the path exists, for where a folder or file really is, such as a project folder against devvm’s own folders or an SSH key against the folders VMs mount. paths.PhysicalParent resolves only the folder’s symlinks and keeps the last element as named, for a path that may itself be a symlink devvm mustn’t follow, such as a key’s recorded path or a Seatbelt rule. filepath.EvalSymlinks itself, which fails when the path doesn’t exist, is for a path that must exist, such as the folder devvm runs in, or a stopped VM’s project folder, which each of a start’s three checks resolves with filepath.EvalSymlinks (an existing VM). Then paths.Within tells whether a path is a folder or inside it, and paths.Below whether it’s inside it only. Both compare names, so both paths are resolved the same way first. A check that keeps a VM away from a folder, such as project.Unsafe’s, an SSH key against the folders VMs mount, or a project folder against an agent’s folder, uses paths.In or paths.Under instead, which also compare the folders themselves and match when the path, or a folder above it, is the same folder as the other, by device and inode. On a volume that ignores case, as macOS’s do by default, ~/.Config/devvm is ~/.config/devvm, which a comparison of names alone misses.
A VM’s state, vm.json, has one owner too, internal/state, which reads and writes the whole file and knows only its core fields. Every other package that keeps something of a VM’s owns one section of it, with its own type, its name (Section), and an Of that reads it through state.Section: internal/netpolicy owns net, internal/gitprotect git, internal/ports ports, internal/sshagent agent, internal/tools tools, internal/secrets secrets, and internal/vm size, clone, devcontainer, desktop and links (internal/vm/state.go). A section’s type keeps what the user asked for at its top level and what devvm made under made. A change goes through state.VM.Update, which takes the VM’s lock, reads the file again, runs the change and writes the file once: the change sets its section with state.SetSection and works out a list’s new value from the file as it is then, never from what the command read earlier, so a change another devvm made meanwhile is kept. A change that fails writes nothing. Update holds one VM’s lock, so a change takes no other lock inside it, and a change to several VMs updates each in turn. Test builds and the tests panic on a lock taken out of that order (the lock rule). state.VM.Claim is Update that also holds the claims lock, for what no two VMs may have (ports.Allocator chooses every VM’s host port through it), and state.VM.Create writes a new VM’s whole state once, its ssh alias chosen under the claims lock. A build VM has no state, so ports.Allocator.Build chooses its ssh port through state.Claims, which holds the claims lock alone. A VM’s alias is one vmname.IsAlias accepts, or devvm doesn’t use it. internal/vm’s checkState reads every section of the folder’s VM’s state as the VM is found, so a section that can’t be read stops the command instead of reading as empty. A new section adds its check there.
data.the-consolidation-pass#The consolidation:
A review of a body of work, and the review before a release, look across the code for copies:
two parsers of one format a path built outside internal/paths a list of files kept beside the folder that holds them a value encoded in a string two messages that say one thing a comment that says to keep two places in sync a test that copies a constant Each copy gets one of three outcomes: extend the owner, make one owner, or leave it. Leave it when the only shared helper would be the wrong one, because a copy costs less than the wrong helper, and wait for a third copy before making one. The pass is part of those reviews, not a step every change runs.
data.the-packages#The packages:
Each package owns these concerns, and a package’s doc.go, where it has one, maps the package itself. internal/fetch, internal/redact, internal/agents, internal/jsonc, internal/shell, internal/vmname, internal/safefile, internal/landlock and internal/daemon use the standard library alone, and internal/proxy uses it with internal/daemon, internal/landlock, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/vmname and nothing else. internal/devcontainer imports no module from outside devvm, but it uses internal/image, internal/jsonc, internal/msg and internal/shell.
Package Owns cmd/devvm the entry point: ui.Main makes the run’s UI and runs the root command with it, and it’s the only os.Exit internal/cli the command line. Each Cobra command has a file of its own, and its about holds its docs page, its help group and the reason it has no --json. The package also holds the run’s services (app.go), the argument and flag checks, whose failures are usage errors, help, --json, the CLI tests, docgen/, which writes the CLI reference, and doctor’s check of Linux’s pins (pins.go) internal/vm what each command does to a folder’s VM, below the command line: Env and its parts, the one start, the finder, the inventory, Launch, the agents’ store, logins and saves, Lifecycle and the one remake, Housekeeping, Settings, Net and Links, which its doc.go maps with their owners. A --clone VM’s copy is cloneseed.go’s: its in-VM scripts initRepos, seedStage and seedApply, sent through the backend’s Exec, with the shallow file read through internal/safefile and the pack made by internal/hostgit’s git. Its uncommitted changes are cloneworktree.go’s seedTree: the index read through internal/safefile and normalised by internal/hostgit’s git, hostgit.DiffFiles for what differs, and each working copy read through a safefile.Root, opening each folder from its parent with OpenDir, so no link on the way is followed, then the record of what went, which clonecheck.go reads back. An operation in progress, the info files and the stash are clonestate.go’s seedState, each file read through internal/safefile, and only the files its stateIDs lists are read for object ids. The settings and hooks are cloneconfig.go’s seedConfig, an allowlist of config keys whose URLs cleanURL takes the credentials out of, and a VM’s stash entry is saved by clonesave.go, without its untracked files. Tools.update is the step devvm tools update takes, which devvm update takes first, and filePorts works out a VM’s ports again from its devcontainer.json’s, with the rules of devvm ports add and devvm ports rm (reading the devcontainer.json again). vm.AgentImport reads each agent’s folder through that folder as an os.Root (links out of an agent’s folder). Launch.buildTools builds the tool images that a VM’s shared tools need and the share lacks, and retainTools is retention’s tools.unused-age. Inventory.GitKeeper names the VM that keeps a path locked, and cloneState is the script that reads a --clone VM’s state back, its stash entries included. A Git LFS object file is opened beneath the common dir through an os.Root, each folder on the way checked first, because an os.Root still follows a link that stays inside it. confinementFor chooses a start’s confinement from the tier, starter.start registers the interrupt’s cleanup around the backend’s Start, vm.Env.Terminal gives an agent’s login the terminal’s files (ui.Terminal), and AgentLogin.endLogin ends the login in the VM internal/shell quoting for a POSIX shell (Quote, QuoteJoin), a word on one line for bash (QuoteLine, ANSI-C quoting) and a shell variable’s names (EnvName), with the standard library alone internal/vmname the name of every machine devvm runs on a backend, VM, which a field or a parameter holds instead of a string, and the parsers that make one where it’s read. Parse reads a project VM’s name from an argument or a file name, and it also reads vm.json’s name and runs in project.Nth. ParseListed reads one that a backend lists. VM’s UnmarshalText reads one in a JSON file, which may be any machine’s, so a field that must hold a project VM’s is still checked with IsProject. Image names an image’s machine, and VM.Aside a remake’s old one. msg.M.VM reads back the VM a message’s function took. It also holds a project VM’s name grammar (Prefix, HashLen, IsVM, and VM’s IsProject, Hash, Slug, Short, ImageKey and a remake’s Aside), with the standard library alone, so the proxy uses it too (the checks on owners) internal/project a project folder: its VM’s name, the hash that names its VM’s state folder (project.Hash), its link targets, the folders that aren’t safe to use and its parents internal/gitprotect .git protection: one scan for each check, a Locker for each host, which is Flags on macOS, Binds on Linux, whose pins the start sets, or else Watch, and the table of its reports. A nested repo is left to another only when that repo’s scan locks its git folder whole (snapshot.covered). gitprotect.Protector.Check is the check of a stopped VM, and for a VM that devvm 0.1.0 or 0.1.1-rc.1 made strict, the converter’s unstrict then takes diff.ignoreSubmodules = all out of its repos’ configs, on a context that an interrupt doesn’t cancel (context.WithoutCancel), and strictLeft does the same for devvm git-protect on and off and devvm rm, without the warning. gitprotect.Keeps says whether another VM’s protection still covers a path. The configs it reads, the watch’s hashed files and git’s .git, commondir and gitdir files all go through internal/safefile (.git protection) internal/hostsafety the folder’s other checks on the host: one Walk once the VM is stopped, which skips .git and finds set-id files and nested repos (hostsafety.Walk, which only starter.walk calls), git’s own test for a bare repo’s shape (hostsafety.IsGitDir), doctor’s read of safe.bareRepository (hostsafety.BareExplicit), and an SSH origin internal/hostgit every git command devvm runs on the host, with no fsmonitor, hooks, filters or signing programs, ssh only, none of the environment’s GIT_* variables and no prompts, and with GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1 and GIT_GRAFT_FILE=/dev/null, so it sees a repo’s real history. hostgit.UserConfig reads one key of git’s global and system config by the files’ names, the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name included internal/sshconfig the ssh config that reaches running VMs by name, and its Include line in ~/.ssh/config internal/sshagent each VM’s choice of SSH agent, devvm’s own agent and its keys internal/build building and rebuilding images, and their records. build.Names checks an image name’s layers and refuses a shared tool’s name internal/image image keys and names, with no side effects, and the shared tools’ registry, SharedTools: one entry for each toolchain, with its members, its detection, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files (the structure test’s names), and whether it’s built for glibc alone (image.ToolDef.GlibcOnly) internal/fetch every HTTP client, with the standard library alone: NewClient, with a timeout and HTTPSOnly or SameScheme, Retry and Transient, ReadCapped, Get, Resolve, which finds where a HEAD’s redirects end, and Download, which checks the SHA-256 and caps the size. fetch.Client.Trust adds your CAs to a client’s roots, for the download of devvm’s own mise and an agent’s OAuth refresh internal/upgrade devvm upgrade: how this devvm was installed (Detect), the releases (Source, with the newest, Check for a notice, and Fetch, which checks minisign’s ED signature by the built-in key, then the SHA-256), the unpack, the link’s switch and its rollback, and Homebrew. upgradetest/, for tests only, has a TLS release server and a minisign signer internal/from --from: references, registry digests with an anonymous token, Docker’s IDs and the recorded digests internal/redact passwords out of logs, with the standard library alone, and Secret, the type of the values that let whoever holds them act as you or as a VM (Secrets in the code). String redacts the run log’s lines, taking out proxy keys and URL passwords. In redacts another program’s log as it grows, in place and keeping its length. It reads a line not yet ended again from its start when the line is within MatchMax of what an earlier look read, and otherwise from MatchMax back, starring what runs on to an @ there, and Look.Cut does the same after a rotation’s cut. Unended redacts a copy’s cut end internal/vmlog every log a VM can drive, except the proxy’s own. Limit is the rate and length of what a VM makes devvm’s background processes write. The port forwarder and the link session write through it, and the link session’s warnings take their turns from its Allow. Capped is a background process’s log, held to its cap as it appends, with Trim at its next start. KeepVM is what the VM’s proxy (through proxy.IO.KeepLogs) and a build run on the logs the backend writes as the VM runs (backend.Run.Logs), the serial consoles’ among them. It watches each log in a goroutine of its own, redacts what each one gained every second (redact.In), so a reboot in place can’t leave the proxy’s password there, and skips a log that hasn’t grown. Redact is Lima’s redaction at the end of a start. Each rotation copies the log’s end to its .1 file, redacting only what the last look didn’t reach and masking a secret cut at its end, and empties it with f.Truncate, counting a log by what it holds past the hole its writer left, as Lima’s programs write at their own offset. Every log is opened through safefile (Opts.Write), never through a link or waiting on a FIFO. The proxy, which imports only the standard library and a few of devvm’s leaves, rotates its own logs itself (proxy.rotating) internal/safefile every read of a file a VM can write or swap, with the standard library alone, so the proxy uses it too (the checks on owners). It refuses a file that isn’t regular with safefile.ErrNotRegular and one past its cap with safefile.ErrTooLong internal/landlock the proxy’s child’s confinement on Linux, with the standard library alone, behind its own build tags: Self, which confines every thread of the process to its folders with no_new_privs, Landlock and the hand-written seccomp filter (filter), checks that it holds, and returns what it got (Result), which the proxy’s confineSelf turns into its line in run/proxy.confined (proxy.Confinement) (the child’s sandbox). It makes each call on every thread through syscall.AllThreadsSyscall, which works only without cgo internal/devcontainer a project’s devcontainer.json, with no side effects: finding it, mapping it to a new VM’s plan, its refusals, and what devvm update’s second reading replaces (Reread): devcontainer.Reread drops the parts the file gave that it no longer calls for and adds the ones it now calls for internal/jsonc JSON with comments (jsonc.Strip), with the standard library alone internal/tools the shared tools: the lock, mise on the host, the daily check, the tool images’ builds and the share. Share.Build builds a VM’s tool images under the making lock, which tools.Making holds, and tools.HasBuilds refuses a glibc-only tool, such as pi, for a musl VM. ShareBusy says whether another devvm holds the share’s lock, so retention skips the tool images that day. Share.NoVM lists the current tool images that no VM’s state lists, and Versions.StaleMise the folders of mise’s other versions, which gc deletes. withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go adds each platform’s dotnet SDK archive to the lock (building tools) internal/netpolicy network policy: the choice of tier, learning the hosts a VM reached, RiskOf, the VM’s proxy and the self-check. netpolicy.Policies lists a VM’s policies for its tier, the built-in ones and yours, and netpolicy.PolicyWarnings warns of the lines that aren’t rules. netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare readies a VM’s proxy at each launch, its policy warnings and the CA bundle included, netpolicy.Proxy.PrepareRunning checks what could refuse a running VM’s new proxy before the old one stops, and netpolicy.Proxy.Refusal runs the company proxy’s check with the check of your CAs. The event log’s readers are netpolicy.Log.Blocks, which gives a quiet block no Allow, netpolicy.Log.Learned, with Learned.NoProxy for the hosts that only transparent mode reached and agentWord for a User-Agent’s first word, Log.Countable and netpolicy.Log.MarkLearning. netpolicy.Judge.Quiet keeps quiet hosts out of what devvm network lock offers, netpolicy.Tickable, with its list tickable, and netpolicy.RiskOf mark the hosts it offers, and quietMark and RuleFile.Quiet show the quiet lines in devvm network (network policy) internal/secrets tokens on the host and the VM’s bindings to them, and your own secrets (custom.go, with their checks, Yours and custom-secrets.json). secrets.BoundSecret records in a VM’s state the definition and hosts a secret of yours was bound with, and the store’s lookup (Store.Get, secrets.Store.Get) checks every binding against that record. secrets.Store.Save saves a secret, secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Login picks the one Claude Code login devvm keeps, and secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Sums gives that login’s checksums internal/trust your CAs in ~/.config/devvm/ca, read and checked, sent to VMs, the build VMs’ Trust scripts and the guest environment, and each VM’s own CA and its next one (InitCA, in vms//run/ca/). trust.Env holds the CAs’ variables that a build’s scripts and every project VM start with. trust.Read reads your CA folder, looking at each file with os.Lstat and following no link, trust.CAs.Host writes the bundle for the host’s mise on Linux, and trust.InitCA readies each VM’s CA and its next one internal/agents the coding agents’ registry, with the standard library alone: one Def for each agent, with its shared tool, settings, logins, history, guest environment, ways to log in and [pass-keys], which every list of the agents comes from. Code about one agent names it by its constant (the structure test’s names). agents.Def’s PassKeys says whether an agent’s keys are withheld by default, and agents.Providers lists the providers whose keys the proxy puts in internal/agentlogin agents’ login and settings files on the host: the VM’s copies with placeholders, the bindings, the values and the OAuth refresh (File, with a format for each kind of login), the shape of every placeholder (Placeholder), Redact, and Restore, which puts the store’s values back for a VM’s placeholders. The package agentlogin saves a captured login (agentlogin.File.Capture), refreshes and reads one (agentlogin.File.Get) and makes the VM’s copy (agentlogin.File.VMCopy), whose VMFile reports PassBound, the bound providers that [pass-keys] lists. agentlogin.Pick tells whose login a request is by its User-Agent, agentlogin.Endpoints lists every format’s endpoints, agentlogin.SetupToken recognises claude setup-token’s request, agentlogin.ClaudeOAuthBindings makes the Claude login’s bindings, agentlogin.OpencodeImport makes opencode’s import entries, and agentlogin.PiSettings drops the pi settings that would undo devvm’s. The formats’ field lists are codexKeep, claudeAccountKeep and cursorFormat, internal/agentlogin/logins.go holds opencodeVM and withheldEntry, and internal/agentlogin/pi.go holds pi’s format (agents’ logins and settings) internal/proxy the proxy, as its README.md describes. It runs as two processes, its broker, devvm _proxy (broker.go, process.go), and its child, devvm _proxy-child (child.go), which talk over a socketpair in the broker’s protocol (wire.go). The package also holds the relay of a VM’s SSH agent on paths.Dirs.AgentRelay (Config.Agent, agent.go), which is the only socket of an agent that a VM’s backend forwards. And it holds the one form of a host that every package judges and compares hosts in (Host, NormHost, HostOK), which the structure test holds every package to (the checks on owners). The desktop’s local proxy listens in the VM at proxy.LocalProxyAddr and proxy.LocalProxyPort (the local proxy). The package proxy reads policies in policy.go: proxy.ParsePolicy is the one parser of every policy file, which returns each line with its number and whether it’s a rule, proxy.ValidRule decides what’s a rule, proxy.BrokenDeny marks a broken ! line, and proxy.ReadPolicy reads a file through internal/safefile. readBuiltins keeps a built-in policy’s quiet lines (PolicyLine.Quiet), and loadPolicy drops any other file’s. proxy.NarrowRule writes a rule by method and path in its canonical form, in proxy.Methods’ order, and proxy.ExactRule the exact rule for one host and port. proxy.ReadAllowlist reads the allowlist tier’s policies, whose Allowlist.Allows, Allowlist.Denies and Allowlist.Quiet are the proxy’s own decisions. A decision reads the rules that cover a host and port in one read (policy.rulesFor, a hostRules), policy.all leaves the quiet rules out and policy.quiet matches them. hostRules.byRequest says when requests are judged one by one, by policy.judge, and hostRules.unjudgeable covers a request that names a method outside proxy.Methods. request.go judges each request in an intercepted tunnel (server.judgeRequest) with the one matcher of rules and bindings, proxy.match, which uses plainPath, proxy.PathOK and matchPath for paths and patterns, overrides and overrideLike for the methods a request names, and match.allows, match.denies and trimDots, and Go’s url.ParseQuery, whose ParseQuery reads a query differently from some servers (requests by method and path). In proxy.go, server.blocked marks a block’s event Quiet only for the reason notAllowed, blockPage writes the block page, and proxy.Public is the one judge of a public address. secrets.go holds the bindings file (proxy.BindingList.Encode), how a secret binding’s value goes in (Binding.secretValue) and a login binding’s (Binding.takes), and the refusals githubMinting and cursorMints. cursor.go holds Cursor’s routes and refusals (cursorRoutes, cursorPersists, cursorStore, cursorChanges) and the reply scanners (frameScanner, jwtScanner). upstream.go holds the route to a company proxy (proxy.Upstream.WithPassword, proxy.Upstream.Route), which a lookup’s context carries with proxy.WithRoute and gives back with proxy.RouteOf, and the CAs a lookup trusts (proxy.WithRoots, proxy.RootsOf). The config is proxy.Config, and proxy.Config.Sum tells devvm whether a running proxy must start again internal/seatbelt macOS’s sandbox as devvm uses it: sandbox-exec’s path (Exec), a Seatbelt string and a real path in a profile (String, Path), the links a sandboxed lookup goes through (Links), and the profile of a VM’s proxy’s child (ChildProfile), which Sandbox.ProxyChild gives the broker through proxy.IO.Seatbelt, because the proxy imports the standard library alone. Lima’s profile for its hostagent (lima/seatbelt.go) is written with the same strings and paths. How the child is confined, its report in run/proxy.confined (proxy.Confinement), the check that it holds (checkConfined) and the hook where a platform confines the child in the process (confineSelf) are internal/proxy’s confine.go, which every platform’s confinement shares internal/daemon devvm’s background processes, with the standard library alone: detached starts in a session of their own (daemon.Detach), pid files checked against the process’s arguments before any signal (daemon.Proc), stopping with TERM and then KILL, each sent to the process’s group (daemon.SignalGroup), readiness by a status file, the lifeline, and an accept loop’s wait after an error that leaves its listener open (AcceptRetry), which the port forwarder, the link session, a login’s forward, the proxy’s SSH agent relay and the desktop relay share. It’s the only place that signals a process by its pid. Processes has what each of those processes holds, reads, writes and is confined by internal/desktop devvm desktop’s relay on the host, which checks VNC’s password, then opens an ssh channel to the VM’s socket and drops the viewer’s clipboard, and the desktop’s passwords internal/backend Backend and its roles, Caps, Require, Check, the registry and its guard (As), as how a backend plugs in describes. Below it are backendtest/, the fake, registry/, which holds every backend, and lima/, whose pins.go has QEMU’s user and mount namespace on Linux, its pins, their events and the probe, while platform’s pinrun_linux.go is the namespace’s side. A build’s ImageSpec.Trust, a Trust, holds the Add and Remove scripts made from ca.sh and the Env each script gets, and a tools build runs ToolsSpec.Trust.Add alone. A backend runs Add before anything downloads and Remove once the scripts are done: Lima runs Add right after the start and Remove before the final sync, and a tools build needs no Remove. backend.NetProxy confines a VM to its proxy and backend.NetDirect puts it on its backend’s own network, Confinement.GuestProxy says whether the guest’s proxy settings name devvm’s proxy, and Lima’s clone sets the VM’s environment from VMSpec.Env (a company’s CA in builds) internal/vmssh devvm’s own use of a VM’s ssh, on every backend. Checked is the one way to a VM’s ssh (how a backend plugs in), and Forwards is the port forwarder’s one owner, which locks, stops and starts it with its ports from vm.json. The package also holds a login’s forward of this machine’s loopback ports, in devvm’s own process (ForwardLoopback), the links’ sessions, and each VM’s one record of its host keys for each start (PinHostKeys, in vms//run/known_hosts), which every ssh of devvm’s checks internal/ui the only package that prints: ui.UI, with messages, prompts, the status line, the run log and the cleanups, and ui.Main, which handles signals. It has no package state internal/msg, locales messages: en.toml, the generated functions, the doc links (docs.go), the generator (gen/), Reporter and Question (messages) internal/ports a VM’s ports section, with the forwards asked for and the host ports chosen, and the one allocator of host ports, under the claims lock, which puts VMs’ ssh only on the ports browsers refuse (SSHPorts) internal/paths every folder and file devvm uses, a VM’s in its folder (Dirs.VM, and a project VM’s folder, vms//, from Dirs.VMDir), and host paths resolved and compared (Physical, PhysicalParent, Within, Below, In and Under, where resolve.go says which one is for what). Among the locks, paths.Dirs.GitLock is the host’s lock of .git protection, taken before any VM’s own, and Dirs.MakingLock is the tool images’ making lock internal/state a VM’s state, vm.json, with its core fields and one section for each package, which changes only in VM.Update under the VM’s lock. It also owns the layout version (CheckLayout and migrations, while testdata/script/layout.txtar lists every file), every file written whole (WriteFile, WriteFileMode) and private folders (PrivateDir) internal/settings the defaults (Defaults, Read, Save), with your config.toml, read strictly, over devvm’s settings.json, and each value’s check (ParsePorts, ParseCPUs, ParseGiB and the retention settings). settings.CompanyProxy.Upstream checks the company proxy’s settings and its password, settings.CompanyProxy.Route is the route devvm’s own clients take through it, and settings.PassKeys is config.toml’s [pass-keys] internal/platform the code for each system, behind build tags, such as platform.SameFolder, which tells whether a project folder whose device number changed after a restart is still the VM’s (an existing VM), and platform.FoldsCase, whether the system’s file systems fold case internal/ubuntu finding Ubuntu’s cloud image and verifying it, without ever downloading one, the release pocket’s date (ubuntu.Released), and versions ordered as dpkg --compare-versions orders them (ubuntu.CompareVersions) internal/testbuild whether this is a test build, which ldflags set: only a test build reads the test overrides (cli’s readOverrides) assets the files devvm ships, embedded as assets.FS, which cli passes to constructors. base.yaml is base’s Lima template, and prelude.sh, with $devvm_arch, $devvm_libc and devvm_sha, comes first in each build script run with bash, the user’s layers included, and is put in place of a script’s #! line, as one eval line quoted by shell.QuoteLine, by image.WithPrelude, which image.OwnScript calls for devvm’s own. layers/ holds base’s scripts, its policy and Ubuntu’s signing keys, and the built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, each with its policy. network/ holds the network tiers’ own policies, features/ base’s optional features, and shared-tools/ its mise.toml, build.sh and *.policy files. guest/ holds the scripts in the VM that every launch sends, and the port forwarder’s ports.sh, and oci/ is --from’s conversion, as its README.md describes. So the How it works pages’ scripts are, in the repo, assets/base.yaml, assets/prelude.sh, assets/layers/apt.sh, whose first step is assets/layers/apt.sh begin, assets/layers/base.sh, assets/layers/.sh for each built-in layer, which are assets/layers/desktop.sh, assets/layers/docker.sh and assets/layers/nix.sh, with assets/layers/desktop.policy, assets/layers/docker.policy and assets/layers/nix.policy, Ubuntu’s keys, assets/layers/ubuntu-cloud.gpg and assets/layers/ubuntu-archive.gpg, base’s features, assets/features/.sh, the shared tools’ assets/shared-tools/mise.toml and assets/shared-tools/build.sh, the conversion’s assets/oci/build.sh and assets/oci/bootify.sh, and the CA script, assets/guest/ca.sh, which assets/guest/ca.sh DIR runs to install the CAs in a VM. The built-in policies are paths in assets/ (images) internal/structure the structure test, for tests only, and owners_doc_test.go, which writes the checks on owners internal/stubtest the test stubs, for tests only internal/leaktest the goroutine leak checks, Main for a package’s TestMain and Check for one test, for tests only, and the standard library only, so the proxy’s tests use it too internal/memnet the network in memory for tests in a synctest bubble: connections (Pipe) that close their writing side alone, hold a buffer’s worth and have deadlines, and listeners by address (Network), for tests only, and the standard library only, so the proxy’s tests use it too testdata the CLI tests (script/*.txtar), the golden fixtures (golden//), a lock to test with (mise.lock), each package’s coverage baseline on each system (coverage/.txt), each release’s state fixture (v//), and the lines that break each forbidigo rule (lint/, Go lint rules) tests/e2e, tests/e2e-mise.lock the end-to-end tests on real VMs, in Go with the tag e2e and a file for each section. TestE2E is the run, sandbox_test.go has the sandbox, its slot’s paths and lock and e2eUbuntuRelease, and slots_test.go runs the slots. The lock file holds the shared tools’ versions that every section but tools uses (scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools) scripts, packaging, .goreleaser.yaml, VERSION, CHANGELOG.md bump.sh updates the pins. release.sh runs the signed tag’s checks around GoReleaser, then minisign, and publish.sh makes the release itself, with its checks, release.sh, one yes, then the pushes, gh release and the tap. The test and coverage tasks run test.sh, which runs coverage.sh to check each package’s coverage against its baseline. packaging/ holds the Homebrew formula and key.go, which embeds its folder, so devvm upgrade’s key is minisign.pub’s, and a build without that file has none. Only the scripts read VERSION (releasing) install.sh curl | bash: it installs the host’s archive, with the binary, the README, the changelog and the license, checked, into ~/.local/lib/devvm/, then runs doctor’s fixes, asking first. Tests source it (DEVVM_INSTALL_TEST)
data.the-structure-test#The structure test:
internal/structure parses every Go file in the repo, tests and every platform’s included, generated files left out, and checks what linters don’t. mise run test runs it. Each failure starts with its rule and the file and line:
Rule Checks max-methods no type has more than 24 methods, value and pointer receivers together, and no interface declares more than 24, not counting the interfaces it embeds; a larger one splits by what its methods do no-init no func init() package-vars a package-level var is a blank interface check, an Err*/err* sentinel from errors.New or fmt.Errorf, a regexp.MustCompile, template.Must or sync.Once* result, a //go:embed file, or listed in allowedVars; anything else becomes a field, a const or a local layers which packages import which, in non-test files (tests may wire packages together) owners in non-test files, only its owner runs a host command that commands lists, only the files execSites lists make a host command, only guardOwner asserts a backend package’s type, only envOwner reads a DEVVM_ variable, but the settings envSettings lists, only its file in envOwners reads HOME, only its owner’s string literals hold a text that literals lists, only its owner’s string literals are, whole, a name that names lists, only its owner’s calls to package strings split or join on a separator that separators lists, only pathsOwner builds a path in devvm’s data or config folder, and only its file in callers calls a function that callers lists (details) goroutines in non-test files, a function that starts a goroutine, with a go statement, a wait group’s Go or time’s or context’s AfterFunc, is in goroutineSites, with what waits for its goroutines to end, or detached: and why nothing does, and a package that starts one calls leaktest.Main in its tests’ TestMain dropped-errors in non-test files, no function assigns a Wait’s error, or a strconv parse’s, to _, such as _ = cmd.Wait() or n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s), unless droppedErrors lists it with why, because a failed wait would read as a clean exit and text that isn’t a number as 0 read-limits in non-test files, every io.ReadAll reads through an io.LimitReader made in its call, such as io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, limit+1)), unless unboundedReads lists its function with why, so a peer or a file that never ends can’t fill the memory folder-ids in non-test files outside internal/platform, no function compares a folder’s identity or its volume with == or !=, except with "", switches on one, passes one to strings.EqualFold, strings.Compare, slices.Contains or slices.Index, or keys a map by one, whether indexed or in a map’s literal, with its type written out or as a named map type of the module’s. A folder’s identity is a field named Folder or GitID, a call of a state’s Folder or FolderVolume, a call of FolderID, folderID or FolderDevice, or a name in the same function that one of those, or such a name, was assigned to. A function passes when exactFolderIDs lists it with why. The rule is there because a boot can number an unchanged folder’s device anew, which only platform.SameFolder and platform.SameOpenFolder allow for status-lines in non-test files outside the folders statusFree lists, a function that does slow work shows a status line itself, with a Reporter’s Status, a LoggedCmd step or its Runner’s Run, unless statusSites lists it with why, so the user sees what devvm waits for (status lines). Slow work is making a host command with exec.Command or exec.CommandContext, running host git through internal/hostgit, walking a folder with fs.WalkDir, filepath.Walk, filepath.WalkDir, hostsafety.Walk or safefile.Walk, looking up a volume with platform.VolumeUUID, making a request with internal/fetch’s Open, Resolve, Get or Download, waiting for a lock with platform.LockFile, LockFileShared or LockDir whose waiting is nil or platform.NoWait, or running a backend’s command outside a step with its Runner’s Output or Attach The layers:
Only cmd/devvm and internal/cli import internal/ui; only internal/cli imports internal/vm; only cmd/devvm imports internal/cli. internal/backend/... imports none of internal/vm, build, tools, netpolicy, secrets, project, gitprotect, sshconfig, sshagent, trust or vmssh, so the port forwarder and the link sessions stay devvm’s on every backend. Only internal/backend/registry and internal/cli import a backend (lima); only tests import backendtest, internal/leaktest, internal/memnet, and internal/stubtest and the packages below it, which import only internal/msg and each other. The stubs’ binary, internal/stubtest/stub, and its state, internal/stubtest/stubstate, import nothing else of devvm’s, because the binary stands in for the tools devvm runs and is built apart from it. internal/proxy imports no other devvm package except internal/daemon, internal/landlock, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/vmname. assets, locales, internal/platform, internal/msg/gen, internal/testbuild, internal/hostgit, internal/shell, internal/vmname, internal/daemon, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/redact, internal/agents, internal/safefile, internal/landlock, internal/leaktest and internal/memnet import no devvm package; internal/agentlogin only internal/agents, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/platform, internal/proxy, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/state, because it holds agents’ logins; internal/msg only locales and internal/vmname; internal/paths only internal/msg and internal/vmname; internal/state only internal/msg, internal/paths, internal/platform and internal/vmname; internal/image only assets, internal/agents, internal/msg, internal/paths and internal/shell; internal/devcontainer only internal/image, internal/jsonc, internal/msg and internal/shell. Everything it holds the code to is in devvm() in internal/structure/structure_test.go:
largeTypes lists the types allowed more methods, which are paths.Dirs and ui.UI, each with its count as its maximum and why. A backend isn’t one of them, because its methods are split by backend.Backend’s roles (how a backend plugs in). One that grows fails; one that shrinks fails until its maximum is lowered. allowedVars lists the other package-level vars, by package folder and name, each with why: values set by -ldflags, fixed tables, test fixtures. An entry whose var is gone fails. layers is the layering table: a layer’s packages (from, but not exceptFrom) import none of to (but exceptTo); x/... is x and the packages below it. commands maps a host command to the one package that runs it. execSites lists the files that make a host command with exec.Command or exec.CommandContext, each with why, and a listed file that no longer makes one fails. guardOwner names internal/backend/guard.go, the one file that asserts a backend’s type. envOwner names the one file that reads devvm’s DEVVM_ variables. envSettings lists the variables read elsewhere, each with the files that read it and why. A listed file that no longer reads its variable fails. envOwners maps another variable to the one file that reads it, which for HOME is internal/paths/dirs.go. literals maps a text that only one package’s string literals may hold to that package and what the others use instead. names maps a name that only one package’s string literals may be, whole, to that package and what the others use, and namesFree lists the folders whose literals may be one anyway: internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for. goroutineSites lists every function outside tests that starts a goroutine, as its file and its name (internal/proxy/splice.go: splice, or Type.Method for a method). A function literal’s goroutine counts in the function it’s in, or in the package-level var whose value it is. A goroutine starts with a go statement, a wait group’s Go, or time’s or context’s AfterFunc, whose function runs in a goroutine of its own. Goroutines that the standard library starts otherwise, such as an HTTP server’s for each connection, are for the leak checks to find, not the registry. Each entry says what waits for the goroutines to end, such as scanAll's wg.Wait, or starts with detached: and says why nothing does and what ends them anyway, such as a look at a folder whose disk may hang, which folderWithin leaves to finish on its own. A new goroutine fails until its function is listed, and a listed function that no longer starts one fails, so the list stays current. A package that starts a goroutine also fails until a test file of its calls leaktest.Main. The tests’ own goroutines are the leak checks’. droppedErrors lists the functions outside tests that assign a Wait’s or a strconv parse’s error to _, each named as in goroutineSites and with why, and none does today. The check reads no types, so a call of any method named Wait counts, and the parses are Atoi, the Parse functions, Unquote, UnquoteChar and QuotedPrefix. A listed function that no longer drops one fails, so the list stays current. unboundedReads lists the functions outside tests whose io.ReadAll reads with no limit, in the same way, each with why its reader ends: the status line’s look at the end of the run’s own log, which only that run writes, and the test stubs’ reads of the standard input that devvm under test writes and closes. A reader limited before the call, held in a variable, counts as unlimited, so the limit goes in the call itself. A listed function that no longer reads with no limit fails. exactFolderIDs lists the functions outside tests and internal/platform that compare a field named Folder or GitID with == or !=, in the same way, each with why: the agents’ and exports’ fields of that name, which are paths, recordMove’s check that the state is as it was read, and folderChanged, which runs after a start recorded the folder’s identity as it is now. The check reads no types, so any field by those names counts. A listed function that no longer compares one fails. statusSites lists the functions outside tests that do slow work and show no status line of their own, in the same way, each with why: the status line of the caller it runs under, named by its message, such as checking_vm for a launch’s checks of the project folder, work that takes the terminal, such as ssh-add asking for a passphrase, a process with no UI, such as a forwarder or a link session, or a command made for its caller to run. statusFree lists the folders whose code shows none, each with why: internal/ui, which draws the status line, the proxy’s and devvm’s background processes, internal/hostgit and internal/fetch, whose callers’ functions are the sites, and the tests’ stubs. The check reads no types, so it doesn’t see a backend’s methods, such as Exec, which TestLaunchStatusLines checks for a launch, and a caller’s status line is only named, so a reviewer checks that it covers the call. A listed function that no longer does slow work without one fails. callers maps a function to the one file outside its package that calls it, and a listed file that no longer calls it fails. A method is listed as pkg.Type.Name, such as internal/paths.Dirs.AgentSettings, and any call of a method by that name outside its package counts, because the check reads no types, so a listed method’s name is its type’s alone. TestRulesFail breaks each rule, and each layer, on small sources and checks the failure names it.
Shell scripts that live in Go strings get shellcheck too, since lint’s shellcheck only finds files with a shebang. TestEmbeddedScripts in internal/structure finds every call site that runs a script as sh -c, /bin/sh -c or bash -c (or -lc), in a []string literal or a call’s arguments, outside tests and the stubs. When the script is a constant, a literal, or a sum of them, such as seedApply with seedMarker in it, the test writes it to a file and runs shellcheck -s sh or -s bash, as its shell reads it, at -S warning, skipping when shellcheck isn’t installed. A script built at run time can’t be read there, so the test fails on one until dynamicScripts lists its file and expression with why: a fixed command around quoted paths, a devcontainer’s own command, or a builder that a test of its package checks, as internal/vm’s TestBuiltScriptsShellcheck does for the scripts built from the agents’ registry. A listed site that’s gone fails too, so the list stays current. A shell given any other flag, such as sh -ec or sh -e -c, fails as well, because the test would miss its script: put options such as set -e in the script instead. -s, for a script on standard input, is fine.
data.the-support-window#The support window: An upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 works until 1.0. When a release leaves the window, its fixture and the code that only its state needs, such as a reader of a field that only that release wrote, go together, in one commit that says which release left and why. The commit deletes testdata/v/, its scripts and its entries in the tables above.
data.the-tests-on-every-fixture#The tests on:
The unit tests read every fixture’s files with today’s readers. stateFixtures in internal/vm/fixture_test.go lists each release’s expectations: its VMs, the version of their vm.json, its layout version, its clones of one repo, and functions that check its VMs, its defaults and its agent store. 0.1.0’s entry is v010Fixture in fixture_v010_test.go. TestFixtureVMStates, TestFixtureVMsRead, TestFixtureSettings, TestFixtureAgentStore and TestFixtureClonesReadAsOneRepo run once for each release and system, and they check that each field the release wrote reads and writes back unchanged. TestStateFixturesListed fails when a folder in testdata has no entry, or an entry has no folder. Two packages keep a table of their own for what only they read. In internal/proxy, fixtureBinaries records the SHA-256 of the binary that made each release’s state, which its proxy configs name, and TestFixtureBindings and TestFixtureProxyConfig read every release’s bindings files and proxy configs. In internal/secrets, storeFixtures names a secret that each release’s store on Linux keeps as a file, which TestFixtureStoreGet reads through a VM’s binding. TestV010Rules is a copy of 0.1.0’s own tests of the proxy’s rules, kept apart from today’s.
The CLI tests run today’s commands on each fixture. A release’s scripts are in testdata/script/, named fixture_v and the release’s version without its dots, such as fixture_v010.txtar, fixture_v010_clone.txtar and fixture_v010_network.txtar for 0.1.0. Each one puts the state into a sandbox with fixture v, which moves it to the sandbox’s folder: the folder’s path, each VM’s name hash, its folder’s and .git’s identities and its backend’s place become what they are there, each host port, and each port that a VM or the defaults forward, becomes one of the sandbox’s own that nothing on this host listens on, and nothing else changes. The ports change because a launch that finds a VM’s port taken, by a program of yours or by another run of the tests, rightly chooses another one and edits the VM’s Lima config. It also warns that it can’t forward a port that a program has, such as a web server of yours on 3000. A script names a forwarded port by what it was, as $FIXTURE_PORT_3000. The script then runs today’s devvm on it. Each --json must have everything the release’s had (json_superset), the read-only commands must change no file, and a launch must start each VM as it is, without a Lima edit. The scripts stay separate for each release, because their checks name that release’s VMs and what each one has, and TestFixtureScripts in internal/cli fails when a fixture has no script or a script names a fixture that isn’t there.
data.what-a-fixture-holds#What a fixture hold:
A release’s fixture is the folder testdata/v/. Its darwin/ folder holds the state that the release left on a Mac, and its linux/ folder the state it left on Linux. For 0.1.0, that’s four VMs’ states, its defaults, its agent store and logins, the stubs’ record of the VMs, and what its --json printed for them, and the folder’s README.md lists what each VM has. The release made these files itself. Its generate.sh checks out the release’s tag in a temporary folder and runs generate.txtar with that version’s own CLI test harness, then copies what the run left, with each file’s mode in modes, because git doesn’t keep modes.
A fixture is frozen. It’s generated once, from the release’s own binary, and never edited or generated again, so never run its generate.sh from a newer devvm and never change its files. A release whose state is the same as the one before it adds no fixture, and neither does a release candidate, such as 0.1.1-rc.1, because only a final release that changes the state gets one.

data: For contributors. The everyday tests, CLI tests and end-to-end tests are in Contributing, and how to raise a package’s coverage baseline is in Coverage; this page is about running them on a host other than your Mac.
data.a-host-of-any-size#A host of any size:
devvm reads this machine’s CPUs, its memory and the free space on its disks when it fits base to the host, checks a size you give it, checks free space before a build or a new VM, and warns in devvm doctor. All of these reads go through platform.Host, so the CLI tests can stand in for a host of any size and pass the same way on a large Mac and on a small CI runner. In a test build, three environment variables replace what platform.Host reads:
Variable Replaces DEVVM_TEST_CPUS the number of CPUs DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB the memory, in GiB DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB the free space in GiB, on every disk Only a test build reads them, and a release ignores all three, so no variable can make devvm see more free space or more memory than this machine has. Each one that isn’t set leaves the machine’s own value. internal/cli/script_test.go sets a large host in every script: 8 CPUs, 16 GiB of memory and 500 GiB free, which is more than base asks for and more than any build checks for. A script that tests a small host sets its own values with env, as small_host.txtar does with 2 CPUs, 7 GiB and 1 GiB free:
env DEVVM_TEST_CPUS=2 env DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB=7 ! exec devvm size -g --cpus 3 stderr '^devvm: too_many_cpus have=2 want=3$' To go back to the large host later in the same script, set the large values again, because an empty value leaves the machine’s own. The fake host covers only size and free space. What differs between operating systems, such as Lima’s disk floors on Linux, ports already in use, Docker on PATH, or tmpfs and 9p mounts, still differs, and the Linux CI job is what catches it.
data.adding-a-section#Adding a section:
Each section is a file of its own in tests/e2e, such as gc_test.go, so sections can change at the same time without touching each other’s files. A new check goes in its section’s function, where its setup steps run, because a check’s time counts from the end of the one before it. To add a section:
Write Section(s *S) in tests/e2e/ _test.go. Add it to sections (tests/e2e/sections_test.go), in the order the run runs it, with a guess of its time for --slots to place it before it has run, and the host commands it needs beyond limactl and pkill, each with what installs it. Run it with mise run e2e -- --only on a Mac and on a Linux host, and check that each check passes. A helper that more than one section needs goes in the harness’s files, beside those above, so that every section shares one copy, and a fixture that two sections share, such as an image, stays in the sandbox’s cache. These are the ones the sections share so far, each with what it does in a shell’s terms:
