data.any-time-zone#Any time zone:
The tests pass in any time zone and on any date, because a test that compares times counts them from an instant it parsed or fixed, or works in UTC, and never sets time.Local. A testscript that needs an old file uses a date far in the past, such as touch -t 202001010000, and one that needs a file that stays new uses a date far in the future, such as an export named 20991231-235959, so the scripts keep passing as the calendar moves on. CI runs mise run test on macOS in UTC and on Linux with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, which has daylight saving time, so a test that only passes in one zone fails in CI and not only on a laptop. To check a change the same way, run the tests with another zone, including one with an odd offset or a half-hour DST change:
TZ=America/Los_Angeles mise run test TZ=Pacific/Chatham mise run test TZ=Australia/Lord_Howe mise run test
data.end-to-end-tests-in-go#End-to-end tests: The end-to-end tests are in Go, in tests/e2e, a file for each section. That package builds only with the e2e build tag, and its TestE2E is the run.
data.fuzzing#Fuzzing:
devvm’s fuzz targets use Go’s built-in fuzzing, and each one checks a property of what it fuzzes, not only that nothing panics. go test runs only each target’s seed inputs, the ones its f.Add lines give and the files in its package’s testdata/fuzz// folder, so every run of the tests checks them. To fuzz one target on your machine, or to run one failing input again:
go test -run '^$' -fuzz '^FuzzNoProxy$' -fuzztime 2m ./internal/proxy # fuzz one target for two minutes go test -run '^$' -fuzz '^FuzzNoProxy$' -parallel 2 ./internal/proxy # with two workers, on a busy machine go test -run '^$' -fuzz '^FuzzUnpack$' -fuzzminimizetime 1000x ./internal/upgrade # minimizing each new input in 1,000 runs go test -run '^FuzzNoProxy/e9e4d242dc7b413a$' ./internal/proxy # one input in testdata/fuzz/FuzzNoProxy/ When a target fails, go test writes the input that broke it to the package’s testdata/fuzz// folder. Fix the code, add a test of the fix beside the code’s other tests, and commit the input with them, because go test then runs it as a seed every time.
data.golden-fixtures#Golden fixtures:
The golden fixtures are what the real tools printed, kept in testdata/golden/darwin/ and testdata/golden/linux/, so the tests can check both devvm’s parsers and the stubs against real output on any machine. Each system’s folder holds what its tools printed there:
Fixture The real output of Captured from limactl-version.txt limactl --version TestLimactlStubContract’s run on real Lima limactl-list-stopped.json limactl list --json the contract test’s dummy instances, after the step that leaves the most limactl-list-running.json limactl list --json of a running VM the project section’s first VM qemu-img-info.json qemu-img info -U --output=json of base’s disk the images section, on Linux qemu-img-info-overlay.json the same, of a project VM’s overlay disk the project section, on Linux security-missing.txt security find-generic-password for an item that isn’t there, and its exit status the images section, on macOS tmutil-isexcluded.txt tmutil isexcluded the images section, on macOS mise run e2e -- --golden captures them on a real machine, into the checkout, and you commit what changed. It runs the contract test with STUB_GOLDEN set to the system’s folder for the dummy instances’ fixtures, and runs the other commands itself, so a run needs the images section, and the project section for a running VM. Each fixture has this machine’s home folder replaced with /home/me, the user’s name with me, and the user’s full name, the timezone and a VM’s environment made up, so it holds nothing of yours. A capture isn’t a check, so a run with --golden runs as many checks as one without, and a capture that fails says so and keeps the fixture it had. Run it on a Mac and on a Linux host after Lima or QEMU changes what it prints.
TestGoldenLimactlVersion, TestGoldenLimactlList and TestGoldenQemuImgInfo in internal/backend/lima/golden_test.go read every system’s fixtures with devvm’s own parsers, so a change in what the tools print that devvm would misread fails them on any machine. Each also runs the stub and checks that its output has the same form, or the same shape for JSON: every field the stub prints is one that the real tool prints, with a value of the same kind. For limactl list --json, the stub’s output is its listing after the contract test’s scenario. TestGoldenSecurityTmutil in internal/platform checks the stub’s security and tmutil against macOS’s fixtures the same way, on macOS.
data.linux-hosts#Linux hosts:
Test in a Lima VM with nested virtualization, which needs an M3 or newer and macOS 15 or newer. Give it a Lima home of its own, so its VMs stay apart from yours:
Make it from Lima’s Ubuntu template, with nested virtualization, room for nested VMs, its user at uid 1000, and only the repo mounted, read-only:
REPO=$(pwd) && cd /tmp export LIMA_HOME=~/.lt-linux-go limactl create --name=linuxhost --tty=false --vm-type=vz --cpus=8 --memory=16 --disk=150 \ --containerd=none --set '.nestedVirtualization=true | .user.uid=1000' --mount "$REPO" template:ubuntu-24.04 limactl edit --tty=false --set '.mounts=[{"location":"'"$REPO"'","writable":false}]' linuxhost limactl start --tty=false linuxhost Run it from the main checkout of the repo, which the VM mounts at the same path, and not from a git worktree. A worktree’s .git is a file that points into the main checkout’s .git folder, outside the mount, so git in the VM can’t read it, and the VM’s only mount goes when the worktree does. --mount alone keeps the template’s home mount, hence the edit. Lima gives the VM’s user your Mac’s uid unless user.uid sets another, and a Mac’s first user has uid 501. Most Linux hosts’ first user has uid 1000, and so does the user that some container images ship, such as the ubuntu user of Ubuntu’s images. With the VM’s user at uid 1000, the end-to-end tests’ from section meets that clash, as devvm does on most Linux hosts.
Inside it, install the packages, then Lima and mise from their release tarballs, each checked against its release’s checksums (SHA256SUMS, SHASUMS256.txt) with sha256sum -c, and add yourself to the kvm group:
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils qemu-efi-aarch64 virtiofsd build-essential git curl jq rsync sudo usermod -aG kvm "$USER" Then restart the VM, so a fresh login has the group.
Copy the repo into the VM’s home, so the read-only mount stays untouched, install the pinned tools and run the gate, then the end-to-end tests:
rsync -a --delete /path/to/your/checkout/ ~/devvm/ && cd ~/devvm mise trust && mise install mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test mise run e2e -- --from The copy keeps the checkout’s .git folder, which the gate needs, because mise run lint finds the shell scripts it checks with git ls-files, and the docs’ build reads each page’s git information (enableGitInfo). A copy without .git, such as one that git archive makes, fails the lint. To test a branch that a worktree has checked out, commit it, and clone that branch from the main checkout instead of copying the checkout, because a worktree’s branches are the main checkout’s too:
rm -rf ~/devvm && git clone --branch BRANCH /path/to/your/checkout ~/devvm && cd ~/devvm A clone has only what’s committed, so commit a change before you test it this way.
The first --from run builds every image and takes about half an hour on an M3 Max. Later ones reuse them, because every section but tools uses the pinned shared tools’ versions and --from images, and those images stay valid until scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools or scripts/bump.sh e2e-from moves a pin (end-to-end tests). Stop the VM when done (limactl stop linuxhost); it keeps its images for the next run.
Gotchas of this setup:
The Linux host’s home and its VMs’ homes are both /home/.guest, so a file under $HOME in a VM isn’t proof of a mount: the end-to-end tests check the VM’s mounts list instead. A VM booting while another one works boots degraded and its downloads time out: the end-to-end tests stop a VM it’s done with before starting the next. minisign, for signing releases, has no linux/arm64 build, so mise skips it there.
data.manual-checks#Manual checks:
What the end-to-end tests leave out, as it would change something of yours or needs something it doesn’t have:
Screen Sharing on devvm desktop: e2e speaks VNC itself (TestE2EDesktop), because it can’t drive a window. In a VM made with --layers desktop, run devvm desktop. Screen Sharing opens and asks for the password devvm shows, and the Xfce desktop answers the mouse and keys. A wrong password gets refused. With Edit > Use Shared Clipboard on, text you copy on this machine doesn’t paste in the VM, and with devvm desktop --clipboard it does. ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/ has no line saying the relay doesn’t know a message (which the relay doesn't know).
A VM’s clock after this machine sleeps: e2e can’t sleep a Mac, and hosted CI can’t either. With an open VM and an allowlist VM running, compare each VM’s date +%s.%N over ssh with this machine’s clock, halfway through the ssh round trip. Then sleep the Mac for over 30 minutes and compare again right after it wakes and 2 minutes later. Each VM stays within about 0.1 s of this machine, the same as before the sleep, and the clock catches up without NTP: chrony in the allowlist VM has never synced, yet it stays right, while chrony in each VM logs Forward time jump detected! after the wake. Before you sleep the Mac, check that pmset -g assertions shows PreventSystemSleep 0. An app running caffeinate -s on AC power turns a sleep into a dark wake where the CPU keeps running, so the VMs never pause and the check proves nothing. In a real sleep, a measurement you run every few minutes in the background leaves a gap.
workerd under wrangler dev, without proxy settings: e2e stands in for it with curl and a static Go client, because npm’s download of workerd would make the run depend on it. In a node VM on the allowlist tier with devvm network allow api.open-meteo.com, make a Worker whose fetch handler returns fetch("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=0&longitude=0¤t=temperature_2m"), then run npx wrangler dev and curl localhost:8787 in the VM. It answers with the forecast, and devvm network log has api.open-meteo.com:443 without proxy settings. With the host taken out of the rules, the Worker’s fetch fails with the proxy’s 403 or a certificate error, as workerd may not trust the VM’s CA, and the log has the block. With devvm network transparent off and a launch, the fetch fails at once, and wrangler dev’s output has Temporary failure in name resolution. Run it from a folder in the VM’s home, such as a copy in ~/wk, because workerd’s SQLite fails with SQLITE_IOERR_SHMMAP in the project folder on a Linux host’s 9p mount.
--from an image only Docker has (built locally, never pushed): it would build an image in your Docker. Build a small one (docker build -t devvm-local-test . from a Dockerfile with FROM alpine:3), run devvm --from devvm-local-test in a new folder, check the VM boots from it, then devvm rm and docker image rm devvm-local-test.
data.running-the-runner#Running the runner:
mise run e2e runs TestE2E from tests/e2e, with the run’s flags after --. You can also run go test yourself from that folder:
mise run e2e -- --only gc cd tests/e2e && CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -tags e2e -count=1 -timeout 0 -run '^TestE2E$' -args --only gc Run go test from tests/e2e without naming a package, because only then does go test show the run’s lines as they come, and in a package list it holds them until the package ends. TestE2E refuses any -timeout but 0, because go test’s default of 10 minutes would end a long section in the middle of a check, and -count=1 keeps go test from showing a cached result. The run’s flags, which Contributing lists, come after -args. --reuse keeps the VMs that a section makes with Reuse for the next run, which takes each one as it finds it when it’s still running, so iterating on one check doesn’t launch its VM again.
The runner uses a sandbox for each slot, with its own fixed ports, it refuses your real Lima home, and it builds devvm from the checkout into src-go in the sandbox’s state folder, as a test build with its files embedded. It writes a config.toml that chooses base’s features, so nothing asks, and puts the pinned tool lock in place, after checking the lock’s first line. Base starts from the dated Ubuntu release in e2eUbuntuRelease (tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go), which scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves. The runner takes the slot’s lock, a symlink to its pid, and it deletes only the VMs, files and project folders that it made, which include any VM whose folder is in one of the run’s project folders, even one that a failed check made without registering it. Before the first section, it stops with a setup failure when the slot’s Lima home has a project VM that an earlier run left, unless --reuse keeps them, and it prints the commands that delete each one and its state folder. Before anything else, it names each host command that the chosen sections need and this machine lacks, with what installs it. Its lines are each section’s == name heading, then PASS, FAIL, SKIP or RETRY with [n/N], the check’s title, its time, the run’s time and the time left. A heartbeat every minute shows the newest line of the check’s output or devvm’s run log, and the run ends with a summary line. It keeps each section’s times in slot 0’s timings folder, under its tier, and beside them a checksum of tests/e2e’s Go files, so a section’s check count is compared only with a run of the same Go files. With --slots, it plans, seeds and runs the slots, each slot a run of the same test binary, and it adds up their results. On macOS it seeds each slot with APFS clones (clonefile), and on Linux with reflinks. With --newest-base, its last lines name the release Ubuntu lists as its newest and the one devvm pinned, and a failure is named as upstream drift.
Each check’s time limit is three times its longest time in its section’s last complete run, and the steps between two checks get an hour. Each command a check runs is in a process group of its own, and when the check’s time runs out, the group gets TERM, then KILL 30 seconds later. The check then fails with the heartbeat’s last line, and the run goes on to the next check. The runner’s own tests, the TestHarness tests, need no VM, and mise run test runs them with the e2e tag.
data.slots-for-each-host#Slots for each host:
mise run e2e -- --slots N runs the end-to-end sections in N sandboxes at once (slots), and each slot runs its own VMs, up to three at a time in the link section. How many slots a host can run depends on its cores and memory:
Host Slots A bare-metal Linux host with 32 cores and 124 GB of memory 3 or 4 A Mac 2 A Linux host nested in a VM, such as the Linux host above 1, the default: a VM booting while another one works boots degraded there A Mac clones the images it gives each slot, because /tmp and your home folder are on the same APFS volume. A Linux host reflinks the Lima instances in your home folder when its file system can, as XFS made with reflink=1 and Btrfs can, but a /tmp on tmpfs can’t reflink, so there each slot other than slot 0 builds its own tool images. Every slot keeps its images between runs, so only its first run builds them.
data.test-builds#Test builds:
The tests run a test build of devvm, which is one made with -ldflags "-X github.com/devvmhq/devvm/internal/testbuild.testBuild=yes", as the end-to-end tests and the CLI tests make theirs. Only a test build reads the environment variables that stand in for what devvm would find on this machine. Releases (GoReleaser, the Homebrew formula) don’t set the flag, so a release ignores every one of these variables, whatever its environment says. devvm reads them in one place, readOverrides in internal/cli/overrides.go, into an Overrides struct, and passes each one to the package that uses it:
Variable Stands in for DEVVM_HOST_MISE devvm’s pinned and checked mise on the host DEVVM_KVM Linux’s /dev/kvm DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/resolute, where devvm finds Ubuntu’s dated releases DEVVM_UBUNTU_RELEASE the newest dated release, which devvm pins base to: the end-to-end tests pin their own, e2eUbuntuRelease, so its images stay cached between runs, and devvm checks it as it does the newest DEVVM_UNREVIEWED the refusal of unreviewed emulations (unreviewed emulations) DEVVM_SSH_PORTS the 17 ports every browser refuses, which VMs’ ssh comes from (ports.SSHPorts). It’s a comma-separated list of the CLI test sandbox’s own ports, so sandboxes running at once never share them DEVVM_TEST_CPUS, DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_LIST_TIMEOUT this machine’s size and how long devvm waits for a backend’s listings (a host of any size) DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS a terminal to answer questions in: with 1, each question reads its answer as a line of input that isn’t a terminal, without its prompt, where devvm would refuse it DEVVM_VOLUME the volume of every folder, such as uuid:…, in place of diskutil’s on macOS and the file system’s ID on Linux, as devvm records and matches it when it makes, launches, adopts, moves, deletes or lists a VM, so a script needn’t depend on the real one, and fail makes each lookup fail DEVVM_HISTORY_MAX the 2 GiB that an export of agents’ history holds at most, in bytes, so a script whose VM writes an export without end reaches the cap at once DEVVM_CLIP_TOOLS where devvm paste finds the clipboard tools: macOS’s /usr/bin/osascript and /usr/bin/pbcopy, and wl-paste, wl-copy and xclip in Linux’s system folders, so the tests’ stand-ins run in their place DEVVM_PASTE_WAIT how long devvm paste waits for its script in the VM, in seconds, in place of 10 minutes for a write and 2 for a count or a delete, so a script whose VM never answers reaches the limit at once The settings that the environment table lists, such as DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, are yours to set, so every build reads them.
data.tests-on-real-lima#Tests on real Lima:
Most Go tests run the limactl stub, which can’t tell whether real Lima accepts what devvm gives it. The tests in internal/backend/lima/real_test.go run the real limactl instead, on dummy instances, as Lima’s own tests do. A dummy instance’s image is a small local file, so it can’t boot, but limactl still creates, clones, edits, lists and deletes it. The tests run in a sandbox of their own, with a Lima home under /tmp and a HOME of their own, so they never touch your VMs or your Lima home, and they never start a VM. They run in mise run test wherever limactl is on PATH, and where it isn’t, they skip and say why.
Each test walks through scenario, which makes every kind of Lima config devvm makes, through the same code devvm runs. It makes base from Ubuntu’s image and from a --from conversion, a layer, the shared tools’ build VM, the conversion’s VM, and a project VM with its mounts, ports, size and environment. Then it makes the edits that a build’s start makes, and those of the project VM’s starts: its first start, a confined start with the proxy’s password that changes its agents’ folders, agent forwarding and size in the same edit, and an open start and one with no network. In the end it deletes everything. TestLimaConfigsValid runs limactl validate on every instance’s lima.yaml after each step. That covers the proxy’s password too, which devvm writes into lima.yaml itself, so limactl edit never checks it.
TestLimactlStubContract in contract_test.go keeps the limactl stub in internal/stubtest/stub honest, because the CLI tests and most Go tests trust it to act as Lima does. It runs scenario twice, once through the real limactl and once through the stub, and after each step it compares every instance as devvm reads it from limactl list --json. It compares the order of the instances, each one’s status, size, mounts, agent forwarding, ssh port and networks, and the edits each kind of start would make to it. When Lima and the stub differ, the test names the step and the fields that differ, and the stub gets fixed to match Lima.
data.the-nightly-run#The nightly run:
The Fuzz workflow (.github/workflows/fuzz.yml) fuzzes every target for five minutes each night, eight targets at a time, and you can start it by hand from the Actions tab. It minimizes each new input in at most 1,000 runs (-fuzzminimizetime 1000x), because by default go test minimizes each one for up to a minute, and a target whose runs write files, such as FuzzUnpack, would spend its five minutes doing that. It finds the targets by reading each func Fuzz in the tests, so a new target is fuzzed without any change to the workflow, and the proxy’s targets run first. A target’s name must be its own across the packages, because the workflow names the target’s artifacts and its line in the issue after it, and two targets of one name fail the run.
Each target starts from its corpus, the inputs that its earlier nights found reaching new code, so each night goes further than the last rather than starting again from the seeds. go test keeps a target’s corpus in the fuzz folder of GOCACHE, and the workflow restores it from a cache of the target’s own before fuzzing and saves it afterwards, whether the target failed or not. When a target fails, the workflow uploads the input that broke it as an artifact named crash-, and it adds the input to the target’s corpus, so the target fails on it again each night until the fix is on main.
The workflow keeps the failures in one issue, “Fuzzing found failing inputs”:
It opens the issue on the first night a target fails. The issue lists each failing target with its package and how its run ended, and links the night’s run, where the crash- artifacts are. A target whose job reported nothing also counts as failing. It comments on the issue when the failing targets change, so a new failure notifies you, and otherwise it only updates the issue’s link to the latest run. It closes the issue on the first night every target passes, the inputs that failed included. Only a run on main updates the issue, so a run started on another branch never closes it. The fuzz jobs run the repo’s code with read access alone, and the issue job, the only one that can write issues, runs none of it.
data.unreviewed-emulations#Unreviewed emulati:
devvm refuses an emulated feature until its review passes, yet the review needs end-to-end checks of it. In a test build, DEVVM_UNREVIEWED lets the ones it names through, as backend:feature pairs, comma-separated, each time with a warning (backend_unreviewed_used). A release ignores it:
DEVVM_UNREVIEWED=lima:ports-all devvm It’s for tests only, of an emulation before its review: none needs it now, as every emulation is reviewed. It never makes a feature a backend lacks usable, and devvm doctor still shows the feature unreviewed.
data.what-each-target-checks#What each target:
The parsers of what a VM can write, its output and its files, and of what comes from the network fail closed, so they take only what their format allows, within its caps. A secret’s value goes only where it’s bound, and a redaction leaves no planted secret behind. The host readers’ targets are differential, which means each one checks one reader against a frozen copy of how it read a host before devvm read every host in one form, and allows only the differences that One form of a host lists.
Target Package What it checks FuzzCursorFrames internal/proxy A reply from a Cursor host, of any type, encodings, body and trailers, read in reads of any size, passes only what came, from its start. A Connect or gRPC stream passes whole messages alone, none over frameMax as it came or as it decompresses, so a gzip bomb is refused, and none holding a JWT’s start once decompressed and, in JSON, with its escapes undone. Another body passes no JWT’s start of up to jwtWindow bytes, and a trailer holding one never lets the body end cleanly. FuzzInject internal/proxy Whatever a request’s host, method, path and headers, each binding’s value goes in only for a host the binding names, judged apart from the policy’s matcher, in NormHost’s form, for a path and methods it allows. It goes in its own header alone, once, and only when exactly one of that header’s values held its exact placeholder. Every other header stays as it came. FuzzParseBindings internal/proxy A bindings file is read only at a version the proxy knows, with each binding’s kind, path, methods and scheme ones it takes, and none of version 1 that a proxy of that version reads otherwise. A file that’s read reads back as itself from what Encode writes. FuzzLinkList internal/proxy A links list is read only at its version, and a host and port find only an entry that names them, at a link’s address in 127.77.0.0/16 as netip writes it, whose socket is this VM’s link’s for that address and port. FuzzBrokerFrames internal/proxy Whatever frame a child sends, the broker’s read never panics, refuses a frame past 2 MiB without reading it, takes only a frame of a type the protocol’s version knows, with its fields alone, and answers a request only with what its own config names: a value looked up with its own binding, a file of its own list, no link its list lacks, a token exchange at its own endpoints for its own VM, a lookup of a host name alone, and a connection only to an address that its own floor allows, never this machine’s loopback or its own address, which no rule of its names. FuzzFrameStreams internal/proxy Whatever stream of frames reaches either side, the broker answers each request with a frame of its ID and type and one of the protocol’s error codes alone, the child takes no reply to a request it never sent, nor a second start, and both end at the first frame that breaks the rules or at the stream’s end, never panicking or hanging. FuzzParseUpstream internal/proxy A company proxy’s URL is taken only as http://, with a host, a port that is one or none, and no path but / or query, and the upstream made of it has that host and port and Basic credentials only when it names a user. Its errors hold no more of the URL than its scheme. FuzzNoProxy internal/proxy Each NO_PROXY entry sends directly only what it names: every host for *, addresses alone for an address or a CIDR, a name and the names under it, only those after a leading . or *., and only the port an entry names. A list sends directly what any of its entries does. FuzzParseNarinfo internal/proxy A narinfo is taken only when cache.nixos.org-1 signed it, for the path asked for, and what the signature doesn’t cover keeps to its forms: a NAR’s URL named by its NarHash or FileHash, and sizes from 1 byte to 1 TiB. FuzzParseTokenRequest internal/agentlogin A token request is read only as a form, or with no type, or as one JSON object alone, with no field named twice however its name is written, and its fields are what it sent. FuzzRedact internal/agentlogin No secret planted in an agent’s settings file, JSON or TOML, survives into the VM’s copy, which reads back: a known key’s shape as a value or among other words, a URL’s password or query value, a value under a secret-looking key, an env or headers table’s value, and a flag’s argument. Claude Code’s own settings in its top-level env stay, as Redact keeps them. FuzzCapture internal/agentlogin Whatever an agent’s token endpoint replies to whatever request, for every agent whose login devvm captures, the VM’s reply is a JSON object holding none of the reply’s tokens, and a reply that isn’t captured leaves the store unwritten. FuzzSplit internal/redact A password that String finds in a line, in a URL of at most the tail’s length, never reaches the log when the line comes in parts of any size and is written after each part as far as Split lets it, as the run log writes it. FuzzStrip internal/jsonc Strip keeps every offset, blanking bytes with spaces and keeping newlines, leaves JSON as it is, and, against encoding/json, makes JSON with comments, trailing commas and a byte order mark read as the same value as the JSON without them. FuzzParsePublicKey internal/upgrade A minisign public key is read only from one base64 line, alone or after its untrusted comment, as exactly its key ID and its Ed25519 key. FuzzVerify internal/upgrade A signature verifies only the data its key’s holder signed, with the trusted comment that was signed. FuzzEntryName internal/upgrade An archive’s entry is taken only as the release’s folder or as a regular file right in it, which lands in the folder unpack makes and nowhere else. FuzzUnpack internal/upgrade unpack writes only regular files right in the folder it makes, devvm among them, each as the archive has it, devvm executable and the rest not, at most unpackCap in all and nothing outside the folder. An archive it refuses leaves no folder. FuzzParseHostKeys internal/vmssh Each host key taken from what a VM shows is of a type ssh has, with no certificate, marker or pattern, in strict base64 of at most keyMax that names its own type, from a line of the VM’s own, in order. Its line in the record is three fields, which read back as that key. FuzzParsePorts internal/vmssh A forwarder’s record, which other VMs’ forwarders read, gives only ports that are ones, each an entry of its line, in order, and the ports it writes read back as themselves. FuzzParseCloneState internal/vm A --clone VM’s answer to the check is taken only whole: every repo asked for is gone or has its branches and status, within cloneRefsMax branches in all and cloneWorktreesMax worktrees a repo, each worktree once, at a clean path below the project folder, with a commit’s name or none for its HEAD. Nothing taken is more than the answer. FuzzParseInit internal/vm The VM’s answer to its repos’ setup names a seed as landed, or of another format, only when a line names that seed’s path, and an old git only by what git --version prints, else as unknown. FuzzParseKept internal/vm What a seed’s apply kept, which devvm only shows, is the VM’s own lines and names as it wrote them, none of them empty. FuzzParseLFSPointer internal/vm A blob is taken as a Git LFS pointer only as the spec writes one, with its version line first and each line ended, one oid of 64 lowercase hex digits, which names its object’s path, and one size of at least 0. FuzzHandshakeVM internal/desktop The relay’s handshake with the VM’s VNC server succeeds only for version 3.8 or later, a list of security types that has None, and an OK result, and reads no more than those. It writes only version 3.8, then None, and None only from a list that has it, and its error, which goes in the log, stays short. FuzzHostSites internal/proxy Each of the proxy’s readers of a host reads it as its frozen copy did, except for the listed differences. FuzzClaudeHostSite, FuzzPromisorHostSite, FuzzPublicHostSite, FuzzRiskSites, FuzzCheckHostSite internal/agentlogin, internal/vm, internal/from, internal/netpolicy, internal/secrets The other readers of a host, an MCP server’s, a promisor remote’s, --from’s registry’s, devvm network lock’s and a secret’s --host, read it as their frozen copies did, except for the listed differences. FuzzParseRule internal/proxy A rule’s text parses back to the same rule, a host rule never holds a space or a slash, and ParsePolicy marks a line a rule exactly when ValidRule takes it. FuzzRequest internal/proxy A request target the proxy accepts is a plain host, and the allow command it suggests allows exactly that host and port. FuzzDenyBypass internal/proxy A deny of /gists/ and of POST holds however a request spells the path or the method. FuzzClientHello internal/proxy Reading a tunnel’s first bytes never hangs, a stream whose first byte starts a TLS record counts as TLS, and only a whole record of TLS’s version is returned. FuzzTransparent internal/proxy Whatever its first bytes, a transparent connection to a proxy whose policy allows nothing reaches nothing. FuzzNixPath internal/proxy What nixPath takes is one of the cache’s exact forms and names a file inside its folder. FuzzParse internal/devcontainer A devcontainer.json refuses ${localEnv:…} and ${env:…}. The check reads each variable as devvm does, from ${ to the first } after it, so a nested one such as ${${localEnv:HOME}} is left as text. Its environment variables are names and shell words the environment file holds as they are, and nothing it keeps has a NUL. FuzzParseRef internal/from Any image reference parses into a tag without / or :, and a valid one parses the same once written out in full. FuzzRestrictNetdev internal/backend/lima RestrictNetdev refuses, or returns at most one network, restricted, with nothing else changed. FuzzQuote internal/shell A string that Quote quotes reaches a shell as itself.
data.whats-platform-specific#What’s platform-:
The same code and tests run on macOS and Linux; what differs is behind build tags in internal/platform and the backend’s own checks:
macOS Linux VMs Lima on Apple’s Virtualization framework (vz) Lima on QEMU with KVM Mounts virtiofs 9p, one mount per share per guest Project VM disks APFS copy-on-write clones of the image’s qcow2 overlays of the image’s Confined tiers the VM’s Lima process under a macOS sandbox QEMU’s restrict=on and a guestfwd to the proxy .git protection locked with chflags read-only in QEMU’s namespace, or, where the kernel refuses it, watched, and devvm says so (details) Set-id files dropped by virtiofs reach the host: new VMs check for them Tokens the Keychain files only you can read, in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/ The CA kept out of Time Machine no backup to keep it out of The end-to-end tests check each side where they run: on Linux, the .git protection checks look at QEMU’s namespace and what root in the VM can do, or, on a host whose kernel refuses the namespace, that it’s off and devvm says so, and the Keychain check is left out. The CLI tests run as on a Linux host that can’t pin (DEVVM_PINS), whatever the host’s kernel allows, and the unit tests that pin for real (TestRunPinned, TestProbePin) run only on a Linux host that allows it.
On macOS, the end-to-end tests also need OpenSSL as openssl, because its CA checks serve HTTPS with openssl s_server, and the LibreSSL that macOS ships as /usr/bin/openssl cuts the VM’s OpenSSL client off mid-request. Install it with brew install openssl@3, then put $(brew --prefix openssl@3)/bin first on your PATH, because Homebrew doesn’t link it into its own bin. On Linux, openssl is OpenSSL, and Ubuntu’s images have it installed, as ca-certificates needs it.
Before it builds anything, the runner checks every command of this machine’s that the chosen sections use. It always checks limactl and pkill, and each section lists the others it needs in tests/e2e/sections_test.go, such as git, openssl, which must be OpenSSL and not LibreSSL, OpenSSH’s ssh, ssh-agent, ssh-add and ssh-keygen, tar, ps, lsof on macOS or ss on Linux, and python3. When any of them is missing, e2e lists each one with the command that installs it, through Homebrew on macOS or apt-get or dnf on Linux, and stops. It needs Go too, or mise, which installs the repo’s pinned Go.
data.writing-a-check#Writing a check:
A section is a function that takes the running section, *S, and calls s.Check once for each check:
s.Check("gc deletes a tool image no VM uses, with its record", func() error { if Exists(old) || Exists(old+".json") { return errors.New("the old tool image or its record is still there") } return nil }) The check passes when its function returns nil. Its title is its key in the timings, so a changed title starts its times again: give a new check a title that says what it proves. When a check fails, the runner prints its error, each line led by failed:, and then the last 5 lines that its commands printed, or as many as Tail(n) asks for. It also copies every proxy log in the sandbox that has lines, each VM’s and each build’s, into proxy-logs/ in the sandbox’s state folder, because the run deletes the VMs and builds that wrote them, and it prints that folder and the last 5 lines of each log written since the check began. The next run empties proxy-logs/ before its first check. A check that the run has nothing for is s.Skip(title, why), which counts it, so that runs compare their counts.
The commands a check runs go through the section, so that they run in the sandbox’s environment and within the check’s time limit, and their output goes into the check’s log:
Helper What it runs or reads s.Devvm(dir, args…), s.DevvmNames(dir, args…) the run’s devvm in dir, with no input; DevvmNames in names mode (DEVVM_MESSAGES=names) s.Msg(name, "k=v"…) a message’s text, from devvm _msg, so a check never repeats its wording s.Limactl(args…), s.InVM(vm, script), s.Status(vm) limactl in the sandbox’s Lima home, a script in the VM’s login shell with no input, and a VM’s status s.Run(Cmd{…}) any command, with its own folder, input or variables s.NewProject(name), s.Launch(dir, input, args…), s.Reuse(name, input, args…) a new project folder, deleted at the end, and devvm launched in a folder, its VM recorded for the cleanup s.Paths.State(vm), s.Paths.VMOf(dir), s.Paths.VMDir(vm) a VM’s vm.json, flattened as the CLI tests’ vm_state does, the VM a folder has, and its folder s.Paths.KeysOf(image), s.Paths.Record(key, field), s.Own(image) an image’s keys and records, and its images made the run’s to delete s.Layer(name, script), s.Paths a layer of the run’s (e2e*), deleted at the end, and the sandbox’s folders s.Golden(name, args…) with --golden, a golden fixture captured from what args printed s.GoE2E(test, pkg, "VAR=value"…) a Go test in internal/pkg that needs a real VM, such as TestE2EExecQuoting, with its variables in its environment and never in a process’s arguments s.Until(timeout, fn), Settle a wait for what the check looks for, trying each second, and the one fixed wait, before looking for something that must not have happened s.Port(p), s.Defer(fn) one of slot 0’s fixed ports as this slot has it, and a cleanup of the section’s own Three options change how a check runs. Flaky(reason) marks a check that’s known to flake: when it fails, the runner shows its output and runs it once more, and only a second failure fails it. Its result says retried once, and its timings line and the summary say so too, and every other check fails on its first failure. Builds() marks a check whose own command can build base or a --from base, so it gets at least an hour. Needs(backend.FeatureLink) names the backend features that a check proves: on a backend that has one of them neither natively nor emulated and reviewed, as devvm doctor --json shows its features, the check is skipped and counted, so a check is written once for every backend that has its features. A section whose every check proves a feature takes it once with s.Needing(...), as link takes FeatureLink, nix FeatureNixLayer and --from FeatureFrom, and a section’s own checks of the docker or nix layer and of ports name theirs with Needs.
data.x86_64-hosts#x86_64 hosts:
These need real x86_64 hardware, or an x86_64 VM on such hardware with nested virtualization. An emulated x86_64 VM on a Mac (--arch=x86_64, QEMU TCG; Lima needs its lima-additional-guestagents) runs the unit tests, but VMs nested in it crash in their firmware.
A bare-metal x86_64 Linux host, such as Fedora 43 with SELinux enforcing, runs the gate and mise run e2e -- --from as the Linux host above does, from a clone of the repo, and it can run --slots 3 (slots for each host). Those runs check the x86_64 side of what devvm builds: the _amd64 pins of base, every layer and feature, the shared tools’ linux-x64 lock entries and their checksums, --from’s conversion, whose VM reads its scripts over 9p, and the confined tiers through devvm _qemu and qemu-system-x86_64.
The tests don’t cover the release itself, so check it by hand on that host. Build the archives with scripts/release.sh --head, with DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY and DEVVM_MINISIGN_PUB naming a test key so the signature is checked too, and install devvm--linux-amd64.tar.gz from them in a throwaway HOME, as maintaining shows, with main --yes in place of main --no-deps. With only the system’s folders on PATH, the script finds no Lima, so it installs Lima’s latest release into that HOME’s ~/.local. When the host already has QEMU and access to /dev/kvm, nothing it runs needs sudo. Then run the installed devvm --version and devvm doctor, and check with file that the binary is statically linked.
devvm hasn’t been tested on an Intel Mac. Its release has a darwin-amd64 archive, and that binary runs under Rosetta on Apple silicon, but nobody has run the tests or a VM on Intel hardware.
GitHub’s Linux runners are x86_64 with KVM, and the E2E workflow (.github/workflows/e2e.yml) runs mise run e2e -- --only project on one as a trial. Start it from the repo’s Actions tab, with Run workflow on the E2E workflow, because it has no other trigger yet. It installs QEMU, gives the runner’s user /dev/kvm as Lima’s own CI does, installs Lima at a pinned version checked against its checksum, and runs the section up to three times. It caches Ubuntu’s cloud image under the release that the end-to-end tests pin, and the built images under a hash of assets/, tests/e2e-mise.lock, that release and Lima’s version, because devvm’s image keys are only known once it builds. When the run fails, it uploads the e2e logs, devvm’s run logs and each Lima instance’s serial logs as the e2e-logs artifact.

data.cli-tests#CLI tests:
CLI tests are testscript scripts in testdata/script/*.txtar, run by internal/cli/script_test.go against a freshly built devvm. Call it with exec devvm …:
# An unknown flag fails. ! exec devvm --nope stderr '^devvm: flag_unknown command=devvm flag=--nope$' Scripts see messages by their names, so the example checks which message devvm printed, not its wording. A script that checks a message’s text sets env DEVVM_MESSAGES= first.
Run one script with mise exec -- go test ./internal/cli -run TestScript/.
Each script runs in a sandbox under /tmp, never the real folders:
Variable Points to HOME home/ XDG_DATA_HOME data/ XDG_CONFIG_HOME config/ DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, LIMA_HOME lima/ (short, for Lima’s socket paths) DATA, VMS, RUN devvm’s data folder, data/devvm/, and its vms/ and run/ folders CFG devvm’s config folder, config/devvm/ DEVVM_MESSAGES names, so messages print as their names STUB_DIR stub/, for stubs’ state STUB_LOG stub/calls, the stubs’ call log DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE devvm-test, the Keychain service name DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL ubuntu/, with a dated release as Ubuntu signed it DEVVM_KVM stub/kvm, a file standing in for Linux’s /dev/kvm DEVVM_TEST_CPUS, DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB 8, 16 and 500: a large host, whatever runs the tests (details) DEVVM_HOST_MISE the mise stub, which resolves the shared tools in place of devvm’s own mise DEVVM_CLIP_TOOLS the stubs’ folder, so devvm paste runs the clipboard stubs in place of the system’s tools, such as macOS’s /usr/bin/osascript, and no script reaches the real clipboard MISE_STUB_LOCK testdata/mise.lock, the lock the mise stub writes TOOLCHAINS, AGENTS the toolchains’ and the coding agents’ names, in the registries’ order and joined with spaces, as devvm’s messages list them, so a script that checks a list names no toolchain or agent itself (stderr 'names='$TOOLCHAINS'$') AGENT_CHOICES, LOGIN_AGENTS, KEY_AGENTS every agent’s name, those that devvm agent login logs in, and those with a key for each provider, in the registry’s order and joined with a comma and a space, as a message of choices lists them (stderr 'choices='$AGENT_CHOICES' command=') DEVVM_BIN the folder of the built devvm, alone DEVVM_REPO the checkout, for the scripts in scripts/, which tests copy into a throwaway repo before running, and the scripts in assets/, which tests source to check their pieces DEVVM_SSH_PORTS, SANDBOX_PORT_NEXT, SANDBOX_PORT_END, DEVVM_PORT_RANGE the sandbox’s own ports, as the next paragraph says Each sandbox has a block of 160 ports of its own, between 10000 and 19999, below both the range devvm chooses ports from and the system’s ephemeral range, so neither a devvm that a script runs nor an outgoing connection takes one. The sandbox holds the block’s lock file in /tmp/devvm-test-ports-/, a folder of your user’s alone, while it lasts, so no other sandbox has the same block, whether it’s in the same test process or in another one running at once, such as a second worktree’s gate. While every block is held, a new sandbox waits for one, up to 5 minutes. The block’s first 60 ports are for the scripts. The VMs’ ssh ports (DEVVM_SSH_PORTS) come first, and then the ports for free_port VAR… and the fixtures. Each of those is taken in turn from SANDBOX_PORT_NEXT up to SANDBOX_PORT_END, and it’s free on every address, 127.0.0.1 included, when it’s taken (free_port -range FIRST LAST takes two in a row). The other 100 are the range the sandbox’s devvm chooses its VMs’ proxy and desktop ports from (DEVVM_PORT_RANGE, which only a test build reads), so two sandboxes’ devvms never choose the same port.
The built devvm is a test build, so it reads the stand-ins above that a release ignores, such as DEVVM_KVM and DEVVM_HOST_MISE. A script answers a question in one of two ways: ttyin -stdin FILE gives the next exec a terminal whose input is the file, so devvm asks as it does in yours, and env DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS=1 with stdin FILE has each question read its answer as a line of the file instead, without its prompt. Without either, devvm has no terminal, so it refuses every question, as a script’s devvm does. It has the checkout’s assets/ embedded, as a release has, and no test build reads them from elsewhere: a script that needs other files for devvm (layers, features, policies) puts them in the user’s folders in the sandbox, as a user would.
$WORK, the script’s own folder, is the current folder. project NAME makes the folder $WORK/NAME and goes to it, as a project’s folder, and project NAME git makes it a git repo too. Once devvm has made the folder’s VM, vm_name VAR NAME finds it among the states in $VMS and sets $VAR to the VM’s name, which ends in an ID the test can’t know, so a script can pass it to a stub (exec limactl stop $WEB). It also sets $VAR_dir to the VM’s folder, $VMS/, so a script reads the VM’s state as $WEB_dir/vm.json and its network log as $WEB_dir/logs/network.jsonl. catg GLOB prints the one file a glob matches, and fails when the glob matches none or more than one, so a check never reads two files by mistake. vm_state GLOB prints the one VM state a glob matches as sorted KEY=VALUE lines for stdout to match: a section’s fields are dotted (net.on=true, ports.host.ssh=23456), a list of strings is joined with spaces (tools.names=node claude), a list of objects is indexed (links.links.0.name=db), and anything but a string is JSON. Negated, ! catg GLOB and ! vm_name VAR NAME pass when there isn’t exactly one. json_set GLOB KEY=VALUE… sets string fields in each JSON file the glob matches and keeps the rest, or makes the file when a glob without wildcards matches none. KEY:=JSON sets any JSON value, and a dotted key sets a field of an object, which it makes when it’s missing. Scripts write devvm’s JSON records with it, such as a tool image’s record (json_set $SHARE/node-*.json built=2020-01-01T00:00:00Z), because a record’s times are in the file, where touch can’t change them. renumber FILE changes a VM’s state as a boot that numbered the disks’ devices anew leaves it, as macOS does. The folder’s identity and each .git’s git_id get another device, with their inodes and birth times as they were, and $FOLDER_ID and $GIT_ID hold the folder’s and its own .git’s identities from before the change. fixture VERSION puts a release’s state into the sandbox, and json_superset [-shape] [-changes PATH] WANT GOT checks that one JSON file has everything another has, as Released state says. A VM state a script writes as a fixture needs version, id, name, image, dir and backend, created for a VM whose creation finished, and a hash of its own for its folder (json_set $VMS/12345612345601/vm.json version:=1 id=x name=devvm-live-12345612345601 image=base dir=/p/live backend=lima created=2020-01-01T00:00:00Z net.on:=false).
Tests never touch the network. Downloads are served from a test server (net/http/httptest) or read from a file:// folder. DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL replaces https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/resolute, where devvm finds Ubuntu’s dated releases: point it at a folder of release-YYYYMMDD/ folders, each with its SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.gpg, as file:///path/to/folder. The CLI tests serve internal/ubuntu/testdata/resolute, a release as Ubuntu published and signed it, and Go tests sign their own releases with a key they make (internal/ubuntu/pgp_test.go). devvm’s own releases, which devvm upgrade installs, come from internal/upgrade/upgradetest: a TLS test server laid out as GitHub’s releases, with a minisign key of the test’s own that signs each release’s SHA256SUMS as minisign does. A script starts one with release_server [-badsig] LATEST [VERSION...], which serves a release of each version, the first the newest, each devvm in it a script that prints its version, and with -badsig signs them with another key. It points a test build at the server with DEVVM_REPO_URL, at its key with DEVVM_RELEASE_KEY and at its certificate with DEVVM_RELEASE_CA, and DEVVM_TEST_VERSION gives the test build a release’s version. Container registries (--from) are a TLS test server in Go tests; scripts use pinned digests, which need no lookup, or set HTTPS_PROXY to a closed port, so lookups fail as offline ones do.
A command left running in the background (exec devvm … &name&) can be interrupted with kill -INT name. wait_file FILE waits up to 60 seconds for a file to appear, such as one a stub writes when it gets somewhere, and fails at once when every background command has ended. For anything else, wait_until SCRIPT runs sh -c SCRIPT every 100 ms until it succeeds, for up to 90 seconds. It fails at once when every background command has ended, or when SCRIPT exits 100, which is how a check that can no longer succeed says so, as when it waits on a session that ended. Wait with these two rather than a loop of your own. A script that runs a copy of devvm makes it with cp_exe SRC DST, not cp: on Linux, a command another script starts while the copy is being written keeps the file open for writing until it runs, so running the copy then fails with “text file busy”, and cp_exe writes the file while no command can start.
data.coverage#Coverage:
mise run test measures each package’s test coverage, then fails when a package’s coverage is more than a point below its line in the baseline, so coverage only goes up. That point of room is there because the same tests can cover a little less from one run to the next, with timing or the tools a machine has installed. A package inside it passes and keeps its line. Each system has a baseline of its own, testdata/coverage/darwin.txt and testdata/coverage/linux.txt, because macOS and Linux run different code and skip different tests. On a system without one, mise run test says so and checks nothing. A package’s coverage counts its own Go tests and the CLI tests together. scripts/test.sh sets CLI_GOCOVERDIR, so TestScript builds devvm with -cover for every package of devvm’s, and each devvm a script runs writes its counters to that script’s own folder inside it. Scripts run in parallel, and devvm runs that started at the same moment in one folder would race to write the same meta-data file, so one of them would print coverage meta-data emit failed on stderr and fail any script that checks it. go tool covdata then merges every script’s folder with the Go tests’ own counters. That way internal/cli, and code that only the CLI tests reach, such as a backend’s real runner, count as tested. The end-to-end tests don’t count.
When a change raises a package’s coverage, raise its baseline in the same commit. Run mise run coverage, which runs the tests as mise run test does, then writes each package’s coverage to this system’s baseline where it went up, and commit the file. A change that raises coverage on both systems raises both baselines, so run it on a Linux host too. It never lowers a line: a package within a point below its baseline keeps the line it has, and when a package is more than a point below, it fails and writes nothing. A new package gets its line from mise run coverage too, and a package that’s gone loses its line there, because mise run test fails on both until then. coverage.txtar checks scripts/coverage.sh, which compares the coverage with the baseline.
There’s no target percentage: a package is judged by what’s untested in it, not by its number.
data.end-to-end-tests#End-to-end tests:
mise run e2e runs devvm against real VMs, so it needs Lima and takes minutes: run it in the background. It runs TestE2E in tests/e2e, with the run’s flags after --. First it checks that this machine has every command the chosen sections use, and it names each one that’s missing with what installs it (the list). Then it builds devvm from the checkout into its sandbox, its files embedded, and runs every check through that binary:
Lima home ~/.lt-e2e-go (or $DEVVM_E2E_LIMA_HOME); it refuses ~/.lima and devvm’s own State /tmp/devvm-go-e2e (XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME) Keychain service devvm-go-e2e (DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE), fake tokens only, deleted at the end Lock /tmp/devvm-go-e2e.lock, a symlink to the pid of the run that holds it, so only one run uses the sandbox at a time Git identity GIT_AUTHOR_* and GIT_COMMITTER_* of its own, so the harness’s commits and tags work on a machine with no git config, and yours never goes into them; devvm’s own git ignores them mise run e2e # every section but desktop and from mise run e2e -- --from # every section, from too, and base with every feature: the longest mise run e2e -- --only images,gc # just these sections mise run e2e -- --clean # delete the sandbox's cached images and tool images first mise run e2e -- --every-feature # base with every feature, as a run with from builds it mise run e2e -- --slots 3 # the sections spread over 3 sandboxes that run at once mise run e2e -- --slot 1 # run in slot 1's sandbox, its images as it has them mise run e2e -- --newest-base # base from Ubuntu's newest image and packages, in a sandbox of its own mise run e2e -- --golden # also capture the stubs' golden fixtures from the real tools End-to-end tests in Go says how to run go test yourself, write a check and add a section.
A change that touches VMs passes the sections for what it changed, with --only, and a run with --only that names from builds base with every feature, as --from does. Before you merge a change to assets/ or to --from, run --from, because only it runs every section on base with every feature. GitHub’s hosted runners can’t run the end-to-end tests on macOS, so a Mac of your own runs them there.
--newest-base builds base as a user’s first build does, in place of the pinned release that the other runs use, and Maintaining says when to run it and what to do when it fails. --golden writes the golden fixtures of this system into the checkout, for you to commit.

The store keeps the refreshed login, the VM’s requests to the API and to mcp-proxy.anthropic.com go on with the refreshed access token, and no log holds a value. TestClaudeOAuthGet checks the refresh too. Last, a VM made with --network learn runs on the internet tier, shown as internet (learning), and reaches example.com and example.org; devvm network lock --json lists both, each with its port, and its next launch counts what it learned; devvm network lock --all adds exactly the hosts it learned to its own rules and gives it the allowlist tier at once, the VM running on, so example.com still works on 443, while its port 80 and example.net get a 403. desktop: a VM of base has none of the desktop’s programs, and devvm desktop refuses it, naming the layer. --layers desktop makes a VM of the desktop image, and devvm desktop serves its desktop on this machine’s 127.0.0.1 alone, keeping its port and its password from one run to the next. A viewer with a wrong password is refused, and one with the password gets the VM’s desktop. The VM’s server listens on its user’s own socket and on no TCP port, with the clipboard off, and the password is in no file of the VM’s, in no run log and in no host process’s arguments while devvm desktop starts. With network policy, the VM still reaches only its proxy and not the desktop’s port on this machine, the desktop’s browsers use the VM’s local proxy without a password, a blocked host still gets a 403, and the local proxy isn’t forwarded to this machine. When root in the VM runs a server of its own without a password, a viewer with a wrong password is still refused and one with the password gets in, and the refused viewer never reaches the VM, nor does the viewer’s clipboard, only its key event. Ctrl+C ends devvm desktop and closes its port, and devvm desktop --clipboard starts the server again on the same port with the clipboard on, which a viewer with the password gets. nix: the nix layer. A copy of assets/layers/nix.sh as a layer of the run’s own, built behind a company proxy of the run’s own, reaches Nix’s releases through it and leaves no proxy settings for nix-daemon (and not the company proxy’s password) anywhere on its image’s disk. Then a folder with package.json, flake.nix and .envrc gets a VM with node on the nix layer (--layers nix) on the allowlist tier: Nix and direnv at their pins, a store that’s root’s, sandbox on with no fallback, trusted-users root alone and an untrusted user’s --option substituters ignored, nix-daemon with the VM’s own proxy in devvm’s drop-in alone, nix run nixpkgs#hello from Nix’s cache, a build in Nix’s sandbox, sudo nix and nix over ssh, the flake’s dev shell (nixpkgs at a pinned revision) loaded by direnv in an interactive shell, its node ahead of the shared node prompt after prompt and gone outside the folder, nix-direnv’s cache in the VM’s home with no .direnv in the folder, a fixed-output download from a host that isn’t allowed refused with 403 and named by devvm-why, and after devvm network open and devvm restart, no drop-in and no proxy for the daemon. from: run with a docker that isn’t running, so nothing comes from Docker. Its container images go by their pinned digests, as node:24@sha256:…, so devvm looks them up nowhere, except the company proxy’s alpine:3.21, which keeps its tag so that devvm’s registry lookup is checked too. A VM from node:24 with node, python and Claude Code on the docker and nix layers (Debian 12, in a home of its own) boots, with its base keyed by the pinned digest, its node, python and claude at the locked versions, GNU tar as its commands find it, its tool images built in a clone of devvm’s own Ubuntu base when the run builds them, the docker layer’s Docker from Docker’s Debian repository, and the nix layer’s Nix under systemd running nix run nixpkgs#hello and a build in Nix’s sandbox, then, after devvm network allowlist and devvm restart, transparent mode’s checks as the network section has them, and with its service stopped, Lima’s DNS and a public server answering nothing; a VM from alpine:3 with node and dotnet, which its package.json and global.json call for, on the docker, nix and desktop layers runs node and pnpm from musl tool images, and dotnet’s musl SDK with ICU, which makes and runs a console project, built in its own base and keyed and recorded by its digest, the docker layer’s Docker on OpenRC, the desktop layer’s programs from Alpine’s packages, with no crashed services, and the nix layer’s Nix as an OpenRC service, with nix run nixpkgs#hello and a sandboxed build, then after devvm network allowlist and devvm restart transparent mode’s checks on OpenRC and musl, as for Debian 12, and a download only its daemon makes from a host that isn’t allowed refused with the proxy’s 403, and with GNU tar as its commands find it, devvm history import puts an export into it, while an export with a path outside the agents’ history imports nothing there, and on a Linux host, given Lima’s mmap with no mode chosen, devvm mount-cache none gives it none at its next start, through the restart that a remount Alpine refuses gets, which devvm’s portable check of the folder confirms; base builds from ubuntu:26.04; and the build VM and its temporary folders are gone. link: links between VMs, each check the end-to-end proof of a row of the threat check in the design note. It runs devvm with a soft limit of 256 open files, macOS’s default, as the link sessions it starts get that limit too, and it makes two small open targets, each forwarding no port and running servers on its own 127.0.0.1 (/var/tmp/e2e-link.pl, in perl, which every base has), and a client that forwards every port. Each of the three reserves the link checks’ ports (ip_local_reserved_ports), so Linux never gives one to a connection’s own end, where a connection that just ended would hold it for a minute and a later server or ssh -R couldn’t bind it. sshd -T in each VM shows remote forwards allowed on 127.77.*:* alone, at the address the host asks for, and the client’s own Lima rules ignore every port. A port the target doesn’t publish is refused by devvm link add, and once a port is published, devvm link add on the running client reaches it within seconds as NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT, by curl and by a raw TCP client (bash’s /dev/tcp), while with --as NAME the target’s folder name doesn’t resolve. Two targets on one port are each reached by their own name, port 80 is linked on port 80, devvm link and devvm link publish list what they hold with "version": 1 in their --json, and devvm network allowlist is refused for the client while it links to open targets. A published port that isn’t linked has nothing listening for it, devvm link unpublish refuses the link’s next connection, logs it and names the client, and devvm link rm takes the listener away within seconds. In the client, sshd listens only on its own port and the links’ addresses, and nothing from a link listens on 127.0.0.1, ::1 or every address, so this machine gets no forward of a link, while a server of the client’s own on 127.0.0.1 with a link’s port is forwarded as usual. Each link’s socket is mode 600 in the run folder of mode 700, and the link session and every process it starts listen on no TCP port and connect only to the VMs’ ssh ports. ssh -R into the client binds nothing outside 127.77.0.0/16 (rfwd_links). A program in the client that holds a link’s address first fails that link alone with link_port_taken, 256 connections at once, past the socket’s backlog of 128 on macOS, are all carried, and a 257th is refused and logged as link_limit. Root in the client then loosens its sshd and the link session connects again: with PermitListen any the client binds only the links’ addresses, because the host asks for nothing else, and with GatewayPorts yes too, the link session still listens on no TCP port of this machine and connects only to the VMs’ sshd. devvm network log shows the links’ connections and refusals. A stopped target refuses the connection, logs link_target_stopped and stays stopped, and the client’s launch warns of it. Once it’s restarted, the link works again. devvm rm of the target removes the client’s link, names the client and removes its sockets, and a VM made again in that folder isn’t linked. Then the client and one target get the allowlist tier, the target while it runs. Until the target restarts, devvm ls shows it unenforced, the client’s next connection is refused and logged as unenforced while the target’s server runs, and devvm link add and the client’s launch warn of it (link_target_unenforced). Once both have restarted, the client reaches its link by curl through its proxy settings and by a raw TCP client while a direct connection fails. A link added while the client runs is reached at once by curl through its proxy, by GET and CONNECT, with no link name in NO_PROXY and the client’s boot and host keys unchanged, and the client’s proxy refuses names, ports and addresses that aren’t on its own list, while the target’s proxy refuses the client’s link name. devvm link add refuses an open target, devvm network open is refused for the target, and with the rule broken by hand in the target’s state the next connection is refused and the client’s launch warns and runs without the link until the rule holds again. In the --from tier, an Alpine client reaches its link to port 80. devvm rm of the client leaves no link session, socket, pid file, log or link state. Every section but tools uses the shared tools’ versions pinned in tests/e2e-mise.lock, for both architectures’ glibc and musl VMs, and the --from checks start from container images pinned by digest in tests/e2e/from_test.go (fromNodeDigest, fromAlpineDigest and fromUbuntuDigest). The images built from them stay valid until a pin moves. base starts from the dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image that e2eUbuntuRelease in tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go names, given to devvm as DEVVM_UBUNTU_RELEASE, in place of the newest that a user’s devvm pins, so base’s key stays the same between runs and on every machine of one architecture. devvm keeps a release it has pinned, so when the sandbox’s pin names another release, as it does after scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves e2eUbuntuRelease, the run deletes that pin before its first section, and the next build pins e2eUbuntuRelease. Its packages are those its key recorded at its first build in the sandbox, which stay in the sandbox’s package cache through --clean, so base built again under the same key installs the same packages until assets/ or the release changes its key. scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools moves the lock to upstream’s newest versions, resolved with devvm’s pinned host mise, scripts/bump.sh e2e-from moves the digests to what Docker Hub has for each tag, and scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves the release to the newest Ubuntu lists; scripts/bump.sh --check shows them against upstream. The lock’s first line is the SHA-256 of the assets/shared-tools/mise.toml it was resolved from, and a run stops at once when that file has changed since, until scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools resolves the lock again.
base, the --from bases and the shared tool images stay cached between runs, except what a rebuild or gc deletes: every stale image in the sandbox (other selections’ bases, whose features differ, among them) and every unused tool image (an earlier from run’s musl ones, and the tools section’s newest versions where they differ from the pins); every other VM a run makes is deleted at its end, and its project folders are unlocked and deleted. Each check prints [n/N], how long it took and the time left as the last complete run of each of its sections measured it, and a heartbeat every minute shows the latest output. e2e keeps each section’s times in a file of its own in slot 0’s state folder, timings/plain/SECTION, or timings/features/SECTION for a run whose base has every feature, because that run also checks base’s features. So a run of any selection, in any slot, estimates from and compares with the sections it runs. A check fails on its first failure, except the few marked Flaky, which flake on timing, such as the network section’s check that the proxy’s password was in no host process’s arguments, and the link section’s 256-connection check and its stopped-target check. When one of these fails, e2e shows its output and runs it once more, and a second failure fails it. Its result says retried once, its line in the timings has a third field, retried, and the summary counts the retried checks and names each one. A check a run has nothing for is counted as SKIP: base’s features, with base cached. A section that runs fewer checks than its last complete run with the same tests/e2e Go files fails the run, because an error ended it early, and e2e keeps the times it had. After you edit those files, each section’s first complete run sets the count the next runs compare with. Checks look for devvm’s messages with devvm _msg, never by their wording. The Go tests that need a real VM or desktop, TestE2EExecQuoting, TestE2ESelfCheck and TestE2EDesktop, skip unless their DEVVM_E2E_* variables are set, and e2e runs each of them through s.GoE2E, which sets those variables in the test’s environment, so a value such as the desktop’s password is in no process’s arguments.
Each check’s command has a time limit, counted from when it starts: three times the check’s longest time in its section’s last complete run, at least 2 minutes, or 10 minutes for a check with no time yet. The checks that build base or a --from base, which Builds() marks, get at least an hour, because their last time may have been a cached build. The steps between two checks, such as the launches that build tool images, get an hour too. When a check runs past its limit, the heartbeat stops the processes it started, with TERM as Ctrl+C would and then KILL 30 seconds later, and the check fails with the heartbeat’s last line in its output. When the steps before a check run past their limit, the heartbeat stops their processes the same way, and that check fails without running. Either way, the run goes on to the next check and then to its usual cleanup.
data.go-test-helpers#Go test helpers:
Every change to devvm’s logic comes with a test, and Go tests are table tests next to the code they test. Neither the Go tests nor the CLI tests touch the Keychain, real VMs or your own folders. A Go test that writes state points the XDG folders at t.TempDir(), and a Go test makes VMs only on the fake backend, backendtest. The CLI tests run the built devvm against the stubs, so only the end-to-end tests make real VMs. The Go tests share a few helpers, so each one reads the same way:
stubtest.New(t) puts the stubs first on PATH for one test, as the CLI tests have them, with a new folder under /tmp as their STUB_DIR and its calls file as their STUB_LOG. The folder goes when the test ends. stubtest.New(t, "ssh") puts only the stubs it names on PATH, so the host’s other commands, such as git, stay. Its Calls returns the calls the stubs logged, Reset forgets them, and Touch, Write and Read work on the files the stubs read, such as a switch, a file whose presence makes a stub fail. VM, Size and VMs set and read Lima’s instances in the stubs’ state, and Keychain and SetKeychain the Keychain’s items. stubtest.Command(t, "mise") returns the path of one stub, for a test that runs it by its path, as DEVVM_HOST_MISE does. stubtest.Git(ctx, args...) is plain git for a test’s own repo, and a test runs git only through it, which the structure test checks. Its environment is the test’s without git’s variables that pick a repo, its files or its config, such as GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE and GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS (stubtest.GitEnv), and it reads no global or system config. A git that runs the tests, such as a hook’s or git rebase --exec’s, sets some of those variables, and a test’s git that kept them would work on the checkout itself, writing its config and commits there. A test that runs something else that runs git, such as a script or a stub, calls stubtest.NoGitRepo(t) first, which takes the same variables out of the test’s environment until it ends, and stubtest.New calls it for the stubs. The CLI tests’ environment leaves them out too. stubtest.ExecRunner is a backend’s runner that runs each command as it is, with no run log, so a backend under test runs the stubs. msg.IDOf(err) returns the ID of the message an error carries, or "" when it carries none, and msg.NamesOf(err) returns the message’s names, as names mode prints them, or the error’s own text when it isn’t a message. A test compares either with what it expects. A msg.Fake is the msg.Reporter a package under test prints and asks through. Its zero value is quiet: it prints nothing, has no terminal, so it refuses every question as the UI does where it can’t ask, and runs a logged command as it is. Its fields change that: OnInfo, OnWarn and the other On funcs are given each message or question of their kind, with a question’s context going to OnNote first, OnAny every message, and Terminal, Picks, Interrupt and the writers stand for the terminal, the picker, an interrupt and the output. OnStatus is given each status line’s label and each logged command’s step, and Showing returns the one showing now, for a test that checks slow work runs under its status line (status lines). A msg.Recorder keeps the messages it’s given. Set a msg.Fake’s OnInfo or OnWarn to the recorder’s Add, then compare its Names or its IDs. backendtest.Stored is the fake backend with its disks on the host, for the free-space checks. The proxy’s child in a test’s process gets IO’s confine, a confinement that confines nothing (noConfine), because confineChild would confine the test’s whole process on Linux. ChildMain uses confineChild only when the field is nil, and runChildOn refuses to start without one. A test of confineChild’s own logic calls confineWith with a confinement of its own. A test’s server made with newServer looks up its names and connects in the test’s process, because newChildServer gives it the broker itself. The tests that run the child over a real socketpair (inProcess) send every lookup and connection through the broker instead, and a broker in a test connects through a seam of its own (broker.net’s connect) wherever it could reach the internet. internal/landlock’s TestSelf runs the test binary again as a child that confines itself and logs what it could still do. It runs only without cgo (CGO_ENABLED=0), as CI’s nocgo job and a hand run on a Linux host do, and skips under the race detector, whose cgo keeps Go from reaching every thread. The CLI tests’ devvm is built without cgo, so on Linux their VMs’ proxies’ children run confined too.
data.goroutine-leaks#Goroutine leaks:
A goroutine that outlives its test is one that would outlive its command in devvm, such as a tunnel the proxy carries after it has closed, or a goroutine that passes signals on after its child has ended. internal/leaktest finds them in every package that starts goroutines: internal/proxy, vmssh, daemon, desktop, ui, vm, backend/lima, platform, cli, gitprotect, vmlog and memnet. It imports only the standard library, so the proxy’s and the daemon’s tests use it too.
leaktest.Main(m), in a package’s TestMain, runs the tests and, once they’ve passed, reads every goroutine’s stack. It gives the goroutines that are still ending, such as a closed listener’s accept loop, five seconds, then fails the test binary with the stacks of any still running. It leaves out the standard library’s own goroutines that outlive every test and that no test can end, which allowed lists with why: signal.Notify’s loop and an HTTP client’s idle connections. It then reads Go’s goroutineleak profile, which names each goroutine blocked for good on a channel, a lock or a wait group that nothing still running can reach, and fails on any it names. A TestMain that makes the test binary a helper process runs the helper first and calls leaktest.Main last. leaktest.Check(t), called first in a test, fails that test when a goroutine started while it ran is still running once it has ended, its context cancelled and its cleanups run, after the same five seconds. It counts the goroutines the test started, and theirs, followed through those still running, so a test running in parallel doesn’t count. Nor does a goroutine that a server shared between tests starts for the test, such as a server that TestMain or a sync.Once started. That goroutine leads back to the server’s own goroutine, which ran before the test, and Main finds such goroutines at the end. Check’s failure names the test, where Main’s names only the binary, so a test of something that starts and stops goroutines, such as a link session, the port forwarder or the desktop’s relay, calls it. Anything Main or Check finds is a leak to fix, with a test that fails without the fix. Only a goroutine that the standard library starts and that outlives every test goes in allowed. A new package that starts goroutines gets a main_test.go that calls leaktest.Main, which the structure test checks, and the structure test also lists every goroutine devvm’s code starts, with what waits for it to end (goroutineSites).
data.slots#Slots:
A host with spare cores and memory can run the sections at once, each set in a sandbox of its own called a slot. mise run e2e -- --slots N spreads the chosen sections over N slots, from 1 to 9, and runs each slot as a --slot K run of its own, all at the same time. The default is one slot, which is the run described above. Slot 0 is the sandbox in the table, and slot K adds -K to its Lima home, state folder, Keychain service and lock, as ~/.lt-e2e-go-1, /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-1, devvm-go-e2e-1 and /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-1.lock. Each fixed port the checks use is slot 0’s plus 100 times the slot, so slot 1’s servers use 47260 where slot 0’s use 47160. Slot 0’s ports run from 47160 to 47199, from 47240 to 47249, and 47613, 18765 and 18766, so no two slots ever share one.
e2e places the longest sections first, each in the slot with the least time so far, using each section’s time from its last complete run. A section that has never run gets a guess, from 2 minutes for gc and clone to 30 minutes for from. link always goes in the same slot as from when both run, because in the --from tier link’s Alpine client starts from the image that from builds. Each slot runs its own sections in the usual order, and a slot left without a section isn’t started. When go isn’t on your PATH, e2e finds mise’s Go once and puts its folder first on the slots’ PATH, because slots that each ran mise exec at the same time would each install the repo’s tools over one another. With --from, e2e passes --every-feature to every slot, so each slot’s base has every feature, as a single --from run’s has.
Before the slots start, e2e takes every slot’s lock and gives each other slot what slot 0 has and it lacks: every image’s Lima instance and record, every tool image and its record, and devvm’s caches. It clones the large files and never copies them whole: on macOS each one is an APFS clone, which needs both folders on one APFS volume, and on Linux a reflink. The records and the --from digests are small files, so e2e copies them. When a file can’t be cloned, as on a Linux host whose /tmp is tmpfs, e2e says so and that slot builds its own. With --clean, nothing is cloned, and each slot deletes its own cached images instead. A --slot K run of your own uses that slot’s images as they are.
Each slot’s output appears as it comes, each line led by its slot’s number, such as [1], and stays in the slot’s e2e.log. When every slot has ended, e2e prints each slot’s sections, results and time, then the sums: checks passed, failed, skipped and retried, the failed checks by name, and the time the whole run took. The run fails when any slot fails or ends without its results. TERM or Ctrl+C stops every slot with TERM, and each one cleans up as a single run does.
Testing on other hosts says how many slots each kind of host runs. Testing on other hosts also covers Linux hosts, x86_64 and the checks to run by hand.
data.stubs#Stubs:
