The stubs stand in for every host command devvm runs, so tests never run the real tools: limactl, docker, security, ssh, ssh-add, ssh-agent, ssh-keygen, qemu-img, qemu-system-aarch64, qemu-system-x86_64, chflags, tmutil, sw_vers, uname, open, code, mise, and the clipboard tools wl-paste, wl-copy, xclip, osascript and pbcopy, which read a clipboard the test lays out in $STUB_DIR (clip-types, clip, clip-file) and write what’s copied to $STUB_DIR/copied. They are one Go program, internal/stubtest/stub, which does what the command it’s run as would do: the binary is named stub, each command’s name is a link to it, and it reads its name from its argv[0]. internal/stubtest builds it once, into $TMPDIR/devvm-stubs- with its links, where the hash covers the stub’s sources and Go’s version. Every test process, and every later run until the sources change, finds that folder and uses it, so the binary builds only once, and a folder of an older build is removed once it’s a day old. TestScript puts that folder on PATH right after devvm’s, ahead of the real commands.
Each stub logs its call to $STUB_LOG as one line, its name and its arguments joined by spaces. The stub writes the line itself, in one write to the log opened for appending, so lines from stubs running at once never mix, and its arguments never go to another process’s command line. That matters because endpoint security tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon kill a process whose arguments look like an ssh option next to a proxy URL with a password, which is what a start’s limactl edit passes. stub_calls prints the log for stdout or cmp to check, ! stub_calls fails if anything was logged, and stub_reset empties the log, so the next check sees only the calls after it:
exec devvm … stub_calls cmp stdout calls -- calls -- limactl list uname and sw_vers pretend to be another host when these are set, and run the real command otherwise:
Variable Printed by STUB_UNAME_S uname -s STUB_UNAME_M uname -m STUB_SW_VERS sw_vers -productVersion What the stubs keep between their calls is their state, $STUB_DIR/state.json, which internal/stubtest/stubstate reads and writes as typed JSON under a file lock, so stubs running at once never lose each other’s changes. It holds Lima’s instances, each with its status, size and config, the Keychain’s items, the SSH agent and its keys, and Time Machine’s exclusions. Scripts read and change it with the stub command, and Go tests with the stubtest.Stubs methods VM, Size, VMs, Keychain and SetKeychain:
Command What it does stub vm NAME STATUS Lima lists the instance NAME in STATUS, such as Stopped, Running or Broken, with Lima’s default size when it’s new stub vms prints Lima’s instances, one NAME STATUS line each, sorted stub size NAME CPUS MEMORY DISK gives an instance its size, with the memory and disk in bytes stub keychain ACCOUNT prints the Keychain’s item for ACCOUNT, and fails when there’s none stub keychain-set ACCOUNT saves the item for ACCOUNT from its input, so the value is in no process’s arguments stub agent prints the SSH agent’s keys as ssh-add -l lists them, and fails when no agent runs stub agent-stop stops the SSH agent stub names prints every stub’s name A switch is a file a test makes in $STUB_DIR to change what a stub does, such as start-fails, which makes limactl start fail. The comment above each stub’s function lists its switches, and every switch is named for the command and what happens to it: -fails, -hangs, -fails-on and -waits-on, where an -on switch holds the text that a call’s arguments must contain. A stub that hangs touches $STUB_DIR/hanging first, so wait_file can wait for it. The files a stub writes in $STUB_DIR are what a test checks, such as $STUB_DIR/sync.tar, what a VM’s setup was sent.
limactl keeps its instances in the state and fails or hangs on request. It keeps each instance’s size and config as create, clone and edit set them, and a contract test checks that it does so as real Lima does. Its shell reaches the guest, the VM the stubs make believe in, which ssh reaches too. One module, guest.go, answers whatever devvm runs in a VM, with one set of switches whichever way devvm gets there. limactl shell is also the shell devvm opens in a VM, which then ends, so a script sees it as devvm’s last call. In the shared tools’ build VM, its shell writes the images build.sh is asked for into the build’s folder (or, on request, a symlink instead), and it keeps what a VM’s setup is sent as $STUB_DIR/sync.tar. A base build’s packages go in as $STUB_DIR/packages-in.tar, and what the build gives back is $STUB_DIR/packages-out.tar, or no packages. In the --from build VM, its shell writes what oci/build.sh would (or, on request, a hostile disk, command line, C library or symlink), and a call naming $STUB_DIR/interrupt-on’s text interrupts devvm, as Ctrl+C would. The VM’s ssh host keys are one made-up key for each VM, unless $STUB_DIR/hostkeys-fails exists.
docker stands in only for what --from asks of it. It has an image only when $STUB_DIR/docker-image holds its ID, its save writes a tarball naming that image (or $STUB_DIR/docker-saved’s, a tag that moved), and it isn’t running when $STUB_DIR/docker-down exists. ssh answers a port forwarder’s master with $STUB_DIR/guest-ports, and a link session’s master listens on its control socket. Either master outlives the process that started it, as ssh’s does, until the sandbox’s cleanup stops it or 5 minutes pass. A direct connection from a VM (the self-check’s) fails, as a confined VM’s does, unless $STUB_DIR/net-direct exists. A --clone VM’s git and its seed’s scripts run on the host, with real bash, git and tar, on $STUB_DIR/vmfs/, and ssh fetches from there (it fails with $STUB_DIR/ssh-fails). A clone’s command fails, as any shell does, when $STUB_DIR/shell-fails-on holds text its arguments hold, such as index-pack for the seed’s apply. security stands in for the Keychain and tmutil for Time Machine, both keeping their items in the state, never in the real ones. mise writes $MISE_STUB_LOCK as the lock ($MISE_STUB_OLDER_LOCK for a list of versions), lists $MISE_STUB_VERSIONS, and fails like mise offline with MISE_STUB_FAIL set. chflags sets no flags, so .git protection leaves test folders deletable. qemu-img and QEMU are there so Linux hosts pass devvm’s checks.
To add a stub, write its function in internal/stubtest/stub, with a comment that says what it does and lists its switches, and add it to stubs() under the command’s name. It logs its call with c.log() first, keeps what it must remember in the state through c.update, and reads its switches with c.on and c.text. A new command the state needs goes in control. To add a switch, read it in the stub’s function, name it for what it does as above, and add it to that function’s comment. Each stub has unit tests in stub_test.go, which run it in the test’s own process. Where a stub prints what devvm parses, such as limactl list --json, the golden fixtures check that it prints what the real tool prints.
devvm runs in $WORK or a folder made in it (mkdir, then cd), never in HOME or devvm’s own folders, which it refuses as project folders.
data.the-tests-behind-how-it-works#The tests:
The How it works pages say in words what the tests of a mechanism check, and this section names those tests, so you can find the one to extend when you change the mechanism. Each unit test is named with its package, the CLI tests are files in testdata/script/, and the end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e, in the section the page names. The design notes name the tests of each emulation themselves (design notes).
How the proxy puts secrets in: TestCheckName, TestCheckHost, TestCheckHeader, TestCheckEnv, TestCheckPrefix, TestDefine and TestChangeApply, in internal/secrets, check what a secret of yours may be and what devvm secret set’s flags change. TestReservedEnvAssets and TestEnvReservedForSecrets, in internal/netpolicy, check the variables a secret can’t take. TestInjectSecretShapes and TestSchemeOK, in internal/proxy, check each shape a value goes in and each that keeps the placeholder, and TestPathWithin, TestForRequestMethods and TestInterceptSecretMethods that a binding’s path and methods let it in only for the requests they match. TestGetChecksTheBinding checks that a binding that isn’t the secret’s as it’s saved gets nothing, TestValueMax and TestKeychainLine, in internal/platform, that a value too long for the Keychain’s line is refused, and TestPlaceholders the placeholders’ one shape. TestCustomStore, TestCustomsUnreadable and TestWriteFilesCustom check the list, its mode and its checks, TestValuesCachedByBinding, in internal/proxy, that two bindings of one name are cached apart, and TestCustomSecrets, in internal/vm, use, a new value and the question before a delete. The CLI tests are secret_custom.txtar and layout.txtar, and the end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e’s network section. The VM’s CA: TestInitCA, TestInitCASwitch, TestInitCAReplaced, TestInitCATogether and TestInitCACancelled, in internal/trust, TestPrepareOpen, in internal/netpolicy, and TestNextCASigns, TestLoadCA and TestServersApart. The CLI tests are network.txtar, sync.txtar and layout.txtar. Logins made in a VM: TestCaptureLogin, TestCapturePaths, TestCaptureEarlyHintsAnswerAndSaved, TestCaptureErrorPasses, TestCaptureRefuses and TestCaptureGet, in internal/proxy, check what goes out, what the VM gets and what’s refused. TestCodexCapture, TestOpencodeCapture, TestClaudeCapture, TestClaudeSetupToken, TestClaudeOAuthGet, TestCaptureRefuses, TestEndpoints and TestPick, in internal/agentlogin, check each agent’s file, its placeholders and copies, and its refresh. TestOneClaudeLogin, TestClaudeBindings and TestClaudeOAuthVMCopy, in internal/secrets, check the one Claude Code login and its bindings, and TestCapturer and TestCaptureOwnAgents, in internal/netpolicy, the endpoints in every VM’s config and which agent a capture is. TestAgentLoginTerminal, in internal/vm, and TestTerminal, in internal/ui, check that an agent’s login gets the terminal’s files only when devvm’s input and output are both terminals. The end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e’s network section. Agents’ logins and settings: TestFormatsWithholdUnknown plants a field that no format knows in every login file, ~/.claude.json included, and checks that no VM’s copy holds it. Learning from the log: TestTickable checks that no name devvm network lock ticks is a shared-hosting domain or under one. A company’s CA in builds: tests/e2e’s images section checks that a layer built with a test CA trusts it while its script runs and keeps its key once the folder is emptied, and that a copy of its image booted without devvm has none of devvm’s CA files. Its project and tools sections check a company’s CA in a VM, which tests/e2e runs on real VMs.
data.time-and-lifecycles#Time and lifecycles:
A test of a timeout, a grace or a close, such as the relay’s grace, the forwarder’s close or the proxy’s ClientHello deadline, runs in a testing/synctest bubble, synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { … }), rather than sleeping on the real clock. Inside the bubble, time is fake and moves only when every goroutine of the test is blocked, so time.Sleep(30 * time.Second) returns at once, and synctest.Wait() returns once every other goroutine has done what it can. Such a test takes no time, and a loaded CI machine can’t make it fail, so it never needs the margins a real-clock test does.
A test checks that something happens at the moment it’s due and not a nanosecond before. It sleeps to just short of the moment, calls synctest.Wait() and checks, then sleeps the last nanosecond and checks again. A goroutine that never ends fails the bubble as a deadlock, and a test of something that starts and stops goroutines calls leaktest.Check(t) before the bubble as well.
Time moves only while each goroutine waits on something inside the bubble: a channel, a timer, time.Sleep, a sync.Cond or a wait group. A socket’s read, a process’s wait or any system call that blocks keeps it from moving, so the code under test gets seams. Like every test seam, each one is a field that a test sets to a stand-in in memory:
internal/memnet is a network in memory for tests. memnet.Pipe() makes a connection, and a memnet.Network holds listeners by address, whose Listen, Dial and DialContext stand in for a socket’s. Its connections close their writing side alone (CloseWrite), as TCP’s do and net.Pipe’s don’t. They hold up to 64 KiB that the other end hasn’t read before a write waits, as a socket’s buffer does. They have deadlines on the bubble’s clock, and so do its listeners, through SetDeadline. It uses only the standard library, so the proxy’s tests use it. The forwarder and the link sessions take their listeners from their Listen fields, so a test gives them a memnet.Network’s. The relays carry each connection through an sshRelay, whose start field starts its ssh -W. In production it’s execSSH, and a test’s stand-in, memSSH, is a VM in memory that sends what the test tells it and ends only when its context does, as exec.CommandContext kills ssh. The proxy connects to the far ends through its egress’s connect field, which memServe points at a memnet.Network while it serves the proxy on a listener in memory. A daemon.Proc asks its Alive, Args and Signal fields about its process, so a test of Stop gives it a process table of its own (fakeProc). A test’s own HTTP server, when the test sends the requests itself, is httptest.NewTestServer’s, which serves in memory, and the test sends through its Client(), which reaches it whatever the request’s host. A stand-in can’t show what the real thing does with a kernel’s buffers, a real ssh or a real process, so each kind of lifecycle keeps one test that runs the real one, on the real clock: TestPipeSSHGrace, TestPipeSSHGraceSlowClient and TestPipeSSHGraceWriteError run the relay with an ssh stand-in on PATH, TestForwarderEndsStuckRelay closes a forward whose relay’s ssh never ends, TestLinksBurst fills a link’s real Unix socket, TestSpliceKeepsAnEarlyAnswer splices over TCP and TestProcStop stops real processes. A new seam keeps the real test of its kind.
The proxy’s tests that start a whole proxy, such as TestMainRuns and TestAgentRelay, run its child in the test’s process (inProcess), on real sockets, so they can’t run in a bubble. Their broker waits testStartWait, 30 seconds, for the child to say it’s ready, through IO’s startWait field, where devvm’s own proxy waits 4 seconds, and each test waits as long for the proxy to listen (retryFor). Under the race detector on a loaded Linux host, those starts can take more than 4 seconds, most of it spent hashing the test’s executable, which each broker does as it starts, so a wait of 4 seconds would fail them.

data:
These pages take you from installing devvm to working in your first VM.
Installing: what devvm needs on your machine, how to install it with Homebrew or the install script, and how to check it with devvm doctor. Your first VM: making a VM for a project folder, logging Claude Code in, starting the agent, and coming back to the VM later. Everyday commands: devvm’s commands in the groups devvm --help shows, with the options for a new VM.

This page lists devvm’s commands in the groups that devvm --help shows them in, and each row links to the page with the details. devvm COMMAND --help shows a command’s examples and flags, the command line covers what works the same in every command, and the CLI reference has every command with all its flags.
data.change-your-vm#Change your VM: devvm tools in a terminal, choose this folder’s VM’s toolchains and agents in a list, then open a shell in it, and otherwise show its shared tools, each with its version and any newer one (details) devvm tools add TOOL... add shared tools to this folder’s VM, such as devvm tools add python claude, then open a shell in it (details) devvm tools rm TOOL... take shared tools out of this folder’s VM, such as devvm tools rm python claude, then open a shell in it devvm tools update move this folder’s VM to the newest shared tools, and only those, then open a shell in it (details) devvm size [--cpus N] [--memory GiB] [--disk GiB] show or change this folder’s VM’s CPUs, memory and disk (details) devvm size -g ... show or change the size new VMs get (details) devvm mount-cache [none] show how this folder’s VM caches its project folder on a Linux host, none, which new VMs get, or Lima’s mmap, which can lose writes, or switch it to none from the VM’s next start (details) devvm ports [all|none|LIST] show or change which ports this folder’s VM forwards to this machine’s localhost, even while it runs (details) devvm ports add|rm LIST forward more ports, or stop forwarding some (details) devvm ports -g ... show or change what new VMs forward (details) devvm network [open|internet|learn|allowlist|none] show this folder’s VM’s tier, open, internet, internet (learning), allowlist, none or unenforced, and then its allowlist, file by file, or give it a tier: between the confined tiers at once, and into or out of open from its next start, offering to restart a running VM now, and with learn, internet while it learns the hosts it needs (details) devvm network -g [open|internet|allowlist|none] show or change new VMs’ tier, which is allowlist until you change it (details) devvm network lock [--all] [--none] choose which of the hosts this folder’s VM learned it keeps, add them to its own rules, and give it the allowlist tier (details) devvm network allow|deny|rm RULE... [-g] add allow or deny rules to this folder’s VM’s own, or remove them, at once, and with -g, change yours for every VM (details) devvm network allow|deny|rm RULE... --method METHODS --path PATH narrow those rules to some of a host’s requests, such as only GET and HEAD (details) devvm network log [--follow] [-n N] [--blocked] show what this folder’s VM connected to and what its proxy blocked (details) devvm network transparent [on|off] show whether this folder’s VM sends tools that ignore the proxy settings to its proxy by the names they look up, and where that comes from, or give the VM its own setting, from its next launch (details) devvm ssh-agent [on|devvm|off] show this folder’s VM’s SSH agent forwarding, which is off, on for yours or devvm for devvm’s own, then the keys devvm’s own agent holds and those added to it, or change the forwarding from the VM’s next start (details) devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE [--confirm] [--lifetime DURATION] load a key into devvm’s own agent, and load it again whenever a VM needs it (details) devvm ssh-agent rm KEY_FILE take a key out of devvm’s own agent, so devvm doesn’t load it again (details) devvm git-protect [on|off] show or change this folder’s VM’s .git protection, while it’s stopped (details) devvm clone [on|off] [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home [--no-worktree-check]] [--no-clone-check] [--repos LIST] show whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, or make it again with one, or with the folder mounted, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details) devvm secret, devvm secret rm NAME list the secrets, whether each is saved and the VMs using it, or delete a saved one (details) devvm secret set claude|github [--stdin] save your Claude Code token or GitHub token on this machine, so that VMs get a placeholder and their proxy puts the secret in (details) devvm secret set NAME --host HOST --env VARIABLE save a secret of your own, such as an API key, which VMs that use it send only to its hosts (details) devvm secret use|unuse NAME let this folder’s VM use a secret, or stop it, though a VM with Claude Code always uses claude (details) devvm layer add LAYER... [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home [--no-worktree-check]] make this folder’s VM again with more layers on top, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details) devvm layer rm LAYER... [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home [--no-worktree-check]] make this folder’s VM again without some of its layers, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details)
data.devvm-itself#devvm itself: devvm help [COMMAND] print the help for devvm or a command, as --help and -h do (details) devvm --version print devvm’s version alone, as devvm version also does The folders devvm keeps its state in and the environment variables it reads are in Settings and files.
data.disk-space#Disk space: devvm space show what devvm keeps on this machine, the disk each kind takes, and what frees it (details) devvm gc delete the stale and unfinished images and the tool images no VM uses, after listing them, and never a VM (details) devvm retention [KEY=VALUE...] show the retention settings, which say what devvm deletes on its own, or change them, with KEY=off turning one off (details)
data.images#Images: devvm images list the images, then the shared tool images (details) devvm images rm IMAGE|KEY... delete images, by name or by the key devvm images shows (details) devvm build IMAGE build an image and the images under it, unless they’re built, such as devvm build docker or devvm build foo+bar, where IMAGE is base or layers and never a shared tool (details) devvm rebuild IMAGE build an image of base or layers again from its parent as it is, and delete the stale images no VM uses, while shared tools follow the tools lock instead (details) devvm layer new NAME start a layer of your own, ~/.config/devvm/layers/NAME.sh, with its allowlist, NAME.policy (details) devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm take --from IMAGE to work on a base made from that container image (details).
data.links-between-vms#Links between VMs: devvm link list this folder’s VM’s links, each with its name, port, target VM and folder, the target’s status, and whether the link applies (details) devvm link add TARGET PORT [--as NAME] link this folder’s VM to PORT of the VM that TARGET names, so programs in it reach the port as NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT (details) devvm link rm TARGET PORT remove one of this folder’s VM’s links (details) devvm link publish [PORTS] show the ports this folder’s VM publishes, or offer PORTS to links from any of your other VMs (details) devvm link unpublish PORTS stop offering ports to links (details) devvm group show the group this folder’s VM is in, with each of its VMs, the name the others reach it by, its folder and the ports it publishes (details) devvm group join NAME [--as NAME] put this folder’s VM in the group NAME, which its first VM makes, so each VM in the group reaches the ports the others publish (details) devvm group leave take this folder’s VM out of its group, removing the links the group made (details)
data.this-machine#This machine: devvm setup [--features LIST|none] [--agents LIST|none] [--layers LIST|none] choose base’s features and the coding agents and layers new VMs get, and in a terminal also new VMs’ size and network tier (details) devvm agent import [AGENT...] copy the agents’ settings and logins from your home folder into devvm’s agent store, which every VM gets them from, never their history, asking before it replaces the store’s (details) devvm agent login AGENT [--setup-token] [--device-code] [--api-key] log an agent in inside this folder’s VM, such as Claude Code to your Claude subscription, or get a Claude Code token with --setup-token (details), or log an agent in to ChatGPT there, in a browser on this machine or with a code, or save an API key, and keep the login in devvm’s agent store for every VM (details) devvm agent save [AGENT...] copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s agent store, never their logins or history, after showing what changed and asking (details) devvm doctor check what devvm needs on this machine and say how to get what’s missing (details) devvm upgrade [--check] [--to VERSION] install devvm’s newest release the way you installed devvm, after asking, or with --check only say whether a newer one is out (details) devvm completion SHELL print the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish (details) devvm limactl ARGS... run Lima’s limactl on the VMs and images in devvm’s own Lima home, not ~/.lima, for debugging, which starts VMs unconfined, whatever their tier (details)
data.working-on-a-clone#Working on a clone: devvm --clone make this folder’s VM with its own clone of the repo, copy your repo into it and open a shell in the clone (details) devvm clone fetch [--json] on this machine, fetch the VM’s work as devvm/ into every repo it has a clone of, with its Git LFS objects, to review before you merge it, and list the new or moved branches, each with its repos (details) devvm clone add PATH copy one more repo of a folder of repos into the VM, at the same path (details) devvm rm delete the VM, first offering to keep the work you haven’t fetched as saved/devvm/ branches (details) devvm clone on|off make an existing VM again with its own clone of the repo, or with the folder mounted once devvm has offered to keep the clone’s work as devvm rm does (details)
data.your-vm#Your VM:
devvm open a shell in this folder’s VM, at the same path, making the VM first with the toolchains, agents and layers you choose, or that --tools, --agents and --layers name (details) devvm restart stop this folder’s VM, start it again and open a shell in it, for changes that apply only when it starts (details) devvm stop stop this folder’s VM (details) devvm update [--force] [--no-export] [--clean-home [--no-worktree-check]] move this folder’s VM to the newest shared tools, and when its image or its devcontainer.json has changed, make it again from the image’s new build and the file as it is now, keeping its home folder and settings, after asking, then open a shell in it (details) devvm rm [--force] [--no-export] [--no-clone-check] [--no-worktree-check] delete this folder’s VM after asking, exporting its agents’ history first unless --no-export (details) devvm rm VM [--force] [--no-export] [--no-clone-check] [--no-worktree-check] delete a VM whose folder is gone, by its name or ssh alias, after asking (details), or one whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, only after asking in a terminal (details) devvm adopt use the VM made for an earlier folder at this path here (details), or the VM made for this folder before you moved or renamed it (details) devvm adopt VM move a VM whose folder is gone to this folder, such as a copy of that folder on another disk, after asking (details) devvm ls list the project VMs (details) devvm code get this folder’s VM ready as devvm host does, then open its folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH (VS Code and Cursor) devvm cursor get this folder’s VM ready as devvm host does, then open its folder in Cursor over Remote-SSH (VS Code and Cursor) devvm desktop [--clipboard] [--no-open] serve this folder’s VM’s desktop on 127.0.0.1 with its password until Ctrl+C, and open it in Screen Sharing on macOS (details) devvm host get this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, and show the host name they reach it by, such as devvm-website (details) devvm history list the exports of agents’ history that devvm saved in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports (details) devvm history export [FILE] save the history of this folder’s VM’s agents to FILE, or to a new .tar.gz in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports (details) devvm history import [FILE] put the agents’ history in FILE, or in the newest export devvm saved for this folder, into this folder’s VM (details) devvm paste [--json] [--send-file] send the image, the PDF, or the one copied file, after asking about a file, on this machine’s clipboard into this folder’s running VM’s paste folder, and copy its path there for your terminal’s paste shortcut (details) devvm paste rm [--force] delete the files devvm paste left in this folder’s running VM, after asking (details) In a folder without a VM of its own, each of these commands but devvm adopt uses the VM of the nearest folder with one that it’s inside, and says which VM that is. --here and --parent choose which VM a command uses (a subfolder).
These options are for a new VM, so a VM that exists ignores them with a warning, and only devvm takes them (what a new VM gets):
--tools LIST|none the toolchains the VM gets, such as --tools node,python, in place of those the folder’s files call for (details) --agents LIST|none the coding agents the VM gets, such as --agents claude,codex, in place of those devvm setup chose (details) --layers LIST|none the layers the VM’s image gets, bottom first, such as --layers docker, in place of those devvm setup chose (details) --network TIER create the VM on a network tier: open reaches anything this machine can, internet any public host, allowlist, the default, only the hosts you allow, and none only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts and its links --clone create the VM with its own clone of the repo, or of each repo in a folder of repos, instead of mounting the folder (details) --repos all|none|LIST with --clone in a folder of repos, the repos the VM gets a clone of, such as --repos frontend,backend, in place of the picker (details) --no-git-protect create the VM without .git protection --ssh-agent create the VM forwarding your SSH agent, so while you’re connected, anything in it can use your keys (details) --unsafe-folder mount a folder that devvm refuses, such as one that is or holds your home folder (details) --cpus N, --memory GiB, --disk GiB the VM’s size (details) --ports all|none|LIST which ports the VM forwards (details) --from IMAGE start its base from a container image, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu’s cloud image (details) --no-devcontainer create the VM without reading the folder’s devcontainer.json, which otherwise describes the VM as far as devvm supports it, with the options you give taking priority (details)

data: This page assumes you’ve installed devvm and that devvm doctor finds nothing missing.
data.claude-codes-login#Claude Code’s login:
If the VM has Claude Code, log it in to your Claude account once. Run this in a terminal on this machine, not the VM’s shell, in the project folder:
devvm agent login claude Open the address it shows in a browser, approve the login, and paste the code the browser shows. devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with Claude Code, and the VMs get only a placeholder (Claude Code login). If you already use an agent on this machine, devvm agent import copies its settings and logins into devvm’s agent store instead (devvm’s agent store).
data.coming-back-to-it#Coming back to it:
The VM belongs to its folder, and its subfolders use it too (a subfolder):
devvm # a shell in this folder's VM, started if it's stopped devvm tools # choose its toolchains and agents devvm tools add claude # add Claude Code to this folder's VM devvm code # open it in VS Code devvm stop # stop it devvm ls # list every VM devvm rm # delete it after asking, saving its agents' history first Everyday commands lists the rest, and managing VMs covers restarting, deleting and moving VMs. Before you let an agent loose in the VM, read staying safe.
data.making-the-vm#Making the VM:
Run devvm in a project folder.
cd ~/some-project devvm Answer the first-run questions. The first time, devvm asks for the CPUs and memory new VMs get, the coding agents they get, and the optional extras the base image gets, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. These set devvm’s defaults for every new VM, and devvm setup changes them later (devvm setup).
Check the summary. devvm shows what this folder’s new VM gets: the toolchains your folder’s files call for, the agents and layers you chose for new VMs, its size, its network tier and its ports.
==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets: toolchain node, for package.json agent claude, from devvm setup layers: none size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk network tier: allowlist ports: all Customize it? [y/N] Confirm, or customize it. Confirm to make the VM as shown, or customize it to choose its toolchains, coding agents, layers, network tier, ports and size first (what a new VM gets). Flags such as --agents claude choose a part beforehand, and devvm asks nothing when the flags choose everything.
Tip
Keep allowlist, the default, unless the VM needs more. The allowlist network tier limits the VM to the hosts you allow, and every tier keeps your secrets on your machine. When you don’t know yet which hosts the project needs, choose learn: the VM reaches any public host while it learns them, and devvm network lock then keeps the ones you choose on the allowlist tier (learning the hosts a VM needs).
Wait for the base image. The first time, devvm builds it with the extras you chose, which takes a few minutes once, and later VMs start in seconds (images).
==> building image base (e9f517dddef1) a few minutes, and Ubuntu's cloud image to download the first time (details: ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/20261024-090616-83541.log) ==> image base ready ==> creating devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c from base ==> starting devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c Then devvm opens a shell in the VM at the same path, ~/some-project, with (devvm) at the start of the prompt.
data.starting-the-agent#Starting the agent:
Start the agent in the VM’s shell, so it runs in the VM:
~/some-project $ devvm (devvm) ~/some-project $ claude Run the agent the VM has by its name, such as claude, which the supported agents table lists (running an agent).
data.whats-in-the-vm#What’s in the VM: Your project folder, read-write, so your editor and the VM share the same files. It’s the only folder of yours the VM sees, and its .git hooks and config are locked, except on a Linux host that can’t lock them, such as Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, where devvm only watches them (.git protection). The toolchains, ready at once (toolchains). Your git name and email, so commits made in the VM are yours. Ports: a dev server on :5173 in the VM opens at localhost:5173 on your machine (ports). sudo without a password, so apt install works as on any Ubuntu machine.
data.working-on-a-clone-instead#Working on a:
To keep the VM out of your working tree and .git entirely, make it with its own clone of the repo:
devvm --clone # a VM with its own clone of your branches git fetch devvm # later, on this machine: the VM's work as devvm/ git log -p main..devvm/main # review it before you merge it Use it for an agent working unattended, a repo you don’t trust, or on a Linux host whose kernel doesn’t let devvm protect .git (working on a clone).

data: This page gets devvm installed and checked on your machine. Upgrading and uninstalling covers what comes later.
data.checking-what-devvm-needs#Checking what:
Run devvm doctor:
devvm doctor It lists everything that devvm’s backend, Lima, needs and doesn’t have, each with what to do, then its warnings, such as a machine with less than the recommended memory, and it fails only when something is missing. devvm never installs anything on this machine itself, and every command that needs the backend checks it first and stops at the first thing that’s missing. What devvm doctor checks lists each check and warning.
When devvm doctor finds nothing missing, you’re ready for your first VM. Before you make it, read staying safe, which lists the habits that close most of what devvm leaves open.
data.installing-devvm#Installing devvm:
Run the command for your system:
macOSLinux # Install devvm, and Lima with it brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm The install script in the Linux tab also works on macOS.
# Install devvm and what it needs curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash The script asks before it installs Lima, QEMU or access to /dev/kvm.
Install devvm one way, with Homebrew or with the install script, but not both (one devvm). The install script needs curl, tar, and sha256sum or shasum, it never needs sudo for devvm itself, and it checks the download’s checksum and signature before it installs anything (Installing and updating). To check the script itself against devvm’s release key before you run it, follow checking the install script. It takes options after bash -s --, as in curl -fsSL … | bash -s -- --yes:
Option What it does --yes answer yes to every question --version 0.1.0, or DEVVM_VERSION=0.1.0 install that release --no-deps install devvm only --force install even when Homebrew installed devvm, which leaves you with two copies DEVVM_PREFIX=/some/dir install under that folder instead of ~/.local
data.requirements#Requirements:
devvm runs its VMs on Lima, its default backend. It’s tested on Apple silicon Macs and on Linux on both arm64 and x86_64, but not yet on Intel Macs (Known limits). The last column says whether the install script offers to install a requirement for you.
macOSLinux You need To check To get it The install script macOS at Lima’s minimum, on arm64 or x86_64 sw_vers and uname -m doesn’t 8 GiB of memory and 4 CPUs, recommended sysctl hw.memsize hw.ncpu doesn’t Lima at its minimum limactl --version brew install lima, or Lima’s install guide offers it: Homebrew’s when you have Homebrew, otherwise Lima’s latest release into ~/.local OpenSSH 8.7 or newer, for ssh and editors by name (details) ssh -V macOS 13’s has it doesn’t Docker Desktop, only for --from with an image only Docker has docker version Docker Desktop doesn’t You need To check To get it The install script Linux on arm64 or x86_64 uname -m doesn’t 8 GiB of memory and 4 CPUs, recommended free -g and nproc doesn’t Lima at its minimum limactl --version brew install lima, or Lima’s install guide offers it: Homebrew’s when you have Homebrew, otherwise Lima’s latest release into ~/.local QEMU qemu-img --version your package manager: apt, dnf, pacman or zypper offers it, with sudo Access to /dev/kvm ls -l /dev/kvm sudo usermod -aG kvm $USER, then log out and back in offers it, with sudo OpenSSH 8.7 or newer, for ssh and editors by name (details) ssh -V Ubuntu 22.04’s has it doesn’t Docker’s engine, only for --from with an image only Docker has docker version Docker’s engine doesn’t A smaller machine works too. devvm gives base fewer CPUs and less memory there (size and ports). Your first VM needs 8 GiB of free disk space, for the base image, the VM’s own image and the shared tools (free space). Everything else goes inside the VMs, including the toolchains, the coding agents and Docker for your projects (docker layer), so you don’t install any of the supported coding agents on this machine (devvm’s agent store). Linux hosts have a few limits, such as .git protection that needs a kernel which lets devvm use a user namespace, which Ubuntu 23.10 and newer don’t by default (Known limits).

data:
These pages explain how devvm does what the other sections describe, for readers who want to check a claim, such as security reviewers and agents. They name the files devvm ships and the messages it prints. You don’t need them to use devvm.
Overview: what devvm does, step by step, when it makes, opens, stops and deletes a VM, and the state files it keeps. Installing and updating: what the install script downloads and checks, devvm doctor --json, devvm’s own files, and upgrading. Images and caching: how images and shared tools are built, keyed and cached, and how devvm checks what they start from. Port forwarding: how devvm’s forwarder forwards a VM’s ports to your machine. The desktop: how devvm desktop serves a VM’s desktop on your machine, checks its password and keeps your clipboard out, and why devvm doesn’t forward X11. Network tiers: each tier’s confinement, the proxy, the self-check, and how secrets get into requests. .git protection: what devvm locks, when it checks the locks, and what they can’t stop. Security model: what devvm protects on your machine and how, and what it doesn’t protect. Backends: each backend’s features, native or emulated, and what happens when one is missing. Lima: devvm’s Lima home, confinement, clones and port forwarding on Lima. Processes: what each of devvm’s processes holds, reads, writes and is confined by, the listeners a VM’s bytes reach, and why devvm is written in Go. Coding agents: how the agents’ settings, logins and history reach a VM, and what devvm checks when it imports, saves and exports them. Why devvm is built this way, what failed and what’s still open is in the design notes, under Contributing.

This page explains how devvm gives the coding agents in a VM their settings, logins and history, and what it checks on the way, for the tasks that Coding agents shows. How the proxy holds the agents’ secrets is in agents’ logins and settings.
data.api-keys#API keys:
The proxy puts in opencode’s and pi’s API keys for the providers that API keys the proxy puts in lists, in the headers it names. OpenRouter’s key goes in either of its two headers, because pi sends it in x-api-key for OpenRouter’s Anthropic models, as Anthropic’s own API takes a key, and in Authorization for every other model. The proxy swaps the placeholder only when the header holds the placeholder and nothing else, or for Authorization, Bearer, one space and the placeholder, which is how opencode and pi send each of these keys. A header that holds anything else beside the placeholder, or a second header of the same name, keeps the placeholder, so code in the VM can’t surround your key with text of its own, which a provider that quotes part of a key it refuses could show back to it.
The placeholder for an OpenAI key starts with sk-, as an OpenAI API key does, because pi takes an OpenAI key that starts any other way for a Sign in with ChatGPT login and then leaves settings such as the longest reply it wants out of its requests.
The placeholder keeps a key out of the VM only from the launch that first gives the VM the placeholder. A VM that was given one of these keys as it was before then, such as through [pass-keys] when the proxy didn’t put that provider’s key in, may still hold copies of it. They can be in opencode’s database, its write-ahead log and its freed pages, in the disk’s free space and anywhere that the VM’s own code copied the key. While opencode in the VM fails to import the placeholder, devvm’s record of opencode’s last import, ~/.local/state/devvm/opencode-import.json, holds the key too.
With some of these keys, code in the VM can make a credential of its own that works without the proxy. Google Gemini’s key gets an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. xAI’s key gets a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and OpenAI’s key gets one that lasts up to 2 hours. opencode’s experimental voice mode asks for these itself, so the proxy allows those requests (attack vectors). Some of these providers’ own tools also fetch the URLs that a request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, so code in the VM can reach hosts that the allowlist doesn’t have through them, as it can through Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s.
data.claude-codes-login#Claude Code’s login:
devvm agent login claude runs Claude Code’s own login in the VM, and the VM’s proxy saves the login as it reaches Claude’s token endpoint, and Claude Code in the VM gets only placeholders. devvm then sets the VM up again, so it uses the login at once, and every other VM with Claude Code gets it from its next launch.
A VM gets either ~/.claude/.credentials.json or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from devvm, never both, because Claude Code would use the token in its environment over the login in its file. A VM that started with the login devvm replaced keeps working, because its proxy puts the login devvm keeps now in place of either placeholder. The VM gets placeholders whatever its network tier.
The VM’s setup merges devvm’s copy of the login into the VM’s own ~/.claude/.credentials.json, because Claude Code keeps more than its Claude login in that file, such as its logins to MCP servers under mcpOAuth, which hold an MCP server’s tokens and, while a login is under way, its PKCE verifier. devvm sends its copy beside the setup as claude-credentials.json, and the setup’s merge_claude_credentials replaces the VM’s claudeAiOauth with the copy’s, or takes it out when the copy has none, and keeps every other key of the VM’s file. It reads the file with jq and writes the result whole, mode 600, to a temp file in ~/.cache, which neither an export of the VM’s history nor a VM made again carries, and then moves it over the file. When the VM’s file is a link, isn’t JSON or isn’t one JSON object, the copy replaces it and the setup says so, and a link is taken away first, so the move never writes through it. When it’s a folder, the setup leaves it as it is and says so. When the move fails, the setup removes the temp file and fails. A write that Claude Code makes to the file between the setup’s read and its move, such as a login to an MCP server that finishes in those milliseconds, is lost, and you make that login again. With a Claude Code token, devvm sends no copy, so the VM’s file stays as it is. Claude Code uses the token in its environment over any login left in the file, and that login’s placeholder gets the token at api.anthropic.com and nothing at mcp-proxy.anthropic.com (logins made in a VM).
The MCP servers’ logins stay in the VM. devvm agent save reads only the settings, an export of the VM’s history leaves ~/.claude/.credentials.json out and an import never writes it, and a VM made again doesn’t get it, so nothing of the VM’s file reaches devvm’s store, this machine or another VM. Only the store’s copy goes into the file, and it holds the placeholders alone.
data.claude-codes-plugins#Claude Code’s plugi:
Claude Code keeps everything of its plugins in one folder, ~/.claude/plugins unless CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR names another, and writes there as it runs: each plugin’s data in data/, which a plugin reaches as ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, the plugins it installs in cache, its marketplaces’ copies in marketplaces and their updates, its MCP bundles in mcpb, the plugins claude.ai synced in synced, its trash in .trash, and its records, such as installed_plugins.json. The store’s plugins folder is mounted read-only in every VM with Claude Code, because a VM that could write it could change what Claude Code runs in every other VM (the design note). So each VM’s ~/.claude/plugins is its own folder, on its own disk, and the store’s folder is the VM’s seed, Claude Code’s own support for a plugins folder it only reads. Every shell in the VM sets CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR to ~/.claude/plugins and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR to ~/.claude/plugins-seed, where the VM links the store’s folder. A seed is laid out as a plugins folder, with the marketplaces’ records in known_marketplaces.json, their copies in marketplaces and the plugins in cache. As Claude Code starts, it registers the seed’s marketplaces in the VM’s own folder, turns off their updates, and loads each plugin that enabledPlugins turns on from the seed’s cache, without copying it, and it never writes into the seed. It registers a marketplace from the seed only when the seed has its copy in marketplaces, so a marketplace from a folder on this machine, which Claude Code reads in place and never copies, isn’t one, and Claude Code in the VM adds it from extraKnownMarketplaces in settings.json only when that folder is in the VM too. In claude -p, Claude Code registers the seed’s marketplaces during the first session that the VM’s folder doesn’t have them yet, so a plugin’s hooks for the start of a session run from the next session on.
At every launch, the VM’s setup makes ~/.claude/plugins a folder of the VM’s own when it isn’t one, replacing a link there, and it links ~/.claude/plugins-seed to the store’s folder. A VM made again with other layers keeps its own plugins folder, as it keeps the rest of its home.
A store that devvm 0.1.0’s devvm agent import wrote can hold the whole of ~/.claude/plugins, each plugin’s data included, and every VM with Claude Code mounts the store’s folder whole. So every start, before the VM runs, takes out of the store’s plugins folder each entry that a seed doesn’t have and warns once, naming them. It leaves the folder itself, so no VM’s mounts change and its Lima config needs no edit. A VM that’s already running stops seeing the entries through its mount at once on macOS, while on a Linux host, whose 9p mounts cache what the VM has read, it can keep seeing what it read until its next start. devvm reaches the folder from its config folder, every part of the path below it a folder, never a link, which only a hand-made store has and which the VM’s mount would follow, perhaps to your own ~/.claude/plugins. It takes a link among the entries out without following it, and it leaves the temporary files that a devvm agent import or devvm agent save running at the same time writes known_marketplaces.json through. When it can’t take an entry out, or finds a link on the path, the start of a VM with Claude Code fails, naming the folder and what it should hold, rather than give the VM what it would read, and the start of any other VM warns.
devvm agent import and devvm agent save copy only what a seed has, so neither copies what each machine keeps of its own. The save’s script in the VM excludes, by name, every other entry of the VM’s ~/.claude/plugins when it’s a folder and not a link, and devvm saves nothing when the VM sends any other entry of it, as for any path outside the agents’ settings. The VM’s folder holds only what the VM added to its seed, so the save adds the files that the VM’s folder has and changes those that differ, but it never takes a file out of the store’s folder. The save merges the VM’s known_marketplaces.json into the store’s. It renames each path in the VM’s records that leads to the VM’s own plugins folder to the store’s folder, where every VM mounts it, and then each marketplace whose copy is in the store’s marketplaces, by a path without . or .. parts, replaces the store’s of the same name. The others stay as the store has them, because a seed can’t use them. They are the ones that Claude Code registered from the seed, whose copies are at the seed’s link, which are the store’s own, and those that Claude Code reads where they are, such as a folder in the VM. So a save that changes no marketplace leaves the file as it is. devvm leaves the file out with a warning when it isn’t a JSON object. The save’s script sends an entry whose name has a wildcard’s character, such as *, rather than exclude it by a pattern that could match other names, so devvm then saves nothing, naming it.
An export of a VM’s history leaves out the VM’s ~/.claude/plugins, and an import of one leaves out both it and ~/.claude/plugins-seed. The VM’s plugins folder holds settings, not history. The plugins it installed reach another VM only through devvm agent save, after you read its diff, and each plugin’s data can hold the plugin’s own logins and large caches, which an export on this machine would keep. A new VM gets the store’s plugins from its seed again.
data.codexs-and-opencodes-logins#Codex’s and:
The proxy reads the real API keys and logins from the login files in devvm’s store as it needs them and refreshes ChatGPT logins there. The proxy puts in opencode’s API keys for the providers that API keys the proxy puts in lists, and its OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins. The VM’s entry for such an API key holds only its type and the placeholder, so the entry’s other fields, such as its metadata, stay on this machine.
The VM’s copy of Codex’s auth.json holds only what Codex needs for its API key and its ChatGPT login: the placeholders, how it logs in, when it last refreshed, and the IDs of the account and the login. devvm keeps every other field on this machine, because the VM’s proxy can’t put it in, and it names those fields at every launch. That includes Codex’s other ways to log in, such as a personal access token or an Amazon Bedrock key, so Codex in a VM can’t use them. devvm treats Claude Code’s account state in ~/.claude.json the same way, so the VM gets only the account fields that Claude Code writes there today, and devvm names any other field at every launch.
devvm keeps every other entry of opencode’s auth.json on this machine too, because devvm doesn’t know which hosts it’s for, so the VM gets that entry without its key or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each at every launch. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as Azure’s or a local model server’s, a well-known login, which an organization’s own opencode config sets up, and any other OAuth login, such as Copilot Enterprise’s. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its enterpriseUrl and its expiry, so opencode in the VM doesn’t use that provider.
data.copies#Copies: devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json, so servers added in the VM stay (MCP servers). Your API key, your answers about API keys and your per-project entries never reach the VM. devvm also replaces the secrets in the agents’ settings files with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced. Those are the values under keys that look like secrets, every env value and header, and the secrets in URLs and in arguments. In other text, such as a hook’s command, devvm replaces the secrets in its URLs, the keys that start like a known key, such as sk- or ghp_, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, and keeps the words around them (keys in settings files). pi’s settings files that can hold a key are settings.json, models.json and mcp.json, so a provider’s apiKey in models.json reaches the VM as devvm-redacted, and pi’s keybindings.json and Markdown files reach it as they are. From the env of Claude Code’s settings.json, the VM gets only Claude Code’s own settings, such as ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_* and MAX_* variables and those ending in _TIMEOUT_MS, but none whose name marks it as a credential, such as ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. It also gets the values that only name where a secret is, base URLs without their passwords, true, false and short numbers. Every other env value, and every env value of an MCP server, becomes devvm-redacted. When devvm can’t parse a settings file to take its secrets out, the VM doesn’t get a copy of it, and neither does it get opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env. devvm names each file it doesn’t copy, and when it can’t make the copy of a login, it says why.
data.cursors-cli#Cursor’s CLI:
The VM’s proxy puts the real login only into the requests for the methods that devvm found the CLI calling in its package, on Cursor’s API, its agent’s hosts and its codebase indexing, and into no other. It refuses every other request below /auth/ on those hosts, the methods that make or show a key, a token, a secret or a sign-in, the methods that change your account, and any path it can’t read as Cursor’s hosts do. Those are the real control. As a defence in depth, the proxy also reads every reply from those hosts as it passes, its headers and the agent’s streams included, and cuts one off where a token starts. devvm checked this against one release of the CLI, by reading its code, and against Cursor’s own answers to a login that isn’t there, so a method that Cursor adds that hands out a token in a shape devvm doesn’t know would reach the VM. Such a token would work without the proxy, so if you suspect that one reached a VM, log in again with devvm agent login cursor (logins made in a VM). Neither does devvm guard Cursor’s hosts that the CLI doesn’t use: if one of them also answered /auth/poll, a VM could finish a login there and keep its tokens, though none is known to.
Your Cursor agents on every machine and in the cloud share Cursor’s agent store, your cloud agents follow the skills in it, and your team shares a store of its own, so a VM that could write there could leave instructions for them. So no VM gets the store (why).
data.each-agents-variables#Each agent’s varia: Every VM sets OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=1, as it sets DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 for Claude Code, because the agents are read-only shared tools that can’t update themselves, and devvm keeps their versions. For the same reason every VM sets PI_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1, so pi doesn’t ask you to run pi update, and PI_TELEMETRY=0, which turns off pi’s report of its install and the attribution headers it adds to some providers’ requests. Claude Code’s telemetry and error reports are off with DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1, and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR name its plugins folder and its seed (Claude Code’s plugins). devvm writes every agent’s variables into each VM at every launch, whichever agents the VM has, and every shell in the VM gets them, login or not, so an agent that an editor’s terminal or ssh runs gets them too. pi would download fd and rg into ~/.pi/agent/bin whenever they’re missing, so base has both, from Ubuntu’s or the container image’s own packages, and pi finds Ubuntu’s and Debian’s fd by its name there, fdfind.
data.history-exports#History exports:
The agents’ logins aren’t in the export, which leaves out ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin, and holds nothing of ~/.pi/agent but its sessions, so pi’s auth.json stays out too. It leaves out the VM’s ~/.claude/plugins, which holds settings and each plugin’s data rather than history (Claude Code’s plugins). It also leaves out what of ~/.local/state/opencode is the VM’s own as a machine:
its machine folder, whose home-key is the private key that every machine opencode pairs with opencode machine add trusts its service.json, or service-.json for another channel’s opencode, which holds the password of opencode’s background service, and the handoff tickets and temporary files that opencode writes beside it its pty folder, which holds the sockets of its terminals’ daemons and their access tokens its plugin-approvals.json, with its lock and the temporary files it’s written through, which holds the project plugins you approved in opencode’s native client, which doesn’t ship in opencode 2.4.1 its plugin-staged folder, the approved plugins’ copies, which that client runs without checking their hash again, so an export would otherwise approve a plugin for another VM The copy of opencode’s database leaves out its machine table too, which holds the public keys that the machines it paired log in to it with. An import never writes them either, so the new VM’s opencode makes its own, and a VM made again keeps the VM’s own, because it’s the same machine (what a VM made again keeps).
opencode keeps its sessions and its logins together in one database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, so the export holds a copy of that database without its logins. The VM makes the copy with sqlite3, which every base image has, and the copy has no logins, API keys or opencode account in any part of the file, not even a key you typed into opencode in the VM, while the VM’s own database keeps them (how). The copy also leaves out what opencode 2.4 would act on without asking in the VM that imports it:
its automation table, because opencode runs each automation’s shell command on its schedule or event without asking again its permission table, the requests you said always to allow its job table, the subagents’ jobs, and its session_inbox table, the messages queued for a session’s next turn, because opencode’s service starts those jobs and turns when it starts each session’s allow rules, as the session keeps only the deny and ask rules of its permission rules each suspended session’s mark, so no session resumes its turn on its own each project’s commands, whose start command opencode runs for each worktree it makes The export also leaves out opencode’s git repositories in ~/.local/share/opencode, which are snapshot, repos and worktree, because a repository’s config can name a command that git runs, and opencode’s own git commands would run it in the VM that imports it. So the export doesn’t hold opencode’s worktrees, and the work in them stays in the VM, which a VM made again keeps and devvm rm deletes, after it checks them (opencode’s worktrees). Their commits are in the project’s own repository. A view or a generated column in the database could hide rows from these steps, so the copy drops every view, and it fails its check when a table has a generated column. The export never holds the database’s -wal, -shm or -journal files, which can hold logins that opencode saved last. When the VM has no sqlite3, such as a VM made from an image built without it, the export leaves the database out, so opencode’s sessions aren’t in it, and the run log says so. It does the same when the VM’s sqlite3 can’t read JSON, which the sessions’ rules are. devvm starts a stopped VM for the export as a launch does, so it locks the folder’s .git again and checks the VM’s confinement first, and the VM stays running. devvm writes the file only once the export is complete, so a failed export leaves no file and leaves an existing FILE as it was. An export holds at most 2 GiB, because a VM could otherwise write until this machine’s disk is full. When the VM sends more, devvm stops the export and keeps nothing of it, so devvm history export fails, while devvm rm and the commands that make a VM again warn that they kept no export and go on without one. Only you can read the file, and devvm makes the exports folder yours alone each time it writes one there, whatever its mode was before. When FILE is in a folder of your own, that folder keeps its mode. If the export fails, devvm rm keeps the VM, and devvm rm --no-export deletes it without exporting. devvm rm VM, for a VM whose folder is gone, exports in the same way, but only from a running VM or a --clone VM, because starting any other would make its folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).
data.importing#Importing:
The import copies only the paths in the store’s table, from ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode and ~/.pi/agent, so it never copies your history, such as ~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex’s sessions or ~/.pi/agent/sessions, and never ~/.claude/.credentials.json. Of ~/.claude/plugins it copies only what a seed has, known_marketplaces.json, marketplaces and cache, whether the folder is in ~/.claude or a link you allowed leads to it, so this machine’s own entries, such as each plugin’s data in data, its MCP bundles in mcpb, the plugins that claude.ai synced, its trash and its record of the plugins it installed, never reach the store (Claude Code’s plugins). Claude Code’s plugin records name the plugins’ folders by their paths, so the store’s copies of the JSON files in ~/.claude/plugins name the plugins’ folders in the store, where the VMs mount them.
A link inside an agent’s folder that leads to a file inside it is copied as that file only when the file is one of the settings that the import copies of the folder itself, by the name that the link resolves to, one link at a time. So a link never copies what the import leaves out, such as ~/.claude/projects, ~/.claude/.credentials.json or a plugin’s data in ~/.claude/plugins/data, and the import also leaves out a name that differs from a setting’s only in case, which a Mac’s file system would still find. The import reads each file it listed, and a link’s file by the path that the link resolved to. It reads through the agent’s folder opened one folder at a time, each from its parent, without following a link in any part of the path, and it fails unless the file it opened is the one it listed. A VM whose project folder is inside an agent’s folder, such as a skill you work on in ~/.claude/skills, can change a link or a folder there between the listing and the read, so such a change fails the import rather than copy what the new link leads to, and devvm warns, before it reads anything, of each VM whose project folder is inside an agent’s folder or holds it. A VM whose state devvm can’t read gets a warning of its own, naming its state file, because devvm can’t tell where its project folder is, and while any state can’t be read, devvm leaves out, with a warning naming the state, every path it would read through a link: an agent’s folder or login whose path passes through one, and every link out of an agent’s folder. That also counts the links on the way to your home folder, because a VM made with --unsafe-folder on a folder that holds your home folder holds them. It doesn’t count a link that only root can change, such as macOS’s /var or the /home of Fedora Silverblue, whose folders up to / are root’s alone, by their modes and by what the system says you may write, an ACL included. A VM changes this machine’s files only as you, so no VM can change where such a link leads. devvm opens an agent’s folder twice, as a root to list it and one folder at a time to read it, and fails the import, naming the folder, unless both are the same folder, so a VM can’t swap the folder between the two. A project folder that holds an agent’s folder, such as ~/.pi for pi’s ~/.pi/agent, lets its VM put a link in the agent folder’s place, so devvm resolves the folder’s path one link at a time and leaves the folder out, with a warning, when a link in a VM’s project folder leads it out of that folder, which would let the VM choose any folder of this machine’s, such as your home folder. A login file in a folder left out so, such as pi’s auth.json, is left out with it. Otherwise devvm reads the folder where the path led when it resolved it. It reads an agent’s login file, other than Claude Code’s ~/.claude.json, in the same way: devvm resolves its path one link at a time, leaves it out in the same way, and reads it where the path led, through its folder opened one folder at a time without following a link and never resolved again. It opens the file itself without following a link and reads it only as a regular file of at most 128 MiB, so a link, a FIFO or an endless file that a VM put in its place fails the import. It copies at most 20,000 files, folders and links, 128 MiB, and 16 MiB in one file, of each agent’s folder, the bounds of saving a VM’s settings, so such a VM can’t fill the store that every VM with the agent mounts. It reads each folder 256 entries at a time and counts every entry as it reads it, a link, a socket or a FIFO as much as a file, stopping at 20,000, so a folder of millions of entries never costs it more than that and one batch, and a folder that holds more fails the import before anything is written, naming the folder. It goes at most 128 folders deep, in paths of at most 4,096 bytes, because it opens each folder from the agent’s folder down, one name at a time, through the folder above it, which it opened in the same way. So a chain of folders nested deeper fails the import in the same way, and a link or a FIFO that a VM swaps in for a folder during the walk fails the import instead of leading it elsewhere or holding it. A file that grows past 16 MiB, or past what’s left of the 128 MiB, between the listing and the read fails the import too, naming the file. The copy of a Claude Code plugin record names the store’s longer paths, so it can be larger than the file, and what it grows counts against the same bounds, so a copy that would pass them fails the import, naming the folder.
The import reads and writes every agent’s settings into a staging folder of the agent’s store first, .devvm-import- and a random name, beside the agent’s folder there, so no VM mounts it. When a file fails to read, has changed since it was listed or passes the bounds, the import fails, leaving the store as it was and taking out the staging folder. An interrupt before every agent’s settings are staged does the same, and the run’s cleanups take out its staging folders. Once every agent’s settings are staged, the import moves each file into place and moves what your home folder no longer has aside, into a folder of the staging folder, where a file it replaces is kept too, as a second hard link, so each file is still replaced in one rename. Then it saves the logins, all or none, reading each login file it replaces first. A failure from then on, such as a rename that fails or a login that can’t be saved, puts back every agent’s store and every login as they were, the last change first, and an interrupt waits for that, or for the import to finish, before the run’s cleanups take the staging folder out. It puts back every agent’s store that it changed, even after putting one back fails. Only then, if one did fail, does it say so, naming each store it couldn’t put back and its staging folder. It keeps that staging folder, which holds what devvm couldn’t put back, until the next import or save. A run that’s killed while it puts the settings in place can leave the store partly replaced, so run the import again. The staging folders go once the import is done. The import holds the store’s lock, agents.lock in devvm’s data folder, from its staging to its logins, as the save does while it writes, and a start does while it cleans Claude Code’s plugins or opencode’s service settings, once it finds something to take out, so no two of them change the store at once, and the second waits under a status line until the first is done. A staging folder that a killed import or save left counts as nothing of the agent’s, so the import doesn’t ask before it replaces a store that holds only that, and the next import or save of that agent takes it out first. A replacement keeps the store’s folders, so a running VM’s mounts still show them. The import and the save read names as the volume that holds the store reads them, so on a volume that ignores case, as a Mac’s does by default, a file named foo.md replaces the store’s Foo.md in place, under the store’s name. What they keep when they move aside what a folder no longer has is each file and folder they wrote or keep, found by what it is on the volume rather than by how its name is spelled, so the store’s Foo.md stays. Their staging folder is on the same volume and holds only what they wrote, so a name that’s already there before they write it, under no name they wrote, is one the volume reads as another of theirs, such as a.md after A.md, and then they fail before the store changes and name both. The save also counts the names that it leaves out in this check. The staging folder reads names by its own folder’s rules, which are the store’s wherever a volume’s rules hold for every folder, as on macOS, but Linux’s ext4 can ignore case in some folders alone, so a store whose agent folder alone ignores case gets no such check. A file with a second name, a hard link, which only a hand-made store has, is kept only by the name it’s written or kept under, and the save’s diff shows its other names as removed. Where the store has a folder and the home folder now has a file, or the other way round, as when a link that led to a folder now leads to a file, the import replaces it. Before they write anything, both the import and the save check the path of every folder and file they’ll write, and each part of the path below devvm’s config folder must be a folder, never a link. A link there, which only a hand-made store has and which could lead to your home folder, fails the command before the store changes, for any of the agents that the command handles, and the command names it. A link in the store in place of a settings file is replaced, never followed. They then write only through the agent’s store, or its folder there, opened from devvm’s config folder as a root, every part of its path a folder, so a link put in the store after the check can’t lead a write out of it. They also reach a folder of the store that they empty from devvm’s config folder in the same way, as the start does for Claude Code’s plugins, and devvm’s config folder itself may be a link, as a dotfiles repo’s is.
opencode 2 keeps its logins in its own database rather than in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json, so when this machine’s opencode is version 2 or later, devvm reads its logins with opencode auth export and saves them in the store in the format of auth.json, the file that devvm copies for opencode 1. When opencode auth export fails, the import fails too, and the store keeps the login it had.
data.importing-history#Importing history:
The import works on every VM, whether its base is Ubuntu’s image or a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image (starting from a container image), because it unpacks the export with GNU tar, which Debian and Ubuntu always have and which devvm installs in every base made --from alpine.
An export holds what a VM wrote, so devvm treats it as untrusted. Its transcripts can hold what the old VM’s agents read, and a VM on a less strict tier reaches more, such as your local network on the open tier. So when the export comes from a VM on a less strict tier than the VM you import it into, going from open to internet, allowlist and none, devvm warns you before it imports. devvm knows an export’s tier only from the .folder file beside it in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, so it warns about an export with no tier recorded, or any FILE elsewhere, such as in the project folder that a VM can write, as if it came from an open VM. devvm never unpacks an export on this machine. It streams the file into the VM as it is, and the VM’s own tar unpacks it there as the VM’s user, so it can only write what that user can write. Before unpacking anything, the VM lists the paths in the export, and when one of them is outside ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode, ~/.local/state/opencode, ~/.pi/agent/sessions and ~/.cursor/chats, starts with / or has a ., .. or empty part, such as .claude/./plugins or .claude//plugins, devvm imports nothing and says so, because tar matches the paths it leaves out against each name as the export writes it. Once it has unpacked the export, it also deletes each of those paths by its path, whatever name put a file there. It leaves out of that check, and never unpacks, the AppleDouble files whose names start with ._, which macOS’s tar puts beside each file that has extended attributes, so an export you packed yourself on a Mac imports. The import keeps no owner or mode from the export, so the VM user’s umask applies and no file is set-user-ID. It also takes out every symbolic link that points outside the folder it’s in, which is any link to an absolute path or one with a .. part, so an agent writing to a session file can’t follow a link out of its history. An export that devvm didn’t write, such as a .tar.gz you made yourself, can hold opencode’s database with its logins, so the import takes out the database’s -wal, -shm and -journal files and puts in a copy of the database without its logins or what opencode would act on without asking, as the export makes it (history exports), or leaves the database out when the VM has no sqlite3. It never writes opencode’s git repositories either. opencode in the new VM then reads the logins that devvm gave the VM, as it does when it first makes its database. When the VM already has an opencode database, it keeps its own, and opencode’s sessions from the export aren’t imported.
data.links-out-of-an-agents-folder#Links out:
The import reads each agent’s folder through a handle that’s rooted at that folder, so no link inside it leads out of it (the packages). A link that leads out is resolved, every link on the way, and only then followed, as links out of an agent’s folder says, and the design note explains why:
How it resolves. devvm resolves a link one name at a time, as the system does, and keeps where each link on the way is, so it sees a link that a VM put in its project folder even in the middle of a chain. It compares a target with the refused places and the VMs’ folders by name and by identity, so another spelling of a folder, such as ~/.SSH on a Mac, where case doesn’t count, is still that folder. Where it reads. devvm opens the folder it reads the link’s target through, a follow-links folder, the linked folder or the linked file’s own folder, one folder at a time from /, each opened from its parent and never through a link, so a link that a VM swaps into that path fails the import rather than lead elsewhere. It lists what the link leads to through that folder as a root, and reads each file without blocking, refusing a FIFO, a device or a file that changed into a link as it opened it. What it lists. A linked folder’s folders and files are listed under the link’s own path, and a link inside it is listed as a file when the root resolves it to a regular file. Anything else is left out with a warning. The bounds. It counts every entry it reads, a folder’s read 256 at a time, and the size of every file, across all the links of one import, and leaves out a link that would pass 20,000 entries, 128 MiB or a file of 16 MiB, the bounds of saving a VM’s settings. The walks of all the links read at most 80,000 entries, those of links left out included, and once they have, each link left is left out unread, with the same warning. A file that grows past them between the listing and the read fails the import. A VM’s folder. It reads the state of every VM devvm has, and warns once for each link and VM when the link’s target is in that VM’s project folder or holds it, or when a link inside a linked folder resolves into it. While a VM’s state can’t be read, it follows no link out of an agent’s folder, as importing says.
data.logging-in#Logging in:
When you approve a browser login, the browser comes back to localhost:1455, where the agent’s own server in the VM waits, so devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455, and localhost:1457, which Codex uses when 1455 is taken in the VM, to the same ports in the VM. The forward lasts only while the login runs, and it ends when the login ends, fails or you press Ctrl+C, which ends the agent’s login in the VM too.
Codex in a VM keeps its login in ~/.codex/auth.json, never in a keyring, because devvm sets cli_auth_credentials_store = "file" in the VM’s ~/.codex/config.toml on every launch.
With --api-key, devvm gives the running VM its copy of the login, with a placeholder in place of the key, and the VM’s proxy puts the key in at once. opencode keeps its logins in its own database in the VM, and it reads its auth.json only when it first makes that database, so when opencode has already run in the VM, devvm also gives it the key’s placeholder with opencode auth import. devvm reads at most 1 MiB of what that import prints in the VM, and when it prints more, devvm stops it and fails, so running devvm in the VM’s folder tries again. Every other VM with opencode gets the key’s placeholder at its next launch, the same way, and any credentials that you added to opencode in a VM yourself stay in its database.
data.logins-made-in-a-vm#Logins made in a VM: When Codex or opencode in a VM logs in to OpenAI, whether devvm agent login runs it or you run it yourself, the VM’s proxy saves the login in devvm’s store, in the agent’s own auth.json, and the agent in the VM gets only placeholders, so on every tier but open the VM never holds the login’s tokens.
