The VM you logged in from uses the login at once, and every VM with that agent gets it from its next launch. opencode reads its auth.json only when it first makes its database, so in a VM where opencode has already run, devvm adds the store’s logins to opencode’s database at each launch when they changed since the VM last got them, and makes them the ones opencode uses. Credentials that you added to opencode in the VM yourself stay in its database, labeled with your names rather than devvm, and opencode auth switch changes back to one of them. A login that shows a code to type into a browser on any machine works in a VM as it is, such as codex login --device-auth and opencode’s Codex device code login. opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT doesn’t work in a VM, because it gets its tokens from another endpoint, whose replies the VM’s proxy refuses so that they never reach the VM, so choose one of opencode’s Codex logins instead, as devvm agent login opencode does. A new login replaces the one in the store, together with Codex’s API key, so every VM with the agent uses the account you logged in to last. A VM saves a login only for an agent that it has, so a VM without Codex can’t replace the store’s Codex login, and a VM without opencode can’t replace opencode’s. When a VM sends a login for an agent it doesn’t have, such as one that a program installed in the VM itself, its proxy refuses the login, devvm saves nothing, and the proxy’s own log says so. In a VM with both Codex and opencode, devvm tells their logins apart by the program that sends them. devvm network log shows a login line for each login it saved. On the open tier, a program that goes around the VM’s proxy gets the login’s tokens itself, and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM). Claude Code’s logins in a VM are saved in the same way (Claude Code login).
data.mounts#Mounts:
Absolute paths in the mounted folders, such as Claude Code’s plugin paths, still work, because each is mounted at the same path as in the store on this machine. The VM follows a symlink in these folders among its own files, so a link to a file outside the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, doesn’t reach that file on this machine, on macOS’s virtiofs mounts and on Linux’s 9p mounts alike. devvm doesn’t mount a folder whose path has a comma, on any backend, and it warns you. Lima can’t mount such a path (Lima’s limits).
The VM reads every file in these folders, a Claude Code marketplace’s git clone included, so when devvm agent import or devvm agent save copies a marketplace, it checks the clone for a credential and warns of each one. It reads, with git itself and without its includes, every git config below the clone’s .git, a submodule’s included, and each file a config includes from inside the clone, which the copy holds too, and it looks for an http.extraHeader and a URL with a password or an access token in its user info: a remote’s or a submodule’s URL, a push URL, a proxy, or the base of an insteadOf. It judges a URL as --clone judges a remote, so an scp-like git@host:path is a name, not a credential. It also checks each marketplace’s source in known_marketplaces.json. A warning names the keys, never the credential, and a URL in a key’s name that holds one shows as . When git can’t read such a config, devvm warns that it couldn’t check it, with git’s reason, as the VM reads the file whatever git makes of it.
data.opencodes-service#opencode’s service:
opencode keeps its background service’s settings in ~/.config/opencode/service.json, or in service-.json for a channel other than latest, dev, beta or next (an earlier build named it service-.json), and it writes each one through a temporary file beside it, ..tmp. They hold the service’s password, 32 random bytes that the service makes when it starts and the file has none, and with remote access on, the route that the service is served on, a random name that keeps its address unguessable. So opencode service get with no key hides both, and only opencode service get password shows the password. They also hold the service’s port, host name, CORS origins and environment. That makes them each machine’s own rather than settings, so the import and the save leave out every entry of ~/.config/opencode with one of these names, what’s in a folder of that name included, and the save’s script in the VM never sends them, so the VM’s own file never makes a save fail. The VM’s file stays in the VM, so a VM made again keeps it, and no export of the VM’s history holds it, because ~/.config/opencode isn’t history.
A store that an earlier import filled can hold them, so every start looks for them in the store’s ~/.config/opencode, which it opens as it opens Claude Code’s plugins folder, and once it finds any, it takes them out holding the store’s lock and warns once, naming them. No VM gets them from the store meanwhile, because a VM’s setup copies only the files that the import would copy, so a start whose clean-up fails only warns, naming the folder. devvm writes devvm-redacted in place of a secret in every copy of a settings file that it makes, so a file with one of these names that holds it is a copy that devvm made, whose password every VM with such a copy shares. Each launch’s setup takes out each such regular file in the VM’s ~/.config/opencode and leaves the VM’s own files, links and folders, so the VM’s opencode makes its own password when its service next starts. A service that’s running keeps the password it started with until it stops, as when the VM restarts.
data.opencodes-worktrees#opencode’s worktrees:
opencode 2.4 makes each worktree with git worktree add, in ~/.local/share/opencode/worktree//, where is the first six characters of the project’s ID in opencode. Because an export leaves that folder out, devvm rm, and a command that makes the VM again with --clean-home, read the worktrees there before the VM’s disk goes. devvm runs one command in the running VM, in its home folder, which finds each folder at that depth with a .git in it, those whose names start with a dot too, and prints, for each one, its path, its git status --porcelain, and the commit its HEAD is detached at when no branch, tag or remote-tracking branch in the VM has that commit. A worktree whose git status fails counts as one with changes, because the VM still has its files. The command looks at 100 worktrees at most and says when there are more. devvm reads at most 8 MiB of its answer and stops the command once it sends more, and it waits at most 2 minutes for the answer, so a VM that answers without end, or never, can’t keep devvm rm waiting.
The answer comes from the VM, so devvm checks it before it shows any of it. Each record must be whole, each path must be a clean path below the home folder that opencode’s pattern matches, each worktree must appear once and be followed by its status, and there can be no more than 100 of them. An answer that breaks any of these, a command that fails, an answer over the limit or one that doesn’t come in time keeps the VM, because the VM may hold work devvm can’t see, and devvm names --no-worktree-check. A path or a change devvm shows goes through the same filter as every message, which drops the characters that would move the cursor or hide text. The VM can still leave a worktree out of its answer, which hides only its own work. For a --clone VM, the same question covers the clone check’s findings, so devvm asks once.
devvm checks only that folder. A worktree that opencode’s worktree.directory setting puts elsewhere in the VM’s home folder isn’t checked, and it goes with the VM as any other file there does. One that the setting puts in the project folder is on this machine for a VM that mounts it, and in the clone for a --clone VM, whose check covers the worktrees inside its folder (deleting the VM).
data.pasting#Pasting: How devvm paste reads the clipboard, names a copied file, refuses links and finds Linux’s clipboard programs is in the design note on pasting images.
data.pis-logins#pi’s logins:
devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider PROVIDER saves the key in the store’s ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/pi/.pi/agent/auth.json, in pi’s own format, beside pi’s other providers, as opencode’s --api-key does (logging in with devvm agent login). The VM’s ~/.pi/agent/auth.json holds a placeholder in place of each of those keys, and the VM’s proxy puts the key into pi’s requests to that provider’s hosts, on every network tier, and allows those hosts, as the table in API keys the proxy puts in describes. The VM’s entry for such a provider holds only its type and the placeholder, so it gets none of the entry’s other fields, such as its env, whose values pi uses before the environment’s, and the store keeps them on this machine.
devvm keeps every other entry of pi’s auth.json on this machine too, and the VM gets that entry without its key, its env or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as a local model server’s, a key that’s a command for pi to run, such as !security find-generic-password, and a key that pi fills in from a variable, such as $KEY or ${KEY}, even for a provider whose key the proxy puts in, because devvm can’t tell what pi would send. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its accountId and its expiry.
pi’s Claude and ChatGPT logins use the same token endpoints as Claude Code’s, Codex’s and opencode’s logins, whose replies the VM’s proxy captures for those agents, and devvm never keeps such a login as pi’s. In a VM that also has the matching agent, Claude Code for a Claude login and Codex or opencode for a ChatGPT login, the proxy saves pi’s login as that agent’s own, in place of the one devvm keeps for every VM with that agent. In a VM with none of them, the proxy refuses pi’s login and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM).
data.saving-a-vms-settings#Saving a VM’s sett:
The save reads only the settings in the store’s table from the VM’s home, and never the logins, so it never reads your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, opencode’s auth.json or pi’s. From the VM’s ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, as the import does, and the VM leaves out its per-project entries before it sends anything. devvm puts that part in the store’s logins folder, where the import keeps it too. A folder that the store already has is mounted read-only in the VM, so the agent there can’t change it, and the save leaves it as it is. The exception is Claude Code’s plugins folder, which is the VM’s own, with the store’s as its seed (Claude Code’s plugins). A folder that the store doesn’t have yet is the VM’s own until you save it, and once the VM next starts with the store’s new folder mounted, its setup links that folder in place of its own (mounts).
devvm treats everything the VM sends as untrusted, because the agent in the VM could have changed any of it. It reads at most 128 MiB from the VM, in at most 20,000 files, folders and links, none of the files larger than 16 MiB, at most 128 folders deep and in paths of at most 4,096 bytes, the import’s bounds, because the save opens each folder one name at a time from the store down. When the VM sends more, or sends a path outside the agents’ settings or a name with a character that a terminal wouldn’t show, devvm saves nothing. Each file it saves is yours alone (mode 600), or mode 700 when it was executable in the VM, so it never keeps a set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit. A link in a settings folder that leads to a file in the same folder becomes a copy of that file. devvm leaves out any other link, any other kind of file, such as a socket, and a settings file that it can’t parse whole, such as a settings.json that isn’t JSON, and it warns you about each. When it leaves out a file in a folder, the store keeps its own copy of that file. A settings file that the VM doesn’t have stays in the store. A folder that the VM sends, other than Claude Code’s plugins folder, replaces the store’s folder whole, so devvm writes each of its files again and takes out the files that the VM’s folder doesn’t have, but it keeps the store’s folder itself, so a running VM’s mounts still show it. It compares each of the VM’s names with the store’s file that the store’s volume reads it as, found by what the file is, so where the volume ignores case, the diff shows the VM’s foo.md as a change to the store’s Foo.md rather than a file added and another removed. The save writes holding the store’s lock, as the import does, and once it holds the lock, it plans again from the store as it is then. When that differs from what it showed you, as when an import wrote the store while you read the diff, it saves nothing and says so, rather than write over that change. Where the store has a folder and the VM has a file, or the other way round, the save saves nothing and names the store’s path, because putting one in the other’s place would take out what the store has there, which the diff doesn’t show. It then saves all or nothing, as the import does, so it first writes every agent’s files into a staging folder of the agent’s store first, with the import’s name, .devvm-import- and a random name, and takes out any that a killed import or save left there. Then it moves each file into place and moves aside what a folder the VM sent no longer has, and it saves the part of ~/.claude.json last, holding the lock of the folder of Claude Code’s logins, which a VM’s proxy holds while it saves a Claude Code login made in that VM, so the two take turns. A failure from then on, such as a rename that fails or the login that can’t be saved, puts back every agent’s store and the login as they were, the last change first, and when putting a store back fails too, devvm says so, naming each store it couldn’t put back and its staging folder, which it keeps until the next import or save. A run that’s killed while it puts the settings in place can leave the store partly saved, so run the save again. A Ctrl-C while the save waits for the store’s lock or the login’s ends the wait, and the save leaves the store as it was.
The VM’s copies of the settings files and of ~/.claude.json hold placeholders, such as devvm-redacted, where the store has your secrets. devvm puts the store’s secret back in place of each placeholder, as long as the VM’s copy had that placeholder in that place and nothing around it changed, such as the URL of the MCP server that a header is for. When something around a placeholder changed, devvm leaves the whole file out and warns you, so a VM can’t send a secret it never saw to another host, and you can make that change in the store’s file yourself. devvm also leaves out any other file that holds a placeholder, such as a skill. No VM gets opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env, so devvm leaves out the VM’s own file of that name and keeps the store’s.
data.the-guide-in-every-vm#The guide in every: Each launch installs the guide again whenever it differs from devvm’s, and it belongs to root and is read-only, so nothing that the VM’s user runs without sudo can change what the agents read, and a change made with sudo lasts only until the next launch.

data: This page explains how a backend gives devvm what it needs to run a VM, what devvm does when a backend lacks something, and how devvm names VMs. devvm runs its VMs on Lima, and another backend would plug in the same way, through the features below (how a backend plugs in).
data.features#Features:
Each thing devvm needs from a backend is a feature, such as building images, mounting the project folder or confining a VM to its proxy. devvm doctor lists them as “features” too, but they aren’t the base image features you choose with devvm setup. Each backend declares how it has each feature:
native: the backend does it itself. emulated: devvm builds it from other parts of the backend. none: the backend can’t do it. A backend lists every feature, the ones it lacks too, and devvm refuses to use a backend that leaves one out, so a new feature makes each backend say how it has it. Some features are built on others: read-only-paths and mount-cache on project-mount, ports-all on ports, agent-toggle on agent-forwarding, and link on ssh. A backend has such a feature no better than the one it’s built on, so the feature is emulated wherever its base is emulated, and none wherever its base is none.
devvm uses an emulation only once its review has passed, and until then it refuses the emulation. A review takes a design note, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove the guarantee.
devvm doctor lists Lima’s features, and devvm doctor --json those of every backend devvm has. Both show an emulation whose review hasn’t passed as unreviewed.
data.missing-and-unreviewed-features#Missing:
devvm checks each feature an image or a VM needs this way:
How devvm checks a featureA feature that the image or the VM needs is allowed when the backend has it natively, or emulates it and the emulation is reviewed. An unreviewed emulation, or none, is refused, and devvm stops and names the VM, the feature and the backend, except egress-proxy for a new open VM, which is made open, as asked.native emulated, reviewed emulated, unreviewed,or none no yes a feature the imageor the VM needs how the backend has it allowed egress-proxy, fora new open VM? refused: devvm stopsand names the VM,the feature and the backend the VM is made open,as asked Before devvm builds an image, makes or starts a VM, or changes a VM’s settings, it checks that the backend has every feature the image or the VM needs. The backend itself is behind the same check: every time devvm asks it to build an image or the shared tools, make a VM or start one, devvm checks the features that request needs before the backend sees it, so a request that skipped the first check is refused too. When the backend lacks one, devvm stops and names the VM, the feature and the backend (backend_lacks). It does the same for a feature the backend only emulates when that emulation’s review hasn’t passed (backend_unreviewed). devvm never falls back to something weaker, so a VM on a confined tier never starts with an open network.
To get the feature, use a backend that has it. A VM keeps its backend, so that means making a new VM.
A new VM’s tier is the one exception, because allowlist is the default, and When a backend lacks something says what devvm does instead.
data.the-feature-table#The feature table: Feature What it is Lima build-image build images from the layer and feature scripts native build-confinement builds reach the internet but not the host’s loopback, or nothing native: Seatbelt on macOS. On Linux, QEMU’s restrict=on confines a build with no network, but a build with the internet reaches the host’s loopback (details) from base from a container image (--from) native: devvm converts the image to a disk clone a project VM from an image native: an APFS copy-on-write copy on macOS, and a qcow2 overlay on Linux (details) project-mount the project folder, read-write native: virtiofs on macOS, and 9p on Linux read-only-paths paths in the project folder that the guest can’t change while the VM runs, which .git protection asks for on Linux native on Linux where the kernel lets devvm use a user namespace: QEMU runs in one of its own, with the paths bound read-only over themselves (details). None on macOS, where .git protection locks the host’s files itself, and none where devvm’s check of the kernel fails mount-cache choosing how the guest caches the project folder’s mount, which devvm mount-cache sets native on Linux, where it’s 9p’s cache option, none for new VMs (details). None on macOS, where virtiofs has no such option agent-folders agents’ host folders, read-only native: read-only mounts, enforced by the host tools-share the shared tools, read-only native: a read-only mount, enforced by the host egress-proxy network traffic only through devvm’s proxy native: Seatbelt on macOS, and on Linux QEMU’s restrict=on with a guestfwd to the proxy (details) ssh ssh for editors native: Lima’s ssh forward and config ports the listed ports forwarded to the host’s loopback emulated (reviewed): devvm’s forwarder over Lima’s ssh, for the listed ports alone, with Lima’s own forwards off (details) ports-all every port forwarded, servers on the VM’s loopback included emulated (reviewed): the same forwarder, for whatever listens in the VM from port 1024 up, and never a port the host has (details) agent-forwarding ssh-agent forwarding, chosen when the VM is made native agent-toggle turning a VM’s ssh-agent forwarding on or off later native cpus a VM’s CPUs native memory a VM’s memory native disk a VM’s disk size native: it grows but never shrinks docker-layer the docker layer: Docker’s engine running in the VM native nix-layer the nix layer: Nix’s daemon and its store in the VM, with builds in Nix’s sandbox native (details) link links between VMs: a program in one VM reaches a port another VM publishes, by name native: a link session of devvm’s own over Lima’s ssh, with remote forwards to 127.77.0.0/16 alone (details) egress-proxy is what every network tier but open needs. The open tier needs no feature of its own: every backend must let a VM on its own network reach a port on the host’s loopback and set the guest’s proxy settings from what devvm confines the VM to, which the conformance suite checks (how a backend plugs in), because every VM’s proxy carries its requests. So a backend without egress-proxy still has open VMs, and devvm refuses every other tier on it in one line (net_tier_backend).
data.vm-names#VM names:
A project VM’s name is devvm--. The folder part is up to 20 characters of the folder’s name, in lowercase, with each run of characters other than letters and digits turned into one dash, because Lima refuses a name with separators in a row, so foo (copy) gives foo-copy. The hash part is 14 hex digits of a hash of the folder’s path. devvm takes a name as a project VM’s only when it has that form, so a name in a state file or a backend’s list whose folder part has any other character, starts or ends with a dash, or has two dashes in a row isn’t a project VM’s. A state file whose name has dashes in a row and no created time belongs to a VM that Lima refused to make, so devvm reads it as no VM’s state and the folder’s next VM replaces it.
A backend may need shorter names, and then devvm cuts the folder’s part to fit. When fewer than 4 characters of it would fit, devvm refuses (vm_name_no_room). On Lima the room for a name depends on the Lima home’s path, because Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket under it, so there the fix is a shorter Lima home (lima_home_too_long, limits).
Only a new VM gets a name, which fits the limit of the backend that makes it. devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s path, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s data folder (vms//, named by the hash that ends the VM’s name), so an existing VM keeps the name and the backend its state records, whichever backend new VMs get, and keeps them when its folder moves (a moved folder).
data.what-a-backend-does#What a backend does:
A backend has four roles, and every backend has all of them:
The host: it says what it needs that this machine lacks, which devvm doctor reports, how long a VM’s name can be, where its VMs live, and which folders hold their disks, so devvm can check the free space before a step that writes them. Images: it builds images and the shared tools’ images, keeps the images, and names the files of its own that it puts into base, which base’s key hashes. Machines: it makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, runs commands and shells in them, and says how ssh and devvm’s port forwarder reach them. It also says how a VM runs now: which start it’s on, whether that start is confined to the VM’s proxy, and the file the VM’s proxy and forwarder follow, which ends them when the process that runs the VM ends. Housekeeping: it says how much disk its VMs and caches take for devvm space, lists the VMs with devvm’s label that this devvm has no state for, and lists and deletes devvm’s share of its own caches for devvm gc --caches. A backend that can’t tell one of these returns nothing, so devvm shows no size or deletes nothing. A backend may also keep files of its own for a VM besides the VM, which devvm gc --orphans deletes once the VM is gone. Lima keeps none.
data.what-a-start-changes#What a start change:
A backend makes a VM as devvm asks, and then changes it only when it starts. Each time devvm starts a stopped VM, it tells the backend what the VM’s state asks for, which is its size, the agent folders in devvm’s agent store and whether it forwards your SSH agent, together with how the VM is confined. The backend compares that with the VM it has and changes only what differs, so a start that changes nothing leaves the VM’s config as it was. Nothing changes a stopped VM’s config between starts, so devvm size and devvm ssh-agent save what you ask for in the VM’s state, and the VM gets it when it next starts.
A running VM is left as it is, and devvm says what changes when it next starts. Its ports aren’t the backend’s, so devvm ports changes them at once, and a running VM’s forwarder starts again with the new ones (port forwarding). A disk can’t shrink, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before the backend changes anything (disk_shrink).
Which ports a VM forwards stays in the VM’s state alone, and the backend never hears of them. The backend keeps only what it needs for the start it made, such as Lima’s record of the hostagent it started confined (confinement).
data.what-each-backend-emulates#What each bac:
On Lima, devvm emulates forwarding ports, both the listed ones and every one, through its forwarder, and the emulation is reviewed (port forwarding). Everything else on Lima is Lima’s own.
The forwarder is devvm’s own on every backend, never a backend’s. A backend that has ports turns its own forwards off, and devvm’s forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd the way the backend’s SSH says, which is a user, a key and a port. devvm refuses that target unless it’s on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with the same check it uses for links and the ssh config. devvm reads which ports the VM forwards from its state, chooses which of them are free, pins the VM’s host keys for its current start and starts the forwarder, which follows the backend’s lifeline for the VM.
data.which-backends-a-launch-asks#Which backe: A launch asks a backend about its VMs only when some VM’s state names that backend. It asks them to write the ssh config and to check the SSH agent’s folders. So a backend that no VM uses never runs during a launch, even when it isn’t running or isn’t installed (a VM’s backend).

data: This page explains how devvm desktop serves a VM’s desktop on this machine, how it checks a viewer’s password and keeps the clipboard out of the VM, and why devvm uses VNC and never forwards X11. A VM’s desktop covers adding the desktop and opening it.
data.in-the-vm#In the VM:
The built-in desktop layer installs Xfce, TigerVNC’s Xvnc, socat for the local proxy and a command of devvm’s, devvm-desktop, into the desktop image, which only the VMs with the layer are made from (the desktop layer). Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, and it downloads nothing else. When you run devvm desktop, devvm first checks that the VM has devvm-desktop, and refuses a VM without it (desktop_no_layer). Then it runs devvm-desktop start off, or start on with --clipboard, as the VM’s user.
devvm-desktop starts Xvnc on display :1 unless it’s running. Xvnc listens on the socket /run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock alone, in a folder of the VM’s user’s own (mode 700), the socket itself mode 600. It listens on no TCP port (-rfbport -1), and takes no X11 connections over TCP (-nolisten tcp), so devvm’s port forwarder never sees it, even on a VM that forwards every port. It asks for no password of its own (-SecurityTypes None), because devvm checks the viewer’s password on this machine first. The clipboard settings (AcceptCutText, SendCutText, SetPrimary, SendPrimary) are on or off as asked, and on a desktop that runs already, devvm-desktop changes them in place with vncconfig. Then it starts an Xfce session on the display, in a D-Bus session of its own, with the session’s proxy settings pointed at the VM’s local proxy. Nothing starts the desktop at boot, so a VM whose desktop you never open runs none. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM.
data.on-this-machine#On this machine:
devvm desktop listens on 127.0.0.1 alone, on the VM’s port. That’s the port its state records in its ports section (host.desktop) while no program on this machine has it, and otherwise a new one that no program and no VM has, which devvm chooses and records in its place under the claims lock, as it does every port it chooses for a VM. New ports come from 20000 up to just below the range this machine gives outgoing connections, which starts at 32768 on Linux by default and 49152 on macOS, because Linux refuses a listener on a port that a live outgoing connection holds. devvm reads that range from the system, and when it can’t, or the range leaves fewer than 1000 ports above 20000, it picks from 20000 to 32767. The port is among those devvm records for VMs, with their ssh and proxy ports, so no VM’s port forwarder takes it and no new VM gets it for its ssh or its proxy. devvm listens without address reuse, so a program that has the port on any address keeps it. The listener stays open until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM no longer runs, which devvm checks every 5 seconds (desktop_vm_stopped). Nothing else listens for the desktop on this machine, at any other time.
Each connection to the port goes through devvm’s relay, which runs in devvm desktop:
The relay speaks VNC’s protocol (RFB 3.8, and 3.7 and 3.3 for older viewers) as a server, and offers VNC’s own authentication alone. It sends a random challenge and checks the viewer’s answer against the VM’s password, with one check at a time, so a wrong answer holds every other viewer’s check for a second, and at one guess a second, guessing the password would take thousands of years. A viewer whose answer is wrong is refused and never reaches the VM. Only then does the relay connect to the VM: an ssh channel to the VM’s socket (ssh -W /run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock), through devvm’s ssh config’s entry for the VM, with its pinned host key. The channel opens no session, and it carries no agent and no forwarding either way (IdentityAgent=none, ForwardAgent=no, ForwardX11=no, ClearAllForwardings=yes). The relay does the viewer’s side of the VM’s handshake, asking for no authentication, and tells the viewer it’s in. From then on it carries the viewer’s messages to the VM and the VM’s to the viewer. Without --clipboard, it reads each of the viewer’s messages and drops its clipboard ones (ClientCutText, extended clipboard ones included). It ends a connection that sends a message it doesn’t know, so nothing it can’t read reaches the VM. At most 8 viewers connect at once. The VM’s password is 8 characters of lowercase letters and digits without 0, o, 1, l and i, about 40 bits, because VNC’s authentication uses 8 characters at most. devvm makes it the first time and keeps it in the VM’s state, in its desktop section (made.password), in a file that only you can read. It never goes into the VM, and devvm prints it only with the address, never into the run log. Processes describes the relay alongside devvm’s other processes, and it lists the listeners that a VM’s bytes reach.
data.the-local-proxy#The local proxy:
Every request from the VM to its proxy carries the VM’s password in Proxy-Authorization, and the VM’s proxy settings carry it in their URL, http://devvm:KEY@192.168.5.2:PORT. Command-line tools take the password from that URL, but Chrome, Chromium and Firefox ignore it and ask for the proxy’s username and password instead, on every site. So the desktop’s programs use a local proxy in the VM, devvm-local-proxy, which needs no password and adds the VM’s.
The VM’s setup writes devvm-local-proxy into /usr/local/bin at each launch, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s, with the VM’s proxy address and password in it, and installs it whole, so a connection that’s already running keeps the copy it started with. The VM already holds the same password in its environment. devvm-desktop runs devvm-local-proxy start before it starts Xvnc, which starts socat unless it’s running, so the local proxy starts with the desktop and runs until the VM stops. socat listens on 127.0.77.1:3128 alone, which is on the VM’s loopback, takes connections only from 127.0.0.0/8, carries at most 256 at once, and runs devvm-local-proxy on each connection itself. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-local-proxy.log. The address comes from devvm’s proxy code (the packages), which the setup gets as DEVVM_LOCAL_PROXY, and devvm-desktop sets http_proxy, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY to http://127.0.77.1:3128 for the Xfce session. On Xfce, Chrome and Chromium read those variables for their proxy, and Firefox reads them first when its proxy setting is the system’s, which is its default.
For each connection, devvm-local-proxy reads the request line and the headers, waiting at most 30 seconds for each line and taking at most 100 headers. It takes only what a proxy is sent:
a CONNECT to a host and port, which becomes a tunnel; a request for an absolute http:// or https:// URL, such as GET http://example.com/. Anything else gets 400, and nothing of it reaches the VM’s proxy. That includes a request in origin form, such as GET /, which is what a web page sends when it reaches the local proxy as a server, so a page in the browser can’t use it. The local proxy drops the client’s own Proxy-Authorization and Proxy-Connection headers and adds the VM’s password. For a request that isn’t a CONNECT, it drops Connection and Keep-Alive and asks for Connection: close, because the password goes with each request’s head and the local proxy reads only the first, so each connection carries one request. Then it connects to the VM’s proxy, and to nothing else, sends the head and carries the rest both ways with socat. The VM’s proxy decides as it does for any request: a host the tier allows is reached, and one it doesn’t allow gets the proxy’s 403 with its reason.
devvm’s port forwarder never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, on any port, because a forward would put a proxy that adds the VM’s password on this machine’s localhost, where other users and programs could reach it.
data.what-the-vm-can-and-cant-change#What the:
Root in the VM can change its desktop, or run another server on the socket in its place. The relay doesn’t depend on the VM’s server for its guarantees:
The password: the relay checks it on this machine before it opens the channel, so a VM’s server that asks for none still gets no viewer without it. The address: the relay listens on this machine’s loopback, so no server in the VM reaches other machines through it. A server root starts on a TCP port of the VM’s is an ordinary server of the VM’s, which the VM’s ports forward to this machine’s loopback, or don’t, as for any other. This machine’s clipboard: without --clipboard, the relay drops it, whatever the VM’s server accepts. No way out: every connection starts on this machine, and the VM opens none to it through the relay. The channel is a local forward that devvm’s ssh asks for, which the VM’s sshd connects to the VM’s own socket. On a confined tier, the VM’s own connections still reach only its proxy. The relay can’t stop a VM’s server from sending its clipboard to the viewer, because that would mean reading every screen update the server sends. So the VM’s clipboard stays off this machine only while its server is as devvm set it up, or while the viewer doesn’t take it, which Screen Sharing’s Use Shared Clipboard setting decides.
data.why-not-x11#Why not X11: ssh’s X11 forwarding gives programs in the VM a connection to this machine’s display, and an X11 program on a display can read the keys typed into other windows on it, read their contents and send them input. So devvm turns X11 forwarding off on both sides of the VM’s ssh. Its ssh config’s entries set ForwardX11 no, and the VM’s sshd has X11Forwarding no (ssh into VMs). With VNC, the VM’s programs draw on a display of the VM’s own, and this machine only shows a picture of it, so nothing in the VM reaches this machine’s windows.

data:
This page explains what devvm locks in a project’s git folder, when it locks and checks the locks again, and what the locks can’t stop. .git protection covers what still works, turning protection on or off, VMs that were strict, and what isn’t covered.
On macOS devvm locks with the user-immutable flag (chflags uchg), which even root in the VM can’t clear. A read-only mount wouldn’t hold, because root in the VM can unmount it.
On Linux devvm makes the same paths read-only in the user and mount namespace it runs the VM’s QEMU in (on Linux hosts), so the VM, which reaches the folder only through QEMU, can’t change them.
Each check reads each repo’s .git once, the folder’s own and those nested in it, finding its git folders, submodules, what it would lock, what the locked files hand over and what points git elsewhere, and then locks, unlocks, watches and reports from what it found. The host’s locker does the locking: the flag on macOS, and on Linux nothing at the check itself, because the VM’s next start makes the paths read-only. A Linux host whose kernel refuses devvm the namespace locks nothing, and devvm watches .git there instead.
data.git-lfs-in-the-copy#Git LFS in the copy:
Base’s image has git-lfs, pinned like every other download, but nothing in the image sets its filter, so a VM that mounts its folder sees each LFS file as the pointer git stores. The copy sets the filter in each clone repo it makes, submodules included, with git lfs install --local --skip-repo, which writes the repo’s own config and no hooks, and when that fails, devvm says the clone’s LFS files may be pointers there (clone_lfs_setup_failed). No git-lfs runs on this machine for the copy or for what comes back, and when the repo’s lfs.storage puts its objects outside .git, devvm copies none either way and says so (clone_lfs_storage).
Every object file devvm reads or writes on this machine is opened beneath the repo’s common dir through a root that no path can leave, and before that, each folder on the way, lfs, lfs/objects, both two-character folders and lfs/tmp, must be a folder, never a link, as such a root still follows a link that stays inside it. So a link planted in .git/lfs can’t make devvm send a file from elsewhere on this machine or write the VM’s content anywhere else.
On the way in, devvm reads the pointers among the index’s blobs: those of at most 1,024 bytes, git cat-file --batch-check says, which, read with git cat-file --batch, are a pointer as git-lfs’s spec has it, with its version line first, an oid sha256: of 64 lowercase hex characters and a size, each once, and a newline at its end. Both outputs are read as they come, and at most 200,000 blobs are taken as maybe pointers. Each object the repo has, at lfs/objects/// in its common dir, a regular file of its pointer’s size, is hashed before anything is sent, and one whose SHA-256 isn’t its oid stays on this machine, named (clone_lfs_bad), while the copy goes on. The rest go in the tar as lfs/, hashed again as they’re sent, so one that changed in between fails the copy, its tar cut short. The VM moves each into its repo’s lfs/objects, where it has no file of that name, before the checkout. The checkout runs with GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1, so git-lfs never fetches during the copy, then git lfs checkout, which reads only the objects the repo has, writes each file’s content; a file whose object isn’t there stays a pointer.
On the way back, once each fetch from the VM is in, devvm clone fetch’s and devvm rm’s and devvm clone off’s, devvm lists the objects that what it fetched (FETCH_HEAD) reaches past this repo’s own refs, with git rev-list --objects --missing=allow-promisor, and reads the pointers among them as above. Its own refs are every ref but the saved/ branches and the remote-tracking branches of a devvm VM’s remote, so a commit that a plain git fetch devvm brought earlier, without its LFS objects, still has them looked for. Once that work is merged into a branch of this repo, though, its commits are past that branch, so devvm also has the script in the VM list the files in the clone’s lfs/objects, by name and size, none followed through a link, and takes those this repo lacks whose pointer the history of what it fetched names since the copy. That walk stops at what the copy set the clone’s refs to, which the VM keeps in .git/devvm-seed-tips, so an object the VM fetched for the history it was given isn’t taken for its work, and a long history never has every blob read, or, for a clone an older devvm made, at this repo’s own refs, as above. When the objects this repo lacks come to more than 2 GiB in all, a total that can’t overflow, devvm asks first (clone_lfs_large), and refuses without a terminal. A script in the VM then writes all of them in one stream, its connection carrying no SSH agent: for each, a line with the oid and its size and then the clone’s own .git/lfs/objects/…/, a regular file that isn’t a link, or a line that says the clone lacks it or has it at another size. devvm reads exactly the pointer’s size of each into a new file in this repo’s lfs/tmp and moves it into lfs/objects only when its SHA-256 is the oid. One that the VM lacks, or that isn’t what its pointer names, stays out, named (clone_lfs_kept), and its file is a pointer here until git lfs pull fetches it. A failure is named too (clone_lfs_failed), with its reason in the run log.
An object that the VM’s clone has and that didn’t come back, for a reason other than its content, such as a link in .git/lfs or a stream cut short, would go with the VM, so devvm rm and devvm clone off keep the VM then, as for a commit they couldn’t fetch. Their check also looks for the objects that only the VM’s clone has, of commits this repo has already: it lists them as above from the clone’s refs, merged ones included, asks the script in the VM which it has, sizes only, stopping the script once it writes more than a line for each, or more than 64 MiB of the list, and names them (clone_lfs_unfetched), then asks before the VM goes, which devvm clone fetch answers by bringing them here.
data.nested-repos#Nested repos: devvm protects each git repo nested in the project folder as it protects the folder’s own: it locks the same paths of each, checks each at every launch, pins each on Linux and watches each where the host can’t lock (nested repos).
data.on-each-launch#On each launch:
Every launch of an existing VM, every export of its agents’ history, and devvm stop check .git again. devvm reports each of these once:
A .git that was replaced since devvm locked it (git_replaced). devvm then does nothing else, so check the new .git, and look for the old one, renamed. A repo that appeared in the folder after the VM was made (git_appeared), which devvm then locks, and a nested repo that appeared since the last check (git_nested_appeared). A nested repo devvm protected that’s gone (git_nested_gone). A submodule git folder that appeared, in the working tree or under .git/modules (git_embedded_new), which devvm then locks. devvm compares with the git folders it recorded last time, so devvm git-protect on after a VM was made without protection names none: it locks .git as it is then, as trusted. Hooks in a hooks folder that wasn’t locked, because it wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule (git_hooks_unlocked). devvm also reports these, the first two on every launch and the last two when they change:
A commondir (git_commondir). Linked worktrees whose commondir leads elsewhere (git_worktree_stray). Includes and hook links into the project folder (git_include_inside, git_hook_link_inside), which not covered describes. Submodules whose git folder, in the working tree, isn’t a git folder (git_gitdir_not_git), which devvm doesn’t lock.
data.on-linux-hosts#On Linux hosts:
Linux hosts have no immutable flag that a user can set, so devvm makes what it locks read-only where the VM sees it, in the VM’s QEMU process, which serves the project folder to the guest over 9p. Lima starts QEMU through devvm’s wrapper (devvm _qemu exec), and a start of a VM that’s on gives the wrapper what to pin in a file of its own, run/git-pins.json in the VM’s folder, written private, which DEVVM_QEMU_PINS names, because a VM with many nested repos has more pins than one environment variable holds. The wrapper reads the file through no symlink, and it pins, for the folder’s own repo and each nested repo the VM’s state records protecting, .git and each git folder it locks besides, which stay writable, and every path of what’s locked that’s there, which become read-only. They’re the paths the check before the start found and checked, each a real path in the project folder with no symlink, and the check made a missing hooks folder and config.worktree first, so each has a place to pin. devvm then starts devvm _qemu pinned in a user and mount namespace of its own, as you, with only CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and only in that namespace. It makes the namespace’s mounts private, so nothing it mounts reaches this machine’s, and pins each path in order, a folder before what’s under it. It opens each path once, by the kernel, below the project folder and through no symlink (openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS), refuses anything but a file or a folder, and refuses a file with another name, or a folder holding a regular file with one, because a bind covers one name and macOS’s flag covers the file itself (git_pin_linked, which the check before the start names first). Then it binds what it opened over itself with open_tree, mount_setattr and move_mount, which act on that file descriptor and never on a path again, because mount(2) would follow a symlink that the VM planted. A path it can’t pin, or folders it can’t watch, stop the start (qemu_pins_failed), so the VM never runs unlocked. Then it starts devvm _qemu drop as its child, which clears every capability it has, ambient, permitted, effective and inheritable, sets no-new-privileges and replaces itself with QEMU, which runs as you with no capability at all. Its bounding set stays whole, which only CAP_SETPCAP could change, and gives nothing with no new privileges. QEMU is killed if devvm _qemu pinned ends (PR_SET_PDEATHSIG), which runs as long as QEMU does, keeping the pins, so QEMU never outlives what keeps them. devvm _qemu exec waits for both and passes them the signals Lima sends, and if it’s killed, QEMU is killed with it, an unclean stop for the guest, as if its power went.
The guest reaches the project folder only through QEMU, so a write to a pinned path gets EROFS, and a rename or a removal of one, .git itself included, gets EBUSY, because it’s a mount point. A mount can’t be undone from the guest, and QEMU, which has no capability, can’t undo it either. A bind mount over a folder is a file system of its own to the guest, so a rename between the working tree and .git gets EXDEV. The namespace ends with QEMU, so nothing persists once the VM stops, and nothing changes on this machine’s side, where git works as usual.
A git command on this machine that writes .git/config writes a new file and renames it over the old one, and the new file isn’t pinned in the namespace. devvm _qemu pinned watches each pinned path’s folder with inotify, a few folders for each repo, so the 100 nested repos devvm protects at most stay far below the kernel’s limit of watches, and it pins again whatever lost its pin as soon as one changes, and every two seconds besides. A pin can race the rename, because the kernel takes the old file’s mount away before the new file has its name, so the pin may open the old file and find it gone by the time it binds (move_mount’s ENOENT). devvm _qemu pinned then opens the path again and pins what the rename left, up to 50 times, so on a busy host it never mistakes a rename for a lost pin. Until then the guest can write the new file, rename it away and put its own in its place, which then gets the pin, open it for writing, a handle the pin doesn’t take back, or give it another name. So each pin it makes again, and each it can’t, it records in the VM’s run folder (run/git-pins.jsonl), a JSON object a line, after a first line that says it keeps the pins from then on, which it writes before QEMU starts and without which QEMU doesn’t start (qemu_pins_failed). The next check of the stopped VM, at devvm stop or at the next launch, names them before anything else, one line for each path and kind however often it happened (git_pin_again, git_pin_linked_run, git_pin_lost), then removes the file. An event devvm _qemu pinned can’t add goes to Lima’s log, with a warning, and to the file as a mark if it still takes one. A record the check can’t trust is named (git_pins_unrecorded): one it can’t read, which it keeps, a line that isn’t an event, a mark, or a file that doesn’t start with a run’s first line, as when it was removed while the VM ran and made again. The check also sums what a lock covers, as the watch does, and names what changed since the VM’s last check, so a file the guest changed in that window, or through a handle it kept, is named too. macOS’s flag has no window, because a locked config can’t be replaced on the host either.
Each launch of a running VM that’s on, and devvm stop before it stops it, read QEMU’s mounts (/proc//mountinfo, QEMU’s pid from Lima’s qemu.pid) and name what of .git and of the git folders it locked QEMU lacks (git_pins_missing): .git and each git folder that isn’t a mount point of its own, and each read-only path that QEMU doesn’t see read-only,, such as all of them for a VM that limactl start started. A VM that’s on whose .git has nothing devvm can pin, such as one whose .git is a symlink, is named at its start (git_pins_none).
devvm checks that the host can pin by doing it: it pins a file in a namespace of its own, with its own binary, and checks that writing it fails (devvm _qemu probe). Lima’s read-only-paths feature is native where that works and none elsewhere, and a VM that’s on needs it to start, so where the kernel stops letting devvm in, the start is refused (backend_lacks) and never goes on unlocked. Where the probe fails, new VMs get off, devvm watches .git instead, and devvm doctor says why: Ubuntu’s kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns, kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone or user.max_user_namespaces at 0, or the probe’s own error. devvm offers no AppArmor profile for Ubuntu, because a profile for a binary in a folder you can write gives any program running as you what Ubuntu’s restriction holds back (Ubuntu). devvm makes the namespace itself rather than through unshare(1), so the program that asks for it is devvm.
devvm doesn’t pin .git/commondir against the VM making one, which would point git on this machine at another config: a file has to be there to be pinned, and devvm puts no file in .git that git doesn’t, so it reports a commondir at each check, as on macOS.
data.submodules-in-the-copy#Submodules in the:
Once a repo’s copy is in, and before devvm records it as copied, each of its initialised submodules gets a clone of its own in the VM, nested ones after their parent, so a copy that didn’t finish copies the rest on the next launch. devvm takes the list from this machine’s repo alone, never from the VM or .gitmodules: a submodule is one whose name the repo’s own config gives a URL (submodule..url, as git submodule init sets it), whose git dir is modules/ in the repo’s common dir, whose core.worktree there leads to a folder below the repo where its index has a submodule (a gitlink), and which is its own repo there by the checks above, at a path a terminal can show. An uninitialised submodule has no such git dir, so its folder stays as the parent’s copy left it, empty, and so does one initialised after the copy, or in a VM made before devvm copied submodules. One that’s initialised but fails a check stays on this machine, named (clone_submodule_kept), and so does each of a linked worktree’s, whose submodules’ git dirs are in the common dir, which devvm doesn’t read for them. Each submodule’s copy is a repo’s, checked again just before, as a folder of repos’ repo is: still its own repo’s top, with no grafts and a HEAD, and no other VM mounting it. One that fails that, or any step of its copy, such as a VM that refuses it, is named (clone_submodule_kept), with its own submodules left out, and the repo’s copy goes on without it and is recorded as done, so it’s tried again only on a launch before that, when the repo’s copy didn’t finish. Its record is taken out only when nothing of it can be in the VM: it failed before this launch recorded it, with no record from an earlier launch. Otherwise its record stays, not copied, so whatever of it the VM has is still fetched from and checked by devvm rm, which checks a repo that wasn’t copied when the VM has it, and devvm clone fetch adds its remote. Its remote is chosen as a repo’s is, recorded with its path in the VM’s state before its copy (submodules, in its repo’s entry, nested ones in theirs). The submodule is then made in the VM, in the folder the parent’s checkout left empty, as a repo with a .git folder of its own, which git submodule status reads as a submodule’s, and copied, so its HEAD is detached at the commit the submodule has checked out here, with its refs, its changes, its state and its settings; then its remote added in its repo here, which is its git dir’s config, and the copy recorded. The parent’s settings give it submodule..url and active (the settings in the copy), so git in the VM takes it for initialised.
devvm clone fetch, devvm rm’s and devvm clone off’s check and the remotes’ removal go over each submodule the state records, each named by its path in the folder, as a folder of repos’ repos are, so a submodule you remove or deinitialise here later isn’t passed over: as one another VM mounts, it’s named as one devvm can’t check (clone_submodule_unchecked), and devvm rm and devvm clone off ask before the VM goes, while devvm clone fetch names it and leaves it. devvm clone add of a recorded submodule says it’s the clone’s already. An older devvm ignores the record, so its devvm rm wouldn’t check a submodule, which matters only after a downgrade. A folder of repos’ walk passes over a repo that’s a submodule of a repo in the folder, among that repo’s initialised submodules, which its clone has.
A submodule’s own folder isn’t a repo that --clone takes by itself: its .git file leads into the parent’s .git/modules, or for a parent that’s a linked worktree, into the main repo’s .git, and a VM that mounts the folder of either could swap that git dir under host git, which the check for a VM mounting the repo, looking at the folder and a worktree’s common dir, wouldn’t see. So devvm --clone there, and a folder of repos’ copy of one, refuses it as a .git that points into another repo (clone_git_elsewhere). Only as a submodule of a --clone repo is it copied, and every check of it as one, before its copy, before a fetch and in the clone check, takes that shape.
data.symlinks#Symlinks: devvm never locks or creates anything through a symlink, because the VM could plant one under .git so that devvm would lock a file elsewhere. devvm reports a path that is a symlink, or is under one, instead of locking it (git_not_locked). devvm also checks each lock again once it’s set. If the path moved in the meantime, devvm unlocks it where it landed and reports it (git_lock_raced).
data.the-copy-into-a-clone-vm#The copy into a:
devvm copies a repo into a --clone VM without git push, because git receive-pack in the VM refuses repos that users have: a shallow clone’s push fails with shallow update not allowed, and a SHA-256 repo’s push into a SHA-1 repo fails with the receiving end does not support this repository's hash algorithm. The copy is a snapshot instead, made by devvm’s own git on this machine and applied by plain git in the VM, through the backend’s command channel, which also carries the VM’s agent. The structure test keeps git push out of devvm’s code, so the copy can’t drift back to a second transport (where the code is).
The copy takes three commands in the VM:
One script makes every repo the clone has. For each repo, it gets the repo’s path and the host repo’s object format. A repo that’s copied already is printed as landed and left alone. That’s a repo whose .git/devvm-seeded says done, or one with no such file whose HEAD resolves, which an older devvm’s push made. A repo that isn’t there yet is made with git init, with --object-format=sha256 only for a SHA-256 repo, because git before 2.29 doesn’t know the option. One that’s there, from a copy that didn’t finish, isn’t made again, because git 2.54’s git init in a reftable repo drops its extensions.refStorage setting and breaks the repo. It takes receive.denyCurrentBranch=updateInstead and receive.shallowUpdate=true, for your own git push devvm BRANCH later, and .git/devvm-seeded says pending. A git init that fails for a SHA-256 repo prints the VM’s git --version, and devvm stops before it sends anything (clone_vm_git_old), showing the version only when it reads as git prints one. A tar of small files goes into .git/devvm-seed in the VM’s repo, never /tmp, which is in memory on some systems. It holds the refs to set, each an object and its name, the symbolic refs, such as refs/remotes/origin/HEAD, each with the ref it points to, what to check out, a branch’s name or, for a detached HEAD, its commit, and the host repo’s shallow file, read from the repo’s common dir as a regular file only, never through a link, so a link there can’t send another file. It also holds the working tree (the working tree): the repo’s index, normalised, the paths to check out from it, and the working copies of the tracked files that differ from it. And it holds the repo’s state (the state in the copy): an operation in progress, the stash, and the info files. The pack of the objects those refs and a detached HEAD reach, with the index’s blobs and the commits the state names, from git pack-objects --revs --stdout, goes straight into git index-pack --stdin in the VM, which checks every object it writes, so devvm doesn’t run git fsck as well. pack-objects --revs walks with the repo’s commit-graph and bitmaps when it has them, so a VM that once wrote this repo’s .git, through a mount before .git protection, could have forged one to put objects in the pack that the refs don’t reach, which are this repo’s own objects, never another repo’s or a file’s. Neither end holds the whole pack in memory, and when the command in the VM ends early, devvm closes the pipe so pack-objects stops. The same command then copies the shallow file and sets the refs with git update-ref --stdin, and each symbolic ref with git symbolic-ref, unless a ref of that name is there already. It points HEAD at the branch, with git symbolic-ref, or detaches it at the commit, with git update-ref --no-deref, and puts the host’s index in place, with the working copies sent where the VM has no file. It does that only when HEAD was unborn, is on the branch the copy just set, or is detached at the commit or at one an earlier try set, so a VM that checked out a branch of its own keeps it, and one that moved its detached HEAD keeps it too. A HEAD left where the VM put it, away from this machine’s, is named (clone_kept_head), which covers a repo here switched between a branch and a detached HEAD since the copy that didn’t finish. It checks out the listed paths with git checkout-index -u -z --stdin, or every path with -a when it kept the VM’s HEAD, without -f, so it writes only the files that aren’t there. It removes .git/devvm-seed and writes done to .git/devvm-seeded last. The refs are those of refs/heads, refs/tags, refs/notes, refs/replace and refs/remotes, read in one git for-each-ref, less the remote-tracking branches of each remote any of whose URLs, as git resolves them (git remote get-url --all), reaches a devvm VM by its full name or its shorter one, in any URL form or case, and less a branch that’s no commit, which git won’t set. A linked worktree’s copy takes the smaller set above, and its upstream and default branch pass the same rules, so neither can be another VM’s remote-tracking branch or a ref outside the namespaces, such as refs/stash through branch..remote=.. A symbolic ref goes only when the ref it points to goes. Nothing outside those namespaces goes, such as refs/original, refs/prefetch or refs/stash. The pack carries what a push of the same refs would: the commits, trees, blobs and tags they reach, and nothing unreachable. devvm’s git runs pack-objects with replace refs and grafts off, so each commit goes with its own parents, and a repo with a grafts file is refused before the VM is made (clone_grafts).
A partial clone, one whose config names a promisor remote (remote..promisor, or an older git’s extensions.partialClone), lacks objects its remote has, and pack-objects --revs would want them in its walk, which fails with GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, missing trees and all. Its pack is made from a list instead: git rev-list --objects --missing=allow-promisor --stdin of the tips the repo has, which git cat-file --batch-check picks, as a sparse checkout’s index can name blobs the repo never fetched, piped into git pack-objects --stdout through a pipe of their own, whose ends devvm closes once both have started, so when pack-objects ends early, rev-list’s next write fails and it ends too. devvm holds back the pack’s last 64 bytes, more than its trailing hash, until the pack ends, then waits for rev-list, and when rev-list failed, it ends the pack there, so the VM’s git index-pack gets a pack cut short and refuses it, and the copy fails with rev-list’s error, never with a pack that lacks objects and says nothing. The VM reads the pack with git index-pack --promisor, so it’s a promisor pack, and the settings give the VM’s clone the promisor remote, with its filter, and promisor as git reads it, so yes, 1 or no value at all goes as true. Its git then fetches a missing object from that remote when a command needs one. That fetch goes through the VM’s own network policy, with no credential of this machine’s, as the remote’s URL has none, so a private remote needs the VM’s own login.
devvm reads each ref’s object type with git cat-file --batch-check after listing the refs, because git for-each-ref’s %(objecttype) fails on a ref whose object the repo lacks, such as a partial clone’s tag of a blob it never fetched. Such a ref stays out of the copy, named (clone_partial_refs_kept), and in a repo that isn’t partial, it fails the copy, as that repo is broken (clone_ref_no_object). devvm reads the promisor remotes as git here reads them, includes followed, each remote..promisor on its own, so one value git can’t read as a boolean drops only its own remote, and a remote’s last value wins. It names those whose settings don’t go, as their URL is of a kind that stays or reaches a devvm VM (clone_partial_promisor_kept), and copies the repo anyway, as the VM’s clone works with what it has. For each promisor remote that goes, in name order, it compares the remote’s host and port with the VM’s tier: on the none tier it names the host with how to reach it (clone_partial_blocked_none), on the allowlist tier one the allowlist doesn’t allow (clone_partial_blocked), and on the internet tier one a deny rule blocks or an address that isn’t public, which that tier never reaches (clone_partial_denied). A host it names on a port other than 80 or 443, such as an ssh remote’s 22, is named as the rule that allows that port alone, such as github.com:22, which devvm network allow takes. When devvm can’t read the VM’s policies, it judges nothing against them, and names only the none tier’s hosts and private addresses. A name that resolves to a private address isn’t reached either, which devvm can’t tell before the VM looks it up. It also names a remote on this machine, a file:// URL or a path, which the VM can’t reach (clone_partial_unreachable). A scp-like URL’s host is read as git reads it, up to its first colon, past a bracketed one such as [::1], and a URL whose port isn’t a number names no host.
devvm’s own fetch from the VM keeps GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1, so a VM can’t make this machine’s git fetch anything, and the VM’s git upload-pack fetches no missing object to send it, as git 2.45.1 and newer turn that off. So when the VM’s work names an object its partial clone lacks, such as a blob restored from an old commit, the fetch fails, and devvm says to have git in the VM read the work’s objects first, which fetches them, then fetch again (clone_fetch_partial). devvm doesn’t turn lazy fetching on in the VM’s upload-pack.
A copy that fails before its end leaves pending, so the next launch copies again in full. git index-pack of a pack the repo has, git symbolic-ref and the checkout are all safe to run again. The refs follow one rule, so a copy never moves a branch the VM moved: before it sets a ref, the script records its name and the commit in .git/devvm-seeded-refs, and it then sets a ref that’s missing, at the host’s commit already, or at a commit an earlier try recorded. It leaves any other as it is and prints it, and devvm names those branches (clone_kept_branches). After the checkout, git update-index --refresh and git diff-files -z list the files whose content isn’t the index’s. devvm leaves out the paths that the copy itself sent or deleted, adds the VM’s own files at those paths, and names what’s left as the files the VM wrote (clone_kept_files). What the VM prints is untrusted, so devvm reads at most 1 MiB of it, shows at most 20 names, each cut to 200 bytes and quoted, and acts on none of it. devvm rm and devvm clone off check a clone whose copy didn’t finish as any other, so the VM’s work there is offered for fetching too.
An older devvm made each VM’s repo with plain git init, so with SHA-1 object names. In such a VM whose copy failed, a SHA-256 repo’s empty repo has the wrong object format, which the script prints. devvm then asks whether to make that repo again (clone_repo_format). The repo has no commit, but it may hold the VM’s own hooks or config, so only you can say, and no flag answers the question. Without a terminal devvm refuses, saying what to run (clone_repo_format_kept). On yes, the script deletes that .git only when it still has no HEAD and no ref, and makes it again.
data.the-record-of-what-was-copied#The record:
So that devvm rm and devvm clone off don’t take your own uncommitted changes for the VM’s work, the copy leaves a record of them in the VM’s repo, .git/devvm-seeded-tree, written with the index. It covers each path that git status in the VM would list once the copy is in: those whose staged entry isn’t HEAD’s, found with git diff-index --cached on the normalised index, and those whose working copy differs. For each path it holds what devvm put there: the blob of the working copy, which devvm hashes as it sends the file, with a mark for an executable file, = for one checked out from the index, dir for a gitlink’s empty folder or - for none, and the path’s index entries, each with its mode, blob and stage.
The clone check reads the record back in the VM. For each path, git in the VM hashes the working copy with git hash-object --no-filters, or the link’s target for a symbolic link, or, for one checked out from the index, asks git diff-files --quiet after a refresh whether it’s still the index’s, so a file that info/attributes converts, such as with eol=crlf, matches as git checked it out, and it lists the index entries with git ls-files --format, and the VM prints the paths whose state matches the record. devvm leaves the git status lines that name only those paths out of what it counts and shows, so a path counts once the VM changes its content, its executable bit or what’s staged for it. A deletion that’s still deleted matches. Untracked files’ lines always count, as the copy sends none.
The record is the VM’s side of the copy, not a comparison with the repo here, so it stays right when your working copy changes after the copy, and it needs nothing in devvm’s own state. The VM can write the record, and it can answer for it anything it likes, but all a forged record or answer can do is make the VM’s own work look unchanged, so that devvm rm deletes it without asking, which hurts only the VM’s work. A VM without the record, such as one an older devvm made, or whose git has no ls-files --format (before 2.38), counts every change as before.
data.the-settings-in-the-copy#The settings in:
The copy reads the repo’s own config with git config --local --no-includes --null --list, and, when extensions.worktreeConfig is on, the worktree’s config.worktree after it with --worktree, where git sparse-checkout writes its settings, so neither your global config nor an included file goes. It sends only the keys of an allowlist, each value checked, never the config as a file, and a key written with no value, which git reads as true, goes as true. The VM sets them with git config --add, each key unset first, then writes .git/devvm-seeded-config, so a copy that runs again sets nothing over what the VM changed since:
remote..url, as git remote get-url --all gives them, with insteadOf applied, and pushurl, when git remote get-url --push --all gives other URLs, as it does with a push URL or a pushInsteadOf. Each URL is cleaned: an http or https URL without its user name, password, query or fragment, any of which can be a token; an ssh://, git+ssh:// or ssh+git:// URL without its password, query or fragment, its user kept, as git@ is a name, not a secret; a scp-like [user@]host:path as it is; and a file:// URL or a path as it is. git reads a scp-like URL’s host up to its first colon, past a bracketed host such as [::1], so its user, before an @ there, holds no colon, and one whose path has an @ and then a colon, as in user:token@host:path, which git reads as the host user and a path holding the token, stays. Any other kind, such as git:// or a transport helper’s ext::, stays, named (clone_urls_kept), and a remote with no URL that goes stays with the rest of its settings. A remote that reaches a devvm VM stays, as its refs do, and so does a push URL that reaches one. A remote whose push URLs all stay goes without them, so git push in the VM pushes to its URL, named (clone_push_urls_kept). A remote whose URLs git remote get-url can’t give stays, named (clone_urls_unread). remote..fetch, promisor, partialclonefilter and tagOpt, for a remote that goes. branch..remote, merge, rebase and pushRemote, for a branch the copy sends, so the VM of a worktree learns no other branch’s name, but an upstream on a remote that stays. submodule..url, resolved with git ls-remote --get-url and cleaned as a remote’s, and its active, branch and update, but an update that runs a command (!command). core.sparseCheckout, core.sparseCheckoutCone and index.sparse. core.hooksPath, the last one, when it’s a relative folder inside the repo, never through .. or a .git part, and not one that git expands, as it does ~/ and %(prefix)/. user.name and user.email. Nothing else goes, such as credential.*, http.* and its extra headers, url.*.insteadOf, which the URLs have applied already, core.sshCommand, core.fsmonitor, filter.*, include*, alias.*, or the keys that describe this machine’s filesystem, core.ignorecase, precomposeunicode, filemode and symlinks.
The hooks go as they are, and only as git here runs them, from the common dir’s hooks folder, which git rev-parse --git-path hooks can’t give, as it gives /dev/null under devvm’s own git’s core.hooksPath. They go when the core.hooksPath git uses is none, .git/hooks or that folder. It’s the last of the repo’s own config and its worktree’s, includes followed (git config --includes --show-scope --get-all, its local and worktree ones), so an include after the repo’s own wins, as in git, else your global or system config’s, read from the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name when they’re set. In a linked worktree, whose .git is a file, a relative .git/hooks names no folder, so git there runs no hook, and none goes. A core.hooksPath elsewhere inside the repo goes as the setting alone: the hooks in it are files of the working tree, so the tracked ones reach the VM with the checkout, and the untracked ones, such as husky’s _ folder, stay, as every untracked file does. One outside the repo, or one an included file sets, stays, named (clone_hooks_path_kept), and no hook goes. The hooks folder is opened from the common dir, never through a link, and one that’s missing, a link or unreadable is named (clone_hooks_dir_kept). Only files named as git’s hooks go, the names devvm’s own git turns off, each a regular file of at most 1 MiB and 16 MiB in all. A link, a folder or a bigger file stays, named (clone_hooks_kept). In the VM, a hook goes into the git dir’s hooks folder only where the VM has no file of that name, with its executable bit.
The settings and hooks go in last, after the checkout, and the script’s git runs with core.hooksPath=/dev/null, so neither a hook the copy brings nor one of the VM’s own runs during the copy, and none can fail it or a copy that runs again.
data.the-state-in-the-copy#The state in the c:
The copy sends what git keeps beside the refs and the index that you’d miss in the VM. Every file is read from the repo’s git dir, at the path git rev-parse --git-path gives, so a linked worktree’s own are read, as a regular file only, never through a link, at most 16 MiB each and 64 MiB in all, and a folder is opened from its parent, refusing a link. info/sparse-checkout and info/attributes always go. info/exclude goes too, added below the VM’s own, which holds the lines that keep a folder of repos’ other repos out of each one’s git status.
An operation’s files go only while it’s in progress, and an operation is never told by a file that a reftable repo keeps as a ref:
A rebase, by its folder, rebase-merge or rebase-apply: the folder’s files, the pseudo-refs REBASE_HEAD and AUTO_MERGE, and the refs below refs/rewritten/, with ORIG_HEAD only during git am (rebase-apply/applying), whose --abort needs it. A merge, by its MERGE_HEAD file: MERGE_HEAD, MERGE_MSG, MERGE_MODE, MERGE_AUTOSTASH and SQUASH_MSG, and the pseudo-ref AUTO_MERGE. A cherry-pick or a revert, by the pseudo-ref CHERRY_PICK_HEAD or REVERT_HEAD, or by the sequencer folder: MERGE_MSG, the folder’s files, and the pseudo-refs CHERRY_PICK_HEAD, REVERT_HEAD and AUTO_MERGE. Bisect, by its BISECT_START file: the BISECT_* files, BISECT_FIRST_PARENT included, the pseudo-ref BISECT_HEAD, and the refs below refs/bisect/. A pseudo-ref is read with git rev-parse -q --verify, and only when --symbolic-full-name gives its own name back, so a branch or tag named CHERRY_PICK_HEAD isn’t taken for one. It’s set in the VM with git update-ref, never copied as a file, so a reftable repo, which keeps CHERRY_PICK_HEAD and the rest as refs, works as a files one does. ORIG_HEAD never goes otherwise, not even while an operation is in progress, because a reset made meanwhile points it at what it took back, such as a commit that held a secret, and a stopped rebase or a sequencer folder left behind would carry it along.
The pack carries the commits the operation needs, and only those that its files hold as object ids: the first word of rebase-merge’s onto, orig-head, stopped-sha, amend, autostash and squash-onto, every id in its update-refs, the first two of each line of its rewritten-list and rewritten-pending, rebase-apply’s onto, orig-head and abort-safety, each line of MERGE_HEAD, MERGE_AUTOSTASH, sequencer’s head and abort-safety, BISECT_EXPECTED_REV, and the ids on BISECT_LOG’s lines that mark a commit good, bad, skipped, or with the terms BISECT_TERMS names. Each must be an object the repo has, which git cat-file --batch-check says. Free text never counts, so a commit that only a merge message or a revert’s message names stays on this machine. A new state file that holds object ids needs its entry in that list. The commits the todo lists still have to pick, rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo and sequencer/todo, are never scanned into the pack: devvm resolves each and names those that the copy’s refs and the ids above don’t reach (clone_todo_missing), as that step will fail in the VM.
The stash goes as its entries, oldest first, each with its message, read with git reflog show --format='%H %gs' refs/stash, the newest 1,000, the rest named (clone_stash_over_kept), and the VM stores each with git stash store -m, the commits it was made on with it. An entry with untracked files, a third parent, is taken for one of git stash --all and stays, named (clone_stash_all_kept), because it may hold ignored files, such as .env, when any of those files is a .gitignore, when the entry changes a .gitignore (git stash --all takes back an uncommitted edit of one, so the rules that ignored a file are gone from the working tree), or when the ignore rules ignore any of its untracked files (git check-ignore --no-index), as they are now or as the entry’s own .gitignore files had them, which devvm writes into a folder of their own to check against. The check errs toward keeping an entry back. A linked worktree’s copy sends no stash, which is the whole repo’s. The VM records each entry it stores in .git/devvm-seeded-stash, so a copy that runs again skips as many as the record has, an entry that the stash holds twice is stored twice, and the clone check leaves those entries out of the VM’s own.
The script that reads the clone’s state prints every other entry as SHA stash@{N}, devvm names it as stash-N when this repo doesn’t have its commit, and fetches it by that commit. devvm clone fetch does the same, with a script of its own whose lines devvm takes only for a detached HEAD’s commit and stash entries, so the VM can’t have it save a branch of another name, and an entry it can’t fetch is named, the others saved. For rm and clone off, an entry that can’t be fetched keeps the VM. A stash entry is never saved with its untracked files, because git stash apply writes them, ignored ones too, such as a virtualenv’s sitecustomize.py that Python runs on its own, while git stash show doesn’t list them. devvm makes the entry again with git commit-tree, from its tree and its first two parents, with its own message, author and committer, so the same entry is always the same commit, and saves that as saved/devvm/stash-N. The untracked files go to saved/devvm/stash-N-untracked, and devvm names them, and those that git on this machine ignores (clone_stash_untracked, clone_stash_untracked_ignored). Every fetch from a VM checks each object it receives (transfer.fsckObjects). No ref names an older entry, and devvm’s ssh passes no GIT_PROTOCOL to the VM, so its git upload-pack speaks protocol v0, which refuses a commit no ref names unless the fetch runs it with uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant, as devvm’s does. That only lets the host ask the VM for its own objects. The stubs drop GIT_PROTOCOL too, so the tests fetch over v0.
