The state goes in only when the copy sets HEAD, as the working tree does, since an operation applies to the commit it started from, and so do the refs of an operation, below refs/rewritten/ and refs/bisect/. The stash goes in either way.
data.the-walk#The walk:
devvm finds the nested repos by walking the project folder when it creates the VM, at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop, at devvm git-protect on a stopped VM, and when devvm clone off mounts the folder again. It’s one walk that also finds the set-id files on a Linux host, which only the start runs (the checks on owners), and a launch into a running VM never walks. The walk stays on the project folder’s file system, follows no symlink and never enters a .git folder, so it never finds the repos of .git/modules, which are the folder’s own repo’s to protect. It takes a folder for a repo when the folder has anything named .git, a folder, a file, which a linked worktree or a repo with its git folder elsewhere has, a symlink or anything else, whether git takes it for a repo’s now or not, because the VM can make it one at any time. On macOS, whose file systems fold case, .GIT is .git to git, so the walk takes any case of the name there. It looks for repos at most four folders below the project folder, and not in node_modules, vendor, .venv, __pycache__ or .terraform, which package managers and build tools fill with what they fetch, so on macOS, where there are no set-id files to look for, the walk doesn’t enter those folders at all. On Linux it walks them for set-id files anyway, and counts the .git it sees there and below four folders (git_nested_skipped). It counts the folders it doesn’t enter because they’re on another file system (git_nested_devices). It keeps the first 100 repos it finds, in the walk’s order, and counts the rest, keeping the names of the first ten of those (git_nested_past_bound).
The walk also names each folder up to four folders down that git could take for a bare repo (git_nested_bare), one shaped like a git folder by git’s own test: a HEAD, and objects and refs, files or folders, in the folder or in the folder its commondir names. A git folder that a repo’s scan locks, or that a nested repo’s .git file names, isn’t named. devvm doctor reads safe.bareRepository from git’s global and system config, the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name included, which it reads by name because devvm’s host git ignores every GIT_* variable, and it gives a tip unless the setting is explicit (doctor_git_bare).
A check takes the repos the walk found, the ones the VM’s state records first. A recorded repo stays protected, whether the walk found it or not, while its folder is a real folder of the project with anything at its .git, because the VM can make a .git that the walk or git’s own test passes over while git still takes it: objects and refs renamed with a commondir that leads to a git folder of its own, a .GIT, or a .git it can’t read, which devvm can’t lock and names (git_not_locked). A check without a walk, such as devvm rm and the start that pins, takes the repos the state records. A launch into a running VM checks the folder’s own repo alone and keeps the nested repos’ records as they are, because it locks nothing and the VM can change them until it stops, so it never pays for scanning them, and the check of a running VM’s pins goes by those records without scanning them. devvm scans each repo as it scans the folder’s own, eight at once, because each scan runs a few host git commands: a check of a stopped VM with 50 nested repos, the walk and the locks included, takes under a second on an M3 Max.
data.the-watch#The watch:
Where the host can’t pin, devvm locks nothing, and every VM that mounts its folder gets off as its mode. devvm watches the paths it would lock instead, and names what changed after the fact (git_changed), which Linux hosts tells the user how to check.
devvm hashes the same paths that what’s locked lists, found in the same way, and .git/commondir, there or not, the files that include.path and includeIf.*.path lead to in the project folder, and the folder that core.hooksPath names in it. For a hooks folder, it hashes each entry below it, except git’s .sample files, which git never runs, starting with the entries at its top that have a hook’s name (githooks(5)), which git runs, and then the rest. It hashes a regular file’s contents with SHA-256, opened with O_NOFOLLOW and O_NONBLOCK and checked to be a regular file once it’s open, as devvm reads every file a VM can write. It records a symlink by where it points, and a path under a symlink, such as .git/config when .git is a symlink, by that fact. When the link resolves to a file or folder inside the project folder, it adds that file’s hash, or a hash of that folder’s hashes, and it never follows a link out of the project folder. Anything else, such as a FIFO, is recorded by its type. The work is bounded: past 1,000 entries, a hooks folder is recorded by that count, its inode and its change time, a file larger than 16 MiB by its size, inode and change time, and a watch keeps at most 2,000 hashes of the folder’s own repo and 200 of each nested repo, so a folder with many nested repos never overflows it. The VM can’t set a change time back over 9p, so a change that keeps a large file’s size is still named. Each check names, in its own warning (git_watch_blind), every path that is a symlink or under one, past a bound, or past the 2,000, because the watch can’t see every change there.
The same checks first run what a lock’s check reports, without locking (protect with watching): a .git replaced since the last check (git_replaced), after which the next check compares with the new one, a commondir (git_commondir), linked worktrees whose commondir leads elsewhere, a repo or submodule git folder that appeared, a submodule’s folder that isn’t a git folder (git_gitdir_not_git), which the watch doesn’t hash as one and where devvm creates nothing, and includes, hook links and core.hooksPath into the project folder. They don’t report hooks in folders that aren’t locked, because nothing is, and the watch names their changes. .git’s identity and the git folders and delegations found are recorded in the git section’s made, as a lock’s check records them. A VM whose made isn’t set yet reports as a new VM does.
The watch reads .git only when the VM is stopped, so it misses a change the VM made and undid before it stopped. It’s a report, not a security boundary.
The hashes go in the VM’s state, in the git section’s watched, by each path relative to the project folder, with scanned set once a check has recorded them. devvm records them when it creates the VM, and checks them again on each launch that finds the VM stopped and on devvm stop, the same places that check the locks on macOS. Each check names every path whose hash changed, appeared or went since the last one, in one warning, at most ten of them and then how many more (git_changed_more), and then records the new hashes. A launch of a running VM checks nothing. A VM whose state has no watched yet, such as one an older devvm made, or one that devvm adopt gave this folder, records its first hashes without naming anything.
Each launch also warns that the VM can change .git (git_unprotected), unless the folder has no .git or the VM is a --clone VM. The warning stops once the user has chosen the mode, which devvm records as the git section’s chosen: devvm git-protect off sets it, and so does --no-git-protect when devvm creates the VM.
data.the-working-tree-in-the-copy#The working:
The copy sends your uncommitted changes as git’s own index and the working copies of the files that differ from it, so git status in the VM shows what it shows here. devvm reads the repo’s index, at the path git rev-parse --git-path index gives, as a regular file only, never through a link, into a temporary file of its own, registered for removal before any git command runs, so it goes however the copy ends. The copy keeps the index’s modification time, so git tells a file changed in the second the index was written from one that wasn’t, as it would with the repo’s own index. devvm’s git then refreshes the copy, so a file whose stat changed but not its content isn’t sent, without entering any submodule (--ignore-submodules), and rewrites it as version 3, even when it’s that already (--force-write-index), with no split index, no sparse directories, no untracked cache, no fsmonitor data, no resolve-undo and a real trailing hash. The untracked cache names untracked files and the repo’s path on this machine, so none of that goes, and any git since 1.7 reads the result. Resolve-undo, which git checkout -m uses to bring back a conflict you resolved, can name blobs that no ref reaches and that the pack doesn’t carry, so the VM’s repo would fail git fsck with it. What’s staged is staged in the VM, conflicts, intent-to-add entries and skip-worktree bits included, and the pack carries every blob the index names, but no gitlink’s commit, which isn’t this repo’s. An index with a path that git never checks out, one with a .git part in any case, as macOS and Windows also read one, or with an empty, . or .. part, fails the copy.
git ls-files -s -z on the copy lists the paths, and git diff-files --ignore-submodules=all --name-only -z on it lists those whose working copy differs. Without --ignore-submodules, git diff-files runs git status in each submodule and embedded repo, where that repo’s own config can name a filter that devvm’s git hasn’t turned off, so devvm runs diff-files only through the helper that adds it. Each path that differs is sorted out through a root opened at the repo, and each folder on the way to it is opened from its parent, refusing a symbolic link, so neither a link out of the repo nor one inside it, such as a tracked folder replaced by a link to an ignored folder or to .git, sends another file:
A regular file or a symbolic link, where the index has one of those, goes as it is, under changed/ in the tar, with its permissions and modification time, read without following a link. A file that’s a link now goes as the link, so git status in the VM shows the same type change. A path that’s gone, or whose folder is a symbolic link here, which git takes for a deletion, goes as gone: the VM doesn’t check it out, so it’s deleted there too. Anything else, such as a tracked file that’s a folder now, goes as gone, and devvm names it (clone_typechange_kept), so nothing inside that folder goes. A gitlink, a submodule’s or an embedded repo’s, is checked out as git does, as an empty folder, without its .git or anything in it. A path that a filter attribute names a filter for, in the working tree’s attributes or the index’s, such as git-crypt’s or Git LFS’s, is checked out from the index, as git stores it, and named as one that may differ (clone_filtered_kept). devvm’s git runs no filter, so it can’t tell a real change from the filter’s own. Such a file that’s gone goes as gone. In the VM, when the copy sets HEAD, it puts the index in place, notes which of the paths sent or gone it already has a file at, copies each working copy sent where the VM has no file, with cp -P -p, and checks out the other paths from the index, without -f, except a conflict’s, which has no entry to check out, and a path with the skip-worktree bit that the working tree doesn’t have, which a sparse checkout leaves out, in the VM as here. A skip-worktree path that the working tree has, marked by hand with git update-index --skip-worktree or left by a git older than 2.37 outside a sparse checkout, is checked out from the index, never sent as it is here, because git hides its edits, which are often local settings or secrets: the VM turns the bit off for those paths (skip.list), checks them out and turns it on again, and devvm names them (clone_skip_worktree_kept). An assume-unchanged file’s edits are hidden from git diff-files too, so it goes as the index has it. The VM’s files that the copy didn’t write over are named (clone_kept_files): those at a path you changed or deleted here, and those elsewhere that differ from the index. When the copy keeps the VM’s HEAD, the VM’s index stays, nothing of the working tree is applied, because your changes would apply to something else, and devvm says so (clone_uncommitted_kept) instead of naming the files it would have left out.
data.two-bounds#Two bounds:
Each repo has two bounds. Its own top folder is where its .git is, where .git/modules and a relative core.hooksPath are read from, and where its submodules’ folders are. The project folder, which the VM mounts, is what the VM can write, so it’s the bound for everything else: devvm locks only a real path in the project folder, through no symlink, an include or a hooks path leads inside when it leads into the project folder, and a submodule’s git folder outside the project folder is one devvm can’t lock (git_gitdir_outside). A nested repo’s hooks path that leads into a sibling repo is inside, because the VM can write it.
A nested repo is left to another repo only when that repo’s scan locks its git folder whole: the git folder is that repo’s .git, one under its .git/modules that reads its config from itself, with no commondir that leads elsewhere, or one of its linked worktrees under .git/worktrees whose commondir leads back. Anything else below a .git, such as a .git/evil the VM made for a src/.git file to name, isn’t locked by anything, so the repo is scanned on its own, and named as one that appeared and as one devvm doesn’t protect. A submodule in the working tree is scanned as a repo of its own as well as its parent’s submodule, because the index that names it is the VM’s to write: a gitlink the VM adds, whose .git file names a nested repo’s git folder, would otherwise hide that repo’s own submodules and worktrees behind a scan from the wrong folder. Locking a path twice changes nothing, and unlocking goes by path once. A nested repo whose .git is a file is locked as the folder’s own is when it’s a linked worktree, by its .git file. When the git folder that file names is in the project folder and no repo’s scan locks it, devvm names the repo as one it doesn’t protect, and when it’s outside the project folder, it names the repo as one whose git folder it can’t lock (git_nested_gitdir_outside), as it does a submodule’s.
A scan follows each submodule git folder once, by its resolved path, and one check’s scans follow at most 1,000 of them across every repo, so gitlinks that the VM points back at a git folder already followed, or through a symlinked folder at the repo itself, or many repos full of submodules, can’t make a check run git without end. A repo whose scan stopped there is named at every check (git_scan_bounded).
data.two-vms-one-repo#Two VMs, one repo: A nested repo with a VM of its own is protected by two VMs, the parent folder’s and its own. On macOS both set the same flag on the same files, so when one VM’s protection comes off, at devvm rm or devvm git-protect off, devvm leaves locked every path that another VM’s protection still covers, which is a git folder that VM recorded locking, of its own repo or of a nested one, and names that VM (git_kept_locked). The inventory reads every VM’s state for that. It fails closed: a state it can’t read keeps locked every path in the folder whose hash names that state’s folder, and when it can’t read the VMs’ folder at all, everything stays locked, each named with the state to fix (git_kept_unread). Locking a VM’s repos and recording them, and unlocking another’s, take the host’s lock of .git protection first, before any VM’s own lock, so one VM’s unlock never runs between another’s locks and their record. Taking a strict VM’s diff.ignoreSubmodules out never unlocks a config another VM keeps locked, because that VM, running, could race the unlocked file, so the setting stays there, and devvm names the file, that VM and how to take it out by hand (git_strict_kept). The repo goes in the state’s strict_left, as does one whose config changed since the check, and each later check that finds the VM stopped tries again, until none is left. When git can’t change a config, devvm locks it again all the same. On Linux each VM’s pins are in its own QEMU’s namespace, and the watch locks nothing, so neither needs this.
data.what-a-lock-cant-stop#What a lock can’t:
The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, add .git/commondir to point git at another config, or do the same with a linked worktree’s folder in .git/worktrees. When devvm creates the VM, and on each launch, it reports a commondir that’s there, linked worktrees whose commondir leads somewhere else, and paths it couldn’t lock because they’re symlinks. devvm reads git’s own small files, a .git file, a commondir and a linked worktree’s gitdir, through a symbolic link as git does, but only when each is a regular file of at most 16 MiB, opened without blocking, so a FIFO the VM leaves there can’t hang devvm. devvm doesn’t repair anything, so check what it names before you run git in the folder. When you don’t trust what runs in the VM, use --clone, which mounts no .git at all.
The VM writes .git/index, because it has to in order to commit, so it can also add a submodule with its own config, which git status on the host reads. A submodule’s core.fsmonitor therefore also runs on the host. devvm names a new submodule at the next check that finds the VM stopped, but git on the host reads it before that. No setting in the locked config keeps git on the host out of it. The VM writes .gitmodules, whose ignore line for a submodule beats diff.ignoreSubmodules, and git falls back to the index’s and HEAD’s copies of the file when the working tree has none. git add -A, -u and . enter a submodule whatever any setting says, and git diff-index, git diff-files and git describe --dirty enter one that .gitmodules doesn’t name. A setting for a submodule’s name in .git/config holds only for the name the VM chooses in .gitmodules. Only --clone keeps the VM’s code away from git on the host.
devvm’s own git commands on the host run no program that a repo’s config or .git names, a submodule’s included, whatever the VM wrote there. devvm runs each one with these settings, given as GIT_CONFIG_COUNT pairs, which git takes over any config file:
core.fsmonitor=false, core.hooksPath=/dev/null and core.alternateRefsCommand=true, so git runs no fsmonitor, no hook from a hooks folder and no command for an alternate object store’s refs. hook.EVENT.enabled=false for every event githooks(5) lists, and hook.NAME.enabled=false for each hook the repo’s config names, so git 2.54 and newer run no hook that a config defines. filter.NAME.clean, smudge and process emptied, and filter.NAME.required=false, for each filter driver the repo’s config names, so git hashes files without running a filter and doesn’t fail on a required one. protocol.allow=never and protocol.ssh.allow=always, so git reaches nothing but ssh, not a path, file://, ext::, git:// or http. A repo’s config could still allow one protocol by its own key, such as protocol.ext.allow=always, which git takes over protocol.allow, so devvm also sets GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=ssh, which git takes over every protocol setting. maintenance.auto=false and gc.auto=0, so a fetch starts no maintenance or gc. log.showSignature=false, and gpg.program, gpg.ssh.program and gpg.x509.program all false, so no log or reflog command runs the signing program a repo’s config names to check a signed commit. advice.graftFileDeprecated=false, so git doesn’t warn about the grafts file that the next paragraph sets. Its ssh is false, which reaches nothing, in place of a repo’s core.sshCommand (GIT_SSH_COMMAND=false, with GIT_SSH_VARIANT=ssh over a repo’s ssh.variant), unless the command is a --clone VM’s fetch, and it fetches nothing lazily (GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1), so a repo that says it’s a partial clone can’t make git rev-list or git status connect anywhere for an object it lacks. It sees a repo’s real objects and history, not what its replace refs (GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1) or a grafts file (GIT_GRAFT_FILE=/dev/null) would show, so what it walks, packs or looks up is what the repo holds.
It runs without any GIT_* variable of devvm’s own environment, such as GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE or GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so a hook or a rebase you run devvm from can’t point it at another repo or config, and it reads your global config from its usual place. It keeps only the absolute folders of PATH, because git looks programs up, ssh among them, from the repo’s folder, and it runs with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. Its git status adds --no-optional-locks, so it writes no index, and --ignore-submodules=all, so it never enters a submodule, whose own config could name filters of its own.
A --clone VM’s fetch adds --no-recurse-submodules and an empty --refmap=, so it updates only the branches its own refspecs name, never those of a remote that the repo’s config names after the clone’s address. It runs git with devvm’s own GIT_SSH_COMMAND, which ignores the host, port and options git passes to ssh. It always connects to the VM’s own address and port, the host’s loopback port that the VM’s backend gives, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key, and it reads no ssh config (-F none). It checks the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, with the VM’s own known hosts file and no global one, -o HostKeyAlias= the VM’s name and -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, and it runs with -o BatchMode=yes, -o ForwardAgent=no and -o ClearAllForwardings=yes. In the VM it runs only git-receive-pack or git-upload-pack, whichever git asks for, on the clone’s path, and it refuses any other command. So no url.*.insteadOf or remote URL in the repo’s config can send the fetch to another host or to another path, and it forwards neither your agent nor any port. devvm’s own copy into the VM uses no git transport at all (the copy into a clone VM). A repo’s core.sshCommand doesn’t apply, because devvm sets GIT_SSH_COMMAND, and its diff.external, textconv drivers and pager never run, because none of devvm’s commands shows a diff or writes to a terminal.
Before a --clone VM is made, and again before its copy, devvm checks that what git reads in the folder is the repo’s own, so the copy can’t take another repo into the VM. The folder’s .git is a folder with no commondir, or it’s the .git file of a linked worktree whose link git made both ways. That .git file names /.git/worktrees/, that entry’s gitdir file names the folder’s .git back, and its commondir leads to that /.git, which has no commondir of its own. Or it’s the .git file of a submodule, whose git dir is below its parent repo’s: the parent is the nearest folder above with a .git, itself its own repo by these same checks, and the .git file names a folder modules/ below the parent’s git dir, a nested submodule’s below its parent submodule’s, where it resolves, so no symbolic link leads it out of that git dir, with no commondir, and whose config’s one core.worktree, in a file that includes no other, leads back to the folder. Neither the git dir nor the common dir has objects/info/alternates, or a packed-refs or reftable that’s a symlink, or anything in objects or refs that’s a symlink, such as a pack folder or a loose object’s folder that leads to another repo’s objects. Then git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir --git-common-dir must name the same two folders. The common dir has no info/grafts, because the copy carries each commit with its own parents. A partial clone’s copy carries every object the repo has that its tips reach, and leaves the rest to its promisor remote (below). A worktree’s copy sends its branch, that branch’s upstream when the upstream is one ref, the repo’s default branch, the remote-tracking branches and the tags, so the repo’s other local branches stay on this machine. A branch..merge that’s a pattern, such as refs/heads/*, would make the upstream every branch, so devvm then copies no upstream.
devvm finds the hook and filter names to turn off with one git config before each command, so a VM that keeps swapping the repo’s config could show that git config one config and the command another. Every hook event is turned off by its name as well, which covers config hooks on git that has the event setting, so the gap is a filter that the swap hides, which git status could then run on a file whose stat changed. It needs a VM that writes the repo’s .git, so on macOS, where .git/config is locked, it needs a repo devvm doesn’t lock, such as a nested repo past the walk’s bounds (nested repos).
Two things a repo’s config can still do, and neither runs code. An include.path can make devvm’s git config --get user.name read your name and email from another file in git’s config format, which then go into the VM as its git identity. A config file or included file that is a FIFO makes git, and so devvm, wait until you press Ctrl+C.
data.whats-locked#What’s locked:
devvm locks these paths, of the folder’s own repo and of each nested repo it protects:
.git/hooks and .git/config. A repo without a hooks folder gets an empty one, locked, so the VM can’t make one. The same paths for each submodule devvm finds, submodules of submodules included. Those are the git folders under .git/modules, and those in the working tree, which are sub/.git or the folder that a sub/.git file points to. devvm finds the submodules from the index, which it reads with core.fsmonitor off. It takes a folder for a git folder only when it has what git looks for in one, which is a HEAD, and objects and refs in the folder or in the folder its commondir names, as git’s own test has it. The VM can point a sub/.git file at any folder in the project, such as src, and locking that folder’s hooks and config would lock your own files, so devvm locks and creates nothing in a folder that fails the check and reports it instead. .git/config.worktree, when extensions.worktreeConfig is on. devvm creates it empty if it’s missing. What linked worktrees elsewhere on your machine read from here, which is .git/worktrees//commondir and config.worktree. The project folder’s .git file, if the project folder is itself a linked worktree. The repo it points to is outside the VM.
data.whats-recorded#What’s recorded:
The VM’s state records each protected nested repo in the git section’s made.repos, by its folder relative to the project folder, with the same fields as the folder’s own repo: .git’s identity, the git folders locked besides .git, and a hash of what its locked files hand over. made.nested is set once the VM protects its nested repos, which a new VM does, and so do devvm git-protect on and the watch on a Linux host that can’t lock. A nested repo without a record is scanned for the first time, which records it as a new VM’s repo is recorded, without reporting its git folders. At a check of a VM whose made.nested is set, devvm also reports it as one that appeared, such as a repo the VM cloned while it ran, naming each key of its config that runs a program or reads another config (core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, filters, aliases that start with !, includes and the like) and each hook that isn’t one of git’s samples (git_nested_appeared_runs, else git_nested_appeared), because it locks the repo as it is. A recorded repo with nothing at its .git, or whose folder isn’t a real folder of the project any more, is reported (git_nested_gone), and a recorded repo whose .git is another one is reported as the folder’s own is (git_replaced). The record of a repo devvm stops protecting, as it’s gone or another repo’s protection covers it, moves to made.left, so devvm rm and devvm git-protect off take its locks off with the rest, and name one that isn’t in the folder any more (git_locks_left), whose locks only chflags can take off.
A VM an earlier devvm made has no made.nested, so it protects only the folder’s own repo. The first check of it that finds nested repos names them once (git_nested_protectable, recorded as nested_noticed), and devvm git-protect on protects them. The nested repos that a check finds and the protection doesn’t cover are recorded in nested, with nested_more for how many more the walk counted, and named (git_nested_unprotected, git_nested_past_bound): on a host that locks, all of them when devvm creates the VM and at devvm git-protect on, and at a check of a stopped VM those it hadn’t recorded, and how many are past the bound at every check, because the VM could keep their count and change which they are. On a Linux host that can’t lock, each launch names those the last walk recorded, after git_unprotected, which a folder without a .git of its own gets too when it has nested repos, and devvm git-protect off quiets both.
A VM that devvm 0.1.0 or 0.1.1-rc.1 made strict has strict as its mode, and its repos’ configs have the diff.ignoreSubmodules = all that strict set. devvm reads that mode as on: it locks, pins and keeps the VM’s paths as it does for on, and devvm git-protect, its --json and devvm ls show on. The first check that finds the VM stopped, at a launch, devvm stop, devvm clone on or the undo of a devvm clone off, runs as an on VM’s does, and then converts the VM. Under the host’s lock of .git protection, it takes the value all out of the .git/config of each repo that the VM’s state recorded protecting before that check, the folder’s own and the nested ones, with git config --unset-all diff.ignoreSubmodules '^all$', and leaves any other value. It acts only on a repo whose .git has the identity the state recorded (git_id), so a .git the VM replaced, which the check names and locks nothing in, and a VM with no record, as after devvm adopt, keep their setting, which devvm names once when it’s all (git_strict_unknown). It reads the config through devvm’s reader of files a VM can write first, so a FIFO or a symlink there is never read, and after git writes it, it checks that the config is still a regular file in that .git, else it names the path (git_lock_raced). On a host that watches as well as locks, it leaves a config whose sum isn’t the one the check just recorded, and puts the new sum of each config it changed into the watch’s, so the next check doesn’t name devvm’s own change. It locks each config again even after an interrupt, on a context the interrupt doesn’t cancel, and an interrupt records nothing, so the next check goes again. Then it records on in mode, and in next when an earlier devvm saved strict there for the VM’s next stop, and warns once (git_strict_converted), unless next is off. A config that git can’t change keeps the setting, and devvm names it (git_strict_left). devvm git-protect on and off and the unlock at devvm rm take the setting out the same way, without the warning (the packages names the code).
data.when-devvm-locks#When devvm locks:
devvm records a new VM’s mode in its state before its backend makes the VM, so the mode is never unset: on with locks (macOS, and Linux where the kernel lets devvm use a user namespace), off when you pass --no-git-protect or on hosts without locks, and clone for a --clone VM, which mounts no .git. devvm locks once the backend has made the VM, and again on each launch that finds the VM stopped and on devvm stop, so nothing in the VM can race the locks. A VM whose creation stopped before its first locks, or that devvm adopt moved to this folder, is locked on its next launch as a new VM is, without reports. A running VM keeps the locks it had, and devvm stop or the next launch that finds the VM stopped, such as devvm restart, sets new ones. devvm git-protect on a running VM saves the mode in the VM’s state (the git section’s next).
Each time it locks, devvm records in the VM’s state what it locked and found: the identity of .git (its device and inode, and its birth time where the file system keeps one), every git folder it locked besides .git (those under .git/modules and the submodules’ in the working tree, in one list), and a hash of what the locked files hand over to the project folder. The next check compares with those, so it reports what changed since. When only the device of .git differs, and it’s at the same path with no link on it and has the same inode and birth time, it’s the .git that devvm locked, on a disk that macOS numbered anew at boot, as for one VM per folder. The check then records its identity as it is now and doesn’t report a replaced .git. The same places first check .git under the mode the VM ran with, so a .git that the VM replaced meanwhile is still named (git_replaced), and then set the new mode, which locks .git as it is then.
A new VM that’s interrupted before its first shell is deleted, and devvm takes its locks off. When devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm also takes its locks off. It unlocks what it would lock now and every git folder the VM’s state records locking, so a submodule whose entry the VM dropped from the index since is unlocked too.

data: This page explains how devvm builds images and shared tools, how it keys and caches them, and how it checks what they start from: Ubuntu’s cloud image, a container image from --from, and each tool’s downloads. Images and tools covers choosing, rebuilding and cleaning up images, and Starting from a container image covers --from.
data.a-companys-ca-in-builds#A company’s CA i:
Build VMs trust the CA certificates in ~/.config/devvm/ca (a company’s CA) while they build, and images never keep them. Network tiers describes how devvm reads them and how the guest’s ca.sh installs them.
A build carries two scripts made from ca.sh, which run as root: one to add the CAs, which writes the certificates from heredocs to a temporary folder and installs them, and one to remove them, which is ca.sh without a folder. Each script of the build, build.sh of a tools build too, also gets an environment at its start that exports the CAs’ variables, so its tools find the CAs, and nothing of that is written in the VM. The backend puts it there, as it does the build’s proxy variables (the packages names the types). Each backend runs the add script before anything in the build VM downloads, and the remove script once the scripts are done, before the VM stops:
Lima: the add script runs right after the start, through sudo sh, then base’s or the layer’s scripts, then the remove script, before the final sync and the stop. Lima with --from: the conversion’s build VM, which is deleted afterwards, also runs the add script. oci/build.sh gets ca.sh, from devvm’s guest/ folder mounted read-only, and runs it in the image’s chroot with the CAs before bootify.sh and without them after it, so that Alpine’s apk reaches its HTTPS mirrors. The converted base then builds as Lima’s does. Shared tools: the add script runs before build.sh. devvm deletes the build VM and keeps only its output folder, so it needs no remove script. An image is therefore the same with or without CAs, which is why its key holds none of them, and a tool image’s key stays its lock entry, build.sh, mise’s settings, the C library and the base it builds in. When there are CAs, the build’s numbered steps include the two scripts. A layer script that copies the system’s bundle elsewhere keeps that copy.
End-to-end checks (the images section, the tests behind it): a layer built with a test CA in the folder trusts it while its script runs, keeps its key once the folder is emptied, and a copy of its image booted without devvm has none of devvm’s CA files.
data.bases-packages#Base’s packages:
base’s recipe runs apt.sh begin as root before base.sh, and apt.sh end after the last feature. Both are steps of the recipe, so base’s key hashes the script. What the build gives the script in /var/cache/devvm/packages/in decides where apt’s packages come from:
A first build of a key records them. devvm sends in/mirrors, which holds the mirror that ubuntu-mirror sets, or nothing. apt.sh begin points each of the image’s sources at an apt mirror+file: list of that mirror and then the source’s own archive (archive.ubuntu.com, or ports.ubuntu.com on arm64), so apt tries them in that order, and it keeps every package it downloads. apt also installs phased updates (APT::Get::Always-Include-Phased-Updates), which Ubuntu otherwise rolls out to only some machines at first, so it always takes the newest version that the lists have. apt checks the archive’s signature with Ubuntu’s archive key, which the image has, whichever mirror answers. At the end, apt.sh end moves each downloaded package to out/.deb and writes its entry from apt’s package lists, which apt checked against that signature, to out/Packages. The script fails the build when the lists have no entry with the file’s SHA-256. It also copies each InRelease file and package list that apt used to out/.InRelease or out/.Packages, so devvm can check them on this machine. apt keeps those lists uncompressed while base builds (Acquire::GzipIndexes "false"), as they’re signed. Every later build of the key replays them. devvm sends the files the key recorded, from its cache, and in/Packages, their entries, each naming its file. apt.sh begin moves the image’s sources aside and gives apt only that folder, so base.sh and the features install exactly what the first build did, with no network for them. A --from base gets neither. Its packages come from the container image’s own sources as they are when it builds, and they aren’t pinned. Both ends put the image’s own sources back, remove devvm’s apt settings, empty apt’s cache and delete the package lists, so a first build and a replay make the same image. A VM made from it fetches lists when you run sudo apt update, and each layer’s recipe starts with apt.sh lists, as root, which fetches them from the image’s own sources when there are none, so a layer’s script installs as it would on any Ubuntu. apt.sh turns apt’s retries off and makes a source that sends nothing for 30 seconds fail, and when no source answers, it exits 75, which the backend reports as build_sources_unreachable, not as a script that failed.
The backend sends the build’s input into the VM as a tar stream before the first step, and after the last step it hands devvm a tar stream of out/ and deletes the folder, which is the backend’s packages role (how a backend plugs in). On Lima, both run as root over limactl shell. What comes back is the build VM’s, so devvm checks it before it keeps anything (packages_refused). It takes only regular files named Packages, <64 hex digits>.deb, .InRelease or .Packages, each package’s content must hash to its name, and each entry must name a file that came back with the size and SHA-256 the entry gives, with no file left over. Each InRelease file is at most 4 MiB and all of them 32 MiB, and each package list is at most 512 MiB, with lines of at most 1 MiB and entries of at most 4 MiB, and all the lists 2 GiB. A name that comes back twice is refused.
devvm doesn’t take the build VM’s word for the entries, because anything with root in that VM could write them. It checks each InRelease file’s clearsigned signature itself, in Go, against Ubuntu’s archive key, which devvm’s own files hold (fingerprint F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C), and refuses one that doesn’t check out or isn’t one of the suites an Ubuntu 26.04 image’s sources name: resolute, resolute-updates, resolute-security and resolute-backports, never resolute-proposed. It tries at most 4 signatures in each file, because each one hashes the whole file. It also refuses an InRelease whose Date: is older than the archive state the pinned cloud image was built from, because Ubuntu’s InRelease files carry no Valid-Until, so a mirror that stopped updating still serves validly signed ones. The release pocket, resolute, which Ubuntu stopped changing at release, must be dated no earlier than that day, 2026-04-23, which devvm’s code records. Every other pocket (resolute-updates, resolute-security, resolute-backports) must be dated no more than a day before the pinned release’s date (release-YYYYMMDD). devvm names the mirror that ubuntu-mirror sets (packages_stale_mirror), or Ubuntu’s archive when none is set (packages_stale). devvm compares the lists with the cloud image’s date, not with today’s, so a mirror that’s behind, or one that’s lying, can’t serve lists older than that, but a mirror that fell behind after that date can still give base packages older than Ubuntu’s, which is why ubuntu-mirror should name only a mirror you trust to keep up. Each package list must have the SHA-256 and size that a verified InRelease gives for one of its Packages lists, which devvm checks before it reads the list, and each package’s SHA-256 must be in one of those lists, as the same package, version, architecture and size that apt’s entry says. devvm then keeps the archive’s own entry for the package, not apt’s.
devvm also checks that each package is the newest version that apt would install, because whatever has root in the build VM could hand back only the lists it chooses, such as the release pocket’s, and record an older version than resolute-updates or resolute-security has. A recording must give back the InRelease files of resolute-updates and resolute-security with lists for the architectures whose lists have the recorded packages, such as binary-arm64, so another archive’s InRelease, such as archive.ubuntu.com’s on arm64, where ports.ubuntu.com has the lists, doesn’t count. For each InRelease it gives back, it must also give back every package list that the file gives for those architectures, in every component (main, restricted, universe and multiverse). An empty list is the one exception, because it lists nothing. When one is missing, devvm names the suite and keeps nothing (packages_lists_missing). devvm then refuses a recorded package when the release pocket’s list, resolute-updates’ or resolute-security’s has a newer version of it for that architecture, and it names the package, both versions and the suite (packages_not_newest). resolute-backports doesn’t count, because apt installs its packages only when you ask for them (its InRelease says NotAutomatic). devvm orders versions as dpkg --compare-versions does, in its own Go code: the epoch first, then the upstream version, then the Debian revision, with letters before other characters and ~ before everything, even the end, so 1.0~rc1 is older than 1.0.
A recording that gives back no packages needs no lists. devvm writes the files into a folder of the build’s own in the cache while it checks them, and once the image is built, it moves each into the cache, ~/.local/share/devvm/packages/.deb, and writes the key’s set, ~/.local/share/devvm/packages/sets/.json: each package’s name, version, architecture, SHA-256, size and entry. A file the cache already has under that name is kept only when its checksum still matches it; devvm replaces a changed one with the build’s copy and notes that in the run log. That happens before the image’s record, under a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/packages, and a build that fails keeps nothing.
A key’s set is written once, and the cache holds each file under its own SHA-256, so a build can’t change what another key installs. Before a replay, devvm reads each of the set’s files and checks its SHA-256 and size, and it refuses to build when one is gone or changed (packages_missing), so it never records the key’s packages again. devvm rebuild base gives base a new key, which records anew. devvm gc deletes the sets of keys that are neither base’s key as it is now nor an image the backend has, and then, holding the lock, the package files that no set names then, so a set recorded meanwhile keeps its files. It also deletes a build’s own folder of what it gave back that’s over a day old, which a build that was killed leaves.
data.bases-settings-and-pins#Base’s settings:
Base’s size is 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk, which devvm sets in its own code, and it fits the CPUs and memory to the host (base’s size). On Lima, base’s Lima template holds base’s other VM settings. Base’s script installs base, and the optional features you chose follow it.
Each download in base’s script is pinned to a version and a SHA-256 at the top of the script, and the build fails if a checksum doesn’t match. Each feature pins its downloads in the same way, at the top of its script in the repo, which is built into devvm (the packages has where each script is). apt’s packages are pinned per image key, as base’s packages describes.
data.bases-size#Base’s size:
devvm fits base’s CPUs and memory to the host with one rule that every backend uses. Base gets its 4 CPUs, or the host’s count when the host has fewer, because a Lima vz VM given more CPUs than the Mac has can start so slowly that its ssh never comes up, as Lima’s issue reports. Base gets its 8 GiB of memory, or half the host’s whole GiB when 8 GiB would leave the host less than 2 GiB, because a VM asking for all of the host’s memory doesn’t start.
Lima passes the fitted size to limactl create as --cpus and --memory, and base’s 100 GiB disk as --disk, for base and for the VM that converts a --from image. The images built on base are clones of it, so they and their VMs keep that size. A new VM’s disk is never smaller than base’s, because disks can’t shrink. A size you set with --cpus, --memory or devvm size -g replaces the fitted one. devvm checks that size against the same rule, so it refuses more memory than the host’s whole GiB less 2, or half of them on a host of 4 GiB or less, and the fitted memory always passes (size). The fitted size isn’t in image keys, because the host’s size doesn’t change what an image holds.
base also drops the server extras that Ubuntu’s cloud image comes with, which are snapd, multipath, ModemManager, udisks, firmware updates, crash reporting, tracing tools, kernel headers, and apt’s background updates and upgrades. That saves 0.9 GB of disk and 100 MB of memory per VM, and the everyday tools stay (base).
data.building#Building:
devvm builds each image in a VM of its own, and that VM then is the image:
For base, devvm makes a new VM from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml’s settings, or, with --from, from a container image converted into a disk. A layer’s VM is a copy of its parent image. The VM starts confined, and it forwards no ports. What a build with the internet reaches of the host depends on the backend: on macOS, Lima keeps it out of the host’s loopback, and on Linux it reaches the host’s loopback too, as Lima describes. The script runs. For base, that’s base’s own script, base.sh, and then the features you chose, and for a layer, it’s the layer’s script. The VM stops. devvm writes the image’s record last, ~/.local/share/devvm/images//record.json, with its name, its chain, what base started from and its digest, its C library, the glibc version of a --from base with glibc, when the build finished and the version of the devvm that built it (made_by). The record is JSON that only devvm writes, and devvm ignores fields it doesn’t know, so a newer devvm’s record still reads. While the VM is being built, it already has the image’s final name, so devvm holds a lock for each image it builds, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/, from before it looks for the image until the record is written. Another devvm that builds the same image waits for that lock under a status line (image_build_waiting), and once it gets the lock, it finds the image built. An image without a record is unfinished only when its lock is free, so devvm then deletes it and builds it again (image_leftover). While the lock is held, the image is building, and devvm gc, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm leave it alone (image_building). The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when its devvm ends, however it ends, so a crash never leaves an image looking like it’s still being built. devvm deletes the lock file together with the image’s folder.
Nothing from the host is mounted into a build, because layer scripts run third-party installers, which mustn’t see your files. Behind a company proxy, a build on Lima goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine for that build alone, which goes through the company proxy. The scripts’ commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, so neither the build nor its image ever has the company proxy’s password (a company proxy). A build gets base’s size fitted to the host, which the images built on base, and their VMs, keep (base’s size).
data.building-tools#Building tools:
devvm builds the tool images that a VM’s shared tools need when it makes the VM, after its image, and when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update gives a VM new ones, unless the share already has them. devvm build builds images alone, never tool images. Each tool image builds in a throwaway VM of its own, one after another, which devvm makes from a base image and confines like an image build. Which base it makes the VM from depends on the C library the images are for, because any VM whose tools need an image’s key mounts it:
glibc: devvm’s own base from Ubuntu’s cloud image, on the VM’s backend, whatever base the VM has. A VM on a --from Debian or Ubuntu image gets images built there too, so the container image’s code never runs in the build of images that other VMs mount. When that base isn’t built yet, devvm says so (tools_need_own_base) and builds it first, pinning the cloud image on its first build as usual (Ubuntu’s cloud image). musl: the VM’s own --from base, as it is now, because musl builds need Alpine. Its key hashes that base’s digest, so the images are only ever another VM’s on the same container image. devvm tools add, devvm tools update and devvm update build that base first, looking up its digest, so the keys they work out are those of the base that the images build in. Before a build, devvm reads the record of the base it’s about to clone and refuses to build in it unless it’s the base the images are for (tools_wrong_base): base from Ubuntu’s cloud image for glibc, and for musl a --from base with the digest that the images’ keys hash. A tool’s installer can run anything in its VM, as root too, so a VM and a folder for each tool are what keep one tool from writing into another tool’s image, whose key doesn’t hash it. A build VM gets its one tool and version, and it never sees the share. It writes into a folder of its own, ~/.local/share/devvm/tools-build., which devvm deletes once that tool is done. Lima mounts that folder at boot and goes on when the mount fails, so the build script waits up to 60 seconds for the tools lock that devvm put in the folder, mounting the folder again while it isn’t mounted. If the lock never appears, the build fails, naming the folder and the mount’s last error. devvm then checks that each image is a plain file and not a link (tool_bad_output), moves it into the share and writes its record beside it, never through a name the VM could have planted.
A glibc build also measures the newest glibc version that each tool needs, because each upstream download is built against a glibc of its own and doesn’t run on an older one. After installing the tool, the build script reads the version needs of every ELF program and library in it with readelf, which base’s build-essential installs, and writes the newest GLIBC_ version they name into .glibc, or nothing when none needs one. It leaves out folders named testdata, because Go’s has ELF files from other systems that nothing runs. devvm takes that file only as a plain file holding one version (tool_bad_output) and keeps the version in the image’s record (glibc). Before it gives a VM its tools, devvm compares each image’s version with the glibc of the VM’s --from base, and an older base refuses the tool, naming it and both versions (tool_needs_glibc). It checks the same way when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update gives an existing VM tools, against the glibc its state recorded when it was made. A base from Ubuntu’s cloud image has no glibc version in its record, so its tools aren’t checked, and a musl base gets musl builds, which need no glibc. Only one build at a time writes to the share, because each holds the share’s lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/tools.lock, outside the share that VMs mount. Another devvm waits for it under a status line (share_waiting) until the build ends or you press Ctrl+C. The lock is an OS lock on an open file, so the system releases it when its devvm ends, however it ends, and a devvm that crashed or that you killed never leaves another one waiting.
Each tool image is named --.erofs. Its key hashes the tool’s entry in the tools lock (its version, its downloads and their checksums), the shared tools’ build.sh with the prelude before it, the [settings] table of their mise.toml, the version of mise that base.sh pins, the C library the image is built for, the base it builds in (devvm’s own for glibc, and for musl the digest of the --from base), and the backend’s format. The build VM is made from base, so base’s mise is the one that installs the tool, and a new mise builds every tool image it installs again. A tool that build.sh installs itself, without mise, doesn’t have mise’s version in its key, because mise doesn’t install it: rustup installs rust, and dotnet comes from Microsoft’s own archive (dotnet’s download). The tests check that base.sh pins the same mise as the one devvm runs on the host, with the same Linux checksums. devvm reads the lock as TOML and hashes what the tool’s entry says, the entry of the version the image installs, so a mise that writes the same lock in another order, with other spacing or quoting, leaves every key as it is. The settings are in the key because they change what mise installs, such as python.compile, and the key reads what they say in the same way, so a comment or another way of writing the same settings leaves it as it is. Lima’s format is build.sh’s own, compressed EROFS, which adds nothing to the key. A new version, a new download, an edited build script or a changed setting builds the image again, and a base with a different C library, such as Alpine’s musl, gets an image of its own, and so would a VM on another backend. Every glibc image’s key names devvm’s own base, because glibc images build only there, so a VM on Ubuntu’s base and one on a --from Debian image share them. A musl image’s key has its base’s digest, so when the container image’s tag moves to a new image, its VMs’ next tools build again in the new base. When the lock has no download of a tool for the VM’s platform, devvm doesn’t build it and says to try again later (tool_unbuilt).
An image is base and its layers alone, and a VM’s shared tools are a list in its state (the tools section’s names) beside its image. devvm’s check of an image name refuses a shared tool’s name in it (tool_not_layer), so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse one, because shared tools aren’t images and their versions come from the lock.
data.digests#Digests:
base is keyed by the container image’s digest, not its tag. When devvm builds, it asks the image’s registry for the digest anonymously, with a HEAD request for the image’s manifest, which doesn’t count against Docker Hub’s pull limit. When the registry asks for a token, devvm gets one from the registry’s token service, at an https address only. The digest goes into base’s key, and devvm records it for each container image in its cache, ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/from-digests.json, and in the record of each image it builds on that base. An existing VM’s state records what its base was made from (from).
For a VM made with --from, devvm tells whether the VM is outdated from the container image’s digest that it last recorded, without looking anything up. When devvm makes the VM again, the build looks up the digest as every build does, so a tag that has moved since gives the VM the container image’s newer version too, and a pinned digest stays as it is (outdated VMs).
The cache may be deleted at any time. Without it, devvm takes the digest from the record of the newest base built from the same container image, so every key stays as it was, and images stay current until a lookup finds that the tag has moved. The next lookup writes the cache again.
devvm refuses a reference it can’t read (bad_from). When it can’t reach the registry, it uses the digest it recorded last, with a warning (from_cached_unreachable), and with none recorded, it fails (from_unreachable). Tags and digests covers when a moved tag rebuilds base, how @sha256: pins an image, and how devvm reads a reference.
data.dotnets-download#dotnet’s download:
mise resolves dotnet’s version like any tool’s, but it locks the version alone, without a download, because its installer runs Microsoft’s install script, which nothing pins. So devvm adds each platform’s SDK archive to the lock itself (the packages names the code). For each dotnet entry that lacks a platform’s download, it fetches the channel’s list of releases, https://builds.dotnet.microsoft.com/dotnet/release-metadata//releases.json, over HTTPS and capped at 32 MB, and it records that platform’s dotnet-sdk-.tar.gz with its SHA-512. It keeps a file only when its URL is under https://builds.dotnet.microsoft.com/dotnet/ and its hash is 128 hex digits, and a version that Microsoft doesn’t list gets no download, so devvm doesn’t build it. The image’s key hashes that lock entry, its URLs and checksums included, as it does every tool’s.
build.sh gets the URL and the SHA-512 from devvm and downloads the archive with devvm-fetch, which checks a 128-character checksum as a SHA-512 and any other as a SHA-256, and which deletes the file and fails when the sum differs. The script unpacks the archive and checks that dotnet --list-sdks names the locked version. The SDK’s folder is read-only in VMs, so the script puts a userlocal marker in its metadata/workloads/ folder, for its feature band (10.0.400 for 10.0.403), which makes dotnet workload install install into ~/.dotnet in the VM. In the VM, sync.sh writes the shared SDK’s folder into /etc/dotnet/install_location, where .NET’s programs look for an installed runtime, so global tools find it in every shell and not only those that mise activates, and it sets mise’s dotnet.isolated, which gives each SDK a folder of its own, so the shared one runs from its image.
The trust root is Microsoft’s releases.json, read over HTTPS, which is the same model as the upstream checksums that mise locks for the other tools. An SDK that a project’s global.json asks for is different: mise installs it in the VM with Microsoft’s install script, which checks only HTTPS and the download’s size, and it stays in that VM’s home, so no image or other VM gets it.
data.free-space#Free space:
Before each build and each new VM, devvm checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and free space lists what each step needs. devvm checks the disk that holds the images and VMs, which is the disk of devvm’s Lima home. Shared tool images come out into devvm’s data folder, so a tools build also checks that folder’s disk, which needs 0.5 GiB and 0.25 GiB for each tool, rounded up: 1 GiB for one tool and 3 GiB for all ten. When devvm’s data folder is on a small temporary disk, such as a tmpfs /tmp on Linux, devvm checks that disk.
The numbers leave a margin over what each step took when devvm’s tests measured the free space before, during and after it. Most of a step’s space is only needed while it runs. On Lima on macOS, base took about 1 GiB with Ubuntu’s cloud image already downloaded, and downloading the image takes up to another 0.9 GiB. base’s features add up to 2.5 GiB. A build of all ten shared tools took 6 GiB at its peak and kept 1.5 GiB of images. On macOS, an image built on another and a new VM take only what they write. On Linux hosts, an image and the VM that builds shared tools start as a full copy of their parent’s disk, but a new VM’s disk holds only its own changes. A VM then grows as you work in it, and its disk never shrinks.
data.how-its-converted#How it’s converted:
With --from, devvm turns the container image into a disk in a throwaway VM, devvm-oci-build, which it makes from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml’s settings and base’s size. No Docker is needed:
crane downloads exactly the digest in base’s key, for this machine’s architecture, and flattens its layers. crane is pinned like every download: its version and SHA-256 are at the top of the conversion’s build.sh, checked with sha256sum. bootify.sh, in a chroot of the image, adds what a container lacks to boot as a VM: a kernel and initramfs, an init system (systemd, or OpenRC on Alpine), cloud-init, sshd and sudo, and your user in the VM. Your user has your uid, so bootify.sh first removes a user of the image’s that has it, such as Ubuntu’s own ubuntu (uid 1000, the uid a Linux host’s first user usually has). mke2fs writes the image’s files into a raw ext4 disk, and base grows it to base’s 100 GiB disk. build.sh also writes down the image’s C library, from its /etc/os-release, and for a glibc image, its glibc version, which getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION prints in a chroot of the image. devvm checks both, keeps them in the record of base and of every image on it (libc and glibc), and checks each shared tool against that glibc version (building tools).
devvm then deletes the build VM and creates base from the disk, booting its kernel and initrd directly. One conversion runs at a time, because each holds a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/oci-build.lock, so another devvm’s conversion waits for it under a status line (oci_waiting). The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when its devvm ends, however it ends, so a devvm that crashed never keeps another from converting.
data.images-only-docker-has#Images only Docke: When the registry doesn’t give devvm the image (images only Docker has), devvm keys base by Docker’s image ID instead of a digest. devvm exports the image with docker save into the build VM’s folder, where crane reads it, and it checks that the export is the image it looked up. The image is saved by name, so if the tag has moved since, for example after a rebuild, devvm stops and asks you to run it again. devvm only asks Docker about images, with docker image inspect, docker info and docker save.
data.keys-and-caching#Keys and caching:
devvm builds images in layers and caches them, as Docker does. base comes first, and each layer is built on its parent, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. A layer starts from its parent and runs its script inside it, and devvm stores it under a key, which is a hash of everything that goes into it. When an image with that key already exists, devvm uses it, and otherwise it builds one.
Image Its key hashes base the backend, base’s Lima template (base.yaml), devvm’s prelude (prelude.sh), the apt script (apt.sh), base’s script (base.sh), the chosen features that devvm has, in order (each name and its script), its rebuild counter, and with --from, the image, its digest and the scripts that convert it; on Lima, the Ubuntu cloud image pinned on this machine (its release, file and SHA-256), base’s disk size, and the user that a --from conversion puts in the image (its name, uid and home folder) with the converted disk’s size a built-in layer its parent’s key, its name, the prelude, the apt script, its own script, which devvm ships, and its rebuild counter a custom layer its parent’s key, its name, the prelude, the apt script, its script (~/.config/devvm/layers/.sh) with the prelude before it, and its rebuild counter devvm puts together each image’s recipe once, as the ordered list of steps its build runs. A step is a script with its name, its arguments and whether it runs as root. Each script in a recipe that runs with bash, devvm’s own and a custom layer’s alike, starts with devvm’s prelude, which the scripts’ prelude describes, so the recipe holds the prelude and the script together. The recipe of base starts with the backend’s own steps, which say what the backend makes base’s disk from. On Lima, those are the Ubuntu cloud image pinned on this machine, base’s disk size and base.yaml, and with --from, the conversion’s scripts too, build.sh with its arguments. Then come apt.sh begin, base.sh, the chosen features’ scripts and apt.sh end, while a layer’s recipe is apt.sh lists and then its own script. The key hashes that recipe, and the backend is given the same recipe and runs it as it is, so nothing reaches a build that its key doesn’t hold, apart from base’s packages: those are the ones its key recorded at its first build, or the mirror to record them from, which base’s packages describes. A chosen feature without a script isn’t in the recipe, and devvm warns about it (unknown_feature) when it builds base. The user’s CAs and a company proxy’s variables are added to each step while it runs and taken out again, so they aren’t in the recipe, and the image keeps none of them. A build’s CPUs and memory aren’t in it either, because the host’s size doesn’t change what an image holds, but base’s disk size is, because the disk is part of the image (base’s size).
A key is the first 12 hex digits of a SHA-256. Each input goes into the hash with its length, so different inputs never hash the same bytes. An image’s record keeps its chain, which is the key of each image it’s built on, from base up.
Each key hashes its parent’s, so a new key anywhere in the chain changes the key of every image above it:
Image keys in a chainEach image's key hashes its parent's key, as in base, then foo, then foo+bar. After foo.sh is edited, or devvm rebuild foo, base keeps its key and is reused, and foo and foo+bar get new keys and are built again.built after foo.sh is edited,or devvm rebuild foo its key its key its key its key basekey 1a2b3c4d5e6freused fookey 9a0b1c2d3e4fbuilt again foo+barkey 5a6b7c8d9e0fbuilt again basekey 1a2b3c4d5e6f fookey 7a8b9c0d1e2f foo+barkey 3a4b5c6d7e8f This means:
When you edit a script, its layer and every layer above it rebuild the next time they’re used, and the layers below are reused. Each backend builds its own images and never uses another backend’s. With --from, base’s key has the image’s digest, so when the tag moves to a new image, base and everything on it rebuild. A layer whose script is gone hashes as missing, so its images don’t match any more. Nothing else counts. Features you haven’t chosen change no key, and neither do policy files (*.policy), which the proxy reads at run time and which never go into an image. An image whose key doesn’t match its inputs any more is stale. It stays until it’s deleted (cleaning up), and the next use builds a new one.
data.listing-and-cleaning-up#Listing and clea:
Listing images describes the columns of devvm images. An unfinished image is a build that didn’t finish, so it has no record, and a building image has no record yet because another devvm holds its lock. A tool image’s STATE compares it with the tools lock and with the VMs’ state:
current is the tools lock’s version, for the C library of the base that new VMs get, which --from changes, and for musl, for that base’s digest. in use is another version, which a VM has in its state. unused is neither. not built is the lock’s version of a tool that the share has other versions of. not installed means the share has nothing of that name’s. Listing never resolves the tools lock. Before there is a lock, no tool image is current, and the tool images that no VM has show no state.
A tool image’s name doesn’t say which backend and C library it’s built for, so LIBC comes from its record, which also names the backend that built it, as devvm images --json shows in backend. An image without a record shows -, and has no backend or libc.
devvm images rm deletes images with their records. devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images with their records, and unused tool images with theirs. With --tool-images, it also deletes the current tool images that no VM’s state lists and that have a record, however recently they were built.
A VM’s launch builds its tools before it records them in its state, and a new VM can also pick a tool that was built long before and that no VM has, so deleting current tools needs a reliable sign that no VM is being made. That sign is the making lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/making.lock. Each devvm that makes a VM holds it shared from before it picks the VM’s tools, and devvm tools add, devvm tools update and devvm update hold it until the VM’s state lists the new tools. A new VM’s devvm keeps it until just before the VM’s first shell. Any number of devvms hold it at once, on every backend, because it’s taken before the backend does anything. devvm gc --tool-images and retention’s tools.unused-age take it exclusively without waiting (flock with LOCK_NB), after the share’s lock, and hold it until they’re done, so no VM picks its tools between their list and their deletions. A devvm that starts to make a VM meanwhile waits under a status line (making_waiting). In a terminal, gc holds it while it asks. Every tool image build runs for one of those devvms, under the making lock, and holds the share’s lock while it builds and moves the images in, so gc, which takes the share’s lock first, waits for a build in progress and then finds the making lock held until the VM’s state lists what it built.
When a VM is being made, devvm gc --tool-images keeps every current tool image that no VM’s state lists and names them (gc_tools_making), after the same filters, and deletes the rest of its list. Retention deletes no tool images in that run and leaves their records’ idle_since as it is, then applies its other settings. The lock is an OS lock on an open file, which the system releases when the last descriptor closes, so a devvm that crashes or is killed lets go of it. Its descriptor is close-on-exec, so neither the processes devvm starts (a Lima host agent, a proxy) nor the shell that takes devvm’s place inherit it. gc and retention never wait for it, so they can’t block, and the order the two locks are taken in can’t deadlock: a devvm making a VM takes the making lock and then the share’s, and gc and retention take the share’s and only try the making lock. Retention at a command’s start doesn’t wait for the share’s lock either: while another devvm holds it, as a tool build does, that run deletes no tool images, and they wait for the next day’s run.
When a tool image that a new VM’s state lists is gone by the VM’s setup, devvm-tools can’t mount it, the setup fails with tools_unmounted, and the VM and its state stay, because only an interrupt undoes a new VM. Every launch of the VM fails the same way until devvm tools update builds the missing images, as a launch builds whatever the share lacks.
gc holds the share’s lock throughout, so no tool build or devvm tools update changes the share meanwhile. A tool image is unused only when compared with the tools lock, so before there is a lock, gc deletes none. Because current is for the C library of the base that new VMs get, the musl tool images of an Alpine VM are unused once it’s gone, unless you give gc that --from.
gc also trims the shared Nix cache to its cap, deleting its least recently used files under the lock that the VMs’ proxies take, and with --nix-cache, it deletes all of the cache’s files. devvm images ends with what the cache takes of its cap when it holds anything.
data.rebuilding#Rebuilding:
devvm rebuild works through the rebuild counter, which each image’s key hashes. The counters are in ~/.local/share/devvm/images/rebuilds.json, one for each backend, each image that base starts from, as --from gives it, and each image, so a rebuild on one backend leaves the other backends’ images and their VMs as they are, and so does a rebuild from another container image. A rebuild writes a new value into its counter, made of the time and a random part, so the image gets a new key, and so does every image built on it. A rebuild of base on Lima also pins the newest Ubuntu cloud image first, while a rebuild of a --from base looks up its container image’s digest again and keeps the cloud image pinned. The counters can’t be in an image’s folder, because a counter is an input to the key that names that folder. A devvm changing a counter holds a lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/rebuilds, while it reads the file and writes it whole, so two rebuilds at once both keep their new values. devvm lists those images first (rebuild_replaces). After the build, it deletes every stale image that no VM uses, which includes the old image and those built on it, and they’re built again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. On Linux hosts, an image whose disk VMs are overlays of stays, and devvm says which VMs use it.
A VM keeps the image it was made from, and its state keeps that image’s chain. When a key in the chain changes, after an edited script or a rebuild, devvm warns on each launch that the VM is outdated (vm_outdated) and leaves the VM as it is (outdated VMs). devvm update makes the same check, comparing each image’s key in the recorded chain with its key as it is now, and when one differs, it makes the VM again from the same image name (making a VM again). Otherwise, when the VM also had the newest shared tools, it says the VM is current (vm_current). Shared tool images have keys of their own, which building tools describes, and they’re never in the chain, so newer shared tools alone don’t lead devvm update to make the VM again.
data.the-desktop-layer#The desktop layer: The built-in desktop layer’s script is desktop.sh, and its allowlist, desktop.policy, has no rules, because the layer downloads nothing of its own and its packages come from the distribution’s archive, which base’s allowlist has. base’s image has no package lists, so the layer’s apt.sh lists step fetches them first, and its packages are the archive’s as they are when the layer builds, which aren’t pinned. On --from alpine, the script installs Alpine’s own packages, which aren’t pinned either. Besides Xfce and TigerVNC, the script writes /usr/local/bin/devvm-desktop, which devvm desktop runs in the VM. The layer needs no backend feature of its own, because it runs on any VM that can build an image and reach its ssh.
data.the-docker-layer#The docker layer: The built-in docker layer’s script is docker.sh, embedded in devvm, and its allowlist is docker.policy. The script pins the checksum of the signing key of Docker’s apt repository and each package’s version at the top. On --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages, which aren’t pinned. Running Docker’s engine in a VM is a backend feature of its own, docker-layer (features).
data.the-image-is-untrusted#The image is untr:
The container image’s own code runs as root in the build VM, so devvm treats what it writes as hostile:
The build VM is confined like any build with the internet, which it needs for crane, so on macOS it can’t reach this machine’s loopback, though on Linux it can. It mounts three folders of the conversion’s own temporary folder, devvm-oci., and nothing else. oci/ holds the conversion’s scripts, which devvm writes there from its own files for this build alone, and the VM mounts it read-only. guest/, also read-only, holds only ca.sh, and devvm writes and mounts it only when there are company CAs. vm/ is the one writable folder, and devvm writes nothing there itself except an image only Docker has, before the VM starts. The scripts sit beside vm/, never inside it, so what the image writes can’t replace them on this machine. devvm checks what comes out once the build VM is gone. Each file must be a regular file, because a link could point Lima at a file on this machine. The kernel command line can hold only letters, digits, spaces and =,./:_-, because it goes into Lima’s config. The C library must be gnu or musl. The disk must be raw ext4 as mke2fs writes it into a new file, its first 1024 bytes zero and an ext4 superblock after them, because another format, such as qcow2, can name a file on this machine as its backing file, and its header would sit in those first bytes. A glibc file must be a regular file before devvm reads it, because a link could name a FIFO on this machine, and the read would wait. devvm refuses anything else (convert_bad_output), and it doesn’t create base. devvm deletes the build VM and the temporary folder, with the scripts it wrote there, however the run ends, Ctrl+C included.
data.the-nix-layer#The nix layer:
The built-in nix layer’s script is nix.sh, and its allowlist is nix.policy. The script pins Nix’s release tarball, the direnv binary and nix-direnv’s direnvrc at the top, each with its version and SHA-256, which are per architecture for Nix and direnv, and fetches them with devvm-fetch. The repo’s bump script moves them (updating pinned versions). Nix’s version is the one nixos.org’s installer fetches, at least 2.35.3, which fixes the scripted installer’s store ownership (GHSA-hf6w-2rg9-v84g) and the daemon’s store corruption through repair (CVE-2026-110450). Nix’s newer releases come with another installer, from artifacts.nixos.org, so the layer’s pins change shape when it moves to one of them.
The script runs the tarball’s own installer as install --daemon --yes --no-channel-add, which copies the tarball’s store into /nix, downloading nothing, makes the nixbld build users and, under systemd, starts nix-daemon. On OpenRC, which a base --from alpine runs, the script adds a service of devvm’s, /etc/init.d/nix-daemon, to the default runlevel and starts it, and before the install it adds Alpine’s xz, unpinned, which GNU tar needs for the tarball. Nix’s own binaries are static or linked against the C library in its store, so they run on musl. Its extra settings turn on flakes and the nix command and keep trusted-users = root, so only root can choose caches and signing keys. They also set sandbox = true and sandbox-fallback = false, so a build fails where the kernel can’t sandbox it, rather than run outside the sandbox without a word. The installer writes any proxy variables it finds into a systemd drop-in for the daemon, which would put a build’s proxy into the image, so the script runs it without them. It points Nix at the system’s CAs, which hold devvm’s and yours. After the install, the script checks that every path in the store is root’s, and it fails otherwise.
It also adds Nix’s default profile to the end of sudo’s secure_path, through /etc/sudoers.d/devvm-nix, so sudo nix works, and appends Nix’s profiles to the PATH that BASH_ENV gives shells that read no profile. direnv goes into /usr/local/bin and nix-direnv into /usr/local/share/nix-direnv. A file in ~/.config/direnv/lib loads nix-direnv and puts each project’s direnv layout under ~/.cache/direnv/layouts, named by a hash of the project’s path, so its cached dev shell and garbage collector roots stay in the VM’s home and out of the project folder. direnv’s shell hook is in ~/.bashrc.d/direnv.sh, which bash loads before mise.sh, and since each hook puts itself first in PROMPT_COMMAND, direnv’s runs after mise’s, and a dev shell’s PATH comes before the shared tools'.
The daemon doesn’t read /etc/environment, so the VM’s setup gives it the VM’s proxy on every tier, in a drop-in of its own under systemd, or else in /etc/conf.d/nix-daemon, which OpenRC reads for the service. The setup also puts the shared Nix cache first in Nix’s substituters, in /etc/nix/devvm-cache.conf. It removes both files from a VM whose environment names no proxy. Running the layer is a backend feature, nix-layer (features), and building it also needs the feature, so a backend without it refuses devvm build nix.
