With sandbox-fallback = false, every Nix build fails in a VM that can’t make the kernel namespaces that Nix’s sandbox needs.
data.the-scripts-prelude#The scripts’ prelude:
devvm’s prelude, prelude.sh, comes first in each script that a build runs with bash: base.sh and apt.sh, the built-in layers and features, your own layers, the shared tools’ build.sh, and a --from conversion’s build.sh. devvm puts it before the script on the script’s standard input, and for the conversion, in the copy of build.sh that it writes into the conversion’s own temporary folder, so no copy of either is kept anywhere else. The prelude sets no shell options and runs only uname and command -v. It gives the script three things:
$devvm_arch is the VM’s architecture as the pins name it, arm64 or amd64. On any other architecture, the prelude stops the script. $devvm_libc is the VM’s C library, musl on Alpine, where apk is, and gnu everywhere else. devvm_sha TOOL prints TOOL’s pinned SHA-256 for this VM, which is the script’s own TOOL_sha256__musl on musl when the script pins one, and its TOOL_sha256_ otherwise. A script that pins none for this VM gets an error that names the pin. The prelude goes in as one line, eval $'…', which holds the whole file in bash’s ANSI-C quoting, and that line takes the place of the script’s #! line. Each of the script’s lines then keeps its number in bash’s errors and in $LINENO, and a script without a #! line gets the prelude’s line before its first, so its lines are one further down. A build’s exports for a company proxy and for your CAs go on that same first line, before the eval, so they don’t move the script’s lines either.
Each of devvm’s scripts that uses the prelude checks that it came first, with : "${devvm_arch:?}" for each variable it reads, so it stops at once when run without it. The key of each image and tool image whose build runs one of these scripts hashes the prelude with the script, so a change to the prelude rebuilds every image and every shared tool image. bootify.sh, which runs with the container image’s own sh, and kernel.sh don’t get it.
Your own layer gets the prelude in the same way, so it can pin its downloads as devvm’s scripts do and pick them with devvm_sha, which Customizing’s example shows. The prelude runs first, so a name your script sets or defines afterwards, devvm_arch or devvm_sha included, is your script’s from then on, and a script that never uses the prelude runs just as it would without it. Your layer’s step in its image’s recipe holds the prelude and your script together, so a change to either one rebuilds that image and the images above it.
data.the-share#The share:
devvm builds each tool version once for each backend and C library into a read-only image (EROFS) in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools, with its record next to it in .json. The record is JSON that only devvm writes, with the image’s SHA-256 (sha256), its C library (libc), for glibc the newest glibc version it needs (glibc), for musl the digest of the base it was built in (base), its backend’s format (format), the backend that built it (backend), when it was moved in (built), the version of the devvm that built it (made_by) and, once retention finds that no VM has it, since when (idle_since). The share holds only the images and their records, and Lima’s images are compressed. That folder is mounted read-only in every VM at /mnt/devvm-tools, and each VM mounts the images its tools need at /opt/devvm/tools//, at boot and on every launch. A VM can’t change the shared images, even as root.
A tool that doesn’t mount fails the launch (tools_unmounted). mise’s auto_install stays on for a project’s own version files, so without this check a tool that isn’t mounted would download into the VM on first use without a word. The VM’s mount script, devvm-tools, tries every image in the VM’s list. It leaves out the empty mount point of one that fails, lists each failed image in /run/devvm/tools-unmounted and exits non-zero, which fails the launch’s setup. The setup removes that list before anything else it runs, so a list left from the VM’s boot isn’t read after a failure that has nothing to do with the tools. devvm then reads the first 16 KiB of that list from the VM, and it gives up after 10 seconds, because root in the VM could make the read hang. It counts only a whole line that is one of the VM’s own tool images from its state, so the error shows devvm’s own names, never the VM’s text. devvm reads the list with a command of its own because the setup’s output goes straight to the run log, and a pipe for reading it would keep devvm waiting on any process that the setup left running.
At boot the same failure fails only the devvm-tools service, and the boot goes on. Either way, the launch’s setup runs the mount script again and stops on the failure.
data.ubuntus-cloud-image#Ubuntu’s cloud image:
On Lima, base starts from a dated release of Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image (release-YYYYMMDD on cloud-images.ubuntu.com), which devvm pins on this machine the first time it builds base. devvm’s own files hold only the release, 26.04, and Ubuntu’s cloud image key (fingerprint D2EB44626FDDC30B513D5BB71A5D6C4C7DB87C81), so nothing in devvm needs moving when Ubuntu publishes a new image.
To pin an image, devvm reads the list of dated releases at cloud-images.ubuntu.com and takes the newest one whose checksums list an image for the host:
The release’s SHA256SUMS must carry a valid signature from Ubuntu’s cloud image key, in its SHA256SUMS.gpg. No other key counts. devvm checks the signature itself, with the standard library’s RSA and SHA-2, so it needs no gpgv or other program. When the signature is missing or doesn’t check out, devvm refuses the release (ubuntu_bad_signature), and it never falls back to an older release for that reason. The host’s image, ubuntu-26.04-server-cloudimg-arm64.img or -amd64.img, must be listed with a SHA-256 of 64 hex digits. A release that lists none is passed over for the next older one, and when no release has one, devvm stops (no_ubuntu_release). When devvm can’t read the list, it stops (ubuntu_unreachable), and nothing is pinned. devvm records the pin in ~/.local/share/devvm/images/ubuntu.json: the release, the image’s file name, its SHA-256 and when it was pinned. One devvm pins at a time, holding ~/.local/share/devvm/images/locks/ubuntu, so two first builds pin the same image. Every later build of base on this machine uses the pinned image without looking anything up, so it needs no network for the image once Lima has it cached, and Lima checks the download against the pinned SHA-256. A pin for another architecture, such as in a data folder copied from another machine, counts as none, and the next build pins one for this host. A --from base’s conversion boots the pinned image too, and pins one only when none is.
An image devvm pinned in the same run that doesn’t boot, so that the backend fails to start base’s build VM, gets one second chance. devvm says so (origin_no_boot), pins the newest release older than it, which it checks the same way, and builds base on that, so a broken new release of Ubuntu’s doesn’t stop new machines’ first builds. The older release is what stays pinned. devvm tries this once a run, and never for an image that was pinned before the run, because that one booted then. The build VM that didn’t boot stays, stopped, as a failed build does.
The pin is part of base’s recipe, so base’s key hashes the release, the file and its SHA-256, and a new pin makes a new base. base’s record keeps the address and SHA-256 of the image it was built from. Ubuntu removes its dated releases after a few months, so a base built from one that’s gone can still be used, but building it again needs Lima’s cached copy of the image.
data.versions#Versions:
devvm doesn’t pin the shared tools’ versions (shared tools). Instead, the shared tools’ mise.toml, which devvm ships, says which releases to follow, which is the latest of each tool, and Node 24. The first time a tool is needed, devvm resolves it to upstream’s newest release and writes that into the tools lock, ~/.local/share/devvm/mise.lock, with each download’s checksum for every platform that VMs run (Linux, with glibc and with musl). Builds install exactly the lock’s versions and check them against those checksums. Resolving needs this machine to be online once, and until it has been, devvm says so (tools_need_resolve).
mise’s registry decides where a tool comes from, and a mise release can change its choice, so that mise.toml names the backend of every tool that isn’t one of mise’s own core: tools in its [tool_alias] table. Claude Code, Codex, pnpm and uv come from their GitHub releases through aqua, and opencode comes from its GitHub releases directly (github:anomalyco/opencode), because only that gives musl VMs opencode’s own musl build. pi comes from its GitHub releases directly too (github:earendil-works/pi), one Bun-built program for each platform, which the build checks against the SHA-256 the lock records for it, as it checks every tool’s. Its releases have no musl build, so mise locks the glibc download for musl as well, and devvm refuses pi for a musl VM before any build (tool_glibc_only), because the shared tools’ registry marks it as glibc only. Without the alias, mise’s registry would take opencode 2 from npm, which has no download for each platform. The step back locks the older versions from the backend that the newest came from, and every project VM’s mise config gets the same [tool_alias] table, so the VM’s mise finds each tool where its image came from.
The resolving runs on this machine with a mise of devvm’s own. That mise is a pinned release, which devvm downloads once into ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/mise/ and checks against its SHA-256 before it runs it (mise_checksum). A download that gets no answer, loses it partway or gets a 408, 429 or server error is tried again up to three times, after one second and then twice as long each time, and any other answer fails it at once (mise_download_failed). devvm never uses the mise you have installed, and nothing it does reaches your own mise config. Each run of that mise gets temporary folders for its data, cache, state and config, which devvm deletes afterwards, so cache/mise/ holds only the binary. devvm gc deletes the folders of other versions, unless one changed in the last hour.
Sometimes a tool’s newest version isn’t published for every platform yet, for example when a release is still uploading, when a tag has no release, or for a few days after a Node release until its musl builds appear. A version counts as published only where its lock entry has a download with a checksum, since mise checks the download against it. devvm then takes the newest of the next five older versions that is published everywhere, and says so (tool_stepped_back). When none of them is, devvm says that too (tool_no_download). The next check tries the newest version again.
A new VM gets the lock’s versions, and devvm checks the lock again first when the last check was more than a day ago. When a check fails, devvm uses the versions it found last (tools_check_failed). When the shared tools’ mise.toml changes, as it can in a devvm upgrade, devvm resolves the tools again. A VM lists its tool images in its state, so a newer version never changes a VM that has an older one. Older versions that no VM has are unused, and devvm gc deletes them.

data: This page explains what devvm’s install script downloads and checks, what devvm doctor checks and what devvm doctor --json reports, where devvm keeps its own files, what happens to older versions when you upgrade, and how devvm upgrade checks and installs a release. Installing and Upgrading and uninstalling cover the commands you run.
data.checking-the-install-script#Checking the:
The release key’s public half is:
RWSjzFsn7ETaijKJ2y7F4DtZobXmyv+LmdclJwZP/KmAkLUwOCzWF/2b devvm’s README and security policy show the same key. To check the install script with it, you need minisign (brew install minisign). Download the script, SHA256SUMS and its signature from the release:
base=https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download curl -fsSL -O "$base/install.sh" -O "$base/SHA256SUMS" -O "$base/SHA256SUMS.minisig" Then check that the release key signed SHA256SUMS, check the script against it, and run the script once both checks pass:
minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -P RWSjzFsn7ETaijKJ2y7F4DtZobXmyv+LmdclJwZP/KmAkLUwOCzWF/2b shasum -a 256 -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS bash install.sh minisign prints Signature and comment signature verified and a trusted comment that names the release, as in Trusted comment: devvm 0.1.0, and shasum prints install.sh: OK. On Linux without shasum, sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS does the same. When either check fails, don’t run the script. The script takes the same options as curl … | bash -s --, as in bash install.sh --yes, and it still checks the signature and the archive’s checksum itself, as the install script describes.
data.devvm-doctor-json#devvm doctor –json:
devvm doctor --json prints what doctor finds as one JSON object, for scripts such as the install script, as output for scripts describes. It prints nothing else, because its problems and warnings are in the JSON, and it succeeds whatever is missing. A failure that stops the check, such as a data folder devvm can’t read, still goes to standard error and makes it fail.
backend is the backend that doctor checked, lima, which every new VM gets. problems has what that backend is missing, each with its key, the fix command, and the message that devvm doctor prints for it. The fix is a command whose words are separated by spaces, without shell syntax, or null when there’s none to run, for example when virtualization is turned off in the firmware. warnings has the messages of doctor’s warnings, which have no keys, because there’s nothing for a script to fix. They’re about another devvm on PATH, low free space, a machine with less than 8 GiB of memory or fewer than 4 CPUs, each line of ~/.config/devvm/policy, ~/.config/devvm/layers/*.policy and ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/*/policy that isn’t a rule (policy_not_rule), and each running VM whose proxy runs without its sandbox (proxy_unconfined and the proxy_unconfined_* messages, one for each reason). tips has the messages of doctor’s tips, which aren’t problems: git’s safe.bareRepository (doctor_git_bare). docker says whether Docker is installed, which only --from with an image that only Docker has needs. features has, for each backend, how it has each feature, as native, emulated, unreviewed or none. The example below shows two of Lima’s features. { "version": 1, "backend": "lima", "problems": [ { "key": "lima", "fix": "brew install lima", "message": "Lima isn't installed. Run brew install lima to install it." } ], "warnings": [], "tips": [], "docker": true, "features": { "lima": { "agent-forwarding": "native", "disk": "native" } } } These are the keys:
Key Missing Fix os, arch a host the backend runs on none macos macOS at the backend’s minimum none lima Lima at its minimum, working brew install lima (upgrade, reinstall) with Homebrew, otherwise none qemu QEMU, on Linux your package manager’s install (apt, dnf, pacman or zypper), otherwise none kvm /dev/kvm, on Linux none: turn on virtualization kvm-access access to /dev/kvm sudo usermod -aG kvm USER, then log in again lima-config no Lima global configs in devvm’s Lima home (details) none: move them out The install script reads problems with awk, so it needs no JSON tool on this machine. It relies on the layout that devvm writes, with one field on each line, and it reads a problem’s key, fix and message from their lines, with their escapes undone. It offers to fix three of these keys, asking first, and prints the message for the others:
For lima, it runs the fix when there is one, which is Homebrew’s. Without Homebrew, it offers Lima’s latest release instead, which it checks against that release’s SHA256SUMS and installs into ~/.local. For qemu and kvm-access, it runs the fix when there is one, and the fix uses sudo. After you join the kvm group, the script doesn’t run devvm doctor, because the group applies only to new logins, and it tells you to log out and back in first. With --yes, the script answers yes to every question. Without a terminal and without --yes, it installs none of the fixes and says so.
data.devvm-upgrade#devvm upgrade:
devvm upgrade installs a release in Go, with the same files and checks as the install script, and it never runs the script. It reads the newest release’s version from where GitHub’s releases/latest redirects, releases/tag/v, as the script does, so it needs no API and has no rate limit. Every request goes over HTTPS, and a redirect to anything else is refused.
GitHub’s releases/latest skips the releases marked as prereleases, which are the versions with a suffix, such as 0.2.0-rc.1. devvm upgrade, the daily release check and the install script also refuse a prerelease there, so none of them installs or announces one as the newest release, and a prerelease is installed only when --to or the script’s --version names it. A record of the daily check that names a prerelease as the newest release counts as no record, and the next check replaces it. Versions compare as semver orders them: the numbers as numbers, a prerelease before its release, and a prerelease’s suffix part by part, a number below a word and numbers as numbers, so 0.2.0-rc.9 comes before 0.2.0-rc.10.
Homebrew’s devvm-rc formula is the one exception, because it follows prereleases. For a devvm that devvm-rc installed, devvm upgrade and the daily check read the repository’s releases feed, releases.atom, which lists the newest releases, prereleases among them, and needs no API either. The newest version in it, a prerelease or a release, is the newest release for that devvm. The daily check records it as newest in its record, beside latest, the newest release in the feed that isn’t a prerelease, which stays as it was when the feed lists only prereleases.
data.devvms-own-files#devvm’s own files: devvm is one binary. Its own files are built into it, so a copy of it runs anywhere. They are base.yaml, base’s scripts and policy, the features, the shared tools’ config and build script, what devvm sends into VMs, and --from’s conversion. The binary is the only copy, and devvm never writes them to a folder of its own that outlives a run. Lima gets base.yaml on limactl create’s standard input, VMs’ proxies read devvm’s built-in policies from the binary, and --from’s build writes the conversion’s scripts into its own temporary folder, which it deletes when the build ends. So editing a file on disk can’t change devvm’s built-in rules or what goes into an image.
data.how-it-tells-how-devvm-was-installed#How:
It follows the links of the running binary’s path, and it reads only that path, never running anything:
It’s the install script’s when the binary is devvm in /lib/devvm/, with a release’s version as the folder’s name, and /bin/devvm is a link that resolves to that same binary. The prefix comes from the binary’s own path, so DEVVM_PREFIX needs no setting. It’s Homebrew’s when the path has Cellar/devvm/ in it, a keg of Homebrew’s devvm formula, or Cellar/devvm-rc/, a keg of its devvm-rc formula, which follows prereleases. Anything else is another way. A devvm whose version isn’t a release’s, such as a checkout’s pseudo-version or (devel), was built from the source. One with a release’s version that wasn’t set when it was built, as go install gives, was installed with go install. One that has a release’s version is a copy of a release somewhere else.
data.rollbacks#Rollbacks: A server, or someone in the way of one, can offer an older release that’s still properly signed. devvm upgrade refuses a newest release older than the running devvm, whatever the flags, and installs an older one only when --to names it, after a question that says it’s older. When the running devvm is a prerelease, an older newest release is what’s expected before the prerelease’s own release is out, so devvm upgrade says so and installs nothing, without failing. It can’t tell a server that keeps offering the release you already have from one with nothing newer, which is a limit of reading the newest release from the server.
data.switching-the-link#Switching the link:
The unpacked folder’s devvm runs with --version, which must print the release’s version. The folder is renamed to /lib/devvm/. A folder of that version from before is set aside first, and it’s put back if a later step fails. The link switches in one step: a new link to the new devvm is made beside /bin/devvm and renamed over it, so the link is never missing or half made. The new devvm runs again, through the link. When it fails, the link is switched back to the devvm that ran devvm upgrade, and the new folder goes. Then devvm upgrade removes the other versions in /lib/devvm, as the script does: it keeps the new version, the one that ran devvm upgrade, and any version that a running process’s command line names, such as a VM’s proxy, which it lists with ps. When ps fails, it keeps them all. An interrupted upgrade leaves a ..new. folder at most. The next upgrade removes it once no process has that pid, so it never takes the folder of an upgrade that’s still running, and the script’s next install removes it too.
With Homebrew, devvm upgrade runs brew upgrade devvm, or brew upgrade devvm-rc for a devvm-rc keg, into the run log, after asking, and checks nothing of its own, because Homebrew checks the source against the formula’s checksum.
data.the-install-script#The install script:
The script installs the release it comes with, or the one that --version names, which may be a prerelease, such as 0.2.0-rc.1. Without either, it installs the latest release, never a prerelease. Before it downloads anything, it checks whether Homebrew installed devvm, which it does when brew is on PATH. The check never runs brew, because Homebrew can download its own Ruby when it runs. Instead, the script looks for a version folder in Cellar/devvm or Cellar/devvm-rc, the kegs of Homebrew’s two formulas, in each place Homebrew keeps its Cellar: the folder next to the brew it found on PATH (/../Cellar), HOMEBREW_CELLAR and HOMEBREW_PREFIX/Cellar when they’re set, and the Cellar in /opt/homebrew, /usr/local and /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew. When Homebrew has devvm, the script stops with an error that says to run brew upgrade devvm, or brew uninstall devvm first, each naming devvm-rc for its keg, and exits with status 1, in a terminal or without one. --force skips this check. Then it installs in four steps:
It downloads the archive for this machine and the release’s SHA256SUMS, over HTTPS only. The archive is devvm---.tar.gz, where the OS is darwin or linux and the processor is arm64 or amd64. On Apple silicon, the script picks arm64 even when it runs under Rosetta. It checks the signature of SHA256SUMS, then the archive’s checksum, as the signature describes. When either check fails, it installs nothing. It puts devvm, which is one binary with its README, changelog and license, in ~/.local/lib/devvm/, and links ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. When ~/.local/bin isn’t on PATH, the script says how to add it. Unless you pass --no-deps, it runs devvm doctor --json and offers the fixes that devvm reports, asking before each one. Then it runs devvm doctor, which shows doctor’s warnings too, even when nothing is missing. At the end, when ~/.local/bin is on PATH, the script looks up which devvm PATH finds first with command -v devvm. It resolves that path’s links and those of ~/.local/bin/devvm with readlink -f, and when they differ it warns, naming the other copy’s path and saying to remove it or to put ~/.local/bin first. It only looks the other copy up and never runs it. When ~/.local/bin isn’t on PATH, the script prints only how to add it, so you don’t get both.
devvm doctor makes the same check. It looks up devvm on PATH, resolves its links and those of the running binary, and when they differ it prints a warning naming both. It skips the check when no devvm is on PATH. The warning doesn’t change its exit status, and --json lists it among the warnings rather than the problems, so the install script doesn’t offer it as a fix.
data.the-release-check#The release check:
When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer release (the release check). The check reads only where GitHub’s latest devvm release is, over HTTPS, and sends nothing about you or your machine. The latest release is never a prerelease, so the check never announces one. The exception is a devvm that Homebrew’s devvm-rc formula installed, which follows prereleases: its check reads GitHub’s list of devvm’s newest releases instead, as devvm upgrade describes, and it announces a newer prerelease or release, whichever is newest.
The check runs beside the launch, so it never makes devvm wait, and when you’re offline it says nothing and tries again the next day. The line comes from what the last check found, so a release that came out since then shows up at the launch after the next check. devvm keeps what the check found in ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/release.json, and devvm doctor shows it.
data.the-release-key-and-the-signature#The re:
The release key’s public half is built into devvm from packaging/minisign.pub, the same file the script gets its key from, so devvm upgrade trusts the key in the devvm you have, never one that comes with the release. A build without that file has no key, and devvm upgrade refuses to install a release with it.
devvm checks minisign’s signature itself. SHA256SUMS.minisig holds a signature and a trusted comment, each signed with the key. devvm accepts only minisign’s default, prehashed signature, marked ED, which is Ed25519 over the BLAKE2b-512 hash of SHA256SUMS, and refuses the legacy one, marked Ed, over the file itself. The signature’s key ID must be the release key’s, and the global signature, Ed25519 over the signature followed by the trusted comment, must verify too. The trusted comment must be devvm , as the release script writes it, so a SHA256SUMS signed for one release can’t stand in for another’s. Then the archive for this machine, devvm---.tar.gz for the binary’s own OS and processor, must match its line in SHA256SUMS.
The archive is unpacked into /lib/devvm/..new., beside the version that runs. Only its one top-level folder and the regular files in it are unpacked, at most 512 MiB in all, and an archive with a link, a folder inside that one, or a path out of it is refused. devvm is unpacked with mode 755 and the other files with mode 644.
data.the-signature-and-what-it-trusts#The sig:
curl … | bash trusts everything in the release, and Homebrew checks the same archive against a checksum kept outside it. Both install the release’s own binary, the one SHA256SUMS lists and its signature covers, and Homebrew installs only the binary from it:
How each install checks the releaseIn the GitHub release, install.sh, with the public key, checks the signature on SHA256SUMS, signed in .minisig, and SHA256SUMS checks the archive for this machine. Homebrew's formula, in a repository of its own, checks the same archive against its own checksum.the GitHub release checks the signature checks the checksum checks its checksum install.sh, withthe public key SHA256SUMS,signed in .minisig the archivefor this machine Homebrew's formula,in a repository of its own The release’s SHA256SUMS lists the checksums of its archives and of its install.sh, and it’s signed in SHA256SUMS.minisig, made with the maintainer’s minisign key. The key’s public half is in the script and in packaging/minisign.pub. Without minisign (brew install minisign), the script says so, prints the command to check the signature by hand, and checks only the checksum. A script that isn’t from a release has no key, and it also checks only the checksum.
The signature catches an archive or a SHA256SUMS that someone replaced, which the checksum alone can’t. It can’t catch a release that was replaced whole, because curl … | bash runs the install.sh from that same release, key included, so the one-liner trusts GitHub’s release files. Homebrew doesn’t trust them, because the formula’s checksum lives in a repository of its own, and a replaced GitHub release wouldn’t match it. You can also download install.sh, read it and check it with the key from these docs before you run it, which catches a replaced release too, because that key doesn’t come from the release.
data.upgrading#Upgrading: When the script installs a new version, it removes the older versions in ~/.local/lib/devvm, except a version that a running VM’s proxy, or QEMU on Linux, still runs. A later install removes that version once nothing runs it. A VM’s proxy moves to the new version at the VM’s next launch (devvm in its folder), and QEMU moves when the VM next starts.
data.what-devvm-doctor-checks#What devvm doct:
devvm doctor checks what Lima, devvm’s backend, needs. It lists everything that’s missing, each with what to do, which is the command that installs it when there’s one to run. It then lists what Lima can do, which it calls Lima’s features, each as native, emulated, unreviewed for an emulation that devvm refuses until it’s reviewed, or none. It also says whether Docker is installed, which only --from with an image only Docker has needs. When HTTPS_PROXY is set and ~/.config/devvm/ca has no CA certificates, it says that a proxy that inspects TLS needs its CA there (a company’s CA).
It warns in these cases:
another devvm comes first on your PATH (one devvm), the disk that devvm’s images and VMs go on has less free space than building base needs (free space), this machine has less than the 8 GiB of memory or the 4 CPUs that devvm recommends (requirements), a line of your policy files isn’t a rule, which VMs’ proxies skip (rules), a VM’s state, its vm.json, can’t be read, or has a section that the package which owns that section can’t read, as every command also checks for the VM it finds for a folder. doctor names the VM, or its folder when the file can’t be read, and gives the reason, which names the file, and it leaves the file as it is. It doesn’t check a value that reads but that a launch refuses, such as a size that isn’t a number (a file devvm can’t read), a running VM’s proxy runs without its sandbox, or with only part of it, such as on a Linux kernel whose Landlock is older than ABI 6. The proxy writes how it’s confined in the VM’s run/proxy.confined once it starts, and doctor names what that file says. doctor also names a proxy with no such file that another devvm binary started, which it tells by the devvm_sha256 in the proxy’s config, because that’s an older devvm’s single process, which has no sandbox. A proxy that this devvm started and that hasn’t written the file yet is still starting, so it gets no warning (the proxy runs without a sandbox). It also gives a tip, which isn’t a warning, when safe.bareRepository isn’t explicit in your global or system git config, or in the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name: git then takes any folder shaped like a git folder for a bare repo, so a VM can make one that git run below it uses (bare repos). doctor only reads the setting.
Then it says devvm has everything it needs, or it fails. The warnings and tips never make it fail, so a small machine with everything installed passes.

data: This page explains how devvm runs its VMs on Lima: the Lima home it keeps them in, how it builds images and clones VMs from them, what it sets in each VM’s config, how it confines VMs and builds, and how it forwards their ports. Lima covers what you need to run it, devvm limactl and Lima’s limits.
data.a-commands-output#A command’s output: devvm closes the output of each command that it runs in a VM, apart from a shell and an image build’s steps, a second after the command ends or its time limit runs out, because the ssh that limactl shell runs can leave a process behind that holds the output open. So a VM can’t keep devvm waiting past a command’s time limit, and a command whose output was cut short that way fails.
data.a-lima-home-of-its-own#A Lima home of it:
Lima merges _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home into every VM it creates or starts. A network you set there for your own VMs would give a devvm VM a second network card with a route around its proxy, and an extra mount set there would go unnoticed. So devvm keeps its VMs in a Lima home of their own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima, whatever LIMA_HOME says (devvm’s Lima home says what that means for you).
devvm refuses to start a VM while that home holds either file (lima_global_config), and it refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it (vm_has_networks).
devvm runs limactl from its own data folder. When a config is invalid, Lima writes lima.REJECTED.yaml into the folder it runs in, and a project folder belongs to the VM to write.
data.a-shells-colors#A shell’s colors: devvm opens a VM’s shell, and runs an agent’s login, with limactl shell, which asks ssh to send your terminal’s COLORTERM. That request never reaches the VM, because the session goes over the ssh connection that Lima shares between all of a VM’s sessions, which was opened without it (lima-vm/lima#2208). Closing that connection would end every session and the VM’s SSH agent relay with it, so devvm sets COLORTERM in the command it runs in the VM instead. It passes only truecolor and 24bit, the two values that say a terminal shows 24-bit color, and it quotes them for the VM’s shell. Quoting alone would make any value safe, but devvm sends a VM only values it knows. It passes nothing for any other value or when COLORTERM isn’t set, and then the shell starts as limactl shell starts it by itself.
data.a-stopped-vms-shell#A stopped VM’s shell: Every limactl shell that devvm runs says --start=false. In a terminal, limactl shell of a stopped VM asks whether to start it, and the question’s default is yes, but that start skips every check of devvm’s own start. A VM on a confined tier would run unconfined, without its proxy, and any VM would mount whatever is at the project folder’s path, a folder that replaced it included, and Lima would make the folder again if it’s gone. So a VM that stops while devvm works with it, such as one whose guest shut itself down, makes devvm’s shell or command fail, and devvm’s next launch starts it with every check.
data.clones-and-overlays#Clones and overlays:
An image is a stopped VM in devvm’s Lima home, named devvm-img-. devvm makes base’s from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml, base’s size as --cpus, --memory and --disk, and --mount-none, and it gives limactl create the template on its standard input (-), from the binary, so no copy of base.yaml is on disk. With --from, it makes base’s from the converted disk instead, and boots its kernel and initrd directly (details). A layer’s image is a clone of its parent’s, also made with --mount-none, so a build mounts nothing from the host. A project VM is a clone of its image’s VM, which devvm makes while the image is stopped.
macOS: the clone’s disk is an APFS copy-on-write copy. It shares the image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du overcounts it. Linux: Lima’s disks are qcow2 files, and a clone would be a full copy. So a project VM’s disk is a qcow2 overlay of its image’s, readable only by you, which shares the image’s blocks and holds only the VM’s changes. An image’s disk is read-only once it’s built, and devvm can’t delete an image while VMs’ disks are overlays of it (image_in_use). devvm reads each VM disk’s backing file with qemu-img info -U, which shares the disk with the QEMU of a running VM, because that QEMU’s write lock refuses qemu-img info otherwise.
data.confinement#Confinement:
A VM on a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, reaches nothing but its proxy on the host, which applies its tier’s rules, and even root in the VM can’t get around that. Direct connections, DNS, UDP and connections to the host’s own services fail at once, while forwarded ports, mounts and ssh keep working. Processes has what the hostagent and the QEMU wrapper hold, write and wait for (Lima’s hostagent, the QEMU wrapper).
On each host, the VM’s traffic passes through one process that devvm confines:
The process that confines a VM's trafficOn Linux, the VM's traffic goes through QEMU, with restrict=on, which reaches only its proxy at 192.168.5.4:3128. On macOS, it goes through its Lima hostagent, which is sandboxed, so it reaches only its ssh port, its proxy, its Lima sockets and its SSH agent, and everything else is denied.macOS Linux only to192.168.5.4:3128 allowed denied the VM QEMU,restrict=on its proxy the VM its Limahostagent,sandboxed its ssh portits proxyits Lima socketsits SSH agent everythingelse On macOS, devvm starts the VM’s Lima process, its hostagent, under a macOS sandbox. That’s sandbox-exec with a Seatbelt profile, sandbox.sb in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/.
The profile lets the process connect to the VM’s ssh port and its proxy on the host’s loopback, to the unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder (ssh’s control socket and the VM’s network), and to the socket of the ssh agent the VM forwards, which is its proxy’s relay of your agent or devvm’s own (the SSH agents). It connects nowhere else, so other sockets on the host, such as Docker’s, stay out of the hostagent’s reach. The profile limits only the network, so a compromised hostagent can still write your files, and through them run code as you. The profile lets the process listen only on the VM’s ssh port, over TCP, and on unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, so it can’t open a port of the VM’s on the host even if Lima ignored its rules (ports). Names resolve in the proxy, so Lima’s own DNS server for the VM is off, and the guest’s DNS points at 127.0.0.1, which only transparent mode answers, inside the VM, with no upstream. Without it, nothing listens there, and a lookup through the system’s resolver, such as the ones getent and curl make, asks 127.0.0.1 itself (the VM’s resolver) and fails at once on macOS and on a Linux host alike. The guest reaches the proxy at 192.168.5.2, which is the host as Lima’s network sees it. On Linux, Lima starts every VM’s QEMU through a wrapper that devvm writes (~/.local/share/devvm/run/qemu/) and that runs devvm. It runs QEMU in a namespace that makes .git’s hooks and config read-only, for a VM whose .git protection is on. For a confined VM, the wrapper adds QEMU’s restrict=on to Lima’s network, so no traffic goes in or out but Lima’s own forwards. It also adds one address, 192.168.5.4:3128, which QEMU connects to the VM’s proxy through a process for each connection, at most 256 at once (the QEMU wrapper). If Lima’s QEMU arguments aren’t the shape devvm expects, with one -netdev user,id=net0,… and no other network, the wrapper refuses to start QEMU (qemu_refused), so QEMU never runs unrestricted. DNS points at 127.0.0.1 in the guest, which only transparent mode answers, and without it lookups fail at once.
An open VM isn’t confined: on macOS its hostagent runs without a profile, and on Linux the wrapper runs QEMU with Lima’s network as Lima gives it, without restrict=on and without the guestfwd, as it does for a build with the internet. Its guest reaches its proxy at 192.168.5.2 and the proxy’s own port on both hosts, because Lima’s user-mode network, vz’s and QEMU’s alike, reaches the host’s loopback at that address. Its NO_PROXY adds host.lima.internal and 192.168.5.2, which the proxy on the host couldn’t resolve as the VM does, Lima’s DNS stays on, so names resolve in the VM, and propagateProxyEnv is off, so the guest gets no proxy settings of the host’s.
A process can’t leave its sandbox, so devvm records the hostagent it started (started in the VM’s run folder) and checks that the VM still runs on it (the self-check). A VM started another way, such as with limactl start, runs unconfined, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced. The VM’s proxy follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid in the VM’s Lima folder) and exits with it. devvm writes the record only once limactl start returns, while the hostagent runs on its own from early in the start, so an interrupt during the start stops the VM (how long a proxy runs). Interrupted before the hostagent answers, the VM is one Lima reports as Broken, which limactl stop refuses, so devvm stops a broken VM with limactl stop --force. A hostagent that runs without its driver yet is still starting QEMU, which writes its pid file only once it runs, and that can take seconds on a slow host, such as one with nested virtualization. Stopped with --force then, the hostagent would go and the QEMU it started would run on without it, so devvm waits up to 30 seconds for the driver first and then stops the VM as Lima reports it. A VM whose QEMU still runs without its hostagent holds its disk, so no new QEMU can start on it, and a start stops such a VM with --force first.
Builds are also confined, because they run code devvm didn’t write. On macOS a build’s Lima process runs under a profile that reaches either the internet but not the host’s loopback, where other VMs’ proxies and dev servers listen, or nothing at all. Behind a company proxy, a build with the internet also reaches one port of the host’s loopback, its own proxy’s (a company proxy). On Linux only a build with no network is confined. QEMU can’t keep the internet while dropping the host’s loopback, so other builds reach services on the host’s localhost. Builds forward no ports. A build with the internet reaches your LAN on both hosts, this machine’s own address on it included, because the macOS profile keeps only the loopback from it.
sandbox-exec is deprecated. If macOS drops it, devvm needs another way to confine the hostagent, and until then the self-check catches a VM that runs unconfined.
data.ports#Ports:
devvm’s forwarder forwards a Lima VM’s ports by the rules that Port forwarding sets out. On Lima this is an emulation, and it’s reviewed (design). devvm doesn’t use Lima’s own forwards because they listen with SO_REUSEADDR, and on macOS such a forward takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, along with that program’s localhost connections.
So Lima forwards nothing. Each VM’s portForwards are rules that ignore every guest port, TCP and UDP, on 127.0.0.1 (which also covers ::1), 0.0.0.0 and ::. Lima’s own ssh is its VM driver’s forward, not a rule, so it keeps working. devvm sets the rules when it makes the VM, and a start sets them again only where they differ, because any change gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t rely on the rules alone, because its sandbox refuses the Lima process every port but its ssh port (confinement).
Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm’s forwarder reads, so devvm ports changes the state and never the VM’s Lima config, and the backend never hears of them. Its process and files lists the forwarder’s files and its log.
The forwarder isn’t Lima’s, and it runs only for project VMs. What Lima gives it is how to reach a running VM: Lima’s ssh port on this machine’s loopback, Lima’s user, and Lima’s key (_config/user in devvm’s Lima home), which every VM there authorizes. The forwarder connects there with the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, which the VM’s ssh config checks too. Its lifeline is the VM’s hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid), so it ends when the hostagent does, and devvm rm deletes its files.
data.what-devvm-sets-on-a-vm#What devvm sets:
devvm sets these in each VM’s Lima config:
Mounts: the project folder (read-write), agents’ folders (read-only), and the shared tools at /mnt/devvm-tools (read-only). Each folder but the tools is mounted at its host path. devvm mounts nothing else, and it leaves out the home folder that Lima’s templates mount. On macOS, where Lima runs VMs with vz, the project folder’s mount names the folder by the device and inode that devvm recorded when it made the VM, or recorded again at a start after a boot numbered the folder’s disk anew, as location: /.vol// with mountPoint set to the folder’s path. macOS’s /.vol opens a folder by its device and inode, so Virtualization.framework shares the folder devvm made the VM for, wherever that folder is when the VM starts, and never follows a link put at its path (an existing VM). Virtualization.framework then serves the share by the path the folder had at the start, so a folder moved back while the VM runs answers “Operation not permitted” in the VM until its next start. QEMU’s 9p on Linux has nothing like /.vol, so there the mount is by the folder’s path, with the cache mode the VM’s state records as its 9p: cache: option: none for a new VM, and nothing for a VM whose mode nobody chose, which keeps Lima’s mmap (why). The read-only mounts keep Lima’s fscache, and a build VM’s writable output folder gets none. The start that changes a VM’s cache mode mounts its folder again once the VM runs, because the guest mounted it with the old options before cloud-init wrote the new ones into its /etc/fstab, and it then checks the mount: a folder left unmounted fails the start (why). A start that rewrites the mounts, for a folder that moved, another cache mode or other agents’ folders, keeps each mount’s settings that devvm doesn’t set, such as its other 9p and sshfs options, where they differ from Lima’s defaults, and leaves the defaults out for Lima to fill in. ssh: agent forwarding on or off, and the host port, which Lima always listens on at 127.0.0.1. devvm chooses the port and records it, so no other VM’s forwarded ports take it. It chooses only from the 17 ports on which every browser engine refuses every request, navigations and WebSockets included, which are the Fetch standard’s bad ports from 1024 up that Chromium also blocks (1719, 1720, 1723, 2049, 3659, 4045, 5060, 5061, 6000, 6566, 6665 to 6669, 6697 and 10080). Fetch also lists 4190 and 6679, but Chromium’s own list lacks them, and Chrome loads pages on them. Root in a VM can make what answers on its ssh port speak HTTP, and cookies ignore the port, so on any other port a page opened as http://localhost:PORT would reach a server the VM controls with the cookies of the apps you use on localhost, even in a VM that forwards no ports. So at most 17 VMs run at once, and a start past that fails, naming the VMs whose ports are in use (ports_ssh_limit, or ports_ssh_limit_all when they have all 17), or saying that VMs starting or building, ports a running VM lists to forward, or other programs on this machine have them all (ports_ssh_limit_others). devvm’s other host ports, a VM’s proxy port and desktop port, are never one of these, and one an older devvm chose moves at the VM’s next start. A VM that forwards every port never forwards one of the 17 either. A VM that lists one does forward it, whatever set the list, and devvm ports and each launch warn of it (ports_ssh_listed), and while that VM runs, it keeps the port from VMs’ ssh, as any program on this machine that holds one does. A stopped VM keeps its port at its next start while it’s free, and gets another when another program on the host has it, on any address, when the VM lists it to forward, when another start or a build holds it, when a VM that runs lists it, or when it isn’t one of the 17, because an older devvm chose it. A new port is one no VM’s state records, or else one a stopped VM’s state records, which that VM gives up, getting another at its own next start. A build VM’s port is never the one its clone kept from its image while another is free. The start’s one limactl edit sets a new port, and the VM’s host keys are pinned again, as at every start. A start holds its port, kept or new, for a minute, in run/ports.ssh-hold in the VM’s folder, so that no other start or build takes it before its backend binds it as the start begins. The hold lasts only that minute, so a start whose backend takes longer than that to bind the port can lose it to another start that chooses it then. The slower start then fails, and starting it again gives it another port. A running VM keeps its port until its next start, even one an older devvm chose, and each launch warns of the running VMs still on such a port (ports_ssh_old). Ports: none, because Lima’s own forwards are off and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead (below). Size: CPUs, memory and disk. Guest environment: Lima’s env:, which Lima writes to /etc/environment at every boot. On every tier it holds the VM’s proxy’s address and its settings, and Lima doesn’t pass the host’s proxy settings in. A confined VM reaches the proxy as Lima’s host address on macOS and as QEMU’s guestfwd address on Linux, and an open VM reaches it at Lima’s host address on both, which is this machine’s loopback as Lima’s network has it, with host.lima.internal added to its NO_PROXY. limactl edit sets the proxy’s URL with a stand-in for the password (devvm-proxy-password), and devvm then replaces the stand-in in the VM’s lima.yaml, which it rewrites with mode 600, so the password is in no process’s arguments. Its NO_PROXY and no_proxy name the VM alone, and never its links, which its HTTP clients reach through the proxy, so links never change it. A start runs limactl edit only when the environment differs from the one the VM has, because it compares them first. That edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot, as any edit does, and devvm forgets a VM’s host keys at every start and pins them again once it runs, so devvm’s ssh config, its own connections and your editors keep working. Proxy settings and DNS: Lima’s propagateProxyEnv, which writes this machine’s proxy settings into the guest, is on only for a VM on Lima’s own network without devvm’s proxy, so they never reach a VM that goes through devvm’s proxy. A VM confined to its proxy has Lima’s host resolver off (hostResolver.enabled: false) and dns: ["127.0.0.1"], because its names resolve in the proxy (confinement). An open VM keeps Lima’s own resolver and DNS. Lima changes only a stopped VM’s config, so a change you make while the VM runs applies at its next start. When devvm makes a VM, the clone gets its mounts, agent forwarding, ssh port, ports rules and environment, and devvm then edits the VM’s size where it differs from its image’s. Each start of a stopped VM compares the VM’s config, as limactl list shows it, with what the VM’s state asks for and with how the VM starts. That covers its size, its project folder’s path, which changes once the folder moved (a moved folder), on macOS the device and inode its mount names, which change in that same edit once a boot gave the folder’s disk another device number, and on Linux its cache mode where one was chosen, its agents’ folders, its agent forwarding, its ssh port, its environment, Lima’s proxy settings (propagateProxyEnv), its DNS (hostResolver and dns) and its ports rules. devvm then changes whatever differs in one limactl edit, and runs none when nothing does, because each edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. Lima can’t shrink a disk, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before it changes anything (disk_shrink).
devvm leaves Lima’s mountInotify off, so file watchers in the VM see only the changes made in the VM (file watchers). With it on, Lima’s hostagent watches the project folder on the host and, for each change there, changes the file’s times in the guest as root, which raises an inotify event for the guest’s watchers. The hostagent can’t tell the VM’s own writes from the host’s, so it does this to every file the VM writes too, and on macOS the guest then sees such a file as root’s for a moment. A command that writes a file and then changes its mode fails in that moment, and in a test on macOS, git init in the project folder failed 13 times in 30 with it on and never with it off. Lima also passes on no deletions, and it marks the setting as experimental.

data: This page explains how devvm confines a VM to its proxy on each tier, what the proxy does with each connection, and how your secrets get into the VM’s requests without the VM holding them. Network tiers covers choosing a tier, the allowlists and their rules, the secrets and the logs as you use them.
data.a-companys-ca#A company’s CA:
The CA certificates in ~/.config/devvm/ca (a company’s CA) reach every project VM, whatever its tier, and the VM’s proxy. Builds trust them too, as Images and caching describes, and so does the mise that resolves the shared tools’ versions on this machine, which on macOS trusts them for every connection but its Sigstore client’s, as the host’s mise below explains.
Reading them. devvm reads the folder’s *.pem and *.crt files at each launch, each build, each proxy start and each run of the host’s mise, and nothing outside the folder. It looks at the folder and each of those files itself, never at what a link leads to, and follows no link: a folder that is a link fails with ca_folder_link, and a file that is one, dangling or not, with ca_link. A link into a project folder would otherwise let that project’s VM write the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. A file or folder that it can’t read fails with ca_unreadable or ca_folder_unreadable, which name it and carry the error. It decodes every PEM block and refuses a block that isn’t CERTIFICATE (ca_not_certificate), a certificate that crypto/x509 can’t parse (ca_invalid) and a certificate without CA basic constraints (ca_not_ca). It also refuses a file with no certificate in it. It tells a private key apart by its PEM type, not by the file’s name, and a refusal fails the whole launch or build. What leaves the host is each certificate encoded again from its parsed bytes, once each, so the text around a block never does.
Installing them. devvm’s guest script ca.sh DIR runs as root and makes devvm’s CAs in /usr/local/share/ca-certificates exactly DIR’s devvm-*.crt files: the VM’s own CA and its next one, devvm-proxy.crt and devvm-proxy-next.crt, and the user’s devvm-extra-N.crt. When anything changed, it runs update-ca-certificates --fresh, so a CA that went leaves neither the bundle nor its hashed link. update-ca-certificates tells the hooks in /etc/ca-certificates/update.d only about the CAs it links, never about a file that was deleted, so ca.sh tells them itself. It runs each hook that run-parts would run, with a -/etc/ssl/certs/NAME.pem line on its input for each CA it removed, as Debian’s update-ca-certificates does for a CA it deselects. That way Java’s cacerts (ca-certificates-java’s jks-keystore hook) and Mono’s store drop a removed CA, in a project VM and in an image whose layer installed Java. A hook that rebuilds its store from the bundle ignores that input. A hook that fails stops nothing, and ca.sh says so in the run log. It also writes them all to /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, for Node. In a system without update-ca-certificates, such as a container image before its ca-certificates package, it adds them to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt itself. It keeps the bundle as it was in /var/lib/devvm-ca, or a mark that there was none, and puts it back once they go, and a package that arrives in between makes the bundle again from the same folder. Run without DIR, ca.sh removes every one of devvm’s files. Its unit tests run it in a folder that stands for / (DEVVM_CA_ROOT).
Project VMs. The setup that devvm sends at each launch carries ca.sh and the certificates in ca/, and sync.sh runs it, so a change applies at the next launch and a running VM needs no restart. Every project VM starts with the CAs’ variables below in its environment, whatever its tier and whether there are CAs or not, so adding a CA changes nothing that its backend sets at a start. On Lima, the clone that makes the VM sets the environment too, and the VM’s first start adds its proxy’s address to it in the one edit before its first boot. The variables are NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which is empty when there are none (Node warns only about a missing file), SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and PIP_CERT, set to the system’s bundle, and UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=1.
The proxy. As devvm readies a VM’s proxy, it reads the folder too, and writes the bundle into the proxy’s config, proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, as upstream_cas, which the proxy adds to the system’s roots for its own TLS connections. Each secret lookup’s context carries those roots, and an agent’s OAuth refresh on the host takes them from there and sets them on its client, so it goes through a company proxy that inspects TLS as the VM’s own requests do. devvm’s other host requests, such as registry digests and Ubuntu’s image check, use the host’s own store, as the host’s other programs do. A VM can’t change that file or the folder, so the proxy’s roots grow only by what you put there. A proxy whose bundle differs from the folder’s starts again, as one whose CA was replaced does.
The host’s mise. The client that downloads devvm’s own mise adds the folder’s CAs to the system’s roots, and a download whose server’s certificate it still doesn’t trust fails with tools_untrusted, in place of mise_download_failed. That mise, a release build, uses rustls with the platform’s verifier, so it trusts the system’s roots, and it falls back to Mozilla’s own only when none load. On Linux it reads the system’s roots from files, as OpenSSL does. When the environment sets neither SSL_CERT_FILE nor SSL_CERT_DIR, it reads the first bundle it finds, such as /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, and the folders /etc/ssl/certs and /etc/pki/tls/certs, and otherwise it reads only what they name. On macOS it asks Security.framework, which trusts what the Keychain trusts and reads no variable. With CAs in the folder, each run of mise gets them in its temporary folder, and MISE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS names them, which mise adds to its roots on both systems. mise’s Sigstore client, which fetches the trust root (tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev) that its lock-time provenance checks need, ignores that setting, so on Linux devvm also writes a bundle of the system’s bundle and the folder’s CAs, and SSL_CERT_FILE names it, which every client in mise reads. The system’s bundle is the file that SSL_CERT_FILE names when devvm’s environment sets it. When devvm’s environment sets neither variable, SSL_CERT_DIR names the system’s folders, so mise still reads them. Otherwise mise reads the folders that devvm’s environment names, and none when it sets only SSL_CERT_FILE, so a bundle of your own keeps mise to the CAs that you chose and the folder’s. On macOS nothing but the Keychain reaches that client, so a CA that a proxy signs that host with has to be trusted there. Each run of mise also logs to a file in its folder (MISE_LOG_FILE). When a failed resolve’s log has rustls’s invalid peer certificate, devvm fails with tools_untrusted, which names the folder, in place of tools_resolve_failed or tools_need_resolve.
End-to-end checks: in project, a VM trusts a test CA from its next launch (openssl verify against the system’s bundle, and curl reaching an HTTPS server on the host that the CA signed), has the variables, fails its launch on a file that isn’t a certificate, and trusts the CA no more once the folder is emptied; in tools, Node fetches from that server.
data.agents-logins-and-settings#Agents’ login:
Agents’ login files also stay on the host, in devvm’s agent store, which devvm agent import fills, and so do logins made in a VM (devvm’s agent store). devvm never reads an agent’s own login file in the home folder for a VM. When a VM’s image has the agent and the store has a login file for it, the login’s bindings join the VM’s, and their hosts join its allowlist on port 443.
Codex’s login is ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/codex/.codex/auth.json, opencode’s is ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/opencode/.local/share/opencode/auth.json and pi’s is ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/pi/.pi/agent/auth.json, the store’s copies of ~/.codex/auth.json, ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json and ~/.pi/agent/auth.json. The VM’s copy holds placeholders, shaped like a JWT where the tools read claims, and the bindings put the store’s API key or access token into requests for the provider’s hosts:
For Codex, those are OpenAI’s hosts, api.openai.com, and chatgpt.com for a ChatGPT login. For opencode, they’re the hosts of the API keys of the providers in API keys the proxy puts in, each in the headers that its row names, and of OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins, but not Copilot Enterprise. opencode keeps one entry per provider, {"type":"api","key","metadata"}, {"type":"oauth","refresh","access","expires","accountId","enterpriseUrl"} or {"type":"wellknown","key","token"}. A bound key’s entry reaches the VM as {"type","key"} alone, its key the placeholder, so its metadata stays on this machine, and a bound OAuth login’s keeps only the fields that name its account beside the placeholders (the packages). For pi, they’re the hosts of the same providers’ API keys, each in the same headers. Both agents name each of these providers by the same ID, and neither puts a key in a URL, such as Gemini’s ?key=, which the proxy couldn’t fill in, because it swaps the placeholder in a header alone. pi keeps one entry per provider, {"type":"api_key","key","env"} or {"type":"oauth","access","refresh","expires"}, and devvm binds only the first kind, with a key that’s a value rather than a !command or a $NAME or ${NAME} template, which pi fills in from the entry’s env or the environment ($$ is a literal $). A bound entry reaches the VM as {"type","key"} alone, its key the placeholder, so nothing else of it, its env included, leaves this machine. The store keeps opencode’s login in the auth.json format of opencode 1: one entry per provider, {"type":"api","key"} or {"type":"oauth","access","refresh","expires"} with its expiry in milliseconds. opencode 2 keeps its logins in the credential table of its SQLite database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, and imports auth.json into it once, in the migration that makes the table, so a VM’s opencode gets the VM’s copy when it first runs there. A VM’s placeholders don’t change when the host refreshes a login, so the database’s copies keep working. After that, the store’s opencode logins reach the database through opencode auth import, as auth export entries with the IDs cred_devvm_: the placeholder of each API key that the proxy puts in, each key that [pass-keys] passes, with its metadata, and the OpenAI login’s placeholders from one of opencode’s Codex logins. The VM’s setup sends these entries on every launch, and devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider PROVIDER sends them at once, both on the input of devvm’s guest script opencode.sh, never in a command’s arguments. The script keeps the last entries it got in ~/.local/state/devvm/opencode-import.json in the VM. When opencode has made its database and the new entries differ from the record, or the database no longer holds one of their IDs because it was made again, such as after you delete it or a history import replaces it, it logs out of devvm’s entries from the last ones with opencode auth logout, because opencode auth import skips an ID it already has, and then imports the new ones and makes each of them its provider’s active credential with opencode auth switch, so a ChatGPT login for another account or a key saved from another VM reaches every VM at its next launch. Credentials that you added in the VM yourself have other IDs, so they stay in the database, and opencode auth switch makes one of them active again. Before opencode has made its database, the script does nothing and records nothing, because opencode 2.2.5 doesn’t always import auth.json as it makes the database, so the first launch after opencode has run imports every entry. The script imports each entry on its own, so an entry that opencode refuses doesn’t keep the others out, and devvm agent login names the providers that opencode refused. A failed import leaves the record as it was, so the next launch tries again. The script and its record live in the VM rather than in the VM’s state on the host, because only the VM knows whether its database exists and what it last imported, and a VM that is set up again or has its home copied keeps both together.
Each VM’s placeholders end in its own random value, so no other VM’s placeholder gets its secrets. devvm reads a login file only when it’s a regular file, so a FIFO or a device in its place can’t hold devvm. devvm refreshes OAuth logins on the host, one lookup at a time, and writes them back to the store’s file, so a VM never holds the refresh token of a login devvm keeps. Claude Code’s logins to MCP servers that you make in a VM are that VM’s own (Claude Code’s login). A refresh that has started finishes and is written back even when the request that needed it ends, because OpenAI may already have replaced the refresh token. When a refresh fails, or the store’s login no longer has what a binding names, the proxy puts nothing in, and its own log says to log in again with the agent and import the login again (agent_refresh_failed, agent_provider_refresh_failed for one of opencode’s providers, codex_no_key, codex_no_chatgpt), or names the login file it couldn’t read (login_read_failed). The VM’s copy of Codex’s auth.json holds only the fields that devvm knows, as Codex 0.166.0’s login code reads them. Its API key and its tokens are placeholders, and the copy keeps auth_mode and last_refresh, and in tokens, account_id, login_owner_id and the refresh token’s oauth_provenance, its issuer and client_id, each a plain value. devvm leaves every other field out, at the top of the file or in tokens, Codex’s other logins included (agent_identity, personal_access_token, bedrock_api_key and bedrock_access_keys), because the proxy has no binding for them, and warns you, naming a field in tokens by its path, such as tokens.zz (login_fields_withheld). A unit test plants a field that no format knows in every object of each kind’s login file, as a string, an object and a list, and checks that no VM’s copy holds it (the tests behind it). opencode’s and pi’s logins are withheld by default, by the same rule, which each agent’s entry in devvm’s registry of the agents sets. Every entry that devvm doesn’t bind, an API key, an OAuth login or opencode’s well-known login, reaches the VM with only the fields that name its account or how it logs in, type, expires, accountId, enterpriseUrl, projectId, email, scope, scopes and clientId, each a plain value or a list of strings, and devvm warns you (login_withheld). opencode skips an entry that lacks its key or its tokens as it reads auth.json, so it doesn’t use that provider in the VM. The exception is an API-key entry of a provider that config.toml’s [pass-keys] lists under the agent’s name, which goes as it is, and devvm notes it (login_passed). It’s never an OAuth login, whose tokens a VM never gets, and never a provider that devvm binds, whose key is always its placeholder, so binding wins over the table, and devvm notes each bound provider that the table lists (login_pass_bound). The table has one key per agent, so each agent’s withheld keys are passed on their own. If devvm can’t make the VM’s copy of a login, it stops the VM’s setup (login_copy_failed).
Coding agents lists which files each agent shares.
data.devvm-_proxy#devvm _proxy:
devvm runs the proxy as itself, devvm _proxy -config FILE, and nothing else is in its arguments. That’s the broker, which runs its child as devvm _proxy-child -for FILE, with the same config’s path, which the child never opens. The path is there so devvm can tell each VM’s child apart, by run/proxy-child.pid and those arguments, and stop one that outlived its broker. Their flags take one dash or two, and their errors end in one line, The VM's proxy failed: … (proxy_failed). Processes has what a VM’s proxy holds, what it reads from the VM and its bounds, and a build’s proxy has the build’s.
The config is one JSON file, which a VM’s proxy and a build’s proxy both run with. For a VM it’s proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, and for a build it’s proxy.json in the build proxy’s folder. devvm writes it whole, mode 600, before each start. It holds the VM’s password and the company proxy’s credentials from the environment, though never config.toml’s password, which the proxy looks up itself, so it’s never in a process’s arguments, which other users can see. The proxy reads it once, as it starts, and refuses to start unless it’s a regular file, not a symbolic link, owned by the user the proxy runs as and readable and writable by nobody else, at most 1 MiB, of "version": 1, with no field the proxy doesn’t know. It also refuses a config without a password, one whose listen isn’t a loopback address and port, one with ca and no ca_key or the other way around, and one with a nix_cache_max below 0. A config of another version is never read, so a proxy and the devvm that started it always agree on what each field means.
Field What version 1 listen the loopback address and port to listen on, port 0 for any free one vm the VM’s name, for the log password the VM’s password, which every request carries in Proxy-Authorization with the user devvm; required builtin_policies the built-in policies, paths in devvm’s own files, read from the binary once as the proxy starts, ahead of policies; a missing one refuses to start policies your policy files, in order, each read again when it changes; a missing one has no rules log the JSON-lines event log (none: standard output), rotated past 10 MiB proxy_log the file that the proxy’s output goes to, which is its own log, rotated past 10 MiB by copying lifeline the hostagent’s pid file: exit once it no longer holds what it held when the proxy first saw its process running, or that process is gone ca, ca_key the VM’s own CA, for interception: its certificate and key ca_next, ca_next_key with ca: the VM’s next CA, which signs from an hour after its start secrets the VM’s bindings file, read again when it changes, and the broker looks each binding’s value up in its own process, for the child upstream_cas the CAs in your CA folder (PEM), which the proxy’s own TLS connections trust besides the system’s upstream the company proxy: https, http and no_proxy, as HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY or config.toml’s [proxy] had them, and secret, the secret the proxy looks up as the password of a URL that names a user and none of its own; allowed hosts are reached through it upstream_unresolved with upstream: names this machine can’t resolve go there even when only ** allows them, which builds’ proxies get nix_cache serve the shared Nix cache at http://devvm.proxy/nix/ from this folder, which it makes, only yours (mode 700) nix_cache_max with nix_cache: the cache’s cap, in bytes (none: 10 GiB) links the VM’s links’ list, which devvm _links writes: reach each link through its socket, before any rule (links through the proxy); a missing list has no links link_sockets with links: the folder of the links’ sockets, devvm’s run folder; without it, no link is reached vm_logs the logs that the VM’s backend writes as the VM runs and the VM can drive, such as its serial console’s, which the proxy holds to their cap for as long as it runs (Lima’s hostagent) agent, agent_socket together, as absolute paths: the SSH agent that the VM’s start forwards, your own or devvm’s, and the VM’s own socket in devvm’s run folder, agent-.sock, on which the proxy relays it and which the VM’s backend forwards instead (the SSH agents). devvm keeps a running VM’s as its start set them devvm_sha256, ca_sha256, ca_next_sha256 the SHA-256 of devvm’s binary, of the VM’s CA certificate and of its next CA’s that the proxy started with; the proxy doesn’t read them, and they’re there so that a new binary or a new CA makes another config (how long a proxy runs) -config is the proxy’s only flag, and running the proxy is its only mode. What only this machine does for a VM’s proxy runs inside devvm itself, never through the proxy’s arguments. devvm makes each VM’s CAs, and the VM’s copies of agents’ logins and settings files, their bindings and their values, in its own process (the packages).
data.how-long-a-proxy-runs#How long a proxy r:
The proxy exits when the VM’s Lima hostagent does, which it learns from the hostagent’s pid file, the VM’s lifeline (lifeline in its config). The proxy starts before the VM, so it waits for the lifeline to name a process that runs. What the file held when the proxy started is an earlier start’s, and the proxy waits past it, but when a new start writes the file and its process is already gone, the proxy exits. Once it follows a start, it runs while the file holds what it held then and that process runs, so a VM started again gets a new proxy. If the hostagent never appears, the proxy exits 15 minutes after it started, and devvm stop stops it at once. It’s the broker that follows the lifeline, and its child ends with it, as processes describes. The broker closes the socket between them, the child stops listening, closes its connections and exits, and the broker kills a child that hasn’t ended 6 seconds later. A child that ends ends its broker, and neither starts the other again, so the VM has no network until devvm’s next command starts its proxy again, as after any proxy’s crash. devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans also stop a child that outlived its broker, by run/proxy-child.pid and its arguments.
A VM that starts again gets a new proxy on the same port. A running VM also gets a new proxy when the config devvm would start it with differs from the one it started with, which devvm tells by the SHA-256 of each. The config holds everything that, changed, starts the proxy again: the VM’s list of policies, the VM’s CA and the next one, by the SHA-256 of each certificate, so a CA that was replaced counts, the SHA-256 of devvm’s binary, so a proxy from another devvm binary counts, the CAs in your CA folder, the company proxy settings in devvm’s environment and the shared Nix cache’s cap. A config that’s gone, or that the proxy wouldn’t read, counts as one that differs. To start a new proxy, devvm stops the old one with SIGTERM, and with SIGKILL when it’s still running two seconds later. The old proxy counts as stopped only once its process is gone, not once its arguments can no longer be read, because an ending process loses its memory before its files, and for that moment its port still looks taken by another program, which would fail the launch with proxy_port_taken. SIGKILL goes only to a process whose arguments devvm can still read as the proxy’s, so a proxy still ending gets none, and neither does another process given its pid since, even one whose arguments devvm can’t read. If it still runs two seconds after that, devvm stops with proxy_stop_failed and starts nothing, because the old proxy would go on with its old settings.
devvm counts a proxy as started only once the proxy says it’s listening on the VM’s port and is still running, because a program that took the port first would otherwise get the VM’s traffic. The proxy says so in a status file of its own in the VM’s run folder (vms//run/proxy.status), which devvm names to it when it starts it and removes before each start. The file holds the proxy’s pid and the address it listens on, so a status that an earlier proxy left, or that another program wrote, never counts. While devvm waits, the proxy counts as running as long as its pid file still names it, it hasn’t ended, and its arguments are the VM’s proxy’s, _proxy -config with the VM’s proxy.json, or still devvm’s own, or can’t be read yet. On Linux, a process that has just started shows devvm’s own arguments for a moment, then none, because the kernel lets devvm go on as the new program begins to replace devvm’s copy, and shows the program’s arguments only once it has loaded. If the proxy doesn’t start, devvm stops and names the proxy’s log (proxy_start_failed). When a stopped VM’s port was taken by another program, devvm chooses a new free port. A running VM’s backend holds the port it started with, so when a running VM’s proxy is gone and another program took its port, devvm can’t start the proxy again (proxy_port_taken). devvm then stops the VM (net_proxy_down_stopped), and it does the same when the proxy fails to start for any other reason once the old one was stopped, or when none of the VM’s runs, because a confined VM never runs on without its proxy. The next devvm starts both. A running VM’s old proxy has the VM’s port, so it can’t be kept while the new one starts. On a launch, a link’s change or a devvm network change, what can refuse the proxy’s start is checked before the old one stops: the company proxy and its password, your CAs, and the VM’s CA and secret files. A refusal there leaves the VM and its old proxy running as they were, and devvm says so (net_proxy_kept), but only while the old proxy enforces what the VM’s state asks for now: the same built-in policies, policy files and deny files for the VM’s tier, open or not, from the same devvm binary. An old proxy with a looser tier than the state’s, or from another devvm binary, whose built-in policies’ rules may differ, is stopped with the VM, because it would fail open. The comparison leaves out the company proxy and your CAs that the old proxy started with, so an old proxy kept this way still goes through the company proxy, and trusts the CAs, of its own start. devvm restart checks only the company proxy and your CAs before it stops the VM, and its start checks the rest. An interrupt during the start of a confined VM stops the VM and its proxy too (interrupted_start, a cleanup that the start registers around the backend’s start), because a backend can leave the VM running while its start still waits for it. Lima’s hostagent keeps running the VM after limactl start ends, and devvm records the confined start only once limactl start returns. Without the stop, the VM would run with no record of its confined start, so devvm ls would show it as unenforced and its next launch would offer to restart it.
data.how-the-proxy-puts-them-in#How the proxy:
A secret’s hosts join the VM’s allowlist on port 443, whether a value is saved or not. A secret of yours has exact host names alone, because a wildcard would reach names that others may own under a shared domain, and devvm can’t tell those domains from the rest without the public suffix list.
For each secret that has a value, devvm writes the VM’s bindings to secrets.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, as one JSON object, whole and mode 600. It’s of "version": 1 while every binding has no methods and no path but a prefix longer than / that ends with / and has no *, so a proxy that knows only version 1, still running from before an upgrade, keeps the VM’s bindings, its agents’ logins included. One from after bindings gained paths reads such a file alike. A proxy of devvm 0.1.0 or 0.1.1-rc.1 ignores the path, which for the built-in bindings only widens OpenRouter’s key to all of openrouter.ai, as 0.1.0 bound it, until the VM starts again with a new proxy. A secret of yours saved with the path / has none, as / is every path. A binding with methods or another path makes it "version": 2, which such a proxy refuses, so it puts no value in rather than put one in for every method, and devvm warns about each VM whose proxy is from another devvm binary when it writes one (secrets_other_binary).
