A binding holds the secret’s name, its kind, its hosts, header and placeholder, sometimes a path and methods, and never its value. The kind is secret for one that devvm keeps and login for one of an agent’s logins, with the agent whose login file holds it, so where a value comes from never depends on its name. The proxy reads the file only when it’s a regular file, not a symbolic link, that only you can read or write, and a file it can’t read that way has no bindings until devvm writes it again. For a bound host, the proxy intercepts :443 tunnels instead of passing them through. It terminates TLS with a certificate from the VM’s own CA. Each certificate it makes for a host lasts a day, but never past the CA’s own end or before its start, because a client checks the whole chain. The proxy keeps the certificates of the 1024 hosts it used most recently and makes a new one for any other, so a binding with a wildcard host such as *.example.com, which needs a certificate for each name the VM asks for, can’t grow the proxy’s memory without end. It then puts the real value in the binding’s header and forwards the request over a new TLS connection. Absolute-form https:// requests get the same.
How the proxy puts the value in depends on the binding’s kind. A secret binding’s placeholder is replaced only when exactly one value of its header holds it, as it is or inside Basic credentials, and that value has one of four shapes. It’s the placeholder alone, or for Authorization, Bearer, Token or the binding’s own scheme in any case, one space and the placeholder, because gh sends the GitHub token after token. It’s also Basic credentials, canonical base64 after one space, whose password is the placeholder, after a username of printable ASCII without a colon and at most 64 characters, because git sends the GitHub token as x-access-token: that way. With the binding’s basic_user, it may be the username instead, before a password of printable ASCII of at most 64 characters, as Stripe takes its key. The proxy then puts the value where the placeholder was and nowhere else. A username, framed bytes, a doubled placeholder and a Digest field are all places that a server can echo when it refuses a request, as Elasticsearch names the user it couldn’t authenticate, so those keep the placeholder. A login binding’s placeholder is replaced only when the header has one value and that value is the placeholder alone, or, for Authorization, Bearer in any case, one space and the placeholder. Every agent sends its logins that way: an API key alone in x-api-key or x-goog-api-key, every other key and every OAuth login’s access token after Bearer, and an MCP server’s header as the whole value that the VM’s copy replaced. Any other value keeps the placeholder, and so does a header that’s sent twice, which a server may join into one value. So code in the VM can’t put text of its own before or after a real API key, and a provider that quotes part of a key it refuses, as xAI’s, OpenAI’s and DeepSeek’s errors do, quotes only the placeholder. The proxy’s own log names the binding and its header when it leaves a placeholder for that reason, without a value.
A binding can also have a path, a pattern as a rule’s is, and methods, and then the proxy puts its value in only for a request that they match as a rule’s allow does, with the one matcher of requests by method and path, so a request with another method, or with a method-override header that names another, keeps the placeholder. Only a secret of yours has methods, from devvm secret set’s --method, and a binding without them goes in for every method. A path that ends with / matches everything below it. OpenRouter’s API keys are bound below /api/, because opencode and pi send them only to openrouter.ai/api/v1/, so the rest of the site gets the placeholder. They’re bound in two headers, each a binding of its own with the same name and placeholder. pi sends the key in x-api-key to /api/v1/messages for OpenRouter’s anthropic/* models, which it calls with Anthropic’s API, and in Authorization after Bearer for every other model. opencode sends it in Authorization today, and in x-api-key for a model whose first API in the models.dev catalog is Anthropic’s Messages API, because it uses a model’s first API. The proxy compares the path as it forwards it, after a token endpoint’s capture has set it, and it takes the path only in a form that every server reads alike: clean already, without a . or .. segment or a doubled slash, with nothing percent-encoded, so no encoded slash or dot can move the request elsewhere after the check, and without a backslash or a ;, which some servers read as a separator or drop with what follows. A request for /api/../settings, /api%2F..%2Fsettings or /%61pi/v1 keeps the placeholder. A bindings file with a path that isn’t a pattern, or with methods that aren’t in their canonical form, has no bindings. Each request must name the bound host, and one that names another host gets 421. The proxy checks the bindings file for every request and reads it again when it has changed, so removing a binding applies to tunnels that are already open.
The proxy’s broker is devvm itself, so it looks a value up in its own process, from the Keychain, devvm’s secrets folder or the agent’s login file, by the binding’s kind, when the child asks for it. The child names the binding by its kind, agent and name alone, and the broker finds that binding in its own read of the VM’s bindings file and looks the value up with its own copy of it, so a child can ask for no value that isn’t bound to its VM. It runs no other devvm for it, no devvm command prints a secret, and no value is in any process’s arguments. On macOS it asks the Keychain through security find-generic-password, whose output is the value. A lookup takes at most 20 seconds, and the broker makes one at a time, so two requests never refresh a login at once. The broker keeps values for 5 minutes, or 30 seconds for agents’ logins, and a failed lookup for 5 seconds, so a child can’t make it run security or try a refresh back to back, and it drops them all when the bindings file changes, so a secret set right after a failure goes in at the next request. The child keeps a value only until the broker’s lookup is that old, and neither logs one. Each keeps a value by its binding’s kind, agent and name together, so a binding never gets the value of another one with the same name. A lookup that fails puts nothing in, and the proxy’s own log says why, without the value, such as agent_refresh_failed when refreshing a Codex login failed. It refuses with 403 the GitHub API calls that would make a credential of their own with the GitHub token, which are adding an account or deploy key, registering a runner and adding a webhook, whether the repo or organization is named or given by its ID. Every HTTPS request it forwards is checked, inside an intercepted tunnel and in absolute form alike, before it goes anywhere.
Tests: the unit tests check what a secret of yours may be and what devvm secret set’s flags change, that every variable the VM’s scripts export, and the proxy’s, is one it can’t take, each shape its value goes in and each that keeps the placeholder, and that a binding’s path and methods let it in only for the requests they match, each request of a kept-alive or HTTP/2 connection on its own. They check that a binding that isn’t the secret’s as it’s saved gets nothing, that a value too long for the Keychain’s line is refused before anything runs, and that every secret’s placeholder has one shape, the VM’s own, and is never taken as a value. They check the list, its mode and its checks on reading, that no value is in it or in a VM’s bindings, and that only a VM that uses the secret gets its binding and hosts, that two bindings of one name are cached apart, and use, a new value and the question that names the VMs before a delete. The CLI tests check every refusal before anything runs, the value on stdin and at a prompt and never in a command’s arguments, the list, --json, the binding and the variable a VM gets and the other VM doesn’t, and the delete (the tests behind it). End-to-end checks (network): a secret of yours bound to a host that the run’s company proxy fakes; the VM’s variable is its placeholder, the host gets the real value in the secret’s header, another host gets only the placeholder, and no log holds the value. Once the section has saved, bound and captured its secrets, and again at its end, no VM’s proxy password and none of the tokens, keys and logins the section used are in devvm’s run logs, its other logs or any VM’s proxy logs, as they are or in Basic credentials, and no VM’s proxy password is in Lima’s logs, ha.stderr.log and the serial logs.
data.keys-in-settings-files#Keys in settings:
devvm also takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of the agents’ settings files, which are ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, opencode’s .json, .jsonc and .toml files and pi’s settings.json, models.json and mcp.json. Those are JSON, JSONC or TOML, and devvm parses each file whole and writes the VM’s copy from what it parsed, so a JSONC file’s copy is JSON and a TOML file’s copy has no comments. devvm replaces these with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced (config_redacted):
Every value under a key that looks like a secret’s (*key*, *token*, *secret*, *password*, Authorization), and every string in a list or a table under such a key, but key bindings, such as opencode’s keybinds. A name you choose isn’t judged that way, so an MCP server, a plugin or a marketplace named secret-scanner or token-saver keeps its settings, while its own fields, such as its env or an apiKey, are judged as anywhere else. devvm knows the agents’ tables of names from their docs, and reads every agent’s settings files with all of them: Claude Code’s mcpServers, extraKnownMarketplaces, pluginConfigs, enabledPlugins and skillOverrides among them, Codex’s mcp_servers, model_providers, marketplaces, plugins, projects and hooks.state, opencode’s mcp, provider, agent and command, with their 2.x names, and pi’s providers and mcpServers. In most of those tables, only a table under a name escapes the check, so a string right under mcpServers with a secret-looking key is still replaced. In tables of settings, such as Claude Code’s enabledPlugins and skillOverrides, a table and a setting’s word, such as off or name-only, which has only lower-case letters and dashes, aren’t judged by their name either, while any other value is. A name that’s an env or headers table’s key, such as a server named env, still gets its values replaced. Any string that starts like a known key or token, such as sk-, ghp_ or eyJ, wherever it is. Every value in an env or headers table, whatever its name: env, environment, headers, http_headers, and Codex’s shell_environment_policy.set. A number of up to five digits, true and false stay, because they’re switches and ports. In Claude Code’s own env, the top-level one of settings.json, its configuration variables stay too: ANTHROPIC_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL, the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_MODEL_OPTION families, CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_*, MAX_* and *_TIMEOUT_MS. A variable whose name has KEY, TOKEN as a word, SECRET, PASS, AUTH, CREDENTIAL, COOKIE or HEADER in it is redacted all the same, such as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, and so is its value when it’s a URL. In a URL anywhere in the file, a string’s whole value or a part of other text, its user info and its secret-looking query values and path segments. In every list, the arguments that MCP servers’ arguments in ~/.claude.json lose: the value after a secret-named flag, such as --api-key X, the value of --token=X, and any that looks like a key. In any other string, such as a hook’s command or an argument that holds a header, each word that starts like a known key, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, quoted or not, when it has 16 or more characters, with a digit, +, / or = among them, which words don’t have, and isn’t a path. devvm replaces only those words, so curl -H 'x-api-key: sk-…' URL becomes curl -H 'x-api-key: devvm-redacted' URL, and a reference such as Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN} stays. MCP servers’ arguments, command and headersHelper in ~/.claude.json lose the same words. Values that only name where a secret is stay as they are. Those are an environment variable’s name (env_key = "OPENAI_API_KEY"), {env:X}, ${X} and a path. devvm refuses a file that doesn’t parse as its format, instead of copying any of it unread, so the VM doesn’t get that file (config_not_copied). The VM doesn’t get opencode’s other files in ~/.config/opencode either, such as a .env, because devvm can’t take secrets out of them, apart from its Markdown files, such as AGENTS.md, which hold instructions for the agent (config_not_copied). An MCP server or a provider that needs one of those keys in the VM has to get it another way.
data.learning-from-the-log#Learning from the: A VM that learns the hosts it needs is on the internet tier, and its state’s net section has learning.since, the time it started, which any tier set later clears. Its proxy runs as any internet VM’s does, so nothing else records what it reaches: devvm network lock and each launch’s reminder read the event log, both files. They take each tunnel, intercept and forward event since that time, one row for each host and port, its rule the exact one for that host, which always writes the port, counting its events and the first word of the User-Agent its requests sent most, which a CONNECT’s event records too, when that word is at most 32 of [A-Za-z0-9._/+-]. The proxy caps an event’s path and User-Agent at 512 bytes as it records them, and takes no request headers past 64 KiB, so a VM can’t bloat the log. An address that isn’t public, by the proxy’s one judge of that, and a host the policy doesn’t take are left out. Each host and port is judged once with the policies the VM would have on the allowlist tier, read as the proxy reads them, its built-in policies from the binary included, and with the proxy’s own decisions by its rules, so a host that the allowlist already allows, or that a rule denies, never shows. A host starts ticked when, on port 443, it’s one of devvm’s reviewed registry and vendor names, or under one, each with its reason beside it, and it isn’t risky. Nothing of the VM’s rules, secrets or own policy file makes a host tickable, so a host one lock added never makes its neighbours tick later, and a unit test checks that no name on the list is a shared-hosting domain or under one. The risky hosts, which are marked and start unticked, are an address, a punycode label, a host on its lists of paste and drop sites, storage, tunnels, webhook and OAST services, free hosting and chat endpoints, or under one of them, and the patterns of OAST domains, S3 and API Gateway. Past 30 hosts none starts ticked. The picker reads the terminal’s size, cuts each row to its width and a long name from the left, and scrolls in a window that keeps the same number of lines, so a redraw moves back over exactly what it drew. It refuses a terminal too short for a row and its two “more” lines (pick_too_small), takes a terminal of unknown size as 80 by 24, and on a read that fails, such as the EIO of a terminal that hung up, returns pick_failed and confirms nothing, while the end of the input confirms, as Enter does. The risky hosts are a section of their own under a heading, so their mark never depends on a row’s width, and so are the hosts that only events with "via": "dns" reached, between the others and the risky ones. The lock re-reads the VM’s state under the VM’s lock, in the one update of a VM’s state, before it adds a rule, and changes nothing when its context ended meanwhile or the VM no longer learns since the same time, and it says what it added only once the proxy has the new tier. devvm network learn and devvm group join each check the other’s change under the VM’s lock too, so a learning VM never ends up in a group. A launch’s reminder counts only while both files hold at most 2 MiB. devvm keeps no record of its own beside the log, so a log that rotated twice since the VM started learning has lost its first hosts. As a VM starts learning, devvm writes a learn event into its log with the proxy’s own writer, which devvm network log doesn’t show, and devvm network lock warns when that mark is gone.
data.links-through-the-proxy#Links through th:
A VM’s NO_PROXY names only the VM itself, so an HTTP client that uses the VM’s proxy settings sends a request for a link, such as http://db:5432/, to the proxy. A running VM can’t take a new environment, so the proxy carries those requests itself, and a link added while the VM runs works for every HTTP client at once.
devvm _links writes every link the VM has, carried or not, to a list, links.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, mode 600 in a folder of mode 700, whenever they change or the file is gone. Each entry has the link’s names (NAME and NAME.devvm.internal), its address and port in the VM, its target, and its socket on this machine. The list stays when devvm _links ends, and devvm removes it with the VM, so a link that isn’t carried, which has no socket, is refused rather than asked of the rules. devvm puts the list’s path in the proxy’s config as links, and its run folder, where the links’ sockets are, as link_sockets. The proxy checks the list for every request and reads it again when it has changed, as it does the policy files. A list it can’t read has no links, which its log says once. The list must be a regular file, not a symbolic link, that only you can write, and at most 1 MiB.
The proxy checks a request’s host against the list after the VM’s password and before any rule, as it does for devvm.proxy. It lowercases the host and drops one trailing dot, and then a host and port match only an entry that names them exactly, so DB.:5432 matches db:5432, while db..:5432, db.devvm:5432 and 127.77.0.1:5432 don’t. The request names a host and a port, never a socket. An entry counts only when its socket is the one that devvm _links names for this VM’s link at that address and port, in the run folder of devvm’s data folder, so the proxy never connects to another VM’s link or to any other socket, whatever the list holds. Its address must also be in 127.77.0.0/16. Any other name under devvm.internal is refused with 403 and logged as a refused block, whatever the rules allow, so the rules, the host’s resolver and a company proxy never see one. A host and port on no entry are otherwise the policy’s, as before.
For a match, the proxy’s broker finds the host and port in its own read of the list again, connects to that link’s socket and hands the connection to the child, so the child never reaches devvm’s run folder, where every VM’s link sockets are. It’s the same socket that the link’s remote forward reaches, so devvm _links checks the connection as it checks every other (each connection), and the 256-connection cap counts both. A CONNECT is tunneled as it is, with no SNI check and no interception, and an absolute-form request, such as GET http://db:5432/, goes to the socket in origin form, without Proxy-Authorization or Proxy-Connection, over a new connection for each request, which ends when the client gives up the request. A kept-alive connection to the proxy that asks for a link and then for another host has each request handled on its own. HTTPS in absolute form gets 400, because CONNECT carries it. The proxy puts no secret into a link’s connection, even when a secret’s hosts would match the link’s name, and its rules don’t apply, so devvm network deny db doesn’t stop the link db.
The proxy logs nothing for a link’s connection that it passes on, because devvm _links logs it as link, once. When the socket doesn’t answer, because the link was removed since the proxy read the list or devvm _links isn’t running, the proxy answers 502 and logs link_refused with the reason not carried. A socket whose backlog is full refuses a connection, so the proxy tries again for under a second.
data.log-files#Log files:
The proxy writes every decision (tunnel, intercept, forward, blocked, or nix-cache for a request to the shared Nix cache) as a JSON line in network.jsonl in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/. A line holds the time, the VM, the host and port, the method and path when the proxy sees them, the rule or the reason, and the names of the secrets it put in, never their values. A connection that transparent mode sent to the proxy, and each request on it, has "via": "dns", which devvm network log shows as , without proxy settings.
The proxy’s own lines, such as what it loaded and what failed upstream, go to proxy.log next to it. An upstream error stays there, because it can name addresses that the VM shouldn’t learn. So when a name doesn’t resolve, or a tunnel can’t connect, the VM’s 403, its http://devvm.proxy/blocked and the event log give only the reason. For a name, that’s this machine's DNS has no address for it when the DNS server says the name has none, with and names resolve without its search domain; use the full name, such as jenkins.corp.example.com after it for a name without a dot, this machine's DNS didn't answer in time; see proxy.log on the host when it doesn’t answer, and can't resolve it; see proxy.log on the host for any other failure. A rule allows the name already, so each of these blocks is marked refused, and neither the 403, nor http://devvm.proxy/blocked/new, nor devvm network log --blocked suggests a devvm network allow command for it. For a tunnel, it’s connect failed; see proxy.log on the host. The error itself, which can name this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy’s address and what it answered, goes to proxy.log alone. After a timeout or another failure that may pass, the proxy asks the DNS server once more before it blocks the name. When the client goes away while its name is still resolving, nothing was refused, so the event log and http://devvm.proxy/blocked record no block. The lookup still went out, though, and a name can carry data, so proxy.log names the host and port with the client went away while its name resolved, for at most 20 such lookups a minute, and then says that it stops until the minute is up. The broker’s own line for each of the child’s lookups and connections that failed, such as one to an address that no rule names, is held the same way, to 20 a minute. A name that resolves to an internal address gets the reason it resolves to an internal address; allow the address itself to reach it, which tells the VM that much and not the address (attack vectors). Only you can read the VM’s logs folder and its run folder, and devvm’s run logs never hold a VM’s password. The VM chose the hosts and paths, so devvm network log drops control characters in them.
The event log also holds the VM’s links’ connections, which devvm _links writes in the same format: link for a connection it carried, and link_refused, link_target_stopped or link_limit for one it refused, with the link’s name as the host and the target VM in target. An open VM’s event log holds its proxy’s events and its links’, but nothing it reached directly.
The proxy’s broker and its child are the only programs that write proxy.log, which is the output of both, each line’s prefix saying whether the broker or the child wrote it. Either may rotate it, through the file devvm opened for them and never by its path. It takes the file’s lock, checks the file’s size again, copies the file to proxy.log.1 and empties it, so the two rotate it once. The event log has the child and devvm _links as its writers.
The child writes the VM’s logs folder, so devvm, devvm _links, devvm network log, devvm network lock and the proxy never open the logs there through a link at their end, and they take only a regular file with one link that’s yours. A start that finds a link, a FIFO or another file’s hard link where a log should be removes that name, never what it leads to, and starts a new log there, and devvm network log refuses such a file without waiting on it. The proxy rotates each log before a line would take it past 10 MiB, and devvm _links writes the event log with the proxy’s own code, so it rotates the log by the same rule and a VM that runs for months keeps at most about 20 MiB of each. A line never spans two files, and lines from the proxy’s connections at the same time are written one after another, so a rotation loses none and splits none. Before each line, each writer checks that the file it has open is still network.jsonl, and when the other writer has rotated it, the writer opens the new network.jsonl and writes there, so its lines go on reaching the file that devvm network log --follow follows. Each writer takes the log’s size from the file, so it counts the other writer’s lines too. A writer rotates the log while it holds a lock on the file and checks the name again first, so when both reach the limit at once, only one renames the file and the other writes to the new one. A rotation renames network.jsonl to network.jsonl.1, which replaces the one that was there, and starts a new network.jsonl. proxy.log is also the proxy process’s output, where its last error goes when it stops, so the proxy copies it to proxy.log.1 and empties it instead, and that error still reaches the current file. The proxy takes proxy.log’s size from the file before each line, so what reached it as the processes’ output counts too, and its HTTP server’s errors, such as a handler’s panic, go through the child’s own lines rather than straight to that output. Every log file and its .1 file is readable only by you (mode 600).
devvm network log reads network.jsonl.1 before network.jsonl, so the history it shows and the blocks that devvm network log --blocked counts carry on across a rotation. devvm network log --follow reads the renamed file to its end and then follows the new one from its start. devvm rm deletes the .1 files with the rest of the VM’s logs.
data.logins-made-in-a-vm#Logins made in a VM:
A login that an agent makes inside a VM goes to devvm’s store too, and the VM gets only placeholders for it. The VM’s proxy does this at the agent’s OAuth token endpoint, the one request of a login whose reply holds its tokens. Codex and opencode both log in to OpenAI at auth.openai.com/oauth/token, whether the code comes from a browser’s redirect or from a device code typed into a browser elsewhere. For opencode 2, those are its Codex logins, the methods chatgpt-browser and chatgpt-headless. Its Sign in with ChatGPT, chatgpt-token-sharing, registers a client of its own and gets its tokens from auth.openai.com/api/accounts/oauth/token, then checks the id_token’s signature against OpenAI’s keys, which a placeholder can’t pass, so devvm doesn’t capture that endpoint, and its replies get 502, as the next paragraph says. Every VM’s proxy config lists that endpoint in captures, for Codex and for opencode, whatever the VM’s image holds, because a program in the VM could install either agent itself, and the proxy refuses that agent’s login rather than let its tokens reach the VM. The endpoint’s host joins the VM’s secrets.policy on port 443 only when its image has one of them, so that agent can log in on every tier. The proxy intercepts the host’s :443 tunnels as it does a bound host’s, with a certificate from the VM’s CA, and forwards every request to it. Only a request of the endpoint’s method to its path is captured, a POST for every OAuth token endpoint, and the proxy compares the path once it’s cleaned, each segment without its path parameters, a backslash read as a slash, and in any case, as a host that normalizes paths reads it, so a request for /oauth//token, /OAuth/Token/, /oauth/token;x or /x;/../oauth/token is captured too. A captured request goes to the endpoint’s own path whatever the VM’s spelling of it, and a POST goes without a query. An endpoint can be a GET instead, for a login that the agent polls for, whose request is its query. The proxy then refuses a query that isn’t a form or that names a field twice, which devvm and the endpoint could read apart, and a GET with a body, and the query goes on in a canonical form, its fields sorted, so the endpoint reads what devvm read. Any other successful reply from that host that names an access_token, a refresh_token or an id_token anywhere gets 502, whatever its type, so no other path there, such as another token endpoint’s, hands the VM a login, and so does one that names a field that the endpoint’s agent keeps its tokens in, such as accessToken. The proxy passes only a web page and its parts unread, which are HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and fonts, and it refuses a reply it can’t read for that, one that’s encoded or longer than 1 MiB, and an upgrade (101). No informational reply (1xx) from the host reaches the VM, because its headers could hold a cookie. When the host serves an API of its own beside the endpoint, which these checks would break, with its streamed, encoded or long replies, the endpoint names a path prefix that the endpoint is below, its guard, and the proxy checks only the replies below it. It checks the reply to any path that isn’t already clean too, such as one with path parameters, encoded characters or .., because the host could read it as below the guard where devvm doesn’t. The API’s replies elsewhere pass as they are, their informational replies, upgrades and encodings included. A path there that handed out tokens would hand them to the VM, and the VM’s requests to that API carry the agent’s real login, which the proxy puts in, so the agent’s section names the paths that could.
The proxy’s child judges a captured request by the VM’s rules as any other, reads its body whole, up to 64 KiB, with at most 64 KiB of headers, and hands it to the broker, which does the rest itself, so a login’s real tokens, a new login’s refresh token among them, and the store’s id_token never reach the child. The broker finds the endpoint in its own config by the request’s host, path and method, and refuses a request that matches none. It names the VM itself and sends the request to the endpoint’s host from its own config, on port 443, through the company proxy when there is one, trusting the system’s roots and your CAs, as a refresh does. It refuses one that names a field twice, or a JSON body with more after its object, which devvm and the endpoint could read apart. It drops the VM’s Accept-Encoding header from every request to the host, so each reply comes as it is, or as gzip that Go’s transport undoes. The request goes on unchanged, with two exceptions. After a code’s login, Codex exchanges the login’s id_token for an API key, with a token-exchange grant that asks for openai-api-key. The VM’s request carries the VM’s placeholder of the id_token, so the proxy puts the store’s id_token in its place, and only when the placeholder is that VM’s for the store’s current login. An error reply to that request reaches the VM with its OAuth error code alone, such as {"error":"invalid_grant"}, in case the endpoint’s message quotes the id_token. A refresh whose refresh token is the VM’s own, devvm-proxy-managed, or for opencode its access token’s placeholder, goes nowhere, and the VM gets the store’s login as placeholders again, because the host refreshes the login itself. devvm refuses any other grant than a code’s, a refresh’s or Codex’s exchange before the request leaves the host, because it couldn’t read the reply. Any other error reply reaches the VM as it is, with the few headers below, up to 1 MiB, and one that’s longer gets 502. The child reads at most 8 requests and replies to and from the host whole at once, and the broker runs at most 8 exchanges at once.
A successful reply never reaches the VM as it is. The broker reads it whole, up to 1 MiB, and saves its tokens in the store’s login file, in the agent’s own format, under the file’s lock, so a refresh on the host never runs at the same time. Codex’s goes in tokens of its auth.json, with the account from the id_token, and the exchange’s API key in OPENAI_API_KEY. opencode’s goes in the openai entry of its auth.json, as an OAuth login with its expiry in milliseconds and its account. A code’s reply replaces the login, and for Codex it also replaces the API key of the login before it. A refresh’s reply adds to the login, so the store keeps only the newest refresh token. Then devvm writes the VM’s bindings again, so its proxy puts the new login into requests at once. When that write fails, the login is still saved, the VM gets its reply, its proxy’s own log says why, and the VM’s next launch writes its bindings.
The VM gets a reply with placeholders in place of the tokens. Its access token’s placeholder is the one the store’s login binds, a JWT with the login’s account claims, its API key’s is the one its binding names, and its refresh token is devvm-proxy-managed, which is no token. The reply keeps only the token type and scope, says that the access token lasts until 2099, and holds nothing else of the endpoint’s reply, so the agent in the VM never refreshes the login itself. Its headers are only Content-Type, Cache-Control, Pragma and Date, so no cookie of the endpoint’s reaches the VM. A reply that’s too long, encoded in another way, or not a login devvm reads, such as one without an access token, gets 502 instead, logged as a refused block, and devvm saves nothing of it. An error reply holds no tokens, so it reaches the VM as it is, with the same headers alone. The event log gets a login event for each login saved, which names the agent, and the proxy’s own log says why a capture failed, without a value.
A VM captures a login only for an agent that its image has, because a capture replaces the login that every VM with that agent uses. So a login at OpenAI’s endpoint is the agent’s that the VM’s image has, of Codex and opencode, and in a VM with both, the request’s User-Agent says whose login it is. Each login format that captures logins names its endpoints and the starts of its agent’s User-Agent, and devvm lists every format’s endpoints in the registry’s order. opencode runs on Bun, so a request whose User-Agent starts with Bun/ or opencode/ is opencode’s, and any other is Codex’s, because Codex’s format names none. When the VM’s image has neither and its tier reaches the host, its request gets 502 before it leaves this machine, devvm saves nothing, and the proxy’s own log says why (login_capture_refused).
Claude Code logs in at platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token, and older releases at console.anthropic.com/v1/oauth/token, so every VM’s proxy config lists both in captures for Claude Code, and their hosts join the secrets.policy of a VM whose image has it. Anthropic doesn’t document these requests: devvm reads them from Claude Code 2.1’s bundle, so a release that changes them can break the capture, and the network end-to-end section drives the real Claude Code’s login against a fake endpoint to catch that. Claude Code sends JSON with its public client ID, 9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e, and PKCE, without a client secret. A code’s request holds grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id, code_verifier and state, and a refresh’s grant_type, refresh_token, client_id and scope. The reply holds access_token, refresh_token, expires_in and scope, with the account and the organization.
claude setup-token also sends a code’s request, with expires_in of a year added, and asks only for the user:inference scope, so devvm tells it apart by that field. Its reply’s access token, which must start with sk-ant-oat01-, is saved as the claude secret, and the VM gets the secret’s placeholder in its place, which claude setup-token then prints. Any other code’s login goes in the store’s .claude/.credentials.json, as Claude Code keeps it on Linux: claudeAiOauth with accessToken, refreshToken, expiresAt in Unix milliseconds and scopes. A new login whose scope lacks user:inference gets 502, because it can’t use the model. Such a login is an Anthropic Console login, which Claude Code would use to make an API key at api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/claude_cli/create_api_key with the access token the VM never gets. A login or a refresh whose scope has org:create_api_key also gets 502, whatever else it has, because the proxy puts the login into every request to api.anthropic.com, so a VM could make an API key with it and get the key itself. The access token must start with sk-ant-oat01- and hold no space, quote, backslash or control character, in a capture’s reply and in the host’s refresh’s. Only a VM whose image has Claude Code captures a Claude Code login, because a capture replaces the login every VM with Claude Code uses, so another VM’s gets 502 and devvm saves nothing. The VM’s reply holds sk-ant-oat01-devvm-proxy-managed-oauth- as its access token and devvm-proxy-managed as its refresh token, so the Claude login in the VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json, which Claude Code writes from it, holds no token. A refresh with devvm-proxy-managed goes nowhere, and the VM gets the placeholders again.
devvm keeps one Claude Code login. Saving the claude secret, captured or with devvm secret set claude, deletes the store’s .credentials.json, and capturing an OAuth login deletes the saved claude secret, so the newest login wins. Both happen under the lock of the store’s logins/claude folder, so two at once never leave devvm with neither login, and a saved token that can’t be deleted is a warning in the proxy’s log, as the login is saved. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s environment wins over both, as it does in Claude Code. A launch gives the VM CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN with its placeholder when there’s a token, and otherwise the VM’s copy of .credentials.json, with that placeholder, no refresh token and an expiry of 2099, never both. The copy’s claudeAiOauth replaces the VM’s own in its ~/.claude/.credentials.json, and the rest of that file, such as Claude Code’s logins to MCP servers, stays in the VM (Claude Code’s login). The VM’s bindings hold both logins’ placeholders, the claude secret’s and claude-oauth, whenever devvm keeps either login, and the store’s lookup gives each the login devvm keeps now. So a VM that started with the login that the newest replaced keeps working until its next launch gives it the new one. Both put their value into Authorization for api.anthropic.com. Claude Code lists the connectors of the claude.ai account at api.anthropic.com/v1/mcp_servers, which needs the login’s user:mcp_servers scope, and then reaches each connector at mcp-proxy.anthropic.com/v1/mcp/, with the login’s access token too. So the VM gets a third binding, claude-connectors, with claude-oauth’s placeholder, which puts the login into Authorization for mcp-proxy.anthropic.com below /v1/mcp/ alone. It’s a binding of its own because the proxy looks a value up by its binding’s name, and the store’s lookup gives claude-connectors only the OAuth login, never a token. While devvm keeps a token, saved or in its environment, that binding’s lookup fails and puts nothing in. A token in devvm’s environment isn’t checked for its scope, so it could hold the connectors’ scope, and that’s why a token goes to api.anthropic.com alone. Claude Code sends the anthropic-beta header that names oauth-2025-04-20 itself, so the proxy only swaps the placeholder.
The host refreshes the OAuth login when its access token is due, as Codex’s is: a JSON refresh to platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token with Claude Code’s client ID and the login’s scopes, through the company proxy the VM’s proxy goes through, written back under the file’s lock. When the refresh fails, the proxy’s log says to run devvm agent login claude again (agent_refresh_failed).
devvm agent login claude runs claude auth login --claudeai in the VM, or claude setup-token with --setup-token, without the VM’s CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Claude Code shows the address that comes back to platform.claude.com/oauth/code/callback, which shows the code to paste, so devvm forwards no port. The login runs on your terminal. When devvm’s input and output are both terminals, devvm gives the login its output and errors as the files they are, so Lima’s limactl shell gives it a terminal in the VM with ssh -t, as it does devvm’s shell. claude setup-token draws full-screen, so without that terminal it draws nothing and waits. Without a terminal, such as in a script or most end-to-end checks, the login gets pipes to devvm’s output, and with --setup-token devvm warns first (setup_token_no_terminal). Every agent’s login runs the same way, and either way, the login’s output goes to devvm’s output and never to the run log. On a terminal, ssh holds it in raw mode, so Ctrl-C goes to the login in the VM, which ends, and devvm then says that the login ended or saved nothing, rather than stopping as interrupted. A signal sent to devvm alone, such as kill, ends the login in the VM within 10 seconds, for a VM that ends its login when told, and until then ssh may hold the terminal in raw mode and write the VM’s output to it. devvm saves the terminal’s state before the login starts, and puts it back once the login and its end are done, or in a cleanup if the run ends first, so an ssh that a signal killed in raw mode doesn’t leave your terminal that way. Once the store has a new login of the kind asked for, which devvm tells by the logins’ checksums before and after, devvm sets the VM up again, so its environment and files hold the login devvm keeps now.
Cursor’s CLI logs in by polling: cursor-agent login shows cursor.com/loginDeepControl with a PKCE challenge and a uuid, and asks GET api2.cursor.sh/auth/poll?uuid=…&verifier=… until it answers 200 with accessToken and refreshToken, or gives up. Its endpoint in captures is that GET, as devvm’s format for Cursor’s login names it, checked against the CLI’s Linux package 2026.11.17-f532c45, read but not run). The store’s poll is the request’s query, as a form, with its uuid and its verifier, and nothing else. A pending login’s 404 passes as it is, and the success replaces the store’s ~/.config/cursor/auth.json with the two tokens. The VM gets accessToken as a JWT-shaped placeholder that lasts until 2099, because the CLI reads its exp, with the token’s sub, which the CLI names the repos it indexes by, and refreshToken as devvm-proxy-managed, with the team that the reply chose. A reply without both tokens, such as an xAI sign-in’s, is refused and saves nothing.
The login’s bindings put the token in Authorization only for the methods that the CLI’s package calls, each one by its whole path, /package.Service/Method: on api2.cursor.sh, those of its API’s services, such as DashboardService’s GetMe, never its methods that make API keys, and its traces at /v1/traces. On the agent’s hosts, api5.cursor.sh and *.api5.cursor.sh, which api2.cursor.sh’s server config names, and on api2.cursor.sh, where HTTP/1.1 takes it, only the agent’s stream, Run and RunSSE, and BidiAppend. On repo42.cursor.sh, its indexing, only its five indexing methods. The package checks the agent’s hosts only for being URLs and names none of them, so devvm takes every host below api5.cursor.sh, the one Cursor’s network docs name. On every one of those hosts the proxy refuses, with 403, any request below /auth/ other than the poll it captures, so no other login endpoint there hands the VM tokens. It also refuses the API’s other methods that make, show or exchange a credential, which are the ones that the package defines by name and, in any service, any method whose name has a key, a secret, a token, a login, a session, auth, a cookie, a password, a JWT, an invitation or a link in it. It refuses the methods that change the account in a way that outlasts the VM and acts outside it, as the proxy refuses GitHub’s keys and webhooks, though the CLI calls them on the host: installing, updating and removing plugins and marketplaces, applying, deleting, testing and changing automations, setting and deleting cloud agents’ environments, starting a cloud agent, and checking Bedrock keys, which devvm doesn’t keep. It refuses every method of the agent store’s service, AgentStoreService, and of any service of any package whose name starts with AgentStore, in any case, because the agent store isn’t the VM’s alone. The account’s CLIs on every machine and its cloud agents mount its user store read-write, its cloud agents load the skills in that store as instructions, every member of a team mounts the team’s store, and a path in a store can be shared with the team or the public. The store’s methods also take a token of its own, which MintAgentStoreToken makes and which a VM could send out and use from elsewhere until it expires, so the VM gets neither the token nor the store, and the CLI keeps its sessions in a local database without them. In the services that hold the account’s and its teams’ own state, DashboardService, AutomationsService and BackgroundComposerService, it refuses any method whose name starts with a verb that changes something, such as Set, Install, Start, Commit, Merge, Fork, Write or Pin, as those services define many more. Each verb was checked against every method of those services in the pinned release, and none matches a method the CLI calls. A verb such as Submit, whose SubmitFeedback the CLI calls, or Check or Generate, whose methods also only read, isn’t on the list, so GenerateGrokCollectionDescription, which drafts a description and only returns it, passes. Test matches one method that only reads, TestAutomationFilter, a dry run of an automation’s filter, and stays on the list for TestTeamCustomerTelemetryDestinationConnection, which has Cursor’s servers send a request with any headers to any address. It also refuses every path below /cloud-agent/, where cursor-agent worker, which makes the machine a worker for your cloud agents, gets its identity tokens. That worker connects to api2direct.cursor.sh, which has no bindings, with Host: api2.cursor.sh, so the proxy doesn’t open its tunnel and the login never goes in, and on the allowlist tier the host isn’t allowed either. The list of verbs is defence in depth, because the bindings put the login only into the methods the CLI calls. A changing method whose name starts with a verb that the list doesn’t have, such as ResolveReviewThread, whose verb also starts methods that only read, isn’t refused by the list, but it gets no login from the proxy either. So in a VM, Cursor’s CLI can’t do those, and you do them from Cursor on your machine. It also refuses any path it can’t read as those hosts do, with an escape, path parameters, a backslash, a byte past ASCII’s printable ones, a segment that ends in a dot or a space, or one that cleaning changes, and any request for a part of a reply (Range), as the proxy could then see no more than a part of a token.
api2.cursor.sh also serves the CLI’s API, whose agent replies stream, so the endpoint’s guard is /auth/, with the CLI’s own token fields, such as accessToken, sessionToken and apiKey, and any JWT added to what guard refuses there, and any cookie dropped. The bindings and those refusals are the real control. The rest is a defence in depth. On every one of Cursor’s hosts, the proxy drops the VM’s Accept-Encoding, Connect-Accept-Encoding and Grpc-Accept-Encoding from each request, so each reply comes as it is, or as gzip that Go’s transport undoes. A Connect or gRPC server still compresses a stream’s messages with gzip when the request’s are, as the CLI’s agent stream’s are. It drops any Set-Cookie from the reply, because the CLI keeps no cookies, and it refuses a reply that comes encoded anyway, by HTTP, or by Connect or gRPC in any way but a stream’s gzip, a part of a reply (206), and a reply with a JWT’s start in any header, its name or its value. A Connect or gRPC stream, which its Content-Type names, passes message by message: the proxy reads each message whole, at most 16 MiB as it comes and as it decompresses, gunzips it when its flag says it’s compressed, and checks it for a JWT’s start before any of it passes, as it came. Connect’s end of stream is JSON, and so is every message of a stream whose Content-Type says JSON, so the proxy checks those messages’ strings as they decode, escapes undone. It refuses gRPC-Web’s text variant, a whole body in base64, outright. A token in base64, such as in a -bin header or a protobuf bytes field of a JSON stream, isn’t found, as before. A message with a token, a flag the proxy doesn’t know, a compressed message that isn’t gzip, one over the limit or an envelope cut off ends the stream there, before that message. Every other reply’s body, of any status, length or type, passes through a reader that keeps the last 4 KiB that passed and fails at the read that would complete a JWT’s start, a header and the start of its claims, passing none of that read. The reply then ends there, so the token’s claims and signature never reach the VM, though its header may. At the body’s end the reader checks the reply’s trailers, which HTTP/2 and gRPC send after it, in the same way, and fails before the proxy sends them. Upgrades and informational replies are refused on every path, because the CLI uses neither. A token in another shape, such as an opaque one or one that the reply encodes in a way of its own, could still reach the VM. So could a presigned address that isn’t a JWT, such as one for cloud storage, in the reply of a method the login goes to, and the VM could then use it from anywhere until it expires. Refusing a path stops only the requests the VM makes, so a write that Cursor’s server makes on its own, as a side effect of a method the login goes to, such as one to the agent store, isn’t stopped either. devvm checked the CLI’s behaviour against one release of it by reading its code, not against Cursor’s servers. devvm doesn’t guard Cursor’s other hosts either: if one of them also answered /auth/poll, a VM could finish a login there and keep its tokens, though none is known to. Unauthenticated requests for /auth/poll with an unknown login got 404 Not found from api2.cursor.sh, as a pending login does, and a route-not-found 404 from agent.api5.cursor.sh.
The CLI never refreshes a login with its refresh token: only an API key is exchanged for a token, at /auth/exchange_user_api_key, which the proxy refuses, as devvm keeps no Cursor API key. So the host doesn’t refresh it either, and once the access token’s exp has passed, the lookup fails with agent_refresh_failed, which says to log in again.
Any VM with the agent can replace the store’s login, because the store keeps one login for each agent. A VM you don’t trust can log your other VMs in to an account of its choosing, and their requests then go to that account. Claude Code’s long-lived tokens have the same shape whatever asks for one, so a token that Claude Code mints in a VM for another use, such as claude /install-github-app’s, becomes devvm’s Claude Code login too, and what the VM gets is its placeholder, which works only through its proxy. A VM with Claude Code can also use the login, through its proxy, for whatever else its scopes allow at api.anthropic.com, beyond the model, such as reading the account’s profile, and devvm doesn’t limit the paths it goes to there. At mcp-proxy.anthropic.com, below /v1/mcp/, it can call any of the account’s claude.ai connectors with any method, as Claude Code can, and each connector acts in the service it connects to with the access you gave it, so the VM can read what you connected, such as mail or documents, and send through a connector that sends. A deny of mcp-proxy.anthropic.com in your rules, on every tier but open, keeps connectors from a VM (your claude.ai connectors). devvm doesn’t guard Anthropic’s other hosts either. If one of them also answered /v1/oauth/token, a VM could exchange its code there and keep the login’s tokens, though none is known to. On the open tier, a program in the VM can go around its proxy, and then it gets the login’s tokens itself and devvm saves nothing.
Tests: the unit tests check what goes out and what the VM gets, its headers included, which paths are captured and the one they go to, that tokens from another path are refused, that no 1xx reaches the VM, an answered request and a login saved without its bindings, that an error passes, with its code alone after a real value went out, and that what can’t be read is refused. They check each agent’s file, the VM’s placeholders and copies, the exchange, the VM’s own refresh, a Console login refused, setup-token’s request told apart, the host’s refresh of Claude Code’s login and repeated fields, and that the newest Claude Code login replaces the other, the environment’s token wins, both logins’ bindings get the login devvm keeps while the connectors’ binding gets the OAuth login alone, never a saved token or the environment’s, and the VM’s copy holds placeholders. They also check that every VM’s config has the endpoints on every tier, which agent a capture is, that a VM captures no login for an agent its image doesn’t have, that a capture writes the VM’s bindings, and that an agent’s login gets the terminal’s files only when devvm’s input and output are both terminals, and pipes otherwise (the tests behind it). End-to-end checks (network): a fake token endpoint behind a company proxy of the run’s own, which the VM reaches through its proxy; the store gets the real tokens and the API key, the VM’s replies hold placeholders and no refresh token, no log holds a value, and the VM’s next launch gets the login as placeholders. For Claude Code, the same company proxy fakes Claude’s token endpoint and Anthropic’s API: claude setup-token’s request makes the claude secret and the VM gets its placeholder, the real Claude Code’s claude auth login through devvm agent login claude saves the login in the store and leaves placeholders alone in the VM, devvm agent login claude --setup-token, run in a terminal of its own, shows Claude Code’s address, the API gets the store’s token for the VM’s placeholders, mcp-proxy.anthropic.com gets only placeholders while devvm keeps the claude secret, whichever of the two the VM sends, and a login that’s due makes the host refresh it at Claude’s endpoint through the company proxy, after which both the API and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com get the refreshed access token.
data.mcp-servers#MCP servers:
On each launch, devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json, ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude.json, into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json:
Each of your servers replaces the VM’s server of that name whole. devvm removes the servers it copied before that you no longer have. Servers added in the VM stay. The copy holds only your settings, onboarding and account state, and MCP servers. Everything else stays out, such as primaryApiKey, customApiKeyResponses and your per-project entries, which devvm agent import already leaves out of the store, and the VM keeps its own value of each. So the VM keeps its own per-project entries, such as trust and allowed tools, and yours never go in. Your account state, oauthAccount, keeps only the fields that Claude Code 2.1.319 writes there: its profile (accountUuid, emailAddress, organizationUuid, hasExtraUsageEnabled, billingType, accountCreatedAt, subscriptionCreatedAt, claudeCodeTrialEndsAt, claudeCodeTrialDurationDays, seatTier, planDisplayName, displayName, fullName and profileFetchedAt), its roles (organizationRole, workspaceRole and organizationName) and its rate-limit tiers (organizationType, organizationRateLimitTier and userRateLimitTier), each a plain value. Its ccOnboardingFlags stays as an empty object, because Claude Code fetches your profile again while that field is missing, and the flags in it stay out. devvm leaves every other field of oauthAccount out of the VM’s copy and warns you, naming each by its path, such as oauthAccount.zz (login_fields_withheld), and the unit test that plants unknown fields checks ~/.claude.json as it checks the other login files. If devvm can’t read the store’s .claude.json, it stops the VM’s setup (login_copy_failed).
On every tier, an HTTPS server’s headers become bindings for its host, which must be a DNS name on port 443. devvm replaces these with devvm-redacted: env values, plain-HTTP servers’ headers, user info and secret-looking values in URLs, and secret-named or key-shaped arguments. A server’s command and headersHelper, which are shell commands, lose the same words as other text in settings files (keys in settings files).
data.policy-files#Policy files:
On the allowlist tier, a VM’s proxy reads these policies, in this order, as one list. Allowlists describes what they allow and the rules they hold. The other tiers read fewer, and one list of devvm’s makes each tier’s:
internet: one built-in policy, network/internet.policy, which holds **:*, every host and address on any port, then secrets.policy, then your files below, whose denies alone apply. The proxy’s config lists those files in deny_policies, and the proxy drops their allows as it reads them, keeping their denies and a broken deny. ** lifts no floor, so internal addresses and this machine’s stay refused. none: the built-in policies of the VM’s agents, each agent’s shared-tools/.policy, such as shared-tools/claude.policy, and no other built-in one, then secrets.policy, then your files as denies alone. The VM’s links come before every rule, as on every tier. open: no policy at all. The proxy’s config has "open": true, which allows every host and address on every port, internal ones and this machine’s included, and a config with open and any policy is refused. The floor doesn’t apply, and a name that the host can’t resolve goes to the company proxy unjudged, as it does for a build. Policy Read for layers/base.policy (built in) every VM shared-tools/.policy (built in) each shared tool in the VM’s image layers/.policy (built in) each built-in layer in the VM’s image ~/.config/devvm/layers/.policy each of your layers in the VM’s image ~/.config/devvm/policy every VM ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//policy that VM only ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/secrets.policy every VM, which devvm writes with the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins and of its agents’ token endpoints The built-in policies are paths in devvm’s own files, which are built into the binary, and no copy of them is ever on disk. The same list holds both kinds for a VM: the built-in ones go in the proxy’s config as names in builtin_policies, and your files as paths in policies. The proxy reads the built-in ones from the binary once, as it starts, ahead of your files in the list, and never again, so only an upgrade of devvm changes them, and an upgrade starts every VM’s proxy again because the binary changed. A built-in policy that’s missing, or that holds a line that isn’t a rule, is a bug in devvm, so the proxy refuses to start rather than run with fewer rules than devvm meant, and devvm stops the VM as for any proxy that doesn’t start. A missing file of yours, on the other hand, has no rules. devvm network reads the built-in policies from the binary too, and it labels each with its name (# devvm: layers/base.policy, and "builtin" with --json) where it shows your files’ paths. Both lists are in the config that a proxy started with, so a change to either starts the proxy again.
The proxy, devvm network and devvm doctor read every policy with one parser, which returns each line that holds more than a comment, with its number and whether it’s a rule. A line is a rule only when one check takes it, which is exactly what devvm network allow and deny take (the packages). Each time the proxy reads a file, it logs each line that isn’t a rule, with its file, number and text, quoted, to its own log, proxy.log in the VM’s logs/ folder. It skips such a line, unless the line starts with !, which makes it a broken deny. A broken deny fails closed: while any of the VM’s policy files has one, the proxy’s policy denies every name and every address, and each request gets 403 and a refused block whose reason names the file and the line, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log suggests an allow rule. The VM’s links and the proxy’s own answers at devvm.proxy come before the rules, so they still work, and tunnels already open stay open, as they do for any new deny. Fixing the line lifts it at the proxy’s next read of the file, which is the next connection. The proxy reads a file again when its mtime, size or inode changes, or when it comes back after it was missing, whatever its mtime. It also reads a file again at every connection while its mtime is less than 2 seconds old, because some filesystems keep mtimes only to the second or two, so a second write within that time could leave the stamp as it was. A change of a file’s mode or owner alone, with chmod or chown, changes none of the three, so the proxy doesn’t see it until the file’s next write. The same goes for the bindings file and the links list, so one that you make readable or writable by others after the proxy read it keeps its last contents until it changes, and the proxy refuses it then. A file the proxy refused is read again at the next connection, so fixing its mode works at once. An error other than a missing file keeps its last rules and its broken deny, which the proxy’s log says once. The proxy, devvm network and devvm doctor read a policy file only when it’s a regular file, through a symbolic link if it’s one, of at most 1 MiB, through devvm’s one reader of files a VM can write or swap. They open it without blocking and check the file they opened, so a FIFO or a link to /dev/zero in a policy file’s place can’t hang them, and each refuses it with a named error, one for a file that isn’t regular and one for a file that’s too long. A leading byte-order mark isn’t part of the first line. devvm warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with policy_broken_deny for a broken deny and policy_not_rule for the others. A launch of a confined VM warns about the VM’s policy files as it readies the VM’s proxy, devvm network allow, deny and rm about the file they change, and devvm doctor about the files you edit: ~/.config/devvm/policy, your layers’ and each VM’s own. devvm network also marks the line, and --json lists it in not_rules. A unit test parses every policy file that devvm ships and fails on any line that isn’t a rule.
Each change that devvm network allow, deny or rm makes rewrites the file whole, through a link if the file is one, so a proxy never reads half of it.
data.quiet-hosts#Quiet hosts: A built-in policy can hold quiet HOST or quiet HOST:PORT lines, for one exact host name, never *.name or **, so a quiet line can’t hide a whole domain’s blocks (quiet hosts). The policy parser returns such a line as one that isn’t a rule, marked as a quiet line, so the check of a rule and devvm network allow never take one. The proxy’s read of its built-in policies keeps it as a rule marked quiet, which allows and denies nothing, so the proxy leaves it out of the rules a decision reads. It matches a host and port against the built-in quiet rules alone, as it matches any rule, but only while no rule covers that host and port, whether an allow, a deny or one that narrows, and never on an open policy or one with a broken deny. The proxy drops a quiet line in any other file and logs it, and devvm warns about it with policy_quiet_not_own. A quiet host is blocked as any host no rule allows, and an allow of yours still lifts it. The proxy marks a block’s event quiet only when its reason is the one for a host no rule allows, it isn’t refused whatever the rules say, and a quiet rule matches, for the proxy’s path and the transparent one alike, so a block for another reason, such as an internal address, a failed connection or a deny of yours, keeps its notice. A quiet event is logged with "quiet": true but never counted among the blocks that /blocked and /blocked/new serve, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm-why sees it, and the proxy’s block page writes no allow command for it. devvm network log gives it no allow command and a row of its own apart from the same host’s other blocks, and ends its line , quiet, and devvm network lock leaves it out of what it offers, judging it with the proxy’s own match of quiet rules. devvm network marks a built-in quiet line, its --json lists the hosts in quiet, and the agents’ table on the coding agents page leaves quiet lines out. Each quiet line in devvm’s files has a comment that names the host’s use and the maker’s page that documents it.
data.requests-by-method-and-path#Requests by:
A rule for a host name or *.name can have its methods and then its path after it, each after spaces or tabs, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/ (rules by method and path). The policy parser reads such a line as one rule, whose text is its canonical form: the host as before, the methods in capitals in the order of the proxy’s list of methods, and the path as written, joined by one space. That’s what devvm network allow, deny and rm write from --method and --path, and what they compare a line by, so HEAD,get and GET,HEAD are the same rule. A method outside that list, CONNECT among them, an address, a CIDR or ** with methods or a path, and a path that isn’t a pattern aren’t rules, so a typo in a deny is a broken deny, which denies everything, rather than a deny of nothing.
The proxy judges a host in two steps. For the connection, CONNECT host:port or an absolute-form request, a deny that narrows doesn’t refuse the host, and an allow that narrows allows it, so a host that only rules by method and path allow is reached. Its requests are then judged one by one when a rule that narrows covers the host and either it’s a deny or no rule allows the whole host. Both come from one read of the policy files, the rules that cover the host, so a file that changes between the two can’t give the connection one rule’s verdict and another’s way through. Such a host’s CONNECT on a port the proxy intercepts, :443, is intercepted with the VM’s CA, as a bound host’s is, and on any other port, or without a CA, it’s refused with 403, logged as a refused block, because the proxy can’t see the requests in it. An absolute-form request, plain HTTP on any port or https://, is judged before it’s forwarded.
Inside an intercepted tunnel, the proxy’s own HTTP server reads each request, HTTP/1.1 kept alive or HTTP/2, and calls one handler for each, which checks that the request names the host (421 otherwise), then judges it with the rules as they are then, then forwards it. So every request on a connection is judged, not just the first, and a rule added or removed applies from the tunnel’s next request. A WebSocket is judged by its upgrade request, after which the proxy passes its bytes as they are, so for a host that rules narrow, an Upgrade to any other protocol, such as h2c, whose requests would pass the same way, is refused, and so is a CONNECT inside the tunnel. A refused request gets 403, and the event log gets a blocked event with its method and path. A deny’s refusal is marked refused, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log --blocked suggests an allow, and a request that no allow covers suggests the allow of the whole host. An allowed request’s forward event names the rule that allowed it, as its rule.
The proxy’s judge of a request takes the rules that cover the host and port in order. A whole deny refuses, then a CONNECT and an upgrade to a protocol other than WebSocket are refused when a rule narrows the host, and so is, when a rule narrows it by method, a method that the request names besides its own that isn’t exactly one of the proxy’s methods, then each deny that narrows refuses what it matches, and then the first allow that matches lets the request through. One matcher judges both rules and secrets’ bindings (the packages):
A path in plain form: the path as the proxy forwards it starts with /, has nothing percent-encoded, no \ or ;, and is clean, with no . or .. segment and no doubled slash. The query is no part of it. These are the forms that servers read apart, by decoding an encoded slash or dot, reading \ as /, dropping ; and what follows it, or not cleaning the path, so a request in any of them could reach a path that the proxy didn’t judge. A pattern: its segments are split at /, * matches any run of characters within one, and ** as a whole segment matches one segment or more. A pattern’s last / stands for /**, so /api/ is /api/**, which is a binding’s path below which the value goes in. A path’s one trailing / may be there or not. Matching is a table over the pattern’s and the path’s segments, linear in the path for each of the pattern’s at most 32 segments, so a VM’s long path can’t make it slow. The methods a request names: besides its own, each value of a header that some servers take the method from, X-HTTP-Method or any with method-override in its name, read in any case and with _ for -, as Rack’s and CGI’s servers turn - into _, and each _method parameter of the query, in any case of its name. A value that isn’t exactly one of the proxy’s methods, trimmed, is odd: a list such as DELETE, GET, which servers read apart, lower case or nothing. The proxy reads no body, so a form’s _method field is the POST’s. An allow, and a binding, match strictly: the request’s method, and every method it names besides, as written, must be among the rule’s methods, with none odd, and its path must be plain and match the pattern in its own case. A request the matcher can’t judge alike for every server is never allowed by a rule with a path. A deny matches broadly: the method, or any method the request names besides, every word of a list among them, in any case, or any odd one; and the path in any case, any path that isn’t plain, the path above a pattern that ends with / or /**, the path with its last segment cut at its first ., which frameworks that take a format from a suffix (Rails, Spring) route to the same handler, and the path with each segment’s trailing dots dropped, as servers that drop a trailing dot read it. A query servers read apart: while a rule narrows the host by method, a query with a ;, which some servers split pairs at and Go’s query parser skips the pair around, or with an escape that doesn’t decode, which Go’s parser drops, is odd, so a _method hidden in it can’t pass. In a user’s terms, the methods a request names work like this. Some servers take a request’s method from a header or a parameter instead of the request itself, so the proxy judges a request by every method it names. It reads the X-HTTP-Method-Override and X-HTTP-Method headers and every header with method-override in its name, in any case and with _ for -, as some servers read X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE, and the _method parameter of the query. While a rule by method covers a host, a request there whose header or parameter isn’t exactly one of those methods in capitals, such as DELETE, GET, delete or nothing at all, is refused, because servers could read it either way, and so is a request whose query has a ; in it, which some servers split the query at, or a query with an escape that doesn’t decode. Otherwise an allow needs the request’s own method and every one it names to be among its methods, so an allow of GET refuses a GET that says it’s a DELETE, and a deny refuses a request that names any of its methods. The proxy doesn’t read a request’s body, so a _method field in a form that a POST sends, which some frameworks take as the method, is judged as the POST it is: a deny of POST refuses it, and an allow of POST lets it through whatever the field says.
Paths work like this. Servers don’t all read a request’s path alike, so a rule’s path matches only a path that every server reads the same way: one with nothing percent-encoded, no \ or ;, no . or .. part and no doubled slash. An allow matches exactly, its method and its path in their own case, and no path in any other form. A deny matches broadly instead. It matches in any case and every path that isn’t in that plain form, a deny whose path ends with / also matches the path above it, a path’s last segment matches with what follows its first . cut off too, as frameworks that take a format from a suffix route /admin.json to /admin, and every segment matches with its trailing dots dropped, as some servers drop them, so a deny of /config.json refuses /config.json..
Judging a request costs the policy files’ stat, which every connection already has, and a scan of the host’s rules. Decrypting the tunnel costs a TLS handshake with a certificate from the VM’s CA, which the proxy keeps for the 1024 hosts it used most recently, and another to the host, so the proxy decrypts only the hosts whose rules need it: a host that a whole allow covers, with no deny that narrows, stays a tunnel that the proxy doesn’t read.
data.saving-the-copies-back#Saving the copies: devvm agent save reads the VM’s copies back, and they hold devvm-redacted and the proxy’s placeholders where devvm’s agent store has your secrets (saving a VM’s settings). devvm parses the VM’s file whole, and when it holds a placeholder, devvm also makes the copy the VM got from the store’s file again: the same redaction for a settings file, and for ~/.claude.json the copy with the VM’s own salted placeholders. Each placeholder gets the store’s value at the same path, but only when the copy had the same placeholder there, and when the table the placeholder is in and the table above that one, below the file’s top level, are the same as in the copy. Those tables say where the secret goes, such as an MCP server’s url beside its headers, a provider’s baseURL beside its apiKey and an env table’s base URL beside its key, so a VM can’t keep a placeholder and point it at another host. A placeholder that fails the check leaves the whole file out of the save (agent_save_placeholder), and so does a placeholder in a file without a format devvm parses, such as a skill. A file with placeholders put back is written as devvm writes the VM’s copies, as JSON or as TOML without comments, and a file without placeholders is saved as the VM has it.
data.secrets#Secrets: Secrets lists each secret with its hosts and header. This section describes where devvm keeps them and how the proxy puts them into requests.
data.starting-a-vm-on-its-tier#Starting a VM:
A VM’s state records its tier in its net section, as "tier": open, internet, allowlist or none (network tiers). A section without a tier reads as allowlist, and one with a tier devvm doesn’t know can’t be read, so devvm refuses the VM rather than take it as open. The tier decides the VM’s confinement: on every tier but open, the VM starts confined to its proxy, and an open VM starts on its backend’s own network with its proxy’s port and password in its confinement, so its guest’s proxy settings name the proxy all the same (how a backend plugs in). A running VM keeps the confinement it started with until its next start.
When devvm starts a VM on a confined tier, it takes these steps in order:
It readies the VM’s own CA and the next one (the VM’s CA), and on macOS it keeps them out of Time Machine. It writes the VM’s secrets as the VM’s proxy sees them. It starts the VM’s proxy on a free port on the host’s loopback, and waits for the proxy to say it’s listening. It starts the VM confined, with the VM’s proxy settings pointing at the proxy. It runs the self-check before the VM’s setup and before its shell. It sets the VM up, as the VM’s setup describes. The setup puts the VM’s CA and the next one in the VM, points the tools that don’t read the environment at the proxy, and writes the VM’s placeholders and its agents’ logins and settings with your keys taken out. An open VM’s start takes the same steps, but it starts the VM unconfined and runs the open self-check. Its proxy has the VM’s CAs and its secrets as any VM’s does, and applies no rules. Its setup installs both CAs in the VM, points the same tools at the proxy, and writes the same placeholders and copies of the agents’ logins and settings, so an open VM holds no real secret either. The VM reaches its proxy directly, through the HTTPS_PROXY that names it (Lima), and a request that goes around the proxy carries only the placeholder.
So an open VM runs on its backend’s own network, and it reaches this machine and your LAN directly, as a VM without a proxy would. Its environment names its proxy all the same (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms), and the proxy reaches every host and address for it, this machine’s localhost and your LAN included, so a tool behaves the same through the proxy as it does directly. Its NO_PROXY names the VM itself and this machine as the VM reaches it, host.lima.internal, so requests to those go directly. Every launch checks that an open VM’s proxy is set in the VM and answers it, and when it doesn’t, devvm warns you and opens the VM all the same. An open VM gets a placeholder for each secret it may use, as every VM does, and only its proxy puts the real value in, so a request that goes around the proxy, directly from the VM, carries only the placeholder, and the secret’s host refuses it.
data.the-childs-sandbox#The child’s sandbox:
The child makes no connection of its own, on either system. It asks its broker to look up each name the floor judges, and to open each connection, to an address the child’s floor kept or to a company proxy, and the broker hands it the connection, as it hands it a link’s. The broker connects to an address only once its own read of the VM’s policy files and of this machine’s addresses allows it, as the floor does, and it looks at the policy files at each connection, so a rule such as devvm network allow 127.0.0.1:5432 applies from the next connection. So even a child that a VM took over reaches this machine’s loopback, its own addresses and the private and link-local ranges only where a rule names the address, as the VM does. It still reaches the internet, a host on this machine’s network whose address is public, such as a printer’s global IPv6 address, and whatever a company proxy reaches, which it speaks to with its password, this machine’s loopback included when the company proxy runs here. The broker connects to the company proxy at the address in its own config, so one on this machine’s loopback, such as a VPN client’s, works. It looks names up through this machine’s resolver, whatever its address, so the child sends no DNS. The broker carries at most 256 lookups and 1024 connections at once for the child, each lookup within 20 seconds and each connection within 15, and the child cancels one whose request has gone. The child also holds at most 8448 open files, a limit it sets on itself before it’s confined, so it can’t keep every connection the broker hands it (the design note).
On macOS, the broker starts its child through /usr/bin/sandbox-exec, with a Seatbelt profile that denies everything the child doesn’t need, so the child is confined from its first instruction, before it reads a byte of the VM’s. The broker writes the profile for each start from what the child needs, and passes it to sandbox-exec as an argument, so it’s never a file on disk. It runs devvm’s binary by its real path, with its links resolved, because Seatbelt matches real paths. The profile allows the child the following, and nothing else:
devvm’s binary: running it and reading it, for its SHA-256, and the metadata of its folder, which CoreFoundation looks at for the program’s bundle before Security checks a certificate.
