The system: the rules that the system’s own dyld-support.sb profile gives a program to start, reading the system’s libraries in /usr/lib and /System/Library and the time zone, the metadata of the links /etc, /var and /tmp, through which those paths lead, and reading sysctl, which the floor reads the host’s addresses with, except the process table’s kern.proc names. Its folders: reading and writing in the VM’s logs folder and the shared Nix cache, where it can make only regular files, and change their mode and times, but not their flags, ACLs, owner, set-id bits or extended attributes, and can remove no folder. It makes no hard link anywhere. The broker makes the cache’s folders before the child starts, as the child can’t make a folder. A build’s child gets its own logs/ folder. The files that change: the metadata of your policy files, the VM’s bindings and the links’ list, which the child looks at with stat alone, and of their targets when they’re links, and of every link on the way to any of those files or folders. Checking certificates: the mach services com.apple.trustd and com.apple.trustd.agent, which check certificates for Go’s crypto/x509. The network: accepting on the listener the broker gave it, and reading and writing the connections it accepted and those the broker handed it, which need no rule of their own. The profile allows no network out at all, so the child connects nowhere and sends no datagram itself, because Seatbelt checks every connect and every send with an address. Signals and processes: signals to itself, and looking only at itself. So the child can’t read your home folder or devvm’s other folders, its run folder, its config and the other VMs’ among them, and can’t reach the Keychain, whose service com.apple.SecurityServer the profile never allows, nor any unix socket, such as an ssh master’s control socket or an SSH agent’s. It can’t bind a port, fork or run a program, signal another process, list the processes, or read another process’s path, details or arguments (process-info, kern.proc). macOS answers a process’s arguments (kern.procargs2) to a sandboxed process only within its own process group, and the child runs alone in a session of its own, so it can read only its own. A policy file that’s a link to another file is looked at where it pointed as the proxy started, and when it points elsewhere later, the child’s stat is refused, so the child asks the broker for the file at every request instead, which reads it as before.
On Linux, the child confines itself once it has opened its logs and the Nix cache and loaded the system’s roots and its time zone. It does so before it says it’s ready, so before it reads a byte of the VM’s. It sets no_new_privs on every thread, restricts every thread with Landlock, and installs a seccomp filter on every thread. Landlock and prctl change only the thread that calls them, and Go’s runtime runs the child on several threads, so the child makes each call on every thread at once through Go’s call for all of a process’s threads, which works only in a binary without cgo, as devvm’s releases are. From Landlock’s ABI 8 it restricts every thread in one call instead (LANDLOCK_RESTRICT_SELF_TSYNC), and the filter goes on every thread in one call (SECCOMP_FILTER_FLAG_TSYNC). Landlock holds the child to these files, whatever their permissions:
Its folders: the VM’s logs folder, and for a VM with the nix layer the shared Nix cache, where it reads, writes, lists, makes, deletes, renames and empties regular files, from Landlock’s ABI 2, which lets the cache rename a file from its top folder into nar/. It makes no folder, link, FIFO, socket or device there, and nothing in them runs. Nothing else: it can’t read, write or list any other file, your home folder, devvm’s folders and /etc included, or run a program. Landlock doesn’t restrict stat, so the child still looks at the changing files, and learns whether a file of yours exists, its size and when it changed, but not what it holds. Landlock also doesn’t restrict a file’s mode, owner, extended attributes or times, or, below ABI 3, a truncation by path, so the seccomp filter refuses those. From ABI 4 Landlock also refuses the child a TCP port’s bind and every TCP connection, from ABI 6 a signal to any process outside it and a connection to an abstract unix socket that isn’t its own, from ABI 9 a connection to a named unix socket, and from ABI 10 every UDP bind and datagram. On a kernel at ABI 6 or 7 without Landlock’s fix for signals between a process’s threads, the child leaves its signals unscoped, because Go’s runtime signals each of its threads to restrict itself in turn, and those signals would be refused and hang the start. Landlock’s network rules match only ports, so they can’t refuse an address alone, and the seccomp filter refuses the child every connection of its own on every kernel.
The seccomp filter refuses the child, with EPERM:
Sockets: every socket but a netlink route socket (AF_NETLINK with NETLINK_ROUTE), which the floor reads the host’s addresses through and which reaches the kernel alone, a socketpair, connect, listen, and sendto, sendmsg and sendmmsg with MSG_FASTOPEN, which would connect a TCP socket as it sends, such as its listener once a shutdown has closed it. So the child has no socket of its own to connect, and can’t connect one it holds again. Below Landlock’s ABI 9, the filter is also what keeps it from the ssh masters’ control sockets, docker.sock and your SSH agent’s socket. Calls around the filter: the three io_uring calls, whose operations wouldn’t pass it. Other processes: ptrace, process_vm_readv, process_vm_writev and pidfd_getfd, which reach another process’s memory or descriptors, and what changes how another process runs, which Landlock’s scope of signals doesn’t cover: prlimit64 other than on the child itself, as a limit such as RLIMIT_CPU can kill a process, setpriority, ioprio_set, sched_setaffinity, sched_setscheduler, sched_setparam and sched_setattr. Watching files: inotify_init, inotify_init1, inotify_add_watch, fanotify_init and fanotify_mark, which would tell it the names of files outside its folders as they change. A file’s metadata by its path: chmod, fchmodat and fchmodat2, chown, lchown and fchownat, the extended attributes’ setxattr, lsetxattr, removexattr, lremovexattr, setxattrat and removexattrat, truncate, and the times’ utime, utimes, futimesat, and utimensat with a path. The calls on a descriptor that the child opened, which Landlock checked as it opened it, stay: fchmod, fchown, ftruncate and utimensat on a descriptor, which its logs and the Nix cache use. The kernel’s keyrings: add_key, request_key and keyctl. What it never does: running a program (execve, execveat), a process of its own (fork and vfork, and clone for anything but a thread), a namespace (unshare, setns, and clone with a namespace’s flag), bpf, userfaultfd and perf_event_open. clone3 gets ENOSYS, as a kernel without it answers, because its flags are behind a pointer that the filter can’t read, so a caller falls back to clone, whose flags it can. It kills the child for a system call of any architecture but its own, and on amd64 for the x32 numbers, so the 32-bit calls, socketcall among them, can’t get around it. The child needs none of these, because the broker looks up its names, the listener and the socket to the broker were open before, every connection it opens comes from the broker, and Go’s runtime starts its threads with clone and the thread’s flag. The broker sets itself undumpable (PR_SET_DUMPABLE), so on a kernel without Landlock, where nothing else would, the child can’t read the broker’s memory or open its descriptors through /proc. Other processes of yours stay readable through /proc there, unless the kernel’s Yama restricts ptrace, as Ubuntu’s does. Once confined, the child checks that it lists its own folders, that it fails to list / and to read /etc/hosts with Landlock, and that it fails to make a unix or an IPv4 socket, to connect, to listen and to send with MSG_FASTOPEN with the filter. It also reads the host’s own addresses again, through a netlink socket, and a read that fails or finds none fails the start, because the floor would refuse none of them without it. The confinement takes at most 2 seconds, within the broker’s 4, and a confinement or a check that fails fails the start, which devvm reports as the proxy failing to start (proxy_start_failed). A kernel without Landlock, below ABI 2, or without seccomp filters, leaves that part out, and the child runs with what there is, which it says.
On both systems, the child checks that what confines its files holds before it says it’s ready. It opens its broker’s config, the file named in its arguments, which the profile or Landlock must refuse it, and closes it unread if it opens. Its ready message says how it’s confined, and the broker writes that to run/proxy.confined as one line of a level, full, partial or none, then what confines it and, for a child that isn’t fully confined, why, from a fixed set of words, so devvm never prints what a child wrote:
run/proxy.confined What full seatbelt the profile confines the child, and its check held none seatbelt check-failed the child ran under the profile, but could open its broker’s config none sandbox-exec-missing there’s no /usr/bin/sandbox-exec, so the broker started the child unconfined none sandbox-exec-failed sandbox-exec failed to start the child under its profile, so the broker started it again unconfined none unsupported devvm doesn’t confine the child on this system, or this devvm, built with cgo as the tests’ race detector is, can’t reach its threads full landlock on Linux, Landlock from ABI 6 with its signals scoped, and the seccomp filter, confine the child, and its check held. Below ABI 9 the filter alone refuses it a unix socket, and below ABI 10 a UDP socket partial landlock landlock-signals this kernel’s Landlock is ABI 4 or 5, or 6 or 7 without its fix for signals between threads, so the child can also signal your other processes partial landlock landlock-below-abi4 this kernel’s Landlock is ABI 2 or 3, which refuses no TCP of the child’s, though the filter refuses it every socket and connection of its own partial landlock no-seccomp this kernel has no seccomp filters, so only Landlock confines the child, which below ABI 4 can connect anywhere itself, this machine’s loopback included partial seccomp no-landlock this kernel has no Landlock, or only ABI 1, so only the filter confines the child, which can read and write your files none no-landlock-or-seccomp this kernel has neither, so the child runs with the broker’s access, and can connect anywhere itself none landlock check-failed the child confined itself, but could open its broker’s config The broker starts the child again unconfined only when sandbox-exec failed before devvm’s code ran. That’s when the child had already ended before it answered, either with sandbox-exec’s own exit status, 65 for a profile it refused or 71 for a program it couldn’t run, or killed by SIGABRT or SIGKILL, as the system kills a program that a profile refuses what it needs to load. The broker decides that before it stops the child itself, so a child that its own stop ended never counts. Nothing of a VM’s can cause those failures, so the second start, which has what’s left of the broker’s 4 seconds, never trades a confined child for an unconfined one at a VM’s request. A program of yours that sent the child one of those signals in that moment could, and the proxy’s log and devvm doctor then say the child runs unconfined. A child that answers failed, ends any other way, or doesn’t answer in time fails the start, as it would unconfined, because what it read by then could be a VM’s. A ready that names a sandbox the broker didn’t start the child under, or another than the one it did, breaks the protocol’s rules, so a child can’t claim more than it was given. The broker writes a warning in proxy.log for each child that isn’t fully confined, and devvm doctor warns of each running VM whose proxy says so (the proxy runs without a sandbox). A proxy that hasn’t written run/proxy.confined yet, such as one still starting or one that a devvm from before the broker started, gets no warning.
data.the-proxy#The proxy:
One proxy runs for each VM. It runs on the host as devvm _proxy, a hidden command, and listens on a loopback port. The VM reaches nothing else over its network, so every connection the VM makes goes through its proxy.
The proxy is two processes. devvm _proxy, the broker, does what only the host should do. It looks up each bound value, sends the token requests of logins made in the VM, connects to the VM’s links’ sockets, reads the files that change while the proxy runs, relays the VM’s SSH agent, follows the VM’s lifeline, and looks up the names and opens the connections that the child asks for. Its child, devvm _proxy-child, does everything this section describes with the VM’s requests, and asks the broker over a socketpair for each of those, by something the broker finds in its own config, so a child that a VM took over can’t make the broker act for another VM, another secret or another file. No byte of the VM’s requests crosses that socket, because the broker hands the child each connection, so the broker adds a hop to opening a connection but none to what it carries. On Linux, before it reads a byte of the VM’s, the child confines itself with Landlock and a seccomp filter to its logs and the Nix cache, with no connection of its own, no unix socket and no program to run, and on macOS a Seatbelt profile does the same (the child’s sandbox). So a child that a VM took over can’t read your files, reach an ssh master’s socket or connect to this machine’s loopback. Processes has what each holds, reads and writes, and the proxy’s broker has the protocol and its threat check. The one other way out of the VM is the links you add to it, which this machine carries over ssh to the ports your other VMs publish, so they don’t use the VM’s network. The proxy is a second entrance to those links, for the VM’s HTTP clients (links through the proxy).
Other programs on the host can also reach that port, so the port alone doesn’t identify the VM. Every request must carry the VM’s password in Proxy-Authorization, with the user devvm, or it gets 407. Each VM has its own random password in its proxy settings. The proxy reads the password from its config, a file only you can read, never from its arguments, which other users can see, and it refuses to start without one (devvm _proxy). The VM’s settings also get the password through files (Lima).
For each connection, the proxy does the following:
It sends a request for one of the VM’s own links to that link before any rule, and passes its bytes on as they are (links through the proxy). It checks CONNECT host:port and absolute-form requests (GET http://host/…) against the VM’s policy files, and then tunnels or forwards the allowed ones untouched. It takes only host names, made of letters, digits, -, _ and ., and addresses. It lowercases a name and drops one trailing dot, and the name that’s left may have no empty label, so evil.test.., evil..test and .evil.test get 400 too, because a company proxy that drops trailing dots would otherwise reach a host that a deny of evil.test never matched. It lowercases only ASCII, so a name with any other character keeps that character and gets 400, because Unicode’s case folding turns some letters into ASCII ones, such as the Kelvin sign into k, so the host it judged wouldn’t be the one the VM named. An address is bare, or an IPv6 address in one pair of brackets, so [evil.com]:443, [1.2.3.4]:443 and a stray bracket get 400 too. An IPv6 address with a zone, such as [fe80::1%en0], gets 400, and so does one with an empty zone. An address keeps its trailing dot, because the dot can only be its zone’s, and dropping it would leave an empty zone, which Go’s address parser reads as no address but a resolver may read as the address alone. Anything else gets 400 before the policy or the log sees it. Everything else that reads a host reads it in the same form: a rule’s host, a secret’s hosts, NO_PROXY, devvm network lock’s risks and ticks, a secret’s --host, an MCP server’s host, --from’s registry and a partial clone’s remotes. It refuses devvm.proxy, its own domain, and any name under it, in a CONNECT and as a host, with 403, before the links, the policy or a company proxy see the name, on every tier. Only a request in absolute form for http://devvm.proxy/ itself reaches its endpoints, and CONNECT transparent.devvm.proxy:PORT is transparent mode’s. It refuses the stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, with a reason that says the tool resolved the name itself. It resolves names itself and dials the addresses it checked, through its broker, which checks each address again before it connects (the child’s sandbox). It looks each name up absolute, with a trailing dot, so this machine’s resolver never adds its DNS search domain, which macOS takes from the network’s settings and Linux from /etc/resolv.conf’s search. Otherwise, with api.corp.example.com denied and ** allowing the rest, CONNECT api:443 would reach api.corp.example.com, a name that no rule judged, and so would api.eu reach api.eu.corp.example.com when api.eu itself has no address. It refuses the host’s own addresses and internal ones unless a rule names the address. Internal addresses are loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 and the other ranges that aren’t the public internet, among them IPv4’s documentation ranges 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 and the old 6to4 relays’ 192.88.99.0/24, and IPv6’s Teredo 2001::/32, documentation 2001:db8::/32 and 3fff::/20, discard-only 100::/64, benchmarking 2001:2::/48, ORCHID 2001:10::/28 and ORCHIDv2 2001:20::/28, SRv6 5f00::/16 and IPv4-translated ::ffff:0:a.b.c.d. An address with an IPv6 zone is also internal, whatever its address, because a zone ties it to one of this machine’s links. An address with an IPv4 address in it counts as that IPv4 address, both a NAT64 address 64:ff9b::a.b.c.d and a 6to4 address in 2002::/16, such as 2002:a00:1::1 for 10.0.0.1, and the 6to4 network, a /48, of one of the host’s own 6to4 addresses counts as the host’s, because the machines on its LAN share it. A deny for an IPv4 address covers both forms. An allow for an IPv4 address covers its NAT64 form, which this network’s own translator carries, but not its 6to4 form, because 6to4 traffic goes through relays that anyone may run, so a 6to4 address is allowed only by a rule that names it. A Teredo address holds its IPv4 addresses scrambled, and the proxy doesn’t read them, so a broad IPv6 allow such as ::/0 lets in the Teredo form of a denied IPv4 address. It requires a TLS ClientHello in a tunnel to name the CONNECT host in its SNI, in ASCII, letters’ case aside. The proxy doesn’t see the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that routes by it can reach other sites it serves. For a host with a bound secret, it replaces the placeholder in one header with the real value, as how the proxy puts them in describes. For a host whose rules narrow it to some methods or paths, it decrypts the host’s HTTPS and checks each request, as requests by method and path describes. Everything else passes unread. It carries at most 1024 CONNECT tunnels, holds at most 2048 connections of every kind and has at most 2048 requests to hosts under way at once for the VM, as described below. It logs every decision (log files). A CONNECT tunnel meets the proxy’s checks in this order:
The proxy's checks on a CONNECT tunnelThe proxy checks a CONNECT tunnel from the VM in order: the VM's password, else 407, a host name or an address, else 400, and fewer than 1024 tunnels open, else 503. transparent.devvm.proxy takes the host from its first bytes, TLS's SNI or each HTTP Host, and closes the tunnel when there's none, and devvm.proxy, its names and 198.18.0.1 get 403. One of the VM's links goes to the link's socket untouched, and a transparent connection to one is refused. Any other host must be on the allowlist and not denied, else 403, which a transparent TLS connection gets over the VM's CA, and it must be public and not this machine's or an address a rule names, and on port 443 when rules judge its requests, else 403. A bound host, on port 443, or one whose requests are judged, is intercepted with the VM's CA, where each request must name the host, else 421, and be allowed by the rules, else 403, before its placeholder is swapped for the real value. Any other tunnel passes untouched when its TLS SNI names the CONNECT host, or it isn't TLS.yes no yes no no yes, or not TLS yes CONNECT host:port from the VM the VM's password?no: 407 a host name or an address?no: 400 fewer than 1024 tunnels open?no: 503 transparent.devvm.proxy? the host in its first bytes:TLS's SNI, or each HTTP Hostnone: closed one of the VM's links? devvm.proxy or under it,or 198.18.0.1?yes: 403 the link's socket,tunneled untouched(transparent: refused) on the allowlist, and not denied?no: 403(transparent TLS: 403over the VM's CA) public and not this machine's,or an address a rule names?no: 403 rules by method and pathjudge its requests:on port 443?no: 403 a bound host, on port 443,or its requests judged? its TLS SNI namesthe CONNECT host?no: closed tunneled untouched intercepted, withthe VM's CA each request namesthe host?no: 421 each request allowed bythe rules, by method and path?no: 403 the placeholder swappedfor the real value A tunnel that the proxy doesn’t intercept carries the bytes both ways as they are. When the VM finishes sending, the proxy closes its side of the connection to the far end, so the far end sees the end of what the VM sent and can still answer. The tunnel ends when the far end’s bytes end, or when the proxy can’t pass them on because the VM’s connection has gone, and then the proxy closes both connections. In a tunnel to a host the policy allows, the far end’s bytes reach the VM at once, so a protocol whose server speaks first, such as SMTP, gets its greeting before the VM sends anything. The VM’s bytes wait until the proxy has checked them: when the first one starts a TLS record, the proxy reads the whole ClientHello and checks its SNI before any of it reaches the far end, and any other first byte passes at once. The VM may wait as long as it likes before its first byte, as on any open tunnel, but once a ClientHello starts, it must arrive whole, in one record of at most 16 KiB and 256 bytes, within 10 seconds, or the proxy closes the tunnel and logs why. The proxy reads no record past that length, so a VM can’t make it hold 64 KiB for each of its tunnels, nor hold a slot by sending its ClientHello a byte at a time.
The proxy carries at most 1024 CONNECT tunnels for the VM at once, including tunnels to links and intercepted ones, from the request until the tunnel ends. That’s four times the 256 connections a browser such as Chrome keeps open at most, and many times what a package manager opens, such as npm’s 15 sockets or uv’s 50 downloads, so several installs and builds at once fit. Each tunnel holds two of the proxy’s file descriptors, so the limit keeps a VM that opens tunnels without end from taking them all. A CONNECT past the limit gets 503, which a client may retry, and the reason 1024 tunnels open already, logged as a refused block, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log suggests an allow rule. The proxy’s own log, proxy.log, says when the VM reaches the limit, once until a tunnel ends.
The proxy also holds at most 2048 of the VM’s connections at once, of every kind, which counts plain HTTP requests in absolute form, idle kept-alive connections and a request that goes on after its client has gone, as well as tunnels. That’s twice the tunnels’ limit, so a CONNECT past the tunnels’ limit still gets its 503 first. A connection counts from its first request with the VM’s password, and a request on a connection past the limit gets 503, after which the proxy closes the connection. On a Linux host, the limit of 256 connections that QEMU carries to the proxy at once comes first, and a connection past it gets a 503 before it reaches the proxy (the QEMU wrapper).
Every program on this machine can reach the proxy’s port, an open VM’s included, so a connection that hasn’t sent the VM’s password yet never takes the VM’s room. Such connections wait in a pool of their own, at most 128 at once, and one more closes the one that has waited longest, which a real client rarely is, because it sends its request at once. Holding connections open can’t take the VM’s room, but a program that opens connections as fast as this machine accepts them still slows the proxy for the VM, through the system’s queue of connections waiting to be accepted (design).
The proxy also has at most 2048 requests to hosts under way at once, plain HTTP’s and those inside intercepted tunnels together. Each is a connection of its own to the host, so the tunnels’ HTTP/2 requests, 100 at once in each, can’t add up to more connections than the proxy can open. A request past the limit gets 503, which a client may retry.
proxy.log says when the VM reaches either limit, once a minute at most (attack vectors).
Nothing bounds how long a request or a tunnel lasts, so a long download, a WebSocket, a model’s slow stream and server-sent events go on for as long as they take. The proxy bounds what a connection makes it hold instead:
A connection to the proxy waits at most 10 minutes for its next request, as the HTTP inside an intercepted tunnel or a transparent connection does, which is longer than a client keeps one idle. A request without the VM’s password gets 407, and the proxy closes its connection after it, so nothing without the password keeps a connection open. A request takes at most 64 KiB of headers, including in an intercepted tunnel, a transparent connection and the 403 page’s TLS connection. HTTP/2 inside an intercepted tunnel or a transparent connection carries at most 100 requests at once, which is what most servers allow, and each is a request the proxy makes to the host. A plain HTTP request in absolute form goes on when its client half-closes after sending, because some clients do, so the proxy can’t tell from that alone that the client has gone. The request goes on while its answer keeps coming, and once its client has stopped sending and a minute passes with nothing to pass on, the proxy ends it, so a client that went away doesn’t leave a request waiting on a host that never answers.
data.the-self-check#The self-check:
A confined tier holds only while the VM runs on the process that devvm started confined. A process can’t leave its sandbox, but limactl start starts a new Lima process, unconfined. So on every launch, and whenever an export or devvm rm’s check of a --clone VM needs the VM running, whether devvm started the VM or found it running, devvm checks two things, from the host:
That the VM still runs on the process devvm started. The VM can’t fake this check. That a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. The VM answers this check, so it catches only the honest case. devvm records the result in the VM’s state, as ok or unenforced in the net section’s made.check. When the check fails, what devvm does depends on why:
The VM wasn’t started confined, because it was started outside devvm or has been running since before devvm network moved it from open to a confined tier. In a terminal, devvm offers to restart the VM confined (net_unenforced_restart), and if you decline, it warns you and goes on (net_unenforced). Without a terminal, or if the VM is still unenforced after the restart, devvm stops the VM and ends without opening a shell (net_unenforced_stop). The next devvm starts the VM confined. The VM was started confined, yet it gets out, because it reaches the internet through something devvm didn’t set up, such as a second network. A restart wouldn’t help, so devvm stops the VM and ends (net_direct_route). This is the check, and what devvm does when it fails:
The self-check on every launchOn every launch, devvm checks that the VM runs on the process devvm started and that a direct connection from it fails. If either isn't so, the check is unenforced. A VM started confined is then stopped, because it has another way out. Otherwise, without a terminal, devvm stops the VM without a shell, and the next devvm starts it confined. In a terminal, devvm offers to restart it confined, and warns and goes on if you say no, or stops it if the check still fails after the restart.yes yes no no yes: anotherway out no no yes no yes yes no every launch on the processdevvm started? a direct connectionfrom the VM fails? check: ok check: unenforced started confined? stops the VMand ends a terminal? stops the VM, no shell;the next devvm startsit confined restart it confined? warns, goes on enforced now? check: ok An open VM isn’t confined, so its self-check is another one: a command in the VM asks its proxy for http://devvm.proxy/blocked through the proxy that the VM’s /etc/environment names, the variable’s name in the command and never the password. When the proxy doesn’t answer, devvm warns you (net_proxy_unreachable) and goes on, records no result, and the VM keeps running.
devvm ls and devvm network show such a VM’s tier as unenforced. That’s a VM whose last self-check failed, or a running VM that isn’t on the process devvm started confined, which devvm checks on the host each time.
On Lima, “the process devvm started” is the VM’s Lima process, which devvm starts confined.
data.the-shared-nix-cache#The shared Nix cach:
VMs with the nix layer share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache, so each package comes from cache.nixos.org once per machine instead of once per VM. Each VM keeps its own Nix store and daemon, and only the host writes the cache, so no VM can change what another VM gets. The design note says why it’s a cache that the host fills rather than a shared store.
In the VM. devvm starts the VM’s proxy with nix_cache set to ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/nix-cache in its config when the VM’s image has the nix layer, and the VM’s setup puts http://devvm.proxy/nix before https://cache.nixos.org in Nix’s substituters (the VM’s setup). It leaves trusted-public-keys as Nix has it, which is cache.nixos.org’s key alone. Nix’s daemon reaches devvm.proxy through its own proxy settings, so its requests are absolute-form GETs with the VM’s password, and the proxy answers them itself, as it does /blocked and /ca.pem, and never forwards them. When the cache answers with anything but a file, Nix goes on to cache.nixos.org, through the proxy as any other download.
What a VM can ask for. The proxy takes only GET and HEAD requests with no query, for three kinds of path under /nix/. These are nix-cache-info, a narinfo named .narinfo with a 32-character hash in Nix’s base 32, and a NAR named nar/.nar with a 52-character hash and no suffix or .xz, .zst or .bz2. Anything else gets 400. The proxy makes up nix-cache-info itself, with priority 30, so Nix asks the cache before cache.nixos.org, whose priority is 40. It serves the other files from the folder, or fetches them from https://cache.nixos.org when the VM’s policy allows cache.nixos.org:443 and, when rules by method and path narrow that host, a GET of the file’s path there. That’s the only host it fetches from, and its fetches go through the same address floor and company proxy as the VM’s own requests. It follows no redirect, and nothing of the VM’s request goes with it, so nothing a VM sends is ever stored.
What the host checks. Before it keeps a narinfo, the proxy checks that its StorePath is the path the VM asked for, and that cache.nixos.org-1, whose Ed25519 key devvm pins, signed its fingerprint, 1;StorePath;NarHash;NarSize;References. The signature doesn’t cover the NAR’s URL, so the proxy also checks that the URL is named by the narinfo’s own NarHash or FileHash, and no narinfo can put a file in another NAR’s place. It fetches a NAR only after it checked a narinfo that names it, never for a HEAD, and it keeps the NAR only when its SHA-256 and size are that narinfo’s FileHash and FileSize. The host can’t check a NAR’s NarHash, which is the hash of the archive before compression, because the proxy uses Go’s standard library alone, and that has no xz or zstd. Each VM’s Nix checks the signature and the NarHash again, so a narinfo with an added reference, or a corrupted NAR, fails there too. A file that fails a check, a not-found and an error all get 404, and the proxy keeps nothing of them, so Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself.
The folder and its cap. The proxy writes each file whole into a temporary file in the folder, then renames it into place, mode 600 in folders of 700. The cache’s cap is the nix-cache.size retention setting, 10 GiB when it’s off, which devvm puts in the proxy’s config as nix_cache_max when the proxy starts. The cap counts the disk each file takes, in whole blocks, and a NAR being fetched counts at its full size from the start. When a new file would take the cache past its cap, the proxy deletes the least recently used files, down to nine tenths of the cap, and when the NARs being fetched leave no room, it refuses the fetch. One proxy fetches each NAR once, however many requests ask for it, and at most four at once. A request that missed the cache looks again once it’s its turn to fetch, so a fetch that ended in between is served from the cache, not downloaded and counted against the cap a second time. A hit marks a file used by setting its modification time. Every VM’s proxy and devvm gc take one lock on the folder before they change it, so the cap holds while many VMs fill it, and a running total in the folder saves counting it for each file. Each tries the lock without waiting, again and again for at most 5 seconds, because a proxy’s child that a VM took over could hold it for ever. Past that, the request gets 404, so Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself, and devvm gc skips the trim and says so (nix_cache_locked). devvm gc and the daily retention run also trim the cache to its cap, and devvm gc --nix-cache empties it.
What a child could leave there. A VM’s proxy’s child writes the cache, so devvm reads it as it reads a file a VM can write. Its trim and its count of the cache open the folder as a root that no link leads out of, take nar/ only when it’s a folder and never a link, count and delete only regular files, and delete a link as itself, never what it leads to, so a link a child leaves never leads devvm to your files. Each proxy makes nar/ and sets the cache’s folders to yours alone through the folders it opened, never by their paths. The proxy deletes anything at nar/ that isn’t a folder, such as a link, as itself, makes a folder in its place and warns of it in its log, so its change of mode never reaches a folder of yours. Every proxy reads a cached file only when it’s a regular file, never through a link and without waiting on a FIFO, and takes the lock only on a regular file with one link.
Logs. Each request is a nix-cache event in the VM’s own log, with its path and what came of it: hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found or was refused. devvm network log shows these as cache.
Open VMs have their proxy too, so they share the cache. An open proxy allows cache.nixos.org as it allows every host.
What stays open. What one VM can learn of another through the cache, and how it can push other VMs’ files out, is under Attack vectors. Private caches, such as Cachix or one behind a netrc, are never shared, because only root in a VM can add a substituter, and Nix reaches it directly through the proxy’s allowlist.
data.the-vms-ca#The VM’s CA:
Each VM has a CA of its own, whatever its tier, which only its proxy signs with and only that VM trusts, so a copy of one VM’s key can impersonate sites to that VM alone, and no VM’s proxy can make a certificate that another VM accepts. A CA is ECDSA P-256, valid for 30 days from an hour before it’s made, and it names no host. Its common name holds its serial number, so no two CAs share a name. devvm keeps the VM’s CAs in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/ca/: the current CA as ca.pem and its key ca.key, and the next CA as next.pem and its key next.key. The folder and both keys are yours alone (modes 700 and 600), devvm writes each file whole, a key before its certificate, and on macOS it keeps the folder out of Time Machine. The keys never leave this machine: the VM gets the two certificates and nothing else. The proxy reads each certificate and key only when it’s a regular file, not a symbolic link, and refuses a key that anybody but you may read or write.
At each launch, devvm readies both CAs before the proxy starts, holding the folder’s lock, lock, so two launches of one VM at once take turns. The current CA stays while it has over a week left. When it has less, or there’s none, the next CA takes its place if it has started and has over a week left, and otherwise devvm makes a new current CA. The next CA starts a week and an hour before the current one ends, and lasts 30 days too. When it doesn’t follow the current one that way, by ending after it and starting by the time it’s replaced, devvm makes it again. A key without its certificate, or a CA that lasts longer than 30 days, is made again too. Each launch’s setup installs both certificates in the VM, so the VM trusts the next CA weeks before the proxy uses it.
The proxy holds both CAs, and it signs with the next one from an hour after that CA’s start, which is a week before the current one ends and the moment from which the next launch would make it the current one. The hour lets a VM whose clock is behind see that the CA has started. The switch needs no launch and no new proxy, because the VM already trusts the next CA, so a VM that you don’t open again keeps verifying the proxy’s certificates until the next CA ends, which is at least 30 days less an hour after its last launch. A proxy keeps the CAs it started with, because the VM trusts no others, and a launch that replaced either one starts the proxy again with the new ones, as how long a proxy runs describes. /ca.pem at devvm.proxy serves both certificates.
A VM that runs past its next CA’s end without a launch can’t verify the proxy’s certificates any more. From then on, its proxy answers each CONNECT to a bound host’s :443 with 403 before any tunnel opens, and it logs a refused block with the reason devvm's CA has ended: open the VM again (devvm in its folder) for a new one, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log suggests an allow rule. Absolute-form https:// requests involve no certificate for the VM, so they go on getting their secrets. The VM’s other connections work until you open it again. Running devvm in the VM’s folder then makes a new CA and a next one and starts the proxy again with them, which ends the connections open through the old one, and the launch’s setup installs both in the VM.
The CAs live as long as the VM’s folder. A remake keeps the folder, so the VM keeps its CAs, and so does a change of tier. devvm rm, devvm gc --orphans, and devvm deleting a VM whose creation it interrupted or whose folder an earlier VM of the project left, delete the folder, and the CAs and their keys with it.
In a user’s terms: to put a secret in, the proxy shows the VM a certificate from the VM’s own CA, which every VM has, an open one’s included, and which no other VM trusts, so one VM’s proxy can’t make certificates that another VM accepts. Each CA lasts 30 days, and its key stays on this machine. Each launch installs the VM’s current CA and the next one, which starts a week before the current one ends, and the proxy switches to the next CA then on its own, without a launch. So a VM that you don’t open again keeps working for at least 30 days after its last launch with devvm in its folder. Connecting with ssh alone isn’t a launch. When a VM runs past its next CA’s end without a launch, its proxy refuses its HTTPS connections to secrets’ hosts, and devvm network log --blocked gives the reason devvm's CA has ended. The VM’s other requests keep working. Running devvm in the VM’s folder installs new CAs, which also starts the VM’s proxy again and ends the connections open through it (saving and binding secrets). devvm rm deletes a VM’s CAs with the VM, and a VM keeps them when its tier changes.
Tests: the unit tests check the dates, the modes, the switch and each CA that’s made again, that launches at once take turns on the lock, that an open VM’s proxy has the VM’s CAs, salt and secrets file and that a VM keeps its CAs as its tier changes, that a client trusting both CAs verifies the proxy’s certificates before the switch and after it, with the same proxy, that the proxy refuses a key others may read and a symbolic link, and that two proxies’ certificates come from their own CAs. The CLI tests check each VM’s CA files and modes, that two VMs’ CAs differ, that the setup sends both certificates and no key, an open VM’s too, and that a VM turned off and on again keeps its CAs (the tests behind it). End-to-end checks (network): a second confined VM, whose CAs differ from the first’s; each VM trusts its own two and none of the other’s; no key is anywhere in the VM; each proxy serves its own CAs at /ca.pem, and its certificates verify with its own VM’s CAs and not with the other’s; devvm rm deletes a VM’s CA with its folder.
data.the-vms-resolver#The VM’s resolver:
On a confined VM, Lima’s DNS setting gives the guest one name server, its own 127.0.0.1, and each launch’s setup makes the system’s resolver ask it directly. systemd-resolved’s stub, 127.0.0.53, would ask 127.0.0.1 in turn, and when nothing listens there, because transparent mode is off or stopped, the stub can keep retrying it over UDP and TCP without answering, so a lookup through glibc waits out its own timeout instead of failing. So the setup replaces /etc/resolv.conf, which on Ubuntu is a link to the stub’s file, with a file of its own that names 127.0.0.1 alone, with the stub’s search line and a timeout of one second, tried twice, which is plenty because dnsmasq answers in the VM itself. glibc then gets a refusal at once when nothing listens, and dnsmasq’s answer through the nftables rule when transparent mode runs, as musl on Alpine does.
systemd-resolved still runs, so resolvectl and the programs that ask it over D-Bus still go through it. Docker reads /etc/resolv.conf and finds only a loopback server there, so on its default bridge it gives containers its fallback servers, and on a network of their own, such as Compose’s, its embedded DNS server asks 127.0.0.1 from the VM’s side. The nftables table sends both to dnsmasq. The setup writes its file only on a guest with systemd that has the stub’s file and whose /etc/resolv.conf is the stub’s link or the setup’s own file, so a file or link of your own stays, and it copies the search line again at each launch. When it can’t write the file, it says so in one line and the launch goes on. systemd-resolved reads a file that isn’t its own link as servers and search domains of its own, so while the VM is confined it takes 127.0.0.1 from the setup’s file, and a search line of . sends every name there. It keeps them after the file is a link again, until it restarts. So on an open VM, the setup puts the stub’s link back and restarts systemd-resolved, which then asks Lima’s DNS. Going back needs only the setup’s own file, which it writes nowhere else, and when the stub’s file is missing afterwards, the setup says that names may not resolve.
data.the-vms-setup#The VM’s setup:
On every launch, the VM’s setup does the following:
It installs the VM’s own CA and the next one into the VM’s trust store, as devvm-proxy.crt and devvm-proxy-next.crt, so the proxy’s certificates for hosts with a bound secret verify, in this VM only. It never gets their keys. It points the programs that ignore the proxy variables at the proxy. Those are apt, sudo (which keeps the variables), every ssh connection, Docker’s daemon and containers with the docker layer, and Nix’s daemon with the nix layer. Under systemd, each daemon gets a drop-in, devvm-proxy.conf, that holds the VM’s own proxy address and nothing else, and without systemd, Docker’s settings in /etc/conf.d/docker get a block instead, and Nix’s daemon gets /etc/conf.d/nix-daemon. Every VM has a proxy, an open one’s included, so every VM gets them, and the setup restarts a daemon whose settings changed. An ssh connection gets a ProxyCommand that tunnels through the proxy, and the proxy checks its host and port against the allowlist. It writes devvm-local-proxy, a proxy on the VM’s loopback that adds the VM’s password to each request, for browsers, which ask for a proxy’s password rather than take it from the proxy variables. The desktop layer starts it and points the desktop’s session at it (the local proxy). With the nix layer, it points Nix at the shared Nix cache first: /etc/nix/devvm-cache.conf, which /etc/nix/nix.conf includes with !include, sets substituters = http://devvm.proxy/nix https://cache.nixos.org. Every VM gets that file, an open one’s included, and the setup restarts Nix’s daemon when the file changed. It sets NO_PROXY and no_proxy to the VM itself, localhost,127.0.0.1,::1, in the daemons’ settings above and in Docker’s client settings (~/.docker/config.json), as the VM’s backend does in the environment it sets at each start. The VM’s links aren’t in it, because HTTP clients reach them through the proxy, so a change of links changes no daemon’s settings and restarts nothing. It puts the VM’s placeholders in ~/.config/devvm/env, which login shells read, as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN. When github is bound, it also sets up git’s credential helper for GitHub over HTTPS. It adds devvm-why, the note before each prompt, and the notes for Claude Code and Codex (inside the VM). devvm-why prints the proxy’s /blocked, and when that list is empty, the proxy’s answer adds that a connection refused, or a DNS error, for an allowed host comes from a tool that skipped the proxy where devvm can’t send it there, with a link to troubleshooting. With transparent mode, devvm-why then prints devvm-transparent status as root, through sudo -n. The notes, a block between markers in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, say to run devvm-why after a connection error or a 403 from the proxy, that a tool that ignores the proxy settings still reaches the proxy by name over HTTPS, HTTP and the ports the rules name, and that a refused connection on another port, or a DNS error, while devvm-why shows nothing blocked means the tool skipped the proxy and needs its own proxy setting or $HTTPS_PROXY. The setup writes them only when the VM has a proxy address, and replaces the block on every launch. On a VM that runs confined to its proxy, with transparent mode on, it sets up transparent mode, and on any other VM it takes transparent mode out. Each placeholder ends in a random value of the VM’s own, its salt, which isn’t its password.
data.through-a-company-proxy#Through a compan:
When devvm starts a VM’s proxy, it reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY from its own environment, each in capitals first and then in lowercase, as Go’s clients do. When its environment sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, it reads config.toml’s [proxy] table instead, its https, http and no-proxy, and never a mix of the two. It writes them into the proxy’s config, proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, as upstream, so a password in the environment’s URL is in a file only you can read and in no process’s arguments. devvm checks the settings first: a proxy URL is http://user:password@host:port, or host:port alone, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm refuses an https:// or socks5:// proxy (upstream_proxy_scheme) and a setting it can’t read (upstream_proxy_invalid), so a VM doesn’t start until you change it.
A config.toml URL never holds a password (proxy_password_in_config, as it’s read), because people copy that file between machines and keep it with their dotfiles. When its URL names a user, upstream gets "secret": "proxy", and the proxy looks the proxy secret up as it starts, through the same lookup as the secrets it puts in, the Keychain or ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/proxy, and uses it as the password of each URL that names a user and none of its own. So proxy.json never holds that password. A proxy whose lookup fails doesn’t start, and devvm checks that the secret is saved before it makes a new VM, starts a VM’s proxy, or builds an image or the shared tools (proxy_password_missing), and before it stops a running VM to start it again, as devvm restart does, so a refused restart leaves the VM running. It also checks before it changes a running VM’s tier between internet, allowlist and none, which the VM’s proxy applies at once, so the VM’s state never names a tier that its proxy doesn’t enforce. Each of these is one check of the company proxy’s settings, which devvm runs with the check of your CAs before a VM is made, stopped to start again, or given another confined tier while it runs (the packages).
devvm’s own requests on this machine go through the same company proxy. They are the download of its own mise, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and the registries --from asks for digests. When the environment sets the proxy, their clients use Go’s own environment proxy. When config.toml sets it, devvm’s route to the company proxy is their transport’s proxy. At the first request, the route looks the proxy secret up and puts it in each URL that names a user and none of its own. It routes each request as a VM’s proxy does: HTTPS_PROXY’s for HTTPS, HTTP_PROXY’s for plain HTTP, and directly for NO_PROXY’s hosts, localhost and loopback addresses. Go sends the user and password only to the company proxy, in Proxy-Authorization. A missing password fails the request without a retry. The mise that devvm runs on this machine inherits devvm’s environment, so it uses the environment’s proxy as it is. With config.toml’s proxy, devvm adds HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY to mise’s environment, in capitals and in lowercase, with the password in each URL that names a user. mise takes a proxy’s password only in its URL, so its environment is the one place it can go. It’s never in mise’s arguments or in a file.
A VM’s proxy refreshes Codex’s and opencode’s OAuth logins through the company proxy it sends the VM’s requests through, its upstream, whether that came from the environment or from config.toml. As it starts, it makes that upstream’s route for its own requests, with the proxy secret it looked up as the password, as devvm makes the route for its own requests. It carries the route in each lookup’s context, and the login’s refresh takes it from there as its transport’s proxy. A VM’s proxy without an upstream sends the refresh directly, as it does the VM’s requests.
An open VM’s proxy goes through the company proxy as a confined VM’s does. Its guest gets no proxy settings of devvm’s environment: Lima’s propagateProxyEnv is off for every VM whose guest names devvm’s proxy, so neither the shell’s nor config.toml’s password reaches the guest.
devvm warns (upstream_proxy_gone) when the config the VM’s proxy last started with has an upstream and the one it starts it with now has none, as happens when a shell without the settings starts it.
The proxy decides each request as it does without a company proxy, by the host name the VM asked for, and only then picks the way out:
A host that NO_PROXY names, localhost, a name under .localhost and a loopback or unspecified address go directly, through the checks above. A tunnel, and the connection the proxy makes to a bound host to put a secret in, go through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy. The proxy sends CONNECT host:port with the name the VM asked for, and Proxy-Authorization: Basic from the URL’s user and password, and it reads the answer. Anything but 200 refuses the VM’s request, naming the company proxy by its host and port. Over that tunnel, the proxy’s TLS connection to a bound host checks the server’s certificate against the system’s roots and the CAs in your CA folder, as it does directly. A plain HTTP request goes to HTTP_PROXY’s proxy in absolute form, with its Proxy-Authorization in place of the VM’s. The company proxy’s address in the request has no password, so no error the proxy logs holds one. Without HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY, those requests go directly. NO_PROXY is a comma-separated list, which the proxy reads as Go’s clients read it. In it, * matches every host, and an address or a CIDR matches addresses. A name matches itself and its subdomains, while a name with a leading . or *. matches only its subdomains. Any entry can end in a port, which limits it to that port, and an entry whose port no request has, such as git.test:0, or whose port isn’t in plain decimal, such as git.test:080, matches nothing. The proxy reads a name in NO_PROXY as it reads the host of every request, lowercased in ASCII alone and without one trailing dot, so a name with a character that isn’t printable ASCII matches no host, because Unicode’s case folding would turn the Kelvin sign into k.
The company proxy resolves the names it’s sent, so the proxy can’t hold it to the addresses it checked, and the floor changes for those requests. An address in the VM’s request is checked as before, and a host whose last label is all digits or starts with 0x, such as 127.1, gets 400, because a company proxy may read it as an address. For a name, the proxy asks this machine’s resolver, for at most three seconds, and refuses the request when any answer is internal or denied, unless a rule names the address. A name this machine can’t resolve, which is common behind a company proxy, goes to the company proxy unchecked when a rule names it, as itself or under *.domain. When only ** allows it, the proxy refuses it with 403, and the event log says that this machine can’t resolve it and only ** allows it. The proxy reads at most 64 KiB of the company proxy’s answer to CONNECT. The design note explains what that leaves open, which Attack vectors lists, and how builds reach the company proxy through a proxy of their own.
The event log’s upstream field names the company proxy, by host and port, for each tunnel and request that went through it, and devvm network log adds through host:port to the line. The proxy’s own log names both company proxies by host and port when it starts. Neither holds the user or the password.
data.tools-that-skip-the-proxy#Tools that ski:
On a confined VM, transparent mode sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy by the names it looks up (what it covers). Nothing new runs or listens on the host, and the backends don’t change: the VM reaches its proxy over the path its proxy settings use, and the proxy judges each connection as it judges CONNECT host:port. Every piece in the VM is a program that devvm configures, dnsmasq, nftables and socat, which base installs, and one script, devvm-transparent, which each launch sends. A tool that looks up api.example.com and connects to it goes this way:
Its lookup reaches dnsmasq in the VM. glibc and musl both ask 127.0.0.1:53 themselves, which is where Lima’s DNS setting for a confined VM points (the VM’s resolver). An nftables rule sends 127.0.0.1:53 to dnsmasq, which listens on the stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, alone. That rule takes every connection to 127.0.0.1:53 in the VM, so a DNS server of the user’s own there, or a forward of port 53 to it, gets nothing. dnsmasq answers the A query with 198.18.0.1, with a time to live of 0, and every other type, AAAA and HTTPS included, with an empty answer, never REFUSED, which musl waits 5 seconds on. It has no upstream server, so no query leaves the VM, and it reads /etc/hosts first, so localhost, the VM’s hostname, host.lima.internal and the links’ names keep their own addresses. Names under devvm.internal that aren’t a link’s don’t exist, and neither does a name without a dot, nor a name under the search domains that the VM’s resolver appends to one, which Lima takes from this machine’s network and dnsmasq reads from /etc/resolv.conf as it starts. So a single-label name that isn’t in /etc/hosts doesn’t resolve, rather than turning into a name of this machine’s network. dnsmasq can’t tell a name the resolver made that way from one a tool names whole, so every name under those domains gets no answer, such as git.corp.example.com under corp.example.com. The tool connects to 198.18.0.1:443. The address is on the VM’s loopback interface, so the connection stays in the VM, and an nftables rule sends it to a socat listener on 198.18.0.1:61443. Nothing binds port 443 or 80 itself, so your own servers keep them. socat opens an ordinary CONNECT transparent.devvm.proxy:443 to the VM’s proxy, with the VM’s password, which it reads from a file, never from its arguments. Each port has a listener of its own, so the port reaches the proxy in the target, and nothing the VM sends can change it. The proxy checks the password, takes one of the VM’s 1024 tunnel slots, and reads the connection’s first bytes for at most 10 seconds. A TLS record is read whole, and its ClientHello’s server name (SNI) is the host. An HTTP/1.x request line or HTTP/2’s preface makes each request’s Host the host, judged on its own. Anything else is refused and logged as a refused block of transparent.devvm.proxy, with why: no SNI, an address as the SNI, a name with anything but ASCII, a name under devvm.proxy, or bytes that name no host, such as SSH’s, Postgres’s SSLRequest or a server that speaks first. From there the connection is CONNECT host:443: the links, the policy and the floor, interception for a bound host, the tunnel and its SNI check, the log, and /blocked, in the order CONNECT has them. The ClientHello goes on to whatever serves it first, so the far end gets it byte for byte. The proxy dials the host it judged, by name, so the VM can’t name one host and reach another. Its events carry "via": "dns". A blocked TLS host gets a TLS handshake with a certificate for its SNI name from the VM’s own CA, signed as interception signs, then the proxy’s 403 text for every request on the connection, over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. The proxy resolves nothing and dials nothing for it. Without a CA, or once it has ended, the connection closes, and the block is logged all the same. A plain HTTP request is always forwarded as http://, whatever its request line says, so no secret goes into it, and a Host that names another port than the connection’s gets 400, as does a CONNECT inside it. A link’s name gets a refused block on both ways, because dnsmasq never gives a link’s name the stand-in address. Its name in /etc/hosts reaches it. A Host of devvm.proxy reaches /blocked alone and gets 403 for every other endpoint, the CA, the ports and the Nix cache, because socat adds the password for any client, a container without the proxy settings included.
The ports. The proxy serves the ports to redirect at http://devvm.proxy/transparent/ports: 80 and 443, then each port an allow rule names for hosts by name, **:8443 included, the lowest first, at most 32 of them. It leaves out :*, address rules’ ports, 22 and 53, and every port but 80 and 443 while a deny is broken. The proxy’s own log names the ports past 32, once each time they change. devvm-transparent fetches the list every 10 seconds and at each launch, and takes it only when it’s 2 to 34 ports, each once, with 80 and 443 and neither 22 nor 53. A new port gets the lowest free listener from 61100 to 61131, and a port that stays keeps its own. The list shows the VM the ports its rules name, never their hosts, which it can’t read otherwise. That’s a small disclosure, and it gives the VM nothing to reach: each connection is still judged by its own host and port.
The nftables table. The table inet devvm_transparent is loaded whole, in one transaction, and devvm-transparent loads it again within 10 seconds when something removes it, such as nft flush ruleset. Its NAT chains run at priority -110, before Docker’s at -100, and the first NAT chain that gives a connection a mapping is the only one that does, so they give every TCP and UDP port of the stand-in address one: a redirected port goes to its listener, DNS to dnsmasq, and every other port to port 61079, where nothing listens, so the kernel refuses it at once with a reset, or for UDP, QUIC included, with a port-unreachable. Docker’s chains, which would send a published port’s traffic to a container, so never see the stand-in address, and neither a VM process nor a container that connects to db.example.com:5432 reaches a container that publishes 5432. The refused connections are logged in the kernel’s log, five a second at most, which devvm-transparent status reads. DNS to any public server goes to dnsmasq too, from the VM and from Docker’s bridges (docker0 and br-*), so Docker’s fallback servers, 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4, and resolvers that tools hard-code reach it. So does DNS to the VM’s own name servers but loopback’s, as /etc/resolv.conf and systemd-resolved’s list name them, such as the one Lima’s DHCP adds beside 127.0.0.1, which Docker gives its containers once it drops the loopback one; devvm-transparent reads them again every 10 seconds. Other loopback addresses, private, link-local and CGNAT ones are left alone, so a DNS server on a container’s or the LAN’s address still answers, and Lima’s DNS addresses that aren’t the VM’s name servers answer nothing, as the host’s confinement has it. Two filter chains run before every NAT chain, at priority -150: one drops traffic to the stand-in address from any interface but the loopback and Docker’s bridges, such as Podman’s or LXD’s bridges and Lima’s network, and both drop anything to it but TCP, UDP and ICMP, such as SCTP, which no NAT rule maps. So neither reaches Docker’s DNAT of a published port through the stand-in address. An input rule keeps the same interfaces off it again, and only connections the NAT rules translated, and DNS, reach it. The listeners’ ports, 61080, 61443 and 61100 to 61131, and the dead port, 61079, are above Linux’s range for outgoing connections, 32768 to 60999, so no connection out is given one.
The service. devvm-transparent run is the service, under systemd or OpenRC, as root: it adds 198.18.0.1/32 to lo, loads the table, starts dnsmasq and a socat listener for each port, and then restarts any of them that ends within a second, sends dnsmasq SIGHUP when /etc/hosts changes, and fetches the ports every tenth second. dnsmasq runs as the user devvm-transparent, and so does each socat connection’s process, which reads the password file through its group. When the service stops, it removes the table, the address and what it started, so names stop resolving, and a stopped or broken service never leaves a way out. It starts at each boot, before any launch, with the last ports and settings, and each launch’s setup turns it on, off, or restarts it when its settings changed, such as a new proxy port or password. Its files are root’s, in /etc/devvm/transparent, and the VM’s password, which every program in the VM has in its environment already, is in files only, never in a process’s arguments. On an open VM, and with transparent mode off, the setup stops and removes all of it, and flushes systemd-resolved’s cache. The setup decides by the confinement the VM runs with, so a VM whose tier changed into or out of open keeps what it had until its next start.
What doesn’t change. The host’s confinement is the boundary: root in the VM can change or stop all of this, and then names stop resolving, or a query to Lima’s DNS goes nowhere, as for a VM without transparent mode. The self-check’s direct connection is to an address on port 443, so transparent mode never answers it. The VM’s names never reach the host’s resolver for a blocked host, because the proxy asks the policy before it resolves anything. Design notes has the threat check.
data.vms-that-cant-be-confined#VMs that can’t: A VM whose backend can’t confine it to its proxy (egress-proxy) can only be open: devvm refuses to make it on any other tier, unasked, in one line that names the backend and --network open (net_tier_backend), and the registry’s check refuses devvm network with a confined tier.
data.what-stays-in-the-vms-copies#What stays:
Taking secrets out of a file works only where devvm can tell a secret from the rest, so some go into the VM on every tier, and keys devvm can’t tell apart lists them among what devvm leaves open:
The agents’ mounted folders. devvm mounts Claude Code’s skills, agents, commands, output-styles and plugins, Codex’s prompts and skills, opencode’s subfolders, and pi’s extensions, skills, prompts and themes whole and read-only, so every file in them reaches the VM, a .env in ~/.config/opencode/plugin included. So does a plugin marketplace’s git config in ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces, which holds a password or a token when you added a private marketplace with one in its URL. These folders hold code that the agent runs, such as plugins, hooks and the scripts that skills call, so a copy with only settings and Markdown, as opencode’s config folder’s files get, would break them. A copy without files whose names look secret, such as .env or *.pem, would miss a key in any other file, and it would need a copy of each folder, which can be large, on every launch, while a mount shows the changes to devvm’s agent store at once. So devvm mounts them as they are, and the coding agents page says to keep secrets out of them. Free text of an unknown shape. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic, because devvm can’t tell it from a word. Logins devvm can’t bind. opencode’s and pi’s keys that devvm can’t bind, a local model server’s among them, are withheld unless [pass-keys] lists their provider, and then they go as they are (login_passed). pi’s settings that undo devvm’s. The VM’s copy of pi’s settings.json leaves out httpProxy, sessionDir and selfUpdateCommand (pi_settings_dropped), and devvm warns when it sets defaultProjectTrust to always (pi_trusts_all). Its other settings stay, with their keys taken out as above.
data.where-secrets-are-saved#Where secrets ar:
On macOS, devvm saves a secret in the Keychain, under the service devvm and the account that is the secret’s name, such as claude, github or stripe. It saves it through security -i, giving the value on its input, so the value is in no process’s arguments. DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE names another service, made of letters, digits, ., _ and - only. On other systems, devvm saves a secret in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/, a file only you can read.
A secret of your own keeps its value under custom., as its Keychain account or its file’s name, which no known secret’s name can be, so a known secret that devvm adds later never finds a value of yours. Its definition is in ~/.local/share/devvm/custom-secrets.json: its name, an ID of 16 random bytes made as it’s first saved, its hosts, header, variable, prefix, scheme, path, methods and whether it may be Basic’s username, as one JSON object of "version": 1, written whole and mode 600, and never its value. A path that devvm writes there has "path_pattern": true, as * in it is a wildcard, and devvm refuses a saved path with a * but without it, which was saved as a prefix whose * was itself, rather than read it as wider than it was saved, so the commands that read the list fail and name the file, as for any entry they refuse. devvm changes the list only while it holds custom-secrets.lock beside it, so two runs of devvm secret set at once never lose one another’s secret. It saves the value before the definition, and when a new secret’s definition can’t be written, it deletes the value again. devvm secret rm unbinds a secret’s VMs and deletes it, and devvm secret use binds a VM to the definition that’s there, each under the same lock, so neither can come between the other’s check and its change. A value devvm can’t save whole is refused before the one saved is touched: security -i reads its commands in lines of 4096 bytes, so a value has at most 3,800 bytes, and devvm checks the whole line before it runs security. Each value is printable ASCII alone, because a header carries nothing else and the Keychain gives what isn’t back in hex.
Inside devvm, a secret’s value has a type of its own from the moment devvm reads it, as you paste it, from the Keychain or its file, or from an agent’s login file, until the place that uses it. The same goes for a VM’s proxy password and the company proxy’s password. Printed in any way, in an error, a warning or devvm’s run log, that type shows and never the value, and devvm can’t write it into a file by accident, because only the files that must hold the real value write it: the Keychain or the secret’s file, the proxy’s config, the VM’s state and the agents’ login files (secrets in the code).
Each VM’s state records, for each secret of yours it uses, the definition’s ID and the hosts the secret had when devvm secret use bound it. The VM’s binding has the secret’s hosts that are in that record, so a host the secret gains reaches a VM only once devvm secret use binds it again, and a VM bound to another definition by the name gets no binding at all. The proxy’s lookup checks every secret binding against the secret as it’s saved before it gives a value: its hosts within the secret’s, and its header, scheme, path, methods, Basic username switch, ID and placeholder the secret’s own. A binding that doesn’t match gets nothing, and the proxy logs secret_binding_changed. Writing the bindings of every running VM again goes on past a VM whose files can’t be written and returns every failure together, so one VM never keeps the others’ proxies from dropping a secret. A proxy whose bindings file did change drops every value it has cached at once. One whose file couldn’t be written keeps a cached value for at most its 5 minutes, and only for the hosts it had. devvm checks every entry again each time it reads the list, as devvm secret set checks what you give it, so an entry edited by hand with a wildcard host or a known secret’s name is refused, and a list it can’t read fails the command that reads it, naming the file, rather than leaving a secret out. It reads the list as the proxy reads its own files: a regular file, not a symbolic link, that’s yours and that only you may write. Only a command that needs one of your secrets reads it, so a VM that uses none of them launches whatever the list holds. Your secrets’ names never shadow devvm’s own, nor an agent’s login’s, whose bindings are named after the agent, such as codex-key or pi-openai, and their placeholders have secret- before the name, which no login’s placeholder has. devvm secret rm unbinds a secret of yours from each VM that uses it before it deletes the secret, so a failure part way leaves the secret saved rather than a VM bound to a name that a secret saved later could take.

data: This page explains what devvm does, step by step, when it makes, opens, changes, stops and deletes a VM, and how it keeps each VM’s state. Everyday commands and Managing VMs cover the same commands from your side, and Settings and files lists your settings.
data.a-folder-made-again#A folder made again:
A VM’s state records its project folder’s path (dir) and the folder’s identity (folder), which one VM per folder describes. When either differs from the folder you’re in, the folder was deleted and made again, or another repo was cloned where the old one was. devvm then refuses the VM in every command that opens, stops or changes it (vm_other_folder), and only devvm rm and devvm adopt act on it. Each of them asks first, so without a terminal each one refuses (vm_other_folder_rm, vm_other_folder_adopt), unless devvm adopt --force. A folder made again says what each one does, and devvm does it as follows:
devvm rm asks with delete_other_folder_vm, then deletes the VM without checking a clone, because the VM’s folder is gone. devvm adopt asks with adopt_vm, then records this folder’s path and identity in the VM’s state and clears the inode of .git it recorded, so the next launch locks .git as if it had just appeared (vm_adopted). In a folder the VM already belongs to, it changes nothing (vm_already_here).
data.a-moved-folder#A moved folder:
A VM’s folder in the data folder, vms//, is named by the hash at the end of the VM’s name, which the backend’s machine has too, so neither changes when the project folder moves. What changes is the state’s dir, and devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records its path (a VM’s folder).
When the folder devvm runs in has no VM, devvm looks through every VM’s state for one made for this folder at another path (listing VMs). A state matches when its folder identity is this folder’s, its dir is another path, nothing is at that path any more on the folder’s device (gone, a VM whose folder is gone) or only a symlink that resolves to this folder is, its creation finished, and it isn’t a --clone VM. The folder must be this user’s, and its identity must be one that no other folder can have had. It must have the folder’s birth time, which tells a folder apart from a deleted one with the same inode number, and from a folder with the same inode number on another volume that a later mount gave the same device number, and on macOS the folder must be on APFS or HFS+, which never give a new folder a deleted one’s inode number. On Linux it must be on ext4, XFS, Btrfs, tmpfs, ZFS, F2FS or bcachefs, local file systems that keep a file’s inode number for its life and report its birth time, which devvm reads by the file system’s type from statfs. FUSE, network shares, 9p, overlayfs and FAT may make inode numbers up, so a folder on one never matches. A copy has a new inode, so it never matches, and a folder made again at the old path doesn’t either. At another path, the identity must also match the device in the state’s folder. So a folder that moved after a boot numbered its disk anew, before its VM started again, isn’t offered the VM, and you move the VM to it with devvm adopt VM. When more than one state matches, devvm moves none (vms_moved_here).
For one match, devvm asks in a terminal (move_vm), with no as the default, and refuses without one (vm_moved_here). devvm adopt --force moves it without asking. A no leaves the folder without a VM, so devvm makes a new one. A yes first checks the folder as a new VM’s folder is checked (project folders devvm refuses). Then devvm takes the creation locks of the VM and of the new VM the folder would get, so no other devvm deletes the VM or makes one for the folder meanwhile, and checks again that no state records the folder, and that the folder at the path is still the one it asked about (move_folder_changed). A running VM still mounts the old path, so devvm stops it as devvm stop does, with its proxy, port forwarder and link session (stopped). Last, it records the folder’s path and identity under the VM’s lock, refusing a state whose dir or folder changed since it was read (create_running), and says so (vm_adopted). In the same write, it records the old path in the state’s moved section as from, the path that the agents in the VM keep the folder’s history under. A second move before the VM’s next start keeps the first move’s old path there, because the history is still under it, and a move back to that path clears the section. The .git protection’s record stays as it was, because a folder that moved keeps its .git, whose identity and locks move with it, so the next check compares .git with what it locked.
The backend gets the new path at the VM’s next start, because a start makes a stopped VM what its state asks for, its project folder’s mount included, and Lima does it in the same limactl edit as the rest (what devvm sets on a VM). A VM that runs with its project folder at another path all the same, such as one started outside devvm, mounts that path until it starts again, so devvm asks whether to restart it as it opens the VM (restart_now), with yes as the default, as for agent folders, and otherwise warns that it mounts the folder at the new path only when it next starts (next_start_folder, then next_start).
The VM’s setup, which runs on every launch, moves Claude Code’s history for the folder. Claude Code keeps a folder’s sessions in ~/.claude/projects/SLUG, where SLUG is the folder’s path with each character other than an ASCII letter or digit replaced by a dash, counted in UTF-16 units as JavaScript counts them. A SLUG longer than 200 characters is cut at 200 and gets a dash and the path’s hash in base 36, the 32-bit hash that multiplies by 31 and adds each UTF-16 unit. That rule is Claude Code’s own, read from its 2.1 release. Claude Code also keeps the folder’s trust and MCP servers under the path itself in ~/.claude.json’s projects. When the state has a moved section, devvm sends the setup a moved file with both paths and both slugs, and the setup’s claude.sh renames the old slug’s folder to the new slug. When the new slug’s folder exists already, the setup moves each of the old folder’s entries that the new one doesn’t have into it, and leaves the rest. It moves the projects entry of the old path to the new path, unless the new path has one of its own, and leaves a ~/.claude.json that isn’t JSON as it is, with a warning in the run log. A folder or file that is a symlink stays as it is. All of this runs in the VM, as the VM’s user, on the VM’s own files, and never on the host’s. Running it again changes nothing, so a setup that fails after it moved the history does no harm when it runs again. Once the setup succeeds, devvm clears the moved section under the VM’s lock, unless another move recorded a different path meanwhile. devvm moves nothing of Codex’s or opencode’s. Codex records each session’s folder in the session, and opencode keeps a git repo’s sessions by the repo’s first commit and other folders’ sessions by their path (a moved or renamed folder). Links and groups go by the VM’s name, so they stay as they were, and a link’s TARGET given as a path finds the VM whose dir is that path. A new VM made at the old path can’t use the folder the moved VM keeps, so its name ends with the next hash of that path that names a free folder.
devvm adopt VM moves the VM it names, found as devvm rm VM finds one, to the folder devvm runs in, for a copy of the folder, such as one on another disk. It refuses a --clone VM (adopt_clone), a VM its backend no longer has (rm_vm_lost), a VM whose creation didn’t finish, a VM whose folder is there (adopt_folder_there), and a folder with a VM of its own (adopt_has_vm). It asks in a terminal (adopt_move_vm), which --force answers, and refuses without either (adopt_move_refused). It moves the VM as a match does, and also clears the .git protection’s record, as devvm adopt does, because the copy’s .git is another folder. A VM whose dir is this folder goes through devvm adopt.
data.a-new-vm#A new VM:
When you run devvm in a folder that has no VM, devvm makes one in these steps:
How devvm makes a VMUntil the first shell opens, devvm checks everything first, checks the shared tools for newer versions if due, builds the image if it isn't built, writes the VM's state, makes the VM from its image, locks .git unless --clone, starts its proxy and then the VM, runs the self-check, and sets the VM up, then the clone and devcontainer.json's commands.
