Then it opens the shell. If it's interrupted before then, devvm deletes the VM and what it made for it, and unlocks .git.until the first shell opens interrupted checks everything first:image, size, ports,network tier, SSH agent,features, devcontainer.json checks the shared toolsfor newer versions, if due builds the image,if it isn't built writes the VM's state,with its network choice makes the VMfrom its image locks .git,unless --clone starts its proxy,then the VM the self-check sets the VM up, then the cloneand devcontainer.json's commands opens the shell deletes the VM and whatdevvm made for it,and unlocks .git devvm checks everything the new VM needs before it builds anything, because a build can take minutes. That covers the folder, its toolchains, agents and layers, which it shows in a list in a terminal when you give none of --tools, --agents and --layers (what a new VM gets), the size, the ports, the network tier (choosing a tier), the SSH agent, the backend’s features and what the folder’s devcontainer.json says. Last, when the VM gets an agent and devvm saved an export of agents’ history for this folder before, devvm offers the newest one, asking in a terminal with no as the default (history_import_ask) and naming devvm history import without one (history_import_later). Before any of it, devvm takes the folder’s creation lock, which it holds until it has recorded that it made the VM in step 5. When the VM gets shared tools and the daily check is due, devvm checks for newer versions of them. devvm builds the image if it isn’t built yet (building), then the VM’s shared tools that the share lacks. devvm writes the VM’s state, with the network choice in it, before it makes the VM. If a later step fails, the VM never starts without its network choice. devvm also clears what an earlier VM of this folder that was deleted some other way left behind: it stops that VM’s proxy and link session and deletes the VM’s folder in its data folder, with its own rules, its run files and its logs. devvm makes the VM from its image. The VM mounts only the project folder, read-write, and the shared tools and its agents’ settings folders from devvm’s agent store, read-only. With --clone, devvm doesn’t mount the folder, and the VM gets its own clone of the repo instead (working on a clone). Unless the VM is a --clone VM, devvm locks the folder’s .git hooks and config (.git protection). It warns when the repo’s origin is an SSH remote and the VM has no SSH agent (ssh_remote_hint), and on Linux hosts it names the set-id files in the folder, including those an earlier VM of this folder made. When the VM forwards your SSH agent, devvm checks that the agent has keys. devvm starts the VM’s proxy, then the VM, confined to the proxy on every tier but open. The self-check runs, before the setup and the shell. Then, when you said yes to the export devvm offered, devvm warns when the tier that its .folder file records is less strict than the VM’s, or when it records none (history_import_less_strict, history_import_tier_unknown), and streams it into the VM, whose own tar checks its paths and unpacks it as the VM’s user (importing history), and a failed import only warns. devvm sets the VM up (the VM’s setup) and makes it reachable by name over SSH. It makes a --clone VM’s clone, or a workspace clone’s repos, all in one command in the VM, then copies each repo’s branches into it (the copy into a clone VM) and copies the folder’s own files, and then runs the commands of the folder’s devcontainer.json. devvm opens a shell in the VM in its own place, so devvm ends when the shell does. Without a terminal, the shell reads its commands from devvm’s input. Until the first shell opens, nothing of yours is in the VM yet. If you interrupt devvm before then, it deletes the VM, stops its proxy, deletes its pinned host keys and its folder, with its state, its own rules and its run files, takes the locks off .git, and for a --clone VM removes the repo’s remote for it.
data.a-subfolders-vm#A subfolder’s VM:
devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s physical path (a VM’s folder), so devvm in a subfolder finds no state file and names a new VM that doesn’t exist. When the backend has no VM by that name and devvm has no state file for the folder, and no VM whose folder moved there (a moved folder), devvm checks the folders the current folder is inside, nearest first (a subfolder). It finds each parent’s state file by that parent’s path in the same way, and it passes over only the parents that have no state file. The search stops at the first parent with a state file. devvm uses that parent’s VM when its backend has the VM and the state’s dir and folder match that folder. Otherwise the current folder has no VM, so a command that needs one says there’s no VM for it, and devvm makes a new one. A parent that was deleted and made again since its VM was made fails the folder check, and so does a nested project folder that a VM replaced through its mount, because a folder made again gets a new device and inode. Stopping there keeps devvm from skipping the nested folder’s VM for the VM of a folder further out, such as the VM that replaced it. A folder with a state file of its own uses a parent’s VM only with --parent, even when its backend has lost its own, so devvm rm there never reaches past it to a parent’s unless you ask for that. The current folder’s path is physical, with its links resolved, so a subfolder that is a link to a folder elsewhere is looked up from where it points, never from the folder that holds the link. devvm reads the current folder only for a command that acts on a folder’s VM, so devvm build, devvm rebuild, devvm images, devvm space and devvm gc also run in a folder that has been deleted.
The lookup stops before the home folder, compared by its physical path, and before the filesystem root. Those folders are refused as project folders anyway, but a VM made for one with --unsafe-folder would otherwise open in every folder below it. Using a parent’s VM changes nothing about what it mounts, because the current folder is already inside its project folder at the same path.
Every command that acts on the folder’s VM, devvm included, decides in one place which VM the folder uses, from what it found and the command’s --here or --parent, so they all decide the same way, with or without a terminal. By default, the folder’s own VM wins when it has a state file or its backend has the VM. Otherwise the parent’s VM is used, unless a repo of its own is in between, and otherwise the folder has none. A repo in between doesn’t count when the parent’s VM is a workspace clone whose state records that repo, by its path relative to the parent’s folder (clone.repos), because that VM has the repo’s clone at the same path and mounts nothing of this machine, so its folders are the VM’s as the parent’s own are. --here takes the folder’s own VM and never looks at the parents. --parent looks at the parents even when the folder has a VM of its own, takes the parent’s VM across a repo of its own, and fails when no parent has a VM (no_parent_vm). A command that uses a parent’s VM first names the VM and its folder (using_parent_vm) and asks nothing more, except devvm rm and the commands that give the VM more access. devvm rm then asks before deleting a parent’s VM (delete_parent_vm), with or without -f, and without a terminal it refuses (rm_parent_vm). The commands that give a parent’s VM more access, which a subfolder lists, ask before changing the VM (widen_parent_vm, [y/N]) and refuse without a terminal (widen_parent_vm_refused). They ask because the parent folder’s project chose its VM’s access, and a subfolder can be a project of its own that only happens to sit inside it. devvm adopt looks only for the VM of this folder’s own path, and devvm --clone skips the lookup, as --here does, so it makes the folder’s own VM. devvm passes the current folder to the backend as the shell’s working folder, and devvm host and devvm code use it as the folder to open. For a --clone VM, devvm first checks in the VM that the clone has the folder, and uses the clone’s top folder when it doesn’t.
On the way up, devvm also notes the nearest folder below the parent’s that has a .git of its own, a folder or a file, starting with the current folder. When there is one, the current folder belongs to a separate repo, so without --parent the parent’s VM is passed over. devvm then makes the folder’s own VM without asking, and every other command fails with no_vm.
data.a-vm-whose-folder-is-gone#A VM whose fol:
A VM’s folder is there, gone or not connected, which devvm ls --json gives as folder_state. It’s there when something is at the path its state records as dir (a VM’s state), so a folder made again at that path is there too, and a folder made again covers it, and so is a path devvm can’t read for another reason, such as its permissions. When nothing is at the path, devvm walks up to the nearest folder above it that exists and compares that folder’s device with the device in the folder identity the state records, or, for a state that records the folder’s volume (folder_volume), that folder’s volume with it, so a disk that a restart numbered anew isn’t taken for another (one VM per folder). The same device means the folder was deleted or moved from that filesystem, so it’s gone. Another device means it was on a disk or share that isn’t mounted, so it’s not connected, and a folder moved to another disk and then deleted counts as not connected too, which is the safe mistake. A state with no folder identity, or a device devvm can’t read, counts as gone. devvm ls and devvm space check every VM’s path when they list it, and neither devvm gc nor retention treats such a VM as leftover state, because its backend still has it.
devvm rm VM finds the VM by the name or alias in each state file, and nothing else, so a folder’s name never matches (rm_unknown_vm). A VM whose dir is the folder devvm runs in goes through devvm rm when it’s that folder’s own VM, the one the folder’s lookup finds (a VM’s folder). A VM whose dir names a folder with another VM of its own, which only a state changed by hand can, is a VM whose folder is there, so devvm rm VM never sends the command to that folder’s own VM. Otherwise devvm refuses a VM whose folder is there (rm_vm_folder_there), and one that its backend no longer has (rm_vm_lost). It then refuses a --clone VM unless --no-clone-check (rm_gone_clone), because there’s no repo to fetch the clone’s work into. When the VM has an agent and --no-export isn’t given, it refuses a stopped VM that mounts its folder (rm_gone_stopped), because Lima makes a missing folder that a VM mounts as the VM starts, and the export would make the project folder again. It asks next (delete_gone_folder_vm), which --force answers, and where devvm can’t ask it refuses unless --force (no_input). For a folder that isn’t connected, it refuses where devvm can’t ask, even with --force (rm_vm_not_connected), and otherwise it asks (delete_not_connected_folder_vm), which --force never answers. Once you answer, it reads the VM’s state again and checks that the folder is still in the state it found, and the VM’s status when it’s to be exported, once more, because the folder may have come back while it asked, another devvm may have made the VM again, or stopped it: each of those keeps the VM, with the same refusals. Last, it exports the history from the running VM, or from a --clone VM it starts, and deletes the VM as devvm rm does (deleting a VM). A failed export keeps the VM (export_failed_kept).
data.a-vms-folder#A VM’s folder:
Each VM’s folder, vms//, is named by the hash at the end of the VM’s name, which is the hash of its project folder’s physical path when devvm made the VM, and it holds every file that devvm keeps for the VM in the data folder:
Path in vms// Holds vm.json the VM’s state (a VM’s state) lock the lock that each change to vm.json holds (locks) policy the VM’s own network rules, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change run/ what the VM’s runs leave: its host keys for its current start (known_hosts), which every ssh of devvm’s to the VM checks, its port forwarder’s ports.pid, ports.status and ports.lock, its proxy’s config, proxy.json, which holds everything the proxy started with, its password and the company proxy’s from the environment among it (devvm _proxy), and its proxy.pid and proxy.status, its broker’s child’s proxy-child.pid and how the child is confined, proxy.confined (processes), the VM’s own CA and the next one in ca/ (ca.pem and ca.key, next.pem and next.key, and their lock), whose keys never leave this machine, its secrets’ bindings (secrets.json, secrets.policy), its link session’s links.pid and links.json, the remake lock (remake.lock), the hostagent it was started on (started), the ssh port its last start held for a minute (ports.ssh-hold), and on macOS the hostagent’s sandbox profile (sandbox.sb) logs/ its proxy’s decisions (network.jsonl) and its proxy’s broker’s and child’s own output (proxy.log), which the log files describe, its link session’s output (links.log) and its port forwarder’s (ports.log), each held to 1 MiB with one .1 file. The proxy’s child writes this folder, so devvm never opens the files in it through a link home.tar.gz the VM’s home folder, only while devvm makes the VM again devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s path as its dir, first in the VM folder that the hash of that path names and then in every other VM’s (a moved folder), so an existing VM has the name and the backend its state records, whichever backend you ask for. Only a new VM gets a name, which fits its backend’s limit, and when the VM folder that the path’s hash names holds another VM’s state, the new VM’s name ends with the hash of the path and a number instead, the first whose folder is free. The VM’s folder lasts as long as the VM, because devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop what runs for the VM, delete what devvm keeps for it outside the folder, and then delete the folder whole (deleting a VM), so the next devvm in that folder starts fresh.
No VM’s folder holds a socket, because a unix socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters and ssh adds 17 to a control socket’s while it makes it. The sockets that VMs need are in run/, named by hashes: each port forwarder’s control socket, run/port-.ctl, and each link session’s run/link-.sock and run/link-.ctl. With the default data folder, every socket fits for a home folder of up to 37 characters, and the ssh control sockets are the longest.
data.a-vms-state#A VM’s state:
A VM’s state is vm.json, a JSON file that only devvm writes. It starts with the fields every VM has: the file’s version, the VM’s random id, its name and its ssh alias, the image the VM came from with its build chain and the from image its base started from, its project folder (dir) and that folder’s identity (folder), the volume it’s on (folder_volume, bound to the folder’s inode and birth time, where devvm can tell it), folder_unchecked while that volume is still to check after a renumbering (one VM per folder), its backend and where that backend kept it (backend_at), created, the time its backend finished making it, and made_by, the version of the devvm that made it, which later changes keep. A VM without created never starts, because its creation didn’t finish. devvm takes the alias only when it’s one devvm could have chosen for the VM, which is devvm- with the folder part of the VM’s own name, or the full name. An alias edited to anything else never reaches the ssh config and names no VM, so the VM is reached by its full name. After those fields comes one section for each part of devvm that keeps something of the VM’s:
Section Kept by Holds net network tier the VM’s tier, and what devvm made for it: the proxy’s password, the salt that ends its placeholders and the last self-check’s result git .git protection the mode, the mode chosen while the VM ran, and what locking found: .git’s identity, the git folders it locked besides .git, and a hash of what the locked files hand over to the project folder ports the port allocator which ports the VM forwards, and the host ports devvm chose for its ssh, its proxy and its desktop agent SSH agent forwarding the VM’s choice, the start devvm last started it with, and whether that start forwarded its proxy’s relay of the agent tools the shared tools the VM’s shared tools by name, and their images and C library secrets secrets the secrets bound to the VM size devvm size the CPUs, memory and disk asked for clone --clone whether the VM has its own clone, the repo’s remote for it, and whether its branches were copied in; a folder of repos’ repos, each with the same; and each repo’s submodules the VM has a clone of (submodules), nested ones too, each with its path in its repo’s folder, its remote and whether it was copied, so devvm clone fetch and devvm rm’s check go over each one the VM has, even when this machine’s repo no longer has it. An older devvm ignores submodules, so its devvm rm wouldn’t check them, which matters only after a downgrade devcontainer a devcontainer.json the file the VM was made from, its variables and commands, which of them ran, and what of the VM came from the file and what from you (reading it again) desktop devvm desktop the desktop’s password links links and groups the ports the VM publishes, its links and its group remake devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update while devvm makes the VM again: the new image, the command, whether the home folder is kept and the history exported, what devvm update read again of the devcontainer.json, whether the new machine was made and what the VM had before it, and whether it’s done moved a moved folder the path the folder had before it moved, until the VM’s next setup moves Claude Code’s history from it Each section keeps what you asked for apart from what devvm made, which sits under the section’s made. devvm reads fields it doesn’t know without complaint and keeps them when it writes the file. A file that isn’t JSON, lacks one of version, id, name, image, dir or backend, or holds a section devvm can’t read is refused, and devvm names the file.
A new VM’s whole state is written once, with everything you asked for, before its backend makes the VM.
data.adding-to-a-vm#Adding to a VM: When devvm tools add, or devvm tools in a terminal, adds shared tools to an existing VM (adding to a VM), the tools it builds join the VM’s state and are mounted as devvm then launches the VM, and nothing is installed on the VM’s disk. A new agent’s config folders are mounted as the launch matches the VM’s agent folder mounts, which restarts a running VM after asking. devvm tools shows an existing VM’s layers but can’t change them, and --tools, --agents and --layers change nothing on an existing VM, because a layer goes onto the VM’s disk, which only making the VM again changes.
data.an-existing-vm#An existing VM:
When you run devvm in a folder whose VM exists, devvm opens the VM as it is and starts it if it’s stopped. Each time, it does these steps in this order:
devvm warns when an image the VM was made from has changed since, or when there are newer shared tools than the VM’s, and both warnings name devvm update, which moves the VM to the newer tools and, after asking, makes it again from the changed image (outdated VMs). It also checks for newer tools once a day. devvm ignores the options for new VMs, with a warning for each. The VM keeps its shared tools, which devvm tools changes, and its layers, which devvm layer add and devvm layer rm change. It keeps its network tier, which devvm network changes, and its .git protection, which devvm git-protect changes. It keeps its size, which devvm size changes, its ports, which devvm ports changes, and its SSH agent forwarding, which devvm ssh-agent changes. It also keeps its backend, and ignores --from and --no-devcontainer. devvm warns when the folder’s devcontainer.json isn’t the one the VM was made from, and the warning names devvm update, which makes the VM again as the file says now (details). devvm asks the backend for the VM’s status and config, once for the whole start. It compares the VM’s agent folder mounts with the folders in devvm’s agent store and names the folders that changed. A running VM gets the new mounts when it next starts. When a running VM has changes waiting for its next start, such as these mounts, a new size, a change to its agent forwarding or the open tier given to it while it ran confined, devvm names them in at most two lines, one for each change (next_start_size, next_start_agent, next_start_mounts, next_start_net_off), or past two the first change and how many more (next_start_more). Then it asks once, in a terminal, whether to restart it now (restart_now), yes by default ([Y/n]) when the mounts are among the changes and no by default ([y/N]) otherwise. A yes stops the VM here, so the steps below start it with the changes, and a no leaves it running. devvm checks .git (on each launch) and, on Linux hosts when it finds the VM stopped, names the set-id files in the folder. It skips both for a --clone VM, which mounts neither. devvm checks that the backend can still give the VM what its state asks for: its tier’s confinement, its ports and its SSH agent forwarding, and turning that forwarding on or off when the VM has it the other way. A backend that can’t is refused before anything starts. When the VM forwards your agent, devvm checks that the agent has keys. devvm starts the VM if it’s stopped. The backend’s start gives the VM what its state asks for: its size, the agent folders in devvm’s agent store, its agent forwarding and its ports. It changes only what differs from the VM’s config, together with what the VM’s confinement needs, and it changes nothing on a running VM (on Lima). When the VM uses devvm’s own agent, devvm loads the keys that the agent lacks, whether the VM starts or runs already. A running VM keeps its proxy, unless what the proxy was started with has changed (the proxy), and a VM made open after it started confined stays confined to its proxy, which applies the open tier’s rules, until it next starts. For a VM that runs on, devvm then says in one place what the VM gets only when it next starts, where that differs from what its state asks for: its size, its agent forwarding, its agent folder mounts and the open tier’s direct network. It warns of each with the line that names it in step 4, then once that devvm restart applies them (next_start), which is also what devvm size, devvm network and devvm ssh-agent say for a running VM you don’t restart. The self-check runs, and devvm stops a VM whose confined tier isn’t enforced. devvm sets the VM up and opens the shell, as for a new VM. A --clone VM whose clone wasn’t made yet gets it first. On the first launch after the VM started, the postStartCommand of the devcontainer.json that the VM was made from runs before the shell opens (commands). Steps 4 to 8 are the one way devvm starts a VM, whatever the command, and only a launch matches the agent folder mounts in step 4. So devvm host and devvm code, an export, devvm rm’s check of a --clone VM and a remake’s new machine check .git, check what the backend can give, start the VM with the size, agent folders, agent forwarding and ports its state asks for, and run the self-check in the same way. A new VM goes through steps 5 to 8 once it’s made, and in step 5 devvm locks its .git and checks its folder as step 6 of a new VM says.
devvm never starts a VM whose creation didn’t finish, because the VM would start without its tier (vm_unfinished). That happens when devvm was stopped after it made the VM but before it recorded the VM’s tier. In a terminal and without --no-input, devvm asks whether to delete such a VM and make it again (remake_unfinished, [y/N]), and yes deletes it as devvm rm does, then makes the VM as for a folder without one. Otherwise, and for a parent folder’s VM, devvm refuses, and devvm rm deletes such a VM.
devvm also never starts a VM on a project folder that was replaced after the finder found the VM. A parent folder’s VM mounts a nested project folder too, so code in it can move the folder aside and put a link or another folder at its path. On Linux, Lima passes the path to QEMU as it is, and its 9p share follows a link when it opens the folder at the VM’s start. On macOS, the Lima backend mounts the folder by the device and inode in the state’s folder instead (what devvm sets on a VM), so Virtualization.framework’s virtiofs share opens the folder devvm made the VM for, wherever it is then, and never what replaced it. devvm checks the folder three times in a start of a stopped VM: before step 5’s .git checks, which would otherwise act on what the link points to, just before the backend’s start, and once the backend’s start returns. Each check resolves the path’s links, which must give the same path, and compares the folder’s identity, its device, inode and birth time, with the state’s folder. macOS numbers its disks’ devices in the order they appear at boot, so after a restart the same folder can be on a device with another number. So when only the folder’s device differs and the folder is still the VM’s, the start records the folder’s identity as it is now in the state’s folder, under the VM’s lock, before the first check. The folder is still the VM’s when its identity has its birth time and its file system never gives a new folder a deleted one’s inode number (as for a moved folder). devvm reads that identity from the folder opened at its path with no link followed, so a link swapped in for a moment can’t pass a copy’s identity off as the folder’s. The finder takes such a folder as the VM’s in the same way. The backend then mounts the folder by the device it’s on now, never by the old number, which may be another disk’s after the boot, and each of the three checks compares the identity with the recorded one exactly. A failed check before the start refuses it (project_folder_changed), and one after it stops the VM and its proxy and refuses (project_folder_changed_stopped). The backend’s start returns once the VM has booted, so a VM stopped by the last check ran with what it mounted for as long as its boot took, on its own tier’s network. A running VM’s share never follows a link put in the folder’s place later: QEMU’s 9p share holds the folder it opened at the start, and Virtualization.framework’s virtiofs share answers “Operation not permitted” for it, which the project section of the end-to-end tests checks on both. So a launch into a running VM checks nothing more than the finder did. On Linux, code that replaces the folder only for the moment QEMU opens it, and puts it back before the last check, stays unseen, and the VM keeps what the link pointed to until its next start. On macOS, the same swap leaves the VM with the project folder where it was moved to at the start, and once the folder is back, virtiofs answers “Operation not permitted” for it until the VM’s next start, which the project section of the end-to-end tests checks.
devvm warns about the setup that allows this before it makes or opens a VM that mounts its folder (project_in_vm_folder). The finder walks the folders the VM’s folder is inside, as it does for a subfolder’s VM, and names the nearest one with a state of its own that was made for that folder and isn’t a --clone VM. It reads only the states and asks no backend, so a stopped parent folder’s VM counts too, because it writes to the folder whenever it runs. The warning comes once per run of devvm, and no other command gives it.
data.deleting-a-vm#Deleting a VM:
devvm rm deletes this folder’s VM and what devvm keeps for it: its state, its own allowlist and secret files, its network log, its .git locks, its pinned host keys and its ssh config entry. Other VMs, images and the project folder stay.
After the backend deletes the VM, devvm tears down the rest in one order, which devvm gc --orphans follows too. It stops the VM’s proxy, port forwarder and link session first. Then it deletes what devvm keeps for the VM outside its folder: a clone’s remote and the .git locks, other VMs’ links to it and the links its group made, its pinned host keys, for devvm gc --orphans the backend’s own leftovers, and the old machine of a remake that didn’t finish. Then it deletes the VM’s folder, with every file devvm keeps for it there, and last its ssh config entry.
For a --clone VM, devvm first checks the clone for commits that this repo hasn’t fetched and for uncommitted changes, in the clone and in the worktrees inside it (deleting the VM). It reads every repo of the clone in one command in the VM, a script sent with it that prints each repo’s branches, its status and each linked worktree below the project folder with that worktree’s status, as length-prefixed records. devvm reads at most 8 MiB of the answer and stops the command once it sends more, and it waits at most 2 minutes for the answer, so a VM that answers without end, or never, can’t keep devvm rm waiting. It takes only whole records of the repos it asked for, each worktree’s path clean, relative and below the folder, and any other answer fails the check, which keeps the VM. The repo’s remote for the VM goes with the VM, and devvm keeps the work fetched from it as local branches, which saved branches names. When the VM’s image has an agent, devvm then exports the agents’ history from the VM, starting it if it’s stopped (history), and it keeps the VM if the export fails. devvm reads the VM’s export through a writer that stops at 2 GiB (bounded): past that, it stops the VM’s command, deletes what it wrote and warns (history_too_large), and the delete goes on, as it does for a remake. devvm rm asks first in a terminal (rm_confirm), and where devvm can’t ask it refuses unless --force, the question’s refusal naming --force (no_input). devvm rm --no-export deletes the VM without the export, the clone’s checks still run and ask only in a terminal, and a VM whose creation didn’t finish gets neither, because it never ran.
data.listing-vms#Listing VMs:
Every command that reads all the VMs, such as devvm ls, devvm space, devvm gc and the writing of the ssh config, reads them in one place. It reads each VM’s state file on its own, then asks the backends for their VMs, each within 30 seconds, so one that hangs makes only its own VMs unknown. devvm ls and devvm space ask every backend, so they see a VM whose state is gone too. The ssh config and devvm gc --orphans ask only the backends that some VM’s state names, so a backend you don’t use, such as one that isn’t installed, never slows them down. The commands that need only what the states say read the states alone and ask no backend. They are devvm secret’s list, devvm rm VM, devvm adopt VM and devvm link add finding a VM by its name, finding a folder’s VM by the folder its state records and a VM whose folder moved there (a moved folder), the links’ checks, and the check of whether a key for devvm’s SSH agent is in a folder that a VM mounts, so that check counts the folders of stopped VMs too.
All of them fail in the same cases. A backend that can’t list its VMs, for example because Lima isn’t installed, fails devvm ls and the writing of the ssh config only when a VM’s state names that backend, and the ssh config then stays as it was rather than lose the entries of that backend’s VMs. devvm space and devvm gc --orphans name such a backend and leave its VMs alone instead. A state file that can’t be read never stops the others being read. Its VM never starts, so the commands that only read or show VMs leave it out, and devvm ls lists it with its name and status alone, when its backend has it. The commands that delete by what the states say, such as devvm gc with the shared tools that VMs use, and devvm’s SSH agent with the folders that VMs mount, fail and name the file, because that VM may use any shared tool or mount any folder (a file devvm can’t read).
devvm waits 5 seconds at most to find out whether a VM’s project folder is there, for devvm ls, devvm space, devvm rm VM, devvm adopt VM and a moved folder’s match, so a folder on a network share that hangs counts as there, never as gone. Every cell of its table, and of devvm’s other tables, is shown on one line without control characters, so a folder or a status with an escape sequence or a newline in it can’t change what the terminal shows.
data.locks#Locks:
Reading a VM’s state takes no lock, because each write replaces the file whole. Each change takes the VM’s lock, reads the file again, makes the change and writes the file once, so a command’s changes land together or not at all, and two devvms changing one VM at once lose neither’s change. Deleting a VM’s folder takes the VM’s lock too, so a change that another devvm is making to the VM’s state lands before the folder goes and never after it, and a VM made again in the project folder keeps its own state. A command holds one VM’s lock at a time. A change to other VMs, such as removing every link to a VM that devvm rm deletes, lets go of the first VM’s lock and then takes each other VM’s lock in turn, reading each one’s state again before it changes it. What no two VMs may have, a new VM’s ssh alias and the host ports devvm chooses, is chosen under the claims lock, run/claims.lock, which devvm takes after the VM’s own lock and holds until the VM’s state is written. A build VM has no state, so devvm chooses its ssh port under the claims lock alone and records it in run/build-ports/ while the VM starts, which keeps any other VM from getting that port until Lima has bound it. Each project VM’s start records the ssh port it holds in the VM’s own folder, as run/ports.ssh-hold. Each choice of a port reads that file for a minute while Lima binds the port, so no other start or build takes it, whether the start kept the VM’s port or chose a new one (the ssh port). The port is never the one that the build VM’s config kept from the image it’s a clone of, so its start always sets the new port and a build’s numbered steps are the same each time. The devvm that starts the build holds a file lock on the record while it’s there, so a record whose lock no process holds was left by a devvm that was killed. Once such a record is 15 minutes old, longer than Lima waits for a VM’s ssh, devvm deletes it the next time it chooses a port.
A folder’s creation lock, run/create-.lock, keeps two devvms from making one folder’s VM at once. It lives outside the VM’s folder because a new VM’s creation deletes that folder and makes it again. When devvm finds that the folder has no VM, or has its own VM whose creation didn’t finish, it takes the lock before the new VM’s questions and reads the VM’s state again under it. If another devvm made the VM meanwhile, devvm opens that VM as it is. devvm holds the lock until it has recorded that it made the VM, and lets go of it before the VM’s first start, so another devvm in the folder then opens the VM. After an interrupt, devvm lets go of the lock only once it has deleted what it made. A second devvm that finds the lock held refuses at once (create_running) and never waits on the first one’s questions. devvm rm takes the lock too before it deletes a VM, because a VM whose creation didn’t finish may be one another devvm is making, and one whose machine the backend lost may be being made again. It refuses while another devvm holds the lock, and refuses as well when it finds the VM’s state changed once it has the lock. devvm gc --orphans and retention’s orphans.age take the lock too before they forget a VM, because a VM that a devvm is making again has its state before its backend has it, however old that state is, and they refuse while another devvm holds the lock.
Every lock devvm takes is an OS file lock on an open file, which the system lets go of when the devvm holding it ends, however it ends. So a lock file is empty, it stays when its lock is let go of, and a devvm that was killed never leaves a lock held. The creation lock is the one exception that doesn’t stay: the devvm holding it deletes the file as it lets go, so no file named by the VM stays outside its folder, and a VM’s teardown deletes one that a killed devvm left. Besides each VM’s lock and the claims lock, the data folder has these:
Lock Held by version.lock each devvm checking the layout version vms//run/ports.lock whatever stops a VM’s port forwarder and starts the next one vms//run/ca/lock each launch readying the VM’s CAs vms//run/remake.lock the devvm making a VM again or finishing its remake, which a second devvm finds held and refuses run/create-.lock the devvm making a project folder’s new VM, from before its questions until it has recorded that it made the VM, and devvm rm deleting a VM, which a second devvm finds held and refuses images/locks/ the devvm building an image images/locks/rebuilds a devvm changing a rebuild counter oci-build.lock a Lima build of a base from a container image tools.lock a devvm writing to the share or swapping the tools lock making.lock each devvm making a VM or giving one new shared tools, shared, and devvm gc --tool-images --force, alone (cleaning up) groups.lock a devvm joining or leaving a group, or working its links out again agents.lock a devvm writing the agent store: an import, a save, or a start cleaning Claude Code’s plugins custom-secrets.lock a devvm saving or deleting a secret of yours, or binding a VM to one retention.lock the devvm applying the retention settings
data.making-a-vm-again#Making a VM again:
devvm layer add LAYER... makes the folder’s VM again from a new image, its own layers with the new ones on top, and keeps devvm’s settings for it and its home folder (adding layers to a VM). devvm layer rm LAYER... makes it again from an image of its other layers, in their order (taking layers out of a VM). devvm update first moves the VM to the newest shared tools, the step devvm tools update takes, which needs no remake because the tools are mounted. Then it makes the VM again from the image it has, when that image or one below it has a new key, so the VM gets the image’s new build (outdated VMs), and when the folder’s devcontainer.json isn’t the one the VM was made from, as reading the devcontainer.json again describes. An outdated VM without --force or a terminal is refused before the tools step, so a refusal changes nothing. The remake is one path in the VM’s lifecycle, which takes the image to make the VM from, so each command only works out that image and its own refusals: devvm layer add names the layers the VM has already, devvm layer rm names those it lacks (lacks_layers) and refuses a name that’s no layer’s, though it takes out one of the user’s whose script is gone, and devvm update says the VM is current (vm_current) when it had the newest tools and nothing in its chain changed, or names what changed (vm_changed) before it asks.
Before anything changes, devvm refuses a name that isn’t a layer, a VM made for another folder, one whose creation didn’t finish and, except for devvm clone, a --clone VM, and it checks that the VM’s backend has every feature the VM needs with the new image (missing and unreviewed features) and that the disk has room for a VM. Then it asks (remake_confirm, or remake_confirm_clean_home with --clean-home), and a parent folder’s VM only in a terminal (remake_parent_vm_ask). Then it checks what the remake would lose, as devvm rm does: the clone for devvm clone off, unless --no-clone-check, and with --clean-home opencode’s worktrees, unless --no-worktree-check (opencode’s worktrees). It asks once more when either finds work (remake_anyway). The remake then goes in this order:
devvm builds the new image, as for a new VM. It exports the agents’ history as devvm rm does, unless --no-export, and saves the VM’s home folder, unless --clean-home. The VM runs tar --one-file-system --ignore-failed-read in its home as its user, and devvm reads that stream on this machine and writes only what it keeps to home.tar.gz in the VM’s folder (the home folder’s copy). A failure in either keeps the VM as it was (export_failed_kept, remake_home_failed), but an export over 2 GiB only warns (history_too_large), and the remake goes on without one. devvm records the remake in the VM’s state (remake), stops the VM, its proxy and its link session, and has the backend rename the VM’s machine to its aside name, devvm--old, which is no project VM’s name, so nothing else takes it for one. On Lima that’s limactl rename, which keeps the old disk whole. devvm makes the new machine by the VM’s name from the new image, with what the state records: its project folder, its agents’ folders, the tools share, its SSH agent, its size, its ports and its ssh port. It records that the new machine was made, and it keeps in the remake’s section what the VM had of its base’s from, its shared tools, its ports and its devcontainer section (remake.was), so an undo can give them back. It clears which of its devcontainer.json’s commands ran, so those that run once run again. Then it starts the VM as every start does (an existing VM, steps 4 to 8), which pins its new host keys. devvm puts the saved home folder in, with tar --skip-old-files as the VM’s user, so what the new image has stays the image’s. The new machine is the VM from then on, so devvm records the new image and chain, and that the new machine is done. devvm deletes the old machine and ends the remake, which removes the section, then deletes home.tar.gz and opens the VM as an existing VM, setting it up first. The proxy reads the VM’s layers from its image, so the new layers’ allowlists apply from then, and those of layers taken out no longer do, as what the proxy started with has changed (the proxy). The VM’s id, its alias and every other field stay as they were (a VM made again). Until the new machine has the home folder in step 5, a failure or an interrupt runs the remake’s cleanup (remake_undone). It deletes the new machine, renames the old one back, whose next start makes it what the state asks for, as every start does, records that the machine by the VM’s name is the old one, gives the VM back the from, shared tools, ports and devcontainer section that step 4 kept, and ends the remake. When it can’t, it warns (remake_undo_failed) and leaves the remake recorded. The section goes before home.tar.gz does, so the saved home folder is there for as long as the remake is recorded. After step 5, nothing deletes the new machine, and a failure to delete the old one leaves the remake recorded as done.
devvm clone on and devvm clone off make the VM again from the image it has, in the other clone mode, which the remake records (remake.clone), so a remake that didn’t finish is finished in that mode (switching a VM that exists). Before anything changes, devvm clone on checks the folder as --clone does, and after the question devvm clone off checks the clone as devvm rm does, unless --no-clone-check. In step 4 the new machine mounts the project folder, or mounts none of it and keeps the clone at the folder’s path, and devvm records its mode when it records that the new machine was made. For the folder mounted, the mode comes with the .git protection a new VM gets. Before the new machine starts, devvm removes the repo’s remote for the clone, keeping the work fetched from it as saved branches, and then locks .git, because git can’t change a locked .git/config. After devvm clone on, devvm takes the .git locks off in step 6, once the old machine is deleted and it has checked .git as a launch that finds the VM stopped does. Undoing the remake sets the old mode back, takes off the locks the new machine got, and adds the remote back.
A devvm holds the VM’s remake lock, run/remake.lock in the VM’s folder, from when it finds the VM until the remake ends, and reads the VM’s state again once it has the lock. A second devvm that would make the VM again or finish its remake meanwhile refuses (remake_running), so it never takes a remake that’s still running for one that stopped.
A remake that’s recorded while no devvm holds the lock didn’t finish, because devvm was killed or its cleanup failed. The next devvm, devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update, devvm clone on or devvm clone off in the folder finishes it without asking (remake_resuming). When the new machine is done, devvm deletes the old one and ends the remake. When the old machine is still aside, or the new one was never made, so the machine by the VM’s name is the old one, devvm puts the old machine back and makes the VM again from step 1. Otherwise the old machine is gone, and the new one, made or not, never ran a shell, so devvm checks the remake again as before step 1, deletes the new machine and makes it again from step 4 with the saved home folder, or without one, warning, when the file is gone (remake_home_lost). Meanwhile every other command that acts on the VM refuses (remake_pending), devvm gc --orphans never takes the VM for an orphan, though the backend may have no machine by its name, and devvm rm deletes the VM and its old machine too.
data.reading-the-devcontainerjson-again#Readi:
A VM’s devcontainer section records more than the file’s SHA-256 and what it maps to of the VM’s own. It records which of the VM’s parts came from the file and which from you, so that devvm update can replace only the file’s. parts lists the toolchains and layers the file’s features mapped to when devvm last read it, and gave lists those of them the VM got from the file alone. A part isn’t the file’s when --tools or --layers chose that part’s list, when devvm setup’s layers have it, when the folder’s other files call for it, or when you unchecked it in the list. ports lists the file’s forwardPorts, and ports_gave lists those of them that devvm added to the VM’s ports, as devvm ports add adds them, because your ports didn’t forward them already and you didn’t give --ports. image is the container image the file names, recorded only when the VM’s base starts from it, and from_flag records that you gave --from, which wins over the file’s image for as long as the VM exists.
When the folder’s file isn’t the one the VM was made from, because it changed, it’s gone or it appeared, devvm update reads it again as a new VM’s file is read and refuses what a new VM refuses (devcontainer_reread, or devcontainer_gone for a file that’s gone). Then it works out what the VM is made again with:
Its parts. devvm drops the parts in gave that the file no longer calls for, and adds the ones the file now calls for that weren’t in parts and that the VM lacks. A part you took out stays out, and your own parts stay. Layers go into the new image’s name, after the layers the VM keeps, and toolchains go into its shared tools. Its base. With from_flag, the base stays as it is, and devvm says the file’s image is ignored. When the file names another image, devvm pins it to the digest its registry gives anyone, as for a new VM. When the file no longer names one, the base starts from $DEVVM_FROM, or else from Ubuntu’s cloud image. Its ports. In the same way, devvm takes out the ports in ports_gave that the file no longer lists, with the rule devvm ports rm follows, and adds the ones it lists anew that the VM’s ports don’t already forward, with the rule devvm ports add follows. A port you took out with devvm ports rm stays out, your own ports stay, and with every port forwarded nothing changes. A port of the file’s that’s part of one of your ranges counts as yours. Its variables and commands. The file’s new ones replace the old ones, and the commands that run once run on the new disk. The remake records all of this in its section (remake.reread): the new base’s from, the shared tools, the ports and the new devcontainer section. After step 1 builds the new image from the new base, devvm builds the shared tools for that base, as for a new VM, and records their files there too, holding the lock that new VMs hold so that devvm gc keeps the tool images. In step 4 the VM gets all four, so the port forwarder starts with the new ports when the VM starts, and an undo gives back what it had. A remake that didn’t finish keeps them, so it’s finished with what the file said when devvm update read it.
data.saved-branches#Saved branches: The local branches are named saved//, after the remote, and devvm never overwrites a branch. If a branch named saved/ exists, or one under it, or one it would sit under, devvm uses saved/-2 instead, then -3, and so on up to -99. If none of those names is free, for example because a branch is named saved, devvm rm refuses before it fetches anything and keeps the VM. When that happens as devvm is about to remove the remote, it leaves the remote and its branches in place. Branch names come from the VM, so devvm quotes them when it shows them, and it skips any name that git refuses as a branch name.
data.state-files#State files:
devvm writes nothing into the project folder. It keeps its files in two folders, and the folder a file is in says who writes it:
~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm) holds what you write: config.toml, your rules for every VM in policy, and your own layers and CAs. devvm never rewrites a file of yours there. It changes single lines of policy when devvm network adds or removes a rule for every VM, it writes a new layer’s files when you run devvm layer new, and it writes the folder’s version (the layout version). Your settings lists the folder file by file. ~/.local/share/devvm ($XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm) holds everything devvm writes itself, and you never edit it. devvm’s data folder lists it file by file, with how each one is cleaned up, and what devvm keeps on this machine also lists what Lima keeps outside it. The two folders use two formats. config.toml is TOML, which devvm reads strictly, so a key it doesn’t know or a value that a key can’t take stops the command, and devvm names the file and the line (when devvm can’t read it). devvm’s own records are JSON: settings.json, each VM’s vm.json, each image’s record and each shared tool image’s record. devvm ignores a field it doesn’t know in them, so a field that a newer devvm adds doesn’t stop an older one, and a change that an older devvm would read wrongly goes through the layout version. devvm’s other files are small ones of its own, such as pid files, the ssh config and the pinned host keys.
In the data folder, each VM has a folder of its own, vms// (a VM’s folder), and the rest is shared by every VM:
settings.json holds the defaults devvm’s commands save, below config.toml’s (where a default comes from). ssh_config is the ssh config for running VMs, and each entry checks its VM against the host keys in the VM’s own folder. agent-keys.json lists the keys added to devvm’s own SSH agent, with each one’s file, fingerprint, confirm and lifetime, and agent.sock is that agent’s socket. secrets/ holds each secret in a file of its own, on hosts without a Keychain. custom-secrets.json holds the definitions of your own secrets, their hosts, headers, variables and prefixes, never their values. images//record.json is each image’s record, and images/rebuilds.json holds the rebuild counters, by backend, --from and image. images/ubuntu.json is the Ubuntu cloud image that base starts from on this machine. tools/ holds the shared tools, each image with its record. Beside it are the tools lock, mise.lock, the mise.toml it was resolved from, mise.lock.toml, and mise.lock.checked, which says when devvm last checked for newer versions. logs/runs/ holds the run logs, and logs/tools-check.log the daily tools check’s output. exports/ holds the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save. lima/ is devvm’s own Lima home, unless DEVVM_LIMA_HOME moves it. cache/ holds only what devvm makes again whenever it needs it, so it may be deleted at any time. That’s devvm’s own mise (cache/mise/), the shared Nix cache (cache/nix-cache/) and the digests of the container images that --from bases start from (cache/from-digests.json). run/ holds what running VMs need that isn’t one VM’s, or whose path must be short: the QEMU wrapper on Linux hosts, the claims lock and, while devvm makes a folder’s VM, the folder’s creation lock (locks), the sockets of port forwarders and link sessions, named by hashes, in build-ports/ the ssh port of each build VM that’s starting (locks), and in builds// each build VM’s folder, laid out as a VM’s folder is. devvm deletes a build VM’s folder once its image is built, because an image’s VM never starts again, and otherwise when it deletes the build VM.
Each write replaces a file whole, so a file is never left half written. devvm makes its files readable only by you (mode 600), and the programs it keeps to run, such as its mise and QEMU wrapper, are mode 700, as are its folders. Before every command, devvm makes the data folder and ~/.config/devvm when they’re missing and sets both to mode 700, whatever mode they had. A wider mode on anything beneath them then opens nothing to others, and when devvm can’t set a folder’s mode, it warns and goes on. The folders that hold history, logs, keys or secrets (exports/, logs/, logs/runs/, run/, secrets/, and the run/, run/ca/ and logs/ folders in each VM’s folder) are set to mode 700 again whenever devvm writes an export, a log, a key or a secret into them, whatever mode they had before. devvm refuses to use one of those folders when it’s a symbolic link or not a folder at all, so it never sets the mode of whatever a link points to. The data folder and ~/.config/devvm may be symbolic links, such as into a dotfiles repo, and devvm follows them. When a file can’t be read, devvm names the file and the line, and you fix the line or delete the file.
data.stopping-a-vm#Stopping a VM: devvm stop stops this folder’s VM, then its proxy, its port forwarder and its link session. Once the VM is stopped, devvm applies the .git protection chosen with devvm git-protect while the VM ran, checks .git as a launch that finds the VM stopped does, and sets the locks that were waiting for the VM to stop (on each launch). On Linux hosts it also names the set-id files in the folder. It skips both for a --clone VM. Then devvm removes the VM’s entry from the ssh config. A VM that’s already stopped gets the same checks.
data.the-layout-version#The layout version:
The layout version says which folders and files devvm keeps in its two folders, and in which formats. This devvm’s is 1. The data folder and ~/.config/devvm each record theirs in a file named version, which holds the number alone. Before every command, after it makes both folders private, devvm takes version.lock in the data folder with an OS file lock and reads both files:
When both have this devvm’s version, the command runs. When a folder has no version file, as a new folder doesn’t, devvm writes its own version there. When either one is older, devvm changes the folders to its own layout, one version at a time, and then writes its version into both files. A change that fails stops the command and leaves the versions as they were, so the next command tries again. When either one is newer, a newer devvm changed the folders, so this one would misread them. The command stops before it does anything, with a message that names the file and both versions (a newer devvm changed devvm’s folders). A version file that doesn’t hold a whole number from 1 up stops the command too, naming the file. Help, completion, devvm --version and the commands that devvm runs itself, such as the proxy, skip the check. Each VM’s vm.json, each image’s record and each shared tool image’s record also hold made_by, the version of the devvm that made it, so a file from another devvm can be told apart.
data.the-run-log#The run log:
Each run that runs a command has one log, ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/--.log, which only you can read. devvm keeps the newest 20, or as many as logs.runs sets, and deletes older ones once the logs take more than 256 MiB together. It never deletes the newest log, or the log of a run whose process still runs, which it tells from the pid in the log’s name, so a background process or another devvm never loses the log it’s writing (a command fails). In the log, each command appears as a + line with its arguments, followed by its output, and a numbered step adds a # [2/5] line first. A command that devvm runs in a VM adds at most 4 MiB of output to the log, because a VM could otherwise fill this machine’s disk with it, and a devvm: truncated line marks where devvm left out the rest. A run writes at most 128 MiB to its log in all, because a run that lasts, such as devvm desktop’s, could otherwise log without end, and a devvm: truncated line also marks where that limit cut the log.
A VM’s proxy key and the build proxy’s password are written as devvm:@. Any other password in a URL, in a command’s arguments or its output, is written as user:@, and so is the password in a proxy’s address without a scheme, such as user:password@proxy.corp:8080, when the address has a port. So a company proxy’s password from your shell’s HTTPS_PROXY, which Lima can print as it starts a VM, stays out of the log, even when a command writes it in pieces. This covers the output of the commands devvm runs in a VM too, such as a VM’s setup or a devcontainer.json’s commands.
With -v, the lines devvm shows are the log’s own, so a VM’s proxy key is hidden in them as it is in the log, and devvm drops the control characters a command prints, so its output can’t move the cursor or change your terminal.
Lima keeps a log of its own for each VM, ha.stderr.log in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home, and it writes a proxy password into that log as it starts the VM. Lima also keeps a log of each of the VM’s serial consoles there, serial.log, serialp.log or serialv.log, and its boot scripts write the VM’s proxy URL, with the VM’s proxy password, to the console as they set up the VM’s environment. Once Lima has started the VM, devvm replaces each password in those logs with as many *, so the log keeps its length and Lima goes on writing to it. If devvm can’t change the file, it warns you and names it, and you can delete the file, which Lima makes again at the VM’s next start. While the VM runs, its proxy also replaces each password that these logs gain, within a second of its line ending, so a reboot inside the VM, which on Linux hosts QEMU carries out in place and which runs the boot scripts again, can’t leave the password in the console’s log. The proxy also holds the disk space that each of these logs takes to 10 MiB, with a .1 file of as much, on a file system with holes (Lima’s hostagent). A rotation’s copy, such as ha.stderr.log.1, has each password replaced, whether the start had ended or not.

data:
This page explains how devvm’s forwarder forwards a VM’s ports to this machine, which ports it never takes, and how it runs. Ports and size covers choosing a VM’s ports with --ports and devvm ports.
devvm forwards a VM’s ports with its own forwarder, never with Lima’s own forwards. Lima explains why, and what devvm sets on Lima instead.
data.each-connection#Each connection:
A program in the client that connects to db:5432 takes this path:
A connection over a linkYour program in the client connects to db:5432, which /etc/hosts names as 127.77.0.1. The client's sshd passes it over the link session's ssh, which this machine opened, to devvm _links on this machine, which connects over ssh, with the target's key and pinned host key, to the target's sshd, and so to the server on the target's own loopback, 127.0.0.1:5432.db:5432, which /etc/hostsnames as 127.77.0.1 the link session's ssh,which this machine opened ssh, with the target's keyand pinned host key 127.0.0.1:5432,its own loopback your program, in the client the client's sshd devvm _links,on this machine the target's sshd the server, in the target The client’s sshd carries the connection over the link session to this machine, where ssh connects it to the link’s unix socket. The socket is mode 600, in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700), and named by a hash of the client, the address and the port, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. devvm _links checks the link again. The link must still exist, the target must be the VM it was made for, by its ID, the port must be published, the tier rule must hold, and the target must be running, as its backend says. For a client on a confined tier, the target’s tier must also be enforced as the target runs, as devvm ls shows it, because a target that got a confined tier while it ran stays outside its proxy until its next start, and one whose self-check failed may reach the internet directly. devvm never starts the target for a connection. The link session asks the target’s backend whether the target is running and how its ssh reaches it, and the connections to that target share that answer for one second, so a burst of connections asks the backend once and devvm notices a target that stops within a second. For a client on a confined tier, the check of the target’s tier asks the backend for each connection, so it notices at once that the target stopped, and devvm logs the connection as refused because the target isn’t running, not because its tier isn’t in force. An answer that a connection closing cut short isn’t shared, so the other connections ask again. devvm makes every other check again for each connection, including the check of the target’s tier as it runs. It carries the connection over one ssh connection that it keeps to each target, with the target’s key and pinned host key, and the target’s sshd connects to 127.0.0.1:PORT in the target. That connection to a target ends when the target stops, and the next one reads the target’s host keys again, because a VM whose Lima config changed gets new ones when it boots. An HTTP client that uses the VM’s proxy settings sends db:5432 to the VM’s proxy instead, and the proxy connects to the same link socket on this machine (links through the proxy). Steps 2 and 3 are the same for it, so the link’s checks, its cap and its events hold for both ways in.
At most 256 of a client’s connections are carried at once, and the next one is refused. A link’s socket holds at most 128 connections waiting to be accepted on macOS, and devvm _links accepts nothing while it starts a process, so it accepts a burst of connections whole before it starts any of their ssh processes: it hands them on once 5 ms pass with nothing more to accept, once the first has waited 50 ms, or once 257 wait. Each one it accepted is carried, or refused when 256 are carried already. The ssh connection to a target takes in two file descriptors for each connection it carries, more than macOS’s default limit of 256 open files allows, so devvm _links and the port forwarder give the ssh processes they start the higher limit that devvm runs with. Each connection carried or refused is written to the client’s event log, which devvm network log shows, so every VM gets an event log for its links’ connections, whatever its tier.
data.groups#Groups: A group is recorded in each of its VMs’ own state, with the name the others reach it by, so a VM made again in a folder, which gets new state, is in none. The links a group makes are links in each VM’s state like the ones devvm link add makes, marked as the group’s, so the link session, the proxy’s list and every check of a connection treat them alike. devvm works out each VM’s group links again from its own links and the other VMs’ published ports whenever one of them joins or leaves, publishes or unpublishes a port, or adds or removes a link of its own, and it records and applies only the VMs whose links changed, as above. The design note has the rules and the threat check.
data.how-it-reaches-the-vm#How it reaches the:
The forwarder reaches the VM over the VM’s ssh, with a key and a host key that devvm pins, and it asks for no forwarding into this machine. Only a link session asks a VM for a remote forward, on a connection of its own. Every connection starts on this machine, and the VM opens none to it. The VM sees each forwarded connection only as one to its own loopback, and on a confined tier the VM still reaches only its proxy.
A connection to a forwarded port, such as 5173, takes this path:
A connection to a forwarded portYour browser on this machine connects to localhost:5173, where devvm's forwarder, on this machine, takes it over ssh, with a key and a host key devvm pins, to the VM's sshd, which connects to your server on the VM's own loopback, 127.0.0.1:5173.localhost:5173 ssh, with a key anda host key devvm pins 127.0.0.1:5173,its own loopback your browser, on this machine,where every connection starts devvm's forwarder,on this machine the VM's sshd your server, in the VM The forwarder is devvm’s own, the same on every backend. The backend only says how the forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd, which is a user, a key and a port on this machine’s loopback, and which file the forwarder follows to know the VM still runs, as Lima’s Ports section describes.
Each forwarded connection gets an ssh process of its own, which carries it over the forwarder’s ssh connection to the VM, and the forwarder carries at most 256 connections at once, refusing the next one. When accepting a connection fails while the forward still listens, such as when the forwarder runs out of open files in a burst, it tries again after a wait that starts at 5 ms and doubles with each failure in a row, up to a second, so the port answers again once files are free. Its log gets only the first failure of each run. When a forward closes, because the VM’s server stopped or its port is now another VM’s, the forwarder closes that forward’s open connections and ends their ssh processes too. A VM that never closes its end of a connection therefore can’t keep that connection’s ssh process, or one of the 256, after its port’s forward has gone.
A connection’s ssh process also ends once the program on this machine has closed its side and the VM has sent nothing for 30 seconds, whether or not the VM closes its end. A program that only stops sending, and waits for an answer, still gets one for as long as the VM keeps sending it, however slowly the program reads it, but the VM has to send something at least every 30 seconds, its first byte included. So a program that stops sending and then waits longer than that for the answer to begin, such as nc -N in front of a slow database query, has its connection cut. The same holds for every link’s connections (each connection).
data.its-process-and-files#Its process and fi:
The forwarder runs as a hidden devvm command, devvm _ports, one process for each VM. devvm starts it after each start of the VM, once the backend says the VM runs, and again with the new ports when you change a running VM’s ports. devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it, and a VM that stops some other way ends it, because the forwarder exits once the backend’s process for the VM is gone. Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm reads each time it starts the forwarder, so devvm ports changes the state and never the backend’s config, and the backend never hears of them. The forwarder’s log is ports.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/, and its ports.pid, ports.status, ports.lock and ports.forwarded are in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, beside the VM’s host keys for its current start, known_hosts, which the forwarder checks the VM against, as devvm’s ssh config does (ssh into VMs). Its control socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/run/port-.ctl, named by a hash of the VM’s name, outside the VM’s folder, because a unix socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. Processes has what the forwarder holds, what it reads from the VM and the bounds on its log, and ssh masters and relays has its ssh processes.
devvm reads every list of ports the same way, whether it comes from --ports, devvm ports or the VM’s state. Each entry is a port from 1 to 65535 or a range of them, such as 8000-8010. When the VM’s state holds a list that devvm can’t read this way, such as a file edited by hand, the VM doesn’t start and devvm names the value it couldn’t read with port_invalid, so a bad entry never becomes a port the VM didn’t ask for.
data.links-between-vms#Links between VMs: A link between VMs carries a client VM’s connections to a port that a target VM publishes. Like the forwarder, it goes over ssh, every connection starts on this machine, and it uses neither VM’s network, so no backend’s confinement changes and a confined VM still reaches nothing past its proxy over its own network. The design note has the rules, the threat check and what the prototype showed.
data.ports-other-vms-forward#Ports other VMs:
A host port that two VMs could forward belongs to the running VM that forwards it, never to a stopped one, so a stopped VM’s listed ports are free to the others until it starts again. Each forwarder writes the ports it forwards to ports.forwarded in its VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, after each change, with its pid on the first line and the ports it forwards on the second. The next three lines hold the ports it tried and couldn’t take, by why: those a program on this machine has, those past its limit of 256 forwards, and those this machine refused for another reason, such as a port below 1024 on Linux. It writes an empty record when it starts. A record counts only while that pid is the VM’s running forwarder, as ports.pid and the process’s arguments say, so the record of a VM that stopped or crashed, whose forwarder ended with it, holds nothing. devvm also removes the record under the VM’s ports.lock each time it starts the VM’s forwarder, so a pid used again never makes an old record count.
At each report from its VM, every forwarder reads the other VMs’ states and records again, and it never takes these ports:
a port that another VM’s running forwarder forwards now a port that another VM lists while that VM has a claim on it, unless this VM lists it too. A VM has a claim while its forwarder runs, and while devvm holds its ports.lock to start the forwarder again, so no other VM takes its listed ports between the old forwarder’s stop and the new one’s start. A VM that lists a port comes before one that forwards every port. Besides its VM’s reports, every forwarder checks the ports it forwards against those rules every 10 seconds on its own clock and closes a forward whose port is now another VM’s, so a VM that keeps its session open without reporting can’t keep a port. Closing a forward also closes the connections it accepted that are still open, such as a browser’s keep-alive connections, so none of them reaches the old VM afterwards. A VM that forwards every port therefore gives up a port within about 10 seconds of a running VM listing it.
A port the forwarder never takes for those reasons, and that its VM listens on, waits: the forwarder tries it again at each report, which comes at least every 10 seconds, and forwards it once it’s free, even when an earlier try found it taken. A port the other VM gives up can therefore take up to about 20 seconds to reach this VM: up to 10 for the other forwarder’s check and up to 10 for this one’s next report. When a start or a change of ports finds that another VM forwards one of the VM’s listed ports now, whether that VM lists it or forwards every port, devvm keeps the port in the VM’s list and warns you (ports_held), and devvm ports warns again, with the other VM in its JSON’s held_by. A port that another VM forwards isn’t a program’s, so it never gets ports_taken. A listed port of a running VM that its forwarder tried and couldn’t take is only logged by the forwarder, and devvm ports warns about it, as When it can’t forward describes.
When two VMs that list the same port start at once, neither waits for the other, because neither forwards it yet. The first forwarder to bind the port on this machine’s loopback has it, because the system lets one listener have it, and the other forwarder’s try fails. That forwarder sees the winner’s record at its next report and waits for the port from then on. No lock is needed for this, and no port is shared.
data.the-addresses#The addresses:
Each target that a client links to gets an address of its own in 127.77.0.0/16 in that client, starting at 127.77.0.1. devvm chooses it when the client’s first link to that target is made and keeps it for every port of that target, so two targets can share a port. The client’s /etc/hosts holds a block between # devvm links begin and # devvm links end, with a line 127.77.x.y NAME NAME.devvm.internal for each target. The VM’s setup replaces the block whole at each launch, and again when links change on a running client. The setup writes the file in place, never renaming over it, and only when the block changed.
A link listens at its target’s address on the target’s own port, never on the client’s 127.0.0.1 or ::1. At each start, the setup sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start to 0 where it’s 1024, which is on Lima’s Alpine VMs, so a link to a port below 1024 listens on that port too. Lima’s Ubuntu and Debian VMs already have 0.
The addresses are internal to devvm. devvm link and its JSON never show them, and the forwarder never forwards them (above).
data.the-link-session#The link session:
For each running client with links, devvm runs a hidden command, devvm _links VM, as one detached process on this machine. Its pid is in links.pid in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, and its log is links.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/. It keeps an ssh connection of its own to the client, never the forwarder’s, which starts with no forwards and asks for each link as a remote forward from 127.77.x.y:PORT in the client to a unix socket on this machine. That’s the only remote forward devvm asks a VM for. It reads the client’s links again every second and adds or cancels one forward at a time as they change, and a cancel leaves the connections that are open. A link whose address and port a program in the client already holds fails alone, with link_port_taken in the session’s log, which the next launch shows. Each line that the session’s ssh processes print starts with ssh: in its log, so no line of theirs reads as one of the session’s own, and devvm link add and the launch read only the session’s own lines.
The process ends once the client no longer runs the start it was made for, or has no links left, and devvm stop stops it with the client, which ends its connections and removes its sockets. Processes has what the session holds, what it reads from the VMs and the bounds on its log.
Every VM’s sshd allows remote forwards on 127.77.0.0/16 alone, with AllowTcpForwarding all, GatewayPorts clientspecified and PermitListen 127.77.*:*, written once into every image, so links never change or reload sshd. sshd matches the address a request names against that rule as text, so a remote forward on localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Root in the client can change sshd, so those settings protect only an honest VM. What keeps the VM from choosing where its connections go on this machine is the host’s ssh client, which accepts a forwarded channel only for a forward it asked for and connects it only to that link’s socket.
data.what-it-forwards#What it forwards:
Ports lists which ports the forwarder forwards, for --ports all, the default, and for a list such as --ports 5173,8000-8010, and how soon. A listed port also carries a server on the VM’s loopback (127.0.0.1 or ::1) to this machine. You can list port 22, which forwards the VM’s sshd to port 22 on this machine, while ssh by name keeps using the VM’s own ssh port.
The forwarder never forwards a server on an address in 127.77.0.0/16, on any VM, because that’s where a VM listens for its links to other VMs, so a link never appears on this machine’s localhost. A server of the VM’s own on 127.0.0.1 with the same port is forwarded as usual. It also never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, where the desktop’s local proxy listens, because the local proxy adds the VM’s password to what it sends to the VM’s proxy, and on this machine’s localhost other users and programs could use it.
data.what-it-never-takes#What it never takes:
The forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine has on any address. That program keeps the port and its localhost connections, and the forward waits until the VM’s server stops and starts again.
The forwarder also never takes a port that devvm records for a VM, even while that port is free. Those are the ssh, proxy and desktop ports that devvm chooses for VMs, running or not, and the VM’s own ssh port. devvm chooses and records every VM’s ssh port, whatever its tier, so no forwarder takes it in the seconds before Lima binds it (the threat check). It chooses that port only from the 17 ports that every browser refuses (the ssh port), which devvm’s proxy and desktop ports never take. A forwarder never takes one of those 17 either, unless its VM lists it, so a VM that forwards every port can’t take the ports other VMs’ ssh needs. When devvm chooses one of those ports, it also avoids every port that any VM lists, running or not, so a stopped VM’s listed ports stay free for it.
When a start, or a change of a running VM’s ports, finds that a program on this machine has a listed port, devvm doesn’t forward that port and warns you (ports_taken). The VM starts or runs on all the same, and the next start or change that finds the port free forwards it again. Ports says what happens to a program that binds a port on all addresses after the forwarder has forwarded it.
data.when-it-cant-forward#When it can’t forwa:
When a forwarder doesn’t start, devvm warns you and names its log (ports_forward_failed), and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.
When a running forwarder tries a listed port and can’t take it, it logs the port with the system’s error and records why in ports.forwarded. devvm ports warns about each such port by why:
ports_taken, when a program on this machine has the port, which the system reports as the address being in use. The forwarder tries the port again only once the VM’s server on it stops and starts again. ports_limit, when the VM already forwards 256 ports, the most a forwarder forwards at once, so the forwarder didn’t try it. The forwarder tries the port again at the VM’s next report once it forwards fewer. ports_refused, when this machine denied the forwarder the port, such as Linux keeping ports below 1024 for root. The forwarder tries the port again only once the VM’s server on it stops and starts again. Any other error, such as running out of open files for a moment, says nothing about the port, so the forwarder logs it alone, records nothing, and tries the port again at the VM’s next report.
The forwarder listens on both 127.0.0.1 and ::1, and it treats an error on ::1 as it would treat one on 127.0.0.1, closing the port’s 127.0.0.1 listener as well. A program that listens on the port’s ::1 makes the port count as in use, and after any other error the forwarder tries the port again at the next report, so an error that passes never leaves a forward on IPv4 alone. A machine without IPv6 on its loopback gets the port on 127.0.0.1 alone, and so does one that refuses the forwarder ::1 while it allows 127.0.0.1, such as one whose security module denies IPv6 sockets, and the forwarder logs that.
