devvm ports reads these from the forwarder’s record and binds nothing to find out, so it never takes a port that the forwarder is opening at that moment. A port that another VM forwards isn’t one of these, so it gets ports_held instead. A record that the running forwarder didn’t write, or none, gives none of these warnings, and neither does a record from an older devvm’s forwarder after an upgrade, which lists every port it couldn’t take on one line, without saying why, so devvm never says a port is in use when it may not be.
data.when-links-change#When links change:
devvm link add and devvm link rm record the change in the client’s state on this machine, never in a VM. On a running client they send its setup again, which rewrites /etc/hosts, and they start devvm _links if it isn’t running. devvm _links reads the links again every second and writes the list that the client’s proxy reads, so the proxy reaches a new link as soon as its forward is in place. A stopped client gets the change when it next starts. Links change nothing else in the VM: no link name is in its NO_PROXY (the VM’s setup), so no daemon restarts, and on Lima no link changes the VM’s Lima config or its ssh host keys.
When a link goes, devvm _links stops listening for it and ends the connections that are open through it, with their ssh processes. Each connection’s ssh process waits for the target’s sshd to end its channel, so ending it is what keeps a target that never closes its end from holding that process, and one of the client’s 256 connections, after the link has gone. When a target starts again, the connections still open through its old ssh connection end once the next connection to the target arrives, which makes a new ssh connection, or once the old one dies. A link whose name now leads to another target at the same address and port, because one link was removed and another added within the same second, ends the old target’s connections the same way.
devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from every client’s state and updates the running clients, and devvm gc --orphans removes links to VMs whose state is gone and the sockets that a killed link session left.

data:
This page goes through every process that devvm runs on this machine for a VM, one section each: what it holds, such as secrets and keys, the input a VM controls that it reads, what it writes and how far that can grow, how it’s confined, and who starts it and waits for it. Then it lists every listener on this machine whose bytes a VM controls, and why devvm is written in Go. The pages each section links to have the details, and the security model has what these processes protect.
Every process here runs as you. devvm runs its own long-running processes as itself, devvm with a hidden command, so their code is the binary you installed, and the other long-running programs it runs are OpenSSH’s ssh and ssh-agent, Lima and, on Linux, QEMU.
Process Started by Ends Confinement devvm itself you when its command ends none A VM’s proxy: its broker, devvm _proxy each start of the VM with the VM’s hostagent, its child, or devvm stop none A VM’s proxy: its child, devvm _proxy-child the broker with its broker a Seatbelt profile on macOS, and Landlock and a seccomp filter on Linux (the child’s sandbox) A build’s proxy, devvm _proxy and its child a build behind a company proxy with the build its child’s, as a VM’s proxy’s child’s The port forwarder, devvm _ports each start of a project VM, and each change of its ports with the VM’s hostagent, or devvm stop none The link session, devvm _links a start or a change of links, for a client with links when the client stops or has no links, or devvm stop none ssh masters and relays the forwarder, the link session and devvm with the process that started them none The QEMU wrapper, devvm _qemu Lima, on Linux hosts with QEMU QEMU’s restricted network, and a user namespace for a VM with .git pins The daily tools check, devvm _refresh-tools a launch of an existing VM, once a day when the check is done none The desktop relay devvm desktop with devvm desktop none The SSH agents you, or devvm for devvm’s own devvm’s own: at logout or a reboot none Lima’s hostagent limactl start when the VM stops a Seatbelt profile on macOS, for a confined VM or a build
data.a-builds-proxy#A build’s proxy:
A build gets a proxy of its own only behind a company proxy, because a build VM otherwise reaches the internet directly (a company proxy). It’s the same devvm _proxy broker and its child, with a config in the build VM’s run/build-proxy folder, which devvm makes again for each build.
Holds: a password made for the build, and the company proxy’s credentials. It has no CA, no secrets, no links and no Nix cache, so its broker looks up only the proxy secret, when config.toml’s company proxy names one. Reads from the build: its requests, in the child, with the same checks as a VM’s proxy, under a policy that allows any host on ports 80 and 443, but not this machine’s own or internal addresses. Writes: events.jsonl and proxy.log, in the build proxy’s logs/ folder, which its child writes and which holds nothing else of the build proxy’s, each rotated as a VM’s proxy rotates its own. devvm deletes the build proxy’s folder after a build that succeeds and keeps it after one that fails. The build’s devvm process holds the build VM’s own logs to their caps, with a company proxy or without one, as a VM’s proxy holds a VM’s. Confinement: none for the broker. Its child is confined as a VM’s proxy’s child is, under the same Seatbelt profile on macOS and with Landlock and the seccomp filter on Linux, and its only folder is the build proxy’s logs/ folder. Starts and ends: the build starts its broker, keeps its process and stops it when the build ends, which ends the child as devvm stop does, and a cleanup stops it when the build fails or is interrupted. It also follows the build VM’s hostagent, as a VM’s proxy does.
data.a-vms-proxy#A VM’s proxy:
Each running VM’s proxy is two processes, so the code that reads every byte the VM sends never holds what only the host should. The two are a broker, devvm _proxy -config FILE, with the VM’s proxy.json in its run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/, and its child, devvm _proxy-child -for FILE, which the broker starts and which reads the VM’s network (the proxy). The child asks the broker over a socketpair between them for a bound value, a changed file, a connection to a link, a login’s token exchange, a name’s addresses and a connection to an address or the company proxy, each by something the broker finds in its own config, which is one VM’s (the proxy’s broker has the design and its threat check).
The broker:
Holds: the VM’s password and the company proxy’s credentials, which it reads from the config and hands the child as it starts. It looks up each bound secret’s value itself, through the Keychain or the secret’s file, keeps a value for 5 minutes, an agent’s login for 30 seconds and a failed lookup for 5 seconds, and drops them all when the VM’s bindings change. It reads the agents’ login files in devvm’s store and refreshes their OAuth logins there, and it sends each login that the VM makes to the agent’s token endpoint itself, saves it into the store and rewrites the VM’s bindings, so a login’s real tokens never reach the child (logins made in a VM). Reads from the VM: the child’s frames, each at most 2 MiB, and through them a login’s token request, at most 64 KiB of headers and 64 KiB of body, and its endpoint’s reply, at most 1 MiB. It also reads your policy files and the VM’s bindings, each at most 1 MiB, and the links’ list, links.json, at most 1 MiB, which devvm _links writes. It reads them for the child once they change, reads the bindings and the links’ list again at each request that uses them, and reads the policy files again at each connection it opens for the child. For a VM that forwards an SSH agent, it reads the agent’s requests that the VM sends, each at most 256 KiB (the SSH agents). Writes: its own lines in proxy.log, its child’s pid file, run/proxy-child.pid, and how the child is confined, run/proxy.confined, and the login files and bindings above. It also holds the logs that the VM’s backend writes as the VM runs to 10 MiB each, with a .1 file of as much, the VM’s serial console’s among them, looking at each every second in a goroutine of its own (Lima’s hostagent), because they’re in the backend’s folder for the VM, beside its disk, which the child must never write. A proxy that an older devvm started doesn’t hold them, so a VM that’s running when you upgrade gets this once its next devvm command starts its proxy again. Bounds: one value, 8 token exchanges, 4 files, 256 links, 256 lookups and 1024 connections at once from its child, and an error for a request past them. Connects: for the child, to an address only once its own read of the VM’s policy files and of this machine’s addresses allows it, as the floor does, and to the company proxy of its config, each within 15 seconds. It also looks up names through this machine’s resolver for the child, each within 20 seconds. Listens: on the VM’s agent socket, ~/.local/share/devvm/run/agent-.sock, for a VM that forwards an SSH agent. It also opens the VM’s proxy port and hands the listener to its child (listeners). Confinement: none. It runs as you, with your Keychain and your files. Starts and ends: devvm starts it before each start of the VM, on every tier, and waits up to 5 seconds for it to say it’s listening. The broker says so once its child has said it’s ready, within 4 seconds of the broker’s start. It exits when the hostagent it follows ends, 15 minutes after it starts if the hostagent never appears, or when its child ends, and devvm stop also stops it (how long a proxy runs). The child:
Holds: the VM’s password, the VM’s CA and the next one, with their keys, the company proxy’s credentials, and each value that the broker gave it, until the broker’s lookup of that value is as old as the broker keeps one. Reads from the VM: every request the VM sends. It takes at most 64 KiB of a request’s headers within 30 seconds, also in an intercepted or transparent connection, and it requires the VM’s password before anything else. It reads a ClientHello of at most 16 KiB and 256 bytes within 10 seconds of its first byte. It looks at the changing files with stat alone and asks the broker for one once it changed. Writes: its event log, network.jsonl, and its own lines in proxy.log, in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/, each rotated before it passes 10 MiB, with one .1 file kept (log files). Its HTTP server’s errors go to proxy.log too, and so does what reaches either process’s error output, which counts toward the 10 MiB. For a VM with the nix layer, it fills the shared Nix cache, at most 10 GiB unless its config sets another cap. It reads and writes nothing else of yours or devvm’s. Bounds: at most 8448 open files, a limit it sets on itself before it’s confined, at most 1024 CONNECT tunnels at once, at most 2048 connections of every kind with the VM’s password, plain HTTP and idle ones included, at most 128 more that haven’t sent the password yet, and at most 2048 requests to hosts under way, its tunnels’ included. It keeps at most 1024 of the certificates it made for intercepted hosts for each CA, dropping the one used longest ago. A connection to the proxy, and the HTTP inside an intercepted or transparent connection, waits at most 10 minutes between requests, and HTTP/2 inside one carries at most 100 requests at once. A request without the VM’s password gets its 407 and its connection closed. A plain HTTP request whose client has stopped sending goes on while its answer keeps coming, and ends after a minute with nothing to pass on, so a client that went away frees what its request holds (the proxy). Nothing bounds how long a request or a tunnel lasts, so long downloads, WebSockets and slow streams go on. Listens: on 127.0.0.1, on the VM’s proxy port, through the listener the broker opened (listeners). Connects: nowhere itself. It asks the broker to look up each name and to open each connection to a host or to the company proxy, and the broker hands it the connection, so it reaches this machine’s loopback, its own addresses and the private and link-local ranges only where a rule names the address, or through a company proxy (the child’s sandbox). Inherits: standard input from the null device, proxy.log as its output and its error output, the socket to the broker as descriptor 3 and the listener as descriptor 4, and from the environment only TZ, SSL_CERT_FILE, SSL_CERT_DIR and GODEBUG. Run by hand without those two sockets, it refuses to start. Confinement: on macOS, a Seatbelt profile that denies everything but what the child needs, from its first instruction, because the broker starts it through /usr/bin/sandbox-exec with the profile as an argument, never as a file (the child’s sandbox). The profile lets it run and read devvm’s binary, write regular files in its logs folder and the shared Nix cache, look at the changing files with stat, and ask trustd to check certificates. It denies the child your home folder, devvm’s other folders, the Keychain, every connection of its own, over TCP, UDP or a unix socket, a bind, a fork, a signal to another process, and a look at another process, its arguments included. The child checks that the sandbox holds before it says it’s ready, and it says how it’s confined in run/proxy.confined, which is full seatbelt when it is. The broker adds a second line with its pid and when the system says it started, and devvm doctor reads the file only when that line names the broker that runs now. So doctor ignores a file that a newer devvm’s broker left behind when, after a downgrade, an older devvm started the VM’s proxy, and it names that proxy as one an older devvm started. When doctor can’t read when the running broker started, it says it can’t tell whether the proxy runs in its sandbox. Where sandbox-exec is missing or fails to start it, the broker starts it unconfined, writes a warning in proxy.log, and devvm doctor warns while the VM runs (the proxy runs without a sandbox). On Linux it confines itself before it reads a byte of the VM’s. It sets no_new_privs, limits itself to the same folders with Landlock, and installs a seccomp filter that refuses it every socket but a netlink route socket, connect, TCP Fast Open, a listen, io_uring, the calls that reach another process, a change to a file’s metadata by its path, the kernel’s keyrings, a program, a process or a namespace of its own. It says full landlock when the kernel has Landlock’s ABI 6 and its fix for signals between threads. An older kernel confines it in part, which it says, and the broker and devvm doctor warn of it the same way. Starts and ends: the broker starts it, devvm’s own binary, by its real path on macOS and as /proc/self/exe on Linux, and on Linux the system kills it when the broker’s thread that started it ends. It ends when it reads the end of its socket to the broker. It then stops listening, closes every connection it accepted, including the tunnels it carries and the WebSocket upgrades it passes on, and refuses one that arrives after that. It then waits for the handlers to return, 5 seconds at most, because Go’s HTTP server neither closes a connection that a handler took from it nor waits for a handler. When the hostagent ends, the broker closes the socket and kills the child a second past those 5 seconds. devvm stop’s SIGTERM reaches the broker, which sends the child SIGTERM, which ends it at once, and kills it if it hasn’t ended within a second. A child that ends, however it ends, ends its broker, and neither starts the other again.
data.devvm-itself#devvm itself: Holds: everything you keep with devvm. It reads secrets from the macOS Keychain with the security command or from files only you can read, and it writes each VM’s proxy password and the company proxy’s credentials into files only you can read, never into a process’s arguments (where secrets are saved). Reads from a VM: the output of the commands it runs there, such as a VM’s host keys, its settings to save and a history export, and the files a VM can write or swap, such as the project folder’s devcontainer.json. It reads such a file without following a link out of the folder, and with a cap on its size, and each kind of output has a cap of its own, such as 128 MiB for a VM’s settings and 2 GiB for a history export (coding agents). Writes: its run log, ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/--.log, with at most 4 MiB of output for each command it runs in a VM and at most 128 MiB in all, after which one line says the rest was left out. It keeps the newest 20 logs, or as many as logs.runs sets, and deletes older ones once the logs take more than 256 MiB together. It never deletes the newest log, or one whose run still runs, which it tells from the pid in the log’s name. It writes state files whole, renamed into place (state files). Listens: only in devvm desktop (the desktop relay) and while devvm agent login waits for a browser’s login (listeners). Confinement: none. devvm needs your Keychain and your files, and it’s the program you chose to run.
data.how-devvm-starts-them#How devvm starts t:
devvm starts the proxy, the port forwarder, the link session and the daily tools check detached, in a session of their own, so they outlive the run that started them and the terminal it ran in (the packages). Each gets no input and devvm’s environment without SSH_AUTH_SOCK, so none of them uses your SSH agent of its own accord, and its output goes to its own log or nowhere. The one exception is a VM’s proxy, which relays the agent that the VM’s start forwards, named in its config (the SSH agents). devvm marks every file it was given past standard input, output and error close-on-exec as it starts, so a terminal or a pipe that devvm inherited never stays open in them (things learned).
devvm finds such a process again by its pid file and its arguments, and it signals a process only while both still say it’s that process, so a pid that the system gave another program since is never signalled. A stop sends SIGTERM, waits two seconds, and sends SIGKILL only to a process whose arguments are still the ones devvm started. Each signal goes to the process’s group, which its own session makes it the leader of, so what it started ends with it, such as the forwarder’s and the link session’s ssh masters and relays, even when it’s killed and can’t stop them itself. A forwarder or a link session that gets SIGTERM from anything else, such as kill, stops its ssh before it exits, waiting up to two seconds for that, as devvm does for its cleanups. A process that devvm waits for, such as the proxy, says it’s ready in a status file of its own, which holds its pid and its address, so a file that another process left never counts (how long a proxy runs).
The run that starts a process reaps it if it ends first, and once that run ends, nothing on this machine waits for it. Instead, each one ends on its own. The proxy and the forwarder follow the VM’s hostagent through its pid file, ha.pid, which is the VM’s lifeline, and the link session asks the VM’s backend every 5 seconds whether the VM still runs the start it was made for. devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop a VM’s proxy, forwarder and link session while they still run.
data.limas-hostagent#Lima’s hostagent:
Each running VM has a hostagent, limactl hostagent, which limactl start runs and which runs the VM: on macOS it runs Apple’s Virtualization framework in its own process, and on Linux it starts QEMU.
Holds: Lima’s login key, _config/user in devvm’s Lima home, which every VM there authorizes, and the VM’s disk. Reads from the VM: everything the VM’s network sends, on macOS. On Linux, QEMU carries it. Writes: its logs, ha.stdout.log and ha.stderr.log, in the VM’s Lima folder, which also get QEMU’s errors on Linux, and the VM’s serial console logs there, serial.log, serialv.log and serialp.log, which QEMU or Apple’s Virtualization framework writes for it and which the VM’s root writes to through /dev/hvc0 and the other consoles. Each start writes them anew. devvm replaces each proxy password in ha.stderr.log and the serial consoles’ logs with as many * once the start ends, in the first 64 MiB of each log. While the VM runs, its proxy looks at each of these logs every second, skipping one that hasn’t grown. It replaces each password in what the log gained since, because a reboot inside the VM, which QEMU on Linux carries out in place, runs Lima’s boot scripts again and writes the password to the console again, and it rotates a log once it holds more than 10 MiB. When a line hasn’t ended yet, the next look reads it again from its start if that’s within 64 KiB of where the last look stopped, and otherwise from 64 KiB before that point, where it stars everything up to an @ as the rest of a secret. So a line that never ends costs at most 64 KiB more than what’s new in it, and a secret of any length is found. A rotation copies the log’s last 10 MiB, from a line’s start, to the log’s .1 file, replacing the one there, and then empties the log. The copy has each password and proxy key replaced, and the start of one that the copy cuts before its @ masked. The next look stars the rest of that one, which the writer goes on with, up to its @. So each of these logs takes at most 10 MiB and 10 MiB more in its .1 file, plus what a VM writes in a second. The log’s writer goes on at its own offset, past a hole that takes no disk, so the cap is on the space the log takes on disk rather than on its length, which keeps growing. The cap holds only on a file system with holes, such as APFS, ext4, XFS and btrfs, because one without them would write the emptied part out as zeros. What the writer adds between the copy and the emptying is lost. On macOS, a reboot inside the VM stops it, as Apple’s Virtualization framework ends a VM that restarts. Listens: on macOS, on the VM’s ssh port on this machine’s loopback, which QEMU listens on instead on Linux. It also listens on unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder and, for an open VM or a build, on loopback ports for Lima’s DNS resolver (listeners). Confinement: on macOS, a confined VM’s hostagent and a build’s run under a Seatbelt profile, sandbox.sb in the VM’s run folder, which denies com.apple.dnssd.service. A confined VM’s profile lets it connect only to the VM’s ssh port and its proxy on the host’s loopback, to the unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder and, when the VM forwards an agent, to that SSH agent, and it lets the hostagent listen only on the VM’s ssh port and those unix sockets. A build’s profile lets it reach either the internet, but not the host’s loopback apart from its ssh port and its build proxy’s port, or nothing, and it doesn’t limit what the hostagent listens on. Every profile limits only the network, so the hostagent can still read and write your files. An open VM’s hostagent and every hostagent on Linux run unconfined, and on Linux, QEMU’s restricted network confines a confined VM instead (confinement). Starts and ends: devvm records the hostagent it started in started in the VM’s run folder and checks that the VM still runs on it (the self-check), and the proxy and the forwarder follow its ha.pid. Nothing waits for it, and limactl stop, which devvm stop runs, ends it.
data.listeners-a-vm-reaches#Listeners a VM re:
These are the listeners on this machine that carry bytes a VM controls. Every one listens on this machine’s loopback or on a unix socket, so other machines never reach them, but every program and every user on this machine can connect to a TCP port on its loopback.
Listener Process Gate What the VM controls each forwarded port, on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 the port forwarder none: whatever connects reaches the VM’s server, 256 connections at once everything its server VM’s pinned host key, and browsers’ own refusal of the port everything the VM’s sshd sends, which root in the VM can make speak HTTP Lima’s DNS resolver, on loopback ports the system picks the hostagent, for an open VM and every build, never for a VM confined to its proxy none its lookups the unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder: the network socket on macOS, which carries the VM’s network frames, and Lima’s ssh control socket, ssh.sock the hostagent, and Lima’s ssh the folder’s mode its network frames, and everything its sshd sends the VM’s proxy port, on 127.0.0.1 the VM’s proxy’s child the VM’s password, before anything else its requests a build’s proxy port, on 127.0.0.1 the build’s proxy’s child the build’s password its requests the desktop port, on 127.0.0.1 devvm desktop the VM’s desktop password, checked on this machine its screen, once a viewer is in 127.0.0.1:1455, with ::1:1455 and port 1457 on both when they’re free devvm agent login, while Codex’s or opencode’s browser login to ChatGPT waits, but not with --device-code none: whatever connects reaches the agent’s login server in the VM, 16 connections at once the login server’s answers each link’s unix socket the link session the socket’s mode, 600 in a folder of mode 700 the client’s bytes, through its sshd’s remote forward or its proxy, and the target’s answers the ssh masters’ control sockets, run/port-.ctl and run/link-.ctl in ~/.local/share/devvm the forwarder’s and the link session’s ssh masters the folder’s mode: any process of yours that connects gets a channel into the VM everything the VM sends on that channel the VM’s agent socket, run/agent-.sock in ~/.local/share/devvm the VM’s proxy’s broker, for a VM that forwards an SSH agent the socket’s mode, 600 in a folder of mode 700 the agent’s requests, of which the proxy passes on only listing keys, signing and binding a session to a host A forwarded port and the login’s port carry whatever connects to them into the VM, a data.ssh-masters-and-relays#ssh masters and r:
The forwarder and the link session each reach a VM over one ssh connection of their own, its master. The forwarder’s master runs the VM’s report of its ports, and the link session keeps one master to the client, which asks for the links’ remote forwards, and one to each target. Every master checks the VM’s pinned host key, sets ControlPersist=no, and sends a keepalive every 10 seconds, giving up after 3 that get no answer.
Each connection that the forwarder or the link session carries gets an ssh process of its own, a relay, which runs ssh -W. A link’s relay can only ride on its target’s master. A forwarder’s relay rides on the VM’s master when it can, and it checks the same pinned host key either way, so it reaches only that VM.
Holds: the login key, and no agent (IdentityAgent=none). Reads from the VM: the bytes of the connection it carries. Writes: nothing of its own. A master’s messages go to its process’s log. Ends: a relay ends when either side ends, when its forward or its link goes, and 30 seconds after the program on this machine closes its side if the VM sends nothing in that time (how it reaches the VM). Each process that starts a master or a relay waits for it, and kills it when it ends that connection. devvm desktop and devvm agent login start relays of their own, one ssh process for each connection, which rides on no master (ControlMaster=no, ControlPath=none). A login’s relay ends as the forwarder’s do, and a login carries at most 16 connections at once, closing any past that, so whatever else on this machine connects to its port can’t start ssh processes without end. A viewer’s ssh process gets 2 seconds to end once its viewer leaves, and is then killed.
data.the-daily-tools-check#The daily tools ch:
devvm _refresh-tools asks for the shared tools’ newest versions once a day, so a later launch can offer them (shared tools).
Holds: the company proxy’s password, when config.toml sets the proxy, in the environment of the mise it runs. Reads: nothing from a VM. It downloads devvm’s pinned mise, checked by its SHA-256, mise reads the tools’ versions from the internet, and the check fetches .NET’s release data. Writes: the shared tools’ lock, under its lock, the time of the check, and its output to ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/tools-check.log, which each check starts empty. Starts and ends: a launch of an existing VM starts it when the shared tools have a lock file and a day has passed since the last check, and doesn’t wait for it. DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK turns it off.
data.the-desktop-relay#The desktop relay:
devvm desktop runs the relay in its own process, for as long as it runs (on this machine).
Holds: the VM’s desktop password, which never goes into the VM. Reads from the VM: the VM’s side of VNC’s handshake, which is a version, at most 255 security types and a result, within 15 seconds, and then the VM’s screen, which it passes to the viewer as it is. Writes: lines to the run log when each viewer connects and disconnects, and for each connection it refuses, and each ssh process’s messages. Bounds: at most 8 connections at once, counting those still in their handshake, one check of a password at a time, and a second’s wait after a wrong one. Listens: on 127.0.0.1 alone, on the VM’s desktop port (listeners). When accepting a connection fails but the port stays open, as when it runs out of open files, it tries again after 5 ms and then twice as long each time, up to a second, and logs only the first failure of a run. Starts and ends: it ends when you press Ctrl+C, or when the VM no longer runs, which it checks every 5 seconds, and it waits for each viewer’s connection.
data.the-link-session#The link session:
One link session runs for each running client VM with links, as devvm _links VM (the link session).
Holds: the login key and the pinned host keys of the client and of each target it connects to. Reads from the VMs: the bytes of each link’s connection, both ways, and the messages of the client’s sshd, such as its refusal of a forward, each cut at 512 bytes. Writes: links.json in the client’s run folder, the client’s event log, network.jsonl, with the proxy’s own writer, so it rotates by the same rule, and its log, links.log, in the client’s logs folder, which it writes, limits and rotates past 1 MiB as the forwarder does its own. Its warning that the client refused to listen for a link carries the client’s sshd’s words, and the client chooses how often it comes, so each warning takes its turn from the same limit as the log’s lines. Bounds: at most 256 of the client’s connections at once. Listens: on a unix socket for each link, mode 600, in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700). Confinement: none. Starts and ends: a start of the client and a change of its links start it. It ends once the client no longer runs the start it was made for, which it checks every 5 seconds, or has no links left, and devvm stop stops it with the client.
data.the-port-forwarder#The port forwarder:
One forwarder runs for each running project VM that forwards ports, as devvm _ports (its process and files).
Holds: the key that the backend logs in to the VM with, which on Lima is Lima’s _config/user, and the VM’s host keys for its current start. Its ssh uses no agent. Reads from the VM: the VM’s report of the ports it listens on, which comes over one ssh session about every 10 seconds, as the VM paces it. A line of the report has at most 127 bytes and its newline, and a longer line, or a report of more than 4096 lines, ends the session, which the forwarder opens again, so nothing is cut. The forwarder applies at most one report every 500 ms. It also reads the bytes of each forwarded connection, which it carries as they are, and the other VMs’ records of their ports. Writes: ports.forwarded in the VM’s run folder, and its log, ports.log, in the VM’s logs folder. The VM chooses some of what goes in the log, so the forwarder makes at most 200 writes at once and then one every 10 seconds, each cut at 512 bytes and without control characters other than newlines and tabs. The log is also its process’s output, and before each line the forwarder checks its size on disk, so a line that would take it past 1 MiB rotates it first. The log’s end goes to ports.log.1, replacing the one there, and the log starts empty. devvm rotates a log that an earlier forwarder left past 1 MiB as it starts the next one. Bounds: at most 256 forwards, and at most 256 connections at once. When accepting a connection fails while the port still listens, such as when the forwarder runs out of open files, it tries again after a wait that starts at 5 ms and doubles with each failure in a row, up to a second, and logs only the first failure of a run, as the link session and a login’s forward do. Listens: on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 for each forwarded port (listeners). Confinement: none. Its ssh processes get the higher limit of open files that devvm runs with. Starts and ends: devvm starts it once the backend says the VM runs, and again when the VM’s ports change. It exits once the VM’s hostagent is gone, which it checks every 2 seconds, and devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it.
data.the-qemu-wrapper-and-its-keeper#The QEMU:
On Linux hosts, Lima starts each VM’s QEMU through a wrapper that devvm writes into ~/.local/share/devvm/run/qemu/, which runs devvm _qemu exec (confinement).
devvm _qemu exec reads Lima’s arguments for QEMU and adds restrict=on to Lima’s one network, except for an open VM and a build with the internet, and for a VM confined to its proxy it adds a guestfwd to that proxy. It refuses arguments of any other shape (qemu_refused). It then runs QEMU in its place, or, for a VM with .git pins, which a VM whose .git protection is on has, starts the keeper and waits for it. Only such a VM gets a user namespace. The keeper, devvm _qemu pinned, runs in a user namespace and a mount namespace of its own, as you, with the capability to mount in that namespace alone. It makes .git’s hooks and config read-only there, and it pins a path again after any change in a folder it watches, and every 2 seconds. It records each pin it makes again in git-pins.jsonl in the VM’s run folder, and on QEMU’s error output, which Lima logs. Past 1 MiB, the file takes no more events, only a line for each that says it went unrecorded, up to 64 KiB more, and the next check names those. It starts QEMU through devvm _qemu drop, which clears its ambient, permitted, effective and inheritable capabilities, keeping the bounding set, sets no_new_privs, and runs QEMU. devvm _qemu probe DIR checks, in a namespace of its own, that a file in DIR can be pinned. devvm _qemu connect is what QEMU’s guestfwd runs for each connection that the VM makes to 192.168.5.4:3128. It connects to the VM’s proxy and carries the bytes both ways, so it reads only what the VM sends to its proxy, which the proxy checks. Each one is a process of its own, about 7.7 MB of memory, so it carries at most 256 of the VM’s connections at once, about 2 GB for a VM that holds them all, each holding a slot, which is a lock file in the proxy.slots folder of the VM’s run folder. A connection past that gets a 503 and is closed before it reaches the proxy, and QEMU’s error output, which Lima logs, says so at most once a minute (qemu_connects_full). A VM that was running when devvm was upgraded has no slots, and so no limit, until its next start. It has no idle timeout and no limit on the bytes it carries, because the proxy bounds what each connection carries, and a long download or a quiet stream must go on. The keeper dies with devvm _qemu exec, and QEMU with the keeper. devvm _qemu connect ends when its connection ends, and its slot is free again.
data.the-ssh-agents#The SSH agents:
A VM whose SSH agent choice is on gets your own agent, which devvm doesn’t start, stop or confine. A VM whose choice is devvm gets devvm’s own agent, which is OpenSSH’s ssh-agent, run as ssh-agent -a ~/.local/share/devvm/agent.sock.
Holds: only the keys you add with devvm ssh-agent add, each for 12 hours unless you chose another lifetime. devvm refuses a key in a folder that a VM mounts. Reads from the VM: only the requests that the VM’s proxy passes on. A VM can use the keys while it’s connected, and it can’t copy them. Starts and ends: devvm starts it when a VM that uses it starts, or when you add a key, and doesn’t stop it, so it runs until you log out or restart this machine. devvm keeps no pid file for it. Apart from the exceptions below, a VM that devvm starts never reaches either agent’s socket itself. ssh-agent answers every request that reaches it by its own rules, and a forwarded connection may send any of them, so a VM with the agent’s own socket could remove every key with ssh-add -D, lock the agent with a password of its own with ssh-add -x, or add keys to it without bound. Every VM that uses the agent would lose it then, and with your own agent, so would you. Instead, the VM’s proxy’s broker, never its child, listens on a socket of the VM’s own, ~/.local/share/devvm/run/agent-.sock, mode 600, and the VM’s start forwards that socket, as devvm’s own connections to the VM and its ssh entry do, so an editor forwards it too. The proxy passes on only three requests to the agent: listing its keys, signing with one, and session-bind@openssh.com, which ssh sends as it forwards an agent and as it logs in with one, so a key you added with destination constraints (ssh-add -h) keeps them. It answers any other request with SSH_AGENT_FAILURE itself, and logs the first one on each connection in its own log, so removing a key, locking the agent, adding a key and loading a smartcard’s keys never reach the agent. It reads each message whole, at most 256 KiB, as ssh-agent does, and ends a connection that sends a longer one. Each VM’s proxy carries at most 16 connections at once, each with a connection of its own to the agent, and it closes a connection that sends no whole request for 2 minutes. The cap is each VM’s own, not the agent’s, so VMs that share an agent can hold 16 connections each, and enough of them could still use up the agent’s open files, 256 by default on macOS. A request that the agent asks you about, for a key added with --confirm, waits as long as the agent does, and ssh-agent answers one request at a time, so while it waits for your answer, every other VM that shares the agent, and you, wait too.
devvm records in the VM’s state each start it made. For a start whose choice forwards an agent, it also records that the start forwarded the relay, even when devvm ran the start without SSH_AUTH_SOCK and so had no agent to relay. For such a start, devvm’s own connections and the ssh entry name the relay even while the proxy starts again or is gone, or relays nothing, so the VM then has no agent, never the agent’s own socket, even when a later command runs from a shell that has one. A VM running a start that devvm didn’t record, such as one started with devvm limactl start, gets no agent in its ssh entry, and devvm’s own connections get its proxy’s relay of the agent that devvm last started it with, or none, never the agent’s own socket. Only a VM that an earlier devvm started without the relay keeps the agent’s own socket, in devvm’s connections and its ssh entry, until its next start.
The proxy relays the agent that the VM’s start chose, and it keeps relaying that agent until the VM’s next start, even when it starts again for a running VM, so a change of choice waits for the next start, as it does for the VM’s backend. The proxy deletes the socket when it ends with the VM’s hostagent, devvm deletes it when it stops the proxy, and devvm gc --orphans deletes one that a killed proxy left, which nothing listens on.
data.why-go#Why Go:
devvm stays in Go, and its own history shows why. None of its first 712 commits fixes a memory-safety bug, and none fixes a data race that got past Go’s race detector, which every test run uses. devvm’s own code imports unsafe only for a few raw system calls on Linux, which confine the proxy’s child and set a file’s times through its descriptor, and it builds without cgo. Its security and reliability fixes fall mostly into five classes, which a language’s types don’t prevent:
Lifecycles and resources, such as a relay that outlived its link, a VM’s QEMU left running without its hostagent, and a VM that could make devvm read more than it should. Policy semantics, such as a 6to4 address judged by its IPv4 address, and a placeholder swapped only when it’s the whole value. Secret leaks, such as a proxy password in Lima’s log, and a resolver’s error in a VM’s refusal reason. Races between processes, such as a proxy that had just started looking gone, and two runs choosing ports or making a folder’s VM at once. File-system trust, such as a project folder replaced after devvm found it, a folder that a VM names as a git folder, a link under a folder’s path, and a project folder mounted by its path rather than as the folder itself. A port to Rust would cost what keeps devvm easy to keep:
One static binary, built with CGO_ENABLED=0 for every platform from one machine. Go’s crypto/tls needs no C toolchain, while rustls’s usual providers, aws-lc-rs and ring, have C in them. A small dependency tree: Go’s standard library, Go’s own x modules, Cobra and pflag, a TOML parser and go-i18n, with the few modules that cobra/doc brings in, where a Rust proxy on the usual async, HTTP and TLS crates brings in about a hundred. One owner for each concern, which depguard, forbidigo and the structure test enforce, and which none of them could see across a language boundary. The proxy is the only part that could be split off, and it’s bound to the rest: its broker looks up secrets and refreshes agents’ logins with devvm’s own code, its config is a schema that every release’s state keeps, and its child reads its built-in policies from devvm’s binary.
The answer changes only for a requirement Go can’t meet, such as intercepting QUIC. Even then, only that piece would move, as a process of its own.

data:
devvm treats everything in a VM as untrusted, including a coding agent with root, because the VM’s user has passwordless sudo. This page explains how devvm keeps that code away from the rest of your machine. Staying safe lists what a VM can reach and the habits that keep you safe, and Attack vectors goes through common attacks one by one and lists what devvm leaves open.
All of it rests on the VM’s boundary. Processes goes through each process on this machine that a VM’s bytes reach, what it holds and how it’s confined, and lists the listeners a VM reaches.
data.a-projects-devcontainerjson#A project’s:
A project’s devcontainer.json belongs to the project, and so to the VM, which can rewrite it for the folder’s next VM, or for the VM itself when you run devvm update. devvm reads it only when it makes a VM, new or again, and uses only what it can do inside the VM. Nothing in it runs on this machine, so initializeCommand never runs. Nothing in it reaches this machine’s files, because devvm doesn’t follow a link out of the folder, or this machine’s environment, because devvm refuses ${localEnv:…} before it makes anything. It can’t add a mount or change the VM’s network tier or other confinement.
Its commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, confined like anything else in it. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script, and it refuses docker-outside-of-docker. devvm uses its image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks anonymously, so it never uses a container image that only your Docker has or that only your registry login reaches. It refuses a registry named localhost or by an address that isn’t the internet’s, and its lookup connects only to the internet’s addresses, so it never uses an image on this machine or its network, except through a company proxy, which resolves the registry’s name itself (attack vectors).
An existing VM never changes when the file does, until you run devvm update, which says it reads the file again and asks before it makes the VM again. The file read again is held to the same refusals as a new VM’s, and it can’t replace a base you chose with --from, bring back a port you took out with devvm ports rm, or change its network tier, size, SSH agent or .git protection, which devvm keeps.
Its forwardPorts are added to the VM’s ports, as devvm ports add adds them, even beyond a list you narrowed, both when devvm makes the VM and when devvm update reads the file again. They go through the one port forwarder, so they listen on this machine’s loopback alone (127.0.0.1 and ::1), never take a port that a program on this machine has, and never take a port another VM forwards (port forwarding). What a cloned repo’s file opens is so only what devvm ports add could open, but it reaches whatever on this machine connects to those ports, a browser’s pages included (attack vectors).
data.git-protection#.git protection: The VM can’t change the parts of .git that run code on the host, because devvm locks hooks and config. On macOS it sets a flag the VM can’t clear, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the user namespace that QEMU runs in. A Linux host whose kernel doesn’t let devvm use a user namespace has no locks, and devvm only watches .git there (details).
data.network-tiers#Network tiers:
A VM on a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, reaches nothing but its own proxy on the host and the links you added to it. On macOS its Lima process runs under a macOS sandbox, and on Linux QEMU’s network is restricted (details). Even root in the VM can’t get around that. A link’s connections don’t use the VM’s network, because this machine carries them over ssh, and only to a port that another VM on the same tier or a stricter one publishes. An open VM runs on its backend’s own network, and its proxy applies no rules.
The proxy applies the tier’s rules, and it refuses the host’s own addresses and internal addresses unless a rule names them (the proxy). The one thing that VMs share through their proxies is the shared Nix cache, for those with the nix layer. Only the host writes it, with packages from cache.nixos.org whose signature it checked, and nothing a VM sends is stored, so a VM can make the host fetch but can’t change what another VM gets. After each start, devvm checks that the VM still runs confined and can’t connect out directly, and it stops a VM that fails the check instead of opening it (the self-check).
data.one-vm-per-folder#One VM per folder:
A VM belongs to the folder it was made for, which devvm knows by its path and by the folder itself: its device and inode, and its birth time where the file system keeps one. macOS numbers its disks’ devices in the order they appear at boot, so after a restart an unchanged folder can be on a device with another number. devvm still takes it as the same folder when it’s at the same path, with no link on that path, and has the same inode and birth time on a file system that never gives a new folder a deleted one’s inode number. That’s safe because nothing in a VM can give a folder an inode and a birth time, and a copy that keeps both, such as a snapshot, is at another path unless you mount it at the folder’s own. devvm reads the folder’s identity from the folder opened at its path with no link followed, so a link that a VM puts there for a moment can’t pass such a copy off as the folder. For a VM whose state records the folder’s volume (below), the folder on the renumbered disk must also be on that volume when devvm can tell it, so a copy of the disk that has a volume ID of its own but keeps the folder’s inode and birth time, mounted at the folder’s own path, is another folder. A copy that keeps the volume ID too, as dd makes, still matches, as below. The VM’s next start records the folder on its device as it is now, before the start mounts it, and never when the folder is on another volume (an existing VM). When you delete a folder and make it again at the same path, or clone another repo where an old one was, devvm refuses to give the new folder the old folder’s VM, so the new folder never quietly gets what’s in the old VM’s disk. devvm rm deletes the old VM and devvm adopt gives it to the new folder, and each does so only after you confirm (a folder made again). When you move or rename the folder, the folder at its new path is the same folder, so devvm offers it the VM, and moves the VM only after you confirm (a moved or renamed folder). It never offers a VM to a copy, to a folder another user owns, or on a file system that may give a new folder the inode number of a deleted one, so a VM never moves to a folder that only looks like its own. The folders that get the offer are those whose file system records a birth time: on macOS, folders on APFS and HFS+, and on Linux, folders on ext4, XFS, Btrfs, tmpfs, ZFS, F2FS and bcachefs. Folders on network shares, FUSE file systems and USB drives formatted with FAT or exFAT never get the offer.
A folder that moved, and whose disk was numbered anew since, is on another device at another path, so its device, inode and birth time alone don’t name it. So the VM’s state also records the folder’s volume, which no renumbering changes. On macOS that’s its volume UUID, as diskutil info gives it for the folder’s mount point, and on Linux it’s the file system’s own ID (f_fsid) on ext4, Btrfs, where each subvolume has its own, and ZFS. XFS, F2FS and tmpfs derive that ID from the device or the mount, so a folder on them, or on any other file system, records no volume and keeps the rule above. devvm reads the folder’s mount point, its device and its file system’s ID from the folder opened with no link on its path, and on macOS it takes diskutil’s answer only when it names that mount point and that device, so a volume mounted there meanwhile isn’t taken for it. A folder on a volume mounted read-only, or a snapshot, records no volume and matches none. The state records the volume bound to the folder’s inode and birth time, so a record that an older devvm left beside a folder it moved, whose inode is another, names no volume and is recorded again. devvm offers a moved folder the VM when its volume, inode and birth time are the recorded ones and the conditions above hold. When the record’s volume is marked unchecked, devvm offers the VM only once it has read the volume and found the one recorded. It looks the volume up only once the inode and birth time match. A command looks each mount’s volume up once, and looks up none after one lookup fails. A lookup has 1 second when a launch records it or when devvm ls and devvm space check whether a folder is gone, and 5 seconds when devvm makes, adopts or moves a VM, offers a move, or checks a renumbered folder at its own path. A lookup that fails or takes longer records nothing, and a later launch tries again. When devvm can’t tell a renumbered folder’s volume, it judges the folder by the rule above, as one whose state records no volume. The launch then records the folder’s new device with the volume it had, marked unchecked (folder_unchecked in vm.json), so each later launch looks the volume up again and takes the folder for another one when it’s on another volume, until a lookup finds the volume recorded and clears the mark. On Linux, where the folder’s volume is read in the process at no cost, every launch compares it with the volume recorded, so a copy with a volume ID of its own, such as a Btrfs snapshot or a ZFS clone, mounted at the folder’s path is another folder even on the device the original had. A copy made with dd or an LVM snapshot of ext4 keeps the volume’s UUID, and so its ID, as above. A Btrfs snapshot rolled back at the folder’s path is another subvolume, with an ID of its own, so its folder is another folder, which devvm adopt gives the VM, and so is the folder after you give its volume a new UUID, as tune2fs -U does. devvm reads the folder’s owner, which the offer of a move needs, from the same open folder as its identity, so the folder that’s checked as yours is the one whose identity devvm matches and records. It reads the owner as the system reports it, so on a macOS volume that ignores ownership, as disk images and external disks often do, every folder is yours, and that check tells nothing there. A clone of a disk, by asr or dd, or an LVM snapshot mounted for writing, keeps the volume, inode and birth time, so its copy of the folder at another path matches too, when nothing is left at the old path, as at the same path it already did. A volume ID can also be forged by anyone who can write a volume’s metadata, which takes root, or a disk or disk image that someone crafted and you attach. Such a forgery gets no more than a copy that keeps all three does, which is an offer of the VM that you confirm at another path, and the VM itself at the folder’s own path, where it has to be mounted. Nothing in a VM can make one (a folder’s volume). A folder whose state records its volume is also on its disk when the first folder above its old path is on that volume, so a renumbered disk isn’t taken for an unmounted one (“not connected”). The state records the volume when the VM is made, adopted or moved, and, for a VM whose state doesn’t record one yet, at its first launch that finds its folder.
data.only-the-project-folder#Only the project:
A VM mounts its project folder read-write at the same path. The only other things it mounts from the host are the shared tools and its agents’ config folders, both read-only, so it never mounts your home folder, which Lima’s own templates do. A --clone VM doesn’t mount the project folder either. It has its own clone, and its work reaches the repo only when you fetch it. When you run devvm in a subfolder and it uses the project folder’s VM, that VM mounts nothing more than it already did (a subfolder’s VM).
devvm refuses a project folder that would hand the VM more than the project:
A folder that is or holds your home folder, devvm’s settings (~/.config/devvm), its state (~/.local/share/devvm, which holds its binaries and other VMs’ disks) or its Lima home (unsafe_folder). A folder inside devvm’s own folders (unsafe_folder_inside). A VM in ~/.config/devvm/layers could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, and a VM in devvm’s data folder could rewrite the files devvm runs on the host. devvm compares each of these folders with the project folder both by path and by the folder itself, so it also catches a project folder, or a folder above it, that is the same folder as one of devvm’s by device and inode, or the other way round. So on a volume that ignores case, as a Mac’s does by default, a project at ~/.Config/devvm/layers is inside ~/.config/devvm, although the two paths differ. --unsafe-folder mounts such a folder anyway, and devvm says so. A --clone VM mounts nothing, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.
A project folder inside a coding agent’s folder in your home folder, such as ~/.claude/skills/mine, or one that holds an agent’s folder, such as ~/.pi for pi’s ~/.pi/agent, gives its VM read-write access to that agent’s settings on this machine, such as Claude Code’s hooks, which run on the host. devvm doesn’t refuse such a folder, because working on a skill in place is common, but each launch of a VM that mounts it warns once, naming every agent’s folder it overlaps (project_agent_folder). devvm finds them by the same comparison and also by the agent folder’s name, so a folder that the VM could make later counts. A --clone VM gets no warning.
data.read-only-and-confined-builds#Read-only:
devvm builds images with nothing from the host mounted, and it confines their builds (details). Every build reaches the internet. On macOS it can’t reach the host’s loopback, but it reaches your LAN, the host’s own address on it included, and on Linux it reaches the host’s loopback too. Credentials never go into images.
A tool build writes into a folder of its own and never into the shared tools, and devvm checks each tool image, moves it in and writes its record, with its hash (details). Tool images for glibc, which any VM may mount, build only in devvm’s own Ubuntu base, never in a --from image, and musl ones are keyed by the digest of the --from base they build in, so a container image’s code never reaches another VM’s tools. devvm’s VMs live in a Lima home of their own, so Lima settings you made for other VMs never reach them. devvm also refuses a VM with a network it didn’t give the VM, because that network would reach around the proxy (details).
data.secrets-stay-on-the-host#Secrets stay on:
devvm saves secrets in the macOS Keychain, or elsewhere in files only you can read, and it never puts a secret in a process’s arguments (where secrets are saved). A VM uses only the Claude Code token, when its image has claude, and the secrets you bind to it. On every tier, a VM’s secrets and its agents’ logins stay on your machine, and its proxy puts them only into requests for their own hosts.
The secrets work only for that VM. Its proxy needs the VM’s own password, and the VM’s placeholders end in a random value of the VM’s own, which isn’t the password, so a placeholder that the VM sends elsewhere gives nothing away. Another VM, or a program on the host that reaches the proxy’s port, gets no secret. The password is in files only you can read, and never in a process’s arguments or in devvm’s run logs, and only you can read the proxy’s logs.
Each VM’s proxy reads traffic to the hosts it puts secrets in for with the VM’s own CA, which devvm keeps in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/ca/ (the VM’s CA). Your machine never trusts it, but inside its VM it vouches for any site, and no other VM trusts it. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, and the next one, which the VM already trusts, takes over a week before the current one ends. The certificates that the proxy makes never outlast their CA. What a copy of a key could do, and for how long, is under the proxy’s CA keys.
data.set-id-files-on-linux-hosts#Set-id files:
Root in a VM can set the set-user-id and set-group-id bits on files in the project folder. On macOS these bits don’t reach the host, because virtiofs drops them, but on Linux they do. A file that a Lima VM writes is yours, so a set-user-id file runs as you for anyone else on the machine who runs it. A set-user-id file that your machine’s root owns runs as root for anyone who runs it, you included, and since the VM’s writes are yours, such a file came from something else on this machine.
devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, by devvm stop or found stopped at a launch, but not at a launch into a running VM, because the search reads every file’s metadata and takes about a second for 200,000 files. It skips .git folders, which hold most of a big project’s files and whose files nothing runs by their path. It lists root’s files apart with setid_root_files, and you shouldn’t run them but delete them with sudo rm. It lists the rest with setid_files, and chmod u-s,g-s FILE clears their bits.
data.ssh-into-vms#ssh into VMs:
ssh and editors reach a running VM by name through the entries that devvm writes (ssh access by name). Each entry is built so that ssh connects only to that VM and the connection gives the VM nothing else of this machine’s:
Each entry checks the VM’s own host keys, which devvm keeps in the VM’s folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/known_hosts, as a record of the VM’s current start. devvm reads them from the VM through its backend, instead of over the network, once each start, after the VM runs, whatever ports the VM forwards, and the record names the start it was read for, so the keys of an earlier start are read again rather than trusted, whoever started the VM. devvm also removes the record before each start of its own. A VM whose Lima config changed gets new host keys when it boots. A VM whose keys devvm can’t read gets no entry, and ssh refuses a host key that doesn’t match. devvm’s port forwarder, the sessions of links between VMs and a --clone VM’s git all check the VM against the same record. Only host keys go into the record. devvm keeps a line the VM shows only when its key decodes and names its own type, which works for every key type ssh has, and it drops certificates, markers such as @cert-authority, patterns and anything else. So the VM can’t add a line that would make ssh trust another host, or trust a key for another name. Each connection is its own. The entries set ControlMaster no, so a session never rides on a connection that another program opened. Of Lima’s own ssh settings for the VM, devvm copies only the address, port, user and login key, because Lima’s settings turn host key checks off. The entries turn off everything else your ssh could share with the VM. They set ForwardX11 no, ForwardX11Trusted no, Tunnel no, PermitRemoteOpen none, AddKeysToAgent no, ProxyJump none, ProxyCommand none, UpdateHostKeys no and HashKnownHosts no, whatever your own Host * says. That turns off X11, tunnels, remote SOCKS forwards and adding keys to an agent. PermitRemoteOpen needs OpenSSH 8.7 or newer (ssh -V), and an older ssh refuses the entries. Of your environment, the entries send only COLORTERM (SendEnv COLORTERM), which says whether your terminal shows 24-bit color. The VM gets it only where its sshd accepts it, as Ubuntu’s does in devvm’s base. devvm doesn’t set that up itself, so a VM made --from a container image whose sshd doesn’t accept it, such as Alpine’s, gets none. ssh sends it as your terminal has it, and it adds to the variables your own Host * sends, such as macOS’s LANG and LC_*, rather than replacing them. Your agent is forwarded only as the VM’s SSH agent choice says. devvm’s own connections to a VM follow the same choice, the one the VM’s current start was made with, and each carries that VM’s agent alone. devvm finds the VM’s agent, which is yours, devvm’s own or none, and the VM’s proxy relays it on a socket of the VM’s own, passing on only listing keys, signing and binding a session to a host, so the VM can’t remove the agent’s keys, lock it or add keys to it (the SSH agents). devvm gives that socket to the backend’s start of the VM, to its shell and to the commands that set it up, such as the setup devvm sends and the devcontainer.json commands. The backend’s other commands get no agent, and neither do the reads of a VM’s host keys, the self-check’s probe, the checks of a --clone VM’s clone or devvm paste’s writes and counts. devvm never changes its own environment, so when one run reaches several VMs, such as a group’s links, no VM gets another VM’s agent. devvm’s background processes, such as the proxy and the port forwarder, start without an agent in their environment, and the proxy reaches only the one its config names. devvm’s own ssh to a VM uses the VM’s login key alone. devvm limactl runs without your agent too, because Lima’s ssh shares one connection per VM, kept open after the command ends, and an agent forwarded over it is the agent of whichever command opened it. With your agent, a devvm limactl shell could open that connection and pass your agent to devvm’s later sessions of a VM whose choice is devvm’s agent or none. A session carries the VM’s connections through your machine only where your ssh asks for it. The entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type, so a RemoteForward still applies. The VM’s sshd allows local forwarding (-L and -D, which VS Code uses), and it allows remote forwards only on addresses in 127.77.0.0/16, which devvm keeps for links between VMs, so a remote forward on the VM’s localhost, as ssh -R asks by default, is refused. It allows no tunnels or X11. Root in the VM can change all of that, so it’s your ssh that decides, and remote forwards you add says what’s left open.
data.what-it-doesnt-protect#What it doesn’t p:
Each defense on this page leaves something open, such as what allowed hosts and secrets permit, open VMs, files the VM writes into the project folder, links between VMs, and escapes from the VM itself through bugs in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU. Attack vectors keeps the one list of them, under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you, and each entry there links back to its mechanism.
Found a way out of a VM? See SECURITY.md.

data:
Each release has a page here with the full story of every change it makes: what was wrong or missing, how it showed, how devvm now works, and what you do about it. The changelog on GitHub, which is each release’s notes, keeps one or two sentences for each change, with a link to its section here, its issue and the commit that made it.
0.2.0: VMs’ ssh on ports that browsers refuse, the proxy split into two processes with a sandbox around the one that reads the VM’s network, Claude Code’s plugins and MCP servers’ logins in a VM, project folders after your Mac restarts, status lines for slow steps, and many hardening fixes. These are the one part of the docs that describes what changed. Every other page describes how devvm works now.

This page covers 0.2.0 and its release candidates, so far 0.2.0-rc.1, and it’s written as 0.2.0 is made, so each release candidate adds its changes here. 0.2.0-rc.1 adds to 0.1.1-rc.3, and 0.2.0 takes 0.1.1’s place, because its breaking changes need a new minor version. Install the release candidate with devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1, the install script’s --version 0.2.0-rc.1, or brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc, while Homebrew’s devvm stays on 0.1.0.
Each change below has a section of its own, which says what was wrong or missing, how it showed, how devvm works now and what you do. The changelog’s entry for each release gives each of the same changes in one sentence, sorted by who notices it, and its What to do section lists what to do once you’ve upgraded.
data.24-bit-color-in-a-vm#24-bit color in a V:
Programs in a VM, such as coding agents, fell back to fewer colors, as #54 reported, because devvm’s shell in a VM never got your terminal’s COLORTERM, and neither did an agent’s login or ssh to a VM by name.
devvm’s shell in a VM and an agent’s login with devvm agent login now get your terminal’s COLORTERM when it’s truecolor or 24bit, and no other value (opening a VM). The ssh config entries for reaching a VM by name now send it as your terminal has it, from the next time devvm launches or stops a VM, which writes them again. A VM made with --from gets it over ssh only when its image’s sshd accepts it (ssh access by name).
data.a-child-without-its-whole-sandbox#A chil: A proxy that can’t get its whole sandbox keeps the VM’s network, and devvm doctor warns. On macOS, if sandbox-exec is missing or fails to start the child, the child runs without the sandbox. On Linux, a kernel without Landlock or seccomp filters, or whose Landlock is older than ABI 6 or lacks its fix for signals between threads, confines the child only in part. Either way the VM keeps its network, and devvm doctor warns for each VM whose proxy runs that way, naming what the kernel lacks on Linux (the proxy runs without a sandbox).
data.a-clone-check-that-never-ends#A clone ch:
Before devvm rm or devvm clone off lets a --clone VM’s clone go, devvm reads what the VM has of it. devvm kept at most 8 MiB of the answer, but it went on reading the rest and waited for the VM’s command to end, so a VM that wrote without end, or never answered, kept the command waiting until you pressed Ctrl+C. devvm now stops the VM’s command once it sends more than 8 MiB, and it waits at most 2 minutes for the answer, the same bounds as its read of opencode’s worktrees. Either way the check fails, and devvm keeps the VM and names --no-clone-check (deleting the VM).
On Lima, the ssh that limactl shell runs can leave a process behind that holds a command’s output open, and such a process could keep devvm waiting past devvm paste’s time limit. devvm now closes a command’s output a second after the command ends or its time limit runs out, so such a process can’t outlast that limit or the clone check’s 2 minutes, and a command whose output was cut short that way fails (a command’s output).
data.a-closed-connections-ssh-process#A close: When a VM never closed its end of a forwarded port’s or a link’s connection, that connection’s ssh process used to stay on this machine after the program here, or in the client, had closed its side, so a hostile VM could take all 256 connections that a forwarder or a client’s links carry at once. The ssh process now ends once its client has closed and the VM has sent nothing for 30 seconds. So a program that stops sending and waits more than 30 seconds for an answer to begin, such as nc -N in front of a slow query, has its connection cut (how it reaches the VM).
data.a-failed-import-changes-nothing#A failed: A failed devvm agent import leaves the store as it was. That holds whether the import fails while it reads, such as at a file that changed meanwhile, or while it puts the settings and logins in place, such as at a login it can’t save. In the rare case that putting the store back fails too, the import names what it kept (importing from this machine).
data.a-failed-save-changes-nothing#A failed s: A save that failed partway, such as at a file it couldn’t write in one agent’s store or at the Claude Code login it saves last, used to leave the agents it had saved before the failure saved and the rest not. A failed devvm agent save now leaves the store as it was, because a save saves all or nothing, as an import does, and in the rare case that putting the store back fails too, it names what it kept. A file in the VM where the store has a folder, or the other way round, now fails the save before anything changes, naming the store’s path (saving a VM’s settings).
data.a-folder-moved-across-a-restart#A folder:
devvm used to miss a folder that moved while a restart gave its disk another device number, and make it a second VM, and it called the gone folder of a VM whose disk was renumbered not connected. Each VM now records its folder’s volume, which no renumbering changes, so devvm finds such a folder. Once the VM has recorded its volume, devvm offers a moved folder its VM by its volume, inode and birth time, and calls a VM’s gone folder gone (a moved or renamed folder).
Each VM records its project folder’s volume at its first launch that finds the folder. Until then, a folder that moves while a restart gives its disk another device number still needs devvm adopt VM, and after a restart, the VM’s gone folder can still be called not connected. Both stay true for a VM whose folder was already gone before the upgrade, because it never records a volume.
data.a-folder-on-another-volume#A folder on a: A folder at the VM’s own path whose disk was renumbered, but on another volume than the one recorded, such as a copy of the disk with a volume ID of its own mounted there, is another folder, so devvm gives it the VM only after devvm adopt. On Linux, every launch checks the volume, so a Btrfs snapshot rolled back at the folder’s path, or the folder after you give its volume a new UUID, also needs devvm adopt (a folder made again). When devvm can’t read the volume at the launch after a renumbering, such as when diskutil doesn’t answer, each launch looks it up until it can (one VM per folder).
data.a-forwarder-after-a-burst#A forwarder af: When the port forwarder ran out of open files while accepting a connection, it used to stop accepting connections on that port while it still listened there, so the port took connections that nothing answered until the server in the VM restarted. It now tries again shortly after, and so do a link’s socket and a browser login’s forward, which also carries at most 16 connections at once (how it reaches the VM).
data.a-history-exports-names#A history export: devvm history import used to leave out the agents’ logins and the files that devvm’s setup writes by their names as the export wrote them, so an export that spelled one another way, such as .claude/./settings.json or .claude//plugins, got it into the VM’s home. It now refuses a name with a . or empty part, and once the export is unpacked, it deletes what it leaves out by its path (importing history).
data.a-linked-agent-store-is-refused#A linked:
devvm agent import and devvm agent save used to write through a link in devvm’s agent store and take out whatever they hadn’t written in the folder it led to, which for a link to your home folder deleted your files.
Now they refuse a linked store: they fail before they change anything, naming the link, when a folder on the way to what they write in the store is a link, from ~/.config/devvm/agents down, such as ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude linked into a dotfiles repo. Make that folder one of its own, then run the command again (devvm’s agent store).
data.a-nix-package-downloaded-twice#A Nix pac: When two requests for a package that wasn’t in the shared Nix cache yet came close together, the second could download it again after the first had kept it, and the cache counted it twice against its cap. devvm now looks in the cache again before it downloads a package, so each package is downloaded once (the shared Nix cache).
data.a-no_proxy-address-with-a-zone#A NO_PROX: An IPv6 address with a zone in your company proxy’s NO_PROXY, such as fe80::1%eth0, used to send that address past the company proxy without its zone, as #59 reported. Such an entry now matches nothing, as it does in Go’s HTTP clients (behind a company proxy).
data.a-no_proxy-entrys-port#A NO_PROXY entry’: The proxy used to read git.test:0 as git.test on every port, so it sent those hosts directly instead of through your company proxy, and it read git.test:080 or git.test:+80 as port 80, which Go’s clients don’t. An entry whose port no request has, such as git.test:0, or whose port isn’t in plain decimal, now matches no host, as one past 65535 already didn’t (through a company proxy).
data.a-pin-that-meets-gits-rename-on-linux#A: On Linux hosts, .git/config could seem to lose its pin. When git on this machine replaced .git/config just as devvm pinned it again, the pin used to fail, and devvm warned that the file lost its pin and couldn’t be pinned again, then that it was pinned again, at the VM’s next check, and a VM’s start could fail the same way. devvm now pins the file that the rename left, and warns only that it was pinned again (how a Linux host locks .git).
data.a-project-folder-after-your-mac-restarts:
After a restart, an unchanged folder could be on a device with another number, and devvm took it for another folder, as #60 reported. So every command on its VM refused it as made for an earlier folder at its path, a stopped VM’s start refused it as replaced, and the next check of .git called it replaced.
A folder at the same path, with no link on it and with the same inode and birth time, is now the same folder on whichever device it’s on. The VM’s next start records the folder on its new device before it mounts it, in the one change devvm makes to its Lima config. A folder that moved after a restart, before its VM started again, isn’t offered the VM, so devvm adopt VM moves it (one VM per folder).
data.a-project-folder-devvm-cant-read#A proje: When you, or code in a VM that mounts it, took away your read permission on a project folder, devvm used to say that the folder’s VM was made for an earlier folder that was deleted or replaced, and offer devvm rm and devvm adopt. devvm now names the folder and why it can’t be read, so make it readable again (a folder made again).
data.a-project-in-an-agents-folder#A project:
When a VM’s project folder is inside a coding agent’s folder on this machine, such as a skill you work on in ~/.claude/skills/mine, or holds one, such as ~/.pi, code in the VM can change that agent’s settings on this machine, and so the settings that devvm agent import copies for every VM.
Each launch of the VM now warns of it in one line, and so does the import, which also leaves out an agent’s folder that a link in a VM’s project folder leads elsewhere (project folders devvm refuses).
data.a-refused-launch#A refused launch:
When config.toml’s proxy named a user and no proxy secret was saved, devvm in the folder of a running VM used to refuse, as it should, but also stop the VM, and devvm restart stopped it before it refused. The same happened when your CAs folder couldn’t be used, or the VM’s CA or secret files couldn’t be readied.
On a launch or a devvm network change, devvm now checks the company proxy, your CAs, the VM’s CA and its secret files before it stops the VM’s proxy, and when it refuses, it says it left the VM and its proxy running as they were. devvm restart checks the company proxy and your CAs before it stops the VM (the proxy).
data.a-removed-links-connections#A removed li: Removing a link with devvm link rm used to stop only the link’s new connections, so a target that never closed its end kept each open connection’s ssh process on this machine, and one of the 256 connections a client’s links carry at once, until the client or the target stopped. Removing a link now ends its open connections within a few seconds, and when a target starts again, the connections still open through its earlier start end as well (removing a link).
data.a-settings-file-thats-one-string#A setti: When an agent’s settings file in the VM was a single JSON string holding a placeholder, devvm agent save used to crash, and it now puts the saved value back in it. A login file on this machine that holds only null is now refused as not a JSON object, where saving a Codex or opencode login made in a VM failed on it (saving a VM’s settings).
data.a-size-that-isnt-a-number#A size that is: When a VM’s state file held a size devvm couldn’t read as a number, such as "cpus": "four" after an edit by hand, the VM used to start with the image’s size without a word. devvm now refuses to start the VM or show its size, names the value, and says to set it again with devvm size. --cpus, --memory, --disk, config.toml and devvm size -g also refuse a number too big for devvm to read, which for a disk reached Lima as infinity (size).
data.a-stopped-vms-shell#A stopped VM’s shell: In a terminal, limactl shell of a stopped VM asks whether to start it, yes by default. When a VM shut itself down as devvm opened its shell or ran a command in it, you could get that question, and a yes, or just Enter, started the VM as Lima does: unconfined and without its proxy, mounting a folder that replaced the project folder, or making the project folder again if it was gone. devvm’s own start refuses each of these. Every limactl shell that devvm runs now says not to start the VM, so the shell or command fails, and devvm’s next launch starts the VM with every check (a stopped VM’s shell).
data.a-vm-and-its-ssh-agent#A VM and its SSH:
A VM that forwarded your agent or devvm’s own used to be able to remove every key from it with ssh-add -D, lock it with a password of its own with ssh-add -x, or add keys to it, and every VM that shares devvm’s agent lost it then, and with your own agent, so did you.
A VM now reaches its agent only through its proxy, which passes on listing keys, signing and binding a session to a host, and refuses everything else, so ssh-add in a VM can still list and use the keys, but not remove, lock or add them. An editor’s connection gets the same agent as devvm’s shell, the one the VM started with (the SSH agents).
