A VM that forwards an SSH agent and runs as you upgrade keeps the agent as it was until its next start, so it can still remove, lock or add keys, and devvm warns of it each time it opens the VM or changes its links. Run devvm restart in its folder to give it the relay at once (agent forwarding).
data.a-vm-never-runs-without-its-proxy#A VM n: A devvm network change could leave a VM running without its proxy. A change between internet, allowlist and none on a running VM is now refused before the VM’s tier changes, so its tier never says one thing while its proxy enforces another. A VM whose proxy doesn’t enforce the tier the VM has now, or whose proxy is stopped for new settings and then can’t start again, is still stopped, and a devvm network change now stops it in that case as well (the proxy).
data.a-vms-logs-and-their-caps#A VM’s logs an: Root in a VM could write to its serial console, /dev/hvc0, without end, and the console log grew until this machine’s disk was full, and so could Lima’s own logs for the VM until its next start. While a VM runs, its proxy now keeps the disk space that Lima’s console log for the VM and Lima’s own logs for the VM each take under 10 MiB, with a .1 file of up to 10 MiB more, and replaces the VM’s proxy password in them as they grow. A VM that’s running when you upgrade gets this once a devvm command starts its proxy again (Lima’s hostagent).
data.an-import-while-a-vms-state-cant-be-read: devvm agent import can’t tell where a VM’s project folder is while it can’t read that VM’s state, so it follows no links then. It warns of each VM whose state it can’t read, naming the state. Until that’s fixed, it leaves out every link out of an agent’s folder, and an agent’s folder or login whose path leads through a link, one on the way to your home folder included unless only root can change it, so run devvm doctor and import again (importing from this machine).
data.at-most-17-vms-run-at-once#At most 17 VM:
Root in a VM could make the VM’s ssh port answer as a web server, and because that port is on localhost, a page it served could get the cookies of the apps you use on localhost, even in a VM that forwards no ports. Each VM’s ssh now uses one of the 17 ports from 1024 up that every browser refuses, so no page in your browser reaches a server in a VM through that port.
So at most 17 VMs run at once. A start past 17 fails and names the VMs that run on those ports, so stop one of them first (too many VMs at once).
A VM that forwards every port leaves out those 17 ports, so that a VM can’t take the ports that other VMs’ ssh needs. A server in the VM on one of them, such as an X server on 6000, reaches this machine only when you list its port with devvm ports, and devvm ports and each launch warn when a VM’s list names one of them (ports).
Each existing VM’s ssh moves to one of those ports at the VM’s next start. That’s the one change devvm makes to the VM’s Lima config, and like any change there, it gives the VM new ssh host keys. A VM that runs as you upgrade keeps its old port until then, and devvm warns of it at each launch, so run devvm stop in its folder, and its next start moves it.
data.claude-codes-plugins-in-a-vm#Claude Code:
Each VM’s ~/.claude/plugins used to be devvm’s agent store’s folder, mounted read-only, so whatever Claude Code writes there failed, such as a plugin’s data in ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, installing a plugin and updating a marketplace, as #56 reported.
Each VM’s ~/.claude/plugins is now its own folder, so all of those work. The store’s plugins are Claude Code’s read-only seed at ~/.claude/plugins-seed, so they load as before, a plugin keeps its data in the VM, and a plugin you install in a VM stays in that VM until devvm agent save copies it into the store. A store that devvm 0.1.0’s import filled keeps only what a seed has, as Claude Code’s plugins in the agent store says (Claude Code’s plugins).
Each VM gets its own ~/.claude/plugins at its next launch, without a restart, in place of its link to the store’s folder. Claude Code started in a shell that was open before that launch finds none of the store’s plugins, so start it in a new shell.
data.claude-codes-plugins-in-the-agent-store#:
devvm 0.1.0’s devvm agent import copied your whole ~/.claude/plugins into devvm’s agent store, where every VM with Claude Code could read it, plugins’ data included. The store now keeps only what a seed has of Claude Code’s plugins, as Claude Code’s plugins in a VM describes.
If you imported Claude Code’s settings with devvm 0.1.0, the first start of any VM takes your plugins’ data out of the store, along with the folder’s other entries that are this machine’s own, such as installed_plugins.json. It warns once, naming what it took, and it leaves your own ~/.claude/plugins as it is (Claude Code’s plugins).
If the store’s plugins folder is a link, or below one, which only a store you made yourself can be, no VM with Claude Code starts until you make it a folder of its own, because a VM’s mount would follow the link.
If a plugin’s data held a login of the plugin’s own, every VM with Claude Code could read that login, so sign in to that plugin again where you don’t trust those VMs. A VM that runs as you upgrade loses the store’s entries that are this machine’s own from its mount at the first start of any VM, so Claude Code there may not find the store’s plugins until that VM’s next launch. On a Linux host, the VM can keep seeing what it had read of them until its next start.
data.claude-codes-setup-token-login#Claude Co: devvm agent login claude --setup-token showed nothing and waited, as #57 reported. The login in the VM got no terminal, so claude setup-token, which draws full-screen, showed nothing. When devvm runs in a terminal, an agent’s login in the VM now gets a terminal of its own, as devvm’s shell does, so Claude Code shows the address to open and the prompt for its code. Without a terminal, --setup-token warns that the login may show nothing (Claude Code login).
data.connections-to-the-proxy-on-linux-hosts#: Each connection that a VM confined to its proxy makes to the proxy starts a devvm process on a Linux host, and with no limit, a VM that opened connections without end could start thousands of them and fill the host with processes. devvm now carries at most 256 of a VM’s connections to its proxy at once, and answers any past that with 503 before it reaches the proxy. A VM that’s running when you upgrade has no limit until its next start (the QEMU wrapper).
data.credentials-in-a-copied-marketplace#Cred: A Claude Code marketplace can have a password or an access token in its clone’s git config or in its source in known_marketplaces.json, and every VM with Claude Code can read it once it’s in devvm’s agent store. devvm agent import and devvm agent save now warn when they copy such a marketplace. The warning names the marketplace, the store’s file and the keys, and the marketplace is copied as before (mounts).
data.ctrl-c-in-an-agents-login#Ctrl-C in an a: In a terminal, Ctrl-C now goes to the agent’s login in the VM and ends it, and devvm then says that the login ended or saved nothing. devvm puts the terminal back as it was before the login, even when a signal ends devvm itself (Claude Code login).
data.cursors-cli-and-your-cursor-account#Curs: Cursor’s CLI in a VM can change less of your Cursor account. Its proxy refuses more of the methods that change your account, your team or your cloud agents, such as merging a cloud agent’s pull request, forking or pinning a cloud agent, or writing to its machine, and every call that the CLI itself makes still passes. Do those from Cursor on your machine (Cursor CLI login).
data.devvm-agent-imports-bounds#devvm agent i: devvm agent import copies at most 20,000 files, folders and links, 128 MiB, and 16 MiB in one file, of each agent’s folder. An agent’s folder that holds more, such as one that a VM’s project inside it filled, fails the import before the store changes, naming the folder, so take out what it doesn’t need and import again (importing from this machine).
data.devvm-agent-save-and-a-new-claude-code-l: devvm agent save and a VM’s new Claude Code login take turns. While it saves Claude Code’s part of ~/.claude.json, the save holds the lock on Claude Code’s logins, the lock that a VM’s proxy holds while it saves a Claude Code login made in that VM. Ctrl-C while the save waits for either lock ends the wait (saving a VM’s settings).
data.devvm-desktop-after-a-burst#devvm deskto: When devvm desktop’s relay ran out of open files while accepting a viewer, devvm desktop used to end with an error, and the desktop’s port with it. The relay now tries again shortly, as the port forwarder does (the desktop relay).
data.devvm-doctor-checks-every-vms-state#devv: devvm doctor warns once of each VM whose state devvm can’t read, naming the VM, the file and why, even when it can’t read the VM’s folder, and it changes nothing. It reads each VM’s vm.json as every command on a VM does. Such a VM used to hide doctor’s warnings about the other VMs’ policy files, and the warnings that devvm network gives for every VM, and it no longer does (a file devvm can’t read).
data.devvms-other-logs#devvm’s other logs:
devvm’s other logs are held to their caps as well:
The port forwarder’s and the link session’s logs now stay under 1 MiB while they run, not only from their next start, and a link’s warnings take turns with the session’s other lines. The build proxy’s log stays under 10 MiB, as a VM’s proxy’s does. A run writes at most 128 MiB to its run log, and the run logs take at most 256 MiB together, though devvm never deletes the newest or one that a running devvm still writes (the run log).
data.devvms-own-folders-in-another-case#devvm: On a Mac, where a name’s case doesn’t count, a project at ~/.Config/devvm/layers used to get a VM with read-write access to devvm’s settings and layer scripts, because devvm compared a project folder with your home folder and its own folders by name alone. It now compares them by the folders themselves as well, so it refuses that project as it refuses ~/.config/devvm/layers. A VM already made in such a folder still mounts it, so delete it with devvm rm there. devvm also refuses an SSH key in a folder that a VM mounts by a name in another case (project folders devvm refuses).
data.each-vms-proxy-runs-as-two-processes#Eac:
A VM’s proxy used to be one process, which read every byte the VM sent and held all of your secrets. It’s now two. Only devvm _proxy reads your Keychain, your agents’ login files and your other files, and devvm _proxy-child, which reads the VM’s network, asks devvm _proxy for the rest, such as each connection and each value bound to the VM.
So besides the VM’s own proxy password and CAs and your company proxy’s password, the code that reads every byte a VM sends holds only the values that the VM’s own bindings name, each for a few minutes after it was last asked for, and never a new login’s tokens, its refresh token among them (a VM’s proxy).
With the split, an error reply from an agent’s token endpoint reaches the VM as it is up to 1 MiB, and gets 502 past that, and a build’s proxy writes its logs to a logs/ folder of their own in its folder.
A VM’s proxy that runs as you upgrade stays one process, without a sandbox, until the VM’s next launch. That launch starts it again as two processes, because a launch starts a VM’s proxy again for every new devvm, and until then, devvm doctor names each VM whose proxy an older devvm started (the proxy runs without a sandbox).
data.every-host-in-one-form#Every host in one:
A few of devvm’s checks used to read a host in a way of their own. devvm secret set --host, an MCP server’s URL and a NO_PROXY entry took a name with a letter that isn’t plain ASCII, such as the Kelvin sign, which Unicode’s case folding turns into k, as the ASCII name it folds into. --from took a registry’s host with such a letter, or an address in brackets before a trailing dot such as [::1]., as one on the internet.
Every host is now read as the proxy reads it. The proxy refuses a host with such a letter, so now:
devvm secret set refuses it an MCP server with one gets no secret a NO_PROXY entry with one matches no host --from doesn’t take such a registry as public devvm network rm with it never removes the rule with the plain letter The proxy also answers 400 to a host with brackets around anything but an IPv6 address, such as [evil.com]:443, and a partial clone’s warnings now read a remote’s host without its trailing dot, so they name example.com, not example.com., and a remote at localhost. gets the same warning as one at localhost (how the proxy reads a host).
data.folder-names-with-separators-in-a-row#Fo: devvm used to turn each character other than letters and digits in a folder’s name into its own dash, and Lima refuses a name with dashes in a row, so a folder named x--y, foo (copy) or C++ stuff got no VM, as #52 reported. devvm now turns each run of such characters into one dash, so those folders get a VM, and foo (copy) gets devvm-foo-copy-. The state that such a folder’s failed VM left is replaced when you run devvm there again (VM names). Thanks to @se6a for the report.
data.forwarded-ports-over-ipv6#Forwarded port: When this machine briefly couldn’t listen on a port’s IPv6 address, such as when it ran out of open files, the forwarder used to forward the port on 127.0.0.1 alone until the server in the VM restarted. So a client that connects only over IPv6, such as http://[::1]:PORT or a tool that doesn’t fall back to 127.0.0.1, didn’t reach the VM, and another program on this machine could take ::1 on that port and get those connections instead. The forwarder now tries the port again at the VM’s next report and forwards it on both addresses (when it can’t forward).
data.hardening#Hardening: These fixes close ways that code in a VM, or a file it wrote, could reach past what devvm lets a VM do. Most of them change nothing you see.
data.host-keys-whatever-a-vms-ports#Host keys:
When other programs on this machine, such as your own dev servers, held every port a VM lists, or the VM forwarded none with devvm ports none, a start that went no further than starting the VM, such as devvm clone fetch on a stopped --clone VM, used to leave the VM’s ssh host keys unpinned. devvm’s own ssh to the VM then failed until something else pinned them, so devvm clone fetch and devvm rm’s fetch failed with clone_fetch_failed.
devvm now pins a VM’s ssh host keys each time it starts the VM, whatever the VM forwards, and a command that finds the VM running without them pins them first (ssh into VMs).
data.how-deep-a-save-goes#How deep a save goe: A chain of thousands of folders used to keep devvm agent save busy for a long time while it held the agent store’s lock. The save now has an import’s bounds on depth, so a VM that sends folders nested more than 128 deep, or a path of more than 4,096 bytes, gets nothing saved, as an import of such folders does (saving a VM’s settings).
data.links-inside-an-agents-folder#Links insi: devvm agent import used to copy a link inside an agent’s folder as the file it led to, wherever that file was in the folder, so a link in ~/.claude/skills or ~/.claude/plugins/cache could put your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json or a plugin’s data into the store, where every VM with the agent reads it. It now copies such a link only when it leads to one of the settings the import copies, and leaves any other out with a warning that names where it leads (importing from this machine).
data.lookups-with-transparent-mode-off#Lookup:
In a VM confined to its proxy, with transparent mode off or stopped, a lookup through the system’s resolver on a Linux host used to wait out its timeout, because systemd-resolved’s stub kept retrying a name server where nothing listened, and workerd under wrangler dev waited about 40 seconds for each lookup.
The VM’s programs now ask the VM’s own name server, at 127.0.0.1, directly, from each VM’s next launch, so a lookup through the system’s resolver, such as getent’s or curl’s, fails at once, and so does workerd’s. A VM on the open tier keeps systemd-resolved’s stub (the VM’s resolver).
data.mcp-servers-logins#MCP servers’ logins:
Claude Code keeps its logins to MCP servers in the VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json, the file where devvm puts the Claude login. Each launch and each devvm agent login claude used to write devvm’s copy of the login over the whole file, as #62 reported. So a login to an MCP server that you started with /mcp in a VM failed when devvm set the VM up again before it finished, such as when you ran devvm in its folder from another terminal, and one that finished was gone at the VM’s next launch.
With your subscription’s login, devvm now replaces only the Claude login in that file and keeps the rest, so the MCP servers’ logins you make in a VM stay in that VM, and they never reach this machine or another VM. With a Claude Code token, the VM’s file stays as it is (MCP servers’ logins).
data.names-are-looked-up-as-theyre-written#Na:
The proxy used to look names up with this machine’s DNS search domain, which macOS takes from the network’s settings and Linux from /etc/resolv.conf. When either host had a public address, no rule judged the name that the search domain made, so with api.corp.example.com denied and ** allowing the rest, a VM could reach that host as api, or api.eu.corp.example.com as api.eu.
The proxy now looks each name up as it’s written, and it no longer adds this machine’s DNS search domain, so a short host name no longer reaches a host through the proxy. A tool in a VM that reached a host on your company’s network by a name such as jenkins now needs the host’s full name, such as jenkins.corp.example.com, and a block for a name without a dot says to use its full name (a name that doesn’t resolve).
data.names-that-differ-only-in-case#Names tha:
On a Mac, when the VM, or your home folder for devvm agent import, had a file whose name differed from the store’s only in case, such as foo.md where the store has Foo.md, devvm agent save and devvm agent import used to delete the store’s file and report success. They now treat such a file as one file, as macOS’s volume does, so the store’s file gets the new content and keeps its name, and the save’s diff shows it as changed.
Two names in the VM that differ only in case, such as A.md and a.md, would be one file in the store, so the save now saves nothing and names both, and so does an import of two such names from a home folder on a volume that tells case apart (saving a VM’s settings).
data.names-you-choose-in-an-agents-settings#N:
devvm used to take a plugin, a marketplace or an MCP server whose name had key, token, secret or passw in it, such as tokeneconomizer or secret-scanner, for a secret, as #55 reported. It put devvm-redacted in place of all its settings in the VM’s copy, so Claude Code refused the VM’s settings.json whole and every plugin was off in the VM.
devvm now knows the agents’ tables of names, such as Claude Code’s mcpServers, and judges only the fields under a name, so a server named secret-scanner keeps its command and still loses its env and its apiKey (keys in settings files).
If a VM’s copy of an agent’s settings file had devvm-redacted under a name you chose, such as a plugin’s marketplace, the VM’s next launch writes the whole copy over the VM’s own. Until then, devvm agent save leaves that file out and warns, so make any change to it in devvm’s agent store, or launch the VM again and make the change there.
Thanks to @jspiro for the report and @dhruv1220 for the tests’ idea in #58.
data.opencodes-automations-and-permissions-in:
opencode 2.4 keeps its automations in its database, each with a schedule or an event that triggers it and a shell command that it runs, which opencode asks you to approve once, as the automation is made, and then runs without asking again. The database also keeps the requests you said always to allow in a project, and each session’s own permission rules. A copy of the database in a history export kept all of them, so a hostile VM could write an automation, an allow rule or a session that allows every command into its database, and devvm history import would put it into the VM you imported the export into, where opencode would run its command without asking. The same went for what opencode’s service starts by itself when it starts: a suspended session’s turn, a subagent’s job and a message queued for a session’s next turn. A project’s start command, which opencode runs for each worktree it makes, was in the copy too. opencode’s git repositories in ~/.local/share/opencode, its snapshots, its cache of repositories and its worktrees, were in the export too, and a repository’s config can name a command that opencode’s own git commands then run.
The copy in an export, and the copy that an import makes of a database in any export, now has:
no automations, subagents’ jobs or queued messages no requests you said always to allow, and each session keeps only its deny and ask rules, each written again as sqlite3 reads it no suspended sessions, so no turn resumes on its own no project commands The copy drops every view and refuses a table with a generated column, which could hide rows from these steps, and its own check counts what’s left and leaves the database out unless nothing is. An export also leaves out opencode’s snapshot, repos and worktree folders, and an import never writes them, so an export doesn’t hold opencode’s worktrees. The worktrees’ commits are in your project’s own repository, and devvm rm, which deletes their folders with the VM, now checks them for uncommitted changes first (opencode’s worktrees before a VM goes). An export also leaves out the project plugins you approved in opencode’s native client, which doesn’t ship yet: plugin-approvals.json and the plugin-staged folder in ~/.local/state/opencode. That client runs the staged copies without checking their hash again, so without this a hostile VM’s export could approve a plugin for the VM you import it into. In the new VM, make again any automation you want, and opencode asks again before the requests you had always allowed. A VM made again keeps its own, because its home folder’s copy isn’t an export (what an export holds).
data.opencodes-lock-files-in-a-save#opencode’: devvm agent save refused a VM whose ~/.config/opencode held a lock file, such as the bun.lock that opencode’s plugins’ installs write or a package-lock.json, or another file the store doesn’t keep, such as .gitignore or .DS_Store. The VM sent every file in that folder, while devvm’s store keeps none of these, so devvm took each as a path outside the agents’ settings and saved nothing. The VM now doesn’t send them, so they stay in the VM, and the save goes on (saving a VM’s settings).
data.opencodes-machine-key-in-history-exports:
opencode 2.4 keeps a private key in ~/.local/state/opencode/machine/home-key, which it makes when it first needs one, such as when you pair a machine with opencode machine add. Every machine it pairs trusts that key, and opencode never replaces it. It sits in opencode’s state folder beside its prompt history, so devvm history export, and the export that devvm rm and a VM made again write, used to copy it into the export, and devvm history import put it into the VM it imported into. The export also held the password of opencode’s background service, which its state folder keeps in service.json, or in service-.json for another channel’s opencode, with the handoff tickets and temporary files beside it. It held the access tokens of opencode’s terminals’ daemons too, which opencode keeps in the state folder’s pty, as releases before 2.4 do as well. The copy of opencode’s database also kept its machine table, which holds the public keys that the paired machines log in with.
An export now leaves them out and empties that table, and an import never writes them, even from an older export, so the new VM’s opencode makes its own. A VM made again keeps its own, because it’s the same machine (what an export holds).
If an export of a VM with opencode 2.4 or later holds .local/state/opencode/machine/home-key, which tar -tzf FILE lists, that VM’s key is in it, and it may be in each VM you imported it into, unless that VM’s opencode had made a key of its own first. In each such VM that’s still there:
Quit opencode, its TUI and any opencode serve included, and stop its service with opencode service stop, because a running opencode keeps the key in memory. Delete ~/.local/state/opencode/machine/home-key, so opencode makes a new key when it next needs one. Pair each machine you paired there again with opencode machine add NAME --replace, which prints a new join string for that machine to join with. In a VM you imported the export into, remove the machines it brought with opencode machine remove NAME. For a VM that you’ve deleted, unpair each machine it had paired, on that machine. Once the key is replaced, the old exports in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports hold a key that nothing trusts.
data.opencodes-service-settings-in-vms#openco:
opencode 2 keeps its background service’s settings in ~/.config/opencode/service.json, or in service-.json on another channel. They hold the service’s password, which the service makes when the file has none, and with remote access on, the secret route that the service’s address is served on and your consent to remote access, beside its port, host name, CORS origins and environment. devvm agent import copied every file in ~/.config/opencode into devvm’s agent store, these included, and every VM with opencode got a copy at each launch, with devvm-redacted in place of the password and of each value of the environment, and with the route as it was. So each such VM’s opencode service took devvm-redacted as its password, which anyone who knows devvm knows. devvm agent save copied a VM’s own file into the store in the same way, and from there into every VM.
devvm agent import and devvm agent save now leave these files out, and no VM gets them, even from a store that holds them. A VM’s start takes them out of the store and warns once, and each VM’s setup takes out the copy that an earlier devvm gave it, which it knows by the devvm-redacted in it, so each VM’s opencode makes a password of its own the next time its service starts. opencode service get password shows it in the VM (opencode’s service).
If you ran devvm agent import or devvm agent save for opencode, your VMs got such a copy. A service that’s running keeps its password until it stops, so restart each running VM that has opencode, with devvm restart in its folder. If this machine’s opencode has remote access on, its route reached the store and your VMs, so turn remote access off and on again on this machine, which gives its service a new route:
opencode service set remote false # on this machine: drop the route that your VMs got opencode service set remote true # and get a new one When this machine’s service had remote access on but hadn’t started since, its file held a route and no password, so the copy held no devvm-redacted and stays in the VM. Once this machine’s route is new, that copy’s route leads nowhere. A password you set yourself with opencode service set password reached your VMs as it was, with no devvm-redacted to mark the copies, when it looked to devvm like a variable’s name or a number, which is any of these:
capital letters, digits and _, starting with a letter at most five digits true or false If yours is one, set a new password on this machine first, because that’s the one your VMs got, then delete ~/.config/opencode/service.json in each VM with opencode and restart the VM.
data.opencodes-worktrees-before-a-vm-goes#ope:
opencode makes its worktrees in ~/.local/share/opencode/worktree in the VM, and a history export now leaves that folder out, because a git repository’s config can name a command that git runs (opencode’s automations and permissions in history). So the uncommitted changes in those worktrees went with the VM, with nothing to say so.
devvm rm, and a command that makes the VM again with --clean-home, now check those worktrees first, starting a stopped VM for the check. devvm shows each worktree’s uncommitted changes under its path and asks before they go, and it asks too about a detached HEAD’s commits that nothing else in the VM has, a worktree that git can’t read, and more than 100 worktrees. --force never answers that question, so without a terminal devvm refuses and keeps the VM. When only the worktrees have work, its refusal names --no-worktree-check, a new flag that warns and goes ahead without the check. A remake’s messages name the command with --clean-home, because --no-worktree-check works only with it, and so do the clone check’s messages for devvm clone off --clean-home. For a VM whose folder is gone, devvm rm VM reads the worktrees from the running VM, and it refuses a stopped one, even with --no-export, naming devvm rm VM --no-export --no-worktree-check, because starting it would make its folder again. If a script deletes such VMs, or remakes them with --clean-home, give it --no-worktree-check where losing those changes is fine (opencode’s worktrees).
data.passwords-in-limas-console-logs#Password: Lima’s boot scripts write the VM’s proxy settings, with the VM’s own proxy password, to the VM’s serial console, which Lima keeps in its console logs for the VM, serial.log, serialp.log or serialv.log in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home. devvm used to take the passwords out of Lima’s ha.stderr.log only. Once the VM has started, devvm now replaces each password with as many * in Lima’s console log for the VM as well, as it does in ha.stderr.log (the run log).
data.pins#Pins:
mise is 2026.11.10, in base and on this machine, the docker layer’s Docker is 29.10.0 and its compose 5.8.0, and Cursor’s CLI is 2026.11.17-f532c45. The new mise and Docker change what goes into the images, so base, every image built on it and every shared tool that mise installs are built again once.
Run devvm update in each existing VM’s folder. Until you do, a VM made from an older image says it’s outdated, and every existing VM says there are newer shared tools at the same versions. The first update or new VM builds base and each of its shared tools again, one at a time, which takes several minutes.
data.pins-since-020-rc1#Pins since 0.2.0-rc.1:
mise is 2026.11.14, in base and on this machine, the nix layer’s Nix is 2.36.0, and the docker layer’s buildx is 0.39.1 and its model plugin 1.2.10. The new mise changes what goes into base, so base, every image built on it and every shared tool that mise installs are built again once, as they were for 0.2.0-rc.1’s pins.
Run devvm update in each existing VM’s folder, and give the first one several minutes.
data.plain-websockets#Plain WebSockets: A plain ws:// WebSocket now connects through the proxy, where it used to get 502 (the proxy).
data.status-lines-for-slow-steps#Status lines:
Some of devvm’s slow steps used to show nothing while they ran. In a terminal, devvm now shows a status line that says what it’s waiting for during these steps (a command fails):
finding the folder’s VM, checking it before a start, checking its network and reading its host keys, setting it up, running a devcontainer.json’s commands, looking up a folder’s disk, checking Lima, deleting a VM or an image, applying the retention settings and installing an upgrade devvm ls reading the VMs, devvm doctor checking this machine, devvm agent import reading your agents’ folders and copying them into the store, and devvm agent save reading and comparing the VM’s settings devvm clone add, clone fetch, clone on and clone off, devvm git-protect, devvm stop, a --clone VM’s check before devvm rm, a history export or import, and devvm ports as it starts a running VM’s port forwarder again devvm link as it asks about the VMs its links lead to, link add, link rm, link publish and link unpublish, devvm group join and group leave, and devvm rm of a VM that others link to, as they give each running VM its changed links and check the VMs that links lead to devvm network learn and network lock as they give a running VM’s proxy its new tier every stop of a VM, as for devvm restart or a restart you agree to after changing a setting
data.status-lines-while-devvm-waits#Status li: While devvm waits for another devvm that’s changing the same thing, such as a VM’s state, its folders’ layout, a group, an image’s build or the shared tools, a status line says so, and only while it waits. Some of those waits used to show nothing, and others printed a line after a few seconds that stayed. A run with -v, or with its output piped, no longer prints that line, because a status line shows only in a terminal without -v (a command fails).
data.stopped-forwarders-and-link-sessions#Sto: devvm stopping a VM’s port forwarder or link session, or a kill of either, used to leave its ssh connection to the VM running on this machine, with its control socket in devvm’s run folder. Each signal that devvm sends either one now also reaches what the process started, and either one stops its ssh before it exits. devvm gc --orphans also deletes a forwarder’s socket that nothing listens on (how devvm starts them).
data.the-child-connects-only-through-devvm-_p:
Wherever its sandbox runs, a bug that a VM drove in the child can’t reach this machine’s services on localhost, such as your dev servers, Docker’s published ports and other VMs’ proxies, nor this machine’s own addresses or your LAN’s private addresses, unless a rule names the address, just as the VM can’t.
A rule such as devvm network allow 127.0.0.1:5432 still applies from the next connection, and a company proxy on localhost still works, though the child reaches whatever that company proxy reaches, as the VM does. Because devvm _proxy looks up the child’s names, the child reads no file below /etc on Linux and doesn’t talk to mDNSResponder on macOS (the child’s sandbox).
data.the-childs-sandbox-on-linux#The child’s: On Linux, before it reads a byte of the VM’s, devvm _proxy-child confines itself with Landlock and a seccomp filter. A bug that a VM drove there could read and write only its VM’s logs and the shared Nix cache, and couldn’t change any other file’s mode, owner, attributes or times, run a program, or connect to a unix socket, such as an ssh master’s, Docker’s or your SSH agent’s. It could still learn whether a file of yours exists, its size and when it changed (the proxy runs without a sandbox).
data.the-childs-sandbox-on-macos#The child’s: On macOS, devvm _proxy-child starts under sandbox-exec, with a profile that lets it write only its VM’s logs and the shared Nix cache and look at your policy files. A bug that a VM drove there couldn’t read your files, reach the Keychain or connect to this machine’s unix sockets, such as ssh’s and Docker’s (the proxy runs without a sandbox).
data.two-devvms-at-the-agent-store#Two devvms: Two devvms could write the agent store at once, so their files used to mix, or one could fail partway. devvm agent import, devvm agent save and a start that cleans Claude Code’s plugins out of the store now take turns, so a second one says it’s waiting and goes on once the first is done. A save that finds the store changed since it showed what differs now saves nothing instead of writing over an import (importing from this machine).
data.warnings-and-the-status-line#Warnings an: A warning used to be written onto the status line’s own line, and the status line’s next redraw could erase a question’s prompt and what you typed. A message that devvm prints during a slow step now prints above the status line, which comes back below it, and a question, the picker and an agent’s login in the VM take the status line away until they’re done (a command fails).
data.what-a-vms-proxy-holds#What a VM’s proxy:
A VM’s proxy used to count only its tunnels toward its limit, keep idle connections open without end, keep a plain HTTP request running after its client had gone, and take 1 MiB of a request’s headers inside an intercepted tunnel, so a VM could make it hold more and more. It now:
holds at most 2048 of the VM’s connections of every kind at once, where one without the VM’s password doesn’t count, and has at most 2048 requests to hosts under way at once closes a connection that waits 10 minutes for its next request, or that lacked the VM’s password ends a plain HTTP request a minute after its client has stopped sending and nothing has come back takes at most 64 KiB of headers everywhere, and carries at most 100 HTTP/2 requests at once in a tunnel lets long downloads, WebSockets and slow streams go on as long as they last (the proxy)
data.your-claudeai-connectors#Your claude.ai:
The connectors you added in claude.ai didn’t work in a VM, as #61 reported. The proxy put your subscription’s login only into requests to api.anthropic.com, so the connectors’ requests held the login’s placeholder and were refused.
With your subscription’s login, the VM’s proxy now also puts the login into requests to mcp-proxy.anthropic.com below /v1/mcp/, which carry the connectors’ traffic, from each VM’s next launch. So a VM with Claude Code can use every connector you added in claude.ai, as Claude Code on this machine can. A Claude Code token, from claude setup-token or in devvm’s environment, still goes only to api.anthropic.com (Claude Code login).
Code in the VM can now read and act through your connectors, so disconnect the ones you don’t want VMs to use, or deny mcp-proxy.anthropic.com with devvm network deny (your claude.ai connectors).
data.your-plugins-data-stays-on-this-machine#: devvm agent import used to copy all of ~/.claude/plugins into the store, so every VM with Claude Code got the data that your plugins keep on this machine, which can hold their own logins. From that folder, it now copies only the marketplaces, their records and the plugins’ cache, and devvm agent save copies only those from a VM (importing from this machine).

data:
devvm runs installs, project code and coding agents in a VM, so code you didn’t write can’t, on its own, read your credentials, run git hooks on this machine or reach your other projects, and Attack vectors lists the exceptions. On the allowlist tier, which new VMs get by default, that code can send data only to the hosts on the VM’s allowlist, which are devvm’s built-in hosts, such as package registries, GitHub and your agents’ providers, your secrets’ hosts and the hosts you add. A few habits close most of what devvm can’t close on its own, so read this page before you trust a VM with a project.
Some of what devvm protects are your secrets. A secret is a credential devvm keeps on this machine for VMs to use: your GitHub token, Claude Code’s token, an agent’s login or an API key.
data.more-on-staying-safe#More on staying saf: Network tiers: choosing a VM’s tier, allowlists, logs and secrets. .git protection: what the lock stops, what still works and what it doesn’t cover. Attack vectors: common attacks one by one, and what devvm does about each. How it works › Security model: how devvm keeps each of these promises. How it works › Processes: what each of devvm’s processes on this machine holds and how it’s confined.
data.the-habits#The habits: Use --clone for a repo or an agent you don’t trust. The VM then works on a clone of its own instead of your folder, so nothing it writes reaches your folder or its .git until you fetch the VM’s work and review it. It’s the safest way to run a repo you don’t know or an agent with its checks off. Run installs, project code and agents in the VM. Whatever the VM writes into the project folder runs as you when a program on this machine runs it, so npm install, make, tests and agents belong in the VM (files the VM writes). Keep VMs on the allowlist or none tier, and keep allowlists short. New VMs get allowlist by default. On the allowlist tier stolen data can go only to the hosts you allowed, on the internet tier to any public host, and on the open tier code in the VM reaches everything this machine can. Review the VM’s changes before you run them on this machine or merge them. Treat its commits as an untrusted contributor’s. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, and bind only the secrets a VM needs. A VM can do whatever its secrets allow, even when it never sees them (secrets and keys the VM may use). Keep credentials out of the project folder and the settings folders of devvm’s agent store. The VM sees every file in them, including a .env file, whatever the VM’s tier (mounts). Leave SSH agent forwarding off, or use devvm’s own agent with only the keys the VM needs.
data.what-a-vm-can-reach#What a VM can reach:
The diagram sorts what’s on this machine by what a VM can do with it, and the table below gives the details.
What a VM can do with what's on this machineThe VM reaches the project folder, read-write, or its own clone with --clone, and what its network tier allows, through the proxy. It gets the shared tools and devvm's agent store's folders read-only, and copies of its settings files, minus your secrets. Out of its reach are the rest of your home folder, the .git hooks and config, which are locked, your SSH agent, unless you turn it on, and your secrets, which stay on this machine.Out of reach Read-only or copied The VM reaches the projectfolder,read-write,or its ownclone with--clone what itsnetwork tierallows,through theproxy the sharedtools,read-only devvm'sagent store'sfolders,read-only copies ofits settingsfiles, minusyour secrets the rest ofyour homefolder .git hooksand config,locked your SSHagent,unless youturn it on your secretsstay on thismachine The project folder The VM reads and writes it. With --clone the folder isn’t mounted, and the VM has a clone of its own (details). .git hooks and config devvm locks them on macOS, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM where the kernel lets it, and watches them where it doesn’t. It reports what a lock can’t stop without preventing it (details). With --clone they’re out of reach. Your agents’ settings and logins (skills, settings, logins) The VM mounts the folders of devvm’s agent store read-only and gets copies of its files, but never your agents’ history, and never the agents’ own files in your home folder (details). The rest of your home folder, other projects The VM doesn’t mount them. Your SSH keys Only with devvm ssh-agent on, and only while you’re connected. With devvm ssh-agent devvm, the VM can use only the keys you added to devvm’s own agent (details). The network On every tier but open, the VM reaches only its proxy on this machine, which lets it reach what its tier allows. On the open tier it reaches everything this machine reaches, including this machine’s own services on localhost (details). Your secrets Your GitHub token, Claude Code’s token, the coding agents’ logins and API keys and the MCP secrets Claude Code gets from this machine stay on this machine on every network tier, and the proxy puts them into requests, so code in the VM can still use each secret the VM may use (details). opencode’s and pi’s keys that the proxy can’t put in, such as a local model server’s, stay on this machine too, unless you pass one to VMs in config.toml (opencode logins, pi logins). Note
Everything here rests on the VM’s boundary: the VM runs its own kernel, apart from this machine’s.

data: This page lists the common ways that code you didn’t write gets to run on a developer’s machine or gets data off it, and what devvm does about each one. devvm stops most of them on its own, and the habits close most of what’s left. Narrowed, not closed and Left to you are the one list of what devvm leaves open, and each entry links to the page that explains its mechanism.
data.bad-packages-and-images#Bad packages and: Typosquatting, dependency confusion and made-up names. Attackers publish packages under names one typo away from popular ones, under a company’s internal package names with a higher version, and under names that AI coding agents invent and that attackers then register. Their code runs as the scripts above do. Compromised maintainers. A trusted package can turn malicious when its maintainer’s account is taken over or a new maintainer joins with bad intent, as event-stream (2018) and xz (2024) did. Updating such a package runs its new code in the VM. Malicious images. An image from --from or from a devcontainer’s image runs its own code as root in the build VM (the image is untrusted). devvm uses only images that the registry gives to anyone who asks anonymously, never one that only your Docker or your registry login reaches, and it confines builds (read-only and confined builds). On macOS a build can’t reach this machine’s loopback, but Left to you covers what it still reaches. A devcontainer.json’s commands and features. A project’s postCreateCommand and its other commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, as soon as devvm makes the VM. Its image and features decide what’s in the VM, and devvm adds its ports to the ones it forwards to this machine’s localhost, even beyond a list you narrowed, so the VM is the project’s from the start. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script. devvm --no-devcontainer skips the file for a project you don’t trust that far (devcontainer.json).
data.credentials-on-this-machine#Credentials: SSH keys. Malware on a developer’s machine looks in ~/.ssh first, because a private key opens every server and repo that trusts it. A VM never mounts ~/.ssh, and besides the project folder it mounts only the shared tools and the folders of devvm’s agent store, read-only, so there’s no key in it to copy. Agent forwarding, which you turn on yourself, lets the VM use your keys but never copy them. Cloud, cluster and registry logins. Worms that steal credentials collect ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json and the npm publish token in ~/.npmrc. A VM mounts none of them, so a package that goes looking finds nothing. Secrets you keep in the project folder are a different case, which Left to you covers. The Keychain, browsers and password managers. Stealers read saved passwords, cookies and login sessions from browser profiles and the Keychain. The VM has no browser profile of yours, and it can’t reach this machine’s Keychain. Your coding agents’ history. Agent transcripts hold what you pasted into them, such as secrets and code from other projects. Your history never goes into a VM, and each VM’s own history stays in that VM (coding agents). Secrets, on every tier. Every VM, an open one included, gets a placeholder instead of each secret, such as your GitHub token or Claude Code’s token, and the proxy on this machine puts the real value only into requests for that secret’s own hosts (secrets). A placeholder copied out of the VM is worthless elsewhere, because it ends in a random value of that VM’s own, and an open VM that sends a request around its proxy sends only the placeholder. Another VM, or another user’s program on this machine, can’t spend the secret through the proxy either, because the proxy needs the VM’s own password, which only you can read. A program that runs as you can read it, though, as it can read the rest of your files. Codex and opencode logins and the MCP secrets that Claude Code gets from this machine work the same way, and devvm refreshes those OAuth logins on this machine, so a VM never holds their refresh tokens. A login to an MCP server that you make with /mcp in a VM is that VM’s own. Claude Code keeps its real tokens in the VM, where code in the VM can read them, and they never leave it (MCP servers’ logins).
data.files-the-vm-writes#Files the VM writes:
The VM can write anything in the project folder, and devvm locks only .git. Any other file there that a program on this machine runs, or reads as its config, is the VM’s to change. --clone keeps all of these away from this machine until you fetch the VM’s work and review it.
Hooks in the working tree. Hooks kept in the project, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath pointing there, run on this machine, and so do an include.path or a hook symlink that leads into the folder. devvm warns about them when it makes the VM (not covered). Agent config in the project. Claude Code reads a project’s .claude/settings.json, whose hooks run commands, and .mcp.json, which starts MCP servers, and agents follow a project’s CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. pi reads a project’s .pi folder, whose extensions run as code when pi starts, whose settings.json installs packages and sets shellCommandPrefix, which comes before every command pi runs, and whose mcp.json starts MCP servers. pi asks before it loads them, unless your ~/.pi/agent/trust.json on this machine already trusts the folder or your settings trust every folder. Running an agent on this machine in the folder after the VM has worked in it runs what the VM wrote, so run your agents in the VM. Editor and tool config. VS Code runs .vscode/tasks.json tasks set to runOn: folderOpen and starts the interpreters and formatters that .vscode/settings.json names. direnv loads .envrc, and mise reads mise.toml’s environment, hooks and tasks. Keep VS Code’s workspace trust on, and use direnv’s and mise’s own approval prompts. Project code and binaries. npm install, make, a test run or ./bin/tool on this machine runs whatever the VM wrote. Run them in the VM instead. Symlinks out of the folder. The VM can create a link in the project folder that points at a file of yours, such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. A program on this machine that follows it, such as an upload, an archive or an agent reading files, reads your file instead. devvm itself never follows a link out of the folder. Backdoors in code you merge. Treat the VM’s commits as an untrusted contributor’s, and review them before you merge, deploy or publish them. Secrets in the project folder. A .env file, a project .npmrc or a cloud key in the folder is in the VM. On the allowlist tier it can reach only the hosts on the allowlist, on the internet tier any public host, and on the open tier anywhere. Keep secrets out of the project folder, or use --clone, which copies no untracked files into the VM but those of a git stash -u entry, though it copies your repo’s hooks as they are and a folder of repos’ own files (what’s copied). The same goes for your agents’ config folders, which keys devvm can’t tell apart covers (mounts). What you paste in. An image, a PDF or a file you send with devvm paste is a file in the VM, which anything in the VM can read, as it reads the project folder. devvm reads only an image, a PDF or a copied file’s reference from your clipboard, never text, asks before sending a copied file, showing its path, refuses a link anywhere in a copied file’s path but the system’s own, and lets nothing the VM says onto your clipboard, so paste nothing you wouldn’t put in the folder (pasting images).
data.getting-out-over-the-network-on-the-allo: Sending data to the attacker’s server. Most attacks end by sending what they stole to a server the attacker runs. A confined VM reaches only its proxy, and on the allowlist tier the proxy allows only the hosts on the VM’s allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. On the internet tier, which a VM is on while it learns the hosts it needs, the proxy allows every public host, the attacker’s included, so this holds only for this machine and your networks. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of the default allowlist on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out (allowlists). DNS tunnelling. An attacker can encode data into names and look them up at a DNS server of their own. A VM sends no DNS queries out of it, because names resolve in the proxy on this machine. The names that tools look up in the VM are answered in the VM, by transparent mode’s dnsmasq, which has no server to ask, and the proxy resolves a name only once the VM’s rules allow it. Services on this machine and your network. Code in a VM could attack what developers leave open on localhost, such as databases, dev servers, Docker’s API and other VMs’ ports. It could also attack your router, a NAS, or a cloud provider’s metadata service at 169.254.169.254. The proxy refuses this machine’s own addresses and internal ones, such as loopback, private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, unless a rule names the address (the proxy). DNS rebinding and address tricks. A name can resolve to a public address when it’s checked and to an internal one when it’s dialed, and an internal address can hide in an IPv6, NAT64 or 6to4 form. The proxy dials only the address it checked, and it sees through NAT64 and 6to4 forms (the proxy). Going around the proxy. Root in a VM can change its routes and firewall, but devvm confines the VM from outside it, so nothing in the VM reaches anything but the proxy (confinement). devvm catches a VM started outside devvm, or one given a second network, with the self-check. It stops a VM that gets out through a second network, and it offers to restart one started outside devvm confined, or stops it when there’s no terminal to ask in.
data.git#Git: The shell prompt. Many shell prompts and editors run git status as soon as you cd into a folder or open it, and git status runs core.fsmonitor. Where devvm locks .git, the lock covers the .git of the folder and of the nested repos devvm has found, so opening the folder runs nothing that the VM wrote into them. It doesn’t cover a submodule the VM adds, a .git the VM replaces or a repo the VM makes while it runs, which git on this machine reads before devvm’s next check, as the entries below describe. Submodules with their own config. The VM writes .git/index to commit, so it can add a submodule whose config sets core.fsmonitor. git status, git diff, git add -A and git describe --dirty on this machine read that config, and run what it names, before devvm stops the VM or the next launch finds the submodule and locks it. No git setting keeps git on this machine out of a submodule that the VM adds, because the VM writes the .gitmodules file that git reads, and several commands enter a submodule whatever the settings say. So use --clone for a repo where you run git on this machine while the VM runs (not covered). Replacing .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or add a commondir that points git at another config. devvm reports these on each launch but doesn’t prevent them, so check what it names before you run git in the folder (what a lock can’t stop). Nested repos. devvm protects the git repos nested in the folder, but the VM can clone a new one while it runs, or move a protected one aside and put another in its place, and git on this machine runs its config before devvm’s next check names it. devvm also doesn’t protect a nested repo deeper than four folders, in a folder such as node_modules, or past the first 100, which it counts and names (nested repos).
data.git-running-code-on-this-machine#Git run: Git hooks and config. A VM can write the project folder, so without protection it could add a hook such as .git/hooks/post-checkout, or set a command in .git/config: core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, core.editor, a filter.* or diff.*.textconv driver, a credential.helper or a ! alias. Your next git command on this machine would run it. On macOS, devvm locks hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM’s view of the folder (.git protection). A Linux host whose kernel doesn’t let devvm do that, which Left to you covers, has neither. devvm’s own git commands. devvm runs git on this machine itself, for example to read your name and email for the VM, to check a --clone VM’s repo for uncommitted changes, and to fetch from the VM. A VM can write a repo that git on this machine reads, such as the project folder’s on Linux or a repo inside a folder it mounts, so devvm’s git runs none of the programs a repo’s config can name: It turns off the repo’s fsmonitor, its hooks, including those its config defines, and its filters, it never enters a submodule for git status, and it uses no transport but ssh, so git status or a fetch of devvm’s runs nothing that the VM wrote into the repo. It runs no program a repo’s config names to check signatures, and it sees a repo’s real history, whatever replace refs or a grafts file say. It ignores the git variables of the shell you run devvm in, such as GIT_DIR and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so it never works on another repo or config by mistake, and it never asks you anything (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0). Its fetches reach the VM with ssh in batch mode (-o BatchMode=yes), so the VM’s ssh server can’t ask you for a password. They always connect to that VM itself, whatever host the repo’s config sends them to, accept only the host key devvm pinned for it, and forward neither your agent nor any port.
data.how-devvm-handles-each-attack#How devvm:
The rest of this page sorts the attacks by how much of each one devvm stops:
Blocked The attack can’t work, because what it’s after isn’t in the VM or the VM can’t reach it. Kept inside the VM The attacker’s code runs, but it runs in the VM, where it reaches only the project folder and what you gave the VM. Narrowed, not closed devvm closes part of the attack, and the entry says what’s still open. Left to you devvm doesn’t stop the attack, and the entry says what to do instead. Some protections hold only on some network tiers or only on macOS, and each entry names its conditions. Everything here rests on the VM’s boundary. How devvm does each of these is in the security model.
data.install-and-build-scripts#Install and bu: npm, yarn, pnpm and bun lifecycle scripts. A package’s preinstall, install, postinstall and prepare scripts run any command when the package is installed, and most npm attacks use them. pnpm’s build approvals (pnpm approve-builds) and --ignore-scripts narrow which packages run scripts, and they’re still worth using, but a package you approved runs its scripts all the same, even one compromised after you approved it. In a VM, those scripts reach only what this section’s introduction lists. Python packages. Installing a source distribution runs its setup.py or its build backend, and a .pth file in site-packages runs code every time Python starts. Ruby gems. A gem with a native extension runs its extconf.rb when it’s installed, and Bundler can install gems straight from a git repo. Rust build scripts and procedural macros. build.rs and procedural macros run on cargo build and cargo check, and also when rust-analyzer opens the project, so opening the folder in an editor is enough to run them. With devvm code or devvm cursor, the editor’s extensions, rust-analyzer among them, run in the VM (devvm host, devvm code and devvm cursor). Go modules. Go has no install scripts, but cgo passes flags to the C compiler, go generate runs commands, a toolchain line in go.mod makes Go download another toolchain, and a module’s init functions run in every test and program that imports it. Makefiles, task runners and curl | sh. A Makefile, a justfile or a project’s install line from its README runs whatever its author wrote.
data.kept-inside-the-vm#Kept inside the VM: The attacks in this section run the attacker’s code, and devvm doesn’t stop that code from running. It runs in the VM, as the VM’s user, who has passwordless sudo. From there it reaches the project folder, or with --clone the VM’s own clone of it, and the secrets the VM uses, which are placeholders on every tier. It reaches what the VM’s tier allows: the hosts on the allowlist on the allowlist tier, every public host on the internet tier, and the whole network on the open tier. Everything in Blocked still holds. What the code writes into the project folder can still reach you when a program on this machine runs it, which Left to you covers.
data.network#Network: Domain fronting. The proxy checks the host name that a TLS connection asks for, its SNI, but not the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that serves many sites on one address can route an allowed connection to a site that isn’t allowed. The proxy reads the connections to hosts with a bound secret, and it refuses a request in them that names another host. A connection that transparent mode sends to the proxy is judged by its SNI in the same way, and so is a client with an Encrypted Client Hello configuration from somewhere other than DNS, whose outer SNI, the CDN’s public name, is what the proxy sees. The VM’s own names give no client such a configuration. The first seconds of an open start. A VM that was confined and is made open runs transparent mode from its next boot until that launch’s setup takes it out, a few seconds later. In that window, its names resolve to the stand-in address and its connections reach its proxy, which is an open one by then, so they reach what the open tier allows, and nothing keeps those answers after. Model providers that fetch for the VM. The proxy allows a bound API key’s provider hosts on port 443, and some providers’ own tools fetch URLs that the request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, as Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s web fetch and search tools do. Code in the VM can send data out through such a tool to a host that the allowlist doesn’t have (API keys the proxy puts in). Ports the VM listens on. devvm forwards the VM’s TCP ports from 1024 up to this machine’s localhost, unless you list the ports with --ports, so a VM could take a port that a program on this machine trusts while that port is free, and what the VM serves there reaches whatever connects to it. devvm’s forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, or one that devvm records for a VM, but a program that binds a port on all addresses after devvm forwarded it gets its localhost connections sent to the VM. devvm ports limits what a VM forwards, and devvm ports none forwards nothing, though a project’s devcontainer.json adds its forwardPorts to that list when devvm makes the VM or devvm update reads the file (devcontainer.json, ports, port forwarding). A browser login’s port. While devvm agent login waits for Codex’s or opencode’s browser login to ChatGPT, devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455, and localhost:1457 when it’s free, to the agent’s login server in the VM, so any program on this machine that connects in that window reaches the VM’s server and gets what it answers. The forward ends with the login, and --device-code logs in without one (logging in). VS Code’s and Cursor’s relays. Over Remote-SSH, which devvm code and devvm cursor open, the editor forwards the ports that programs in the VM listen on, and it answers git’s prompts with your GitHub sign-in. devvm turns both off in the VM’s settings for each editor each time it sets the VM up, but the VM can turn them back on, and its settings take precedence over your own on this machine. The editor’s extensions also run in the VM, its AI features among them, and they may get the editor’s sign-ins there, such as Copilot’s GitHub token or your Cursor login. Recent Cursor runs its Agent in the VM with your sign-in in memory (Cursor’s Agent). So don’t open a VM you don’t trust with devvm code or devvm cursor, or sign out of the editor’s AI features and its GitHub sign-in first (VS Code and Cursor). What a VM does through a link. A link between VMs joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the service it reaches, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has the target’s network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm limits a link to the ports the target publishes, on the target’s loopback, and a client to targets on its own tier or a stricter one, but it doesn’t limit what the service does. In a group, every VM trusts every other in the same way, and a VM that joins later gets the same reach (links between VMs). History imported from a less strict tier. An export of agents’ history carries what the old VM’s agents read, so importing one from an open VM into a VM on the allowlist tier can bring in credentials and data that the new VM couldn’t reach itself, along with any instructions planted in them. devvm warns before such an import, and before importing an export whose tier it has no record of, but it imports all the same. Import history only from a VM you trusted as much as the new one (importing history). What one VM learns of another through the shared Nix cache. VMs with the nix layer share one cache of Nix’s packages on this machine. A VM can tell by how fast the cache answers whether some VM fetched a public package. The packages are public, and a project’s flake.lock names the ones it needs, so this tells a VM only that another project on this machine uses a package. A VM that fetches many packages can also fill the cache up to its cap and push other VMs’ packages out, so they download them again, but it can’t fill the disk past the cap or keep anything that cache.nixos.org didn’t sign (the shared Nix cache). Through a company proxy. The company proxy looks up the names it’s sent itself, and it may get another answer than this machine did, or a later one, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to there. Under a name that an allowlist names, a VM reaches whatever the company proxy reaches, such as your company’s internal hosts and the company proxy’s own host, which is this machine’s loopback when the company proxy runs on this machine, as a VPN client’s does. A name that the VM’s allowlist doesn’t allow never reaches the company proxy (the design note). Which names resolve to internal addresses. When the proxy refuses a name because this machine’s lookup gives it an internal address, its refusal says so, so a VM can learn which names this machine’s DNS resolves to internal addresses. The refusal never names the address, this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy, which stay in the proxy’s own log (log files).
data.rogue-agents#Rogue agents: Prompt injection. Instructions hidden in a README, an issue, a code comment, a web page, a dependency’s docs or an MCP tool’s output can turn a coding agent against you. devvm can’t tell an agent’s own work from injected work, so it limits what the agent reaches instead. An attack like this needs private data, untrusted input and a way to send the data out. On the allowlist tier, the only way out is the hosts on the allowlist, which Left to you covers. Agents with their checks off. An agent run with claude --dangerously-skip-permissions or codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox acts without asking, and a mistaken rm -rf ~ or sudo command reaches only the VM. The project folder is still the agent’s to change, so commit often, or use --clone to keep the agent’s work apart until you fetch it. Malware that stays. Anything the attacker leaves in the VM, such as a cron job, a changed shell startup file or a backdoored program, stays in that VM’s disk and goes into no other VM’s, unless you save an agent’s settings that it changed with devvm agent save. What it wrote into the project folder stays there, though, and the folder’s next VM gets it, such as a devcontainer.json command that runs as soon as devvm makes the VM, or a hook in the project’s agent settings. devvm never deletes a VM on its own, because it may hold unsaved work, so save what you need and run devvm rm, then check the folder for what the VM writes, or use --clone, before you make the VM again. Mining and resource abuse. A VM’s CPUs, memory and disk are capped by its size, which devvm size shows and changes (size). The VM’s proxy on this machine carries at most 1024 tunnels and 2048 connections of every kind for it at once, and on a Linux host devvm carries at most 256 of its connections to the proxy at once, each a process on this machine, so a VM that opens connections without end can’t fill this machine with them (the proxy).
data.secrets-and-keys-the-vm-may-use#Secrets: Worms that use your GitHub token. Shai-Hulud (2025) spread through npm install scripts. It collected npm, GitHub and cloud credentials, then used them to publish repos and new versions of packages. A VM holds no npm or cloud credentials, and its GitHub token is a placeholder. The proxy still puts the real GitHub token into every request to GitHub’s hosts, so a worm in the VM can push, make repos and do whatever else the GitHub token’s scope allows. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to the repos the VM needs, or bind none (saving and binding secrets). A host that sends your secret back. The proxy puts a secret only into requests for its own hosts, but it passes their replies to the VM as they are. A host that echoes a request’s headers, such as a debug endpoint, or an error page that quotes them, shows the VM the real value. This matters most for your own secrets, whose hosts you choose, so give each one only hosts that you trust with it. A secret’s hosts are on the allowlist of every VM that uses it, on every tier, so on a host where anyone can make an account, code in the VM can also send data to an account of its own there. Minting credentials with a secret. A VM that can use a secret can use it to make another credential that outlasts it. The proxy refuses GitHub REST calls that add an SSH key, a deploy key, a self-hosted runner or a webhook with 403, but it can’t refuse everything, such as GitHub’s GraphQL API, an OAuth app grant or other services. A bound API key can make credentials too. With Google Gemini’s key, code in the VM can ask generativelanguage.googleapis.com for an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. With xAI’s key it can ask api.x.ai for a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and with OpenAI’s key it can ask api.openai.com for one that lasts up to 2 hours. These credentials work without the proxy, and the proxy allows the requests that make them, because opencode’s experimental voice mode makes them itself (API keys the proxy puts in). If a VM may have done this, rotate the secret and check the service’s keys, access tokens and runners. Keys devvm can’t tell apart. devvm takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of your agents’ settings and logins only where it can tell a key from the rest. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic. opencode’s and pi’s keys that devvm can’t bind, such as a local model server’s, stay on this machine unless you list their provider in config.toml’s [pass-keys], and then they go in as they are. The agents’ folders that the VM mounts whole, such as ~/.claude/skills or ~/.config/opencode/plugin, reach the VM with every file in them, so a .env in one is in the VM, and so is a private plugin marketplace’s git config with a password or an access token in its URL. Keep secrets out of those folders (what stays in the VM’s copies). Your SSH agent. While agent forwarding is on, anything in the VM can use the agent’s keys to push, log in to servers or sign any data, though it can’t copy them. It also can’t remove the agent’s keys, lock the agent or add keys to it, so it can’t take the agent away from you or from other VMs (the SSH agents). A VM that has run since before you upgraded devvm to this release can still do those until its next start, so restart such VMs with devvm restart. The VM has the agent while you’re connected. devvm ssh-agent devvm limits it to the keys you add to devvm’s own agent, and an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive, narrows it further.
data.spreading-beyond-the-vm#Spreading beyond: Your agents’ config. A rogue agent could add a hook to ~/.claude/settings.json or a skill to ~/.claude/skills, so that it runs the next time you use the agent on this machine. devvm mounts the agents’ config folders read-only, which this machine enforces, and copies their files in on every launch, so nothing the VM changes goes back (mounts). Only devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into devvm’s agent store, for every VM, and it shows what changed and asks first, so read its diff for hooks, MCP servers and plugins you didn’t add (saving a VM’s settings). Other projects and other VMs. Each project folder gets its own VM with its own disk, and a VM mounts only its own project folder. Each VM’s proxy has its own password, so one VM can’t use another’s secrets. A VM reaches a service in another VM only through a link between VMs that you add in its folder, to a port that the other VM’s folder publishes. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in one can often run code in the other through its service, so a VM links only to a VM on its own tier or a stricter one, and nothing in a VM can add a link (links between VMs). Images, layers and devvm itself. Malware could try to make itself permanent by editing an image, a layer script or devvm’s own files. devvm builds images with nothing from this machine mounted, and the shared tools are read-only in every VM. devvm also refuses a project folder that holds its own folders or sits inside them, so a VM can’t reach the layer scripts that every build runs or the files devvm runs on this machine (only the project folder). A folder made again. If you delete a repo and clone another at the same path, the new folder never gets the old VM’s disk or anything left in it. devvm knows a folder by its inode and birth time as well as its path, which nothing in a VM can give a new folder, so it refuses and offers devvm rm or devvm adopt (a folder made again). A devcontainer.json that reaches this machine. Other tools run a devcontainer’s initializeCommand on the host. devvm never runs it, refuses ${localEnv:…}, adds no mounts from the file and doesn’t follow a link out of the folder (devcontainer.json). devvm uses the file’s image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks, and it refuses a registry on this machine or its network. Behind a company proxy, devvm looks the image up through the company proxy and checks only the registry’s name, so a company proxy that reaches this machine or its network for a name that looks public takes the lookup there (the design note). Impersonating a VM. ssh checks a VM against host keys that devvm reads through the VM’s backend instead of over the network, so a program that answers on the VM’s port in its place is refused (ssh access by name).
data.the-network#The network: Allowed hosts. Anything an allowed host accepts can carry data out. github.com accepts a push from anyone with an account, including an attacker with an account of their own, and the npm registry accepts packages the same way. Keep allowlists short, narrow a host to the methods and paths a VM needs (rules by method and path), and check what a VM reached with devvm network log. A rule by method and path judges each request’s method and path, not its body or its other headers, so what an allowed request sends still reaches the host. A deny of git-receive-pack on github.com, for example, blocks pushes over HTTPS alone: a push over ssh to github.com:22, if a rule allows it, and the commits that GitHub’s Git Data API makes at api.github.com with a GitHub token go on. What your secrets allow. A VM can push with a GitHub token it may use and spend Claude quota. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, bind only the secrets a VM needs, and deny the methods a VM mustn’t use, such as devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE. Your claude.ai connectors. With your Claude subscription’s login, a VM with Claude Code can use every connector you added in claude.ai, as Claude Code on this machine can, so code in the VM can read what they reach, such as your mail or documents, and act through them. Disconnect the connectors you don’t want VMs to use, or keep them from a VM with devvm network deny mcp-proxy.anthropic.com, or from every VM with -g, which works on every tier but open (Claude Code login). Open VMs. An open VM, because you chose open or passed --network open, reaches everything this machine can, including its services on localhost, such as other VMs’ ports, dev servers and databases, and your local network, directly and through its proxy, which applies no rules for it. Its proxy still puts its secrets in, so it can spend them on their hosts as any VM can, but it holds only their placeholders, as every VM does. A VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, or one running since before devvm network gave it a confined tier, runs unconfined in the same way until devvm restarts it confined (the self-check). Your browser. Programs in a VM can open URLs in this machine’s browser, and a page that a VM serves on a forwarded port runs in your browser like any other. From there it can reach the internet past the VM’s tier, and your services on localhost. Browsers send a host’s cookies to every port on it, so a server in the VM on a forwarded localhost port gets the cookies of the apps you use on localhost, such as a local dashboard you’re signed in to. A VM’s ssh port in your browser. Root in a VM can make its ssh port on this machine answer as a web server, so devvm puts every VM’s ssh on one of the ports that every browser refuses, and a VM that forwards no ports gets no page from your browser that way. A browser you’ve told to allow those ports, such as with Chrome’s --explicitly-allowed-ports or Firefox’s network.security.ports.banned.override, reaches it again. Another user on this machine can also take all 17 of those ports, so none of your VMs starts until they let one go (too many VMs at once). Remote forwards you add. A RemoteForward in your ssh config, or an ssh -R you type, makes this machine connect to whatever it names for the VM. devvm’s ssh entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type. The VM’s ssh server refuses a remote forward on any address outside 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, so one on the VM’s localhost, which ssh -R asks for by default, is refused. Root in the VM can change that setting, though, and the server allows a forward on an address in 127.77.0.0/16 for anyone it lets in. A forward you ask for by a host name that begins with 127.77. binds whatever address that name resolves to in the VM. So keep remote forwards out of Host *, and don’t forward into a VM you don’t trust (ssh into VMs). A company CA you add. A company CA that you put in ~/.config/devvm/ca can read the TLS traffic of every VM, whatever its tier, as it can this machine’s, and the proxy trusts it for its own connections. Only that folder adds CAs to the proxy, and nothing a VM sends can.
data.the-platform#The platform: .git on Linux hosts. devvm makes hooks and config read-only in the VM’s view, but a git command on this machine that replaces .git/config while the VM runs leaves the new file the VM’s to change, replace or open for writing until devvm locks it again, which devvm names only when the VM stops (when git replaces a locked file). Where the kernel doesn’t let devvm use a user namespace, such as on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, VMs have no .git protection, and the VM can change hooks and config that run on the host, so use --clone there (Linux hosts). What a build reaches.
