A build, such as a --from image’s or a layer’s, reaches the internet and your local network as well, this machine’s own address on it included, so a service of yours that listens on every address is in its reach. On macOS that’s all it reaches of this machine, because its loopback is out of reach, but on Linux the build reaches the services on this machine’s localhost too, such as other VMs’ proxies and dev servers. Build images only from container images and layers you trust (confinement). Escaping the VM. A bug in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU could let code out of the VM. So could a bug in devvm’s own programs on this machine that read what a VM sends, which are the VM’s proxy, the port forwarder, the sessions of links between VMs, devvm agent save and the export of agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save. The part of the VM’s proxy that reads the VM’s network runs in a sandbox, which is macOS’s on macOS and Landlock with a seccomp filter on Linux. A bug there reaches the secrets bound to that VM, the company proxy’s password, the VM’s logs, the shared Nix cache and the public internet. It doesn’t reach your files, the Keychain, other VMs’ secrets, or this machine’s unix sockets, such as ssh’s and Docker’s. Nor does it reach this machine’s services on localhost, its own addresses or your LAN’s private addresses, unless a rule names the address or a company proxy reaches them. On Linux it can also learn whether a file of yours exists, and an older kernel confines it less (what it still reaches). devvm doctor warns when a VM’s proxy runs without its sandbox, or with only part of it (the proxy runs without a sandbox). Found a way out of a VM? See SECURITY.md.
data.this-machine#This machine: A nested project replaced through its parent folder’s VM. A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM is in both VMs, so code in the parent folder’s VM can replace the nested project folder with a link, such as one to your home folder, which the nested VM would mount at its next start. devvm warns each time it makes or opens such a nested VM, naming the parent folder’s VM. It checks the nested folder, by its path and by the folder itself, just before it starts the nested VM and again once the VM runs, and it refuses the start or stops the VM again when the folder was replaced. On macOS the VM mounts the folder itself rather than its path, so it never mounts what a link points to, even when the folder is put back before devvm checks again. On Linux the VM mounts the folder by its path, so code that replaces the folder for the moment the VM’s backend mounts it and puts it back before devvm checks again stays unseen, and the VM keeps what the link pointed to until its next start. Keep a nested project that you don’t want the parent folder’s VM to reach out of the parent folder (a nested project replaced). Set-id files on Linux hosts. Root in a VM can set the set-user-id bit on a file in the project folder, and on Linux hosts that bit reaches the host, so the file runs as its owner for whoever runs it. devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, but not at a launch into a running VM, and Troubleshooting says how to clear them. Don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (set-id files). The proxy’s CA keys. Inside a VM, its CA vouches for any site, so someone with a copy of its key and a place on your network could impersonate sites to that VM. Each VM has CAs of its own, so a copy reaches one VM and no other. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, so a copy goes stale, but the next CA’s key is on disk for up to 23 days before that CA starts, so a copy of it taken then works until that CA ends, up to 53 days later. Keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of other backup and sync tools as well, and on Linux, which has no Time Machine, out of your backups (the VM’s CA). Your company proxy’s password. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings: an open VM goes through its own proxy, which goes through the company proxy for it. devvm keeps the password out of its run logs only where it can tell it’s a password, so one in an address with neither a scheme nor a port, one with a raw /, ?, # or @ in it, or one in a run of more than 4 KiB without a space that a command writes in pieces can stay. Lima’s own log for the VM holds the password until the VM has started, when devvm replaces it with as many *, so the log still shows its length. If devvm is killed before then, or you run limactl start outside devvm, the log keeps it. Lima’s logs of the VM’s serial consoles hold the VM’s own proxy password in the same way, until the VM has started. A reboot inside the VM writes it to the console’s log again, and while the VM runs, its proxy replaces it within about a second of its line ending. So the log holds it for that second, or for as long as the proxy isn’t running (Lima’s hostagent). With config.toml’s proxy, the mise that devvm runs on this machine gets the password in its environment, where programs that run as you can read it (open VMs and builds, the run log).

data:
The project folder is read-write in the VM, so without protection anything in the VM could add a git hook, or set core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath or core.sshCommand in .git/config, and your next git command on this machine would run it. devvm protects them:
On macOS, devvm locks the git hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear, so nothing the VM does runs through them on this machine. On Linux, devvm makes them read-only in the VM’s own view of the folder, which root in the VM can’t change either (Linux hosts). Nested repos: it does the same for each git repo nested in the folder that it has found, such as the repos of a folder that holds several, but a repo or a submodule that the VM adds while it runs is git’s to use before devvm finds it (nested repos, not covered). Only --clone keeps the VM’s code away from git on this machine.
Every new VM gets .git protection. --no-git-protect creates a VM without it, and devvm git-protect changes it later. How it works › .git protection lists what devvm locks and when it checks the locks again.
data.bare-repos#Bare repos: git also takes a folder shaped like a git folder, with a HEAD, objects and refs, for a bare repo, and its config can name a work tree, so git run in a folder below one uses it, core.fsmonitor and all. The VM can make one anywhere in the folder. devvm names the ones it finds up to four folders down that aren’t a repo’s own git folder, and devvm doctor gives a tip when git on this machine takes a bare repo it isn’t told to use. git 2.38 and newer can refuse that: git config --global safe.bareRepository explicit makes git use a bare repo only when you name it, with --git-dir or GIT_DIR. devvm only checks the setting, and never changes your git config.
data.devvm-git-protect-json#devvm git-protect:
devvm git-protect --json prints the VM’s protection as one JSON object with mode, which is on, off or clone, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on or off with it.
{ "version": 1, "mode": "on" }
data.hard-links#Hard links: A lock in the VM’s view covers one name of a file, and macOS’s flag covers the file itself, whatever its names. So devvm doesn’t start a VM whose .git/config, or a hook in a locked hooks folder, has another name (a hard link), because the VM could change the file through that other name. Make it a file of its own, by copying it and moving the copy over it, and start the VM again. A file that gets another name while the VM runs isn’t locked again, and devvm names it when the VM stops.
data.linux-hosts#Linux hosts:
On Linux, devvm runs each VM’s QEMU in a user namespace of its own, without root, and there it makes the paths that macOS’s flag would lock read-only: the hooks and config of .git and of its submodules, and the rest of what’s locked. The VM reaches the project folder only through QEMU, so root in the VM gets Read-only file system when it writes one of them, and Device or resource busy when it renames or removes one, or renames .git itself.
A nested repo’s own folder isn’t pinned, so the VM can still rename the folder, .git and all, and put another repo in its place, which devvm reports at the next check as a replaced .git. Nothing changes on this machine: your own git commands write .git/config as usual, and the read-only view ends when the VM stops. devvm git-protect works as it does on macOS, and a change to a running VM’s protection applies at its next start. Warning
Start VMs with devvm. A VM that limactl start starts runs without the read-only view, and so does one whose view went for another reason, so each launch of a running VM, and devvm stop, check that the VM still can’t rename .git and still sees its hooks and config read-only, and name what it doesn’t: run devvm restart then. If devvm’s own process that runs the VM ends, the VM ends with it at once, as if you pulled its power, so it never runs without the view.
Because a lock in the VM’s view covers one name of a file, devvm also watches .git as a Linux host without locks does, and names what changed at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop. That includes your own changes, such as a git remote add or git push -u.
data.nested-repos#Nested repos:
A folder can hold git repos of its own besides its submodules, such as ws/repo-a and ws/repo-b in a folder ws, whether ws is a repo itself or only a folder of repos. The VM can write all of them, and git on this machine runs what their .git holds when you run git there, so devvm protects each one it finds as it protects the folder’s own .git: it locks them on macOS, makes them read-only in the VM on Linux, and watches them on a Linux host that can’t lock. It finds them this way:
When: when it creates the VM, at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop. A launch into a running VM doesn’t look again, and it doesn’t check the nested repos either, so they’re checked at the next launch that finds the VM stopped, or at devvm stop. Where: up to four folders below the project folder, for anything named .git (on macOS, .GIT as well). It doesn’t look in the folders that package managers and build tools fill, node_modules, vendor, .venv, __pycache__ and .terraform, nor in a folder on another disk. How many: it protects the first 100 it finds and names the rest, at every check. What still works and what doesn’t is the same in a nested repo as in the folder’s own: git config, git remote add and hook installers fail there on macOS, so run them with protection off. devvm keeps protecting a nested repo for as long as anything is at its .git, even when that .git no longer looks like a repo’s, because the VM can change it back at any time.
When you don’t need the VM to write your working trees, devvm --clone in a folder of repos keeps the VM out of all of them instead:
cd ws && devvm --clone # a VM with its own clone of each repo you choose, mounting none of them devvm clone fetch # bring the VM's work back The VM gets a clone of each repo you choose, at the same path, and mounts nothing of this machine, so it can’t reach any repo’s working tree or .git here, and none of what this page describes applies to it (folders of repos). You get its work back with devvm clone fetch.
devvm can’t protect a repo before it has found it, so when you run git in a folder of a VM’s project while the VM runs, the protection holds only for the repos devvm has already found:
A repo the VM makes in the folder while it runs, by cloning one or by making a .git in a folder of yours, is git’s repo for that folder from the moment it’s there: your git status in the folder, and the shell prompts and editors that run git as you open it, run what its config says. devvm names such a repo only at the next launch that finds the VM stopped, or at devvm stop, with the settings in its config and the hooks that run programs, and then locks it as it is, so check what it names before you run git there. A repo the VM makes more than four folders down, or in a folder devvm doesn’t look in, is never named, only counted where devvm walks the folder for set-id files on Linux. On Linux the VM can also move a nested repo’s folder aside and put another repo in its place while it runs, which devvm names only if it’s still in place when the VM stops (Linux hosts).
data.not-covered#Not covered:
The lock covers .git, and the VM can still put things elsewhere that git on this machine runs. devvm tells you about each of these, so read what it reports before you run git in the folder, and use --clone for a repo you don’t trust.
Hooks in the working tree, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath=.husky, or an absolute path into the project folder. The VM can edit them, and they run on this machine. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM. What the locked files hand over to the project folder, which is an include.path or includeIf.*.path that leads into it, or a hook that’s a symlink into it. The VM can edit those files, and git on this machine reads or runs them. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM, and on a launch after they change. Submodules whose git folder is outside the project. devvm can’t lock that folder, because another project’s VM may write it, and git status on this machine reads its config. devvm names these submodules when it creates the VM. A submodule the VM adds. The VM writes .git/index, because it has to in order to commit, so it can add a submodule with a git folder of its own anywhere in the project folder. Whenever git on this machine enters that submodule, it reads the submodule’s config and runs its hooks, so its core.fsmonitor runs on this machine. git status, git diff, git add -A and git describe --dirty all enter it, and so do the shell prompts and editors that run them. devvm names the submodule and locks its git folder only at devvm stop or at the next launch that finds the VM stopped (when devvm reports .git). A replaced .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or point git at another config. devvm reports this on each launch but doesn’t undo it (what a lock can’t stop). Some of the git repos nested in the folder. devvm protects each repo it finds below the project folder (nested repos), but not one more than four folders down, one in a folder that a package manager fills, such as node_modules, one on another disk, or one past the first 100. It doesn’t lock the git folder that a nested repo’s .git file names unless that’s another repo’s that devvm locks, and a git folder outside the project folder it can’t lock at all. The VM can set core.fsmonitor in such a repo’s config, and your next git status there runs it. devvm names the ones it finds and doesn’t protect, and counts those on other disks, so check them before you run git there, or move them out of the folder. A repo the VM makes while it runs, and a bare repo it makes. git on this machine uses either as soon as it’s there, and devvm finds it only once the VM stops (nested repos).
data.the-warning-at-each-launch#The warning a: On a Linux host that can’t lock, each launch of a VM that mounts a folder with a .git, or with nested repos, warns that the VM can change their hooks and config, which run on this machine, and names the nested repos devvm doesn’t watch. That includes the launch that creates the VM, and launches of a VM that’s already running. Once you’ve read the warning and decided to go on without protection, run devvm git-protect off in the folder. devvm records that you chose it and stops warning for that VM, but it still names the changes that the next section describes. A VM that you create with --no-git-protect doesn’t warn either, and a --clone VM never warns, because it mounts no .git.
data.turning-it-on-or-off#Turning it on or of:
devvm git-protect # show this folder's VM's protection: on, off or clone devvm git-protect off # take the locks off devvm git-protect on # lock .git as it is now devvm git-protect shows the VM’s protection, which is on, off, or clone for a --clone VM, which mounts no .git. devvm git-protect on or off changes it at once when the VM is stopped. A running VM could race the locks, so for a running VM devvm saves your choice and asks in a terminal whether to restart the VM now, which stops anything running in it. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, devvm says it saved the choice. It applies the choice the next time it finds the VM stopped: at the restart you agreed to, at devvm stop, at devvm restart, or, when the VM was stopped some other way, at the next launch, before the VM starts. Until then, devvm git-protect shows the protection the VM has, and a later choice replaces the saved one. Launches lock only a stopped VM for the same reason.
on locks .git as it is now and takes it as yours, so a .git that was replaced since the last lock isn’t reported, and the next launches compare with this one. It reports what a lock can’t stop and what’s not covered, as devvm did when it made the VM. If the folder has no .git yet, devvm locks it on the first launch after one appears. The locks don’t reach a submodule or a nested repo that the VM adds while it runs, so git on this machine runs what that repo’s config and hooks say, such as its core.fsmonitor, until devvm stop or the next launch that finds the VM stopped names it and locks it (not covered). off takes the locks off. The VM can then change .git hooks and config, which run on your machine. On an existing VM, devvm ignores --no-git-protect and warns you. A --clone VM’s protection can’t be changed. devvm clone on takes the locks off once it has made the VM again with its own clone, and devvm clone off makes it mount the folder again with protection as a new VM gets it (switching a VM that exists).
data.two-vms-one-repo#Two VMs, one repo:
A nested repo can have a VM of its own, and then two VMs protect it. On macOS, the flag that locks it is the same for both, so devvm rm or devvm git-protect off for one VM leaves locked what the other VM still protects, and names that VM. Run devvm git-protect off for the other VM too when you want the locks off. When devvm can’t read another VM’s state, it leaves locked what that VM may protect, and names the state to fix. On Linux, each VM has its own read-only view, so each protects the repo from its own VM.
A nested repo devvm stopped protecting, because it’s gone or moved, keeps its locks until devvm takes them off with the rest, at devvm rm or devvm git-protect off. When it’s no longer in the folder, devvm can’t find it to unlock it, so it names it, and chflags -R nouchg on its .git/hooks and .git/config takes the locks off.
data.ubuntu#Ubuntu: Ubuntu 23.10 and newer set kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns to 1, so a program gets a user namespace with the rights to mount in it only when an AppArmor profile names the program with the userns rule. Ubuntu does that to keep programs that don’t need one out of the kernel code behind it. devvm’s binary lives in a folder you can write, such as ~/.local/lib/devvm/, and a profile for that path would let any program running as you put itself there and get the same rights, which undoes what Ubuntu set the restriction for. So devvm doesn’t ask for a profile, and on Ubuntu with the restriction on it doesn’t lock .git: it watches it, and devvm doctor and each launch say so. Use --clone there for any repo where you don’t trust what runs in the VM.
data.vms-an-earlier-devvm-made#VMs an earlier: A VM that an earlier devvm made protects only the folder’s own repo. The first time devvm finds nested repos in its folder, it names them once and tells you to run devvm git-protect on, which protects them all from then on. Until you do, devvm names each nested repo it finds that it hadn’t named before.
data.vms-that-were-strict#VMs that were stric:
devvm git-protect takes only on and off. devvm git-protect strict is a usage error that points to devvm clone on, which keeps the VM’s code away from git on this machine.
An earlier devvm’s strict set diff.ignoreSubmodules = all in the locked .git/config, so that git status and git diff on this machine skipped the submodules the VM adds. That couldn’t keep git on this machine out of them. A .gitmodules line that the VM writes, such as ignore = none, makes git status enter a submodule again, and git add -A, git add -u, git describe --dirty, git diff-index, git diff-files, git fetch and git pull enter one whatever the setting says, as does --ignore-submodules on the command line.
A VM that was made strict shows as on at once, in devvm ls, devvm git-protect and its --json, and its locks stay as they are while it runs. The first time devvm finds it stopped, at a launch, at devvm stop, or at devvm clone on, or when devvm undoes a devvm clone off that didn’t finish, devvm takes diff.ignoreSubmodules = all out of the .git/config of the folder’s own repo and of each nested repo the VM protected, unlocking each file for the moment and locking it again. Then it records the VM as on and says so once, unless you chose devvm git-protect off while it ran, which it applies next. devvm git-protect on and off and devvm rm take the setting out the same way, without saying so.
devvm leaves the setting where it can’t tell that it set it, and names what it leaves:
strict doesn’t record a value that the setting had before it sets its own, so devvm can’t put one back. It takes out only the value all, so a value that you set since, such as none or dirty, stays. devvm leaves the setting alone in a repo whose .git isn’t the one it recorded, because strict never set it there: a .git that the VM replaced, which devvm names, a nested repo that it finds for the first time at that check, and every repo of a VM it has no record of, such as one that devvm adopt moved. When such a config sets all, devvm names it once. On a Linux host that watches .git, it also leaves a config that changed since the check read it, which the next check names. If git can’t change a config, devvm names it, and git status and git diff on this machine go on skipping that repo’s submodules until you take the setting out yourself. A .git/config that another VM’s protection also keeps locked keeps the setting, because unlocking it would let that VM change the file if it runs, and devvm names the file and that VM at each launch that finds this VM stopped. devvm takes the setting out at such a check once the other VM no longer keeps the file locked. To take the setting out of a repo yourself, if you didn’t set it:
devvm stop # in this VM's folder, and in the other VM's when another VM locks the file too devvm git-protect off git config --file .git/config --unset-all diff.ignoreSubmodules '^all$' # in that repo devvm git-protect on # lock .git again as it is then Stop both VMs when another VM keeps the file locked too, because a running VM could change the file while it’s unlocked, and a launch into a running VM locks nothing. In that case, run chflags nouchg .git/config on macOS in place of devvm git-protect off, and the next launch of either VM finds it stopped and locks the file again, and on Linux the other VM’s watch names the change.
data.what-else-differs-in-the-vm#What else di:
Two more things work differently in the VM. The VM sees .git as a file system of its own, so renaming a file between the working tree and .git fails with Invalid cross-device link, which mv handles by copying the file, and git never does. And the VM can’t remove or rename a submodule’s git folder, so git submodule absorbgitdirs, or rm -rf on a submodule, fails while the VM runs.
A VM that a devvm without these locks made on this machine stays off, and each launch says that devvm can lock it now: run devvm git-protect on to lock it, or devvm git-protect off to keep it off and stop the warning.
data.what-still-works#What still works:
git in the VM can commit, branch, check out, stash, fetch and pull, and git worktree add works on this machine. Commands that write .git/config fail in the VM, and on macOS they fail on this machine too, with Operation not permitted. Those are git config, git remote add, push -u to a new branch, and hook installers such as husky or pre-commit. On macOS, git worktree remove and prune also fail for the worktrees that were there when devvm locked .git. On Linux, these commands work on this machine as usual, and the VM sees what they change (Linux hosts).
To run them on macOS, stop the VM, unlock .git, run the commands on this machine, and lock it again:
devvm stop devvm git-protect off git config … devvm git-protect on
data.what-the-watch-cant-see#What the watch c:
The watch isn’t a security boundary, and it doesn’t stop anything. It compares what’s in .git when the VM is stopped with what was there at the last check, so it misses a change that the VM made and then undid before it stopped, even though git on this machine may have run the change in between. It also can’t fully watch some paths, and it names them at every check until they’re gone:
A symlink, or a path under one, such as a hook that’s a symlink, or a .git that’s a symlink. devvm never follows a symlink out of the project folder, so it can’t see changes to what such a link points to. For a link that stays inside the project folder, it hashes what the link leads to as well. A file larger than 16 MiB, which devvm records by its size, inode and change time, so it notices a change that keeps the size but can’t hash the file. A hooks folder with more than 1,000 entries, which devvm records by its count and change time. It always hashes the hooks that git runs, at the folder’s top, before the rest. The VM can fill a hooks folder to blind the watch, the folder’s own or a nested repo’s, so devvm names such a folder at every check. What’s past 2,000 paths in all, across every git folder and hooks folder of the folder’s own repo, or past 200 paths of each nested repo. A repo rarely has any of these, so when devvm names one that you didn’t make, check what it holds, and use --clone for that repo.
data.when-devvm-names-a-change#When devvm nam:
On a Linux host that can’t lock, devvm can’t stop the VM from changing .git, and on one that locks, the VM can change a file that git on this machine replaced, but devvm notices the change afterwards on both. When devvm creates a VM, it records a hash of each of these:
each path that a lock would cover on macOS, which are the hooks in .git/hooks, .git/config and the rest of what’s locked, submodules’ and nested repos’ included .git/commondir, whether it’s there or not what the config hands over to the project folder: the files that an include.path leads to, and the hooks folder that core.hooksPath names, such as husky’s .husky Each launch that finds the VM stopped, and devvm stop, hash them again and name every path that changed since the last check, such as .git/config and .git/hooks/pre-commit. A warning names ten paths at most, and then how many more changed. The same checks report what a lock can’t stop either, as they do on macOS: a .git that was replaced, a commondir, a repo or submodule that appeared, and includes, hook links and a core.hooksPath into the project folder (not covered). A launch of a VM that’s already running checks nothing, so run devvm stop when you want the check. A VM that devvm has no hashes for yet, such as one that an older devvm made, records them at its first check and names nothing.
devvm names a change only after it happened, so git on this machine may already have run a changed hook or read a changed config. devvm can’t tell who made a change, so it also names your own, such as a git remote add or git push -u that you ran on this machine. When it names a path that you didn’t change, check it before you run git in the folder:
git config --list --show-origin shows each setting of the repo and the file it comes from. Look for settings that run a program, such as core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, filter.* and include.path. ls -la .git/hooks lists the hooks, and git runs a hook there by its name, such as pre-commit, so read every file whose name doesn’t end in .sample. If you find something that you didn’t put there, remove it, and use --clone for that repo.
data.when-devvm-reports-git#When devvm report:
Every launch of an existing VM, and devvm stop, check .git again, and devvm reports what it finds there that it didn’t lock. When it names one of these, check it before you run git in the folder, because git on this machine would run what the VM put there:
A repo that appeared in the folder after its VM was made, the folder’s own or a nested one. devvm locks it from then on, but if you didn’t make it, check its hooks and config. A submodule that appeared with its git folder in the project folder. devvm locks it from then on, but git on this machine may already have run what its config and hooks say (not covered), so if you didn’t add it, check them. A nested repo that’s gone or moved, which the VM could have moved aside to put another in its place. Hooks in a folder devvm hadn’t locked, because the folder wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule. A submodule whose git folder isn’t one. The VM can name any folder in the project as a submodule’s git folder, such as your src, so devvm locks nothing in a folder that doesn’t look like a git folder, and names the submodule instead. A path that’s a symlink or under one. devvm never locks anything through a symlink, because the VM could point one at a file elsewhere on this machine, so it leaves that path unlocked. A path that moved while devvm locked it. devvm leaves it unlocked and takes the lock off wherever it landed, so check .git. How it works › .git protection lists every check.
data.when-git-on-this-machine-replaces-a-lock:
The VM sees your changes, because its view is the same folder. A git command on this machine that writes .git/config, such as git config, git remote add or git push -u, writes a new file and renames it over the old one, and the new file isn’t read-only in the VM until devvm locks it again. devvm watches the folders of what it locks, so it locks the new file within milliseconds, but until then the VM can change it, replace it with a file of its own, which devvm then locks as yours, or open it to write it later, which the lock doesn’t stop. A VM running code that watches for that moment can use it, so this is a real gap whenever you change a locked file on this machine while the VM runs.
devvm doesn’t stop it, but it names it:
At devvm stop, or at the next launch when the VM stopped another way, devvm names each file it locked again, once however often it happened, and the watch names each one whose contents changed. If devvm couldn’t record whether its locks held while the VM ran, it says so then, and you should check .git’s hooks and config yourself. Check what it names before you run git in the folder, or stop the VM before you change its .git on this machine.
data.when-linux-cant-lock#When Linux can’t lo:
The locks need a kernel that lets a program make a user namespace and mount in it, which Debian, Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE and Arch do by default. Where the kernel doesn’t, devvm doesn’t lock .git, and it watches it instead. devvm doctor says why, and what lets devvm lock:
AppArmor, on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, lets only programs that a profile names use a user namespace (Ubuntu). kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone is 0, as on Arch’s linux-hardened kernel. sudo sysctl kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1 lets devvm lock, until the next boot unless you set it in /etc/sysctl.d/. user.max_user_namespaces is 0, which sudo sysctl user.max_user_namespaces=15000 changes. Without the locks, VMs get off as their mode, devvm refuses devvm git-protect on, and --clone keeps the VM out of .git instead, so use it for any repo where you don’t trust what runs in the VM. A VM that’s on, made when the kernel let devvm lock, doesn’t start until it can again, or until you run devvm git-protect off.

data:
Every VM goes through a proxy that devvm runs for it on this machine, and the VM’s network tier decides what the proxy lets it reach. New VMs get the allowlist tier by default, so they reach only the hosts on their allowlist, which are devvm’s built-in hosts, your secrets’ hosts and the hosts you add. No VM holds the secrets that devvm saved, whatever its tier, because its proxy puts them into its requests, but code in the VM can still use each secret the VM may use, on that secret’s hosts. A secret is a credential devvm keeps on this machine for VMs to use: your GitHub token, Claude Code’s token, an agent’s login or an API key. An open VM, the one tier that isn’t confined to its proxy, reaches anything this machine can, including this machine’s own services on localhost and your LAN.
A VM's requests through its proxyThe VM sends GET /user with a placeholder to its proxy on this machine, which finds api.github.com on the allowlist and sends the request on with your GitHub token, then passes the response back. A CONNECT to example.com:443 gets a 403, because that host isn't on the allowlist.GET /user, witha placeholder GET /user, withyour GitHub token the response the response CONNECTexample.com:443 403: not onthe allowlist on the allowlist The VM Its proxy,on this machine api.github.com This page covers what you do with a VM’s tier and what you see. How it works › Network tiers explains how devvm confines a VM to its proxy and how the proxy handles each connection.
data.allowlists#Allowlists:
The VM’s proxy reads devvm’s built-in policies first and then your policy files, in order, as one list:
devvm’s own rules for every VM, which allow OS packages, mise’s version lists, the Sigstore and GitHub trust roots that mise checks a download’s attestations against, Node’s downloads for a project’s own node, and GitHub; devvm’s rules for each shared tool in the VM’s image (node, claude and the others), which allow its registries, downloads and APIs; devvm’s rules for each built-in layer in the VM’s image, so the docker layer allows Docker’s packages and the container registries Docker Hub and ghcr.io, and the nix layer allows Nix’s binary cache, channels and flake registry; ~/.config/devvm/layers/.policy, for each of your own layers in the VM’s image; ~/.config/devvm/policy, your own rules for every VM, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change with -g; ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//policy, the rules for that VM only, in the VM’s own folder, which is named by the hash that the VM’s name ends with, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change; the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins, and the host its agents log in at, such as Codex’s and opencode’s auth.openai.com and Claude Code’s platform.claude.com and console.anthropic.com, on port 443, which devvm adds. The first three are built in: they come with devvm, inside its binary, so you can’t edit them, and an upgrade of devvm is what changes them. To change what a VM reaches, add your own rules, and to keep a VM from a host that devvm’s rules allow, add a deny, which beats any allow. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of its defaults on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out. Rules never come from the project folder, because the VM can write it. The proxy reads each of your files again when it changes, so an edit applies at once, from the next connection. How it works lists where each policy comes from.
data.behind-a-company-proxy#Behind a company:
When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy, the VM’s proxy sends the requests it allows through that proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase forms, from the shell you run it in. When that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, devvm reads the [proxy] table of config.toml instead, so the proxy works from every shell, including an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile. The shell’s settings win whole: devvm never mixes them with config.toml’s, so a NO_PROXY alone in the shell still leaves config.toml’s proxy in effect, with its own no-proxy.
[proxy] https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com" devvm passes the settings to the VM’s proxy when the proxy starts, and when you run devvm again with different settings, devvm starts the VM’s proxy again with the new ones. So after you change them, run devvm again in the folder or devvm restart. When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you and names config.toml, because a VM’s proxy that a shell without the settings starts sends the VM’s requests directly.
The VM’s proxy uses the company proxy this way (through a company proxy):
It still decides each request by the host name the VM asked for, against the same allowlists, and only then passes it on. It sends tunnels, which carry HTTPS and the requests it puts your secrets into, through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy, and plain HTTP requests through HTTP_PROXY’s. It reaches the hosts that NO_PROXY names directly, and also localhost and loopback addresses. In NO_PROXY, example.com matches that host and its subdomains, .example.com matches only its subdomains, an address or a CIDR matches addresses, any entry can end in a port, and * matches every host. An IPv6 address with a zone, such as fe80::1%eth0, matches nothing, as it does in Go’s HTTP clients. devvm network log adds through host:port to each request that went through the company proxy. The company proxy’s address and password follow these rules:
The company proxy needs an http:// address, such as http://user:password@proxy.example.com:8080 in HTTPS_PROXY, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm doesn’t start a VM’s proxy while HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or a [proxy] key names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, and it tells you which setting to change. The company proxy’s password stays on this machine. The VM never gets it, and devvm writes it into no log, no image and no process’s arguments. config.toml never holds the password, because it’s a file you might copy to other machines or keep with your dotfiles, and devvm refuses a [proxy] URL that has one. Put only the user in the URL, as http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which keeps it as it keeps the other secrets. devvm’s proxies look it up themselves when they start, so no file of devvm’s holds it in the clear. devvm doesn’t make a new VM, start a VM’s proxy, or build an image or the shared tools while config.toml’s proxy names a user and no password is saved, and it checks before anything starts or stops. So devvm or devvm restart in the folder of a running VM leaves the VM and its proxy running as they were, as long as that proxy still enforces the VM’s network tier, and otherwise devvm stops the VM (the proxy). A VM’s proxy reads the password only when it starts, so after you change it, run devvm restart in each VM’s folder. No VM ever gets the proxy secret, and devvm secret use proxy refuses. devvm secret set proxy # save the company proxy's password, which devvm asks for devvm restart # in each VM's folder, once the password changed Note
The company proxy sees the name and port of every host the VM reaches, and if it inspects TLS, the CA you add for it also lets it read the traffic. The company proxy also looks up each name itself, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to. It still refuses an address that’s this machine’s own or internal, unless a rule names it, and it refuses a name when this machine’s lookup gives an internal or denied address for it. A name that this machine can’t look up goes to the company proxy unchecked only when an allowlist names it, as example.com or *.example.com. When only ** allows a name that this machine can’t look up, the VM’s proxy refuses it, so ** never lets a VM send the company proxy a name of its own making. What a VM can still reach through the company proxy, such as hosts on your company’s network, is under Attack vectors.
data.changing-rules#Changing rules:
devvm network shows this folder’s VM’s allowlist after its tier. It prints each of the VM’s policies that holds more than comments, and then its rules without their comments. A built-in policy has its name after # devvm:, because it has no file you could edit, and one of your files has its path after #, followed by (denies only) on the internet and none tiers, where it shows only the file’s denies. An open VM has no policies, so devvm network prints its tier alone. A built-in policy’s quiet line is marked # blocked, without a notice in the VM, and a line that isn’t a rule is marked # not a rule, skipped, with its line number:
allowlist # devvm: layers/base.policy ports.ubuntu.com github.com # /Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy example.com example.com:x # not a rule, skipped (line 2) devvm network allow RULE... add the rules to the VM’s own file devvm network deny RULE... add them as denies, adding ! when it’s missing devvm network rm RULE... remove the lines with these rules, a deny with its !, and warn about one that isn’t there -g, --global with allow, deny or rm, change ~/.config/devvm/policy, for every VM, instead, which needs no VM --method METHODS, --path PATH with allow, deny or rm, narrow each rule to those requests (rules by method and path) A rule is what Rules lists, without spaces or a comment, and --method and --path add its methods and its path. devvm refuses anything else before it adds any rule, and it also refuses allow !RULE. A rule that’s already in the file, in any case, isn’t added again, and a rule by method and path is the same rule however its methods are written, while its path’s case is its own. Each change applies at once, from the next connection. For an open VM, devvm notes that no rule applies to it, and for an allow on the internet or none tier, that only denies apply there. When devvm network log --blocked or a blocked request in the VM suggests a devvm network allow command, its rule is one that devvm network allow takes.
If a VM was deleted outside devvm, devvm deletes what it kept for that VM when it makes a new VM for the same project folder, so the new VM never gets the old one’s rules.
data.choosing-a-tier#Choosing a tier:
A new VM gets the allowlist tier unless you choose another, and the summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names its tier. When you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm lists the four tiers, each with what it reaches, with learn after internet, and the tier the summary showed is chosen (what a new VM gets):
Network tier for devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c (up/down to choose, enter to confirm): ( ) open reaches anything this machine can ( ) internet reaches any public host ( ) learn reaches any public host while it learns which it needs, until devvm network lock > (*) allowlist reaches only the hosts you allow (recommended) ( ) none reaches only its agents' and secrets' hosts and its links Up and down move the choice, and enter gives the VM the chosen tier, so pressing enter at once keeps the tier the summary showed. learn gives the VM the internet tier while it learns the hosts it needs. --network TIER answers the question up front, such as devvm --network internet or devvm --network learn, and when there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, the VM gets the tier the summary showed. A VM keeps its tier. On an existing VM devvm ignores --network and warns you, naming the devvm network command that changes the tier.
To give every new VM another tier, save it with devvm network -g, or choose it in devvm setup:
devvm network -g none # every new VM gets the none tier devvm network -g # show what new VMs get, and where it came from Neither takes learn, because each VM learns the hosts it needs on its own, so devvm network -g refuses it and names devvm --network learn and devvm network learn. Each new VM’s summary then shows that tier, and customizing the VM still asks, with Enter keeping the saved tier. devvm network -g shows what new VMs get, allowlist until you save another tier, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm network -g --json prints it as policy, with source. devvm reads the saved tier only when it creates a VM, so the VMs you already have keep their own tier, and --network still chooses for one new VM. You can also set it with network in config.toml, which wins over the saved tier, and then devvm network -g refuses to change it and names the file (where a default comes from). Lima confines every VM to its proxy, so every VM can be on any tier, the docker layer’s included. devvm never starts a VM on a confined tier with an open network, so if a VM’s backend couldn’t confine it, the VM could only be open: devvm would refuse to make it on any other tier unless you give --network open, and it would refuse to give it any other tier with devvm network (when a backend lacks something).
devvm network print this folder’s VM’s tier as devvm ls shows it, open, internet, internet (learning), allowlist, none or unenforced, and then its allowlist devvm network open|internet|allowlist|none change it: between confined tiers at once, and into or out of open from the VM’s next start, which devvm restart gives you, and for a running VM, ask in a terminal whether to restart it now devvm network learn give it the internet tier while it learns the hosts it needs, from now on devvm network lock choose which of those hosts it keeps, and give it the allowlist tier (locking it) devvm network -g [open|internet|allowlist|none] show or change what new VMs get When a change into or out of open finds the VM running, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it:
If you answer yes, devvm restarts the VM as devvm restart does, so the change applies at once. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the change waits until the VM starts again. If you give a running open VM a confined tier, the VM isn’t confined yet, so devvm ls shows it as unenforced, and its next launch offers to restart it confined, as it does for a VM started outside devvm. If you make a VM open while it runs confined, its launches keep it confined to its proxy, which now applies an open VM’s rules, until it next starts, and they warn you that the VM leaves its proxy’s confinement when it next starts. In a terminal, each of those launches first asks whether to restart the VM now, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).
data.devvm-network-json#devvm network –json:
devvm network --json prints the VM’s tier and its allowlist as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a tier with it.
Field What it holds policy open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced learning_since for a learning VM, the time it started learning allowlist each policy that holds more than comments, in the order the proxy reads them, with the fields below builtin, file a built-in policy’s name, or the path of one of your files rules the policy’s rules: all of a file’s rules, or on the internet and none tiers, for a file whose denies alone apply, its denies, as devvm network lists them under (denies only) denies_only true for a file whose denies alone apply not_rules each line that isn’t a rule, with its line number and its text quiet a built-in policy’s quiet hosts, there only when it has some transparent the VM’s transparent mode, with on and from, as devvm network transparent --json has it With -g, the object has only policy, which is the tier new VMs get, and source, which says where it came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm network -g or devvm setup saved, or built-in (where a default comes from).
{ "version": 1, "policy": "allowlist", "source": "config.toml" } { "version": 1, "policy": "allowlist", "allowlist": [ { "builtin": "layers/base.policy", "rules": [ "ports.ubuntu.com", "github.com" ], "not_rules": [] }, { "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy", "rules": [ "example.com" ], "not_rules": [ { "line": 2, "text": "example.com:x" } ] } ], "transparent": { "on": true, "from": "default" } } On the none tier, a VM with Claude Code gets Claude Code’s built-in policy whole, and its own file shows only its denies:
{ "version": 1, "policy": "none", "allowlist": [ { "builtin": "shared-tools/claude.policy", "rules": [ "api.anthropic.com", "claude.ai" ], "not_rules": [] }, { "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy", "denies_only": true, "rules": [ "!tracker.example.com" ], "not_rules": [] } ] }
data.devvm-network-lock-json#devvm network lo:
devvm network lock --json prints what the VM learned as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and changes nothing, so devvm refuses it with --all or --none. The hosts come in the list’s order: the tickable ones first, then the others, then those that only tools without proxy settings reached, then the risky ones.
Field What it holds learning_since when the VM started learning partial true when the log no longer goes back that far hosts each host the VM learned, with the fields below rule the rule that devvm network lock adds for it host, port its host and port count the number of its connections last the last time the VM reached it agent the User-Agent’s first word that reached it most, when devvm shows one tickable true for a host on port 443 of a registry or vendor on devvm’s list, which starts ticked unless it’s risky risk for a risky host, address, lookalike, paste, storage, mail, tunnel, webhook, hosting or chat via dns for a host that only tools without proxy settings reached { "version": 1, "learning_since": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z", "hosts": [ { "rule": "files.pythonhosted.org:443", "host": "files.pythonhosted.org", "port": 443, "count": 48, "last": "2026-11-07T10:19:00Z", "agent": "uv/0.9.2", "tickable": true }, { "rule": "registry.example.com:443", "host": "registry.example.com", "port": 443, "count": 12, "last": "2026-11-07T10:20:00Z", "agent": "npm/11.6.2" }, { "rule": "pastebin.com:443", "host": "pastebin.com", "port": 443, "count": 3, "last": "2026-11-07T10:21:00Z", "agent": "curl/8.5.0", "risk": "paste" } ] }
data.devvm-network-log-json#devvm network log:
devvm network log --json prints the last N events as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm refuses it with --follow. Each of the events has what the proxy logged, without the VM’s name, and a log with nothing in it gives "events": []:
Field What it holds time, host, port when, and the host and port, which for a link’s connection is the link’s name event tunnel for an allowed connection, intercept for an allowed tunnel that the proxy decrypted, forward for an allowed request, blocked, or nix-cache for a request to the shared Nix cache. A link’s connection is link when devvm carried it, and link_refused, link_target_stopped or link_limit when devvm refused it method, path the request’s, when the event has them rule the rule that allowed it reason the reason it was blocked, or what came of a cache request agent the request’s User-Agent header secrets the secrets put in refused for a request refused whatever the allowlist says, such as an allowed name that doesn’t resolve quiet for a block of a quiet host upstream the company proxy it went through target the VM that a link’s connection went to via dns for a connection that transparent mode sent to the proxy Each field but time, event, host and port is there only when the event has it.
{ "version": 1, "events": [ { "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:00Z", "event": "blocked", "host": "example.com", "port": 443, "method": "CONNECT", "reason": "not on the allowlist" }, { "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:06Z", "event": "forward", "host": "api.github.com", "port": 443, "method": "GET", "path": "/user", "secrets": [ "github" ] } ] } With --blocked, each of the blocked has the last time it was blocked, the count, the host and the port, and allow, the rule that devvm network allow takes to allow it. A block that ALLOW WITH shows as - has no allow, and a quiet host’s has "quiet": true instead.
{ "version": 1, "blocked": [ { "last": "2026-10-09T10:01:00Z", "count": 2, "host": "example.com", "port": 443, "allow": "example.com" } ] }
data.devvm-secret-json#devvm secret –json:
devvm secret --json prints the list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the secrets has its name, saved, which is true when it’s saved or, for claude, in devvm’s environment, and used_by, the names of the VMs using it. Then custom is true for a secret of your own, and hosts lists the hosts the proxy puts it in for, none for proxy. A secret that VMs get has its header and env, the variable that holds its placeholder, and prefix when its placeholder starts with one. A secret of yours also has its scheme, its path, its methods and basic_user when it has them. The JSON never holds a secret’s value.
{ "version": 1, "secrets": [ { "name": "claude", "saved": true, "used_by": [ "devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c" ], "custom": false, "hosts": [ "api.anthropic.com" ], "header": "Authorization", "env": "CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN", "prefix": "sk-ant-oat01-" }, { "name": "github", "saved": false, "used_by": [], "custom": false, "hosts": [ "api.github.com", "github.com", "codeload.github.com", "raw.githubusercontent.com" ], "header": "Authorization", "env": "GH_TOKEN" }, { "name": "proxy", "saved": false, "used_by": [], "custom": false, "hosts": [] }, { "name": "stripe", "saved": true, "used_by": [ "devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c" ], "custom": true, "hosts": [ "api.stripe.com" ], "header": "Authorization", "env": "STRIPE_API_KEY", "prefix": "sk_" } ] }
data.inside-the-vm#Inside the VM:
Every login in the VM has the proxy settings in its environment (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms, NO_PROXY for the VM itself, and NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY), and the CA variables that every VM has point the tools that don’t read the system’s store at the VM’s own CAs. devvm also points apt, sudo, ssh and Docker at the proxy (how), on every tier.
On a confined tier, a direct connection to an address fails at once, even as root, and no DNS query leaves the VM. Names resolve in the proxy as the tool wrote them, without this machine’s DNS search domain added, so to reach a host on your network, use its full name, such as jenkins.corp.example.com and not jenkins. Inside the VM, every name resolves to one stand-in address, which leads to the proxy too, so a tool that skips the proxy settings still reaches the hosts the rules allow over HTTPS and HTTP (tools that ignore the proxy). Such a tool’s connection to another port of a name is refused at once, and nothing reaches the log for it (what to do).
A blocked request gets 403, and the response names the host, the reason and the rule that would allow it, but for a quiet host. The proxy also answers at http://devvm.proxy/:
/blocked lists the last 50 blocks. /blocked/new?after=N gives the number of blocks so far, then those after the Nth, with each rule once, so a shell prompt can show what a command hit. /ca.pem is the VM’s own CA certificate and the next one’s, never their keys. /nix/ is the shared Nix cache, in a VM with the nix layer (below). /transparent/ports lists the ports that transparent mode sends to the proxy, one a line. A request for http://devvm.proxy/ that comes through transparent mode, without the proxy settings, reaches /blocked alone and gets 403 for the rest, because that way asks the tool for no password, so a container without the proxy settings can’t fetch the VM’s CA or the Nix cache.
devvm-why # in the VM: what the proxy blocked lately In the VM, devvm-why prints what the proxy blocked lately, and a note before each prompt tells you when something new was blocked. These help too:
When the proxy blocked nothing lately, devvm-why says so, and it adds that a connection refused, or a DNS error, for a host the tier allows means the tool skipped the proxy on a port or in a way devvm can’t send to it, so you turn on the tool’s own proxy setting or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY (a tool that skips the proxy fails). With transparent mode on, devvm-why then says which ports it sends to the proxy, lists the connections to other ports that the VM refused lately, by port and time, and lists the names that tools looked up lately. devvm also tells Claude Code and Codex, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail and to run devvm-why, that a tool that ignores the proxy settings still reaches the proxy over HTTPS, HTTP and the ports the rules name, and that a connection refused on another port while devvm-why shows nothing blocked means the tool skipped the proxy.
data.learning-the-hosts-a-vm-needs#Learning t:
Finding every host a project needs one block at a time takes a while, so a VM can learn them instead:
Make the VM learn. For a new VM, choose learn in its tier list when you customize it, or give --network learn, such as devvm --network learn. For an existing VM, run devvm network learn, which gives it the internet tier at once, as devvm network internet does, and starts its learning from now. Run the project’s installs, builds and tests. The VM has the internet tier’s access meanwhile, and its proxy logs each host it reaches, as it does on every tier. Run devvm network lock, which lets you choose which of those hosts the VM keeps, and puts it on the allowlist tier with them (locking it). Learning is for one VM at a time, so no default makes new VMs learn: devvm network -g, devvm setup and config.toml don’t take learn (choosing a tier).
Warning
Learning isn’t a tier of its own. While it lasts, the VM is on the internet tier, so it reaches every public host and only your denies apply, and links and groups treat it as an internet VM. That’s internet access for as long as the VM learns, and that includes the dependency installs you run to teach it, when packages’ install scripts run in the VM. So a compromised dependency that you install meanwhile can reach a host of its attacker’s choosing, and that host then shows up among the learned hosts. That’s why devvm network lock asks, starts with few hosts ticked, and leaves you to read the list before you confirm it. Your secrets stay on this machine as they do on every tier, and the VM still gets only placeholders.
Each launch of a learning VM says that it’s learning, since when, and how many hosts it has reached beyond its allowlist, and it names devvm network lock. Once the VM’s log holds more than 2 MiB, the launch leaves out the count, so it never reads the whole log each time. devvm ls and devvm network show its tier as internet (learning), and their --json adds learning_since, the time it started learning.
devvm network internet, none or open end the learning and give the VM that tier. devvm network allowlist refuses while the VM learns, because devvm network lock is how a learning VM goes to the allowlist tier, and devvm network lock --none does it without adding a host. A VM in a group can’t start learning or be locked, because a group’s VMs are all on one tier, so run devvm group leave first, and for the same reason a learning VM can’t join a group until you lock it.
data.links-between-vms#Links between VMs:
A link between VMs lets a program in one VM, the client, reach a port that another VM, the target, publishes. devvm carries a link’s connections over ssh through this machine, so they use neither VM’s network, and a confined VM reaches only what its tier allows and the links you added to it. A client’s proxy is a second way into its links: it carries a request for one of the client’s own links, by the link’s name and port, to the same link on this machine, and passes it on as it is, without looking into it or putting a secret into it. It reaches no other socket on this machine and no other VM’s links. The allowlist’s rules don’t apply to links, so devvm network deny doesn’t stop one, and devvm link rm does.
A link joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. So devvm keeps two rules:
A client links only to a target on its own tier or a stricter one. An allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target, around its own proxy. An open client may link to any target, and it then has the target’s secrets and project folder within reach as well as its own network. devvm checks this when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection, and for a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must be in force as it runs, so devvm refuses the connection while the target shows as unenforced, and it warns you of such a target when you add the link, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and when the client starts. While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than the client’s, such as devvm network open, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open target. The target publishes. A link reaches only a port that the target’s folder publishes with devvm link publish, and only on the target’s own loopback. Publishing offers the port to any of your VMs, and each link is still added in the client’s folder, so a VM reaches another’s service only when you’ve run a command in both folders. The first rule keeps a client’s tier whole, but it doesn’t keep the target’s data in the target. A client on a confined tier can read whatever the target’s service gives it and send that out through the hosts its own tier reaches. Link two VMs only when you’d trust each with what the other has.
A group links each of its VMs to the ports that the others publish, once you’ve run devvm group join in each VM’s folder. Its VMs are all on one tier, so every link it makes keeps the first rule, and devvm refuses to change a VM’s tier with devvm network while it’s in a group. A group joins the trust of all its VMs, so put VMs in one only when you’d trust each with what the others have.
data.locking-it#Locking it:
devvm network lock reads the hosts the VM reached since it started learning from its network log, and it leaves out these:
what the VM’s allowlist tier would allow already, judged by the proxy’s own rules: devvm’s built-in rules, its shared tools’ and layers’, your own rules for every VM and for this VM, and its secrets’ and logins’ hosts what your rules deny, which no allow would reach blocked requests internal and LAN addresses, which the internet tier never reaches In a terminal it lists the rest, one row for each host and port, with how many connections each had and the first word of the User-Agent that the requests sent most, in three groups:
The hosts that the VM’s tools reached through its proxy come first. The hosts that only tools without proxy settings reached, which transparent mode sent to the proxy, come next, under a heading of their own, because background tools’ telemetry and update checks reach the proxy that way, and you may not want to keep them. The risky hosts come last, under a heading of their own, so neither a long name nor a User-Agent can push off the row what makes them risky. That User-Agent is the VM’s own claim, which any program in it can set to anything, so it’s a hint, not proof of which tool made the connection, and devvm shows it only when it’s at most 32 letters, digits and ._/+-. Which way a connection came is the VM’s own doing, as its User-Agent is, so the second group’s heading is a hint about the tool, not proof of what it is. A host name that doesn’t fit is cut from the left, so its domain shows, and a list longer than the terminal scrolls, with a line above and below that says how many more rows there are. In a terminal too short to show a few rows, devvm refuses rather than draw the list wrong:
Since 2026-11-08 09:03 the VM could reach any public host, so this list can hold a host that a compromised dependency reached. Only a host on port 443 of a package registry or vendor devvm knows starts ticked, so read the others before you tick them. Choose the hosts devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c keeps. Use up and down to move, space to toggle, a to toggle them all and enter to confirm. > [x] files.pythonhosted.org:443 2 connections, User-Agent: uv/0.9.2 [x] static.crates.io:443 1 connection, User-Agent: cargo/1.91.0 [ ] example.com:8443 1 connection [ ] uploads.github.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: git/2.51.0 Reached only by tools without proxy settings, which the VM's names sent to its proxy: [ ] api.open-meteo.com:443 3 connections Risky, each an easy way to send data out: [ ] 203.0.113.5:443 1 connection [ ] docs.google.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: python-requests/2.32 [ ] pastebin.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: curl/8.5.0 A host starts ticked only when it’s on port 443 and belongs to a package registry or vendor on a short list that devvm keeps, each name checked so that nobody but its vendor can make a host or post a page under it:
npm’s registry.npmjs.org, PyPI’s files.pythonhosted.org and crates.io Go’s proxy.golang.org and sum.golang.org, and NuGet’s api.nuget.org the toolchains’ own release hosts, such as nodejs.org and static.rust-lang.org Docker Hub’s and GitHub’s container registries the agents’ APIs, api.anthropic.com and api.openai.com A registry’s packages are its users’, but they only get there through the registry’s own upload, with a token. Nothing else makes a host start ticked: not a domain where anyone can get a subdomain or a page, such as github.io, googleapis.com, amazonaws.com or pypi.org, which takes uploads, not a host beside one your rules or your secrets name, and not one beside a host an earlier lock added. So files.pythonhosted.org:443 starts ticked, while files.pythonhosted.org:8080, docs.google.com and evil.github.io don’t. Every other host starts unticked, and so does every host when the list has more than 30, so read the list, or devvm network lock --json, before you tick them.
A host that’s an easy way to send data out is risky, and it always starts unticked. devvm’s own rules leave all of them out too, so tick one only when the project needs it. These are risky:
an address rather than a host name a name with a punycode (xn--) label, which can look like another name a paste or file drop site such as pastebin.com, paste.ubuntu.com or gist.github.com, or a log that takes entries from anyone, such as rekor.sigstore.dev file storage or file sharing such as transfer.sh, Dropbox, Google Docs, SharePoint or an S3 bucket a mail server such as Gmail’s a tunnel such as ngrok or trycloudflare.com a service that records what it’s sent, such as webhook.site or an OAST domain free hosting such as vercel.app, workers.dev or cloudfront.net a chat service’s endpoint for bots, such as Discord’s, Slack’s hooks or Telegram’s API In the list, these keys choose the hosts:
Space ticks or unticks the row under the cursor. a ticks every row, the risky ones and those on other ports too, and again unticks them all. Enter adds the ticked hosts to the VM’s own policy file. Each is an exact host and port, such as registry.example.com:443 or example.com:8443, with the port written even for 443, so it doesn’t allow port 80 too, and never a *. wildcard. Then devvm gives the VM the allowlist tier at once, as it does between confined tiers, so a running VM keeps running, and its learning ends. When the VM’s tier changed while the list was open, such as with devvm network internet in another terminal, devvm network lock changes nothing and says so. When the terminal doesn’t let devvm read single keys, or goes away while the list is open, or you press Ctrl+C, devvm network lock changes nothing, rather than lock with the hosts as they were ticked then. Later, devvm network allow, deny and rm change those rules as they change any other (changing rules).
devvm network lock list the hosts the VM learned, so you choose which it keeps, then give it the allowlist tier --all keep every host it learned, the unticked ones too, without asking --none keep none of them, without asking --json list the hosts it learned, and change nothing Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm network lock refuses and names --all and --none. When the VM reached no host beyond its allowlist, it locks at once without asking. A VM that isn’t learning has nothing to lock, so devvm network lock refuses and names devvm network learn. While the VM links to a target on a lower tier than allowlist, devvm network lock refuses as devvm network allowlist would (links between VMs).
The proxy keeps each VM’s log to its last 10 to 20 MiB (logs), so a VM that learns for a long time with a lot of traffic can lose the first hosts it reached. When the log no longer goes back to the time the VM started learning, devvm network lock warns you, and its --json sets partial. A host that’s missing then is blocked once the VM is locked, and devvm network log --blocked names the devvm network allow command that allows it.
data.logs#Logs:
devvm network log shows the proxy’s decisions for this folder’s VM, oldest first, one line each. A line has the time, allowed, BLOCKED or cache, and the host and port. An allowed line then has the rule that allowed it (, decrypted for an intercepted tunnel), or the request (GET /user), with the rule by method and path that let it through when one did, and the secrets put in (, token: github). A blocked line has why it was blocked, after the request when the proxy saw one, and a cache line, a request to the shared Nix cache, has the request and what came of it. A line ends , without proxy settings when transparent mode sent the connection to the proxy:
2026-10-09T10:00:00Z BLOCKED example.com:443 not on the allowlist 2026-10-09T10:00:05Z allowed github.com:443 rule github.com 2026-10-09T10:00:06Z allowed api.github.com:443 GET /user, token: github 2026-10-09T10:00:07Z BLOCKED api.github.com:443 POST /gists: denied by !api.github.com POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE 2026-10-09T10:00:08Z cache cache.nixos.org:443 GET /nix/yv1zf3y6all4j99aad30cb8i55dw9zmp.narinfo: hit 2026-10-09T10:00:09Z allowed api.open-meteo.com:443 rule **, without proxy settings -n N, --lines N the last N (default 50) --follow then each new one as it happens, until Ctrl+C --blocked the blocks instead, one row per host and port, by when last blocked: LAST, COUNT, HOST and ALLOW WITH, the devvm network allow command that allows it ALLOW WITH is - for a request that the proxy refuses whatever the allowlist says, such as a GitHub call that makes a credential, and for a host that isn’t a host name or an address, and - (quiet) for a quiet host. An open VM’s log holds what went through its proxy and its links’ connections, but not what the VM reached directly, and devvm network log says so. The proxy keeps each VM’s log to its last 10 to 20 MiB by starting a new file once the current one reaches 10 MiB and keeping one older file, which devvm network log reads too. devvm rm deletes the VM’s logs, and How it works describes the files.
data.network-tiers#Network tiers:
A VM is on one of four tiers, from the lowest to the highest:
Tier What the VM reaches Confined to its proxy open whatever this machine reaches, its localhost and the LAN included; the proxy applies no rules no internet every public host, on any port, apart from your denies; never this machine’s addresses or its networks' yes allowlist only the hosts its allowlists allow, apart from your denies yes none only its agents’ hosts, the hosts of its secrets and logins, and its links, apart from your denies yes devvm --network internet # make this folder's new VM on the internet tier devvm network none # give this folder's VM the none tier devvm network # show its tier and its allowlist --network TIER chooses a new VM’s tier, and devvm network with a tier changes an existing VM’s (choosing a tier). A higher tier is stricter, and a VM on any tier but open is confined: it reaches nothing but its proxy, and a direct connection from it fails. A VM can also start on the internet tier while it learns the hosts it needs, and then go to the allowlist tier with the ones you choose.
An open VM runs on its backend’s own network, so it reaches this machine and your LAN directly, as a VM without a proxy would. It still gets only a placeholder for each secret it may use, so a request that goes around its proxy carries no secret, and every launch checks that its proxy is set in the VM and answers it (an open VM).
Rules by tier: on the internet and none tiers, devvm reads only the denies of your policy files, because the internet tier allows every public host itself and the none tier allows only what the VM’s agents, secrets and links need. devvm network marks each such file (denies only), and when you add an allow to a VM on either tier, devvm says that the allow changes nothing until the VM is on the allowlist tier. On the open tier no rule applies at all. When a change applies: a change from one confined tier to another applies at once, because the VM’s proxy starts again with the new tier’s rules and the VM keeps running. A change into or out of the open tier applies from the VM’s next start, as choosing a tier describes. What you see: devvm ls and devvm network show a VM’s tier, or unenforced when a confined tier isn’t in force (when it isn’t enforced).
data.nix#Nix:
In a VM with the nix layer, Nix’s daemon makes most of Nix’s downloads, and devvm also points it at the proxy, so its downloads go through the same allowlists. The layer’s allowlist has cache.nixos.org for Nix’s binary cache, and channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org for its channels and flake registry, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from, is in devvm’s rules for every VM.
Nix asks the proxy’s shared cache, http://devvm.proxy/nix, before cache.nixos.org, so every VM with the layer shares the packages that any of them downloaded (shared downloads, the shared Nix cache):
The proxy fetches what the cache doesn’t have from cache.nixos.org alone, and only while the VM’s tier and rules let it reach cache.nixos.org. It keeps a package only when cache.nixos.org’s signature on it checks, and the VM’s Nix checks that signature again. A VM can only make the proxy fetch from cache.nixos.org: the proxy refuses anything a VM sends to store, and every request that isn’t for one of Nix’s cache files. Each request shows in devvm network log as cache, with whether it was a hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found. What one VM can learn of another through the cache is under Attack vectors. An open VM has its proxy too, so it shares the cache as well, and its proxy fetches from cache.nixos.org for it. When a package isn’t in the binary cache, Nix builds it from source, and the build downloads its sources from their own hosts, such as ftpmirror.gnu.org. The proxy blocks those hosts until you allow them, so the build fails, and the error, devvm-why and devvm network log --blocked name the host and the devvm network allow command that allows it.
data.not-covered#Not covered: The tiers leave some things open, such as what an allowed host accepts beyond what rules by method and path narrow, whatever your secrets allow, such as pushes and API calls, and what a company CA that you add can read. Attack vectors lists them under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you. What transparent mode leaves to a tool’s own proxy settings, such as other ports, databases’ protocols, addresses and HTTP/3 alone, is under tools that ignore the proxy.
data.open-vms-and-builds#Open VMs and builds:
These go through the company proxy too:
Open VMs. An open VM goes through its proxy as every VM does, and its proxy sends its requests through the company proxy, from the shell’s settings or config.toml’s, so the company proxy’s password stays on this machine for it too. The VM never gets the shell’s proxy settings, and Lima gets none to pass on to it. What an open VM reaches directly, past its proxy, such as the hosts its NO_PROXY names, doesn’t go through the company proxy. Lima prints each proxy setting it gives a VM, password and all, as it starts the VM. devvm keeps the password out of its run log, and once the VM has started, it replaces the password with as many * in the log Lima keeps for the VM. Builds. Builds never get your company proxy’s settings, and images never keep them. A build goes through the shell’s company proxy, or else config.toml’s, as a VM’s proxy does. When devvm builds an image, builds the shared tools or converts a --from container image on Lima behind a company proxy, the build goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine, made for that build alone, which goes through your company proxy. The build’s commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, while they run, and devvm stops the proxy when the build ends. What a build runs. So the code a build runs, which includes a container image’s own, never sees your company proxy’s address or password. That proxy also runs on this machine, so a company proxy on localhost, such as one a VPN client runs, works for builds too. A build’s proxy allows any host, as ** does. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, so builds work where only the company proxy looks up outside names. devvm’s own downloads on this machine. They are devvm’s copy of mise and the versions it looks up for the shared tools, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and a container registry’s answers for --from. With the shell’s settings, each of them uses the shell’s. With config.toml’s, devvm’s own requests send the password only to the company proxy. When a VM’s proxy refreshes a Codex or opencode login on this machine, the refresh goes through the same company proxy as the VM’s requests, with the password kept on this machine. The mise devvm runs on this machine. It gets the proxy’s URL with the password in it, in its environment, because mise takes a proxy’s password nowhere else. devvm percent-encodes the password in that URL and mise decodes it before it sends it, so a password with characters such as @, :, /, #, % or a space works too. devvm never puts that URL in mise’s arguments or in a file.
data.quiet-hosts#Quiet hosts:
Some tools send telemetry to a host of their own, and devvm’s built-in policies leave such hosts out. Cursor’s CLI has no setting that turns its metrics off, so it keeps sending them to api3.cursor.sh and getting blocked, many times a session. devvm’s built-in policies mark a few such hosts quiet, with a quiet HOST line, for one exact host name. A quiet host is blocked as any host that no rule allows, and devvm network log still shows each block, ending , quiet. The VM gets no note before its prompt for it, though, and devvm-why doesn’t list it, the 403 that the tool gets suggests no command, devvm network log --blocked shows - (quiet) instead of one, and devvm network lock never offers it.
A block is quiet only when no rule of yours covers the host and nothing else refused it, such as its address. To allow a quiet host anyway, add it as any other host, such as devvm network allow api3.cursor.sh, and your rule wins. Only devvm’s own policies can mark a host quiet.
