In one of your files, a quiet line isn’t a rule, so the proxy skips it, and devvm warns about it as it warns about any other line that isn’t a rule, saying that only devvm’s policies can mark a host quiet. These are the quiet hosts:
api3.cursor.sh, the host Cursor documents for its editor’s Tab requests, which Cursor’s CLI uses for its metrics (in a devvm cursor window, Tab’s requests come from the Cursor app on this machine, not the VM); telemetry.go.dev, Go’s telemetry uploads, which every VM turns off.
data.rules#Rules:
A policy file holds one rule per line. # starts a comment, and matching a host ignores case.
Rule Matches example.com that host only *.example.com any subdomain, at any depth, not example.com itself ** any host, and any address, though an internal address still needs its own rule 10.0.0.5, 10.0.0.0/8, fd00::/8 addresses, IPv4 or IPv6 (also what lets a connection past the internal-address refusal) RULE:22, [fd00::1]:22, 10.0.0.0/8:8080 only that port; without a port, 443 and 80 RULE:*, **:* any port !RULE deny: a deny beats any allow RULE METHODS PATH, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/ only those requests to a host name, by their methods, their path or both (rules by method and path) A rule is written this way:
A rule is plain ASCII, and a host’s part has no spaces in it, while a rule by method and path has its methods and its path after the host, each after a space. A port is a number from 1 to 65535, or * for any port. A host’s one trailing dot is dropped, so example.com. matches example.com. Brackets hold only an IPv6 address, and an address can’t follow *.. A line that holds anything else, such as example.com:x, a*.example.com or ! example.com with a space after the !, isn’t a rule. A line that isn’t a rule and doesn’t start with ! is skipped, and the file’s other lines still apply. The proxy names each such line in its own log. Warning
When a line that isn’t a rule starts with !, it reads as a deny, but the proxy can’t tell what it would deny. So while the line is there, the proxy of every VM that reads the file denies every new connection apart from the VM’s links, whatever the other rules allow. Connections that are already open stay open. Each refusal names the file and the line, and it suggests no devvm network allow command, because no rule would help.
devvm warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with the file and the line’s number, and the warning for a broken deny says that the proxies deny everything until it’s fixed. It warns when you open a confined VM whose proxy reads the file, when devvm network allow, deny or rm changes the file, and in devvm doctor. devvm network also marks the line. Fix the line or remove it, and the change applies from the next connection.
The proxy never dials a denied address, even for an allowed name that resolves to it or to its NAT64 or 6to4 form. A missing file has no rules. A file that changed but can’t be read keeps its last rules, so a deny never lapses.
data.rules-by-method-and-path#Rules by method:
A rule for a host name can also name the requests it covers, by their methods, their path or both. So a VM can read from an API without changing anything there, or reach a host without pushing to it. devvm network allow, deny and rm take --method and --path for this, and the file gets the rule as one line, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/:
devvm network allow api.example.com --method GET,HEAD let the VM only read from api.example.com, a host that no other rule allows devvm network allow api.example.com --path /v1/ let it reach only the paths below /v1/ there devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE keep it from changing anything through GitHub’s API, which devvm’s rules allow devvm network deny github.com --path '/*/*/git-receive-pack' keep it from pushing to GitHub over HTTPS devvm network deny -g pastebin.com --method POST keep every VM from posting there Allows add up and a deny beats any allow, as for every rule:
An allow by method and path lets through only the requests it names, and the host’s other requests stay blocked unless another rule allows the whole host. So to narrow a host that a rule already allows whole, such as api.github.com, which devvm’s own rules allow, add a deny of what the VM mustn’t do. An allow by method and path for such a host narrows nothing, and devvm warns you so when you add one, naming the VMs where another rule allows the host whole, with -g each VM’s own rules counted, and the deny to add instead. Where a whole allow names port 443 alone, such as api.example.com:443, an allow by method and path still narrows the host’s plain HTTP on port 80, and the warning says that. A deny by method and path refuses only the requests it names, and the host’s other requests go on. You can narrow any host this way, devvm’s built-in ones, a secret’s and an agent’s included, for one VM or with -g for every VM. On the internet and none tiers your denies apply, by method and path too, while your allows apply only on the allowlist tier, as for every rule. The methods are some of GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY, in any case, joined by commas, and devvm writes them in capitals in that order:
GET doesn’t include HEAD, so name both for reading. A deny refuses only the methods it names, so to keep a host read-only, name POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. A GraphQL API, such as GitHub’s at api.github.com/graphql, takes its reads as POST too, so such a deny refuses them as well, and the GitHub CLI, which reads through it, fails there. Some servers take a request’s method from a header or a parameter instead of the request itself, so the proxy judges a request by every method it names, and while a rule by method covers a host, it refuses a request whose method it can’t read alike for every server (requests by method and path). A path is a pattern:
Pattern Example Matches * /repos/*/*/issues, /*/*.git/info/refs any part of one segment **, as a whole segment /repos/** one segment or more a path that ends with / /repos/ everything below it, as /** there would, so /repos/a and /repos/a/b but not /repos itself a path without a / at its end /user also the request’s path with one, so /user/ any path /search whatever the query, so /search?q=x, because the query never counts A path starts with /, and it has no . or .. part, no doubled slash, and no space, %, \, ;, ? or #. Servers don’t all read a request’s path alike, so an allow matches only a path in a plain form that every server reads the same way, and a deny matches broadly. So a deny of /gists/ refuses /gists, /GISTS/1, /gists/, /gists.json, /%67ists/1, /x/../gists/1 and /gists;x/1 alike, and a deny of /admin refuses /admin.json and /admin. but not /administrator. While a rule with a path covers a host, a request there whose path has an encoded character, such as a file name with a space, is refused unless a rule without a path allows it (requests by method and path).
To see each request, the proxy decrypts the host’s HTTPS on port 443 with the VM’s own CA, as it does for a secret’s hosts. That has these effects:
The proxy checks every request on the connection, each one on a kept-alive connection and on HTTP/2 alike, with the rules as they are then, so a change to them applies to a decrypted tunnel from its next request. A tunnel that was open to the host before a rule narrowed it isn’t decrypted, so it carries on unchecked until it closes. A tunnel to such a host on any other port is refused, because the proxy can’t see the requests in it, while plain HTTP on any port gets the same check for each request. A tool in the VM that doesn’t trust the VM’s CA fails there, and devvm network log gives the reason TLS with the VM failed, which is why devvm reminds you when you add such a rule that the host is now decrypted. A host that a whole allow covers, with no deny by method and path, stays a tunnel. A rule by method and path needs a host name or *.name, so devvm refuses --method and --path with an address or a CIDR, which have no name to decrypt by, and with **, which would decrypt every host. A WebSocket is checked by the request that opens it, and what it carries after that isn’t. A switch to any other protocol, such as Upgrade: h2c, and a CONNECT inside a decrypted tunnel are refused, because the proxy couldn’t check the requests that would follow. A request that the rules block gets 403 from the proxy, with the reason, and never reaches the host. devvm network log shows it with its method and its path, and devvm-why lists it. For a request that no allow covers, the proxy suggests the devvm network allow command for the whole host, and for one that a deny refuses it suggests nothing, because no allow lifts a deny. A request that a rule by method and path let through shows that rule in devvm network log:
$ devvm network allow api.example.com --method GET --path /v1/ ==> devvm added api.example.com GET /v1/ to devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c's rules. The proxy now decrypts api.example.com's HTTPS on port 443 to check each request, so a tool that doesn't trust the VM's CA fails there, and a new tunnel to it on another port is refused. Tunnels to it that are open already carry on unchecked until they close. https://devvm.dev/docs/safety/network/#rules-by-method-and-path In the VM, a GET below /v1/ reaches the host, while a POST there gets the proxy’s answer:
$ curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/charges devvm: api.example.com:443 is blocked (no rule allows this method and path). Allow it on the host with: devvm network allow api.example.com And on this machine, devvm network log shows both:
2026-11-08T10:00:01Z allowed api.example.com:443 rule api.example.com GET /v1/, decrypted 2026-11-08T10:00:01Z allowed api.example.com:443 GET /v1/charges, rule api.example.com GET /v1/ 2026-11-08T10:00:02Z BLOCKED api.example.com:443 POST /v1/charges: no rule allows this method and path Learning stays by host: devvm network lock adds whole hosts, and you can narrow them afterwards with these flags (learning the hosts a VM needs). A line with a method that devvm doesn’t know, such as !api.github.com PSOT, isn’t a rule, so as a deny it makes the proxy deny everything until you fix it (rules). The shared Nix cache’s own downloads from cache.nixos.org meet these rules too, as GETs of the paths the VM asked the cache for (Nix).
A VM’s proxy is the devvm binary that started it, which is the one from before an upgrade until the VM’s next launch. A proxy from before rules by method and path reads such a rule as a line that isn’t a rule: it skips an allow by method and path, and a deny by method and path makes it deny the VM everything, until it starts again. Likewise, once one of a VM’s secrets goes in by method or by a path pattern, such a proxy puts none of the VM’s secrets in. So when you add or remove such a rule, or change such a secret, while a VM’s proxy runs from another devvm binary, or from one devvm can’t tell, devvm warns you and names the VM, and running devvm in the VM’s folder starts its proxy again.
data.saving-and-binding-secrets#Saving and bi:
Command What it does devvm secret set claude or github asks for the Claude Code token or the GitHub token without showing it, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead) devvm secret set proxy asks for the company proxy’s password, for the user that config.toml’s [proxy] names, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead) devvm secret set NAME --host HOST --env VARIABLE asks for a secret of your own, such as an API key, and saves it with the hosts it goes to and the variable that VMs find its placeholder in (--stdin reads a line instead) devvm secret rm NAME deletes a saved secret, after asking devvm secret lists the secrets, each with its variable, header and hosts, a secret of your own’s path and methods, whether it’s saved, and the VMs using it devvm secret use NAME lets this folder’s VM use the secret, and reach its hosts on port 443 devvm secret unuse NAME stops this folder’s VM using it, though a VM whose image has claude always uses claude devvm saves a secret in the macOS Keychain, or elsewhere in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/, a file only you can read (details). No devvm command prints a saved secret, because each VM’s proxy reads the values it needs itself. devvm checks each value as you save it:
It drops whitespace in a secret’s value, except inside the proxy password, which loses only the whitespace around it. It refuses a value with a quote, a backslash or a control character, a value that holds a VM’s placeholder, such as one copied from a VM’s GH_TOKEN, and a claude value that isn’t a setup token (sk-ant-oat01-…, from claude setup-token). A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s environment wins over a saved one. Each change applies in its own time:
Saving, deleting, binding and unbinding apply at once to the proxies that are running. From its next launch, the VM gets the placeholder in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, GH_TOKEN or your own secret’s variable, and with github a git credential helper for https://github.com. A secret’s hosts join the allowlist of each VM that uses it, on port 443 alone, whatever the VM’s tier, so a VM on the none tier reaches them too. To put a secret in, the proxy shows the VM a certificate from the VM’s own CA, which no other VM trusts. Each CA lasts 30 days, and a VM that you don’t open again keeps working for at least 30 days after its last launch with devvm in its folder. When its CA has ended, its proxy refuses its HTTPS connections to secrets’ hosts, and devvm network log --blocked gives the reason devvm's CA has ended, so run devvm in the VM’s folder to install new CAs (the VM’s CA).
devvm secret unuse and devvm secret rm take a secret away from a VM at once, because the VM only ever had its placeholder. Neither command revokes what a VM made with the secret (minting credentials with a secret), so rotate it if that matters. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, scoped to the repos your VMs need.
data.secrets#Secrets:
Secrets stay on this machine, whatever the VM’s tier. A VM gets a placeholder of its own for each one, and its proxy puts the real value into requests for that secret’s hosts. An open VM can send a request around its proxy, but then the request carries only the placeholder, which the secret’s host refuses (tools that ignore the proxy). The proxy puts each secret into one header:
Secret Hosts Header Used by claude api.anthropic.com Authorization every VM whose image has claude github api.github.com, github.com, codeload.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com Authorization VMs it’s bound to your own the hosts you give it, for the paths and methods you give it Authorization, or the header you give it VMs it’s bound to Agents’ logins work the same way. When a VM’s image has a coding agent and devvm’s agent store has a login or an API key for it, the VM gets placeholders for the login, and so do Claude Code’s MCP servers’ secrets (agents’ logins and settings). A Claude Code, Codex or opencode login that you make inside a VM goes to the store, and the VM gets placeholders for it too (Claude Code login). A login to an MCP server that you make with /mcp in a VM stays in that VM instead, with real tokens that code in the VM can read (MCP servers’ logins).
The logins a VM saves have two limits (logins made in a VM):
Only its own agents. A VM saves a login only for an agent that its image has, and its proxy refuses a login for any other agent, so a VM without Codex can never replace the store’s Codex login. One login for each agent. Because the store keeps one login for each agent, any VM with the agent can replace it, so a VM you don’t trust can log your other VMs in to an account of its choosing.
data.tools-that-ignore-the-proxy#Tools that i:
On every tier but open, devvm sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy anyway, by the names it looks up. This is transparent mode, and it’s on unless you turn it off. In the VM, every name resolves to one stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, and a connection to that address on port 443, port 80 or a port that one of your allow rules names goes to the VM’s proxy.
devvm network transparent # show whether this folder's VM has transparent mode devvm network transparent off # turn it off for the VM, from its next launch The proxy reads the host from the connection itself, from the TLS server name (SNI) on HTTPS and from each request’s Host on plain HTTP, and it judges that host as it judges a request through the proxy settings, against the same allowlist, with the same secrets and the same log. A blocked HTTPS host gets the proxy’s 403, over a certificate for that host from the VM’s own CA, so the tool shows the same message, with the devvm network allow command, that a request through the proxy settings would show. devvm network log and devvm-why mark each of these connections without proxy settings, and so does the note before the prompt. A tool such as workerd, which wrangler dev runs for Cloudflare’s adapters, makes its own lookups and connections, and transparent mode is what lets it reach your allowed hosts from a confined VM.
Transparent mode covers HTTPS and HTTP to a host by name on ports 443 and 80, and on up to 32 more ports that your allow rules name for hosts by name, such as api.example.com:8443, the lowest first. It never covers port 22 or 53, even when a rule names one, because SSH names no host in its first bytes and port 53 is the VM’s own names’. It leaves these to the tool’s own proxy settings:
Other ports. A connection to another port of a name is refused at once, and so is UDP to any port, QUIC included, so a client that tries HTTP/3 falls back to TCP. A client that uses HTTP/3 alone doesn’t connect. Protocols that name no host in their first bytes, such as Postgres, MySQL, Redis, SSH and raw TCP, and those whose server speaks first, such as SMTP. The proxy refuses such a connection and logs why, even on a port a rule names. Addresses. A URL with an address in it, such as https://1.2.3.4/, is a direct connection, which fails, and so does a tool that looks a name up itself and then gives the proxy the stand-in address, which the proxy refuses with a reason that says so. IPv6. Names have no IPv6 address in the VM, so a client that uses IPv6 alone finds no address. Names without a dot, and your network’s names. A name without a dot, such as db, resolves only when /etc/hosts has it, as the name of a link between VMs does. The VM’s resolver adds the search domain of this machine’s network to such a name, and transparent mode can’t tell db.corp.example.com made that way from one a tool names whole, so every name under that search domain gets no answer either, such as printer.lan or git.corp.example.com when your network’s search domain is corp.example.com. A tool that reaches such a host needs its proxy settings. A DNS server of yours on the VM’s 127.0.0.1:53. Transparent mode sends the VM’s lookups there to its own names, so such a server, and a forward of port 53 to it, gets none. Put the server on another address or port, or turn transparent mode off for the VM. Clients that don’t trust the VM’s CA, such as most Docker containers, and those that pin a certificate. For a blocked HTTPS host they show a certificate error instead of the 403, and the block is logged all the same. With the docker layer, Docker’s containers get the same treatment as the VM’s own programs, on Docker’s default bridge and on the networks that docker network create and Compose make. A container without the proxy settings, whether its environment emptied them or a program made it through Docker’s API without them, reaches what the VM’s rules allow, as every program in the VM does. To give a container no network, run it with --network none, and a container on an --internal network reaches nothing either.
devvm network transparent shows a VM’s transparent mode, on or off, and where that comes from: the VM’s own setting, config.toml’s transparent-proxy, or devvm’s default, which is on. devvm network transparent off and devvm network transparent on give the folder’s VM its own setting, and transparent-proxy = false in config.toml turns it off for every VM that has none of its own. A change applies at the VM’s next launch, without a restart.
$ devvm network transparent on # devvm: default $ devvm network transparent off ==> devvm turns transparent mode off for devvm-web-0c3c7077e29f06 at its next launch, and it applies while the VM is on a confined tier. With transparent mode off, names don’t resolve in a confined VM at all, so a tool that skips the proxy fails with a DNS error. Tools such as curl and workerd under wrangler dev get that error at once, on macOS and on a Linux host alike. On the open tier there’s no transparent mode, and the VM resolves names with Lima’s DNS. A VM made from an image built before devvm had transparent mode lacks the programs it runs, so each launch says so, and devvm update makes the VM again from a newer image.
devvm network transparent --json prints the same as JSON, with on and from, which is vm, config or default, and devvm network --json has it too, as transparent:
{ "version": 1, "on": true, "from": "default" } On the open tier, a tool that ignores the proxy settings in the VM’s environment connects directly, past its proxy. Its connections still work, because an open VM reaches everything this machine can, but they don’t show in devvm network log, they don’t go through your company proxy, and a request of theirs that needs one of your secrets carries only its placeholder, so the secret’s host refuses it. On every other tier, a tool that transparent mode doesn’t cover needs the proxy’s address in its own settings. These common tools don’t read HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY, or read them only when told to:
Node’s fetch reads them only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1, from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0, or with --use-env-proxy, from Node 24.5.0 and 22.21.0. devvm sets NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY in every VM, so an older Node’s fetch is the one that connects directly. Python’s aiohttp reads them only when a program makes its session with trust_env=True. Go programs read them through Go’s default HTTP transport, but a program that makes its own transport without a proxy function connects directly. Java reads none of them. It takes its proxy from the https.proxyHost and https.proxyPort system properties, such as -Dhttps.proxyHost=…, and http.proxyHost and http.proxyPort for plain HTTP. The Docker daemon reads them only from its own environment as it starts, or from its daemon.json, never from your shell. devvm points the daemon at the proxy itself, as Inside the VM says.
data.when-it-isnt-enforced#When it isn’t enfo: On every launch devvm checks on this machine that the VM still runs on the process devvm started confined, and that a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. A VM that fails either check shows as unenforced, and devvm offers to restart it confined or stops it, as the self-check describes.
data.your-own-secrets#Your own secrets:
Any other credential that a tool in a VM sends in a header, such as an API key for Stripe, OpenRouter or your company’s own service, can be a secret of your own. You give it a name, the hosts it goes to and the variable that VMs find its placeholder in, and devvm asks for the value without showing it:
$ devvm secret set stripe --host api.stripe.com --env STRIPE_API_KEY --prefix sk_ Paste the value of stripe, which VMs that use it send to api.stripe.com. The VMs that use it can reach those hosts on port 443. Token: ==> devvm saved the stripe secret in the Keychain. $ devvm secret use stripe ==> devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c uses the stripe secret from its next launch, and its allowlist has api.stripe.com on port 443. From its next launch, the VM has STRIPE_API_KEY set to its own placeholder, such as sk_devvm-proxy-managed-secret-stripe-…, and a tool there sends it as Authorization: Bearer $STRIPE_API_KEY. The proxy puts the real value in place of the placeholder only in requests to api.stripe.com on port 443, over TLS, and a request to any other host goes out with the placeholder alone. A program that loads a .env file gets the placeholder too, as long as the file doesn’t set STRIPE_API_KEY itself, because most dotenv libraries leave a variable that’s already set as it is. Keep the real key out of the project’s .env, which the VM can read.
A secret of yours goes only to the VMs you use it in with devvm secret use, and each one’s hosts then join that VM’s allowlist on port 443. devvm secret set takes these flags:
Flag What it gives the secret --host HOST a host it goes to, such as api.stripe.com: repeat the flag, or join hosts with commas, for up to 16 --env VARIABLE the variable that VMs find its placeholder in, such as STRIPE_API_KEY --header HEADER the header it goes in, such as X-Api-Key, when it isn’t Authorization --prefix PREFIX what its placeholder starts with, such as sk_, for a client that checks how its key starts --path PATH the path of the requests it goes in for, written as a rule’s path is, such as /api/ for everything below /api/, so a request to the host’s other paths carries the placeholder alone, or none for every path --method METHODS the methods of the requests it goes in for, such as GET,HEAD, so a request with another method carries the placeholder alone, or none for every method --scheme SCHEME a scheme of its own before it in Authorization, besides Bearer and Token, such as ApiKey, or none --basic-user lets it go in as the username of Basic credentials, as Stripe and some other services take a key (--basic-user=false takes that away) The proxy puts the value in only when exactly one of the header’s values holds the placeholder, in one of these shapes, so that the value lands where the server reads a credential:
the placeholder alone, such as X-Api-Key: PLACEHOLDER; for Authorization, Bearer, Token or the secret’s own --scheme, in any case, then one space and the placeholder; for Authorization, Basic credentials whose password is the placeholder, after a username of printable ASCII up to 64 characters, such as git’s x-access-token:PLACEHOLDER; with --basic-user, Basic credentials whose username is the placeholder, before a password of printable ASCII up to 64 characters, such as PLACEHOLDER:. The placeholder in any other shape stays as it is, and the proxy’s own log says why without the value. That includes bytes of the VM’s own around it, the placeholder twice, a Digest field, and the username of Basic credentials without --basic-user, because a server can show the VM those parts of a request it refuses, such as a username it doesn’t know. The same shapes apply to the github and claude secrets, which the GitHub CLI, git and Claude Code send as Bearer, token and git’s Basic password.
Without --path and --method, the value goes in for every path and every method. With them, the proxy judges each request as it judges an allow by method and path: by its method as written and each method it names in a method-override header or a _method parameter, and by its path only in a plain form (rules by method and path). So a key that may only read goes in for GET and HEAD alone:
$ devvm secret set reports --host api.example.com --env REPORTS_API_KEY --method GET,HEAD Paste the value of reports, which VMs that use it send to api.example.com. The VMs that use it can reach those hosts on port 443. Token: ==> devvm saved the reports secret in the Keychain. A POST from the VM to api.example.com then carries the placeholder, which the host refuses, while a GET gets the key. The proxy judges every request on a connection, so a kept-alive connection or an HTTP/2 one gets the key only in the requests that have those methods. The github and claude secrets go in for every method. To keep a VM from writing with your GitHub token, give it a deny instead, such as devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE, which refuses those requests before they leave the proxy.
devvm refuses a secret that breaks these rules:
Part Rules name lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and not claude, github or proxy, nor starting with a coding agent’s name, such as codex-key host a host name, such as api.example.com. devvm refuses a wildcard, such as *.example.com, because some domains let anyone own a name under them. It also refuses an address, any port but 443, a name with a character that isn’t plain ASCII, as the proxy refuses such a host, and a name that’s only ever internal, such as localhost, printer.local or a Tailscale or nip.io name. The proxy refuses an internal address whatever name resolves to it anyway header not Host, Cookie, Content-Length, Content-Type, Transfer-Encoding, Expect, Forwarded, Via, an X-Forwarded- or Proxy- header, or one that ends at the next hop, such as Connection, because the proxy drops or sets those itself. Nor one that servers commonly log or send back, such as Origin, Referer, User-Agent, X-Request-Id or Traceparent variable not one that devvm or the VM’s shell sets, such as PATH, GH_TOKEN, HTTPS_PROXY, NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX or any DEVVM_ variable, nor one that changes what a program runs or trusts, such as a GIT_ or PYTHON variable, NODE_OPTIONS, EDITOR or SSL_CERT_DIR, nor another secret’s prefix not holding devvm-proxy-managed, which every placeholder holds after its prefix value printable ASCII alone and at most 3,800 characters, and devvm refuses a longer one before it touches the one saved To save a new value or change a secret, give devvm secret set only what changes:
devvm secret set stripe # save a new value, such as after you rotate the key devvm secret set stripe --host api.stripe.com,files.stripe.com # give it a second host devvm secret rm stripe # delete it, after asking Run without the other flags, devvm secret set NAME keeps the secret’s hosts, header, variable, prefix, path, methods and scheme. To change one of those, give only its flag with the new value, and the rest stay as they are. --host gives the whole list of hosts each time. A host the secret loses goes from every VM at once. A host it gains reaches only the VMs you then run devvm secret use NAME in again, so a host you add never gets the value from a VM you didn’t give it to, and devvm names the VMs that keep the hosts they had. To take a prefix away, delete the secret and save it again. Running VMs keep the variable they launched with, so after you change --env or --prefix, a VM that uses the secret gets the new placeholder at its next launch. devvm secret rm NAME deletes the secret with its definition after asking, and the question names the VMs that use it, which stop using it before it goes. It also deletes a value that a failed save left without its definition. Each VM records the secret it was bound to by an ID that the secret gets as it’s first saved, so a secret saved again later by the same name goes to none of those VMs until you use it there again. A VM still bound to an earlier secret of the name gets nothing of the new one, its launch says so, and devvm secret unuse NAME takes the name away whether a secret has it or not.
devvm keeps your secrets’ hosts, headers, variables, prefixes, paths, methods and schemes in ~/.local/share/devvm/custom-secrets.json, without their values, and checks each entry again whenever it reads the file. When it can’t read the file, or an entry breaks the rules above, such as after an edit by hand, devvm secret and the launch of each VM that uses one of your secrets fail and name the file. Fix the entry, or delete the file and save your secrets again with devvm secret set (details).
Warning
The proxy passes the replies from a secret’s hosts to the VM as they are, so a host that sends the request’s headers back, such as an echo or debug endpoint, shows the VM the real value. Give a secret only hosts that you trust with it, and a key scoped to what the VMs need. A secret’s hosts are also open to the VMs that use it for requests without the placeholder, on every tier, the none tier included. So on a host where anyone can make an account, such as a storage or payments service, code in the VM can send data to an account of its own there.

These pages cover what you change as you work, such as the images VMs are made from, their ports and size, your coding agents, and the editors you connect with.
Coding agents: the supported agents, the config they get in a VM, their logins, and their history. Toolchains: the list of toolchains, with what each brings, the files that choose it, its version files, its global installs and its allowlist. SSH and editors: reaching VMs by name from ssh and VS Code, and forwarding your SSH agent. Ports and size: the ports a VM forwards to your machine, and its CPUs, memory and disk. Managing VMs: restarting, stopping, deleting and listing VMs, and what devvm does in a subfolder or when a project folder is made again, moved, deleted or on a disk that isn’t connected. Images and tools: base, the desktop, docker and nix layers and your own layers, how the shared tools work, which image a new VM gets, and rebuilding, listing and deleting images. Customizing images: your own layers, and the optional features in every VM, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. Settings and files: your settings and the commands that write them, devvm’s state, and the environment variables devvm reads. Working on a clone: --clone, which gives a VM its own clone of the repo instead of mounting the folder. devcontainer.json: what a new VM takes from a project’s devcontainer.json, and what devvm refuses. Links between VMs: devvm link, which lets a program in one VM reach a service in another by name, as in postgres://db:5432/app, once that VM publishes the port. A VM’s desktop: the desktop layer, and opening a VM’s desktop in Screen Sharing with devvm desktop. Starting from a container image: --from, which starts base from node:24, alpine:3 or your own image. What devvm keeps on this machine: everything devvm, its tools and its backends keep outside your project folders, and how each is cleaned up. The command line: the help, flags and their values, the questions devvm asks and what answers them, --json for scripts, and shell completion. Upgrading and uninstalling: devvm upgrade, switching between Homebrew and the install script, and removing devvm with everything it keeps. Troubleshooting: what to do when a command or a build fails, a request is blocked, or a VM won’t start. Known limits: what devvm can’t do, in one list.

devvm --clone gives the VM its own clone of the repo instead of mounting your folder, so nothing in the VM can touch your working tree or .git. Use it when you don’t trust what runs in the VM, such as an agent working unattended, and on Linux hosts that can’t lock .git, such as Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, where devvm only names what changed after the fact (when Linux can’t lock). On Linux hosts it’s also the way to use SQLite in WAL mode, or a program that maps its files for writing, such as LMDB or the mold linker, in the repo, because those fail in the 9p share that VMs there mount the folder with, while the clone is on the VM’s own disk, which is also far faster (programs that map files). Files the VM writes lists what --clone keeps away from this machine.
devvm --clone # create the VM, copy your repo into it and open a shell in its clone devvm clone fetch # later, on this machine, fetch the VM's work as devvm/ git log -p main..devvm/main A clone's lifedevvm --clone copies your repo into the VM, where you or an agent commit. devvm clone fetch brings the VM's commits into your repo as a devvm/ branch, for you to review and merge. devvm rm looks for commits not fetched and fetches them into a saved/devvm/ branch, then deletes the VM and removes its remote.devvm --clone copiesyour repo devvm clone fetch givesdevvm/ devvm rm looks forcommits not fetched fetched intosaved/devvm/ you or an agentcommit in the VM review,then merge the VM is deleted,and its remote removed Your repo The VM's clone When the folder holds several repos, such as a frontend and a backend beside each other, devvm --clone gives the VM a clone of each repo you choose, at the same paths as on this machine (folders of repos).
data.a-copy-that-didnt-finish#A copy that did:
If the copy fails, for example because the VM can’t be reached or its disk is full, devvm copies again in full the next time you run it in the folder:
devvm # in the folder, to copy again The VM’s repo counts as copied only once the whole copy is done, so a copy that stopped part way never leaves a clone that devvm thinks is complete. devvm rm and devvm clone off check a clone whose copy didn’t finish as they check any other, so its commits and changes are never lost without a question (deleting the VM). A copy that runs again keeps what the VM did meanwhile, and devvm names what it kept:
A branch that has commits from the VM stays as it is instead of moving to this machine’s. HEAD stays where the VM put it when the VM checked out something else, such as a branch of its own, or moved its detached HEAD. That includes the case where you switched this repo between a branch and a detached HEAD since the copy that didn’t finish. Your uncommitted changes, and a rebase or other operation in progress, would then apply to something else, so they stay on this machine. A file in the clone’s folder that the VM wrote stays as it is, even where you have a change of your own. devvm names it when it’s at a path you changed or deleted, or when it differs from what you’ve staged, and git status in the VM shows it as changed. Running devvm in the folder again is also how a VM that an older devvm made, whose copy failed, gets its clone. An older devvm made every VM’s repo with SHA-1 object names. When such a VM’s copy failed and your repo uses SHA-256, its empty repo can’t take your commits, so devvm asks before it deletes that empty repo’s .git and makes it again. Only the repo is made again, never the VM. Without a terminal devvm leaves it and says what to run, which is devvm in a terminal, or devvm rm, then devvm --clone.
data.a-git-worktree#A git worktree: When the folder is a git worktree, devvm copies what’s published and the worktree’s own work: its branch, that branch’s upstream, if it has one, the repo’s default branch, the remote-tracking branches and the tags. It leaves the repo’s other local branches on this machine, because they’re other worktrees’ work, and it says so. The default branch is the branch origin/HEAD points to, else main, else master, whichever the repo has, so you can rebase onto it or diff against it in the VM. The worktree’s VM gets no stash, because the stash is the whole repo’s, not the worktree’s, and none of the submodules (submodules).
data.a-partial-clone#A partial clone:
When the VM’s network policy blocks the remote a partial clone fetches its missing objects from, devvm names the remote’s host, and on the allowlist tier you let the VM reach it:
devvm network allow github.com A remote reached over ssh: devvm names the host with its port, such as github.com:22, which you allow as it’s named. The none tier: move the VM to the allowlist tier with devvm network allowlist first. The internet tier: devvm names a host that one of your deny rules blocks, or that’s a private address, which that tier never reaches. What the VM can’t reach or doesn’t get: devvm also names a remote that’s on this machine, a file:// URL or a path, a remote that stays here because its URL is of a kind devvm doesn’t copy, and a branch or tag that points to an object the clone never fetched, which the VM’s clone doesn’t get. Fetching the VM’s work back needs every object that work names, and git in the VM never fetches a missing object just to send it, so when the work names one the clone lacks, such as a file restored from an old commit, devvm clone fetch fails and says so. In the VM’s clone, run a command that reads the work’s objects, which fetches the missing ones from the remote, then fetch again from this machine:
git show agent/search # in the VM's clone, for each commit of the work devvm clone fetch # then on this machine
data.adding-a-repo#Adding a repo:
devvm clone add PATH copies one more repo into the VM, such as a repo you cloned into the folder after the VM was made, or one that you left out. PATH is the repo’s folder, relative to the folder you run it in, and it must be inside the VM’s folder. devvm checks the repo as it checks each repo it copies, starts the VM if it’s stopped, copies the repo’s current and default branches to the same path in the VM and adds its remote. When the copy fails, for example because the VM can’t be reached, devvm keeps the repo in the VM’s list, so devvm rm still checks what reached the VM, and running devvm clone add PATH again copies it again.
git clone git@github.com:me/docs.git devvm clone add docs A repo made in the VM stays in the VM, because the VM can’t add a repo to this machine. To bring it out, clone it from the VM with git clone devvm-my-repos-:/path/to/my-repos/new, using the VM’s full name from devvm ls.
data.agents-across-repos#Agents across repos:
An agent that works on one change across repos uses one branch name in each repo, such as agent/search in frontend and in backend, so devvm clone fetch lists that change as one line with both repos. For several agents at once, give each its own folder with a worktree of each repo, inside the VM’s folder:
for r in frontend backend; do git -C "$r" worktree add -b agent/search "../.worktrees/search/$r"; done cd .worktrees/search # the change's own copy of the folder's repos, then start the agent here devvm copies the folder’s own files only into the folder itself, so copy those the agent needs into the change’s folder too. devvm rm checks each worktree inside the VM’s folder for uncommitted changes, whichever repo it belongs to (deleting the VM).
data.an-operation-in-progress#An operation in:
When you’re in the middle of a rebase, a merge, a cherry-pick, a revert or a bisect, the VM’s clone is in the middle of it too, so you or an agent can go on with it there. Resolve a conflict, then go on as you would here:
git rebase --continue # in the VM's clone, for a rebase git commit # for a merge git cherry-pick --continue # for a cherry-pick A rebase started with --autostash brings its autostashed changes back in the VM. When the rest of a rebase or a cherry-pick names a commit that the VM won’t have, devvm names it, as that step will fail there (the state in the copy).
data.deleting-the-vm#Deleting the VM:
devvm clone fetch # fetch the VM's work first, so the check finds it fetched devvm rm # check for unfetched work and uncommitted changes, then ask devvm rm --no-clone-check # skip both checks, so the VM's work goes with it git branch -D saved/devvm/main # delete a saved branch once you've reviewed it Before devvm rm deletes a --clone VM, it checks the clone for work you’d lose. It starts a stopped VM for the check as a launch does, so the VM’s confinement is checked first:
Work this repo hasn’t fetched. devvm names it and offers to fetch it into new local branches: Branches with commits this repo hasn’t fetched go into saved/devvm/. devvm skips a branch whose name git on this machine refuses and names it, and that branch goes with the VM. To keep such a branch, rename it in the VM with git branch -m before you run devvm rm. A detached HEAD’s commits, when the clone’s HEAD is detached at commits that no branch of the clone has and this repo hasn’t fetched, such as an agent’s work done without a branch, are named as HEAD and go into saved/devvm/HEAD. A stash entry the VM made, which this repo hasn’t fetched, is named as stash-N, after its place in the VM’s git stash list, and goes into saved/devvm/stash-N, from which git stash apply saved/devvm/stash-0 applies it here, its untracked files apart, as devvm clone fetch saves them (fetching the VM’s work). When devvm can’t fetch an entry, it keeps the VM. The stash entries devvm copied in from this machine don’t count. Uncommitted changes in the clone or a worktree inside its folder. devvm lists the first 20 of them in all, with each worktree’s changes under its path, and asks before deleting them along with the VM: The changes devvm copied in from this machine don’t count while the VM leaves them as they came, because they’re your work, not the VM’s, even if you’ve changed or undone them here since. Once the VM changes one of those files, its permissions or what’s staged for it, devvm lists it as the VM’s work. A worktree whose HEAD is detached at commits that nothing else in the clone has, no branch, tag or remote-tracking branch, counts the same way: devvm names it and asks, because those commits go with the VM. To keep them, run git switch -c NAME in that worktree, then fetch the branch. Worktrees it skips: one whose folder is gone or that git would prune, and those outside the clone’s folder. When the clone has more than 100 worktrees inside its folder, devvm checks the first 100 and asks before deleting the VM, even if none of them has changes. Worktrees outside the folder don’t count towards the 100. The worktrees that opencode makes in the VM’s home folder are checked apart, as for any VM with opencode, and devvm asks about them in the same question (opencode’s worktrees). If either check finds something and there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM. These questions are asked only in a terminal, because only you can judge the work, so --force never answers them (questions devvm asks). Without a terminal, when the clone has work this repo hasn’t fetched, devvm’s refusal names devvm clone fetch: run it first, and the check finds every branch, a detached HEAD’s commits and the VM’s stash entries fetched, in every repo of a folder of repos too. Two cases check more:
A folder of repos. devvm checks every repo the VM has a clone of, reading them all from the VM at once, and names the repo of each branch and each change it lists. It asks once whether to fetch the unfetched branches of every repo, each into that repo’s saved// branches, and once before the uncommitted changes go, with the first 20 changes in all the repos shown. A repo whose copy didn’t finish is checked too when its clone is in the VM. Beyond that: When a repo’s clone isn’t at its path in the VM, for example because something in the VM moved it, devvm says so and asks before deleting the VM, as for uncommitted changes. When a repo on this machine isn’t the repo the VM has a clone of any more, for example because its .git is gone, devvm refuses and keeps the VM, because git there would read another repo, so put the repo back, or give --no-clone-check. devvm doesn’t check the VM’s copy of the folder’s own files, nor anything else outside the repos, so copy out what you need of those first. A repo that another VM mounts, such as the VM of a folder the repo is in. Code in that VM could swap the repo under devvm’s git, so devvm runs no git in it on this machine. It still checks the clone in the VM, and every other repo of a folder of repos, but it can’t fetch the clone’s work into the repo, so it names that VM and asks before deleting, as for uncommitted changes, and without a terminal it refuses and keeps the VM. Fetch the work by hand first if you need it, then give --no-clone-check. Once the checks pass, devvm deletes the VM. If the remote still points at the VM, devvm then removes it with git remote remove, in each repo of a folder of repos too, which also deletes its devvm/* branches and their upstream settings. Before it does, devvm keeps every devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a new local branch, named after the remote as saved//, whoever fetched it. devvm never overwrites a branch, so when one is in the way, it uses saved/-2, then -3 and so on, and if it finds no free name, devvm rm refuses and keeps the VM (saved branches). devvm names each branch it creates, and they’re yours to review, merge or delete.
Flag What it skips --force only the question whether to delete the VM at all, so both checks still run --no-export the export of the agents’ history, and it leaves both checks as they are --no-clone-check both checks, so the VM goes with the commits this repo hasn’t fetched and the uncommitted changes, and devvm warns you of that first Use --no-clone-check when a check can’t read the clone, such as when git in the VM is broken or the VM doesn’t answer within 2 minutes, and devvm refuses and keeps the VM. Use it too when the VM doesn’t start for the check, such as when its tier isn’t enforced, because devvm then says what kept it from starting and keeps the VM. devvm still asks whether to delete the VM unless you also give --force, and it still keeps the devvm/* branches you fetched as saved/devvm/ branches.
data.devvm-clone-fetch-json#devvm clone fetch:
devvm clone fetch --json fetches as devvm clone fetch does, then prints one JSON object instead of the list. repos has each repo with new or moved branches, or with its detached HEAD’s commits or stash entries saved, by its folder relative to this one (. for this folder’s own repo), with its remote, those branches, and saved, the local branches the detached HEAD’s commits and the stash entries went into, when there are any. branches has the same branches by name, each with its repos, sorted by name. Both are empty when nothing is new.
{ "version": 1, "repos": [ { "path": "backend", "remote": "devvm", "branches": ["agent/search"] }, { "path": "frontend", "remote": "devvm", "branches": ["agent/search"] } ], "branches": [ { "name": "agent/search", "repos": ["backend", "frontend"] } ] }
data.devvm-clone-json#devvm clone –json:
devvm clone --json prints one JSON object with clone, which is on or off, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on or off with it, and the flags that go with them.
{ "version": 1, "clone": "on" }
data.fetching-the-vms-work#Fetching the VM’s:
git fetch devvm in the repo fetches the VM’s branches as devvm/, as for any remote. devvm clone fetch does the same for every repo the VM has a clone of, which is one repo here, or each repo of a folder of repos, and then lists the branches that are new or have moved since the last fetch, each with the repos it’s in:
$ devvm clone fetch agent/search: backend, frontend main: backend ==> Review each branch in its repo before you merge it, such as with git log -p main..devvm/main. devvm clone fetch starts the VM if it’s stopped. It connects to the VM itself, as the copy does, so it needs neither devvm’s Include line in ~/.ssh/config nor the VM’s name in your ssh config. What it fetches:
Every branch of each clone into its repo’s remote, as devvm/, and it never changes your own branches or tags. A detached HEAD’s commits. When a clone’s HEAD is detached at commits that no branch of the clone has and this repo hasn’t fetched, such as an agent’s work done without a branch, which git fetch devvm doesn’t fetch, devvm clone fetch fetches them into a new local branch, saved/devvm/HEAD, and names it. Each stash entry the VM made, the same way, into saved/devvm/stash-N, after the entry’s place in the VM’s git stash list, but not the entries devvm copied in from this machine. An entry’s untracked files go to a branch of their own, saved/devvm/stash-N-untracked, which devvm names, along with any of them that git ignores here, so git stash apply saved/devvm/stash-N never writes them. Look at them with git show saved/devvm/stash-N-untracked before you use them. The work’s Git LFS objects, which git fetch devvm never brings. It never writes over a branch, so when saved/devvm/ is taken, even by an earlier fetch’s, it uses saved/devvm-2/ and on, and it fetches nothing it has saved before. When a repo’s remote is gone, devvm clone fetch adds it again. When you’ve pointed the remote at another URL, or the folder on this machine isn’t that repo any more, for example because its .git is gone, devvm leaves that repo alone and says so.
git log -p main..devvm/main # review each branch before you merge it Fetching runs nothing from the VM on this machine. git only receives objects, checking each one, and updates the devvm/* branches, or creates new saved/devvm/* branches, for a detached HEAD’s commits, the VM’s stash entries, or when devvm rm does the fetch. The commits themselves are untrusted, though, so treat them as you would a contributor’s branch and review them before you merge them, check them out or run anything they change.
data.folders-of-repos#Folders of repos:
A project is often several repos in one folder, such as a frontend that uses file:../shared in its package.json, or a .NET solution whose projects point at ../Lib/Lib.csproj. devvm --clone in that folder gives one VM a clone of each repo you choose, each at the same path as on this machine, so the paths between them work in the VM as they do here. The folder can be a repo itself or not, and when it is one, you ask for this with --repos, because without it devvm --clone there gives the VM a clone of the folder’s own repo alone, as for any repo, whatever repos are below it.
my-repos/ ├── docker-compose.yml ├── frontend/ (a repo) ├── backend/ (a repo) └── shared/ (a repo) cd my-repos devvm --clone # choose the repos, then create the VM and open a shell in my-repos devvm --clone --repos frontend,shared # or choose them on the command line, as a script must devvm looks for repos up to four folders below this one, as .git protection does, and skips the folders of packages and build tools, such as node_modules and vendor. In a terminal, it lists the repos it found in a picker, each ticked, and you untick those the VM doesn’t need. A repo that --clone can’t copy is listed under its own heading with the reason, such as a repo without commits or one whose .git points into another repo, and it can’t be ticked. devvm lists at most 100 repos, and it names how many more it found. A linked worktree of a repo in the folder, such as one in .worktrees/NAME, isn’t a repo of its own, so devvm doesn’t list it, and its repo’s clone gets every branch of that repo, the worktree’s own included. A repo can’t be ticked when:
--clone can’t copy it, such as a repo without commits or one whose .git points into another repo. It’s listed under its own heading with the reason. Its folder’s name has a character a terminal can’t show, such as a line break or a bidi control. Another VM mounts it, because that VM is a subfolder’s that holds the repo, or the repo’s own, or, for a linked worktree, the VM of the repo it belongs to. Code in that VM could swap the repo for another while devvm’s git works in it, so devvm names that VM, and devvm clone add refuses the repo too. Delete that VM, or move the repo out of its folder, to give this VM a clone of it. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, give --repos, or devvm refuses without creating anything:
--repos all takes every repo --clone can copy. --repos none takes none of them. A list, such as --repos frontend,backend, takes those repos, by their folders relative to this one, with . for this folder’s own repo. devvm names each repo you chose that it can’t copy, and leaves it out, and it records your choice in the VM’s state, never in the folder. When devvm finds no repo below this folder that it can copy, devvm --clone gives the VM a clone of this folder’s own repo, as for a folder that holds no other, and the folder must then be one (requirements). A folder of repos inside another repo’s working tree is refused, because devvm would copy that repo’s files. To clone repos in it, run devvm --clone --repos LIST in that repo’s top folder, and choose them there. Each repo’s clone:
Gets the same refs as a single repo’s (what’s copied), every branch, tag and remote-tracking branch, checked out as the repo is here. When a repo’s HEAD is detached, its clone is detached at the same commit, and devvm says so. A repo that is a linked worktree of a repo outside the folder gets what a worktree’s clone gets. Gets a remote of its own for the VM, named as for one repo’s clone (the remote): devvm, or devvm- when that repo already has a devvm remote, for example from a VM of its own. One repo’s remote names never change the others’. When a repo has all three names taken, devvm leaves that repo out and names it. Leaves the other repos’ clones out of its git status, when it’s the folder’s own repo’s, and what your repo’s .git/info/exclude leaves out too, such as .worktrees/, so the other clones aren’t changes devvm rm asks about. Is left out and named when its repo no longer passes the checks as the copy is made, for example because its last commit went, and the others are copied. When the copy fails, devvm copies what’s left the next time you run it in the folder.
data.git-lfs#Git LFS:
Every VM has git-lfs, and the copy sets up its filter in each clone it makes, so a repo that uses Git LFS works in its clone as it does here. A VM that mounts its folder gets no filter, so its LFS files are the pointers git stores. devvm clone fetch brings back the LFS objects of the VM’s work too:
git lfs ls-files # in the VM's clone: the files, with their content devvm clone fetch # on this machine: the VM's branches and their LFS objects Into the VM, the copy sends the LFS objects that the files you have checked out point to, when your repo has them, and git-lfs in the VM checks those files out with their content. One that isn’t what its pointer names stays on this machine, and devvm names it, and when your repo keeps its objects outside .git, with lfs.storage, none go and devvm says so. A file whose object your repo hasn’t fetched stays a pointer in the VM, as git lfs pull would fetch it, where the VM’s network policy and credentials let it. Back from the VM, when devvm clone fetch, devvm rm or devvm clone off brings the VM’s work back, devvm also brings the LFS objects that the work’s pointers name and your repo lacks, each checked against its pointer before it goes into your repo, without git-lfs running on this machine. A plain git fetch devvm brings none, but devvm clone fetch later brings those of the commits it fetched too, even once you’ve merged them. When the objects come to more than 2 GiB, devvm asks first, and without a terminal it refuses. One that the VM’s clone lacks, or that isn’t what its pointer names, stays out, and devvm names it. Before the VM goes, devvm rm and devvm clone off name the LFS objects that only the VM’s clone has and ask, and an object they couldn’t bring back keeps the VM (how it works).
data.opening-a-repos-folder#Opening a repo’s: In a folder of one of the VM’s repos, such as my-repos/frontend, devvm opens the folder’s VM at that repo’s path, as it opens any parent folder’s VM in a subfolder. A repo of its own in a subfolder usually gets a VM of its own, but the folder’s VM has this repo’s clone at the same path and mounts nothing of this machine, so the VM can’t reach the repo’s folder here. devvm --here in the repo’s folder still creates or opens that repo’s own VM. In a repo the VM has no clone of, devvm doesn’t use the folder’s VM.
data.requirements#Requirements: The folder is the top folder of a git repo that has at least one commit, or it’s a folder of repos (folders of repos). The repo is the folder’s own, or the folder is a worktree that git worktree add made. devvm refuses a .git that points into another repo, because the copy would take that repo’s branches into the VM. That includes a .git file that isn’t a worktree’s, such as a submodule’s, which devvm --clone in its parent repo’s folder copies (submodules), a worktree whose link back to this folder doesn’t match, a commondir that leads to another repo, and objects or refs that are symlinks, or that sit in a folder that is one. devvm also refuses a repo that borrows objects from another repo through objects/info/alternates. To use such a repo, run git repack -a -d in it, then delete that file. The repo has no info/grafts file, which gives some commits other parents than their own, because devvm copies each commit with its own parents. git replace --convert-graft-file turns the file into replace refs, which git supports in its place. devvm copies each commit’s real parents even then, so the history the grafts cut off has to be in the repo on this machine. git is installed on this machine. The VM’s images already have it. A repo that names its objects with SHA-256 also needs git 2.29 or newer in the VM, which devvm’s images have. An image you made with --from might not, and then devvm stops before it copies anything and names the VM’s git version. No other VM mounts the folder, such as the VM of a folder it’s in. Code in that VM could swap the repo under the git commands devvm runs here as it copies your branches, so devvm refuses --clone and devvm clone on there and names that VM. Delete that VM, or move the repo out of its folder. You choose --clone when the VM is created, and once a VM is a --clone VM you don’t need to pass --clone again. devvm refuses --clone for an existing VM that mounts its folder, and devvm clone on switches that VM instead (switching a VM that exists).
data.subfolders#Subfolders:
When you run devvm in a subfolder of the repo’s folder, devvm uses the --clone VM as it uses any parent folder’s VM (a subfolder). The clone is at the repo folder’s path, so the subfolder’s path in the VM is the same subfolder in the clone. When the clone has that subfolder, the shell opens there, and devvm host and devvm code give it as the folder to open. When the clone lacks it, for example because the subfolder is untracked or ignored and so never copied, they use the clone’s top folder instead.
cd src/api # a subfolder of the repo devvm # the repo's --clone VM, its shell in src/api in the clone devvm --clone # a VM of the subfolder's own, when it's a repo's top folder devvm --clone in a subfolder never uses a parent folder’s VM. It makes a new --clone VM for the subfolder, as devvm --here does, and doesn’t take --parent, so the subfolder must be the top folder of a repo of its own.
data.submodules#Submodules:
Each submodule you’ve initialised here, nested ones too, gets a clone of its own in the VM, at its path, copied as the repo is, at the commit you have checked out in it, so git submodule status in the VM shows what it shows here:
git submodule status --recursive # in the VM's clone, as on this machine Its repo here gets a devvm remote for the VM, chosen as the repo’s is, so devvm clone fetch fetches each submodule’s branches into it, and devvm rm checks each one for work you haven’t fetched (how the copy works). The rest:
One you remove or deinitialise here later: devvm remembers each submodule it copied, so devvm rm names it as one it can’t check, and asks before the VM goes. One you haven’t initialised, with git submodule update --init, stays an empty folder in the VM, as it is here, and so does one you initialise after the copy, or in a VM made before devvm copied submodules. One that devvm can’t copy, such as one whose .git doesn’t lead to its own git folder inside the repo’s, stays on this machine, with its own submodules, and devvm names it, while the rest of the copy goes on. A git worktree’s VM gets none of its submodules, which devvm names.
data.switching-a-vm-that-exists#Switching a V:
devvm clone shows whether this folder’s VM has its own clone of the repo, which is on, or mounts the folder, which is off. devvm clone on and devvm clone off switch the VM by making it again from the image it has, as devvm layer add does, and then open a shell in it:
devvm clone # show on or off devvm clone on # make the VM again with its own clone of the repo, after asking devvm clone off # fetch the clone's work, then make the VM again with this folder mounted The VM keeps its home folder and its settings, as a VM made again does, and everything else on its disk is lost. So in a terminal devvm asks first, with no as the default, and without one it refuses unless you give --force. --no-export skips the export of the agents’ history, and --clean-home gives the VM the image’s home folder instead of its own, as for devvm layer add. When the VM is in the mode you ask for already, devvm says so and changes nothing.
devvm clone on:
Needs a folder that --clone takes (requirements), and devvm refuses before it changes anything when the folder isn’t one. In a folder of repos, devvm asks which repos the new VM gets in the picker before it asks to make the VM again, and devvm clone on --repos LIST answers that without a terminal. Loses only the VM’s disk, because your work is in the folder. The new VM mounts nothing of the folder, and as it starts, devvm copies your branches into its clone and adds the remote, as for a new --clone VM (what’s copied). Takes the .git locks off the folder once the new VM is ready and the old one is deleted, because no VM mounts it any more. First it names what the old VM changed that the locks can’t stop, as a launch does (when devvm reports .git). devvm clone off:
Checks the clone first, as devvm rm does (deleting the VM), every repo of a folder of repos included, because the clone is on the VM’s disk and goes with it. It offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched into saved/devvm/ branches, and it asks before the clone’s uncommitted changes go. Only a terminal can answer these questions, and --force never does, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM as it is. devvm clone off --no-clone-check skips the check after a warning, and the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes are lost. Mounts the folder again with .git protection as a new VM gets it, which is on on macOS and off on Linux hosts. Removes the remote before the new VM first starts, and before devvm locks .git, and keeps each devvm/* branch that has commits no other branch has as a saved/devvm/ branch, as devvm rm does. If the switch is then undone, devvm adds the remote back. When a step fails, or you press Ctrl+C, before the new VM has its home folder, devvm puts the old VM back as it was, in its old mode, as it does for any remake.
A --clone VM keeps its clone on its own disk, so devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update refuse it. To change its layers or bring it up to date, switch it off first:
devvm clone off # fetch the clone's work, then mount the folder devvm update # or devvm layer add or devvm layer rm devvm clone on # its own clone again
data.the-folders-own-files#The folder’s own f:
A folder of repos often has files of its own at its top, outside every repo, such as a docker-compose.yml, a Makefile or an .envrc. When the folder isn’t a repo itself, devvm copies these into the VM once, when it creates the clone, at the same paths. It never copies them again, and nothing comes back from the VM, so a later change on either side stays there. To change one in the VM, edit it there, and to bring a change back, copy it out yourself, for example with scp and the VM’s name, which devvm host shows:
devvm host # start the VM and show its name scp devvm-my-repos-:/path/to/my-repos/docker-compose.yml . # copy the VM's version back devvm copies the files and folders outside every repo, whether the VM has a clone of that repo or not. It keeps each file’s permissions but its set-user-id and set-group-id bits, and a link that leads to a path in the folder, as a link. It reads only beneath the folder, one folder at a time, and never through a link. It leaves out:
a .git, a folder shaped like one, such as a bare repo’s, and the folders of packages and build tools, such as node_modules, vendor and .venv a link that leads out of the folder, a file with another hard link, sockets and other special files, and anything on another disk a file over 10 MiB, and the files past 64 MiB or 5,000 entries in all devvm says how many of the files it left out. When the folder is a repo itself, its files are its repo’s, so devvm copies none of them this way. A secret in one of these files, such as an .env at the folder’s top, reaches the VM as any other file does, so move it out of the folder before devvm --clone when the VM mustn’t have it. devvm refuses the folders it refuses to mount, such as your home folder (folders devvm refuses), because it would copy their files.
data.the-remote#The remote:
devvm adds a git remote for the VM to your repo. It’s named devvm, or devvm- if devvm is already taken, or the VM’s full name if both are. The remote’s URL is the VM’s full name followed by the clone’s path, so git connects through devvm’s ssh config, and fetching needs two things:
Your ~/.ssh/config needs devvm’s Include line (SSH access by name). devvm offers to add it when it creates the clone, and again when you run devvm host or devvm code. Until the line is there, or when devvm had no terminal to ask in, fetch with GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config' git fetch devvm. The VM must be running. A stopped VM has no SSH entry, so git fetch fails because it can’t resolve the name. Run devvm or devvm host in the folder first.
data.the-settings#The settings:
Your repo’s own settings go too, from its .git/config and, when git keeps settings for each worktree, as git sparse-checkout does, from the worktree’s config.worktree, never from your global config or a file they include (the settings in the copy):
Its remotes, so git fetch origin and git pull work in the VM wherever its network policy reaches the remote and it has the credentials the remote needs: Each URL goes as git resolves it, after any url.*.insteadOf, without the user name, password, query or fragment of an http or https URL, any of which can hold a token, and without the password of an ssh URL, whose user name goes. A file:// URL or a path goes as it is, though it names a folder on this machine that the VM can’t reach. When git pushes somewhere else, because of a push URL or a url.*.pushInsteadOf, the push URLs go too, cleaned the same way. A remote whose URL is of any other kind, such as git:// or ext::, or a scp-like URL that may hold a token, stays on this machine, and devvm names it. A push URL of those kinds, or one that reaches a devvm VM, stays too, and when none of a remote’s push URLs goes, git push in the VM pushes to the remote’s URL, and devvm says so. The upstream of each branch the copy sends, the submodules’ URLs, cleaned as a remote’s, and their active, branch and update settings, but an update that runs a command. core.sparseCheckout, core.sparseCheckoutCone and index.sparse, so a sparse checkout is one in the VM too. core.hooksPath when it’s a folder inside the repo, such as husky’s, as the setting alone. The hooks in that folder are files of your working tree, so the tracked ones reach the VM with the checkout, and the untracked ones, such as husky’s _ folder, stay here, as every untracked file does, until a tool in the VM makes them, such as npm install. The repo’s own user.name and user.email, so a commit in the VM has your name on it. Its hooks, as they are, the secrets in them included, so a hook that calls a tool only this machine has fails in the VM, as it would on a new machine. Only the files named as git’s hooks go, each a regular file of at most 1 MiB and 16 MiB in all, from the repo’s hooks folder, and only when git here runs them, which it doesn’t once a core.hooksPath is set, in the repo or in your global config. A hook that’s a link, a folder or bigger stays and is named, and so do the hooks of a core.hooksPath outside the repo. devvm also names a hooks folder that’s missing, a link or unreadable. Every other setting stays on this machine, such as credential.helper, http.extraHeader, core.sshCommand, aliases and filters. Your remotes’ URLs are real, though, so when the VM may use your GitHub token, which its proxy puts into requests to github.com (secrets), and its network policy reaches GitHub, code in the VM can push to origin there. To keep a VM from pushing to GitHub or changing anything through its API:
devvm network deny github.com --path '/*/*/git-receive-pack' # no git push over HTTPS devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE # no changes through GitHub's API
data.whats-copied#What’s copied:
From this machine, the VM mounts only the shared tools and its agents’ config folders. Once the VM is running, devvm creates a repo in it at the same path as your folder and copies your repo into it, so git status, git log and git stash list in the VM’s clone show what they show here. What goes into the VM:
Every local branch, your saved/devvm/* branches included, which hold a deleted VM’s work. Every tag, an annotated one staying annotated, and your notes and replace refs. Refs are the repo’s data, so what a tool keeps in them goes too, such as an agent tool that stores its transcripts in git notes or branches. The remote-tracking branches of your remotes, such as origin/main, with origin/HEAD still pointing at its branch. That includes the branches of another private repo that you fetched as a remote. What you have checked out, your current branch or, when HEAD is detached, the same commit, detached, and your shell opens there. Your uncommitted changes. What you’ve staged is staged in the VM, and what you haven’t is changed in its working tree, deleted files and files added with git add -N included. Each working copy goes as it is, but only a regular file or a symbolic link, where git tracks one of those. A rebase, a merge, a cherry-pick, a revert or a bisect that you’re in the middle of (an operation in progress), and your repo’s info/exclude, info/sparse-checkout and info/attributes. Your stash, each entry with its message and the commits it was made on, at most your 1,000 newest, and devvm names the rest. An entry made with git stash -u holds untracked files, so those files reach the VM inside it. Your repo’s own settings, such as its remotes, its hooks as they are and your user.name (the settings), each submodule you’ve initialised, and the content of your Git LFS files. What stays on this machine:
Untracked and ignored files, such as .env and node_modules. Anything that isn’t a tracked file of its kind any more. A tracked file that you turned into a folder is missing in the VM, nothing in that folder goes, and devvm names it. A file whose folder is a symbolic link here goes as deleted, as git sees it, never as the file the link leads to. An embedded repo’s contents, and an uninitialised submodule’s. Its folder is empty in the VM, without its .git, its own changes or its untracked files. The change you haven’t committed to a filtered file, one that goes through a git filter, such as git-crypt’s or Git LFS’s. The file goes as git stores it, because devvm’s git runs no filter, though git-lfs in the VM then checks a Git LFS file out with its content (Git LFS), and devvm names it as one that may differ, because without the filter devvm can’t tell whether it changed. Such a file that you deleted is deleted in the VM too. Your edits to a file marked with git update-index --skip-worktree, which git hides and which are often local settings or secrets. The file goes as git’s index has it, and devvm names it. A file marked --assume-unchanged also goes as the index has it, and a sparse checkout’s files outside it stay out of the VM, as they’re out of your working tree. A stash entry made with git stash --all, which may hold ignored files, such as .env. devvm can’t tell such an entry from a -u one for sure, so it keeps back any entry that may be one, such as one whose untracked files your .gitignore ignores, now or when you made it, and it names each one. Another devvm VM’s work, the remote-tracking branches of its remote, such as an older --clone VM’s devvm/*. Refs outside those namespaces, such as refs/original/, where git filter-branch keeps what it rewrote. So does ORIG_HEAD, with any commit that only it still reaches, such as one a reset took back, except during git am, whose --abort needs it. Your global git config, and every setting of your repo that the settings doesn’t list, such as credential.helper. devvm copies all this without git push, over the same channel that carries every other command devvm runs in the VM, so the copy goes to that VM alone, and no setting in your repo’s config, such as a url.*.insteadOf that rewrites the VM’s URL, can send it anywhere else. It also takes a shallow clone, which gets its shallow history in the VM, and a repo that names its objects with SHA-256, which gets a SHA-256 repo there (how the copy works, the working tree, the state). A partial clone, which git clone --filter makes, gets the objects it has, and the VM’s git fetches the rest from its remote when a command needs one, where the VM’s network policy and credentials let it (a partial clone).

data.api-keys-the-proxy-puts-in#API keys the:
The VM’s proxy puts in opencode’s and pi’s API keys for the providers in this table. The ID is the provider’s entry in the agent’s auth.json and the value that devvm agent login --provider takes. The VM’s copy of the login holds a placeholder in place of each of these keys, and on every network tier the proxy swaps it for the key in the headers that the table names, in requests to the provider’s hosts alone, so any other host gets only the placeholder. Where the table names a path, the proxy swaps it only in requests for paths that start with it, so the rest of that host gets the placeholder too. The proxy also allows those hosts on port 443, as it allows the hosts of every secret it puts in, so you don’t allow them yourself:
ID Provider Hosts Paths Headers anthropic Anthropic api.anthropic.com any x-api-key deepseek DeepSeek api.deepseek.com any Authorization google Google Gemini generativelanguage.googleapis.com any x-goog-api-key groq Groq api.groq.com any Authorization mistral Mistral api.mistral.ai any Authorization openai OpenAI api.openai.com any Authorization openrouter OpenRouter openrouter.ai /api/ Authorization, x-api-key xai xAI api.x.ai any Authorization The Google Gemini key is the Gemini API’s, for Google AI Studio. Vertex AI logs in with a Google Cloud account or a service account instead, so devvm withholds its logins, as it does any other provider’s. These providers’ keys never need [pass-keys], and when it lists one of them all the same, the VM still gets the key’s placeholder, not the key, and devvm notes at each launch that you can take the provider out. With some of these keys, code in the VM can make a credential of its own that works without the proxy, or reach hosts that the allowlist doesn’t have through the provider’s own tools (how the proxy puts them in).
Warning
A VM that was given one of these keys as it was, before the launch that first gave it the placeholder, may still hold copies of it, and those copies still work wherever they are. So when you don’t trust that VM, make a new key at the provider, save it with devvm agent login AGENT --api-key --provider PROVIDER and revoke the old one.
devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider openai # save the new key, then revoke the old one at the provider
data.claude-code-login#Claude Code login:
You log Claude Code in once, from inside any VM that has it, and devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with Claude Code, so this machine never needs Claude Code:
devvm agent login claude # log Claude Code in to your Claude subscription devvm agent login claude --setup-token # get a long-lived Claude Code token with claude setup-token instead devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and then runs Claude Code’s own login in the VM, on your terminal: claude auth login --claudeai, or claude setup-token with --setup-token. Claude Code shows an address, which you open in a browser on any machine.
