When you approve the login there, the browser shows a code, which you paste back at Claude Code’s prompt, so devvm forwards no port. The VM uses the login at once, and every other VM with Claude Code gets it from its next launch (how). When the login ends without a new login in the store, such as when Ctrl-C ends Claude Code’s login in the VM, devvm says so and fails. Run --setup-token in a terminal, because claude setup-token draws on one and shows nothing without it, and devvm warns when there’s none (how the login gets a terminal).
devvm keeps one Claude Code login, either your subscription’s login or a Claude Code token, and the newest replaces the other, so every VM uses the account you logged in to last:
Your subscription’s login, from devvm agent login claude or a claude /login that you run in a VM yourself, goes in devvm’s agent store, in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json, only yours to read. The VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json holds placeholders, with no refresh token and an expiry in 2099, so Claude Code in the VM never refreshes the login itself. The VM’s proxy puts the login into the VM’s requests to api.anthropic.com and to mcp-proxy.anthropic.com, the host of your claude.ai connectors, and refreshes it on this machine when it’s due, through the company proxy when config.toml names one. devvm keeps only a login that can use Claude’s models and can’t make API keys, so a login to an Anthropic Console account, which Claude Code uses to make an API key, fails in a VM, and no API key reaches it. Only a VM that has Claude Code can log it in. A Claude Code token, from devvm agent login claude --setup-token or a claude setup-token that you run in a VM yourself, goes with the other secrets. You can also save one with devvm secret set claude and paste the token that claude setup-token printed on another machine (sk-ant-oat01-…), not the code the browser shows. devvm neither saves nor sends a Claude Code token that isn’t a setup token. Every VM with Claude Code gets the token in its environment as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, holding a placeholder of its own, and its proxy puts the token into its requests. When you set up a token in a VM, claude setup-token prints that VM’s placeholder, not the token, because devvm already saved it. A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s own environment on this machine wins over both, as it does in Claude Code, so VMs get that token, and devvm agent login claude warns you when it’s set. With your subscription’s login, and only with it, a VM can use your claude.ai connectors, and your claude.ai connectors says how to stop that. Anthropic doesn’t document the requests that Claude Code’s login sends, so devvm follows the ones Claude Code sends today, and a new Claude Code release can change them. When a login in a VM stops working, run devvm agent login claude again, or save a Claude Code token instead.
data.claude-codes-plugins#Claude Code’s plugi:
Claude Code writes into its plugins folder as it runs, for each plugin’s data, for the plugins you install and for its marketplaces’ updates, so each VM’s ~/.claude/plugins is its own folder, on the VM’s disk. The store’s ~/.claude/plugins is mounted read-only and linked at ~/.claude/plugins-seed, and Claude Code reads it as its seed, a plugins folder it never writes. Every shell in the VM names both for Claude Code, with CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR (how). What that means in a VM:
A plugin in the store loads when enabledPlugins in ~/.claude/settings.json turns it on, as it does on this machine, and Claude Code keeps its data in the VM’s own ~/.claude/plugins/data. A plugin you install in the VM goes into the VM’s own folder, and only that VM has it until you save it. The save copies the plugins you installed and their marketplaces into the store, and it never takes a plugin out of the store, so remove one in the store’s folder yourself, or import your machine’s plugins again. Claude Code doesn’t update the store’s marketplaces in a VM, and claude plugin marketplace update refuses them, so update a marketplace on this machine and run devvm agent import claude again. Neither devvm agent import nor devvm agent save copies what is each machine’s own, such as each plugin’s data, and an export of the VM’s history leaves out the VM’s plugins folder. When the store holds such entries, as an import by devvm 0.1.0 left there, a VM’s start takes them out of the store and warns once, naming them, and leaves your own folder as it is. When devvm can’t take them out, or the store’s ~/.claude/plugins is a link or below one, a VM with Claude Code doesn’t start until that folder is one of its own that holds only known_marketplaces.json, marketplaces and cache (how). claude plugin list # in the VM: the store's plugins and the VM's own
data.codex-and-opencode-logins#Codex and open:
You log Codex and opencode in from inside a VM, with devvm agent login, and devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with that agent:
devvm agent login codex # log Codex in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine devvm agent login opencode # log opencode in with its Codex login, the same way On every network tier, the VM’s auth.json holds placeholders, and its proxy holds the real API keys and logins, so when the agent in the VM stops getting answers, the proxy’s own log, proxy.log in ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/, may say that refreshing a login failed or that you’re no longer logged in that way. To log in again, run devvm agent login codex or devvm agent login opencode in the VM’s folder, which also gives that VM the new login’s placeholders, and the other VMs get them on their next launch. Some logins stay on this machine, and devvm names each at every launch (how):
Codex’s other logins, such as a personal access token or an Amazon Bedrock key, so to use Codex in a VM, log in with ChatGPT or an OpenAI API key (logging in with devvm agent login). opencode’s other entries, such as another provider’s API key or an OAuth login, which the VM gets without its key or its tokens. To use an OAuth login’s provider in the VM, log in to it with an API key on this machine and import the login again. Claude Code’s account fields in ~/.claude.json other than the ones it writes there today. To give the VM one provider’s API key as it is, such as a local model server’s that the VM’s proxy can’t put in, list the provider under opencode in config.toml’s [pass-keys] table (config.toml), as you would for pi. The provider is its entry’s name in opencode’s auth.json, such as ollama. Every VM with opencode then gets that entry whole, its metadata included, and opencode 2 in the VM imports it into its database too, and devvm says so at each launch. It applies only to entries with an API key, because a VM never gets a login’s tokens, and only to providers whose keys the proxy doesn’t put in, because a key the proxy puts in is always its placeholder:
[pass-keys] opencode = ["ollama"] So when opencode in a VM can’t reach a provider whose key works on this machine, such as a local model server’s, and devvm’s warning at launch names that provider, add it to [pass-keys] and run devvm in the folder again.
data.copied-files#Copied files:
Before devvm sends a copied file, it shows the file’s path on this machine and asks, [y/N], because the clipboard can name any file of yours, such as a key in ~/.ssh that you didn’t mean to copy. Answer no and nothing is sent. An image or a PDF is sent without a question, because it’s only what you copied. devvm sends a copied file under a name of its own that keeps only the file’s extension, when it’s letters and digits alone and at most 16 of them, so my shot (1).png becomes paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png, and Makefile becomes paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01 (why).
It sends one file at a time, and it refuses:
several files; a folder; a file with a symbolic link anywhere in its path, your own included, because a link the VM planted in the project folder could point at a file of yours. The only links devvm follows are the system’s own, which root owns, such as macOS’s /tmp, so copy the file from the folder it’s really in. devvm paste --send-file answers the question for a file in the project folder, which it sends without asking, as a script must, because the VM can read that folder already. It doesn’t answer for the rest:
A file anywhere else is still asked about, so only you can send it, at a terminal. A file whose path goes through a symbolic link is asked about too, even through one of the system’s that devvm follows, because the file may not be where its path says. A clone VM’s files, because a clone VM, made with --clone, doesn’t mount the folder. Where devvm can’t ask, such as without a terminal, it sends nothing, and it names --send-file for a file in the folder, the file and the folder for one outside it, and the file for one reached through a link. So don’t bind devvm paste --send-file to a hotkey to send files from outside the project, because a hotkey has no terminal to ask in, and devvm refuses those files.
data.copies#Copies: devvm copies the store’s files into the VM’s home on every launch, over the VM’s own. On every network tier, the copies of the logins and settings files have your secrets taken out, and the VM’s proxy puts them into requests instead (agents’ logins and settings). devvm merges the store’s .claude.json into the VM’s own, so servers added in the VM stay, and it merges Claude Code’s login into the VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json, so MCP servers’ logins made in the VM also stay. It writes devvm-redacted in place of each secret in the settings files, names what it replaced in each file, and names each file it didn’t copy (what it takes out).
data.cursor-cli-login#Cursor CLI login:
Cursor’s CLI runs in the VM as cursor-agent, or agent, its other name. You log it in once, from inside any VM that has it, and devvm keeps the login on this machine for every VM with the CLI:
devvm agent login cursor devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and then runs cursor-agent login in the VM, on your terminal, with NO_OPEN_BROWSER=1, so the CLI prints an address rather than opening a browser in the VM. You open that address in a browser on any machine and approve the login, and the CLI waits for it, so devvm forwards no port. The VM’s proxy saves the login as Cursor’s API hands it to the CLI, in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/cursor/.config/cursor/auth.json, only yours to read, and the CLI in the VM gets placeholders. A cursor-agent login that you run in a VM yourself is saved in the same way, and every VM with the CLI gets the login from its next launch.
Cursor’s CLI never refreshes a login, so devvm doesn’t either. When the login expires, the proxy puts nothing in, and its own log says to log in again with devvm agent login cursor. devvm doesn’t keep a Cursor API key, so devvm agent login cursor takes neither --api-key nor --device-code. devvm agent import cursor copies the CLI’s settings from ~/.cursor on this machine, which are cli-config.json, mcp.json and the rules and commands folders. On Linux it copies the CLI’s login from ~/.config/cursor/auth.json too. On macOS the CLI keeps its login in the Keychain, which devvm doesn’t read, so log in from a VM instead. The CLI would update itself in the VM, but every VM sets its channel to static in ~/.cursor/cli-config.json at each launch, which the CLI never updates on, so it stays the release that devvm pins. Cursor’s CLI has no setting that turns off its reports to Cursor, so its allowlist leaves out the host it sends its metrics to, api3.cursor.sh, which Cursor documents for its editor’s Tab requests, and the reports it sends to Cursor’s API go with the rest. That host is quiet, so its blocks never show in the VM. If Cursor Tab doesn’t work in a devvm cursor window on the allowlist tier, devvm network allow api3.cursor.sh lets it through. In a VM, Cursor’s CLI can’t install, update or remove plugins and marketplaces, change automations or cloud agents’ environments, start, fork, pin or merge the work of a cloud agent, or change your team, because each of those changes your Cursor account in a way that outlasts the VM and acts outside it. Do them from Cursor on your machine. Cursor’s agent store isn’t available in a VM either, so use it from Cursor on your machine. The CLI in a VM keeps its own chats without the store. Checking Amazon Bedrock keys doesn’t work in a VM either, as devvm doesn’t keep them. cursor-agent worker, which makes the machine a worker that runs your cloud agents’ work, doesn’t work in a VM, because the proxy never puts the login into its requests, and its host, api2direct.cursor.sh, isn’t among the Cursor hosts the allowlist tier lets through (how). The VM’s proxy puts the real login only into the requests that the CLI’s own methods make, and cuts a reply off where a token starts, but a token in a shape devvm doesn’t know could still reach the VM, so if you suspect that one did, log in again with devvm agent login cursor (how).
data.deleting-exports#Deleting exports:
After devvm rm, an export is the only copy of that VM’s history, so devvm keeps the exports until you ask it to delete them. devvm gc --history also deletes the exports in that folder, and devvm gc --history --older-than 30d deletes only those written 30 days ago or more. An export’s age counts from the date and time in its name, which is this machine’s local time when devvm wrote it, so across a change to or from daylight saving time an export reaches an age such as 30d an hour earlier or later, for --older-than and for the history.age retention setting alike. gc lists each one by its VM and date first, and in a terminal it asks. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own stay where they are. To delete only the older ones:
devvm gc --history --older-than 30d # also delete the exports written 30 days ago or more, after asking
data.deleting-pasted-files#Deleting pasted fi:
devvm paste rm # delete the files devvm paste left in the folder, after asking in a terminal devvm paste rm --force # delete them without asking, as a script must devvm never deletes a pasted file on its own, because Codex reads the image when you submit your message and pi when the model calls read, which may be some time after the paste. devvm paste rm deletes only the files devvm paste named, and nothing else in the folder, so a paste-dir of your own, such as /home/USER/pastes where USER is your user in the VM, can hold other files. The VM’s /tmp is emptied when the VM boots, so with the default folder the files are gone after a restart anyway. With a paste-dir of your own, they stay, and a command that starts a stopped VM and opens its shell offers to delete them, [y/N], once the VM is set up. Those commands are:
devvm and devvm restart; devvm tools, devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update; devvm layer add and devvm layer rm; devvm update; devvm clone on and devvm clone off. Without a terminal, devvm keeps the files and says nothing, and if deleting them fails, it warns you and opens the shell anyway. Commands that start a VM without opening its shell, such as devvm code and devvm agent save, don’t ask, so run devvm paste rm when you want the files gone.
data.devvm-history-json#devvm history –json:
devvm history --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the exports has its file, its vm, the VM’s folder, which is "" when devvm has no record of it, the date devvm wrote it in RFC 3339 with this machine’s time zone, and its size in bytes.
{ "version": 1, "exports": [ { "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/exports/devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c-20261001-120000.tar.gz", "vm": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c", "folder": "/Users/you/code/website", "date": "2026-10-01T12:00:00+02:00", "size": 1048576 } ] }
data.devvm-paste-json#devvm paste –json:
devvm paste --json does the same and prints what it sent as one object, with "version": 1 first. It has whether anything was sent, which is false when you answered no about a file, the VM, and the file’s path in it ("" when nothing was sent). Then its kind (image, pdf or file), an image’s or a PDF’s type (image/png, image/jpeg, image/gif, image/webp or application/pdf, and "" for a file), and a copied file’s source, its path on this machine ("" otherwise). Last come its size in bytes, and whether the path was copied to the clipboard:
{"version": 1, "sent": true, "vm": "devvm-website-3f9a1c2b4d5e6f", "path": "/tmp/devvm-paste/paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png", "kind": "image", "type": "image/png", "source": "", "bytes": 48213, "copied": true}
data.devvms-agent-store#devvm’s agent store:
devvm keeps the agents’ settings and logins on this machine in a store of its own, and every VM with an agent gets that agent’s settings and logins from there. devvm never reads the agents’ own files in your home folder for a VM, such as ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode or ~/.pi/agent, so a VM gets the same settings and logins whether or not this machine has the agent. The one command that reads those files is devvm agent import, which copies them into the store when you run it, and devvm agent save copies the settings you changed in a VM into the store.
The store has two folders for each agent, and each one holds the agent’s files at the same paths below it as the agent keeps them in a home folder:
Settings go in ~/.config/devvm/agents//, such as ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/settings.json and ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/skills. You can edit these files and make or delete these folders yourself, and a VM gets the change on its next launch, as mounts and copies describe. Keep every folder from ~/.config/devvm/agents down a real folder, because devvm agent import and devvm agent save never write the store through a link. When a link is on the path to what they’d write, they fail and name it before they change anything. Logins go in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins//, such as ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/codex/.codex/auth.json and ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude.json, and so does a login that you make inside a VM, such as Codex’s (Codex and opencode logins) or Claude Code’s in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/claude/.claude/.credentials.json (Claude Code login). Only you can read them, because devvm makes each agent’s logins folder yours alone (mode 700) and each login file mode 600. On macOS, devvm keeps each agent’s logins folder out of Time Machine’s backups. Each VM gets its agents’ settings and logins from the store, but never your history. Transcripts, sessions and databases aren’t in the store, and each VM’s own stay in that VM. Before you leave an agent running unattended, read staying safe and rogue agents.
The agent store and a VMdevvm agent import copies the agents' files from your home folder into devvm's agent store, but never your history. The store's settings folders are mounted into each VM read-only, and its settings files and logins are copied in on every launch, without your secrets. devvm agent save brings changed copies back after a diff and a yes. Each VM's own history goes to a .tar.gz on this machine with devvm history export or devvm rm, and comes back with devvm history import, or with yes when a new VM offers it.The VM devvm's agent store devvm agent import,never your history mountedread-only copied on everylaunch, withoutyour secrets devvm agent save,after a diff and a yes devvm history export,devvm rm devvm history import,or yes when a new VMoffers it the agents' filesin your home folder settings folders:skills, plugins… settings filesand logins linked into ~ copies in ~ its own history a .tar.gzon this machine Each row lists the agent’s paths in the VM’s home, and the store keeps each one at the same path below the agent’s settings or logins folder:
Mounted read-only, linked into ~ Copied in on every launch claude ~/.claude/{skills,agents,commands,output-styles}, and the store’s ~/.claude/plugins at ~/.claude/plugins-seed (Claude Code’s plugins) ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and from the logins ~/.claude.json (merged, only its settings, account state and MCP servers) codex ~/.codex/{prompts,skills} ~/.codex/{config.toml,AGENTS.md}, and from the logins ~/.codex/auth.json opencode the subfolders of ~/.config/opencode (not node_modules) the files in ~/.config/opencode (not lock files, .gitignore, .DS_Store or its service’s settings), and from the logins ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json pi ~/.pi/agent/{extensions,skills,prompts,themes} ~/.pi/agent/{settings.json,keybindings.json,models.json,mcp.json,AGENTS.md,SYSTEM.md,APPEND_SYSTEM.md}, and from the logins ~/.pi/agent/auth.json
data.history#History:
Each VM’s transcripts and sessions stay in that VM. devvm history export [FILE] saves them, and devvm rm saves them before it deletes a VM that has an agent. The export is a .tar.gz of the agents’ history in the VM, ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode, ~/.local/state/opencode, ~/.pi/agent/sessions and ~/.cursor/chats, written to FILE or to ~/.local/share/devvm/exports/--.tar.gz. An export in that folder gets a --.folder file beside it, which names the VM’s project folder and the VM’s network tier when devvm wrote the export. The agents’ logins are never in an export, and neither is the key that every machine paired with the VM’s opencode trusts. An export holds at most 2 GiB (what an export holds). The commands:
devvm history # list the exports devvm saved devvm history export # save this folder's VM's agents' history devvm history export ~/backup.tgz # or save it to a file of your own devvm history import # put this folder's newest export into its VM devvm history lists the exports in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, oldest first, in a table with a header. It shows each export’s file, the VM it’s of, that VM’s folder, the date and time devvm wrote it, and its size, with - for a folder devvm has no record of. Exports you wrote to a FILE of your own aren’t listed, and devvm history changes nothing and starts no VM.
data.importing-from-this-machine#Importing fr:
When you already use an agent on this machine, devvm agent import copies its settings and logins from your home folder into the store, so your VMs get them. With no argument it imports every agent that your home folder has files of, and devvm agent import claude codex imports only the agents you name:
devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins into the store devvm agent import codex # copy only Codex's devvm agent import --force # replace what the store has without asking devvm agent import --follow-links # copy what links out of the agents' folders lead to as well devvm says which agents it imported and where, and an agent you named that your home folder has nothing of gets a warning. What the import copies and asks:
The import copies only the paths in the table above, so it never copies your history or ~/.claude/.credentials.json (what it copies). From ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, so your API key and your per-project entries stay out of the store. From ~/.claude/plugins it copies only the marketplaces, their records and the plugins’ cache, never what is this machine’s own, such as each plugin’s data. devvm reads each agent’s settings inside the agent’s own folder, such as ~/.claude. A link to a file inside the folder becomes a copy of that file when that file is one of the settings that the import copies, such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. devvm leaves out a link to anything else inside the folder, such as your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json or a plugin’s data, with a warning that names where it leads. It does the same with a link to a folder inside it and a link that leads nowhere, and it always leaves out a login file that’s a link, with a warning. A link that leads out of the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, is copied only when you allow it (links out of an agent’s folder). One import copies at most 20,000 files, folders and links, 128 MiB, and 16 MiB in one file, of each agent’s own folder, at most 128 folders deep. When the folder holds more, devvm imports nothing and names the folder, so take out what it doesn’t need, such as a plugin’s build files, and import again. An import that fails leaves the store’s settings and logins as they were, so run it again (how). That holds whether it fails while it reads, such as at a file that changed meanwhile, or while it puts them in place, such as at a login it can’t save. In the rare case that putting the store back also fails, devvm names the stores it couldn’t put back and the folders that hold what it moved aside, so copy what you need from those before you import again, which deletes them. On a Mac, whose volume ignores case by default, a file whose name differs from the store’s only in case, such as foo.md where the store has Foo.md, replaces the store’s file, which keeps its name. Two names that differ only in case, which your home folder can have only on a volume that tells case apart, would be one file in the store, so devvm imports nothing and names both. Runs that write the store take turns. While another devvm agent import or devvm agent save writes it, or a start cleans it, devvm says it’s waiting and goes on once that one is done. When a VM’s project folder is inside an agent’s folder, such as a skill you work on in ~/.claude/skills, or holds one, such as ~/.pi, devvm warns that the VM can change the settings it imports for every VM, and each launch of such a VM also warns (project folders devvm refuses). Keep such a project somewhere else unless you trust that VM. When the path to an agent’s folder passes through a link in a VM’s project folder that leads elsewhere, devvm leaves that agent’s folder out with a warning. A VM whose state devvm can’t read gets a warning that names the file, because devvm can’t tell where its project folder is, and devvm doctor says what’s wrong with it. That VM’s project folder could hold a link, so until the state is fixed, devvm leaves out, with a warning that names the state, every link out of an agent’s folder, and every agent’s folder or login whose path leads through a link, such as an agent’s folder that’s a link to your dotfiles. When the store already has settings or a login of an agent you import, devvm asks in a terminal whether to replace them, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and names --force, which replaces them without asking. An agent whose settings aren’t in your home folder keeps the store’s settings, and one without a login there keeps the store’s login. On macOS, Claude Code keeps its own login in the Keychain, and devvm neither reads it nor copies it. You log Claude Code in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login claude, and every VM with Claude Code gets that login (Claude Code login). When this machine’s opencode is version 2 or later, devvm saves the API key of each provider, and your OpenAI login when you made it with one of opencode’s Codex logins, the browser or the headless one. Any other login is left out with a warning that names it, such as opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT, whose tokens a VM can’t use, or another provider’s OAuth login, and you log in from a VM instead, with devvm agent login opencode (logging in with devvm agent login). When opencode auth export fails, the import fails too, and the store keeps the login it had.
data.importing-history#Importing history:
devvm history import # put this folder's newest export into its VM devvm history import ~/backup.tar.gz # or an export of your own devvm history import [FILE] puts an export back into this folder’s VM, so the agents’ transcripts and sessions carry over when you delete a VM and make it again. Without FILE, it imports the newest export in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports that devvm saved for this folder, going by the .folder file beside each one, and it never picks an export made for another folder. With FILE, it imports that .tar.gz, such as one you saved with devvm history export FILE. devvm starts a stopped VM for the import, as it does for an export, and the import works on every VM, whatever its base (how):
When devvm makes a new VM that has an agent, and it saved an export for the same folder before, it offers that export. In a terminal it asks whether to import it into the new VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, it doesn’t ask, and it says which export it found and that devvm history import in the folder puts it into the VM. devvm imports the export once the VM has started and before its setup, and if the import fails, devvm warns and makes the VM anyway, so you can run devvm history import later.
An export holds what a VM wrote, so devvm treats it as untrusted, and when it comes from a VM on a less strict tier than the VM you import it into, devvm warns you before it imports. It treats an export with no tier recorded, or a FILE elsewhere, as if it came from an open VM. When an export holds a path outside the agents’ history folders, devvm imports nothing.
The import leaves out what devvm puts in the VM itself. That’s the agents’ logins, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, with the old VM’s own MCP servers’ logins in it, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin. It’s also ~/.claude.json, whose copy in the old VM held that VM’s own placeholders, and every agent’s mounted folders and copied files, which the new VM’s setup links and copies from devvm’s agent store.
The import also leaves out the old VM’s opencode identity, as an export does: opencode’s ~/.local/state/opencode/machine, with the key that every machine paired with the old VM’s opencode trusts, and its service.json, or service-.json for another channel’s opencode, and pty, which hold the password of the old VM’s opencode service and the access tokens of its terminals’ daemons. The new VM’s opencode makes its own. The import also leaves out the project plugins you approved in opencode’s native client, plugin-approvals.json and plugin-staged, so opencode asks again before it runs one.
opencode’s sessions come without what opencode would act on without asking. Neither an export nor an import keeps:
automations, whose shell commands run on their schedule without asking again the requests you said always to allow subagents’ jobs and queued messages a project’s commands opencode’s git repositories and worktrees No session resumes its turn on its own, and each session keeps only its deny and ask rules (what an export holds). In the new VM, make again any automation you want, and opencode asks again before the requests you had always allowed. devvm rm deletes opencode’s worktrees with the VM, so it asks before their uncommitted changes go (opencode’s worktrees).
A file or folder the VM already has stays as it is, so importing into a VM that has history of its own adds the export’s files without replacing any of its own.
data.links-out-of-an-agents-folder#Links out:
When your settings live elsewhere, such as in a dotfiles repo with links into ~/.claude, devvm copies what those links lead to only when you allow it, because every VM with the agent gets what’s in the store. In a terminal, devvm names each link and where it leads, and asks whether to copy them, with no as the default. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, it leaves them out with a warning that names --follow-links. You allow them for one run with the flag, or for good with config.toml’s follow-links, which lists the folders whose links devvm follows without asking:
devvm agent import --follow-links # copy what the links lead to, naming each, without asking # in ~/.config/devvm/config.toml: follow links into these folders without asking follow-links = ["~/dotfiles"] What devvm copies through a link, and what it refuses:
Copies, never links. A linked file becomes a file in the store, and a linked folder, such as a skill that ~/.claude/skills/x links to, becomes a folder of copies. Each import copies them again, and takes a copy out once its link is gone. Only inside the folder you allowed. devvm reads what a link leads to through a follow-links folder, or with --follow-links through the linked folder itself, or the linked file’s own folder. A link inside a linked folder becomes a copy of the file it leads to only when that file is inside the same folder, and any other is left out with a warning. Never your secrets or devvm’s own files. devvm never follows a link to your home folder or a folder that holds it, to devvm’s own folders, to ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/Library/Keychains, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.netrc, ~/.config/gh, ~/.docker or ~/.kube, or to an agent’s logins or history, such as ~/.codex, nor into one of these or to a folder that holds one. It leaves such a link out with a warning, even with --follow-links. A follow-links folder must be safe as a whole. A folder that is, holds or is inside one of those places fails the import, naming it, so name a folder inside it instead, such as ~/dotfiles/skills when ~/.claude is a link to ~/dotfiles/claude. Write each folder as an absolute path or one that starts with ~/, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). A VM’s project folder gets a warning. When a link leads into the folder of one of your VMs, --clone VMs included, devvm names that VM and warns that it can change what every VM’s agent reads from the next import on. Follow such links only when you trust that VM. A link that passes through a link in a VM’s project folder to a place outside that folder is left out with a warning naming the VM, whatever allows it, because that VM chose where it leads. While a VM’s state can’t be read, devvm can’t tell where that VM’s project folder is, so it leaves out every link, with a warning that names the state. At most 20,000 files and folders, 128 MiB, and 16 MiB in one file, for all the links of one import together. A link whose files would pass that is left out whole, with a warning. Settings files and folders keep their kind. A link that is one of an agent’s settings files, such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, must lead to a file, and one that is a settings folder, such as ~/.claude/skills, must lead to a folder. Any other is left out with a warning. Without either, two layouts keep your settings in a dotfiles repo and import them as they are. You can link the agent’s whole folder, such as ~/.config/opencode, to a folder in the repo, and devvm then reads that folder as the agent’s folder, so its links to files inside it become copies. Or your dotfiles manager can write real files rather than links, as chezmoi does by default, so your home folder has files that devvm copies.
data.logging-in-with-devvm-agent-login#Loggin:
devvm agent login logs Codex or opencode in from inside this folder’s VM, so this machine never needs either agent, and devvm’s agent store keeps the login for every VM with that agent. Claude Code’s login is devvm agent login claude (Claude Code login), and pi’s is an API key alone (pi logins):
devvm agent login codex # log Codex in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine devvm agent login opencode --device-code # log opencode in with a code, in a browser on any machine devvm agent login codex --api-key # save Codex's OpenAI API key, asking for it devvm agent login codex --api-key --stdin < key.txt # save it from a file or a pipe devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider anthropic # save opencode's Anthropic API key devvm starts the folder’s VM first if it’s stopped, as devvm host does, and the VM must have the agent, which devvm tools add codex gives it. Then devvm logs the agent in one of three ways:
In a browser on this machine, by default: codex login for Codex, and opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-browser, opencode’s Codex browser login, for opencode. The agent shows an address, which you open in a browser on this machine, and devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455 to the VM while the login runs (how). When another program on this machine has port 1455, devvm refuses and names --device-code. With --device-code, the agent shows a code instead, which you type into a browser on any machine, and devvm forwards nothing. Codex’s device code login is codex login --device-auth, which your ChatGPT account’s security settings must allow, and opencode’s is opencode auth login openai --method chatgpt-headless, its Codex device code login. With --api-key, devvm asks for the API key without showing it, or reads it from a line of input with --stdin, and saves it in the store itself, so the key never goes into the VM. Codex’s key is an OpenAI key, and it replaces Codex’s ChatGPT login in the store, as codex login --with-api-key does. opencode’s key is for the provider that --provider names, by one of the IDs in API keys the proxy puts in, and the store keeps opencode’s other providers beside it. opencode’s Anthropic login is an API key, because opencode itself has no other way to log in to Anthropic. opencode’s Claude Agent provider uses Claude Code’s own login instead, so it works in a VM that has Claude Code too, with the login that devvm agent login claude saves. When the agent logs in, the VM’s proxy saves the login in the store, and the agent in the VM gets placeholders, as the next section describes. devvm then says what the store saved and the account’s email, and the VM uses the login at once. When the login ends without a new login in the store, for example because you chose another way to log in, devvm says so and fails, and devvm network log shows each login the proxy saved.
data.logins-made-in-a-vm#Logins made in a VM: A login that Codex or opencode makes in a VM, whether devvm agent login runs it or you run it yourself, is saved in devvm’s store, and every VM with that agent gets it from its next launch. A login that shows a code to type into a browser works in a VM as it is, but opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT doesn’t, so choose one of opencode’s Codex logins instead, as devvm agent login opencode does (how a VM’s logins are saved). On the open tier, a program that goes around the VM’s proxy gets the login’s tokens itself, and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM).
data.mcp-servers-logins#MCP servers’ logins:
You log Claude Code in to an MCP server that asks for a login inside the VM, the way you would on this machine:
/mcp # in Claude Code in the VM: pick the server and log in to it Claude Code keeps these logins in the VM’s ~/.claude/.credentials.json, beside the Claude login, and they’re the VM’s own (how):
They stay in the VM. Each launch replaces only the Claude login in that file and keeps the rest, so a login you make lasts across launches. They hold real tokens, which code in the VM can read, and they never reach this machine, another VM, devvm agent save or an export of the VM’s history. They don’t come along when devvm makes the VM again, such as to add a layer, so you log in to those servers again there (what a VM made again keeps).
data.mounts#Mounts:
devvm mounts the store’s settings folders that exist when it creates the VM read-only, at the same path as in the store on this machine, and links them from the VM’s home. This machine enforces read-only, so even root in the VM can’t write to them (links and paths in them).
devvm mounts each folder whole, whatever the VM’s network tier, so the VM reads every file in it, a .env or a key file in a plugin’s folder included, and the git config of a private plugin marketplace whose URL holds a password. devvm takes no secrets out of these folders, because they hold plugins, skills and their scripts that the agent runs as they are. So keep secrets out of these folders, as you keep them out of the project folder (why devvm mounts them whole). When devvm agent import or devvm agent save copies a Claude Code marketplace that has a password or an access token in its clone’s git config, or in its source in known_marketplaces.json, it copies it as it is and warns, naming the marketplace, the store’s file and the keys that hold it, never the credential (what it checks). Take the credential out of that file and of the marketplace on this machine, and keep it in a credential helper instead. devvm doesn’t mount a folder whose path has a comma, on any backend, and it warns you. When you make or delete one of these folders in the store later, by hand or with devvm agent import, devvm notices on the VM’s next launch and names the folder. A VM’s mounts change only when it starts, so a stopped VM gets the new mounts as the launch starts it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, in the one question that covers every change waiting for the VM’s next start, and because the mounts are among those changes, the default answer is yes (restarting). If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the mounts change when the VM next starts, for example with devvm restart:
devvm restart # give a running VM the store's new folders now
data.on-linux#On Linux:
devvm reads and writes the clipboard with wl-paste and wl-copy in a Wayland session, which WAYLAND_DISPLAY names, and with xclip in an X11 session, which DISPLAY names. It tells you which one is missing, and installs nothing itself, so install wl-clipboard or xclip with your distribution’s package manager:
sudo apt install wl-clipboard # or xclip for X11; dnf, pacman and zypper have both devvm looks for them only in the system’s folders, never elsewhere on your PATH (which folders, and why). Run devvm paste from a terminal in your desktop session, because without either variable there’s no clipboard to read. If WAYLAND_DISPLAY or DISPLAY names a session that’s over, as in a tmux window left from an earlier login, devvm tells you that wl-paste or xclip failed and what it said, rather than that the clipboard is empty. Copying the path leaves wl-copy or xclip running until you copy something else, because a Linux clipboard’s contents live in the program that copied them.
data.opencodes-service#opencode’s service:
opencode’s background service, which opencode starts when it needs one, asks for a password when you sign in to it, and each VM’s opencode makes its own the first time its service starts. To sign in to a VM’s service, such as from opencode’s app, read that VM’s password in the VM:
opencode service get password # in the VM: its service's password, made now if it has none opencode service set password PASSWORD # in the VM: choose another, which stops its service devvm never copies this machine’s opencode service settings into its agent store or a VM. They’re service.json in ~/.config/opencode, or service-.json for another channel’s opencode, and they hold this machine’s service password and, with remote access on, the secret route that the service is served on. So devvm agent import and devvm agent save leave them out, and each VM’s service settings stay in that VM. When devvm’s agent store holds them, a VM’s start takes them out and warns once, and each VM’s setup takes out any copy of them that devvm made, so the VM’s opencode makes its own password (how). A service that’s running keeps the password it started with, so after that warning, restart each running VM that has opencode: devvm restart # in the VM's folder: its opencode service starts again with a password of its own
data.opencodes-worktrees#opencode’s worktrees:
devvm rm # show opencode's worktrees' uncommitted changes, then ask devvm rm --no-worktree-check # delete the VM without checking them, losing those changes devvm update --clean-home # a remake that starts from the image's home folder checks them too opencode makes its worktrees in ~/.local/share/opencode/worktree in the VM, and an export leaves that folder out, so their uncommitted changes go with the VM. Before devvm rm deletes the VM, and before a command that makes it again with --clean-home gives it the image’s home folder, devvm checks each of those worktrees, starting a stopped VM for the check as a launch does. It asks before what it finds is lost, only in a terminal, so --force never answers. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm refuses and keeps the VM, and when only the worktrees have work, the refusal names --no-worktree-check, which warns and goes ahead without the check.
devvm asks about:
Uncommitted changes: it lists the first 20 in all, under each worktree’s path. A detached HEAD’s commits that no branch, tag or remote-tracking branch in the VM has. To keep them, run git switch -c NAME in that worktree first. A worktree that git can’t read, such as one whose entry your project’s repository pruned, because it may hold changes devvm can’t see. More than 100 worktrees, of which devvm checks the first 100. To keep the work, commit it in the worktree, which puts it in your project’s repository for a VM that mounts the folder, or in the clone, whose branches devvm rm offers to fetch, for a --clone VM (deleting the VM). For a --clone VM, the clone’s check and the worktrees’ share one question, and when the clone has work too, the refusal tells you to run the command in a terminal, as the clone’s own does. When reading the worktrees fails, or the VM doesn’t start for the check, devvm keeps the VM and names --no-worktree-check. A command that keeps the VM’s home folder, such as devvm update without --clean-home, keeps the worktrees too, so it doesn’t check them (how devvm checks).
data.pasting-images#Pasting images:
An agent in the VM can’t see this machine’s clipboard, so an image you copied, such as a screenshot, gets to it through devvm paste, which sends the image into the VM and copies its path there for you to paste:
Copy an image on this machine, such as a screenshot, copy pages in a PDF viewer such as Preview, or copy a file in Finder or your file manager. In a terminal on this machine, run devvm paste in the project folder. devvm says where the image is in the VM, such as /tmp/devvm-paste/paste-20261109-153012-7f3a9c01.png, and puts that path on your clipboard. If putting it there fails, devvm warns you and still says where the image is, so you can paste that path yourself. Paste the path into the agent with your terminal’s paste shortcut, which is Cmd+V on macOS and usually Ctrl+Shift+V on Linux. Ctrl+V on its own asks the agent to read the VM’s clipboard, and the VM has none. Claude Code, Codex and opencode attach an image whose path you paste, and pi reads it with its read tool. The VM must be running, because devvm paste is for an agent that runs in it, and devvm refuses a stopped one.
devvm paste # send what you copied, asking first about a copied file devvm paste --send-file # send a file in the project folder without asking, as a script must devvm paste --json # the same, and print what it sent devvm paste rm # delete the files devvm paste left in the VM, after asking
data.pi-logins#pi logins:
pi in a VM uses API keys that devvm keeps on this machine, for the providers whose keys the VM’s proxy puts in, which API keys the proxy puts in lists. You save one with devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider PROVIDER, because pi’s login always takes both flags, or you import the API keys in your own ~/.pi/agent/auth.json with devvm agent import pi:
devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider anthropic # save pi's Anthropic API key, asking for it devvm agent import pi # copy pi's settings and auth.json from this machine The login needs a VM with pi in this folder, which it gives its copy of the login at once, and every other VM with pi gets it at its next launch. The VM gets a placeholder in place of each key, and devvm keeps pi’s other entries on this machine, such as a local model server’s API key, a key that’s a command for pi to run and a key that pi fills in from a variable, even for a provider whose key the proxy puts in, and warns you about each (how). To give the VM one provider’s API key as it is, such as a local model server’s that the VM’s proxy can’t put in, list the provider under pi in config.toml’s [pass-keys] table (config.toml). Every VM with pi then gets that entry whole, its env included, and devvm says so at each launch. It applies only to entries with an API key, because a VM never gets a login’s tokens, and only to providers whose keys the proxy doesn’t put in, because a key the proxy puts in is always its placeholder:
[pass-keys] pi = ["ollama"] pi’s own logins with an account, which /login and pi auth login make for a subscription, such as Claude’s, ChatGPT’s or GitHub Copilot’s, aren’t among the logins devvm keeps, so save the provider’s API key instead. Don’t log pi in with an account inside a VM either, because the VM’s proxy would save it as another agent’s login or refuse it (pi’s logins).
data.pis-settings#pi’s settings:
Two of pi’s settings act differently in a VM:
The VM’s copy of pi’s settings.json leaves out three keys, because each would undo what devvm sets in the VM, and devvm names the ones it left out. httpProxy would send pi around the VM’s proxy, sessionDir would keep pi’s sessions outside ~/.pi/agent/sessions, where history exports look for them, and selfUpdateCommand would run a command of the file’s on pi update. When devvm agent save pi saves the VM’s settings.json, its diff shows those keys as taken out, so save it only when you mean to drop them from the store’s copy too. When the store’s settings.json sets defaultProjectTrust to always, devvm warns you at each launch. That setting makes pi load a project folder’s own .pi extensions, settings and MCP servers without asking, and they run in the VM with pi, so set it to ask in devvm’s agent store unless you trust every project you open.
data.running-an-agent#Running an agent:
An agent runs where you start it, so you start it in the VM’s shell, not on this machine. On this machine, devvm opens the VM’s shell, and the VM’s prompt starts with (devvm):
~/some-project $ devvm (devvm) ~/some-project $ claude In the VM the agent sees only your project folder, and your agents’ settings from devvm’s agent store, which it gets read-only. Whatever it runs, such as a script a package installs, runs in the VM too. You don’t install any agent on this machine, because devvm installs each one in the VMs that have it. How devvm gives each agent its settings, logins and history is in how it works.
data.saving-a-vms-settings#Saving a VM’s sett:
When you change an agent’s settings in a VM, for example by installing a Claude Code plugin there with claude plugin install or /plugin, or by changing ~/.claude/settings.json, devvm agent save copies them into the store, so every VM with that agent gets them. With no argument it saves every agent that the folder’s VM has, and devvm agent save claude saves only the agents you name. devvm starts a stopped VM for it. It reads only the settings, never the logins or your history, treats everything the VM sends as untrusted, and puts your secrets back where the VM’s copies hold placeholders (how).
devvm agent save # show what changed in the VM's agents' settings, then save them devvm agent save codex # save only Codex's It reads at most 128 MiB from the VM, in at most 20,000 files, folders and links, none of the files larger than 16 MiB, at most 128 folders deep and in paths of at most 4,096 bytes. The VM sends only what the store keeps, as the table above lists, so opencode’s lock files, such as the bun.lock that its plugins’ installs write, stay in the VM. When the VM sends more, or sends a path outside the agents’ settings, devvm saves nothing. A save that fails partway leaves the store as it was.
For example, to give every VM a plugin that you install in one:
claude plugin install my-plugin@my-marketplace # in the VM: installs into the VM's own ~/.claude/plugins devvm agent save claude # on this machine, in the project folder: copies it into the store Before it saves anything, devvm shows what would change:
For each folder it lists the files it adds (A), changes (M) and removes (D), and then it shows a diff of each file it adds or changes against the store’s copy, with a line when a file’s mode changes. The diff shows the settings files and ~/.claude.json as a VM gets them, written out again with devvm-redacted in place of the values that look like secrets, so it never prints your secrets, and it says so when only those values or the file’s layout changed. Every character that a terminal wouldn’t show, such as a control character, a zero-width character or a character that reverses the text, appears in the diff as its code, such as \u{200b}, so a VM can’t hide a line from you. The diff names a binary file without showing it, and it shows a file of more than 1 MiB or 10,000 lines, and every line past the first 20,000 of the whole diff, only as a count. On a Mac, whose volume ignores case by default, a file whose name differs from the store’s only in case, such as foo.md where the store has Foo.md, is the store’s file, so the diff shows it as changed and the store keeps its name. Two names in the VM that differ only in case, such as A.md and a.md, would be one file in the store on a Mac, so once you say yes, devvm saves nothing and names both, and you rename one of them in the VM. Then devvm says that every VM with these agents runs the hooks, the MCP servers’ commands and the plugins you save, and it asks whether to save them, with no as the default. Read the diff before you answer, because a hook or a plugin that a rogue agent added in one VM runs in every VM once you save it. devvm agent save always asks, and no flag answers for you, so without a terminal, or with --no-input, it shows what would change and then refuses. What devvm doesn’t save:
A file where the VM changed what’s around a placeholder, which devvm leaves out with a warning, so make that change in the store’s file yourself. Anything, when the store changed after devvm showed what differs, as when you ran devvm agent import meanwhile, so run devvm agent save again to see what differs now.
data.setups-default-agents#Setup’s default ag: devvm setup chooses the agents that the list checks for every new VM, and that a new VM gets without a terminal. devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal and again in devvm setup’s questions, and devvm setup --agents claude,codex or devvm setup --agents none sets them without asking. They’re a setting for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents (devvm setup).
data.supported-agents#Supported agents:
A new VM gets an agent when you choose it as you customize the VM, or when you name it with --agents. A VM that exists gets one from devvm tools, which shows the same list with the VM’s agents already chosen, or from devvm tools add:
devvm # a new VM: customize it, then choose its agents in the list devvm --agents claude,codex # a new VM with Claude Code and Codex, without the list devvm tools # the VM that exists: choose its agents in the list devvm tools add opencode # the VM that exists: add opencode without the list In the VM, you run each agent by its name in the table, such as claude.
Name Agent What devvm adds Allowlist, on the allowlist and none tiers claude Claude Code the newest release, with its auto-update off, since the shared copy is read-only, and its telemetry off Anthropic’s API, Claude’s login, Claude Code’s downloads and claude.ai’s connectors: api.anthropic.com, claude.ai, downloads.claude.ai, platform.claude.com and mcp-proxy.anthropic.com codex Codex the newest release, with its analytics and metrics off unless your config sets them the OpenAI API and the ChatGPT login: api.openai.com, chatgpt.com and auth.openai.com opencode opencode the newest 2.x release, because opencode marks its 1.x releases as its latest on GitHub opencode’s own service and its model catalog: opencode.ai and models.opencode.ai pi pi the newest release, with its check for a newer pi and its install report off, and fd, which pi finds files with, in base pi’s model catalog: pi.dev cursor Cursor CLI the release devvm pins, run as cursor-agent or agent, with its self-update off through its static channel Cursor’s API, its agent’s hosts and its codebase indexing: api2.cursor.sh, api5.cursor.sh, *.api5.cursor.sh and repo42.cursor.sh opencode and pi talk to the model provider you choose, so on the allowlist tier you allow that provider’s API host yourself, such as devvm network allow api.anthropic.com (changing rules), unless devvm keeps the agent’s login or API key for that provider, because the VM’s proxy then allows its host. Claude Code’s telemetry hosts aren’t on its allowlist, because blocking them costs nothing. Every VM turns off each agent’s self-update and telemetry with the agent’s own variables, in every shell (each agent’s variables). pi’s releases are built for glibc alone, so a VM made --from an Alpine-based container image can’t have pi, and devvm refuses it there (shared tools and glibc). Every other agent runs on Alpine too. Agents are shared tools, like the toolchains, so you can combine them with any layers and with each other, as in devvm --tools node --agents claude,codex. devvm follows each agent’s newest release, because agents release several times a week, and devvm update or devvm tools update moves a VM to newer versions (adding and removing tools).
data.the-guide-in-every-vm#The guide in every:
Every VM has a guide to devvm for the agents in it, at /usr/share/doc/devvm/README.md, and devvm-help in the VM prints it:
devvm-help # in the VM: print the guide to devvm It tells an agent what a devvm VM is, how its network tiers and secrets work, where its installs go, and which commands to ask you to run on this machine, such as devvm network allow for a blocked host or devvm agent login for a login. The guide is the same in every VM, so it says nothing about the VM’s own tier, ports or layers, and nothing in the VM can change it for long (the guide). Ask your agent to read it, or to run devvm-help, when it doesn’t know where it’s running. devvm adds nothing about it to the agents’ instruction files.
data.the-paste-folder-and-your-agents-setting:
The files go into the VM’s paste folder, /tmp/devvm-paste unless config.toml’s paste-dir names another (the paste folder), and they keep their mode, 600, so only the VM’s user reads them. The folder is a fixed path so that you can allow it once in an agent’s settings. Claude Code refuses to read a path outside the project folder when its permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories setting is on, until you add the folder in Claude Code:
/add-dir /tmp/devvm-paste Or list it in permissions.additionalDirectories in your settings, which devvm’s agent store keeps for every VM, in ~/.config/devvm/agents/claude/.claude/settings.json:
{ "permissions": { "additionalDirectories": ["/tmp/devvm-paste"] } } Anything in the VM can read what you send, as it can read any file in the project folder, so paste nothing you wouldn’t put in the folder.
data.the-vms-setup#The VM’s setup:
Besides the agents’ config, every launch sets the VM up from this machine’s settings:
its hostname, which is the folder’s part of the VM’s name; the timezone (TZ, else this machine’s) and, when it’s UTF-8, the locale (LC_ALL, else LANG); git’s user.name and user.email, as git has them in the project folder; telemetry off where an environment variable can’t turn it off, which is Go’s, and Codex’s analytics and metrics; every agent’s environment variables, which turn off its self-update and its telemetry (supported agents); every toolchain’s environment variables, such as the ones that turn off .NET’s telemetry and send npm i -g into your home, and the folders where the toolchains’ global installs go, on the PATH (toolchains); (devvm) at the start of the prompt. On every network tier, the launch also installs the VM’s own CA and the next one, points apt, sudo, ssh, the docker layer’s Docker and the nix layer’s Nix at the proxy, and adds devvm-why, which shows what the proxy blocked lately. It also tells the agents, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail (inside the VM). The VM’s secrets go in ~/.config/devvm/env in the VM, which login shells read, and that file holds their placeholders.
data.what-devvm-paste-sends#What devvm paste:
devvm reads only an image, a PDF or a copied file’s reference from the clipboard, never text, so a password you copied never reaches it:
An image: PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, and on macOS also a TIFF, which many Mac apps copy, sent as a PNG. A PDF, such as pages you copied in Preview, sent as it is, as a .pdf file, because most models read PDFs. One copied file, after devvm asks you about it. Nothing over 64 MiB, whether it’s an image, a PDF or a file. devvm checks that an image’s or a PDF’s bytes are the type the clipboard claims (how). Text is never sent, so paste text, such as an error message, into the agent’s terminal yourself. The app you copied from hands over what you copied when devvm asks for it, and devvm waits for it at most 30 seconds, then stops waiting, sends nothing and says so, so copy it again, or wait until the app responds, then run devvm paste again. On macOS, devvm reads the clipboard of the session you’re logged in to, so run devvm paste in a terminal on that Mac, not over ssh.
What devvm gets depends on the app you copied from:
A browser’s Copy Image hands over a PNG, never the original JPEG, GIF or WebP, and Safari hands over a TIFF, which devvm makes a PNG, so an animated GIF arrives as one still frame. To send the original, save it and copy the saved file instead. A PDF viewer puts a picture of what you copied beside the PDF, and devvm sends the PDF, never the picture. When you copy a page’s thumbnail in Preview, Preview also puts a temporary file of its own on the clipboard, and devvm sends the PDF without asking about that file. Finder, on macOS, puts the copied file’s icon on the clipboard as an image beside the file, and devvm sends the file, not the icon. If the file is gone by the time you run devvm paste, devvm says so and sends nothing, rather than the icon. Text is never taken for a file, even when it’s a path, so copy the file itself in Finder. Photos puts a file of the Photos library beside a photo you copy, so devvm asks about that file, as it does about any copied file.

data: This page covers what works the same way in every command: the help, flags and their values, the questions devvm asks and what answers them beforehand, --json for scripts, and shell completion. Everyday commands lists the commands, and the CLI reference has every command with all its flags.
data.flags-and-values#Flags and values:
These rules hold for every command:
Each flag belongs to the commands that list it in their help, and only -h or --help, -v or --verbose and --no-input work with every command. -v shows the output of the commands devvm runs as they run (details), and --no-input makes devvm ask nothing (questions devvm asks). A flag can come before or after the command’s arguments, and options that take a value also work with an equals sign, such as --cpus=N. The options for a new VM, such as --tools and --cpus, are taken only by devvm. Another command given one of them, such as devvm ls --cpus 4, fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (what a new VM gets). When a flag or a setting can mean none or off, you write that as a word: devvm setup --features none, devvm --agents none, devvm ports none, devvm retention history.age=off and devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE --lifetime forever. devvm refuses an empty value, such as --features '', and an empty argument, so a blank never stands for none or for a default. Every duration is a whole number followed by a unit, which is m for minutes, h for hours, d for days or w for weeks, as in 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. That covers devvm gc --older-than, the retention settings’ ages and devvm ssh-agent add --lifetime, and only --lifetime also takes forever, for a key that devvm’s agent keeps until it ends.
data.help#Help:
devvm help COMMAND, devvm COMMAND --help and devvm COMMAND -h print a command’s help. It starts with a few sentences on what the command does, then its usage line and its examples, the most common first, each with a comment. Then come its commands, if it has any, and its flags, and the help ends with the address of the docs page that covers the command. devvm --help lists the commands in the groups that Everyday commands has, which are Your VM, Change your VM, Images, Disk space and This machine, with help under Additional Commands, and it ends with devvm’s issue tracker after its docs page.
devvm itself takes no word after it but a command’s name, so every word there is a command, and a layer may have any name a command has. When the word after devvm isn’t a command, devvm refuses it as a usage error. If the word names a toolchain, an agent or a layer, your own layers included, devvm points you to the flag that chooses it for a new VM, such as devvm --tools node for devvm node, and a word that joins several with + or a comma gets one line with each flag, such as devvm --tools node --agents claude for devvm node+claude. Any other word gets the closest command, such as devvm stop for devvm stpo. devvm stpo --help and devvm help stpo are refused the same way.
data.output-for-scripts#Output for scripts:
Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which prints what the command shows as one JSON object instead of a table or lines, so a script can read it. The page for each command lists its fields with an example, and every command’s JSON follows the same rules:
The object’s first field is "version": 1. A shape only ever gains fields. devvm adds new fields to version 1, and any other change to a shape, such as a field renamed, removed or given another type, comes with a new version. With --json, standard output gets only the JSON. devvm’s messages, such as warnings and notes, still go to standard error, as they do without it, and the JSON is never colored. A list with nothing in it is [], never null. Sizes are in bytes, unless a field’s name gives the unit, such as memory_gib. A field that doesn’t apply, such as a VM’s from when its base is Ubuntu’s cloud image, is left out. A command that shows a setting when you run it bare and changes the setting when you give it a value, such as devvm network or devvm size, only shows with --json. devvm refuses a value given with --json, such as devvm network open with --json, and changes nothing.
Command Its JSON devvm ls --json the project VMs devvm images --json the images and the shared tool images devvm tools --json this folder’s VM’s shared tools devvm size --json, devvm ports --json this folder’s VM’s size and ports, or with -g, new VMs' devvm network --json this folder’s VM’s network tier and allowlist, or with -g, new VMs’ choice devvm network log --json this folder’s VM’s network log, or with --blocked its blocks devvm secret --json the secrets, whether each is saved and the VMs using it devvm ssh-agent --json this folder’s VM’s SSH agent forwarding and devvm’s own agent’s keys devvm link --json this folder’s VM’s links devvm link publish --json the ports this folder’s VM publishes to links devvm git-protect --json this folder’s VM’s .git protection devvm history --json the saved exports of agents’ history devvm space --json what devvm keeps on this machine devvm retention --json the retention settings devvm doctor --json what devvm needs on this machine and what’s missing, and it prints nothing else devvm upgrade --json the newest release and how this devvm was installed, and it installs nothing
data.questions-devvm-asks#Questions devvm ask:
devvm asks a question only in a terminal, and each question has a flag or a command that answers it beforehand, so a script never needs to answer one. Without a terminal, with --no-input, or when the input ends before an answer, devvm can’t ask, and every question is handled the same way in all three cases. A question that only adds something, such as an agent’s folders or the Include line, gets its usual answer or a warning that says what to do, and a command that deletes something refuses unless you give it --force.
Question Answered by the CPUs and memory new VMs get, on the first run --cpus and --memory, or devvm size -g, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, new VMs get the size they would anyway the coding agents new VMs get, on the first run and in devvm setup devvm setup --agents LIST or devvm setup --agents none base’s features, on the first run before the new VM’s summary, or on the first build devvm setup --features LIST or devvm setup --features none whether to customize a new VM, after its summary --tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --ports, --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets what the summary shows a new VM’s toolchains, coding agents and layers, when you customize it --tools, --agents and --layers a new VM’s network tier, chosen from a list when you customize it --network TIER, or devvm network -g with a tier for every new VM, or nothing: where devvm can’t show the list, the VM gets the tier the summary shows the ports a new VM forwards, chosen from a list when you customize it: every port, none, or the ports you type --ports, or devvm ports -g with the ports every new VM forwards, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM forwards the ports the summary shows a new VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, when you customize it --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets the size the summary shows the layers new VMs get, in devvm setup devvm setup --layers LIST or devvm setup --layers none a VM’s toolchains and agents, in devvm tools devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, or --json to show them new VMs’ network tier, in devvm setup devvm network -g whether to load an SSH key into your agent devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE beforehand whether to restart a running VM to apply a change from devvm size, devvm network, devvm ssh-agent or devvm git-protect, or, as devvm opens it, the changes that wait for its next start, such as an agent’s new folders devvm restart afterwards, or nothing: without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for the VM’s next start whether to add the Include line to ~/.ssh/config --ssh-config on devvm, devvm host and devvm code a Claude Code token or a GitHub token devvm secret set NAME --stdin an agent’s API key, in devvm agent login --api-key --stdin whether to delete, in devvm rm, devvm gc, devvm gc --caches, devvm images rm and devvm secret rm --force whether to replace the images built on one, in devvm rebuild --force whether to replace what devvm’s agent store has, in devvm agent import --force whether to install a release, in devvm upgrade --force whether to use the VM made for an earlier folder here, in devvm adopt, or to move a VM to this folder, in devvm adopt VM --force whether to move the VM made for this folder at the path it had before, in any command on this folder’s VM devvm adopt --force --force only skips a confirmation, and it never deletes more than the command does without it. A command that would delete something asks first in a terminal, and where devvm can’t ask, it refuses unless you give --force.
A few questions protect work that only you can judge, so no flag answers them, and devvm asks them only in a terminal. Where devvm can’t ask, each of them refuses and says what to run instead. They are these:
devvm rm deleting the VM of a folder this one is inside or the VM made for an earlier folder at this path a --clone VM’s commits that this repo hasn’t fetched and its uncommitted changes a command giving the VM of a folder this one is inside more access devvm agent save saving a VM’s settings for every VM With --no-input, devvm asks nothing even in a terminal, and it never reads an answer from a pipe or a file either. A question that has no usual answer fails instead, after devvm shows the question, and the error names the flag or command that answers it. A question fails the same way when the input ends before an answer, as it does when you press Ctrl+D at the prompt.
data.shell-completion#Shell completion:
devvm completion SHELL prints the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish. The script completes commands, flags and the image names that devvm build and devvm rebuild take, including layers joined with + after the ones you’ve already typed. It also completes shared tools for devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, the lists that --tools, --agents and --layers take, after the names you’ve already typed and their commas, and all and none for --ports and devvm ports. Load it from your shell’s startup file:
Shell Line In bash source <(devvm completion bash) ~/.bashrc, with the bash-completion package installed zsh source <(devvm completion zsh) ~/.zshrc, after compinit fish devvm completion fish | source ~/.config/fish/config.fish

data: You customize images with your own layers, which add what a project needs, and by choosing base’s features, which are devvm’s optional extras that every VM gets. Your layers live in ~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm), not next to devvm’s binary, so upgrading devvm keeps them. To give every new VM something of your own, write it as a layer and make it one of the layers new VMs get (extras of your own).
data.base-image-features#Base image features:
Features are optional extras that devvm builds into base after base’s own setup, so every VM has them.
Feature What it adds omb oh-my-bash: a themed prompt, completions and aliases, with auto-update off fzf fuzzy Ctrl-R history and Ctrl-T file search cli-tools bat, fd, eza, zoxide (z), btop, tree, tldr The desktop that devvm desktop opens isn’t a feature but a built-in layer, desktop, so only the VMs you choose it for get it.
data.choosing-features#Choosing features:
On its first run, devvm asks which features base gets, after the size and coding agents that new VMs get and before it shows what the folder’s new VM gets. devvm build and devvm rebuild ask too, until the features are chosen. The list starts with every feature chosen, and you choose in it as in any of devvm’s lists. Without a terminal, devvm chooses every feature. devvm prints the choice and saves it, in the order the features run. When features in config.toml chooses them, devvm doesn’t ask.
To change the choice:
devvm setup # asks again, starting from the current choice devvm setup --features fzf,omb # without asking devvm setup --features none # without asking, and base gets no features In a terminal, devvm setup asks for the features among its other questions, which devvm setup lists in order. --features asks for none of the others. Without a terminal, devvm setup keeps the choice. devvm refuses a name that isn’t a feature, and an empty --features '', and then nothing changes. You can also choose them by hand with features in config.toml, such as features = ["fzf", "omb"], which wins over what devvm setup saved, and then devvm setup --features refuses to change them. features = [] chooses none, and devvm skips a name without a script, with a warning.
A new choice makes base and the images built on it rebuild the next time they’re used, and devvm setup says so. The old images are then stale, and devvm gc deletes them.
data.example-mailpit#Example: mailpit:
This layer installs Mailpit, which catches the emails your app sends while you develop it, and starts it with the VM. Point your app’s SMTP settings at localhost:1025, and read the emails at localhost:8025 in your browser, because devvm forwards both ports to your machine. Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail:
mailpit_version=1.32.0 mailpit_sha256_amd64=4b5993c978e8604c70d43927e2ad103b311bba3b1822fa0cf1d4ee4ec890a93c mailpit_sha256_arm64=e1e45d1dc72bd497fb262a1e4100178eee057c42c5fc36d143eb8621769e1137 devvm-fetch "https://github.com/axllent/mailpit/releases/download/v$mailpit_version/mailpit-linux-$devvm_arch.tar.gz" \ "$(devvm_sha mailpit)" /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz sudo tar -xzf /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin mailpit rm /tmp/mailpit.tar.gz printf '%s\n' '[Unit]' 'Description=Mailpit' '[Service]' 'ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/mailpit' \ 'DynamicUser=yes' '[Install]' 'WantedBy=multi-user.target' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/mailpit.service >/dev/null sudo systemctl enable --now mailpit The version and each download’s SHA-256 sit at the top, so devvm-fetch refuses a download that doesn’t match. $devvm_arch names the VM’s build in the address, and devvm_sha mailpit picks the matching pin, mailpit_sha256_arm64 or mailpit_sha256_amd64, or names the pin the script lacks, so the download fails. On Alpine, it takes mailpit_sha256_arm64_musl instead when you pin one, for a tool with a separate musl build. To update Mailpit, change all three and rebuild the image. The downloads come from GitHub’s releases, which base’s allowlist has, so mailpit.policy can stay empty. On a base made --from an Alpine container image, start it with OpenRC (rc-update, rc-service) instead of systemd.
data.extras-of-your-own#Extras of your own:
Base’s features are the ones in the table above, and devvm ships all of them. To give every new VM an extra of your own, such as your shell setup or a tool you always use, write it as a layer of your own and choose it as one of the layers new VMs get:
devvm layer new dotfiles # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh $EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/dotfiles.sh devvm setup --layers dotfiles # every new VM gets it A new VM’s summary then shows dotfiles, and when you customize the VM, its list shows dotfiles under Layers, already chosen because devvm setup chose it, so you can leave it out of that VM (layers for new VMs). A layer is an image built on top of base, so the images that have it are named with it, such as dotfiles or docker+dotfiles, and editing its script rebuilds only those images, never base.
data.your-own-layers#Your own layers:
devvm layer new mailpit # writes ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh and mailpit.policy $EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/mailpit.sh devvm --layers mailpit # a new VM with your layer; or devvm build mailpit When you customize a new VM, its list also shows your layers under Layers, so you can choose mailpit there instead of giving --layers (what a new VM gets). To give every new VM your layer, choose it with devvm setup --layers mailpit, or add it to the layers key in config.toml (layers for new VMs). When you delete a layer’s script that you chose there, new VMs are made without it, and devvm warns you.
A layer is a script, ~/.config/devvm/layers/.sh, that bash runs once as the VM’s user, who has sudo, in an image on top of its parent. devvm layer new NAME writes a starter script, and also NAME.policy next to it unless that file exists. It refuses to overwrite a script that exists.
Names are made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and start with a letter or digit. A name can’t be base, a built-in layer’s name (desktop, docker or nix) or a shared tool’s name (node, claude and so on). A command’s name, such as log, is fine, because devvm takes layers only through --layers, the list and image names. Built-in layers go in the same image names as yours, bottom first, as in devvm --layers docker,mailpit, which makes the image docker+mailpit. Put interactive shell setup in ~/.bashrc.d/.sh, which every VM’s ~/.bashrc reads, and PATH changes in ~/.profile. Download files with devvm-fetch URL SHA256 OUT, which base installs.
