It fails when the file’s checksum doesn’t match. devvm runs a line of its own in place of your script’s #! line, which gives it $devvm_arch, the VM’s architecture as arm64 or amd64, $devvm_libc, which is musl on Alpine and gnu elsewhere, and devvm_sha TOOL, which prints the checksum you pinned for this VM, as the example shows. Names that start with devvm_ are devvm’s, and one your script sets is your script’s from then on. Bash’s errors give your file’s own line numbers, or one more without a #! line (the prelude). NAME.policy lists the hosts that VMs with the layer can reach on the allowlist tier, one rule per line. Editing the script rebuilds its image, and the ones built on it, the next time they’re used (rebuilding). A layer’s script changes the VM’s disk, so devvm layer add mailpit gives a VM you have the layer by making the VM again, keeping its home folder and settings (adding layers to a VM), and devvm layer rm mailpit takes it out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM). To edit layers with an agent in a VM, keep them in a repo of their own and copy them in, because devvm refuses a VM for a folder inside ~/.config/devvm (details).

data: A VM has no screen of its own, but with the desktop layer it gets an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens in a window on this machine. This page covers adding the desktop, opening it, its password and the clipboard, and what it costs. The desktop explains how devvm keeps it to this machine.
data.adding-the-desktop#Adding the desktop:
The desktop is one of devvm’s built-in layers, so only the VMs you choose it for get it, and base and the other VMs stay without it. To add it to a new VM, check desktop under Layers in the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM, or name it with --layers:
devvm --layers desktop # a VM of base with the desktop devvm --layers docker,desktop # the desktop on top of the docker layer devvm builds the desktop image the first time a VM needs it, and VMs that choose it share that image. --layers is the exact list of the VM’s layers, so name every layer you want the VM to have.
devvm setup --layers desktop # every new VM gets the desktop devvm setup --layers docker,desktop # the desktop on top of docker, for every new VM To give every new VM the desktop, choose it with devvm setup --layers desktop, or add it to the layers you already chose, such as devvm setup --layers docker,desktop. New VMs then get it unless you leave it out when you customize them or give --layers without it (layers for new VMs). VMs that exist keep the layers they were made with.
A VM made without the desktop has none, and devvm desktop says so. To give it one, run devvm layer add desktop, which makes the VM again from an image with the desktop on top of its own layers, such as docker+desktop. The VM keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings, and loses the rest of its disk, such as the packages you installed, so devvm asks first (adding layers to a VM). devvm layer rm desktop takes the desktop out again in the same way (taking layers out of a VM).
devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop, after asking devvm layer rm desktop # make it again without the desktop The desktop works on base, and on a base made --from a Debian, Ubuntu or Alpine container image.
data.browsers#Browsers:
The desktop has no browser of its own, so install the one you want in the VM, such as Google Chrome, Chromium or Firefox. Browsers reach the web through the VM’s proxy without asking you for a password, and so do the desktop’s other programs. Browsers ask for a proxy’s password rather than read it from the VM’s proxy settings, so the desktop’s programs use the VM’s local proxy instead. The local proxy is a small proxy in the VM, at http://127.0.77.1:3128, which adds the VM’s password to each request and sends it on to the VM’s proxy. A browser follows the desktop’s proxy settings unless you’ve given it one of its own. The local proxy listens on the VM’s loopback alone, and devvm never forwards it to this machine, even on a VM that forwards every port (the local proxy).
The local proxy changes nothing about what the VM may reach. A host that the VM’s network tier doesn’t allow is still blocked, and a plain http:// page shows the proxy’s reason and the devvm network allow command that allows it. An https:// page shows the browser’s own error instead, such as Chrome’s ERR_TUNNEL_CONNECTION_FAILED, so run devvm-why in the desktop’s terminal to see what was blocked.
data.opening-it#Opening it:
devvm desktop # serves this folder's VM's desktop and opens it in Screen Sharing devvm desktop --no-open # only shows its address and password devvm desktop --clipboard # shares the clipboard both ways, for this run devvm desktop gets the VM ready as devvm host does, and starts it if it’s stopped. Then it starts the VM’s desktop, unless it’s running already, and shows its address and password:
devvm-website-0123456789abcd's desktop is at vnc://127.0.0.1:41234 Password: k3mxq7tw It stays there until you press Ctrl+C. On macOS, devvm opens the address in Screen Sharing, which comes with macOS and asks for the password. Screen Sharing can keep the password in your keychain, and the address stays the same each time. On Linux, open the address in a VNC viewer of your own, such as TigerVNC’s vncviewer or Remmina.
The desktop stays at that address until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM stops, and then devvm desktop ends. The desktop goes on running in the VM, so the windows you left open are there the next time you run devvm desktop. It’s 1600 by 1000 pixels.
The desktop is only ever on this machine, and only while devvm desktop runs:
devvm serves it on this machine’s 127.0.0.1 alone, so nothing else on your network reaches it. Each VM keeps its port, which no other VM and no program on this machine has. When a program has taken it, devvm chooses another one and keeps that. In the VM, the desktop listens on no port at all, so a VM that forwards every port never forwards it. On a confined network tier, the VM still reaches only its proxy while you use its desktop.
data.the-clipboard#The clipboard:
devvm desktop --clipboard # share the clipboard both ways, for this run devvm desktop # the next run without it shares nothing The clipboard isn’t shared unless you add --clipboard. With sharing on, what you copy on this machine goes into the VM, where a coding agent can read it, and what the VM copies lands on this machine’s clipboard. Without --clipboard, devvm keeps this machine’s clipboard out of the VM, even when something in the VM has changed its desktop’s settings, and the VM’s desktop doesn’t send its clipboard.
--clipboard turns sharing on in both directions for that run, and the next run without it turns sharing off again. devvm can’t stop a VM whose desktop was changed from sending its clipboard to Screen Sharing, so when you don’t want the VM’s clipboard on this machine, also turn off Use Shared Clipboard in Screen Sharing’s Edit menu.
data.the-password#The password: Each VM has its own password of eight lowercase letters and digits. devvm makes it the first time you run devvm desktop and keeps it with the VM’s state on this machine, so devvm rm deletes it. The password never goes into the VM, and it isn’t in devvm’s run log. devvm checks it on this machine before a viewer reaches the VM, whatever the VM’s own desktop asks for. Other users and programs on this machine can also connect to 127.0.0.1, so the password is what keeps them out, and devvm lets a viewer try only one password a second (on this machine).
data.what-it-costs#What it costs: About 370 MB of disk for the desktop image, which every VM with the layer shares, while base and the VMs without the layer stay that much smaller. About 500 MB of the VM’s memory while its desktop runs, which it does from your first devvm desktop until the VM stops. A VM whose desktop you never open uses none.
data.when-the-desktop-doesnt-open#When the de: The VM has no desktop: it was made without the desktop layer. Run devvm layer add desktop to make it again with the layer, as adding the desktop explains. The desktop didn’t start: devvm shows the end of its run log. The desktop’s own log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM. Screen Sharing didn’t open: open the address devvm shows in Screen Sharing yourself, by typing it into Finder’s Go > Connect to Server, or in another VNC viewer. Screen Sharing says the password is wrong: use the password devvm desktop shows for this VM. Each VM has its own.

data.commands#Commands:
A command is a string, which devvm runs with sh -c, an array, which it runs as it is, or an object of named commands, which it runs one by one, sorted by name. The commands run in the VM, as its user, in the project folder, in a login shell, and never on this machine. Their output goes to the run log.
When a command fails, devvm names it in one line, and the commands after it that would run once, or at that start, don’t run. devvm keeps the VM and opens it, because the command is the project’s and not devvm’s. The commands reach only what the VM’s network tier allows, like anything else in the VM.
data.properties#Properties: Property What devvm does image The VM’s base starts from it, as with --from. devvm uses only an image that its registry gives anyone who asks anonymously, pinned to that digest. It never uses an image only Docker has, one only your registry login reaches, or one on this machine or its network, which is localhost or a registry whose address is loopback, private or link-local, by name or as it resolves. features ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker is devvm’s docker layer. A feature under ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/ named after one of devvm’s toolchains, such as ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node, is that shared toolchain. devvm ignores their options and says so in one line. It refuses docker-outside-of-docker, which is this machine’s Docker, and every other feature. devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script. forwardPorts devvm forwards numbers, localhost:N and 127.0.0.1:N to this machine’s localhost alone, adding them to your ports as devvm ports add does (ports). With every port forwarded, which is the default, they’re among them already. devvm ports rm takes one out, as for any port. It ignores other hosts’ ports and says so in one line. containerEnv, remoteEnv The VM’s environment, which login shells and the commands below get. remoteEnv wins over containerEnv, and devvm’s own variables, such as LANG and secrets, win over both. A remoteEnv of null sets nothing. onCreateCommand, updateContentCommand, postCreateCommand They run once, in that order, once the VM is made and set up (commands). postStartCommand It runs at each start, on the first launch after the VM started. initializeCommand It never runs, because it would run on this machine, and devvm says so in one line. build, dockerFile, dockerfile, dockerComposeFile Refused, because devvm starts a VM only from an image. postAttachCommand, privileged, capAdd, securityOpt, mounts, runArgs, workspaceMount, workspaceFolder, remoteUser, containerUser, updateRemoteUserUID, init, shutdownAction, overrideCommand, hostRequirements, appPort, portsAttributes, otherPortsAttributes, userEnvProbe, waitFor, overrideFeatureInstallOrder, context, service, runServices Ignored, and named in one line. name, customizations, $schema Ignored. anything else Ignored, and named in one line.
data.security#Security:
The file belongs to the project, so a VM can rewrite it for the folder’s next VM, or for itself when you run devvm update, and devvm never lets it run anything on this machine, reach this machine’s files or environment, add a mount or weaken confinement. An image from it can still be any public container image, whose own code runs as root while devvm builds the VM’s base, as with --from (security model).
Its forwardPorts open ports on this machine, even when you’ve narrowed your ports with devvm ports -g or devvm ports. devvm forwards them only to this machine’s localhost, never to its other addresses, and never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, just as for devvm ports add. Anything on this machine that connects to such a port reaches what the VM serves there, including a web page in your browser, so for a repo you don’t trust, check its file first, or run devvm --ports none or devvm --no-devcontainer (ports the VM listens on).
data.updating-a-vm-from-the-file#Updating a V:
When you change the file, run devvm update. devvm reads the file as it is now, and before it changes anything, it refuses what it would refuse for a new VM. Then it asks to make the VM again from the file, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, as for an outdated VM, and everything else on the VM’s disk is lost. devvm update --force doesn’t ask, and without a terminal devvm refuses unless you give --force.
devvm replaces only what the file gave the VM, and it keeps what you chose:
Toolchains and layers. The ones the file’s features gave the VM go when the file no longer has those features, and the ones the file’s new features map to are added. The ones you chose yourself stay, whether you gave them with --tools or --layers, devvm setup chose them, or the folder’s other files call for them. One you left out in the list, or took out later, stays out. The container image. The VM’s base starts from the file’s new image, pinned as for a new VM. When the file no longer has one, the base starts from $DEVVM_FROM, or else from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A VM made with --from keeps its base, and devvm says that it ignores image. The ports. The ports the file added go when the file no longer lists them, and the ones it lists anew are added, as devvm ports add adds them. The ports you added with devvm ports add stay, and one of the file’s that you took out with devvm ports rm stays out. A VM made with --ports gets the ports the file lists anew, but not the ones --ports won over. The environment and the commands. They’re the file’s new ones, and the commands that run once run again on the new disk. When the file is gone, devvm makes the VM again without it, so what the file gave goes, and so do its environment and commands. When a file appears for a VM made without one, devvm makes the VM again as the file says, as it would a new VM.
data.variables#Variables: Variable ${containerWorkspaceFolder}, ${containerWorkspaceFolderBasename} the project folder, at the same path in the VM, and its name ${containerEnv:NAME} in a string command and in containerEnv and remoteEnv, the VM’s own NAME ${localEnv:NAME}, ${env:NAME} refused, because devvm never puts this machine’s environment in a VM ${localWorkspaceFolder}, ${localWorkspaceFolderBasename}, ${devcontainerId}, ${containerEnv:NAME} elsewhere refused devvm leaves any other ${…} as it is, for the VM’s shell, such as ${HOME} in a command.
data.when-its-read#When it’s read:
When the folder’s VM is made, and again by devvm update. Comments and trailing commas are allowed. devvm reads the file only within the folder, so it doesn’t follow a link out of the folder, and it reads only a regular file of up to 1 MiB. devvm never writes anything to the project folder. What you give on the command line wins. --from wins over image, which wins over $DEVVM_FROM, and --ports wins over forwardPorts, and devvm says so in one line for each. The new VM gets the toolchains and layers that the features map to, which its summary shows, and when you customize the VM, they’re already chosen in its list, each row naming the file, so you can leave them out there. --tools and --layers replace them, as they replace any part’s default (what a new VM gets). An existing VM changes only when devvm makes it again. Its state records the file’s SHA-256. When the file differs from it on a launch, or is gone, or has appeared since, devvm warns once and names devvm update. devvm doesn’t check a VM made with --no-devcontainer, and devvm update doesn’t read the file for it. A new VM takes each of these from the first place that sets it.
Where a new VM's ports and base come fromA new VM's ports are --ports, or else your ports with the file's forwardPorts added. Its base starts from --from, or else the file's image, or else $DEVVM_FROM, or else Ubuntu's cloud image.Its base starts from Its ports or else or else or else or else --ports your ports, withforwardPorts added --from the file's image $DEVVM_FROM Ubuntu's cloud image When devvm refuses something in the file, it stops with one line that names the file, before it makes anything. For invalid JSON, it names the line and column.

data:
By default base starts from Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image. --from IMAGE starts it from a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image instead, such as node:24, python:3.13, debian:13, alpine:3 or an image you built yourself. Use it when your project needs a distribution or a system package set that Ubuntu doesn’t give you.
devvm --from node:24 # a new VM whose base is node:24 devvm build --from alpine:3 base # just the image DEVVM_FROM=node:24 devvm # a default for every new VM and build Everything above base builds and runs as usual, including base’s own setup and the layers (docker and yours). The VM gets its shared tools as any VM does, and shared tools and glibc describes where devvm builds them. devvm keeps the images from each container image apart, so each base and the images on it sit side by side with the others, and each image’s record keeps the container image its base came from and that image’s digest.
--from applies to new VMs and to devvm build and devvm rebuild, and devvm images rm takes it to delete an image on a base from that container image. An existing VM keeps what it was made from, and devvm tools add and devvm tools update build its shared tools for that base. devvm ignores another --from for an existing VM, with a warning. Images and caching explains how devvm turns a container image into a VM’s disk and how it treats the image’s code as untrusted.
data.backends#Backends: Lima starts base from a container image by converting the image into a disk (backends).
data.images-only-docker-has#Images only Docke:
Public images work from any registry, such as Docker Hub, ghcr.io or quay.io. When a registry doesn’t give devvm the image, devvm takes it from Docker, as long as Docker runs and has it. That covers an image you built and never pushed, and a private one, which you get with docker login and then docker pull. devvm itself never logs in to a registry, and it never pulls, builds or deletes Docker’s images.
If the image’s tag moves to another image while devvm builds, for example because you rebuilt it, devvm stops and asks you to run it again.
data.shared-tools-and-glibc#Shared tools and:
A shared tool’s build is mounted by every VM that gets the same version of the tool, so devvm never builds one where a container image’s code could change it for other VMs:
On a Debian- or Ubuntu-based container image, VMs get the same builds of the shared tools as VMs on Ubuntu’s own image, which devvm builds in its own base from Ubuntu’s cloud image, never in the container image. When that base isn’t built yet, devvm says so and builds it first, as it does for a VM on Ubuntu’s image. On an Alpine-based container image, musl builds need Alpine, so devvm builds them in the VM’s own base and keeps them for the VMs on that exact container image, by its digest. When the container image’s tag moves to a new container image, devvm builds the tools it gives those VMs next again, on the new one. The shared tools are their projects’ own prebuilt releases, and each one is built against a glibc version that it needs at least. devvm reads that version from each tool’s files when it builds the tool’s image, and it reads the container image’s glibc version when it converts the image (building tools). When a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image has an older glibc than a tool needs, devvm refuses to give that tool to the VM. The error names the tool, the glibc version it needs and the one the image has, and devvm doesn’t make the VM. The same happens when devvm tools add, devvm tools update or devvm update would give an existing VM such a tool.
To fix it, start from a newer container image with --from, or leave that tool out. Today no shared tool needs a glibc newer than 2.28, so Debian 10 and Ubuntu 20.04 and newer images run all of them, and toolchains lists what each one needs. devvm measures it again for every new version it builds. Alpine-based images get musl builds of the tools, which need no glibc. pi is the one shared tool without a musl build, because its project releases it for glibc alone, so devvm refuses to give pi to a VM on an Alpine-based image, before it builds anything, and the error names pi. Leave pi out of that VM, or start from a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image. devvm doesn’t check base from Ubuntu’s own image, whose glibc is newer than any shared tool needs.
data.supported-images#Supported images: Debian, Ubuntu and Alpine and the distributions based on them. devvm refuses any other, and an image without a shell or /etc/os-release. This machine’s architecture. devvm refuses an image without an arm64 build (or amd64), and names the ones it has. Alpine uses OpenRC and musl, so its VMs get musl builds of the shared tools, built on that image and kept apart for it. Its base also gets GNU tar from Alpine’s packages in place of busybox’s, because devvm sends the VM’s setup and imports agents’ history with it. Unpinned packages. While base builds, its packages come from the container image’s own sources as they are then, apt’s or Alpine’s, and so do the desktop layer’s, the docker layer’s on Alpine and the nix layer’s. devvm keeps no copy of them, unlike base from Ubuntu’s image, so building the same base again installs the sources’ packages of that day, and it needs the network for them. A glibc new enough for your shared tools. A Debian- or Ubuntu-based container image’s glibc must be at least as new as each shared tool needs, which shared tools and glibc covers. Tested. The end-to-end tests make VMs from node:24 (Debian 12, with node, python, claude and the docker and nix layers) and alpine:3 (with node, dotnet and the docker, nix and desktop layers), and build base from ubuntu:26.04.
data.tags-and-digests#Tags and digests:
devvm builds base from the exact image that a tag names when it builds, which is the image’s digest, and it records that digest:
When the tag moves to a new image, such as a new node:24, the next build makes a new base. That build happens for a new VM with --from, devvm build, devvm rebuild, devvm layer add or devvm update. The old base is then stale, and the VMs made from it are outdated, which devvm update changes (outdated VMs). Offline, or when the registry doesn’t have the image any more, devvm uses the digest it recorded last, with a warning. With none recorded, it fails. Opening an existing VM never looks anything up, because only builds do. --from node:24@sha256: pins an exact image, and devvm never looks it up. devvm reads a reference the way Docker does, so node:24 is Docker Hub’s library/node with the tag 24. A first part with a dot or a port, or localhost, names the registry, as in ghcr.io/org/image:tag or localhost:5000/app. A reference without a tag means latest. Digests explains how devvm asks a registry for them.

data:
Every VM is a copy of an image. An image is base with your choice of layers on it, and nothing else. A VM also gets the shared tools you chose for it, such as node or Claude Code, which are mounted into it and are never part of an image. This page covers what a new VM gets, what base brings, the layers and adding them to a VM or taking them out, how the shared tools work, rebuilding, bringing an outdated VM up to date, and how to list, delete and clean up images. Images and caching explains how devvm builds, pins and caches them, and toolchains and coding agents list the shared tools.
Images, VMs and the shared toolsUbuntu's cloud image, or a --from image, is the start of base, with the features you chose, and docker is a layer on base. Each VM is a copy of one image, and the shared tools, such as node and claude, are mounted into each VM read-only.a copy a copy mountedread-only mountedread-only Ubuntu's cloud image,or a --from image base, withthe features you chose docker, a layeron base VM of base,with node VM of docker,with node and claude shared tools:node, claude…
data.a-remake-that-stops-halfway#A remake tha: If devvm itself is killed while it makes a VM again, such as when this machine loses power, the VM’s state records the remake. The next devvm, devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update, devvm clone on or devvm clone off in the folder finishes it without asking. When the new VM already has its home folder, devvm only deletes the old disk. When the old disk is still set aside otherwise, devvm puts it back and makes the VM again from the start, and when it’s gone, devvm makes the new VM with the home folder it saved. Until then, other commands on the VM refuse and name devvm, and devvm rm deletes the VM together with its old disk.
data.adding-layers-to-a-vm#Adding layers to a:
A VM keeps the layers devvm made it with, because a layer’s script changes the VM’s disk. devvm layer add LAYER... gives a VM more layers by making it again. devvm builds an image with the new layers on top of the VM’s own, in the order you give them, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker with desktop added is made again from docker+desktop, so the images it already uses stay as they are. devvm names the layers the VM has already and leaves them where they are, and when the VM has all of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.
devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop layer on top devvm layer add docker nix # docker, then nix on top of it devvm layer add desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must Everything on the VM’s disk that devvm doesn’t keep is lost, so in a terminal devvm names the image and asks first, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses unless you give --force. When the VM has a coding agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, as devvm rm does, unless you give --no-export (history). In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one.
devvm refuses before it changes anything in these cases:
A name isn’t a layer, or is a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools add adds instead. The VM’s backend can’t run one of the layers. The VM’s creation didn’t finish. The VM is a --clone VM, whose clone of the repo is on its disk. To give a --clone VM more layers, run devvm clone off, which offers to fetch the clone’s work first, then devvm layer add and devvm clone on (switching a VM that exists). devvm then works in this order:
It builds the new image, so a build that fails leaves the VM as it was. It exports the agents’ history and saves the VM’s home folder on this machine. It stops the VM and sets its old disk aside under another name. It makes the VM again from the new image, with the same name and settings, and starts it. It copies the home folder onto the new disk and deletes the old disk, then opens a shell in the VM. Until the new VM has started with its home folder, a step that fails, or Ctrl+C, deletes the new disk and puts the old one back as it was. While one devvm makes a VM again, another devvm that would make the same VM again refuses, and so does devvm in its folder, so wait for the first to finish. While devvm makes the VM again, the old disk, the new one and the saved home folder take room on this machine at the same time, and devvm checks for free space before it starts.
data.base#Base:
base is the image that every other image is built on. It is Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image with git, git-lfs, build-essential, ripgrep, jq, sqlite3 and mise added, followed by the optional features you chose, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. Docker comes as a layer of devvm’s, so you choose it when you customize a new VM, or give devvm --layers docker. With --from, base starts from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s (details). A VM made from base gets 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk unless you give it another size, and on a small machine it gets fewer CPUs and less memory (size and ports).
Your VMs use Ubuntu’s live archive, and base keeps no package lists, so run sudo apt update in a VM before you install a package, and apt upgrade then gets the current updates:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install PACKAGE # in the VM: fetch the lists first, as base keeps none sudo apt upgrade # the current updates base drops the server extras that Ubuntu’s cloud image comes with, such as snapd and apt’s background updates, which saves 0.9 GB of disk and 100 MB of memory per VM (base’s size). The everyday tools stay, such as htop, tmux, lsof, strace, tcpdump, rsync and nano.
The first time devvm builds base on this machine, it starts from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image and installs the newest packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from a mirror you set. devvm keeps a copy of each package it installed, so building the same base again, such as after devvm images rm base, installs exactly those packages from the copies, with no network for them. devvm rebuild base starts again from the newest image and packages (rebuilding).
data.built-in-layers#Built-in layers: devvm ships three layers, desktop, docker and nix. You choose them like any other layer, in the list devvm shows for a new VM or as in devvm --layers docker, and you build one with devvm build nix. To give every new VM one, choose it with devvm setup --layers, and to give a VM you have one, run devvm layer add (adding layers to a VM). Their names are reserved, so devvm refuses devvm layer new docker and never reads a desktop.sh, docker.sh or nix.sh of yours. The hosts that each layer needs are in its own allowlist.
data.choosing-in-a-list#Choosing in a list:
devvm’s lists work the same way everywhere: the new VM’s list, its network tiers and ports, devvm tools, base’s features in devvm setup, and the hosts in devvm network lock.
Key What it does Up and down, or k and j move the cursor, and in a list where you choose one, such as the network tiers, moving chooses it Space in a list where you choose several, such as the toolchains, coding agents and layers, chooses or unchooses the row under the cursor a in a list where you choose several, chooses every row, or unchooses them all when they’re all chosen already Enter confirms, and at a question with a value in brackets, such as a size, keeps that value A row that’s greyed out, such as a part a flag gave or a VM’s layers in devvm tools, can’t change, and the cursor skips it. A list longer than the terminal scrolls with the cursor, with a line above and below that says how many more rows there are, and each row is cut to the terminal’s width.
data.cleaning-up#Cleaning up:
devvm gc # stale and unfinished images, unused tools, old mise, the Nix cache over its cap devvm gc --tool-images node # also node's current builds that no VM has devvm gc --history --older-than 30d # also the history exports written 30 days ago or more devvm gc --orphans # also what's left of VMs deleted outside devvm devvm gc --caches # also devvm's share of Lima's caches devvm gc deletes four things:
what devvm images lists as stale or unfinished the shared tools it lists as unused the older versions of the mise that devvm runs on this machine to look up the tools’ versions, which an upgrade of devvm leaves behind, except one that changed in the last hour, because another devvm may be downloading it the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than its cap, the nix-cache.size retention setting, which is 10 GiB when it’s off devvm’s mise and the shared Nix cache are both in cache/ in devvm’s data folder, which holds only what devvm makes again when it needs it, so you can also delete that folder yourself at any time. gc lists them all first and, in a terminal, asks. Without a terminal, it deletes nothing unless you give --force, which deletes without asking, in a terminal too. Its flags do more:
devvm gc --tool-images also deletes the current shared tools that no VM has, such as a toolchain you tried once, for every C library. devvm gc --tool-images node claude deletes only those tools’ builds, by the names you choose them by, so node also covers pnpm and bun. A tool that a VM’s state lists stays, including a stopped VM’s, and a tool that no VM has goes however recently it was built. While devvm is making a VM, or giving one new shared tools through devvm tools add or devvm tools update, gc keeps every current shared tool that no VM has, names them, and deletes the rest of what it would, so run it again once that’s done. A devvm that starts to make a VM meanwhile waits for gc and says so, and in a terminal, gc makes it wait while gc asks you, so answer it first (listing and cleaning up). A VM that has a deleted tool builds it again when it needs it. When a shared tool that a new VM’s state lists is gone before the VM’s first shell, for example because you deleted it by hand, devvm names the tools it couldn’t mount and stops, and the VM stays. Run devvm tools update in the folder, which builds the missing tools again and opens the VM (a shared tool doesn’t mount). devvm gc --history also deletes the exports of agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm saved, which are the only copy of a deleted VM’s history, and --older-than DURATION keeps those newer than that duration, such as 12h, 30d or 2w. gc never deletes exports without --history. devvm gc --nix-cache also deletes the rest of the shared Nix cache. VMs download its packages again when they need them. devvm gc --orphans also deletes what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, such as one you deleted with limactl delete instead of devvm rm, and with it the hold their state has on their shared tools (leftovers). devvm gc --caches then frees devvm’s share of Lima’s own caches, such as its downloads of Ubuntu’s cloud image, after asking, or without asking with --force, which it needs without a terminal (Lima’s caches). devvm gc --retention then applies the retention settings at once, which devvm otherwise applies at most once a day. They’re all off until you set them. When Lima can’t list its images while one of your VMs uses it, for example because Lima isn’t installed, gc warns and leaves Lima’s images, shared tools, VM leftovers and caches alone. It also leaves the shared tools whose record doesn’t name the backend that built them, because they may be Lima’s. gc still succeeds, so run devvm doctor to see what’s wrong with Lima, then run gc again once it answers. devvm images fails instead, because it lists all the images or none. gc never deletes VMs, and it keeps current images, which devvm images rm deletes (deleting images). Without --tool-images it keeps the current shared tools. It always keeps every shared tool that any VM has, including a stopped VM’s and that of a VM deleted outside devvm whose state is left, until --orphans deletes that state. On Linux hosts, a stale image whose disk VMs are overlays of stays, and devvm says which VMs use it. After an Alpine VM is gone, the shared tools built for Alpine are unused, unless you give gc that --from. Images and caching has the details of what counts as current and unused. To see what gc would free before you run it, and what takes the rest of the space, run devvm space (what devvm keeps).
data.deleting-images#Deleting images:
devvm images rm IMAGE|KEY... deletes images. You name each one by its name or by the key that devvm images shows:
A name means its image as it is now, on base from --from when you give it. A stale or unfinished image has only its key. Each image must be built, or devvm deletes nothing. Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm refuses a name that has one, such as node+foo, and devvm gc deletes the shared tools no VM has. devvm also deletes nothing while another devvm is building one of the images, so run the command again once that build ends. devvm gc and devvm rebuild leave such an image alone too. A deleted image is built again the next time it’s needed. VMs made from it keep working, because on macOS they’re clones of its disk. On Linux hosts, devvm refuses to delete an image whose disk VMs are overlays of, and names those VMs.
data.desktop#desktop: The desktop layer installs an Xfce desktop with TigerVNC’s server, which devvm desktop opens in Screen Sharing, and adds about 370 MB to the image. Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, which on a base made --from alpine means Alpine’s own packages, and they aren’t pinned. It needs no hosts of its own on the allowlist tier, and a VM without the layer has no desktop.
data.devvm-images-json#devvm images –json:
devvm images --json prints the same as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm still says the same on stderr. images and tools have the tables’ columns as fields, with sizes in bytes, and a value an image lacks, such as an unfinished build’s name, is "". These fields go beyond the tables:
Field What it holds backend the backend that has the image or built the tool, lima. Only a built tool has it digest an image’s full SHA-256 of what its base started from sized whether devvm knows an image’s size built whether devvm has built a tool image. Only a built one has backend and libc total the disk the images and shared tools take together unused_tools the part the unused tool images take nix_cache the shared Nix cache’s files, the disk they take and its cap { "version": 1, "images": [ { "name": "base", "from": "ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)", "digest": "sha256:8eb876c2ccc4b6ff89e4a65d511815923b285e04503ba465809bf587f763da24", "key": "7a76021c46ef", "state": "current", "size": 2254857830, "sized": true, "backend": "lima" } ], "tools": [ { "name": "node", "tool": "node", "version": "24.11.0", "built": true, "backend": "lima", "libc": "gnu", "size": 125829120, "vms": 1, "state": "current" } ], "total": 2380686950, "unused_tools": 0, "nix_cache": { "files": 0, "size": 0, "cap": 10737418240 } }
data.docker#docker:
The docker layer installs Docker’s engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose from Docker’s apt repository, adds the VM’s user to the docker group, and starts the daemon at each boot. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages instead. A VM without the layer has no Docker.
A VM with the layer can be on any network tier like any other, because its containers’ connections go through the VM’s network, which devvm confines from outside the VM (network tiers). devvm gives every container the VM’s proxy settings, and on a confined tier, a container that ignores them, or was made without them through Docker’s API, reaches the hosts the VM’s rules allow by name through transparent mode, on Docker’s default bridge and on networks that docker network create and Compose make. Such a container doesn’t trust the VM’s CA, so a blocked HTTPS host gives it a certificate error rather than the proxy’s 403, and the block is logged all the same. A container run with --network none, or on an --internal network, reaches nothing.
data.layers#Layers:
An image is base with layers on it, named bottom first and joined with +, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. You can leave base itself out, which makes base+foo the same as foo. An image name never holds shared tools, which aren’t layers, so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse a shared tool’s name, such as node, and point you to devvm tools.
A layer is a script that bash runs in the image’s VM as the VM’s user, who has sudo. It is either one of devvm’s built-in layers or one of yours, at ~/.config/devvm/layers/.sh, and devvm layer new NAME starts a layer of your own (details). devvm refuses a layer whose script is missing, and it refuses any name in an image that breaks these rules:
A layer’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes. It starts with a letter or digit. It is neither base, a built-in layer’s name nor a shared tool’s name. devvm build foo+bar # builds base, foo and foo+bar, unless they're built devvm rebuild foo # builds foo again, and deletes the old foo and foo+bar
data.listing-images#Listing images:
devvm images prints two tables, each with a header, and it shows what a row lacks as -. The first table lists the images by name, with unfinished builds last:
Column IMAGE its name, such as base or foo+bar FROM what its base started from: the --from image, or Ubuntu’s cloud image with its release’s date, ubuntu 26.04 (20261001) DIGEST the first 12 hex digits of that image’s SHA-256 KEY its key, which devvm images rm also takes STATE current, stale when what it’s built from has changed since it was built, unfinished for a build that didn’t finish, or building while another devvm builds it SIZE the disk it takes, in powers of 1024 (2.1G). On macOS an image is a clone of its parent’s disk, and the blocks they share count for both The second table lists the shared tools that devvm has built, by the name you choose them by, such as node for node, pnpm and bun. The toolchains come first, then the agents, with each tool’s versions newest first:
Column NAME a toolchain’s name, such as node, or an agent’s, such as claude TOOL, VERSION the tool and its version LIBC the C library (gnu, or musl for an Alpine base) that this build is for, because each gets a build of its own, or - when devvm can’t tell SIZE the disk it takes VMS how many VMs have it STATE current for the version new VMs get, in use for another version a VM has, unused for neither, not built for the current version of a tool devvm has other versions of, and not installed when devvm has no version of it After the tables, devvm says on stderr how many images are stale or unfinished and how much disk the unused tools take, when there are any. It ends with the disk that the images and shared tools take together, and when the shared Nix cache holds anything, the disk it takes of its cap. devvm space shows the rest of what devvm keeps (what devvm keeps).
data.nix#nix:
The nix layer installs Nix with flakes and the nix command turned on, and direnv with nix-direnv, so a project’s flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix can supply its toolchain. Each VM has a Nix store and daemon of its own, which no other VM and nothing on this machine shares. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache through a cache on this machine that only devvm fills. Nix projects explains that cache, and how a flake’s dev shell and the shared tools work together.
The nix layer works on a base from Ubuntu, Debian or Alpine. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s xz package, which isn’t pinned, and runs Nix’s daemon as an OpenRC service.
data.outdated-vms#Outdated VMs:
A VM keeps the image it was made from. When that image, or one it’s built on, changes after an edited script, another choice of base’s features or a rebuild, the VM is outdated. devvm then warns on each launch, names the images that changed and devvm update, and leaves the VM as it is.
devvm update # move the VM to the newest shared tools, and to its image's new build after asking devvm update --force # the same without asking, as a script must devvm update --clean-home # the same, with the new image's home folder devvm update brings this folder’s VM up to date in two steps:
It moves the VM to the newest shared tools, as devvm tools update does, and that needs no question, because the shared tools aren’t part of the image and nothing on the VM’s disk changes (adding and removing tools). When the VM is outdated, devvm makes it again from its own image as it builds now, with the same layers, in the same way that devvm layer add makes a VM again with more layers. devvm builds the image first, then gives the VM a new disk copied from it, and keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings (what a VM made again keeps). Everything else on its disk is lost, such as the packages you installed with apt and Docker’s images, so in a terminal devvm names the images that changed and asks first, with no as the default. When the folder’s devcontainer.json changed since devvm made the VM, or is gone, or has appeared, devvm also makes the VM again, after asking, as the file says now (updating a VM from the file).
What devvm update does in each case:
When only the shared tools are newer, devvm moves the VM to them and opens a shell in it without asking, because newer tools don’t need the VM made again. When you answer no, devvm keeps the VM with any newer shared tools it moved to, and opens a shell in it if there were some. Without a terminal, devvm refuses an outdated VM unless you give --force, and it refuses before it changes anything, the VM’s shared tools included. When the VM has the newest shared tools and nothing it was made from has changed, devvm says that the VM is current and changes nothing. To make a current VM again with the newest packages that a script installs without a pin, run devvm rebuild on its image first, which makes the VM outdated, then devvm update (rebuilding). For a VM made with --from, devvm tells whether the VM is outdated from the digest it last recorded, without looking anything up, so a moved tag shows only once a build has looked it up. When devvm makes the VM again, a tag that has moved gives the VM the container image’s newer version, and a pinned digest stays as it is (tags and digests, digests). devvm update takes the same flags as devvm layer add, and it refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run its layers. It exports the agents’ history first unless you give --no-export, and --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead of its own. In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one. The steps, and what happens when one fails, are those of adding layers to a VM.
devvm tools update moves the VM to newer shared tools alone, and it never makes the VM again, even when the VM is outdated (adding and removing tools).
data.rebuilding#Rebuilding:
When you edit a layer’s script, devvm builds that layer again the next time it’s used, together with every layer built on it, and it reuses the layers below. A new choice of base’s features rebuilds base and everything on it in the same way. To build an image again yourself:
devvm rebuild base # base again from the newest packages (on Lima, the newest cloud image too) devvm rebuild docker # the docker layer again, on base as it is now devvm rebuild IMAGE builds an image again from its parent as the parent is now, where IMAGE is base or a stack of layers, such as docker or foo+bar. That’s how you get the newest packages that a script installs without a pin. On Lima, devvm rebuild base also starts base again from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image, which devvm otherwise picks only the first time it builds base on this machine. devvm also builds the images on it again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. When there are such images, devvm lists them first and, in a terminal, asks before it goes on. After the build, devvm deletes the old images that no VM uses.
Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm rebuild refuses a shared tool’s name, and devvm update and devvm tools update get their newer versions. Rebuilding explains how devvm tells which images to build again.
data.shared-tools#Shared tools:
The toolchains and coding agents are shared tools, not image layers. A VM of any image can have them, in any mix, such as node and Claude Code on base, or go and Codex on foo. A VM’s state lists its shared tools apart from its image. Toolchains lists the toolchains, with what each brings, and supported agents lists the coding agents.
devvm builds each tool version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, so any mix of tools works without building anything new, and ten VMs with node share one copy of it. The builds are in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools. Each C library gets a build of its own, so when an Alpine VM and an Ubuntu VM both have node 24, devvm images lists two builds of that version (what devvm keeps). An Alpine VM’s builds are only ever shared with VMs on the same container image, as shared tools and glibc explains. mise runs the tools:
They work as usual. Each toolchain’s commands, such as npm i -g (into ~/.npm-global) or go install (into ~/go/bin), work from any shell, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Global installs go into your home, as each toolchain’s section says. A project’s own version files win. A toolchain’s version files, such as .nvmrc for node, pick its version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used, and each toolchain’s section names its files. mise also reads a mise.toml in the project folder, and devvm trusts it without asking, because the folder is yours. They’re read-only. A VM can’t change the shared tools, even as root. The tools can’t update themselves, and rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain. They’re mounted, or the launch stops. When one of a VM’s tools is missing or the VM can’t mount it, devvm stops the launch and names the tool, and the VM never downloads its own copy in its place (a shared tool doesn’t mount). Only the versions that a project’s own version files pick install into the VM. devvm doesn’t pin the tools’ versions, because agents like Claude Code release several times a week. It follows the newest release of each tool, with Node 24 for node and opencode 2 for opencode. The first time a tool is needed, devvm looks up its newest release, which needs this machine to be online once. When it makes a new VM, devvm also checks for newer releases if its last check was more than a day ago, and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 turns that check off.
A new VM gets the tools chosen for it when devvm makes it, and keeps those versions. devvm tools shows them, and in a terminal lets you choose them. devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update change them too, as does the first step of devvm update, and changing them never changes the VM’s disk (adding and removing tools).
data.taking-layers-out-of-a-vm#Taking layers:
devvm layer rm LAYER... takes layers out of a VM by making it again, in the same way that devvm layer add puts them in. devvm builds an image of the VM’s other layers, in the order they had, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker+nix+desktop without nix is made again from docker+desktop, and a VM without any of its layers is made again from base. devvm names the layers that the VM doesn’t have and leaves them out, and when the VM has none of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.
devvm layer rm desktop # make this folder's VM again without the desktop layer devvm layer rm docker nix # take out docker and nix devvm layer rm desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must The VM keeps what a VM made again keeps, its home folder included, and everything else on its disk is lost, such as what the layers you took out installed and Docker’s images. So devvm asks first in a terminal, with no as the default, and refuses without one unless you give --force. It takes the same flags as devvm layer add and works in the same steps. Before it changes anything, it refuses these:
It refuses the same VMs as devvm layer add, which are a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run the layers left. It refuses base, and a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools rm takes out instead. It refuses a name that isn’t a layer. You can still take out a layer of yours whose script you deleted, and that’s the one way to make such a VM again with its home folder and settings, because devvm layer add and devvm update need every layer’s script to build the VM’s image.
data.what-a-new-vm-gets#What a new VM gets:
What a new VM getsdevvm starts from the defaults, the folder's toolchains and devvm setup's agents and layers, each flag given replaces its part, and the summary says what the VM gets. In a terminal, without --no-input and with something left to choose, devvm asks whether to customize it, and y opens the list, the tier, the CPUs, memory and disk. Then devvm builds the image if it isn't built and makes the VM as a copy of it, with its shared tools mounted.no yes Enter y devvm in a folderwithout a VM the defaults: the folder's toolchains,devvm setup's agents and layers each flag given replaces its part:--tools, --agents, --layers,--network, --cpus, --memory the summary says what the VM gets a terminal, without --no-input,and something left to choose? its image built if it isn't,and the VM is a copy of it,with its shared tools mounted Customize it? [y/N] the list, then the tier,then the CPUs, memory and disk Before devvm makes a new VM, it shows a summary of what the VM gets. The summary names each toolchain, coding agent and layer with why the VM gets it, such as for package.json, from devvm setup or from --tools, and then the VM’s size, its network tier, its ports and the folder’s devcontainer.json, when there is one:
==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets: toolchain node, for package.json agent claude, from devvm setup layers: none size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk network tier: allowlist ports: all devcontainer.json: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, which devvm --no-devcontainer skips Customize it? [y/N] In a terminal, devvm then asks whether to customize the VM, with no as the default, so confirming makes it as shown. When you customize it, devvm shows the three parts in one list under three headings, Toolchains, Coding agents and Layers, with what the summary showed already chosen (choosing in a list). The Layers heading says that a layer is extra software built into the VM’s image:
Choose what devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c gets. Use up and down to move, space to toggle and enter to confirm. Toolchains > [x] node for package.json [ ] python [ ] rust [ ] go Coding agents, which you start in the VM's shell [x] claude from devvm setup [ ] codex [ ] opencode [ ] pi Layers: extra software built into the VM's image, such as docker, nix or desktop [ ] desktop an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens [ ] docker Docker's engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose [ ] nix Nix, direnv and nix-direnv After the list, devvm asks three more questions, in this order:
Unless you gave --network, devvm lists the four network tiers, with learn after internet for a VM that learns the hosts it needs, each with what it reaches, and you choose one, starting from the tier the summary showed: allowlist, or the tier you saved for new VMs with devvm network -g (choosing a tier). Unless you gave --ports, devvm lists the ports the VM can forward: every port, none, which you add later with devvm ports add, or the ports you type, which devvm checks as --ports checks them and asks for again when they aren’t a list. The list starts on what the summary showed, every port unless config.toml or devvm ports -g set another (size and ports), and the ports you choose are this VM’s alone. Last, it asks for the VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, starting from the summary’s, and confirming keeps each one. Each question is skipped when you gave its flag, --cpus, --memory or --disk. Before the disk’s question, devvm says that the disk can grow later with devvm size --disk but never shrinks, and that it takes up only the space the VM writes. A disk smaller than the image’s, 100 GiB for base, is refused as --disk refuses it, and devvm asks again, as it does for a value that isn’t a size. The size you type is this VM’s alone, and devvm saves it for no other VM. Each part has a default:
Toolchains: the ones the folder’s files call for, each naming its file in the summary and the list, such as package.json. Coding agents: the ones you chose with devvm setup, which the summary and the list say. The summary says from config.toml for the ones that config.toml sets. Until you choose some, there are none. Layers: the ones you chose with devvm setup, bottom first, which the summary and the list say in the same way. Until you choose some, there are none. A layer that a project file calls for, such as nix for a flake.nix, names the file in its row of the list but isn’t chosen unless devvm setup chose it, so you choose it when you want it. Three flags choose the parts on the command line. --tools takes the toolchains, as in --tools node,python, --agents takes the coding agents, as in --agents claude,codex, and --layers takes the layers bottom first, as in --layers docker,mine:
devvm --tools node,python --agents claude,codex --layers docker # choose every part, without the list devvm --agents none # no agents, the rest as the summary shows Each is the exact list for its part and replaces that part’s default, and none chooses none of it, as in --agents none. A part whose flag you leave out takes its default. devvm checks each name before it does anything. For a name that belongs to another part, such as --tools claude, it names the flag that takes it, and for a name it doesn’t know, it suggests the closest one.
A part, tier or size that a flag gives is taken as given, and the summary says so. devvm still asks whether to customize the VM while anything is left to choose, because a flag answers only its own part. When you customize it, the list shows a part that a flag gave greyed out, and the cursor skips it. Each question is skipped in its own case:
Question Skipped when the list --tools, --agents and --layers give all three parts the tier you give --network or saved a tier, or the backend’s VMs can only be open the ports you give --ports the CPUs, the memory or the disk you give --cpus, --memory or --disk whether to customize the VM the flags give every part, the ports, the CPUs, the memory and the disk, and the tier is given or saved Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing and doesn’t fail. The VM gets what the summary shows, and the summary ends with the flags that choose others.
devvm looks at the folder’s top level for the files that call for a toolchain, in this order:
Toolchain Files node package.json, bun.lock, bun.lockb python pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py, Pipfile rust Cargo.toml go go.mod The defaults combine this way:
If more than one toolchain matches, the VM gets them all, so package.json and pyproject.toml give node and python. A Nix project’s files call for the nix layer, whose row names them. Those files are flake.nix, shell.nix and devenv.nix, and a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell. In a folder with none of these files, the default is no toolchains, so a VM made without a terminal or flags gets devvm setup’s layers and agents. A folder’s devcontainer.json adds what its features map to, such as toolchains or the docker layer, to the defaults, each naming the file in the summary and the list (devcontainer.json). Its layers go on top of devvm setup’s. The VM’s image is base with its layers, in the order you give them, bottom first, so --layers docker,mine makes the image docker+mine. When you check layers in the list, devvm setup’s stay in their order at the bottom, and the ones you add go on top in the list’s order. Its shared tools are a list of their own, the toolchains first, then the agents. If the image isn’t built yet, devvm builds it first, then the shared tools the share lacks, and the VM is a copy of the image with its shared tools mounted. A VM keeps the image and tools it was made from, and the options for a new VM change nothing on a VM that exists, which ignores them with a warning. The warning names the command that changes the same on that VM:
Option The command the warning names --tools devvm tools, which changes its shared tools --layers devvm layer add, which adds layers --cpus devvm size --from, --no-devcontainer none Only devvm takes these options, and another command given one fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (flags and values).
data.what-a-vm-made-again-keeps#What a VM mad:
devvm keeps the project folder, which is on this machine, the VM’s home folder, and everything it keeps for the VM:
The VM keeps its name, its shared tools, its size, its ports, its network tier and allowlist, its secrets’ bindings, its SSH agent choice and its .git protection. It keeps its links, group and published ports, its desktop’s password and port, and what its devcontainer.json gave it. The commands in its devcontainer.json that run once, such as postCreateCommand, run again on the new disk. It keeps its identity, so links to it still reach it. It gets new SSH host keys, which devvm pins as it does for any new VM. devvm reads the home folder as the VM’s user before it stops the VM, and copies it onto the new disk before devvm’s own setup runs there. --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead. Some of the home folder stays behind:
What other shells in the VM write after devvm reads the folder is lost, so close them first. A file that the new image puts in your home itself, such as ~/.bashrc, stays the image’s, so put shell settings of your own in a file of yours in ~/.bashrc.d. devvm leaves out what the new VM gets from devvm itself: ~/.config/devvm, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the agents’ logins, and the agents’ folders and files that devvm links or copies from this machine. It leaves out ~/.cache too. It keeps opencode’s ~/.local/state/opencode/machine, which an export of the VM’s history leaves out, so the machines that opencode paired still trust the VM. Claude Code’s logins to MCP servers, which it keeps in its login file, don’t come along, so you log in to those servers again in the new VM (MCP servers’ logins). devvm keeps only files, folders and symlinks, without setuid bits, and nothing from a filesystem mounted inside your home. Everything else on the VM’s disk is lost:
the packages you installed with apt programs installed outside your home Docker’s images, containers and volumes the Nix store the processes that ran in it When saving the home folder fails, devvm keeps the VM as it was, and --clean-home goes ahead without it. With --clean-home, opencode’s worktrees go with the home folder, so devvm checks them for uncommitted changes first and asks before they go, as devvm rm does. --no-worktree-check, which works only with --clean-home, skips that check (opencode’s worktrees).

data: These are the things devvm can’t do, everywhere, on Linux hosts and on Intel Macs.
data.everywhere#Everywhere: devvm runs on macOS and Linux only, not on Windows (requirements). Shared tools are read-only, so a tool can’t update itself or add components, for example with rustup component add (details). A layer goes in and comes out by making the VM again. A layer’s script changes the VM’s disk, so devvm layer add gives a VM more layers by making it again, and everything on its disk but its home folder is lost (details). devvm layer rm takes layers out in the same way (details). Shared tools go in with devvm tools add and come out with devvm tools rm, and the VM’s disk stays as it is (details). --from takes only Debian-, Ubuntu- and Alpine-based images, and Alpine, Debian 12 (node:24) and Ubuntu before 26.04 on arm64 build with unpinned packages (details). Agent folders that you make or delete on this machine reach a running VM only after a restart, which devvm offers (details). Ports are forwarded over TCP only, and forwarding every port means every port from 1024 up. You can tunnel UDP over a forwarded TCP port with socat (details). Links between VMs carry TCP over IPv4 alone, and a container in a VM reaches them only with --network host (details). Tools that ignore the proxy settings reach a confined VM’s proxy only over HTTPS and HTTP to a host by name, on ports 443 and 80 and up to 32 more that your allow rules name. Other ports, protocols that name no host in their first bytes, such as a database’s, addresses in URLs, HTTP/3 alone and IPv6 alone need the tool’s own proxy settings, and a client that doesn’t trust the VM’s CA sees a certificate error for a blocked HTTPS host (details). Changing a running VM’s ports closes the connections that are open through its forwards (details). With Lima, project paths can’t contain commas, folder names in VM names are cut short, and disks grow but never shrink (details). File watchers in a Lima VM don’t see the edits you make on this machine, only those made in the VM, so set a dev server that should reload on your edits to poll the project folder (details).
data.intel-macs#Intel Macs: devvm has a release for Intel Macs, which the install script and Homebrew install, but nobody has tested it on one yet. The tested systems are Apple silicon Macs and Linux on arm64 and x86_64, so on an Intel Mac, VMs, --from and the network tiers’ confinement may fail in ways that devvm’s tests haven’t caught.
data.linux-hosts#Linux hosts: .git protection is read-only in the VM’s view, not a lock on the host’s files, so after a git command on this machine replaces .git/config while the VM runs, the VM can change or replace the new file until devvm locks it again. devvm names each such file when the VM stops (details). A VM whose .git/config or hook has another name doesn’t start, and the VM can’t rename a file between the working tree and .git (details). Where the kernel doesn’t let devvm use a user namespace, such as on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, there’s no .git protection. devvm warns about it at each launch, and it names the .git hooks and config that changed, but only after the fact, so use --clone there (details). VMs mount the project folder with 9p instead of virtiofs, so file watchers in a VM also miss the VM’s own changes in the folder’s subfolders, and need polling there (details). New VMs cache the project folder with the none mode, because Linux’s 9p client loses data with Lima’s mmap. A VM made before devvm chose none keeps mmap, with a warning at each launch, until you run devvm mount-cache none (details). A program can’t map a file in the project folder for shared writing, and gets Invalid argument, such as LMDB, which Parcel’s .parcel-cache and Gatsby’s cache use, numpy’s memmap in r+ or w+ mode, Java’s read-write mappings and the mold linker. Keep their files on the VM’s own disk, or use a --clone VM (details). SQLite’s WAL mode fails in the project folder unless the connection sets PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE first, while SQLite’s default journal works. Use a --clone VM for a project that needs WAL mode, as its repo is on the VM’s own disk, or keep the database outside the folder (details). Set-id bits that root in a VM sets on files in the project folder reach the host, and devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped (what to do). devvm keeps your secrets in files under ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/, which only you can read, instead of the Keychain (details). devvm has no Time Machine to keep VMs’ CAs out of, so keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of your backups (details).

data:
A link lets a program in one of your VMs reach a TCP service in another by name, as in postgres://db:5432/app or fetch("http://api:3000"). The VM with the service is the target, and you publish its port in its folder. The VM that reaches it is the client, and you add the link in the client’s folder. Links work on every backend, whatever the two VMs’ network tiers, as long as the target’s tier is the client’s or a stricter one. devvm carries each connection over ssh through this machine, so neither VM’s network changes, and How it works › Links between VMs explains how.
For a database in ~/code/db and an app in ~/code/app, both with VMs:
cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 # offer the database's port to links cd ~/code/app && devvm link add db 5432 # programs in app's VM reach it as db:5432 Programs in the app’s VM then reach the database as db:5432 and as db.devvm.internal:5432. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, so add one only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach (below). To link several VMs to each other at once, put them in a group.
data.a-group-joins-the-trust-of-all-its-vms#A: A group joins the trust of every VM in it, as a link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in any of them can often run code in the others through the ports they publish. A VM that joins later gets the same reach into every VM in the group, and they get the same reach into it, so devvm says so on every join. Put VMs in a group only when you’d trust each of them with the others’ reach.
data.a-link-joins-the-two-vms-trust#A link jo: Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s own service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM. It then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm doesn’t stop that, because it’s what the service itself allows. So add a link only between VMs you’d trust with each other’s reach, and publish only the ports that you mean other VMs to use. Network tiers explains what this means for each tier.
data.adding-a-link#Adding a link:
In the client’s folder, devvm link add TARGET PORT links its VM to PORT of the VM that TARGET names, once that VM publishes the port:
devvm link add db 5432 # reach port 5432 of the VM for the folder db as db:5432 devvm link add db 5432 --as pg # reach it as pg:5432 instead devvm link add ../api 8080 # name the target by its folder's path devvm link add devvm-api-71a99b1076d92c 8080 # or by its VM's name TARGET takes one of four forms:
A folder’s name, as VM names have it, such as db for devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c. devvm matches it against the folder that each VM was made for, so a VM whose backend needed a shorter name still matches its whole folder name. When more than one VM has a folder of that name, devvm refuses and lists each VM with its folder, so you can give the VM’s name or the folder’s path instead. A folder’s path, which starts with . or holds a /, such as ../api or /Users/you/code/api. A VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it. A VM’s ssh alias, such as devvm-db, as you’d give it to ssh (SSH access by name). devvm refuses a target that has no VM, the client’s own VM, and a port that the target doesn’t publish. It also refuses a link that the two VMs’ tiers don’t allow. When devvm makes the link, it says what the client reaches it as, and that the link joins the two VMs’ trust.
data.containers-in-the-vm#Containers in the V: A container that the docker layer runs in the client has a network of its own, so it neither resolves a link’s names nor reaches its address. Run it with --network host, as in docker run --network host IMAGE, so it shares the VM’s network and reaches the links as the VM does.
data.devvm-group-json#devvm group –json:
devvm group --json prints the group as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. group is the group’s name, or "" when the VM is in none, and members is [] then. Each of the members has its name in the group, its vm, its folder, and the ports it publishes as published, written as devvm link publish lists them, or none.
{ "version": 1, "group": "web", "members": [ { "name": "db", "vm": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c", "folder": "/Users/you/code/db", "published": "5432" } ] }
data.devvm-link-json#devvm link –json:
devvm link --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the links has its name, its port, the target VM, the target’s folder as target_folder and its status as target_status, both "" when devvm doesn’t know them, applies, which is true or false, and reason, which is why the link doesn’t apply, as APPLIES shows it, or "" when it does.
{ "version": 1, "links": [ { "name": "db", "port": 5432, "target": "devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c", "target_folder": "/Users/you/code/db", "target_status": "Running", "applies": true, "reason": "" } ] }
data.devvm-link-publish-json#devvm link publi:
devvm link publish --json prints what the VM publishes as one JSON object, and it only shows, so devvm refuses a list of ports with it. ports is none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm link publish takes it.
{ "version": 1, "ports": "5432,8000-8010" }
data.groups#Groups:
A group is a set of your VMs that reach each other’s published ports by name, without a devvm link add for each pair. You join each VM in its own folder, and devvm makes the links between them, so every VM in the group gets a link to each port that every other VM in it publishes. A VM is in one group at a time.
For a database in ~/code/db, an API in ~/code/api and an app in ~/code/app, each with a VM:
cd ~/code/db && devvm link publish 5432 && devvm group join web cd ~/code/api && devvm link publish 8080 && devvm group join web cd ~/code/app && devvm group join web Programs in the app’s VM then reach db:5432 and api:8080, programs in the API’s VM reach db:5432, and programs in the database’s VM reach api:8080. The links a group makes are links like any other, so what this page says about names, ports, network tiers, the link log and stopped targets holds for them too, and devvm link lists them.
data.groups-and-network-tiers#Groups and netw:
A group’s VMs are all on one tier. devvm refuses to put a VM in a group whose VMs are on another tier, and it names both tiers. It checks joins one at a time, so when two VMs join a group at once, the second is checked against the first, and a devvm that waits for another says so. While a VM is in a group, devvm refuses to change its tier with devvm network, so run devvm group leave first.
Because every VM in a group is on one tier, the group’s links keep the rule that a client links only to a target on its tier or a stricter one. Each of their connections is still refused while the target’s tier isn’t in force as it runs, and devvm warns you of such a target when the group makes a link to it.
data.joining-a-group#Joining a group:
devvm group join NAME puts this folder’s VM in the group NAME. The first VM to join makes the group, and devvm says so. A group’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts and ends with a letter or a digit, and isn’t all digits.
devvm group join web # join the group web devvm group join web --as api2 # join it as api2 instead of this folder's name devvm group # the group, its VMs and the ports each one publishes devvm group leave # leave it When the VM joins, devvm makes the group’s links in it and in each of the group’s other VMs, and it names the links that each VM gains. The links reach a running VM at once and a stopped one when it next starts, as When links change describes. devvm refuses a VM that’s in another group already, so run devvm group leave first, and it refuses a VM whose backend can’t carry links. A VM made again in a folder isn’t in the group that the folder’s old VM was in.
devvm group shows the group this folder’s VM is in, with one row for each of its VMs:
NAME VM FOLDER PUBLISHED api devvm-api-0f3c2a91b7d4e6 /Users/you/code/api 8080 app devvm-app-5e1d7c08a2b9f4 /Users/you/code/app none db devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db 5432 NAME is what the group’s other VMs reach that VM by, and PUBLISHED is the ports it publishes, or none. When this folder’s VM isn’t in a group, devvm says so.
data.leaving-a-group#Leaving a group:
devvm group leave takes this folder’s VM out of its group. It removes the links that the group made, in this VM and in the group’s other VMs, and names the links that each VM loses. The links that you made with devvm link add stay. devvm link rm doesn’t remove a link that the group made, so leave the group, or unpublish the port in its target’s folder.
devvm rm of a VM takes it out of its group, and when the group’s last VM leaves, the group is gone.
data.links-and-network-tiers#Links and networ:
A client links only to a target on its own network tier or a stricter one, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target. So an allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, and an open client may link to any target. When devvm can’t read a client’s or a target’s tier, because that part of its state was changed by hand, it refuses the link rather than take it as open (a file devvm can’t read).
devvm checks this rule when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection (each connection):
For a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must also be in force as the target runs. If you move the target from open to a confined tier while it’s running, devvm ls shows it as unenforced until the target starts again behind its proxy, and devvm refuses the client’s connections to it until then, so start the target again with devvm restart in its folder. devvm also warns you of such a target when you add a link to it, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and each time the client starts. The warning names the target and refuses nothing, and devvm doesn’t warn of a stopped target, because its tier applies when it next starts. While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than a client’s, such as devvm network open in its folder, and names the clients that link to it, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open VM. Remove those links with devvm link rm first, or give the target the client’s tier:
devvm link rm db 5432 # in the client's folder: remove the link to db's port 5432 devvm network allowlist # or, in the target's folder, give the target an allowlist client's tier Every VM has its proxy, so a program that uses the VM’s proxy settings, such as curl, sends its requests for a link to the VM’s proxy, and the proxy carries a request for one of the link’s names and its port, such as db:5432 or db.devvm.internal:5432, to the link. Other programs reach the link by its name directly. The proxy passes a link’s connection on as it is, so it doesn’t look into it and puts none of your secrets into it.
The network rules don’t apply to links. The allowlist doesn’t allow or block a link’s connections, and devvm network deny db doesn’t stop the link db. The rule above and the published ports decide which connections a link carries, and devvm network log shows them (the link log). To stop a link, remove it with devvm link rm, or unpublish its port in the target’s folder.
data.listing-links#Listing links:
devvm link lists this folder’s VM’s links, with one row for each port:
NAME PORT TARGET FOLDER STATUS APPLIES db 5432 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running yes db 8000 devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c /Users/you/code/db Running unpublished STATUS is the target’s status as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped, and it’s empty when devvm can’t tell. APPLIES is yes for a link that works while the target runs, or else it says why the link doesn’t apply:
gone: the target VM no longer exists. replaced: the target’s folder has another VM, made again since the link was. unpublished: the target doesn’t publish the port. policy: the target is on a lower network tier than the client. ungrouped: a group made the link, and the two VMs aren’t in that group together any more. You can remove such a link with devvm link rm. devvm ls shows how many links each VM has, in its LINKS column.
data.names#Names:
Programs in the client reach a link at NAME:PORT and NAME.devvm.internal:PORT.
