NAME is the target’s folder name, as VM names have it, unless you give --as NAME. .internal is reserved for private networks, so NAME.devvm.internal never names a host on the internet, and it’s the name to use when the short one could clash with a name your network resolves.
A client has one name for each VM it links to. The first link to a target sets the name, and later links to that target take it too, so after devvm link add db 5432 --as pg, devvm link add db 8000 reaches pg:8000. To change the name, remove that target’s links and add them again. A name is one DNS label, made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, which starts and ends with a letter or a digit and isn’t all digits. devvm refuses localhost, the client’s own hostname and a name that another of the client’s links has. When the target’s folder name isn’t a valid name, or it’s taken, give another with --as NAME. A link is reached only by its names, never at the client’s localhost, so localhost:5432 in the client stays the client’s own. A link’s name hides the same name from anywhere else in the client, such as a host db under your network’s search domain.
data.names-in-a-group#Names in a group:
The group’s other VMs reach a VM by its folder name, as VM names have it, unless it joined with --as NAME. The name follows the rules for link names, and devvm refuses localhost.
Two VMs in a group can’t have the same name, so when another VM in the group has the name this VM would join as, devvm refuses the join until you give this VM another with --as NAME. devvm also refuses a name that’s another VM’s folder name, because that’s the other VM’s own hostname. To change a VM’s name in its group, leave the group, then join it again with --as NAME. A VM’s folder name is its own hostname, so devvm refuses to put a VM in a group where another VM’s name is this VM’s folder name, whatever --as NAME you give, because the name would reach the joining VM itself. For two folders with the same name, such as ~/work/api and ~/old/api, have the VM that’s in the group leave it and join again with another name, such as devvm group join web --as api1, then join the other with --as api2. A VM whose folder has a name of its own needs neither. The links that you make with devvm link add take precedence over the group’s. When you link to a VM in the group yourself, the group’s links to that VM take the name your link gives it, and a port that you linked gets no link from the group. When one of your links has the name of another VM in the group, the group’s links to that VM go, and devvm warns you of it, until you remove your link with devvm link rm.
data.ports#Ports:
The client reaches the target’s port on the same port number, so devvm link add web 80 gives web:80, and ports below 1024 work like any other. Two targets can publish the same port, because the client reaches each one by its own name.
Links carry TCP over IPv4 alone. Each name resolves to an IPv4 address, so a program that connects only over IPv6 doesn’t reach it, and UDP isn’t carried.
data.ports-in-a-group#Ports in a group: The group’s links reach every port that a VM in it publishes, so you publish and unpublish ports in each VM’s folder, as Publishing a port describes. A port that you publish reaches the links of every other VM in the group, and a port that you take out goes from them, at once on a running VM and at its next start on a stopped one. devvm names the links that each VM gains or loses. A range that you publish gives a link for each port in it.
data.publishing-a-port#Publishing a port:
Links reach only the ports a VM publishes, so you publish a port in the target’s folder before any VM can link to it:
devvm link publish # what this folder's VM publishes: none, or a list devvm link publish 5432 # offer port 5432 to links devvm link publish 8000-8010 # offer a range devvm link unpublish 5432 # stop offering it devvm link publish takes ports and ranges as devvm ports does, such as 5432,8000-8010, but not all or none. A port you publish is offered to links from any of your VMs, and each link is still made in its client’s folder with devvm link add. devvm link unpublish takes ports as devvm link publish lists them, and it refuses a port that isn’t published. The server in the VM keeps running. When other VMs link to a port you take out, devvm names them, and their next connections to that port are refused, while connections that are open stay until they close. To remove those links, run devvm link rm in their folders. A change applies at once, whether the VM is running or stopped. Publishing forwards nothing to this machine, and it doesn’t change the ports the VM forwards. A link connects to the target’s own 127.0.0.1, so the server in the target has to listen there or on all its addresses. A server that listens on ::1 alone isn’t reached.
data.removing-a-link#Removing a link:
devvm link rm TARGET PORT removes one of this folder’s VM’s links, where TARGET is the link’s name or anything that devvm link add takes:
devvm link rm db 5432 # stop reaching db:5432 devvm link rm pg 5432 # by the name given with --as On a running client, the link’s next connection is refused, and the connections that are open through it end within a few seconds, so a program in the client that keeps one open, such as a database client, sees it closed.
data.the-link-log#The link log:
devvm network log in the client’s folder shows its links’ connections, whatever its tier. A line has the time, link for a connection devvm carried or REFUSED for one it refused, the link’s name and port, and the target VM, with why devvm refused it:
2026-11-01T10:00:00Z link db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c 2026-11-01T10:05:00Z REFUSED db:5432 to devvm-db-71a99b1076d92c: it isn't running When the client is on a confined tier and the target’s isn’t in force yet, the line says unenforced, as Links and network tiers describes.
A client has at most 256 of its links’ connections carried at once, and devvm refuses and logs the next one. devvm network log –json describes the events in JSON.
data.when-a-target-stops-or-goes#When a targe:
devvm never starts a VM for a link. A connection to a stopped target fails, and each launch of the client warns about each stopped target, until you start it with devvm in its folder. The client’s links then work again without any change to the client. When the target stops, the connections that were open through it end. A link also needs both VMs’ backends to carry links, which every backend of devvm’s does, and when one can’t, each launch of the client says so.
devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from your other VMs and names the clients that lost one. A VM that you make again in that folder isn’t linked, so publish its ports and add the links again. devvm rm of a client removes its links, and devvm stop of a client ends its links’ connections. A link can’t listen when a program in the client already holds its port in a way that covers the link’s address, such as a server of the client’s own on all its addresses with the same port. That link alone doesn’t work, devvm says so, and the client’s other links work. Stop that program, then run devvm restart.
data.when-links-change#When links change: A change of links reaches a running client at once and a stopped one when it next starts, and devvm says which. On a running client, the names resolve at once, because devvm rewrites the client’s /etc/hosts, and a link’s port answers within a few seconds. The VM’s proxy reaches a new link as soon as its port answers, so the programs that use the VM’s proxy settings also reach it, including those that were already running. Nothing in the VM restarts, and the VM’s environment doesn’t change, whatever its tier.
data.which-vm-a-link-reaches#Which VM a link: A link stays with the VM it was made for, because devvm records the target VM’s identity with the link. A VM made again in the target’s folder after devvm rm, or another VM with the same folder name that appears later, isn’t the linked target. devvm layer add, devvm layer rm and devvm update keep the target’s identity as they make the VM again, so its links still reach it (adding layers to a VM).

data: This page covers the ports a VM forwards to this machine and the CPUs, memory and disk it gets. You choose both when devvm makes a VM, and you can change both later with devvm ports and devvm size. Port forwarding explains how devvm’s forwarder works.
data.as-json#As JSON:
devvm size --json and devvm ports --json print what the commands show as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. With -g, they print the same fields for new VMs. With --json they only show, so devvm refuses --cpus, --memory, --disk or a list of ports with it.
devvm size --json has cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib, and leaves out what isn’t set. For -g, that’s what new VMs take from the image. When the VM’s size changes at its next start, pending has the cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib that change.
{ "version": 1, "cpus": 4, "memory_gib": 8, "disk_gib": 100, "pending": { "memory_gib": 16 } } With -g, devvm size --json also has sources, which says where each of cpus, memory and disk came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm saved, or built-in for the image’s (where a default comes from).
{ "version": 1, "cpus": 6, "memory_gib": 16, "sources": { "cpus": "settings.json", "disk": "built-in", "memory": "config.toml" } } devvm ports --json has ports, which is all, none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm ports takes it. With -g, it also has source, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.
{ "version": 1, "ports": "5173,8000-8010" } When another running VM forwards some of the VM’s listed ports, devvm ports --json also has held_by, with each such VM’s vm, its name, and ports, the ports it forwards that this VM waits for (two VMs and one port).
{ "version": 1, "ports": "5173,8000-8010", "held_by": [ { "vm": "devvm-b-0123456789abcd", "ports": "5173" } ] }
data.choosing-new-vms-size#Choosing new VMs’:
devvm asks for the CPUs and memory that new VMs get on your first run, before it asks which features base gets, and again whenever you run devvm setup:
devvm setup # asks its questions, the size among them devvm size -g --cpus 6 --memory 16 # only the size, without asking Before the two questions, devvm says how many CPUs and how much memory this machine has. Each question shows in brackets the value new VMs get now. That’s what config.toml sets or devvm size -g saved, or else base’s own size fitted to this machine: 4 CPUs and 8 GiB, or less on a machine that doesn’t have room for them (size and ports). Confirm to keep the value, or enter another one. devvm checks what you type as it checks --cpus and --memory, and when this machine can’t give it, devvm says why and asks again.
devvm doesn’t ask for a value that config.toml sets, and says so. It saves only the values you type, where devvm size -g saves them, and keeps a saved disk size as it is. When you keep both values, devvm saves nothing, so new VMs go on getting the image’s size. Either way, devvm prints the size new VMs get. A new size changes only the VMs made after it, and nothing is rebuilt, so existing VMs keep their size until you change it with devvm size.
The first run asks once, because that run also chooses base’s features, and devvm asks only before they’re chosen. It asks only when all of these hold (questions devvm asks):
devvm runs in a terminal no size is set you didn’t give --cpus or --memory Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing, and new VMs get the image’s size. devvm setup asks only in a terminal, without --no-input, and only when you give it no flags (devvm setup). To set the size without asking, use devvm size -g --cpus N --memory GiB, which takes the same values and has the same limits.
data.disk-use#Disk use:
A VM’s disk size is how far the disk can grow, not how much space it takes. A project VM starts as a copy of its image’s disk that shares the image’s blocks, so a new VM takes almost nothing until it writes (clones and overlays):
macOS: the copy is an APFS clone. du counts the shared blocks as the clone’s own, so it overcounts. Linux: the copy is a qcow2 overlay of the image’s disk, which holds only the VM’s changes, about 12 MB for a new VM instead of 2 GB.
data.free-space#Free space:
Before devvm builds an image or makes a VM, it checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses to start the step when there’s less free than the step needs:
Step macOS Linux building base 8 GiB 8 GiB building any other image 2 GiB 8 GiB building shared tool images 3 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool 9 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool making a VM 2 GiB 2 GiB devvm rounds each number up to whole GiB, so building one shared tool with Lima on macOS needs 4 GiB, and building all ten needs 8 GiB. Each build checks again before it starts, so the first VM on a Mac, which builds base, needs 8 GiB free. A tools build also checks the disk of devvm’s data folder, where the shared tool images come out, and free space explains which disks devvm checks, what each one needs and how the numbers were measured.
devvm doctor also warns when that disk has less free space than building base needs, but the warning doesn’t make doctor fail. When devvm refuses, see Not enough free space for how to make room.
data.ports#Ports:
A VM forwards the TCP ports it listens on to the same port on this machine’s localhost, so a server on :5173 in the VM is at localhost:5173 here. To change which ports a VM forwards:
devvm ports # what this folder's VM forwards: all, none or a list devvm ports 5173,8000-8010 # only these ports and ranges devvm ports add 5432 # one more devvm ports rm 5173 # one fewer, as listed; the last leaves none devvm ports none # nothing; devvm ports all forwards every port again devvm ports -g none # what new VMs forward (default: all) A change applies at once. A stopped VM forwards the new ports from its next start. On a running VM, devvm starts its forwarder again with the new ports while the VM runs on, so a server on an added port reaches this machine within a few seconds. The connections that were open through the old forwarder close, so a client that was connected through it has to connect again. add and rm take ports and ranges, not all or none. devvm refuses rm on a VM that forwards every port, because there’s no list to remove from. -g also works with add and rm. devvm ports -g shows what new VMs forward, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm ports -g --json adds it as source. When config.toml sets ports, devvm ports -g refuses to change it and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from). devvm forwards ports on every network tier, and it forwards no ports from builds. When a VM forwards every port, devvm forwards each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in the VM listens on, whether on the VM’s loopback or on all its addresses. When a VM lists its ports, devvm forwards those ports alone, however many there are, ports below 1024 included. A port reaches this machine within a few seconds of the server starting, only on localhost (127.0.0.1 and ::1), and the forward goes away when the server stops. At most 256 ports are forwarded at once (when it can’t forward). Your browser sends the cookies of every app you use on localhost to a forwarded port as well, so the server in the VM gets them (your browser).
A VM never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, a port that another running VM forwards or lists, or a port that devvm uses for its VMs’ ssh and proxies (what it never takes):
When a port you listed is taken by a program on this machine as the VM starts, or as you change its ports, devvm warns you and the VM runs on without that port. The next start or change that finds the port free forwards it. A program that starts on a port after the VM’s forward does can still bind it on all addresses, as most servers do, and then that program’s localhost connections reach the VM. When the VM’s server listens on a listed port that the VM can’t forward, because a program on this machine has it, the VM already forwards 256 ports, or this machine doesn’t let devvm use the port, such as one below 1024 on Linux, devvm ports warns you and says which of these it is (a listed port isn’t forwarded). If the forwarder can’t start at all, devvm warns you and names its log, and the VM runs on without forwarded ports. The ports devvm uses for its VMs’ ssh are the 17 that every browser refuses, so no page in your browser reaches a VM’s ssh, and at most 17 VMs run at once (too many VMs at once). A VM that forwards every port leaves those 17 out, and forwards one only when you list it, which devvm ports and each launch warn of. UDP isn’t forwarded, on any backend. Run the UDP client in the VM instead, or tunnel it over a forwarded TCP port with socat, installed on both sides. For a UDP server on port 8125 in the VM, with TCP port 9125 forwarded:
socat TCP-LISTEN:9125,fork,reuseaddr UDP:127.0.0.1:8125 # in the VM socat UDP-LISTEN:8125,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:9125 # on this machine TCP is a stream, so datagrams can arrive merged or split. This suits low-rate request and response traffic, such as DNS, statsd or syslog, but not high-rate or latency-sensitive traffic, such as games, QUIC or WebRTC media.
data.size#Size:
To see or change a VM’s size:
devvm size # what this folder's VM has: cpus=4 memory=8GiB disk=100GiB devvm size --cpus 6 --memory 16 # change it; what isn't given stays devvm size --disk 200 # a bigger disk; never a smaller one devvm size -g --memory 16 # the size new VMs get (default: the image's) devvm size -g # cpus=, memory= and disk= lines, empty for the image's, each with its source The flags take the same values as for a new VM and have the same limits, so devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has and more memory than a VM can have (size and ports). devvm size -g checks a default size in the same way when you set it. A VM that already has more memory keeps it and still starts, because devvm checks a size only when you set one. devvm size -g ends each line with where its value came from, after a #: the path of config.toml, devvm: settings.json for what devvm size -g or devvm setup saved, or devvm: default for the image’s. When config.toml sets cpus, memory or disk, devvm size -g refuses to change that one and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from). A stopped VM gets its new size when it next starts, such as with devvm, and until then devvm size shows what the VM has now and says what changes. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does. Otherwise, and without a terminal or with --no-input, the VM keeps its size until it next starts, for example with devvm restart. When devvm opens the running VM while its new size still waits, it asks once more in a terminal, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too, and a yes restarts the VM with its new size before the shell opens (restarting). Disks grow but never shrink, so devvm refuses a disk smaller than the VM’s. When a VM’s state file holds a size that isn’t a number, such as after an edit by hand, devvm refuses to start the VM or show its size and names the value, so set that part again, such as with devvm size --cpus 4.
data.size-and-ports#Size and ports:
A new VM gets its image’s size unless you set one with --cpus, --memory and --disk, as in devvm --cpus 6. For base that’s 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk. On a machine with fewer than 4 CPUs, base gets as many CPUs as the machine has, and when 8 GiB would leave the machine less than 2 GiB of its own, base gets half of the machine’s memory, which is 4 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. When devvm builds base on such a machine, it says how many CPUs and how much memory base gets, and devvm size -g sets the size that new VMs get instead.
--cpus takes a whole number. --memory and --disk take a size in GiB, written 16, 16G or 16GiB, and decimals are allowed. What the flags leave unset comes from the [size] table of config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm size -g and devvm setup saved (choosing new VMs’ size). devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has, and a disk smaller than the image’s, because disks can’t shrink. It refuses them before it builds anything. devvm also refuses more memory than a VM can have, because a VM that asks for all of this machine’s memory doesn’t start. A VM can have this machine’s memory less 2 GiB, counted in whole GiB, so 6 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. On a machine with 4 GiB or less, it can have half, so 2 GiB on a 4 GiB machine. When you ask for more, devvm says how much memory this machine has and the most you can give a VM, so you can run the command again with that. A new VM forwards every TCP port from 1024 up that it listens on, unless --ports says otherwise, as in devvm --ports 5173.
--ports takes all, none, or ports and ranges such as 5173,8000-8010. Without --ports, the default comes from ports in config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm ports -g saved, and without either, a new VM forwards every port. When you customize a new VM without --ports, devvm asks whether it forwards every port, none or the ports you type, starting from the default, and saves the answer for that VM alone (what a new VM gets). devvm refuses a default that isn’t a valid value, as it refuses a bad flag, and for one in config.toml it names the file and the line (when devvm can’t read it).
data.two-vms-and-one-port#Two VMs and one por:
Only a running VM holds a port. A stopped VM’s listed ports are what it forwards when it runs again, so another VM can forward them meanwhile:
cd ~/code/a && devvm ports add 5173 && devvm stop # a lists 5173, then stops cd ~/code/b && devvm # b forwards 5173 while a is stopped cd ~/code/a && devvm # a starts, and warns that b has 5173 devvm ports # in a: 5173, and the same warning The running VM that forwards a port keeps it. When a VM that lists the same port starts, or you change its ports, devvm warns that it forwards the port once the other VM stops forwarding it, and devvm ports repeats that warning while it lasts. When the other VM stops, or stops forwarding the port, the VM forwards it within about 20 seconds, without a restart. A VM that lists a port comes before a VM that forwards every port. A VM that forwards every port takes no port that a running VM lists, and it gives up such a port within about 10 seconds of that VM listing it, even when the VM that forwards every port goes quiet. devvm warns about it as about any other VM. While devvm starts a VM again, its listed ports stay its own, so no other VM takes them in between. When two VMs that list the same port start at once, the first one whose server listens on the port forwards it, and the other waits for it. A VM that crashed holds no port, because its forwarder ends with it. The ports devvm chooses for VMs’ ssh, proxies and desktops never take a port that any VM lists, running or not. devvm ports also warns when a program on this machine has one of a running VM’s listed ports, which the VM then doesn’t forward. While a VM is stopped, another VM serving on its port gets that port’s place in your browser. Your browser keeps site data, storage and service workers for localhost:5173 whichever VM answers there, as it would for two projects that use one port on any machine. A service worker that the other VM’s app registered can keep answering for localhost:5173 after the first VM takes the port back, so clear that site’s data in your browser when you switch.

data: devvm writes nothing into your project folders. It keeps the settings you edit in ~/.config/devvm and everything it writes itself in ~/.local/share/devvm, and it reads a few environment variables. Your settings lists the files you edit, devvm’s data folder lists the ones devvm writes, and Overview explains how devvm keeps them.
data.a-companys-ca#A company’s CA:
Some company networks inspect TLS through a proxy, such as Zscaler or Netskope, that shows its own certificates, signed by the company’s certificate authority (CA). This machine trusts that CA, but VMs and the VMs that devvm builds images in don’t, so their TLS connections fail. To make them trust it, put the CA’s certificate in ~/.config/devvm/ca:
mkdir -p ~/.config/devvm/ca cp company-root.pem ~/.config/devvm/ca/ devvm reads every *.pem and *.crt file in that folder each time you open a VM, each time it builds an image and each time it resolves the shared tools’ versions, and it leaves other files alone. A file can hold one certificate or several, in PEM, the text form that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. devvm accepts only CA certificates, and it sends only the certificates it read out of a file, never the rest of the file. It refuses the whole folder, naming the file, in these cases:
Anything else in a file, such as a private key, a certificate devvm can’t read or a certificate that isn’t a CA’s. A link: a *.pem or *.crt file that is a link, or a folder that is one, because a link into a project folder would let that project’s VM replace the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. devvm doesn’t follow links there, so copy each certificate into the folder rather than linking to it. A file it can’t read, or a folder it can’t read. These trust the CAs:
Every project VM, in its system’s store, from its next launch. Every build VM, for an image or for shared tools. devvm takes them out of a build VM before the image is finished, so images never keep them, and adding or removing a CA rebuilds nothing. A layer script of yours that copies the system’s CA bundle somewhere else does keep that copy (a company’s CA in builds). The VM’s proxy, on every network tier, for the connections it makes itself, the refresh of a coding agent’s login included, which the proxy makes on this machine when the login is due, so a company proxy that inspects TLS doesn’t make the refresh fail. devvm’s own mise, which devvm downloads once to resolve the shared tools’ versions on this machine. That download trusts these CAs as well as this machine’s own store, and on Linux so does that mise. On macOS, mise trusts them for most of its connections, but the part of it that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only the CAs that macOS trusts, which Keychain Access shows. So on macOS, a company’s CA that mise needs has to be there too, where a Mac that your company manages usually has it already. When mise doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, devvm says so and names this folder. devvm’s other connections from this machine, such as checking an image’s registry or Ubuntu’s image, trust this machine’s own store, as your other programs here do. When you take a certificate out of the folder, VMs stop trusting it at their next launch, and stores that copy the system’s CAs, such as Java’s cacerts, drop it too.
Most tools read the system’s store, among them apt, apk, curl, git and Python’s ssl module. For those that don’t, every VM’s environment points them at it:
Variable Value For NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which holds only devvm’s CAs and is empty when there are none Node, npm and Bun SSL_CERT_FILE /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, the system’s bundle Go programs, and Rust programs that read the system’s roots REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, PIP_CERT the system’s bundle Python’s requests and pip, which use their own CA list otherwise UV_SYSTEM_CERTS 1 uv A CA in the folder can read every TLS connection a VM makes, as it can this machine’s, so put only CAs there that you trust as much as this machine does. How it works › Network tiers explains how the CAs reach VMs, and Images and caching how builds use them.
data.an-ubuntu-mirror#An Ubuntu mirror:
ubuntu-mirror = "http://mirror.example.com/ubuntu-ports" # in ~/.config/devvm/config.toml ubuntu-mirror is a mirror of Ubuntu’s archive, such as one your company or university runs, which the first build of base gets its packages from before it tries Ubuntu’s own. It must mirror the archive for this machine’s architecture: archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu on an Intel or AMD machine, or ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports on an Apple silicon Mac or another arm64 machine. Give it as an http:// or https:// address without a user, a query or spaces, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). A package that the mirror doesn’t have, or a mirror that doesn’t answer, falls back to Ubuntu’s archive for that file.
What it can’t do: a mirror can’t give base a package that Ubuntu didn’t publish, because apt and devvm both check every list and package against Ubuntu’s archive key. A mirror that’s behind can still serve old lists, and devvm refuses lists more than a day older than the Ubuntu cloud image base starts from, names the mirror and keeps none of the build’s packages (old package lists). A mirror that fell behind after that image’s date can still give base packages older than Ubuntu’s, so set only a mirror you trust to keep up (base’s packages). What uses it: only the first build of each base, because a later build of the same base installs the packages devvm kept from that first build (base). VMs don’t use it, and neither do layers or a --from base. Where it’s set: no command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.
data.coding-agents-for-new-vms#Coding agents:
The coding agents you choose in devvm setup are the ones a new VM gets unless you choose others for it. The summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup, and when you customize the VM, they’re checked in the list (what a new VM gets). --agents chooses others for one VM. The choice is for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents, and devvm tools changes them.
devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal, together with the size and base’s features, until you’ve chosen them. Until then, and when you choose none, new VMs get no agents by default. devvm setup --agents claude,codex and devvm setup --agents none choose them without asking, and devvm refuses a name that isn’t an agent’s, suggesting the closest.
data.colors#Colors:
In a terminal, devvm colors the labels and links around its messages, while the messages’ own text stays in your terminal’s usual color. The tables that devvm ls, devvm images, devvm space and devvm doctor print are colored too, and their columns line up the same with colors or without:
What Color the values a message fills in, such as a VM’s name, a path, a port or a count, so they stand out from the words around them bold an error’s devvm: label red a warning’s devvm: label yellow a doc link blue and underlined the ==> before what devvm did bold the end of the run log that devvm prints when a step fails, the log’s latest line on the status line, and each line that -v shows dim the mark a slow step leaves when it’s done green each table’s header row and the totals row bold a state that’s good, such as current, Running or native green a state that needs your attention, such as stale, unused, Stopped or emulated yellow a state that says something is wrong, such as an unenforced tier or an unreviewed emulation red digests, image keys and a feature a backend doesn’t have, which devvm doctor lists as none dim names, paths, sizes and counts in a table your terminal’s usual color devvm uses only your terminal’s 16 base colors, so your theme picks shades that read well on its background, light or dark. It never sets a background color.
devvm decides for standard output and standard error apart, and colors one only when it’s a terminal, so output you pipe or redirect to a file stays plain, tables included. What a command prints with --json is plain even in a terminal, and the run log is never colored. These environment variables change when devvm colors, and the first one that applies decides:
NO_COLOR, set to anything but an empty value, turns colors off. FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, set to anything but 0, turns them on even when the output isn’t a terminal. TERM=dumb turns them off.
data.configtoml#config.toml:
~/.config/devvm/config.toml sets the defaults that new VMs get, the retention settings, the company proxy, an Ubuntu mirror, the release check, transparent mode, the API keys that VMs get as they are and the folders that devvm agent import follows links into, in a file you write by hand. devvm reads it and never writes it. Every key is optional, and devvm has no config.toml until you write one. This example sets every key:
# The network tier new VMs get: open, internet, allowlist or none. network = "allowlist" # The ports new VMs forward: all, none, or ports and ranges. ports = "5173,8000-8010" # The features base gets, in the order they run, or [] for none. features = ["cli-tools", "fzf", "omb"] # The coding agents new VMs get, or [] for none. agents = ["claude", "codex"] # The layers new VMs get, bottom first, or [] for none. layers = ["docker"] # A mirror of Ubuntu's archive that base's first build tries first. ubuntu-mirror = "http://mirror.example.com/ubuntu-ports" # Whether a launch checks once a day for a newer devvm release. release-check = true # Whether confined VMs send tools that ignore the proxy settings to their proxy. transparent-proxy = true # The folder in every VM that devvm paste puts images and files in. paste-dir = "/tmp/devvm-paste" # The folders devvm agent import follows links into without asking. follow-links = ["~/dotfiles"] # New VMs' CPUs, and their memory and disk in GiB. [size] cpus = 4 memory = 8 disk = 100 # What devvm deletes on its own, with the keys devvm retention takes. [retention] logs.runs = 20 history.age = "90d" history.count = 10 tools.unused-age = "30d" orphans.age = "30d" nix-cache.size = "20G" # The company proxy, when the shell you run devvm in sets none. [proxy] https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com" # Providers whose API keys an agent's VMs get as they are. [pass-keys] opencode = ["ollama"] pi = ["ollama"] Each key takes what its command takes:
Key What it takes network a tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, as devvm network -g sets it (choosing a tier), and never learn, because each VM learns the hosts it needs on its own ports all, none or a list, as devvm ports -g takes it (size and ports) features the features that base gets agents the coding agents that new VMs get layers the layers that new VMs get, bottom first cpus a whole number, as devvm size -g takes it memory, disk a number of GiB, such as 8, 8.5 or "8G", as devvm size -g takes them the [retention] keys the retention settings, with a duration such as "90d" or a size such as "20G" in quotes, and a count as a number follow-links the folders whose files devvm agent import copies through a link out of an agent’s folder without asking, each an absolute path or one that starts with ~/ (links out of an agent’s folder), which no command saves The [proxy] table is the company proxy that every VM’s proxy, builds and devvm’s own downloads go through when the shell you run devvm in sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, whatever the VM’s tier. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings itself. That shell’s settings win over the whole table. https and http take what HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY take, an http:// URL or host:port, and no-proxy takes what NO_PROXY takes. A URL never holds a password, and devvm refuses one that does, so put only the user in it and save the password with devvm secret set proxy. No command saves the proxy, so it’s only ever in config.toml.
The [pass-keys] table names, for an agent, the providers whose API keys its VMs get as they are, which devvm otherwise keeps on this machine because the VM’s proxy can’t put them in, such as a local model server’s. Every VM with the agent gets a change at its next launch, and no command saves the table, so it’s only ever in config.toml. This is what it takes and refuses:
It takes opencode and pi, each with a list of the agent’s provider IDs as its auth.json names them, in lower case, such as ["ollama"] (opencode logins, pi logins). devvm refuses another agent, a name that isn’t a provider’s ID and a repeat (config.toml names the line). A provider whose key the VM’s proxy puts in (API keys the proxy puts in) never needs the table, because the proxy puts its key in without it. When the table lists one all the same, the VM gets that key’s placeholder from its next launch on, not the key, and devvm notes at each launch that you can take the provider out. A VM that got such a key as it was before then may still hold copies of it, which keep working, so make a new key when you don’t trust that VM (API keys the proxy puts in).
data.devvm-retention-json#devvm retention –js:
devvm retention --json prints the settings as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. settings has every key with its value as you wrote it, and off for each one that isn’t set. sources has every key with where its value came from: config.toml, settings.json for one that devvm retention saved, or built-in for one that’s off. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a KEY=VALUE with it.
{ "version": 1, "settings": { "history.age": "90d", "history.count": "off", "logs.runs": "off", "nix-cache.size": "off", "orphans.age": "off", "tools.unused-age": "30d" }, "sources": { "history.age": "config.toml", "history.count": "built-in", "logs.runs": "built-in", "nix-cache.size": "built-in", "orphans.age": "built-in", "tools.unused-age": "settings.json" } }
data.devvm-setup#devvm setup:
devvm setup chooses what new VMs get. In a terminal, it asks five questions, each starting from the current choice, and saves each answer in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json, as the command for that setting saves it. It skips a question that config.toml answers, saying so, and it refuses a flag that would change what config.toml sets.
The features that base gets. The CPUs and memory that new VMs get, as devvm size -g saves them. The network tier that new VMs get, as devvm network -g saves it: open, internet, allowlist, which is the default, or none. Each new VM’s summary shows that tier, and when you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm asks for its tier, with Enter keeping the one the summary showed (what a new VM gets). --network TIER chooses for one VM and wins over the saved choice. The coding agents that new VMs get. The layers that new VMs get. devvm setup # asks all five questions devvm setup --features fzf,omb # base's features, without asking devvm setup --features none # base gets no features devvm setup --agents claude,codex # new VMs' coding agents, without asking devvm setup --layers docker # new VMs' layers, without asking devvm setup has three flags of its own, and each one chooses without asking anything. --features LIST chooses base’s features, as a comma-separated list or none for none, and devvm refuses an empty --features ''. --agents LIST chooses new VMs’ coding agents in the same way, and --layers LIST chooses new VMs’ layers. With any of the flags, what the flags leave out stays as it is. Without a terminal and without flags, devvm setup asks nothing and keeps base’s features, saving every feature when none was chosen yet. To change new VMs’ size without asking, use devvm size -g (choosing new VMs’ size), and to change their network tier, use devvm network -g (choosing a tier).
data.devvms-state#devvm’s state:
~/.local/share/devvm ($XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm) holds what devvm makes and keeps for you, and devvm writes everything in it, so don’t edit it by hand. It holds the defaults that devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in settings.json, below config.toml’s, and a folder for each VM in vms/, with the VM’s state, its own allowlist and its network logs. It also holds the images and the shared tools, the run logs, the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save, the ssh config for your VMs, and devvm’s own Lima home (lima/), where the Lima backend’s VMs and images live. devvm’s data folder lists each file and folder in it, with how each one is cleaned up.
On Linux hosts this folder also holds your secrets, in files under secrets/ that only you can read, so keep that in mind when you back it up. On macOS they’re in the Keychain. devvm’s Lima home is its own, whatever LIMA_HOME says, so Lima settings meant for other VMs never reach devvm’s. Set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to move it, for example to a sandbox or to a shorter path. Only you can read devvm’s files, in either folder, because each time devvm runs, it makes both folders yours alone (devvm’s data folder). When devvm can’t read one of its files, it names the file and the line (a file devvm can’t read).
data.environment#Environment: NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE turn devvm’s colors off, or on when the output isn’t a terminal (details) DEVVM_LIMA_HOME move devvm’s own Lima home (details) DEVVM_FROM the container image that the base of new VMs and builds starts from when there’s no --from (details) DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 don’t check for newer shared tools once a day (details) DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 don’t check for a newer devvm release once a day (details) DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE the Keychain service devvm saves and reads secrets in, instead of devvm (details) CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN the Claude Code token that VMs get, over the saved Claude Code login, whichever it is (details)
data.layers-for-new-vms#Layers for new VMs:
The layers you choose in devvm setup are the ones every new VM gets unless you choose others for it. They can be devvm’s built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, and your own, which is how you give every new VM an extra of your own (extras of your own). The summary devvm shows before it makes a new VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup. When you customize the VM in a terminal, they’re already chosen under Layers in the list, and you can leave any of them out of that VM (what a new VM gets).
devvm setup --layers docker,desktop # every new VM gets docker, with desktop on top devvm setup --layers none # new VMs get no layers devvm --layers nix # this VM gets nix alone, not setup's layers devvm --layers none # this VM gets no layers devvm setup --layers takes the layers bottom first, in the order the image’s name joins them, so --layers docker,desktop gives new VMs the image docker+desktop. It refuses a name that isn’t a layer’s, suggesting the closest, and changes nothing. Until you choose some, new VMs get no layers by default, and devvm doesn’t ask for them on its first run. In a terminal, devvm setup asks for them last, after the coding agents. To set them by hand, use the layers key in config.toml, which devvm setup --layers then refuses to change.
--layers on devvm is the exact list of one VM’s layers, so it replaces setup’s layers, and --layers none makes a VM without any. A devcontainer.json’s layers go on top of setup’s (devcontainer.json). The choice is for new VMs only. A VM that exists keeps the layers it was made with, and devvm setup says so when it saves the choice. To give that VM more layers, run devvm layer add in its folder (adding layers to a VM), and to take some out, devvm layer rm (taking layers out of a VM). When a layer of yours that you chose in devvm setup has no script in ~/.config/devvm/layers, such as after you delete it, a new VM is made without it, and devvm warns, naming the layer. Run devvm setup --layers to choose the layers again. When the VM’s backend can’t run a layer you chose, such as docker on a backend without Docker’s engine, devvm makes no VM and names the layer. Then choose other layers for that VM with --layers, or change new VMs’ layers with devvm setup --layers.
data.project-folders-devvm-refuses#Project fo:
A VM mounts its project folder read-write, so devvm refuses to make a VM for a folder that would give the VM more than the project:
Your home folder and devvm’s folders, and any folder that holds one: your home folder, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.local/share/devvm or devvm’s Lima home. A folder inside one of devvm’s own folders, because a VM there could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, or the files that devvm runs on this machine. Another name for one of these folders. devvm compares the folders themselves, not only their names, so on a Mac, where a name’s case doesn’t count, ~/.Config/devvm is refused as ~/.config/devvm is. When devvm refuses a folder, make the VM in a project folder inside it, or keep the project somewhere else. A --clone VM mounts nothing from the folder, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.
Warning
If you mean to give the VM the whole folder, pass --unsafe-folder when you make the VM, and devvm warns you that the VM gets read-write access to it (only the project folder).
A folder inside a coding agent’s folder on this machine, such as a skill you work on in ~/.claude/skills, or one that holds an agent’s folder, such as ~/.pi, isn’t refused, but devvm warns at each launch, because code in the VM can change that agent’s settings on this machine. Keep such a project somewhere else unless you trust what runs in its VM.
data.retention#Retention:
devvm keeps what it makes until you delete it, and the retention settings tell it to delete some of it on its own. Every setting is off until you set it, so first run devvm space to see what each one would free: its RETAIN column shows each setting that’s on, beside the row it applies to, with what it would delete now (devvm space).
devvm space # see what each setting would free devvm retention # show every setting devvm retention history.age=90d tools.unused-age=30d # set some devvm retention history.age=off # turn one off devvm gc --retention # gc as usual, then apply them now devvm retention shows every setting and its value, and off for each one that isn’t set. devvm retention KEY=VALUE... sets them, and devvm retention KEY=off turns one off, for example devvm retention history.age=90d tools.unused-age=30d. devvm refuses a key or value it doesn’t know, and a key with no value such as history.age=, and then it writes nothing. devvm saves the settings in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json. The [retention] table of config.toml sets them too, and a setting there wins over the saved one, so devvm retention refuses to change it. Each line that devvm retention shows ends with where its value came from, after a #. When devvm can’t read a file that sets them, it names the file, and the line for config.toml, and applies none of them.
Key What devvm deletes logs.runs the run logs beyond the newest this many, which is 20 when it’s off, and older ones past 256 MiB together whatever it is history.age the exports of agents’ history written this long ago or more, such as 90d history.count the exports of agents’ history beyond the newest this many tools.unused-age the current shared tools that no VM has had for this long, counted from when devvm first found that no VM has them. While a VM is being made or is getting new shared tools, retention deletes none of them in that run, because that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, and it still applies the other settings orphans.age what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, once their state hasn’t changed for this long, as devvm gc --orphans does nix-cache.size the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than this, such as 20G; it’s 10 GiB when it’s off Value Written as Examples an age a duration, a whole number of minutes, hours, days or weeks 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w a size a whole number of K, M, G or T, each 1024 of the one before, as devvm space shows them 500M or 20G When they apply: devvm applies the settings at the start of a command, at most once a day, except for orphans.age, which needs to ask each backend about its VMs, so only devvm gc --retention applies it. devvm gc --retention applies all of them at once. When two devvms start at once, only one of them applies the settings, and when it deletes something, devvm says what in one line. The Nix cache’s size: the shared Nix cache also keeps to its size while VMs fill it, because a VM’s proxy deletes the cache’s least recently used files before a new file would take it past that size. A size you set applies to each VM from its next start. What it never deletes: retention never deletes a VM, an image, a shared tool that any VM’s state lists, or anything in the backends’ own caches, which only devvm gc --caches frees. In cache/, the folder in devvm’s data folder that holds what devvm makes again when it needs it, retention deletes only the shared Nix cache’s files.
data.the-paste-folder#The paste folder:
paste-dir is the folder in every VM that devvm paste puts images, PDFs and copied files in, /tmp/devvm-paste unless you set it. Each launch makes the folder in the VM when it’s missing, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s own. It leaves a folder that’s there as it is, so a folder of your own, such as /home/USER/pastes where USER is your user in the VM, keeps its mode and its other files. A launch warns, and goes on, when:
what’s at the path is a symbolic link, isn’t a folder or isn’t the VM’s user’s, and devvm paste then refuses the folder; it can’t make the folder, as under a file. It’s one fixed path for every VM so that you can allow it once in an agent’s settings. Give it as an absolute path without a trailing slash, made of letters, digits and ., _ and -, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line), because the path goes into a shell in the VM and onto your clipboard. A change applies to each VM at its next launch, which makes the new folder, and devvm paste uses the new folder at once. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.
data.the-release-check#The release check:
When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer devvm release, and when one is out it says so in one line before it opens the VM, naming the release, the version you have and devvm upgrade. devvm never installs anything on its own, so you upgrade with devvm upgrade when you choose to. release-check = false turns the check off, and so does setting DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment, as CI can. release-check must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.
The check never announces a prerelease, unless Homebrew’s devvm-rc formula installed devvm, which follows prereleases and announces a newer prerelease or release, whichever is newest (trying a prerelease). It never makes devvm wait, and devvm doctor shows what it found last. devvm says nothing without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed, which devvm upgrade can’t upgrade. The release check explains what the check reads and when its line shows a new release.
data.transparent-mode#Transparent mode: On every tier but open, devvm sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy by the names it looks up, which is transparent mode. It’s on unless you turn it off. transparent-proxy = false turns it off for every VM that has no setting of its own, and devvm network transparent on or off gives one VM its own, which comes first. A change applies at each VM’s next launch. transparent-proxy must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.
data.when-devvm-cant-read-it#When devvm can’t: devvm reads all of config.toml each time it needs a default, and it checks every key and value. A key it doesn’t know, such as a typo, a value that a key can’t take, and a file that isn’t TOML each stop the command, and devvm names the file and the line. Fix the line, and run the command again. config.toml has no key for the backend, because every new VM runs on Lima, so a backend key stops the command as an unknown key.
data.where-a-default-comes-from#Where a defau:
For each default, devvm uses the first of these that sets it:
A flag for one VM, such as --ports or --cpus. config.toml. What devvm’s commands saved: devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json. devvm’s own default. A command that would save a default that config.toml sets refuses, names the file and the key, and changes nothing, because the value in config.toml would still win. To change that default, edit it in config.toml, or delete it there to let devvm’s commands set it again. In a terminal, devvm setup doesn’t ask about what config.toml sets, and it says so.
devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention show where each value came from, after a #. They show config.toml’s path for a value from config.toml, devvm: settings.json for one that a command saved, and devvm: default for devvm’s own:
$ devvm ports -g 5173,8000-8010 # /Users/you/.config/devvm/config.toml $ devvm network -g allowlist # devvm: default With --json, the same commands add source, or sources for each value of devvm size -g and devvm retention, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.
data.your-settings#Your settings:
~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm) holds what you edit, and it’s the only folder of devvm’s that you should change by hand. devvm never rewrites a file of yours there. It reads config.toml and your own layers and CAs, it creates a new layer’s files when you run devvm layer new, it changes single lines of policy when you add or remove a rule for every VM, and it writes version when the folder has none and when it changes its folders to a newer layout.
File What it holds Written by config.toml the defaults that new VMs get and the retention settings, which win over what devvm’s commands save, the company proxy and an Ubuntu mirror (config.toml) you policy your network rules for every VM devvm network allow -g, deny -g, rm -g, or you layers/ your own layers and their allowlists devvm layer new, then you agents/ your agents’ settings in devvm’s agent store, one folder for each agent devvm agent import, devvm agent save, or you ca/ your company’s CA certificates, which VMs and builds trust you version the folder’s layout version, which says how devvm keeps its files here devvm, when it’s missing or older Edit the files in ~/.config/devvm, and never edit the ones in ~/.local/share/devvm. devvm writes those itself and rewrites them whole, so a change you make there can be lost, or can stop devvm from reading the file. To set a default by hand, put it in config.toml instead.
Upgrading devvm keeps this folder as it is. Back it up, such as in a dotfiles repo, to keep your settings and layers.

data: devvm, the tools it runs and Lima keep files on this machine outside your project folders. This page lists each of them: what it is, who makes it, where it is, whether devvm can make it again, and how it’s cleaned up. Most of it is in devvm’s data folder, ~/.local/share/devvm, and devvm can make all of that again except your exports and what your commands saved, such as your agents’ logins and your secrets. Lima’s own caches hold more, and they can also hold your own downloads.
data.devvm-space#devvm space:
devvm space shows what devvm keeps on this machine and how much disk each kind of thing takes. It changes nothing and starts no VM, and it gives Lima 30 seconds to answer. devvm space --json prints the same as JSON, for scripts (devvm space –json). The first table has a row for each kind of thing devvm has, followed by a total:
Column WHAT VMs, images, tools gnu or tools musl for the shared tools’ builds for each C library, history for the exports of agents’ history, network logs for the VMs’ logs and the daily tools check’s log, run logs, mise, packages for the copies of base’s packages, Nix cache for the shared Nix cache, leftover state for the whole folder of each VM that devvm gc --orphans would forget, and state for the rest of devvm’s data folder, which includes the rest of the VMs’ folders COUNT, SIZE how many there are and the disk they take, in powers of 1024 (2.1G) KEPT remade when devvm makes it again when it’s needed, only copy for VMs and exports, which nothing else has, log for logs, state for what devvm knows of its VMs and images, and leftover GC what devvm gc frees of it now, which for the Nix cache is what it takes beyond its cap FREED BY what frees the rest, such as devvm rm, images rm, which deletes images that are current, or gc --nix-cache RETAIN the retention setting that applies to the row when it’s on, such as 30d, with what it would delete now in brackets, and - when none is on Sizes count each file’s blocks once, as du does. When Lima doesn’t answer while one of your VMs uses it, devvm says so, and its VMs and images aren’t counted.
data.devvms-data-folder#devvm’s data folder:
devvm keeps its state in ~/.local/share/devvm, or in $XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm when XDG_DATA_HOME is set. Everything in it is devvm’s own, and devvm makes most of it again when it’s needed. The exceptions are the exports, which are the only copy of a deleted VM’s agent history, and the defaults, agents’ logins, keys and secrets that your commands saved.
Only you can read it, because each time devvm runs, it makes this folder and the settings folder, ~/.config/devvm, yours alone (mode 700), whatever mode they had, so nothing inside either one is open to others. If devvm can’t, for example because someone else owns a folder, it warns and goes on. Whenever devvm writes into the folders that hold history, logs, keys and secrets, which are exports/, logs/, logs/runs/, run/, secrets/, and the run/, run/ca/ and logs/ folders in each VM’s folder, it makes them only yours again as well, whatever mode they had.

vms//logs/ and the rest in vms//run/. devvm rm deletes them with the VM. The retention settings, which are all off until you set them, make devvm delete some of these on its own, and that section lists what each one deletes. Retention also writes retention.run in the data folder, when it last ran, and records in each current shared tool’s record since when no VM has had it. It never deletes anything in cache/ but the shared Nix cache’s files. A build also makes a temporary folder in the data folder, tools-build. for the shared tools, and devvm deletes it when the build ends, even after a failure or Ctrl+C.
data.exports#Exports: devvm rm saves the history of a VM whose image has an agent before it deletes the VM, so each export in exports/ can be the only copy of that VM’s transcripts and sessions. devvm deletes an export only when you ask it to. devvm history lists the exports, which are named --.tar.gz, with their VM, its folder, their date and their size. devvm gc --history lists them by their VM and date, then deletes them, each with the .folder file beside it, after asking in a terminal, and devvm gc --history --older-than 30d deletes only those written 30 days ago or more. gc leaves anything else in the folder alone, such as an export that devvm history export is still writing.
data.leftovers-of-a-vm-deleted-outside-devvm#:
When you delete a VM with its backend’s own command instead of devvm rm, such as limactl delete, devvm still keeps the VM’s folder, with its state, its logs and its backend’s files, the VM’s sockets in run/, its ssh config entry and its host keys. devvm gc also keeps the shared tools that the VM’s state names. devvm rm deletes these only together with the VM, so once the VM is gone it says the folder has no VM.
devvm gc --orphans deletes what devvm keeps for such a VM, as devvm rm does after it deletes a VM. That includes, for a --clone VM, the devvm remote in your repo. gc first asks each VM’s backend whether it still has the VM, lists the VMs it would forget with their project folders, and in a terminal asks. It never deletes a VM, and it leaves a VM’s state alone in these cases, saying why:
The backend doesn’t answer, for example because it isn’t installed. When a backend that one of your VMs uses can’t list its images, gc warns and leaves all of that backend’s VMs’ state alone, as it does the rest of that backend’s (cleaning up).
The VM was made elsewhere. devvm records where each new VM’s backend keeps it: the Lima home, which DEVVM_LIMA_HOME moves. When this run looks somewhere else, the VM may still exist there. A VM whose state doesn’t record it counts as made in the backend’s default place, so while DEVVM_LIMA_HOME is set, gc leaves such a VM alone.
Its state changed in the last hour, because the VM may still be being made.
When another devvm starts to make the VM again in its folder after gc listed it, gc refuses to forget it and stops there, and so does retention’s orphans.age.
Forgetting a VM also removes your other VMs’ links to it, as devvm rm does. devvm gc --orphans also removes links to VMs whose state is already gone, naming each one, and deletes the sockets that a link session, a port forwarder or a VM’s proxy leaves on your machine when it’s killed, which are the ones nothing listens on.
Once a VM’s state is gone, devvm gc treats its shared tools like any others. devvm space counts the whole folder of each VM that devvm gc --orphans would forget as leftover state, and each socket a link session, a port forwarder or a proxy left counts there too. A VM that gc leaves alone for one of the reasons above isn’t leftover state, so its folder counts as state and its logs as network logs.
data.lima#Lima:
The Lima backend’s VMs and images are in devvm’s Lima home, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima. Each image is a stopped VM named devvm-img-, and each project VM is a clone of one. On macOS a clone’s disk shares its image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du counts those blocks twice. On Linux hosts a VM’s disk is an overlay of its image’s. devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images, and devvm images rm deletes any image you name.
Lima keeps a download cache of its own, ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/lima when XDG_CACHE_HOME is set. When devvm builds base, Lima downloads Ubuntu’s cloud image into that cache, which is 600 to 900 MB for each release, and on macOS it also keeps a copy converted to a raw disk, which takes about 2.4 GB more. The cache is Lima’s and it isn’t in devvm’s Lima home, so your own Lima VMs’ downloads share it.
devvm gc --caches # free devvm's share of Lima's cache, after asking devvm deletes something in it only when you run devvm gc --caches. Lima keeps each download in a folder named by the SHA-256 of its address, and gc frees only the folders of Ubuntu’s cloud images at the address devvm downloads base from, for its Ubuntu release, that no image record of devvm’s names and that haven’t changed in the last hour. A cloud image that one of your own Lima VMs downloaded from that same address can be among them, and Lima downloads it again the next time it needs it. No VM needs its entry once it’s made, because Lima copies the disk out of the cache. limactl prune deletes the whole cache, your own downloads included, so devvm never runs it.
data.limas-caches#Lima’s caches:
The second table lists the caches that belong to Lima, with what each cache holds, how many entries it has, its size and where it is. That’s Lima’s download cache. devvm’s builds fill it, but it can also hold your own downloads, so it isn’t in the total. The Lima section below says what it holds.
devvm gc --caches # gc as usual, then free devvm's share of Lima's caches, after asking devvm gc --caches --force # the same without asking, as a script must devvm never prunes these caches on its own. devvm gc --caches cleans up as devvm gc does, then frees devvm’s share of them, which is what devvm’s builds put there and nothing of devvm’s needs. It lists the entries it would delete with their sizes and asks. Without a terminal it refuses unless you give --force, which frees them without asking.
data.outside-devvms-folders#Outside devvm’s f:
devvm also changes a few things outside its own folders:
The Keychain: on macOS, the secrets you save are Keychain items under the service devvm. devvm secret rm deletes one. ~/.ssh/config: when you let it, devvm adds the line Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config so that ssh reaches VMs by name (SSH and editors). Time Machine: on macOS, devvm keeps each VM’s run/ca/ out of Time Machine’s backups, because a copy of a key elsewhere could impersonate any site to that VM. devvm itself: the install script puts each version in ~/.local/lib/devvm/ and links ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. A newer install removes older versions that nothing runs (upgrading). Homebrew keeps devvm in its own folders. Uninstalling removes all of it.
data.shared-tools#Shared tools: Each tool version is built once for each kind of VM that uses it, so tools/ can hold more than one build of the same version. A base on Alpine needs its tools built for its C library, musl, rather than glibc, so a node 24 that both an Ubuntu VM and an Alpine VM use is two builds, and devvm images lists both. Each Alpine container image gets builds of its own, so VMs on two different Alpine images have two musl builds of it. Cleaning up says which ones devvm gc deletes.
data.vms-devvm-has-no-state-for#VMs devvm has: A VM can also be the other way around: the backend has it, with devvm’s label, but devvm has no state for it. Usually it belongs to another devvm, such as one run with another XDG_DATA_HOME for a test or a sandbox. devvm space names each one, with the data folder its label names, and devvm never deletes it, because the other devvm may still use it. To delete one yourself, run devvm limactl delete NAME.
data.vms-whose-folder-is-gone#VMs whose folde:
A VM whose project folder you deleted or moved still takes its disk, and it isn’t leftover state, because its backend still has it and it may hold that project’s work. devvm space names each VM whose backend has it and whose folder is gone, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs. Neither devvm gc nor retention ever deletes one. devvm rm VM deletes it after asking, exporting its agents’ history first (a VM whose folder is gone).
devvm space also names each VM whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs too. Connect the disk to use the VM again. devvm rm VM deletes one only after you confirm in a terminal, and --force never answers that question (a folder on a disk that isn’t connected).
data.what-devvm-doctor-finds-in-vms#What devv:
vms/ should hold only VMs’ folders, each named by a hash of 14 hexadecimal digits and holding the VM’s vm.json. devvm doctor warns about anything else it finds there, says what to do, and changes nothing:
An entry that isn’t a VM’s folder, such as a file or a folder with another name, which devvm never uses. Move it out of vms/ or delete it. A VM’s folder without vm.json, which a devvm that stopped while making or deleting a VM leaves, for example one holding only the VM’s lock. No VM uses the folder, so delete it. A folder doctor can’t read, vms/ itself or a VM’s folder, so it can’t check what’s in it. Check that you own it and can read it, for example with ls -ld. These warnings never make doctor fail, and devvm doctor --json lists them in warnings.
data.your-settings#Your settings: ~/.config/devvm holds what you edit: config.toml, your network rules, your agents’ settings, your own layers, and your company’s CA certificates. devvm also writes the folder’s layout version into version there when the file is missing or older. Your settings lists each file. devvm never deletes any of them.

/docs/using/space/.title: What devvm keeps on this machine

data: You can reach each running VM by name from ssh and from editors such as VS Code and Cursor, and you choose for each VM whether it can use your SSH keys. ssh into VMs explains how devvm’s ssh entries keep a VM away from the rest of this machine.
data.agent-forwarding#Agent forwarding:
SSH agent forwarding is off by default. While it’s on and you’re connected, anything in the VM, coding agents included, can use the agent’s keys, for example to push, to log in to servers or to sign any data, as ssh-keygen -Y sign does. It can’t copy or remove them, lock the agent or add keys to it (the SSH agents). Turn forwarding on for one VM when you need git over SSH there.
devvm --ssh-agent # a new VM that forwards your SSH agent devvm ssh-agent # show this folder's VM's choice and devvm's agent's keys devvm ssh-agent on # forward your SSH agent to this folder's VM from its next start devvm ssh-agent add ~/.ssh/deploy_key # or load one key into devvm's own agent devvm ssh-agent devvm # and forward that agent instead of yours devvm ssh-agent off # stop forwarding from the VM's next start The SSH agent a VM getsWith devvm ssh-agent off, the default, the VM has no agent, so git over SSH fails. With on, it has your agent while you're connected, and with devvm, it has devvm's own agent, with only the keys you added.off, the default on devvm devvm ssh-agent no agent:git over SSH fails your agent, whileyou're connected devvm's own agent,with only the keysyou added devvm --ssh-agent creates the VM forwarding your agent. devvm ssh-agent on, devvm or off changes it for an existing VM from its next start, and devvm ssh-agent shows it. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, as devvm restart does, and otherwise, or without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for devvm restart or the VM’s next start. Until then, each time devvm opens the running VM it asks in a terminal whether to restart it with the change, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting). The choice applies to devvm’s shells and to the ssh entries alike, both as the VM’s current start was made with, so a change reaches neither until the VM next starts, whichever folder devvm runs from. When forwarding is on, an entry names the VM’s own agent socket, ~/.local/share/devvm/run/agent-.sock, as the agent, so an editor forwards the agent the VM started with however the editor was started. When forwarding is off, an entry says ForwardAgent no, whatever your own Host * settings say, and none of devvm’s own connections to the VM carry your agent. A VM started outside devvm, such as with devvm limactl start, gets no agent in its ssh entry, because nothing says which agent that start forwards. devvm’s shells get its proxy’s relay of the agent that devvm last started it with, if any, until devvm starts it again. A VM that has run since before you upgraded devvm to this release can still remove the agent’s keys, lock the agent and add keys to it until its next start. devvm warns of such a VM each time it opens it or changes its links, and devvm restart in its folder gives it the relay at once. With forwarding off, git over SSH in the VM fails. devvm says so when it creates a VM for a repo whose origin is an SSH URL. Use an HTTPS remote with a GitHub token instead, or turn forwarding on. No keys loaded. When a VM forwards your agent, the agent has no keys and ~/.ssh has one, devvm offers to load it (ssh-add --apple-use-keychain on macOS). To keep it loaded across reboots, add AddKeysToAgent yes, and UseKeychain yes on macOS, under Host * in ~/.ssh/config. You can also use an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive. GitHub’s host keys are preinstalled in every VM, so a first connection to GitHub doesn’t prompt.
data.cursors-agent#Cursor’s Agent:
Recent releases of Cursor run its Agent in the editor’s server in the VM, not in the Cursor app on this machine. That server holds your Cursor sign-in in memory and uses it to talk to Cursor, so code in the VM could use your sign-in while the window is open.
The safest way to use devvm cursor is a VM on the allowlist or none tier without Cursor’s CLI:
devvm --network allowlist --agents claude # any agents but cursor devvm cursor The VM can’t reach Cursor’s hosts, so its server can’t use your sign-in. Agent and Tab still work: Cursor sends their requests through the app on this machine when the VM can’t reach Cursor. devvm network log shows the VM’s server trying api2.cursor.sh and downloads.cursor.com, blocked. The second is the server trying to download itself into the VM; Cursor then downloads it on this machine and copies it in. A VM with Cursor’s CLI has Cursor’s hosts on its allowlist, so there the editor’s server can use your sign-in. To send Agent’s own requests through the app either way, add this line to your Cursor user settings, ~/Library/Application Support/Cursor/User/settings.json on macOS or Cursor/User/settings.json in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, by default ~/.config, on Linux:
"cursorAgentHost.remoteInferenceRoute": "always" Once it finds Cursor’s cursor command, devvm cursor reads that file, without changing it, and warns before it opens Cursor when the line isn’t there, or when it can’t read the file. Cursor reads the setting only from your user settings, never from the VM’s. The setting doesn’t take your sign-in out of the VM, though: the editor’s server still signs in to Cursor where it can reach it, so open only VMs you trust with devvm cursor.
data.devvm-host-devvm-code-and-devvm-cursor#d:
devvm host # get this folder's VM ready, and show the name ssh and editors reach it by devvm code # the same, then open its folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH devvm cursor # the same, then open its folder in Cursor over Remote-SSH devvm host gets this folder’s VM ready for ssh and editors, then shows its host name (devvm-website) and its folder in the VM. It does what a launch of an existing VM does, without opening a shell. It checks .git, applies the size, ports and agent forwarding that a stopped VM’s state asks for, starts the VM if it’s stopped, runs the self-check, sets the VM up and writes the ssh config. A VM whose tier isn’t enforced is stopped, and it gets no name. The editors’ commands start the same way:
devvm code does the same, then opens the folder in VS Code over Remote-SSH with VS Code’s code command, as in code --remote ssh-remote+devvm-website ~/website. VS Code gets the SSH agent that devvm was started with, not the one that devvm’s own connections to the VM carry. Without code on PATH, devvm names the host to connect to with Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. devvm cursor does the same in Cursor, the editor, with its cursor command, as in cursor --remote ssh-remote+devvm-website ~/website. Cursor gets the SSH agent that devvm was started with too, and without cursor on PATH, devvm names the host to connect to from Cursor. Cursor installs its cursor command from its command palette, as VS Code does its code. Cursor’s CLI agent, which runs in the VM, is another program, with commands of its own (Cursor CLI login).
data.devvm-ssh-agent-json#devvm ssh-agent –js:
devvm ssh-agent --json prints what devvm ssh-agent shows as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. mode is this folder’s VM’s choice, off, on or devvm. Each of the keys is a key you added to devvm’s agent, with its file, the fingerprint devvm recorded, confirm, its lifetime and loaded, which says whether the agent holds it. As without --json, devvm loads the keys the agent lacks first, and with no key added, keys is [] and devvm doesn’t start its agent. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on, devvm or off with it.
{ "version": 1, "mode": "devvm", "keys": [ { "file": "/Users/you/.ssh/deploy_key", "fingerprint": "SHA256:mVPwvezndPv/ARoIadVY98vAC0g+P/5633yTC4d/wXE", "confirm": false, "lifetime": "12h", "loaded": true } ] }
data.devvms-own-agent#devvm’s own agent:
devvm’s own agent keeps your other keys out of reach, because it holds only the keys you add to it, such as a deploy key or a key with access to fewer repos.
devvm ssh-agent add ~/.ssh/deploy_key starts the agent and loads the key. The agent’s socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/agent.sock. devvm ssh-agent devvm makes this folder’s VM forward that agent instead of yours, in devvm’s shells and in the ssh entries alike. VMs share the agent, but none of them can remove its keys or lock it for the others. devvm ssh-agent shows this folder’s VM’s choice, and once you’ve added a key, it then lists the keys devvm’s agent holds, as ssh-add -l does, and each key you added, with its file, its fingerprint and how it’s loaded. It loads the keys the agent lacks before it lists them. devvm ssh-agent rm ~/.ssh/deploy_key takes the key out of devvm’s agent and out of ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, so devvm doesn’t load it again. devvm finds the key in the agent by the fingerprint it recorded, so the key file can have changed or be gone, and devvm leaves the file itself as it is. devvm refuses a key you didn’t add, and devvm ssh-agent lists the ones you did. devvm loads a key again when a VM that uses the agent launches without it, such as after a reboot or once the key’s lifetime ran out, and it asks for the key’s passphrase if it has one. It does so only while the file holds the key you added. add records the key’s fingerprint, so devvm doesn’t load a file that was replaced since, or a link that was swapped to another key. A key you replaced in place needs devvm ssh-agent add again. devvm refuses a key inside a folder a VM mounts, and doesn’t load it, because that VM could read it. That’s every folder that a VM’s state says it mounts, whether the VM is running or stopped: its project folder, its agents’ config folders and the shared tools. Keep the keys for devvm’s agent outside project folders. An encrypted key in the old PEM format needs converting first, with ssh-keygen -p -f KEY, because devvm can’t read its fingerprint without the passphrase. The agent drops each key 12 hours after it loads it, so a VM can’t keep using the key indefinitely. --lifetime 30m changes that for one key, and it takes a duration in minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 8h or 1d, or forever. --confirm makes the agent ask you before each use, such as each push or each login, through an ssh-askpass program. macOS doesn’t include one, so install one and put it on your PATH, or set SSH_ASKPASS to it. devvm keeps the keys and their options in ~/.local/share/devvm/agent-keys.json, and running devvm ssh-agent add on the same key again replaces its options.
data.ssh-access-by-name#SSH access by name:
Each running project VM can be reached as devvm-, as in ssh devvm-website or VS Code’s Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. devvm chooses this alias once, when it makes the VM, and records it, so it never changes. A VM gets devvm- unless another VM already has that alias, and then its alias is its full name. So when two folders share a name, the first VM made keeps devvm-website, and the second one’s alias is its full name, whichever of them you delete first. The VM’s full name (devvm-website-) always works as well.
devvm writes these entries to ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config each time it launches or stops a VM, because a VM’s SSH port can change each time it starts. To use them, add this line to the top of ~/.ssh/config, before any Host block:
Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config You can also point ssh at the file, as in ssh -F ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config devvm-website. devvm host, devvm code, devvm cursor and a new --clone VM offer to add the line in a terminal, and without one, they show it.
Only running VMs are listed. A stopped VM’s port is free for any program on this machine to take, so an entry for it could hand your connection, and your agent, to that program. Start the VM with devvm host or devvm before you connect from an editor.
