Each entry checks the VM’s own host keys, which devvm reads from the VM once each time it starts and keeps in the VM’s folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//run/known_hosts. ssh refuses a host key that doesn’t match, and a VM whose keys devvm can’t read gets no entry. Each entry reaches the VM on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key. A VM whose backend names any other address, or no user or key, gets no entry, so ssh never takes your connection somewhere else. The entries need OpenSSH 8.7 or newer (ssh -V), and an older ssh refuses them. ssh sends your terminal’s COLORTERM, so programs in the VM show 24-bit color when your terminal does. It’s the only variable the entries send beyond the ones your own ssh config sends, and a VM made with --from gets it only when its image’s sshd accepts it, as devvm’s base does. Keep remote forwards out of Host *. The entries turn off what else your ssh config could share with a VM, but they can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours.
data.vs-code-and-cursor#VS Code and Cursor:
Over Remote-SSH, VS Code and Cursor reach further than ssh:
Ports. They forward the ports that programs they start in the VM listen on to this machine’s localhost, whatever devvm ports says. Those programs include their terminals, their tasks and an agent. Git sign-in. They answer git’s credential prompts in the VM with your GitHub sign-in in the editor. Your editor’s own sign-ins. The editor’s extensions run in the VM, its AI features among them, such as GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Cursor’s own AI and codebase indexing. They may get the editor’s sign-ins to work there, such as Copilot’s GitHub token or your Cursor login, and devvm’s proxy doesn’t hold those back. devvm hasn’t checked what reaches the VM, so take it that a program in the VM could read them. devvm turns the first two off in each editor’s settings for the VM, which are ~/.vscode-server/data/Machine/settings.json in the VM for VS Code and ~/.cursor-server/data/Machine/settings.json for Cursor. Each time devvm sets the VM up, it sets remote.autoForwardPorts, git.terminalAuthentication and github.gitAuthentication to false in both files and keeps their other settings. A file with comments isn’t plain JSON, so devvm leaves it as it is and says so in the run log. A file or folder that devvm can’t write is said in the run log too, and the rest of the setup goes on.
Those settings only cover ordinary use:
The VM can turn the three back on, and setting them in your own settings on this machine doesn’t stop it: in VS Code, the settings on the remote machine and the opened folder’s .vscode/settings.json, both of which the VM can write, take precedence over yours for all three. Only a policy that an administrator sets takes precedence over the VM’s. Even with port forwarding off, an extension or a URL that the editor opens can still forward a port. Cursor is built on VS Code, so it most likely works the same way, though devvm hasn’t checked it. So don’t open a VM you don’t trust with devvm code or devvm cursor, and use ssh or devvm’s shell instead, or sign out of the editor’s AI features and its GitHub sign-in first. Programs in the VM can also open URLs in this machine’s browser ($BROWSER).

data:
devvm has these toolchains:
Toolchain What it brings node Node 24, with npm, pnpm, yarn and bun python CPython, with pip and uv rust rustup, cargo and the stable toolchain go Go dotnet the .NET SDK and its runtimes A new VM gets the ones its folder’s files call for, which the summary of the new VM shows, unless you customize the VM and check others in the list or give others with --tools, as in devvm --tools node,python (what a new VM gets). Each section below says what the toolchain brings and which files make devvm choose it. A project that gets its toolchain from Nix uses the nix layer, which Nix projects covers.
data.adding-and-removing-tools#Adding and rem:
A new VM gets the shared tools chosen when devvm makes it, the toolchains and the coding agents, and keeps those versions. On each launch, devvm warns when there are newer ones and names devvm update, which moves the VM to them, and also makes the VM again when its image has changed, after asking (outdated VMs).
devvm tools # choose this folder's VM's toolchains and agents in a list devvm tools add python claude # add tools without the list devvm tools rm python # take one out devvm tools update # move the VM to the newest shared tools In a terminal, devvm tools shows the same list as for a new VM, with this folder’s VM’s toolchains and agents already chosen and its layers greyed out, because they’re built into the VM’s image, which keeps them until devvm layer add or devvm layer rm makes it again. The Layers heading names devvm layer add and devvm layer rm, which change a VM’s layers by making it again (adding layers to a VM). Choose the tools and confirm, and devvm adds and takes out what changed, as devvm tools add and devvm tools rm do, then opens a shell in the VM. When a new agent’s config folders need the running VM to start again, devvm asks first. When nothing changed, devvm says so and opens nothing.
Without a terminal, or with --no-input or --json, devvm tools shows the tools of this folder’s VM in a table, one row per tool, with node’s pnpm and bun and python’s uv in rows of their own:
Column TOOL the tool’s name, such as node or pnpm VERSION the version the VM has NEWER the version in devvm’s tools lock when the VM has another build, which is usually a newer version, or - when the VM has the lock’s build BUILT yes when that newer version is built, no when devvm tools update builds it first, or - The table changes nothing and starts no VM. devvm reads the tools lock as it is, without going online, so a release that came out since devvm last checked isn’t in it yet.
data.devvm-tools-json#devvm tools –json:
devvm tools --json prints the same table as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the tools has the tool’s name and the VM’s version. A tool that the lock has another build of also has newer, which is the lock’s version, and newer_built, which says whether that version is built.
{ "version": 1, "tools": [ { "tool": "node", "version": "24.10.0", "newer": "24.11.0", "newer_built": false }, { "tool": "pnpm", "version": "10.18.0" } ] } The commands below change the VM’s tools from a script or the command line. They don’t change the VM’s disk, because its tools are mounted, so a change takes effect when devvm then opens a shell in the VM. Each takes the tools’ names as separate words, as in devvm tools add python claude, and devvm refuses names joined with + or a comma.
devvm tools add TOOL... builds the tools that the share lacks, and they join the VM’s list at once. It says which of the tools the VM has already and leaves those as they are. A new agent’s config folders are mounted too, which needs the VM to start again. A stopped VM gets them as it starts, and for a running VM devvm asks before restarting it, because anything running in it stops (restarting). If you answer no, there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input, the VM gets them at its next start. devvm tools rm TOOL... takes tools out. What the VM installed itself, such as other versions or global packages, stays. devvm tools update checks upstream for newer versions, builds what’s missing, and moves the VM to them. When the VM already has the newest versions, it builds any of them that are missing. It changes only the shared tools, and never makes the VM again. devvm update does the same first, without asking, and then asks to make the VM again only when the VM’s image has changed (outdated VMs), or its devcontainer.json has (updating a VM from the file). --tools, --agents and --layers choose only what a new VM gets, so on a VM that exists they change nothing, and devvm warns and names devvm tools. Layers aren’t shared tools, so devvm tools can’t add or take out a layer such as docker or nix. A VM gets its layers when devvm makes it, so devvm layer add and devvm layer rm change them by making the VM again, after asking (adding layers to a VM).
data.dotnet#dotnet:
dotnet brings the newest release of the .NET SDK, with the .NET and ASP.NET Core runtimes that come with it, and devvm turns off .NET’s telemetry and its first-run banner in the VM.
Files. devvm chooses dotnet for a folder with a solution (*.sln or *.slnx), a C# or F# project (*.csproj or *.fsproj) or global.json at its top level. Versions. The sdk.version in a project’s global.json picks its SDK, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used. mise installs exactly that version and doesn’t follow rollForward, so a global.json that allows a newer SDK still gets the one it names, and a global.json without an SDK version keeps the shared one. mise installs that SDK with Microsoft’s install script, which checks only the download’s size, while devvm checks the shared SDK against the SHA-512 that Microsoft publishes for it. Global installs. dotnet tool install -g installs into ~/.dotnet/tools in the VM, which is on the PATH, and NuGet keeps its packages in ~/.nuget/packages. The shared SDK is read-only, so dotnet workload install installs workloads into ~/.dotnet in the VM instead of the SDK’s folder. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach NuGet, the revocation lists that NuGet checks packages’ signatures against and the OCSP responder it asks when a list can’t be fetched, and the SDK downloads that a global.json asks for, which are api.nuget.org, crl3.digicert.com and ocsp.digicert.com on port 80, dot.net and builds.dotnet.microsoft.com. Microsoft’s telemetry isn’t on the allowlist.
data.go#go:
go brings the newest Go release, and devvm turns Go’s telemetry off in the VM.
Files. devvm chooses go for a folder with go.mod at its top level. Versions. The toolchain line in a project’s go.mod picks its Go version, and Go itself downloads that version into the VM the first time it’s used. Global installs. go install installs into ~/go/bin in the VM, which is on the PATH. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach Go’s module proxy, its checksum database and Go’s downloads, which are proxy.golang.org, sum.golang.org, go.dev and dl.google.com. Go’s telemetry uploads, to telemetry.go.dev, are a quiet host, so their blocks never show in the VM.
data.how-toolchains-are-shared-and-updated#Ho:
The toolchains are shared tools, like the coding agents, so they aren’t part of any image. devvm builds each version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, and mise runs it, so each toolchain’s commands, such as node or cargo, work from any shell in the VM, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Because the shared copy is read-only, a toolchain can’t update itself, and anything you install globally goes into your home in the VM, as each section above says.
devvm follows each toolchain’s newest release, and Node 24 for node:
Which bases they run on says what each one needs from a VM’s base. Adding and removing tools explains how devvm update and devvm tools update move a VM to newer versions, how devvm tools add adds a toolchain to an existing VM, and how devvm tools rm takes one out. What a new VM gets explains what happens when a folder calls for more than one toolchain.
data.nix-projects#Nix projects:
A project whose toolchain comes from Nix gets the nix layer, which brings Nix, direnv and nix-direnv into its VM. For a folder with flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix at its top level, or with a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell, the list devvm shows when you customize a new VM names that file in the nix row, and you choose it there. A layer isn’t chosen by default, so a VM made as its summary shows, or without a terminal, gets it only with --layers nix, as in devvm --layers nix in a folder with package.json and flake.nix, which gives node on the nix layer.
Dev shells. Put use flake (or use nix for a shell.nix) in the project’s .envrc and run direnv allow in the VM once. From then on, each shell that changes into the folder loads the dev shell, and leaving the folder unloads it. This works in your terminal and in the terminals of editors connected over SSH. The flake’s tools come first. While the dev shell is loaded, its tools are ahead of the shared tools on the PATH, so a flake’s node wins over the shared node, and the shared tools come back when you leave the folder. Files in the project. nix-direnv keeps its cache of the dev shell in your home in the VM, so the project gets no .direnv folder. Nix itself writes a flake.lock next to a flake.nix that has none, and in a git repository it marks that file to be added, as it does on any machine. One store per VM. Each VM has its own Nix store, so a package one VM builds isn’t in another’s. nix run nixpkgs#hello works in any VM with the layer. Shared downloads. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache, on every network tier, an open VM’s included, because every VM’s Nix goes through its proxy. The first VM that needs a package gets it from cache.nixos.org through devvm, which keeps a copy on this machine, and the other VMs get that copy, so each package downloads once per machine instead of once per VM. Only devvm adds to this shared cache, and only what cache.nixos.org signed, so no VM can change what another VM gets. When the cache doesn’t have a package or can’t get it, Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself. The cache keeps to 10 GiB, deleting the packages used least recently first, unless you set another size with devvm retention nix-cache.size=20G (retention). devvm space shows what it takes, and devvm gc --nix-cache empties it (how it works). Trust. Only root is a trusted Nix user, so the VM’s user can’t add caches or signing keys of their own, and Nix ignores --option substituters from them. sudo nix works. Nix builds every package in its sandbox, and a build fails rather than run without it. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach Nix’s binary cache and its channels and flake registry, which are cache.nixos.org, channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from. A package that isn’t in Nix’s binary cache builds from source, which downloads its sources from their own hosts, and those are blocked until you allow them (Nix through the proxy).
data.node#node:
node brings the newest release of Node 24, with npm, pnpm, yarn through corepack, and bun. devvm stays on Node 24 because newer releases drop corepack.
Files. devvm chooses node for a folder with package.json, bun.lock or bun.lockb at its top level. Versions. A project’s .nvmrc or .node-version picks its Node version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used. Global installs. npm i -g installs into ~/.npm-global in the VM, which is on the PATH. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach npm’s, yarn’s, pnpm’s and bun’s registries and Node’s downloads, which are registry.npmjs.org, registry.yarnpkg.com, repo.yarnpkg.com, nodejs.org and bun.sh.
data.python#python:
python brings a prebuilt build of the newest CPython release, and uv, so pip and uv work as usual.
Files. devvm chooses python for a folder with pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py or Pipfile at its top level. Versions. A project’s .python-version picks its Python version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used. Global installs. The shared Python is read-only, so packages go into a project’s virtual environment or into your home in the VM, and ~/.local/bin is on the PATH. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach PyPI and the Python downloads that uv uses, which are pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org and releases.astral.sh.
data.rust#rust:
rust brings rustup, cargo and the newest stable toolchain, with the rust-src and rust-analyzer components already added.
Files. devvm chooses rust for a folder with Cargo.toml at its top level. Versions. A project’s rust-toolchain.toml picks its toolchain, which rustup installs into the VM next to the shared one the first time it’s used. Global installs. cargo install installs into ~/.cargo/bin in the VM, which is on the PATH. rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain, which is why it comes with rust-src and rust-analyzer. Allowlist. On the allowlist tier, the VM can reach crates.io and Rust’s toolchain downloads, which are crates.io, index.crates.io, static.crates.io and static.rust-lang.org.
data.sharing-a-teams-packages#Sharing a team’:
When your team’s projects use one flake for their dev shell, you can put that dev shell’s packages into an image, so every VM made from the image starts with them in its store and downloads none of them. VMs made from one image share its disk, because on macOS each VM’s disk is a copy-on-write clone of the image’s, and on Linux hosts it’s an overlay of the image’s, so the packages take their space once. This works with the stable Nix that the nix layer installs, on every network tier.
To do it, make a layer of your own that builds the dev shell while the image builds, and give it after nix, so that it runs on top of the nix layer:
devvm layer new myteam $EDITOR ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh devvm --layers nix,myteam # a new VM of the image nix+myteam Put these lines in ~/.config/devvm/layers/myteam.sh, below the starter’s set -euo pipefail, with your team’s flake at the commit you want:
# The team's flake at a commit, so the image holds exactly that dev shell. flake=github:myorg/devshell/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567 bin=/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/bin "$bin/nix" develop "$flake" --profile /tmp/myteam-shell --command true # A garbage collector root in the VM's home keeps the dev shell's packages in the store. mkdir -p ~/.cache/myteam "$bin/nix-store" --add-root ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell --realise "$(readlink -f /tmp/myteam-shell)" rm -f /tmp/myteam-shell /tmp/myteam-shell-*-link nix develop builds or downloads every package of the flake’s dev shell into the image’s store and records the dev shell in a profile. nix-store --add-root then makes ~/.cache/myteam/dev-shell a garbage collector root, so nix-collect-garbage in a VM never deletes those packages. A project that loads the same dev shell, with use flake github:myorg/devshell/ in its .envrc, finds every package already in its VM’s store, and so does most of a project whose own flake pins the same nixpkgs revision. The image is built without your credentials, because credentials never go into images, so the flake has to be one that anyone can fetch, such as a public repository.
What this doesn’t cover:
Packages a VM gets after it’s made stay on that VM’s own disk. The shared downloads at least save downloading them again. A new version of the flake needs a new image. Moving flake to another commit edits the script, so devvm builds the image again the next time it’s used, while VMs made earlier keep the packages they have. When the script names a branch instead of a commit, a changed flake.lock upstream doesn’t change the script, so run devvm rebuild myteam to build the image again. A flake that pins another nixpkgs revision shares few packages with the image, and its VM downloads the rest. Nix’s local overlay store, which would let VMs share one store as it changes, is left out until Nix makes it stable.
data.which-bases-they-run-on#Which bases they:
Every toolchain runs on base from Ubuntu’s own image, and on an Alpine-based image with --from, which gets musl builds of the tools. dotnet also needs ICU, the Unicode library that .NET’s globalization uses, so devvm installs ICU in base, whether it’s made from Ubuntu’s image or --from a container image. On a Debian- or Ubuntu-based image, each tool needs at least the glibc version that its prebuilt release was built against. devvm measures that version from the tool’s files whenever it builds a new version, and it refuses a tool whose version is newer than the image’s glibc (shared tools and glibc). Today the shared tools need these glibc versions, so Debian 10 and Ubuntu 20.04 and newer images run all of them:
Shared tool arm64 amd64 node 2.28 2.28 pnpm and bun, with node 2.18 and 2.17 2.18 and 2.17 python 2.17 2.17 uv, with python 2.28 2.17 rust, with rustup 2.17 2.17 go none, because its programs need no glibc none dotnet 2.27 2.27 claude, opencode and pi 2.17 2.17 codex 2.28, for its voice helper 2.28 cursor 2.28, for the node it bundles 2.28

data: Each section below starts with what you see, then says what to do, with a link to the details.
data.a-build-fails#A build fails:
When an image’s build fails in its script, or as the build VM starts or stops, devvm keeps the build VM, stopped and without a record, so you can look inside. devvm’s error names the VM and says how to open a shell in it. On Lima, that’s devvm limactl:
devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img- --start starts the VM first, outside the build’s confinement. What happens next depends on the failure:
The next build of that image deletes the VM and starts over, and devvm gc also deletes it. A build whose create or clone fails deletes the image, once devvm has shown the end of the log, because there’s nothing in the image to look at. A first build of base also fails when the packages its VM gives back aren’t exactly the packages apt downloaded, each named by its own checksum with apt’s entry for it. devvm then keeps none of them, so nothing it didn’t check reaches its package cache (base’s packages). Either way, the images under it, which are already built, stay. devvm deletes and builds again any image it finds without its record, such as a failed build’s or one devvm couldn’t clean up after a crash or a power cut.
data.a-command-fails#A command fails:
devvm prints its own steps and sends the output of the commands it runs to a log, and when a step fails, it prints the end of that log. To watch the output as it runs, add -v or --verbose to any command:
devvm -v # open this folder's VM, showing each command's output devvm -v build base # the same for any command With -v, devvm shows each line on standard error as the log gets it, in place of the status line, and it still writes the log. When a step fails with -v, devvm names the log instead of printing its end again.
The status line, which devvm shows in a terminal without -v, says what devvm is waiting for, such as a command it runs, a check of the VM, a look through a folder or another devvm that’s changing the same thing. It also shows how long the wait has run and the log’s latest line, and a step that takes more than a few seconds leaves a line with its time. A wait for another devvm shows nothing with -v or without a terminal. A warning prints above the status line, and a question takes the status line away until you answer it. The log is ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/--.log, one for each run that runs a command, which only you can read, and devvm keeps the newest 20, fewer when they take more than 256 MiB together. Each command appears in it as a + line with its arguments, followed by its output, and a numbered step adds a # [2/5] line first. Passwords and a VM’s proxy key stay out of it, written as user:@ and devvm:@, including a company proxy’s password from your shell’s HTTPS_PROXY (the run log).
data.a-command-is-refused-before-it-runs#A co:
devvm checks a command’s arguments and flags before it does anything else, so a mistyped one never reaches your VM. When one is wrong, such as a missing argument, one too many, a value the command doesn’t take or a flag it doesn’t have, devvm says what the command expected, then names that command’s own help on the last line:
$ devvm ports 5173 8080 devvm: The command devvm ports takes [all|none|LIST], not 5173 8080. devvm: https://devvm.dev/docs/using/troubleshooting/#a-command-is-refused-before-it-runs Run devvm ports --help to see how to use it. Nothing has changed at that point, so you can fix the command and run it again.
data.a-download-doesnt-check-out#A download d: devvm checks Ubuntu’s cloud image and its own mise against checksums before it uses them, and it refuses a download that doesn’t match. Ubuntu’s checksums must also carry a valid signature from Ubuntu’s cloud image key, which devvm checks itself, with nothing to install. When devvm refuses one, try again later, and if it keeps failing, the server or the network between may be serving something else. In the same way, when devvm rebuild base finds Ubuntu’s list of releases ending before the release that base starts from, it says so and keeps that release (Ubuntu’s cloud image).
data.a-file-devvm-cant-read#A file devvm can’:
When devvm can’t read one of its settings or state files, it names the file, and the line when the problem is on one. Fix the line or delete the file. Your settings lists what each file you edit holds, and devvm’s data folder what each file devvm writes holds.
A VM’s own state file, vm.json in its folder in vms/, is the one to fix rather than delete, because it’s what devvm knows of that VM. While devvm can’t read it:
Every command on that VM fails, and the commands that read every VM leave that VM out and carry on with the rest. devvm ls warns and lists the VM with its name and status alone, when its backend has it, and devvm gc --orphans never forgets it. devvm doesn’t know which shared tools such a VM uses or which folders it mounts, so devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc fail and name the file. devvm refuses to add a key to its own SSH agent, or to load one into it as a VM starts, because it can’t tell whether that VM mounts the key’s folder. Every command on such a VM fails until you fix its file. To find every VM whose state devvm can’t read, run doctor:
devvm doctor # warns of each VM whose vm.json, or a section of it, devvm can't read doctor reads each VM’s vm.json and each of its sections as every command on a VM reads them, without changing anything. It names each VM it can’t read once, with the file and why, even when it can’t read the VM’s folder, and such a VM doesn’t hide doctor’s other warnings, such as a line of another VM’s policy file that isn’t a rule.
data.a-listed-port-isnt-forwarded#A listed po:
When a program on this machine already has a port that the VM lists, devvm warns that the VM doesn’t forward it, and the VM runs on without it. Stop that program, then run devvm restart, or change the VM’s ports with devvm ports, and devvm forwards the port once it’s free (ports).
devvm warns about two other reasons too, each in its own words, and devvm ports repeats the warning while the VM runs:
The VM already forwards 256 ports, the most it forwards at once. Stop the servers you don’t need in the VM, or list fewer ports with devvm ports, and devvm forwards the port within about 10 seconds of the VM forwarding fewer. This machine doesn’t let devvm use the port. On Linux, only root can listen on a port below 1024, so a listed port such as 80 isn’t forwarded. Have the server in the VM listen on a port from 1024 up and list that port instead.
data.a-name-that-doesnt-resolve#A name that d:
curl https://jenkins.corp.example.com/ # in the VM: the host's full name, not jenkins The proxy looks each name up on this machine as it’s written, without this machine’s DNS search domain, so name the host in full in the tool’s URL or settings. What the block’s reason says (inside the VM):
This machine’s DNS has no address for the name: a rule allows the name, but the proxy couldn’t resolve it on this machine. So the block suggests no devvm network allow command, and devvm network log --blocked shows - for it. A name without a dot, such as jenkins, which your other tools may reach as jenkins.corp.example.com, gets a reason that says to use the full name. The DNS didn’t answer in time, or can’t resolve the name: the block names proxy.log on this machine, which holds the resolver’s error.
data.a-new-tool-release-isnt-there-yet#A new: A shared tool’s newest release is sometimes not published for every platform yet, such as for a few days after a Node release. devvm then uses the newest older version that is, and says so, and the next daily check tries the newest again. When a release has no download for a VM’s platform yet, try again the next day (versions).
data.a-newer-devvm-changed-devvms-folders#A n: devvm’s data folder, ~/.local/share/devvm, and its settings folder, ~/.config/devvm, each record their layout version in a file named version, which says how devvm keeps its files there, and devvm checks both before each command. When either one has a newer version than this devvm’s, a newer devvm has changed the folders, so this one refuses to run rather than misread them, and it names the file and both versions. Run the newer devvm, or upgrade this one to it, for example after going back to an older version by mistake. devvm --version, help and completion still run. An older version is never refused, because devvm changes the folders to its own layout before the command runs, and a folder without a version file gets this devvm’s (the layout version).
data.a-request-is-blocked#A request is blocke: On the allowlist tier, a VM reaches only the hosts on its allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. To see what the proxy blocked, run devvm network log --blocked on this machine, or devvm-why in the VM. devvm network log --blocked also shows the devvm network allow command that allows each host, and the rule applies at once, to the next connection (logs).
data.a-servers-port-is-taken-in-a-confined-vm: In a confined VM, transparent mode’s programs listen on the stand-in address 198.18.0.1, on port 53 and on ports 61080 and 61443 and 61100 to 61131, so a server of yours that binds one of those ports on every address, such as 0.0.0.0:61443, fails with EADDRINUSE. Ports 80 and 443 stay free for your own servers. A DNS server of yours on 127.0.0.1:53 binds, but gets no lookups, from the VM or through a forward of port 53, because transparent mode sends them to its own names. Move the server to another port, or turn transparent mode off for the VM with devvm network transparent off, which applies at its next launch (tools that ignore the proxy).
data.a-shared-tool-doesnt-mount#A shared tool:
When a VM can’t mount one of its shared tools, devvm stops the launch with an error that names the VM and the tools, and the VM keeps running. That happens when the tool’s image is missing from the folder that devvm keeps the shared tools in, such as after you deleted it by hand, or when the VM can’t mount the image. devvm doesn’t let the VM download the tool in its place, because that copy would be the VM’s own, a download you didn’t ask for, and one that the VM’s tier may block.
devvm tools update # in the project folder: build the missing tools, then open the shell When the VM has the newest versions, devvm tools update builds those, and otherwise it builds the newest versions and moves the VM to them. If the launch still stops, the run log says why the VM couldn’t mount the image (a command fails). A tool that doesn’t mount never keeps the VM from booting. The VM mounts the tools it can and boots as usual, and only devvm’s launch stops (the share).
data.a-tool-that-skips-the-proxy-fails#A tool:
On a confined tier, devvm’s transparent mode sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the proxy by the names it looks up, over HTTPS and HTTP, on ports 443 and 80 and the ports your allow rules name. Such a tool still fails in these cases, and devvm network log shows nothing for it, because the connection never reached the proxy:
A connection refused on another port, such as ECONNREFUSED or Connection refused for db.example.com:5432. devvm-why lists the port under the connections the VM refused lately. Give the tool the proxy’s address in $HTTPS_PROXY or its own setting, or, for HTTPS or HTTP on that port, allow the host with that port, such as devvm network allow db.example.com:8443, which redirects the port within 10 seconds. A protocol that names no host, such as a database’s or SSH, which the proxy refuses and logs as a refused block of transparent.devvm.proxy. SSH in the VM goes through the proxy already, and a database client needs a proxy setting of its own. A DNS error, such as no such host, Temporary failure in name resolution, ENOTFOUND or EAI_AGAIN, which means transparent mode is off for the VM (devvm network transparent), or the VM comes from an image that predates it, which each launch says, and devvm update makes it again from a newer image. The tool gets the error at once. Some tools read the proxy variables only when a setting of their own turns them on, or never. Turn on the tool’s own proxy setting, so that it uses the environment, or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY. Hugo’s resources.GetRemote, for example, uses the proxy only when security.http.proxyFromEnvironment is true in the site’s config (inside the VM).
data.a-vm-shows-as-unenforced#A VM shows as u:
devvm ls and devvm network show a VM’s tier as unenforced when the VM is on a confined tier but devvm didn’t start it confined. That happens when it was started outside devvm, such as with devvm limactl start, or when it has been running since before devvm network moved it from open to a confined tier, such as with devvm network allowlist. The VM then reaches the network without its proxy.
On the VM’s next launch, devvm offers in a terminal to restart it confined, and if you decline, it warns and goes on. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm stops the VM instead, and the next devvm starts it confined (the self-check). To confine it at once:
devvm restart # in the VM's folder: start it again behind its proxy If you press Ctrl+C while devvm starts a confined VM, devvm stops the VM and its proxy before it exits, so the VM never runs on without the proxy, and the next devvm starts both again confined.
data.a-vm-whose-creation-didnt-finish#A VM wh:
When devvm stops after it made a VM but before the VM was ready, such as when you press Ctrl+C at the wrong moment, devvm never starts that VM. The VM never opened a shell, so nothing of yours is in it. In a terminal, devvm asks whether to delete the VM and make it again, with no as the default. Without a terminal, with --no-input or when you answer no, devvm keeps the VM and says so, and you run devvm rm to delete it, then devvm to make it again:
devvm rm && devvm # delete the unfinished VM, after asking, then make it again While another devvm is still making the folder’s VM, such as one waiting for your answers in another terminal, devvm and devvm rm in that folder refuse at once and say so. Finish or stop the other devvm, then run the command again: once the VM is made, devvm opens it.
data.a-vm-wont-boot#A VM won’t boot:
A Lima VM that doesn’t answer over ssh within a minute of starting is stopped. Read the end of its console log before you start it again, because every start overwrites the log:
tail -n 100 ~/.local/share/devvm/lima//serialv.log The log is serialv.log, or another serial*.log, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home, which is ~/.local/share/devvm/lima// unless you set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME (Lima’s limits). A log that passed 10 MiB while the VM ran has its earlier lines in the same name with .1 added, and the log then starts with a long run of empty bytes, so tail reads it better than an editor does.
data.an-open-vm-resolves-no-names-after-a-dow:
A confined VM’s programs ask the VM’s own name server directly, through an /etc/resolv.conf that devvm writes, and devvm puts systemd-resolved’s back when the VM runs open (the VM’s resolver). An older devvm doesn’t know that file, so after a downgrade, a VM that was confined and now runs open can keep it and resolve no names. When the VM’s /etc/resolv.conf starts with # devvm:, launch it with a current devvm, or put systemd-resolved’s file back yourself:
head -1 /etc/resolv.conf # in the VM: "# devvm: ..." means devvm's file sudo ln -sfn /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf /etc/resolv.conf && sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved
data.an-outdated-vm-or-newer-shared-tools#An: devvm warns on each launch when an image the VM was made from has changed, and when there are newer shared tools than the VM’s, and it leaves the VM as it is. Both warnings name devvm update, which moves the VM to the newest shared tools first, without asking. Then, only when the VM’s image has changed, it makes the VM again from the new image, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, after asking (outdated VMs). devvm tools update moves the VM to the newest shared tools alone (adding and removing tools).
data.base-cant-build-on-lima#base can’t build:
On Lima, base starts from a dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image. The first time devvm builds base, it finds the newest release on cloud-images.ubuntu.com and pins it on this machine, so that build needs to reach Ubuntu’s list of releases and the release’s checksums. When it can’t, devvm says so and pins nothing, so check that you’re online and run the command again. When the newest release doesn’t boot, devvm says so and builds base from the release before it (Ubuntu’s cloud image).
Once an image is pinned, building base again needs Lima’s cached copy of it or the release itself, which Ubuntu removes after a few months. Building the same base again also needs the copies of its packages that devvm kept from its first build, and when one of them is gone or changed, devvm names it and builds nothing (base’s packages). Either way, start base again from the newest release and packages:
devvm rebuild base # pin the newest cloud image again, and install the newest packages
data.base-gets-old-package-lists#Base gets ol: The first build of base checks that the package lists it got are as new as the Ubuntu cloud image it starts from, because Ubuntu’s signed lists don’t expire, and a server that stopped updating still serves them. When the lists for one part of the archive, such as resolute-updates, are more than a day older than the cloud image, devvm refuses them, keeps none of the build’s packages and names that part, its date and the image. When you set a mirror, devvm names it, so set ubuntu-mirror to one that’s up to date, or remove it to use Ubuntu’s archive. Without a mirror, the old lists came from Ubuntu’s archive itself, so check that no proxy or cache between you and the archive serves an old copy, then run the command again.
data.behind-a-company-proxy#Behind a company:
When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy and nothing in a VM or a build gets through, check where devvm finds the proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY from the shell you run it in, as env | grep -i _proxy shows, and when that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, it reads the [proxy] table of ~/.config/devvm/config.toml instead (behind a company proxy). A shell without the settings, such as an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile, starts the VM’s proxy without a company proxy, unless config.toml names one. So set the proxy in config.toml, and it works from every shell:
[proxy] https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080" no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com" config.toml never holds the company proxy’s password. Put only the user in the URL, as above, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which asks for it. Then run devvm again in the folder, which starts the VM’s proxy again with the new settings:
devvm secret set proxy # asks for the company proxy's password devvm # start the VM's proxy again with the new settings Other messages and cases:
When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you, names config.toml and starts the proxy without one, so the VM’s requests go directly. Set the proxy in that shell or in config.toml, then run devvm restart in the folder. When devvm says that HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or one of config.toml’s [proxy] keys names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, ask your IT team for the proxy’s http:// address, and set that. A company proxy that inspects TLS also needs its CA, as the next section describes. Builds behind a company proxy go through a proxy of devvm’s, which allows any host. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, which resolves it (open VMs and builds).
data.devvm-names-set-id-files#devvm names set:
On a Linux host, root in a VM can set the set-user-id and set-group-id bits on files in the project folder, and those bits reach this machine, so such a file runs as its owner for anyone who runs it. devvm names these files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, by devvm stop or found stopped at a launch, but not at a launch into a running VM, because looking through a big folder takes a while. It names the ones that root owns apart from the rest, because those run as root, and it doesn’t look in .git folders.
For a file that root owns, don’t run it, and delete it with sudo rm FILE. For any other file, chmod u-s,g-s FILE clears its bits. Either way, don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (files the VM writes).
data.devvm-says-a-newer-release-is-out#devvm:
When you run devvm in a terminal and a newer release is out, devvm says so in one line before it opens the VM, and it opens the VM as usual. Run devvm upgrade to install the release, or carry on with the devvm you have, because devvm never upgrades on its own. The line comes from devvm’s daily check, and devvm doctor shows the newest release that check found and the day it found it. When you’d rather not see the line, set release-check = false in config.toml, or DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment (the release check).
When devvm never says it, even though a newer release is out, the check may not have run yet, because it runs once a day and the line comes from what it found the time before. It also doesn’t run while you’re offline, without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed. devvm upgrade --check asks GitHub at once:
devvm upgrade --check # ask GitHub for the newest release now, and install nothing devvm upgrade # install it, after asking
data.exit-codes#Exit codes:
devvm exits with one of four codes, so a script can tell what happened:
Code Meaning 0 The command succeeded. 1 The command failed, and devvm’s error says why. 2 devvm refused the command line, such as a bad argument or flag or an unknown command, before anything ran. 130 The command was interrupted by Ctrl+C or a closed terminal (you pressed Ctrl+C). Two programs can take devvm’s place and exit with their own codes. Once devvm opens a shell in your VM, the shell replaces devvm, so the code is the shell’s, and devvm limactl exits with limactl’s code.
data.home-isnt-an-absolute-path#HOME isn’t an: devvm finds its folders from HOME, so it stops when HOME is empty or isn’t an absolute path. Set HOME to your home folder, such as /Users/you on macOS or /home/you on Linux, and run devvm again.
data.no-package-source-answers#No package sou: The first build of base on this machine gets its packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from the mirror you set. When neither answers, devvm stops at once and says so, without trying again, and it keeps the build VM stopped as for any failed build. Check that you’re online, and that the mirror’s address is right, then run the command again. Building the same base again later needs neither, because devvm installs the packages it kept from the first build.
data.not-enough-free-space#Not enough free sp:
Before each build and each new VM, devvm checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses when there’s less than the step needs. With Lima on macOS, that’s 8 GiB for base, 2 GiB for another image or a VM, and from 4 GiB for one shared tool to 8 GiB for all ten, and free space gives the numbers for Linux hosts. The message says which folder’s disk it checked, how much is free and how much the step needs. Nothing has been built or made yet, so you can make room and run the same command again:
devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images and unused shared tool images (cleaning up). devvm images lists the images and shared tool images with the space each takes, and devvm images rm deletes those you don’t need (deleting images). devvm ls lists your VMs, and devvm rm deletes one. devvm never deletes a VM to make room, because a VM may hold work you haven’t saved. When devvm says it couldn’t read the free space, the error after the message says why, such as a folder it can’t reach.
data.reporting-a-bug#Reporting a bug: When none of this fixes it, open an issue on devvm’s issue tracker and choose its form for bugs, features, toolchains, built-in layers or docs. The bug report asks for what devvm --version, devvm doctor and limactl --version print, your OS and its version, the command you ran with what it printed, and the run log (a command fails). devvm hides a VM’s proxy key and passwords in the log, but it can still hold folder names, host names and a command’s output, so read it before you paste it. A security problem goes to private vulnerability reporting instead, never to a public issue.
data.the-folder-is-gone#The folder is gone: When you delete or move a project folder, its VM stays and keeps its disk, and devvm ls writes (gone) after its folder. To keep the VM, move the folder back to its path. To delete it, run devvm rm VM with the name that devvm ls lists, in any folder. devvm asks first, and when the VM is stopped and has an agent, it needs --no-export, because starting the VM to export the history would make the folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).
data.the-folder-is-on-a-disk-that-isnt-connec: When a project folder is on an external disk, a USB stick or a network share that isn’t connected, devvm ls writes (not connected) after its folder, and devvm space names the VM. Connect the disk and the VM works as before. If you mean to delete the VM, run devvm rm VM in a terminal and answer yes, because devvm refuses without one, even with --force, as the disk may still hold the project’s work (a folder on a disk that isn’t connected).
data.the-folder-was-made-again#The folder was: When you delete a project folder and make a new one at the same path, such as by cloning another repo there, devvm refuses the old folder’s VM. Run devvm rm to delete the old VM, or devvm adopt to give it to the new folder (a folder made again).
data.the-proxy-doesnt-start#The proxy doesn’t:
A confined VM runs only with its proxy, so when the proxy doesn’t start, devvm stops the VM, and the next devvm starts both again. When devvm refuses before it has stopped the running proxy, such as when your company proxy’s password isn’t saved, the VM and that proxy run on as long as the proxy still enforces the VM’s tier. Otherwise devvm stops the VM.
The proxy didn’t start: read the log devvm names for why. A VM’s is proxy.log in its logs folder, where the proxy’s two processes, its broker and its child, each write their own lines, and a build’s is proxy.log in the build proxy’s logs/ folder. Another program took the proxy’s port: devvm picks another port the next time it starts the VM, so run devvm restart. The proxy doesn’t stop for new settings: run devvm stop, then devvm (the proxy). An open VM’s proxy doesn’t answer it: the VM runs on, and devvm warns you, because its tools that use the proxy fail, so run devvm restart, which starts both again.
data.the-proxy-runs-without-a-sandbox#The pro:
The part of a VM’s proxy that reads the VM’s network runs in a sandbox, which is macOS’s on macOS, and Landlock and a seccomp filter on Linux. If a VM ever took that part over, the sandbox keeps it from your files, your unix sockets, this machine’s services on localhost and the rest of this machine. When the sandbox can’t start, or the kernel has only part of it, the proxy runs with what there is, so the VM keeps its network, and devvm doctor warns for each running VM:
devvm doctor # names each VM whose proxy runs without a sandbox tail ~/.local/share/devvm/vms//logs/proxy.log # the proxy's own warning, with why devvm restart # in the VM's folder: start the proxy again, sandboxed if it can be sandbox-exec is missing: macOS’s /usr/bin/sandbox-exec runs the sandbox, and Lima’s hostagent also needs it, so check that it’s there, and run devvm restart once it is. sandbox-exec couldn’t start it: proxy.log has sandbox-exec’s own error, which says why, such as a profile that this macOS refused. Run devvm restart once you’ve fixed what it names, and if it names devvm’s profile, report it as a bug (reporting a bug), with your macOS version. Its sandbox let it open a file it mustn’t: the sandbox started but didn’t hold, so the proxy runs as if it had none. Report it as a bug (reporting a bug), with your macOS version. This kernel has no Landlock, or an older one, or no seccomp filters: on Linux, the proxy gets what the kernel has. Check that Landlock is turned on with cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm, whose list should name landlock, and turn it on as your distribution’s docs describe, or update the kernel. The proxy is fully confined with the seccomp filter and Landlock’s ABI 8 or later, or ABI 6 or 7 with its fix for signals between threads. Then run devvm restart. An older devvm started it: a VM that ran as you upgraded devvm keeps the proxy that the older devvm started, one process without a sandbox, until devvm next opens the VM. Run devvm in the VM’s folder, which starts its proxy again with the sandbox, while the VM runs on. devvm can’t tell: devvm doctor reads how the proxy is confined only from the proxy that runs now, which it knows by when the system says it started. When it can’t read that, it says it can’t tell whether the proxy runs in its sandbox, and why. Run devvm restart in the VM’s folder, and if the warning stays, report it as a bug (reporting a bug). devvm can’t confine it on this system yet: this devvm, or this machine’s architecture, has no sandbox for it, though devvm’s releases for macOS and for Linux on Intel and Arm have one, so install a release (installing devvm). The child’s sandbox has what the sandbox allows and how the proxy decides to run without it.
data.tls-errors-behind-a-company-proxy#TLS er:
When apt, npm install, pip install, git clone over HTTPS or an image’s build fails with an error such as certificate verify failed, self-signed certificate in certificate chain or unable to get local issuer certificate, the network you’re on may inspect TLS. Ask your IT team for the CA’s certificate, or export it from this machine’s store, such as Keychain Access on macOS. Put it in ~/.config/devvm/ca and open the VM again (a company’s CA):
mkdir -p ~/.config/devvm/ca && cp company-root.pem ~/.config/devvm/ca/ devvm # open the VM again, which now trusts the CA When resolving the shared tools’ versions fails because this machine doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, mise’s lines in the run log end with invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer. On Linux, put the CA in ~/.config/devvm/ca, or add it to this machine’s own store, as update-ca-certificates does on Debian and Ubuntu, and run devvm again:
# on a Debian or Ubuntu host, not in the VM (Fedora: /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ and sudo update-ca-trust) sudo cp company-root.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/company-root.crt && sudo update-ca-certificates A bundle that SSL_CERT_FILE names in devvm’s environment works too, because that mise reads it in place of the system’s. On macOS, open the CA’s certificate in Keychain Access and set it to be trusted, because the part of that mise that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only what macOS trusts.
devvm doctor says so when HTTPS_PROXY or config.toml’s proxy.https is set and the folder has no CA certificates. Many proxies don’t inspect TLS, so that line isn’t a problem in itself. When devvm refuses a file in the folder, it names the file, and you take out anything that isn’t a CA certificate, such as a private key or a server’s certificate.
data.too-many-vms-at-once#Too many VMs at onc:
At most 17 VMs run at once, because each VM’s ssh is on one of the 17 ports that every browser refuses, so no page in your browser can reach it. A start past that fails and names the VMs that run on those ports, so stop one of them first:
devvm stop # in a running VM's folder devvm ls # which VMs run A stopped VM can give up its port to a VM that starts, and it gets another at its own next start. When the message says the ports are taken on this machine without naming your VMs, one of these has them:
VMs that are starting or building. A running VM that lists them to forward, which you change with devvm ports in its folder. Another program, such as another user’s on this machine, whom you’d ask to end it. A VM that an older devvm started keeps its old ssh port until you stop it and start it again, and devvm warns of it at each launch until then (the ssh port).
data.you-pressed-ctrlc#You pressed Ctrl+C:
Ctrl+C, or closing the terminal, stops the command that’s running, cleans up what the run left unfinished, and exits with code 130. A second Ctrl+C doesn’t stop the cleanup. At a question, Ctrl+C ends the run at once, and devvm doesn’t take an answer you type after it, so nothing goes ahead.
devvm deletes an interrupted new VM, with its state, until its first shell opens, because nothing of yours is in it yet. An interrupted build deletes the image it was building.

data: This page covers upgrading devvm, switching between Homebrew and the install script, and removing devvm with everything it keeps. Each depends on how you installed devvm, and your images, VMs and settings stay through an upgrade or a switch, because they don’t live with devvm. Installing and updating explains what the install script and devvm upgrade check.
data.an-older-release#An older release:
When the newest release is older than the devvm you have, devvm upgrade refuses to install it, even with --force. A server that offers an old release in place of the newest could bring back problems that a newer release fixed, so devvm upgrade never goes back a version unless you name it. devvm upgrade --to VERSION installs the release you name, newer or older, and it asks first, saying when the release is older than the devvm you have. When the devvm you have is a prerelease of a release that isn’t out yet, the newest release is older too, and devvm upgrade says so and installs nothing, without failing (trying a prerelease).
Homebrew installs only its formula’s release, so with Homebrew devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to.
data.devvm-upgrade-json#devvm upgrade –json:
devvm upgrade --json prints what devvm upgrade --check says as one JSON object, for scripts, as output for scripts describes, and installs nothing:
current is the version of the devvm you ran. latest is the newest release’s version, which is never a prerelease’s, except with Homebrew’s devvm-rc, where it’s the newest prerelease’s or release’s, whichever is newer. newer says whether that’s newer than current. install is how devvm was installed, install.sh, homebrew or other. path is where the devvm you ran is, its links followed. { "version": 1, "current": "0.1.0", "latest": "0.2.0", "newer": true, "install": "install.sh", "path": "/Users/you/.local/lib/devvm/0.1.0/devvm" }
data.how-devvm-upgrade-upgrades#How devvm upg:
devvm upgrade tells how devvm was installed from where the devvm you ran is, and it never runs anything to find out:
With the install script, devvm is ~/.local/lib/devvm//devvm, and ~/.local/bin/devvm links to it, or the same folders under DEVVM_PREFIX. devvm upgrade downloads the new release and checks it, as What devvm upgrade checks describes. It unpacks the release into a folder of its own beside the devvm you have, runs the new devvm to see that it works, and then switches ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. When anything fails before the new devvm runs through ~/.local/bin/devvm, the link goes back, so the devvm you had stays the one that runs. The version you upgraded from stays in ~/.local/lib/devvm, and so does any older version that a running VM still uses, until a later upgrade finds nothing using it. With Homebrew, devvm is in Homebrew’s Cellar, and devvm upgrade runs brew upgrade devvm after asking, or brew upgrade devvm-rc when you installed the formula for prereleases. Homebrew may upgrade Lima at the same time, because the formula needs it. Homebrew installs the release its formula names, which can come out a little after the release itself, so until then brew upgrade devvm finds nothing to upgrade. Any other way, such as go install, a build from devvm’s source, or a copy of devvm somewhere else, devvm upgrade can’t upgrade. It says how that devvm was installed and how to upgrade it, such as with go install github.com/devvmhq/devvm/cmd/devvm@latest, and fails. A devvm built without devvm’s release key can’t check a release’s signature, so devvm upgrade refuses to install a release with it and says to run the install script again.
data.one-devvm#One devvm:
Install devvm one way, with Homebrew or with the install script, but not both. With two copies, the one that comes first on your PATH is the one that runs, and brew upgrade devvm may update the one you don’t run. So when Homebrew installed devvm, the install script stops before it downloads anything and says to run brew upgrade devvm instead, or brew uninstall devvm first if you want to use the script, and its --force installs a second copy anyway (the install script).
To switch from one way to the other, remove devvm with the command for the way you installed it, as step 5 of Uninstalling shows, and then install it the other way. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm:
# from Homebrew to the install script brew uninstall devvm # or devvm-rc, if that's the formula you installed curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash # from the install script to Homebrew rm -rf ~/.local/lib/devvm ~/.local/bin/devvm brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm After it installs devvm, the script warns when another devvm comes before ~/.local/bin on your PATH. The warning names that copy’s path and says to remove it, or to put ~/.local/bin before its folder in PATH. devvm doctor warns the same way when the devvm first on your PATH isn’t the one you ran, naming both, and the warning doesn’t make it fail.
data.trying-a-prerelease#Trying a prerelease:
A prerelease is a version of devvm that you can try before its release is out, such as a release candidate, 0.2.0-rc.1, or a beta, 0.2.0-beta.1. devvm upgrade and the install script never pick a prerelease as the newest release, and the daily release check never announces one, so you get a prerelease only when you name it or when you install devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases.
Note
The docs at devvm.dev are for the newest release. The docs for the next release, which a prerelease comes before, are at next.devvm.dev, and they change as that release is written, so they can describe more than a prerelease has.
Versions go in this order: a prerelease comes before its release, a beta before a release candidate, and the numbers in order, so 0.2.0-beta.3 comes before 0.2.0-rc.1, then 0.2.0-rc.2, then 0.2.0.
data.uninstalling#Uninstalling:
Delete your VMs: devvm ls, then devvm rm in each folder. For a --clone VM, this also removes the devvm git remote from the repo.
Delete the images: devvm gc, then devvm images rm with every name devvm images lists. Images built --from a container image need the same --from: devvm images rm --from node:24 base.
Free Lima’s cache. In a terminal, devvm gc --caches frees devvm’s share of it, after asking. If you don’t use Lima yourself, you can also empty its cache: Lima keeps Ubuntu’s cloud images in ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, and limactl prune deletes that whole cache.
Delete your saved secrets: devvm secret rm NAME for each one devvm secret lists. On macOS they’re in the Keychain under the service devvm, and on Linux in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/.
Remove devvm itself, with the command for the way you installed it:
macOSLinux brew uninstall devvm If you installed devvm-rc, run brew uninstall devvm-rc instead. If you installed devvm with the install script, remove it as on Linux.
rm -rf ~/.local/lib/devvm ~/.local/bin/devvm Remove its state: rm -rf ~/.local/share/devvm ~/.config/devvm. That includes your layers, in ~/.config/devvm/layers, so copy them somewhere first to keep them. It also includes your exports, the agents’ history that devvm rm saved, and devvm’s agent store, the agents’ settings in ~/.config/devvm/agents and their logins in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins. On macOS, the Time Machine exclusions that devvm set on its CA folders and logins folders go with the folders.
If you let devvm add it, remove the Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config line from ~/.ssh/config.
data.upgrading#Upgrading:
To upgrade devvm, run devvm upgrade, which installs the newest release the way you installed devvm:
devvm upgrade # install the newest release, asking first devvm upgrade --check # say whether a newer release is out, and install nothing devvm upgrade --force # install it without asking, as a script must devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0 # install that release, even one older than the devvm you have devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 # install a prerelease, which only --to installs It says which release it will install in place of the devvm you have, and asks first, so without a terminal or with --no-input it needs --force.
You don’t have to remember to check. When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer release without making you wait, and when one is out it says so in one line that names devvm upgrade. It never upgrades on its own, and release-check = false in config.toml or DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 turns the check off (the release check).
You can also upgrade devvm without devvm upgrade, with the command for the way you installed it:
macOSLinux brew upgrade devvm If you installed devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases, run brew upgrade devvm-rc instead (trying a prerelease). If you installed devvm with the install script, run the script again, as on Linux.
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash Running the install script again installs the newest release.
Your images and VMs stay, because they live in ~/.local/share/devvm, and your settings and layers stay in ~/.config/devvm, apart from devvm itself.
Images whose inputs changed are built again the next time you use them. Existing VMs keep working, and devvm tools update moves a VM to the new shared tools. devvm gc deletes the copies of devvm’s files that older versions wrote out, except those that a VM’s proxy was started with.
data.what-devvm-upgrade-checks#What devvm upg:
devvm upgrade downloads over HTTPS only, and checks each file before it uses the next:
It downloads the release’s SHA256SUMS and its signature, SHA256SUMS.minisig, and checks that devvm’s release key signed it for that release’s version. The key is built into the devvm you have, so a replaced release can’t bring its own. It downloads the archive for this machine and checks it against its checksum in SHA256SUMS. It unpacks the archive, which must hold only devvm’s files in one folder. It runs the new devvm with --version, which must say the release’s version. When a check fails, devvm upgrade installs nothing, and the devvm you have stays the one that runs. It checks the signature itself, so it doesn’t need minisign on this machine, as the install script does. It never runs a script that it downloaded, only the new devvm’s --version.
data.with-homebrew#With Homebrew:
Homebrew’s devvm formula always names the newest release, and the devvm-rc formula names the newest prerelease, or the newest release when that’s newer. Both install the same devvm command, so Homebrew installs only one of them at a time. To switch from devvm to devvm-rc, uninstall devvm first, then trust and install devvm-rc:
brew uninstall devvm brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc To install devvm-rc when Homebrew hasn’t installed devvm before, run only the last two lines. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm.
brew upgrade devvm-rc moves to the next prerelease once it’s out, and to the release once that’s out, so devvm-rc never leaves you on an old prerelease. devvm upgrade runs it for you, after asking, and the daily release check announces each newer prerelease and release. Homebrew installs only its formula’s version, so devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to here either.
To go back to releases only, uninstall devvm-rc and install devvm again, after trusting it if you never installed it before:
brew uninstall devvm-rc brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm devvm installs the newest release, even when that’s older than the prerelease you had.
data.with-the-install-script#With the install:
To install a prerelease with the install script, run the copy of the script that comes with the prerelease, which installs that prerelease, or give its version to the newest release’s script with --version:
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.1/install.sh | bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --version 0.2.0-rc.1 When the install script installed the devvm you have, devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 installs the prerelease too. Both check a prerelease’s signature and checksum as they check a release’s.
While you run a prerelease that the install script installed, devvm upgrade offers the release it comes before once that release is out, and the daily check says so. It never offers a newer prerelease, such as 0.2.0-rc.2, so install one with devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.2. To go back to the newest release before the prerelease’s own release is out, name the newest release’s version, such as devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0. devvm upgrade asks first, because that release is older than the prerelease you have.

data: This page covers a VM from the time devvm makes it until you delete it: opening, restarting and stopping it, deleting it, listing your VMs, and what devvm does when you run a command in a subfolder or when the project folder is made again, moved, deleted or on a disk that isn’t connected. Overview has each step devvm takes for a new VM and an existing one.
data.a-folder-made-again#A folder made again:
A VM belongs to the folder it was made for, which devvm knows by its path and by the folder itself (one VM per folder). When that folder was deleted and a new one made at the same path, every command that opens, stops or changes the VM refuses it, such as devvm, devvm stop, devvm restart and devvm tools. Two commands deal with a folder made again, and each acts only after you confirm in a terminal:
devvm rm deletes the VM and never exports its history, because its folder is gone. The VM may hold that project’s work, so --force never answers this question. devvm adopt gives the VM to this folder, with its files, secrets and allowlist. Its .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared. devvm adopt --force gives it without asking, which devvm adopt needs when there’s no terminal. What devvm does in the cases between:
A restart of your Mac can give the folder’s disk another device number, but that doesn’t make it a new folder, so the VM opens as before. The exception is a VM that has recorded its folder’s volume, when the folder is on another volume now, such as a copy of the disk with a volume ID of its own, mounted at the same path. A folder devvm can’t read at all, as when code in a VM that mounts it took away your read permission, leaves devvm unable to tell whether the folder is the VM’s, so every command on the folder’s VM refuses it, naming the folder and why it can’t be read. Make the folder readable to you again, with chmod u+rx on it, and the VM opens as before. A Btrfs snapshot on Linux that you roll back to at the folder’s path is another subvolume, once the VM has recorded its folder’s volume, so its folder is another folder, as is the folder after you give its volume a new UUID. You give it the VM with devvm adopt.
data.a-folder-on-a-disk-that-isnt-connected#A:
When a project folder is on an external disk, a USB stick or a network share that isn’t connected, nothing is at its path, but the folder may still hold the project’s work, and so may the VM. devvm tells this apart from a deleted folder by the disk: it finds the nearest folder above the path that’s still there, and when that folder is on another disk than the project folder was, the project folder isn’t connected. devvm ls writes (not connected) after such a folder, and devvm space names each such VM with its folder. To use the VM again, connect the disk.
devvm rm VM refuses such a VM when there’s no terminal, even with --force, and tells you to connect the disk, or to run devvm rm VM in a terminal to delete the VM anyway. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question. Otherwise it deletes the VM as it deletes one whose folder is gone. A folder that you moved to another disk and then deleted counts as not connected too, so devvm asks in that case as well.
data.a-moved-or-renamed-folder#A moved or ren:
mv ~/code/app ~/work/app cd ~/work/app && devvm # devvm asks whether to move the VM here devvm adopt --force # the same without asking, as a script must devvm adopt VM # give a copy on another disk the VM, by its name from devvm ls When you move or rename a project folder on the same disk, as with mv ~/code/app ~/work/app, the folder keeps its VM once you say so. The first time you run a command on this folder’s VM at the folder’s new path, such as devvm or devvm stop, devvm finds the VM made for the folder at its old path, names the VM and that path, and asks whether to move the VM here, with no as the default:
Yes: the VM belongs to the folder at its new path, with its home folder, secrets, allowlist, links and settings, and devvm finds it there from then on without asking. No: the folder has no VM, so devvm makes a new one, and the old VM stays with the old path, where devvm rm VM deletes it (a VM whose folder is gone). Without a terminal, devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm adopt in a terminal, or devvm adopt --force, which moves the VM without asking. Once the VM has moved, this is what changes:
The VM mounts the folder at its new path from its next start. When the VM is running as you move it, it still mounts the old path, so devvm stops it before it moves it, and devvm then starts it with the folder at its new path. If a VM runs with its folder at another path all the same, devvm asks whether to restart it as it opens the VM, with yes as the default, and when you answer no, it warns that the VM mounts the folder at its new path only when it next starts. The folder’s .git moves with it, locks and all, so its .git protection goes on as before. Links to the VM and its group go by the VM’s name, so they stay, and a link whose TARGET is the folder’s path finds the VM at its new path. The folder’s path in the VM changes with it. Claude Code’s history follows the folder. Claude Code keeps a folder’s sessions and its settings for that folder, such as whether you trust it and the MCP servers you added there, by the folder’s path. At the VM’s next start, devvm moves them in the VM from the old path to the new one, so claude --continue and claude --resume offer the sessions from before the move. When Claude Code already has sessions at the new path, the old path’s sessions join them, and a session the new path already has stays as it is. Settings that Claude Code already keeps for the new path stay as they are, and the old path’s stay under the old path. devvm moves only what Claude Code keeps for the project folder itself, so sessions you started in one of its subfolders stay under that subfolder’s old path.
Codex records each session’s folder in the session, and codex resume and codex resume --last look only at the current folder’s sessions, so they miss the ones from the old path. To find them:
codex resume --all # list the sessions of every folder, the old path's included codex resume ID # resume a session by its ID, wherever it started opencode keeps the sessions of a git repo by the repo’s first commit, so they follow the folder without any change. In a folder that isn’t a git repo, opencode keeps sessions by the folder’s path, so they stay under the old path.
devvm offers the move only when the folder at the new path is the folder the VM was made for, and when nothing is at the old path any more, or only a symlink to the new path. devvm knows the folder by its device, inode and birth time, or by its volume, inode and birth time after a restart gave its disk another device number (one VM per folder). There’s no offer in these cases:
A copy: a copy of the folder is another folder. Some file systems: a folder on a file system that may give a new folder the inode number of a deleted one, such as a network share, a FUSE file system or a USB drive formatted with FAT or exFAT, never gets the offer. One VM per folder lists the file systems that do. Another user’s folder: devvm offers no VM for a folder that another user owns. On a Mac, a volume that ignores ownership, as disk images and external disks often do, shows every folder as yours, so devvm can’t tell another user’s folder there from yours. Check that a folder on such a volume is yours before you say yes. Moved after a restart, before its volume was recorded: a VM records its folder’s volume when it’s made, adopted or moved, and a VM made before records it at its first launch that finds its folder. Until then, a folder moved after a restart gets no offer, because the restart may have given its disk another device number. The same goes for a folder whose volume is still to check after a restart when devvm also can’t read the volume at the move, and for a folder on a file system whose volume devvm can’t tell, such as XFS or tmpfs on Linux. devvm adopt VM moves the VM to it. A --clone VM, which keeps its own clone of the repo at the old path inside the VM. Several VMs: when more than one VM was made for the folder at paths it had before, devvm moves none of them and names them, so you can choose one with devvm adopt VM. devvm refuses to move a VM to a folder that it wouldn’t make a new VM for, such as your home folder (project folders devvm refuses). A new folder at the old path gets a new VM of its own, with another name.
Moving a folder to another disk copies it, so the folder at the new path is another folder, which devvm never offers the VM to on its own. To give the copy the VM, delete the folder at the old path or disconnect its disk, then run devvm adopt VM in the copy, with the VM’s name as devvm ls lists it. devvm names the VM and its old path and asks first, with no as the default, and --force moves it without asking, which devvm adopt VM needs when there’s no terminal. The VM’s .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared, because the copy’s .git is another folder too. devvm refuses a VM whose folder is still there, a --clone VM, and a folder that has a VM of its own, which you delete first with devvm rm.
data.a-nested-project-replaced#A nested proje:
A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM, such as a nested repo, is in both VMs, because the parent folder’s VM mounts everything inside its folder. Code in the parent folder’s VM can do two things to it:
It can change the nested project’s files, though not the hooks and config of its .git while the parent folder’s VM protects it, as .git protection does for the repos nested in a VM’s folder. It can move the nested project folder aside and put a link in its place, or another folder. On Linux, if devvm then started the nested project’s VM, the VM would mount whatever the link points to, such as your home folder. On macOS the VM mounts the project folder itself, wherever it was moved, and never what a link at its path points to. On both, devvm checks the nested project folder just before it starts the VM and again once the VM runs. If the folder is now a link, sits below a link, or is another folder, devvm doesn’t start the VM, or it stops the VM again, and it tells you which. Then:
Find what replaced the folder. Move the project folder back to its path. Run the command again. Replacing the folder while the VM runs never shows the VM what the link points to. On Linux the VM keeps the folder it mounted when it started, and on macOS the VM gets “Operation not permitted” for its project folder, as it does when the folder was moved aside while the VM started and put back later, so run devvm restart once the folder is back. To keep a nested project out of the parent folder’s VM altogether, move it out of the parent folder.
Each time devvm makes or opens the nested project’s VM, it warns once and names the VM of the nearest parent folder that mounts the project. It warns whether that VM runs or not, because the VM can write to the folder whenever it runs. A --clone VM mounts nothing, so devvm doesn’t warn when you open one, and a parent folder’s --clone VM never counts. The other commands, devvm restart included, don’t warn.
data.a-subfolder#A subfolder:
cd ~/some-project/src devvm # open the parent folder's VM, with the shell here devvm --here # make a VM for this subfolder instead devvm --parent # use the parent folder's VM even in a repo of its own A VM mounts its whole project folder, so the folders inside it are in the VM at the same paths. When the folder you run a command in has no VM of its own, devvm looks for one in the folders it’s inside, starting with the nearest. It stops before your home folder and the filesystem root, so it never uses a VM made for either. It stops at the nearest folder that has a VM, and when that VM was made for an earlier folder at its path (a folder made again), or its backend has lost it, the folder you’re in has no VM, so devvm never reaches past it to a VM further out. Using a parent folder’s VM mounts nothing new, because the subfolder is already inside the folder that VM mounts.
In such a subfolder, such as ~/some-project/src, each command does this:
Command In a subfolder devvm opens the parent folder’s VM there, with the shell at the subfolder’s path, and first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. It does the same with or without a terminal, and it asks nothing. --tools, --agents and --layers change nothing on the parent folder’s VM, as on any VM that exists, and devvm warns that they don’t (adding and removing tools). In a parent folder’s --clone VM, the shell opens in the subfolder when the clone has it (subfolders) devvm --here, devvm --clone make a new VM for the subfolder instead, and devvm --clone makes the subfolder’s own clone VM. Once the subfolder has its own VM, devvm opens that one devvm stop, restart, tools, size, ports, host and code use the parent folder’s VM in the same way, without asking. Each one first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. devvm host gives the subfolder as the folder to open in the VM, and devvm code opens the subfolder devvm rm never deletes a parent folder’s VM unasked. In a terminal, it names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question.
