Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run devvm rm in the parent folder instead devvm adopt acts only on the VM made for this folder’s own path, never on a parent folder’s The commands that give the VM more access ask in the same way as devvm rm, because the parent folder’s project may not expect them:
devvm secret use devvm ssh-agent on and devvm ssh-agent devvm devvm network with a lower tier, such as devvm network open devvm network allow, and devvm network rm when it removes a deny devvm git-protect off In a terminal, each one names the VM and its folder and asks before it changes the VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run it in the parent folder, or in a terminal to confirm. The commands that take access away, such as devvm secret unuse and devvm network deny, ask nothing.
A subfolder that is a git repo of its own is treated as a separate project, and so is a subfolder inside such a repo, when the repo is below the folder with the VM. That covers a nested repo, a submodule and a worktree, which each have a .git folder or file of their own. When you run devvm there, devvm makes a new VM for the subfolder, with or without a terminal, and asks nothing. The other commands don’t use the parent folder’s VM there, and they say this folder has no VM, as in any folder without one.
Every command that acts on this folder’s VM, devvm included, takes --here and --parent, and each finds the VM in the same way:
--here uses only this folder’s own VM, so devvm --here makes one when the folder has none, and the other commands say this folder has no VM. --parent uses the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, even across a git repo of its own and even when this folder has a VM of its own, so devvm --parent in a repo of its own opens the project’s VM there. When no folder that this folder is inside has a VM, a command given --parent fails and changes nothing. You can’t give the two together, or either of them with -g, and devvm --clone doesn’t take --parent, because a clone VM is always the folder’s own. devvm rm VM takes neither, because it deletes the VM you name, and neither does devvm adopt, because it acts only on this folder’s own path. With --parent, devvm rm and the commands that give the VM more access still ask before they change the parent folder’s VM.
data.a-vm-whose-folder-is-gone#A VM whose fol:
When you delete or move a project folder, its VM stays, because the VM may hold work that’s nowhere else and devvm never deletes a VM on its own. A folder you moved gets its VM back at its new path once you say so (a moved or renamed folder), and until then the VM’s folder counts as gone. devvm ls writes (gone) after the folder of each VM whose folder is gone (listing VMs), and devvm space names each one with its folder. A folder on a disk that isn’t connected isn’t gone, and a folder on a disk that isn’t connected covers it. A folder that was deleted and made again at the same path isn’t gone, and devvm handles it as a folder made again. A VM whose folder is gone explains how devvm tells.
devvm ls # the VMs, with (gone) after a folder that's gone devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c # delete one by its name, after asking devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c --no-export # a stopped one with an agent, without its history devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c --no-export --no-worktree-check # a stopped one with opencode, without checking its worktrees devvm rm VM deletes a VM whose folder is gone, and you can run it in any folder. VM is the VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it, or the alias that ssh reaches it by. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default. --force deletes it without asking, which devvm rm VM needs when there’s no terminal. Like devvm rm, it deletes what devvm keeps for the VM, and when the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history unless you give --no-export (history).
The export reads the history from the running VM. Starting a stopped VM would make its folder again, because Lima makes a missing folder that a VM mounts, so for a stopped VM with an agent devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm rm VM --no-export. devvm reads opencode’s worktrees from the running VM too, so for a stopped VM with opencode it tells you to run devvm rm VM --no-export --no-worktree-check. If you moved the folder and want the history, run devvm history export or devvm rm in the folder at its new path, which moves the VM there first (a moved or renamed folder). A --clone VM mounts no project folder, so devvm starts it to export the history. Its clone’s work can’t be fetched into a repo that’s gone, though, so devvm refuses to delete it unless you give --no-clone-check, which deletes the VM and that work with it.
Given this folder’s own VM, devvm rm VM does what devvm rm does. It refuses these:
A folder that’s still there: devvm refuses a VM whose folder is still there, including a VM made for an earlier folder at that path, and tells you to run devvm rm in that folder. A state changed by hand: a VM whose state names this folder while the folder has a VM of its own, which only a state changed by hand can do, is refused as a VM whose folder is still there, so devvm rm VM never deletes the folder’s own VM in its place. An unknown name: devvm refuses a name that isn’t one of your VMs. A VM its backend lost: devvm refuses a VM that its backend no longer has, for which devvm gc --orphans deletes what devvm keeps (leftovers of a VM deleted outside devvm).
data.deleting-a-vm#Deleting a VM:
devvm rm # delete this folder's VM, after asking devvm rm --force # the same without asking, as a script must devvm rm --no-export # without exporting its agents' history first devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c # a VM whose folder is gone, by its name from devvm ls devvm rm deletes this folder’s VM together with what devvm keeps for it. That’s the VM’s state, its own allowlist, its network log, its .git locks or, for a --clone VM, the repo’s devvm remote, and its ssh config entry (deleting a VM). It asks first in a terminal, and --force deletes without asking, which devvm rm needs when there’s no terminal.
When the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, unless you give --no-export, and when the export fails, devvm keeps the VM (history). For a --clone VM, devvm offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched, and it deletes the VM’s uncommitted changes only after you confirm. --no-clone-check skips that check and warns you that the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes go with the VM (deleting the VM). When the VM has opencode, devvm also checks the worktrees opencode made in it, which an export leaves out, and asks before their uncommitted changes go. It starts a stopped VM for that check, even with --no-export, and --no-worktree-check skips the check, so with --no-export as well, devvm deletes a stopped VM without starting it (opencode’s worktrees).
Some VMs devvm deletes only after you confirm, and it asks these questions only in a terminal, where --force never answers them:
the VM made for an earlier folder at this path (a folder made again) in a folder without a VM of its own, the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, which devvm rm acts on and names (a subfolder) To delete a VM whose folder you deleted or moved, give its name, as in devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c (a VM whose folder is gone).
data.devvm-ls-json#devvm ls –json:
devvm ls --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. vms has a VM’s columns as fields, sorted by name. image is the image alone, tools is the list of its shared tools, [] for none, and from is the container image its base started from, which is left out for a base from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A value the VM’s state doesn’t have is "". folder is the folder alone, and folder_state is there when something is at its path, gone when nothing is, and not_connected when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected. links is how many links the VM has, 0 for none. net is the tier alone, and a VM that’s learning the hosts it needs also has learning_since, the time it started learning.
{ "version": 1, "vms": [ { "name": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c", "status": "Running", "image": "base", "tools": ["node", "claude"], "from": "node:24", "git": "on", "net": "internet", "learning_since": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z", "backend": "lima", "folder": "/Users/you/code/website", "folder_state": "there", "links": 0 } ] }
data.listing-vms#Listing VMs:
devvm ls prints a table of the project VMs, sorted by name, with a header first. Images and build VMs aren’t in it.
Column NAME the VM’s name, devvm-- STATUS its state as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped IMAGE its image, base and its layers, with a base from a container image as base (from node:24) (details) TOOLS its shared tools, joined with commas, such as node,claude, or - for none GIT its .git protection, on or off, or clone for a --clone VM NET its network tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, or unenforced (the self-check), and internet (learning) while it learns the hosts it needs LINKS how many links it has to ports of your other VMs, or - for none FOLDER its project folder, with (gone) after it when nothing is at that path, which devvm rm VM deals with (a VM whose folder is gone), or (not connected) when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected (details) A value the VM’s state doesn’t have shows as -, so a VM whose creation didn’t finish shows only its name and status.
data.opening-a-vm#Opening a VM:
devvm makes a new VM from its image of base and the layers you chose, building the image first if it isn’t built yet, then starts the VM and opens a shell in it in devvm’s place, so devvm ends when the shell does. The VM mounts only the project folder, read-write, and the shared tools and its agents’ config folders, read-only, or with --clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead of the folder. devvm also locks the .git hooks and config of the folder and of the repos nested in it against changes from the VM. On macOS it locks them with a file flag, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM where the kernel lets it and only watches them where it doesn’t (.git protection). For a VM that exists, devvm starts it if it’s stopped and opens it as it is.
A VM is running or stopped from the time devvm makes it until you delete it.
A VM's statesdevvm makes a VM, which is then running. devvm restart and devvm update keep it running, devvm stop stops it, and devvm, devvm restart or devvm update start it again. devvm rm deletes it, running or stopped. When its image changes, a VM is outdated, and it keeps its image until devvm update.devvm devvm restart,devvm update devvm stop devvm,devvm restart,devvm update devvm rm devvm rm no VM running stopped deleted When its image changes, a VMis outdated, and it keepsits image until devvm update. The shell, and an agent’s login with devvm agent login, get your terminal’s COLORTERM when it’s truecolor or 24bit, so programs in the VM, such as coding agents, show 24-bit color as they do on this machine (how).
data.restarting-and-stopping#Restarting and s:
devvm restart # stop this folder's VM, start it again and open a shell in it devvm stop # stop it and its proxy devvm restart stops this folder’s VM, then starts it and opens a shell in it as devvm does. Some changes apply only when a VM starts, and a restart applies them:
a new size for a running VM a change into or out of the open tier a change to its SSH agent forwarding the config folders of an agent that devvm tools add added When you make one of these changes to a running VM with devvm size, devvm network into or out of open or devvm ssh-agent, or change its .git protection on macOS with devvm git-protect, which waits for the VM to stop, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart the VM now, because anything running in it stops. If you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, devvm keeps the change and says that devvm restart applies it, and it does the same without asking when there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input.
When devvm opens a running VM that still has changes waiting for its next start, it names them, such as its size and its agent folder mounts, and asks in a terminal once whether to restart the VM now. It names each change on a line of its own, and when more than two wait, it names the first and says how many more there are. The default answer depends on what waits:
Yes ([Y/n]) when the VM’s agent folder mounts are among the changes, because an agent you just added needs its folders. No ([y/N]) otherwise, because the VM is already running and you may only want its shell. If you answer yes, devvm stops the VM, starts it with the changes and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, devvm warns about each change and opens a shell in the running VM.
devvm stop stops this folder’s VM and its proxy (stopping a VM). Once the VM is stopped, devvm locks its .git again and checks it, as a launch that finds the VM stopped does, and it takes the VM’s entry out of devvm’s ssh config. devvm, devvm restart, and the commands that need the VM running, such as devvm host, start it again.
